articles.title: ESMA enforcement priorities for 2026
articles.text:
Highlights

– Financial reporting– Sustainability reporting– ESEF reporting– Find out more

The European securities regulator, ESMA1, has issued its priorities and reminders for 2026 annual reporting, highlighting the areas for companies to focus on.

Ramon Jubels

KPMG EMA Department of Professional Practice

KPMG in the Netherlands

mail

call

For financial reporting, regulatory bodies outside the EU are also likely to focus on similar topics.

ESMA’s 2026 priorities highlight the importance of consistent and connected corporate reporting. Companies need to consider these priorities and reminders when preparing their annual reports, and tell their own story.

Ramon Jubels

Chair, Global Corporate & Sustainability Reporting Topic Team

Financial reporting

Companies continue to face heightened geopolitical risks and uncertainties. ESMA continues to view these as some of the most significant challenges affecting financial reporting. Therefore, companies need to assess:how geopolitical tensions, trade policies, sanctions, shifting trade flows and regional conflicts affect their own operations, financing, asset valuations and cash flow projections;how their estimates and judgements may be impacted; andwhat information is relevant to users of their financial statements.ESMA highlights the following financial reporting areas for particular attention by companies, reminding them of the importance of meaningful disclosures about risks, uncertainties and judgements made. Area Focus Operations
Restructuring: timing of restructuring provisions and termination benefits, and impacts on defined benefit arrangements.Assets held for sale and discontinued operations: timing of the classification of assets or disposal groups as held for sale and/or discontinued operations. Financing
Debt and liquidity: liquidity risk disclosures, including:
maturity analysis for financial liabilities;changes in risk exposures, refinancing risks and funding sources;restrictions on cash balances; andcompliance with debt covenants. Debt restructuring: assessment of whether modifications of financial liabilities result in derecognition under IFRS 9 Financial Instruments. Asset valuations
Fair value measurement: use of relevant observable market inputs and appropriate valuation techniques and transparent company-specific disclosures.Expected credit losses: review of existing models, assumptions and management’s judgements to appropriately capture the effects of heightened uncertainty.

ESMA urges companies to ensure high-quality, timely implementation of IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements, including transparent and meaningful disclosure of the expected impacts ahead of its effective date of 1 January 2027. The new presentation and disclosure requirements will also affect the first interim reporting period in 2027. ESMA refers companies to its Statement on implementation of IFRS 18. TransitionFor 2026 financial statements, companies are expected to provide specific information about the anticipated impacts of IFRS 18. This may include:quantitative changes to the income statement, where possible;significant judgements, including the assessment of specified main business activities;expected management-defined performance measures (MPMs), including any changes to measures currently used in public communications; andother significant judgements and key accounting policy decisions.Ongoing developmentsESMA also urges companies to monitor IFRS Interpretations Committee discussions and decisions relating to IFRS 18 as they may provide clarity on specific application issues.Other public communicationsIFRS 18 implementation can extend beyond the financial statements. ESMA notes that it may affect a company’s public communications, performance metrics and European Single Electronic Format (ESEF) reporting.Companies are also reminded to consider ESMA’s Guidelines on Alternative Performance Measures (APMs). They need to carefully assess new APMs and any adjustments to existing APMs, particularly for performance measures based on hypothetical income and expenses. Measures used need to:enhance, rather than reduce, transparency, comparability and reliability; andprovide decision-useful information for investors.

Sustainability reporting

2026 is a transitional year for sustainability reporting. Eligible companies can apply European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) Set 12, revised ESRS3, or ESRS Set 1 with specified revised ESRS reliefs4. ESMA expects companies to clearly disclose which version of ESRS they apply, helping users to understand the basis of their reporting. ESMA also reminds companies moving from ESRS Set 1 to revised ESRS that the transition relief for comparative information applies only to quantitative metrics that differ between the two versions of ESRS.

ESMA calls for balance in reporting positive and negative impacts and for a comparable level of detail in related disclosures. It highlights the need for companies to:consider both own operations and their upstream and downstream value chain; anddisclose materiality thresholds, particularly if they differ by impact type.ESMA expects concise, company-specific disclosures about the double materiality assessment process, including significant differences in the process used for different sustainability topics. It also expects companies to use the topics and subtopics specified in ESRS 1 General Requirements to categorise material impacts, risks or opportunities (IROs), wherever possible. Companies use the ‘entity-specific’ category only when the topic-specific ESRS does not adequately cover the IRO.

ESMA expects companies to:provide aligned disclosures on IROs and related policies, actions and targets, together with associated metrics5;explain how policies and targets address identified IROs, keeping consistent levels of detail; andclearly state if no policy, action or target exists for a material IRO, or if the company addresses only certain aspects of the IRO.ESMA also reminds companies to be transparent about the link between their reported actions and the current and future resources, including capex and opex, allocated to implement them.ESMA reminds companies who choose to include an executive summary in their sustainability statement that the qualitative characteristics of information in ESRS 1 (e.g. neutrality) also apply to this summary.

ESMA emphasises that disclosures about targets are most useful when they are measurable, time-bound and outcome-oriented, and include relevant information about methodologies applied. Reporting may include:progress towards a target;explanations of targets achieved, missed, abandoned or unlikely to be met; andchanges to baselines, target years or values.Climate-related targets described as ‘science-based’ or aligned with limiting global warming to 1.5°C need to be accompanied by clear, supporting information about how they meet these characteristics. ESMA recommends disclosing absolute values together with intensity values and distinguishing gross GHG emissions reduction targets from targets presented on a net basis.Companies also need to be clear about whether they disclose broad commitments or actual targets.

As 2030 target deadlines approach, ESMA expects companies to disclose when they become aware that they can no longer achieve previously set sustainability targets.Companies not applying revised ESRS in 2026 need to prepare for their application in 2027.

ESEF reporting

ESMA’s 2026 ESEF priorities address common filing errors in the statement of changes in equity, including the following areas:correct, complete and consistent tagging (i.e. mark-ups);consistent structure and presentation;appropriate use of extensions; andcorrect signs, scales and balances.

Find out more

Use our 2026 guides to financial statements to help you tell your own connected and consistent story across your reporting.Use resources on our IFRS 18 hub, including our Illustrative disclosures that reflect the initial application of IFRS 18.See our EU sustainability page for our latest insights and guidance on ESRS.See our digital hubs on Uncertain times and Clear on climate reporting for further practical guidance.

1 European Securities and Markets Authority (the EU’s financial markets regulatory body).2 Under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772, as corrected and amended.3 Under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1563. Referred by ESMA as ‘ESRS Set 2’.4 Reliefs specified under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1563, Article 2.5 In 2026, enforcers are expected to focus on ESRS E1 Climate change and ESRS S1 Own workforce.

articles.title: Is your portfolio ready for the next decade?
articles.text:
Better Vantage podcast

Is your portfolio ready for the next decade?

November 11, 2026

Video length: 20 minutes 33 seconds

Read the transcript

Rebecca Choo Quan: For much of the last decade, building a portfolio often seemed pretty straightforward--buy U.S. stocks, lean into technology, and let the markets do the work. And work it did.
But the environment investors face today--AI disruption, shifting interest rates, and growing market concentration is raising a question every investor should ask--is the portfolio that worked for the last 10 years right for the next ten?
Welcome to season three of Better Vantage by Vanguard, a podcast series hosted by Custom Content from WSJ and Vanguard. I'm Rebecca Choo Quan from Vanguard's Investment Strategy Group, sitting in today for Christine Kashkari of WSJ Custom Content. And with me is my co-host and our resident expert Joe Davis, global chief economist and head of investment strategy at Vanguard.
Today, we are exploring how investors at different stages of life, from those just starting out to mid-career professionals building wealth to retirees drawing income, should approach portfolio construction in a rapidly evolving world.
Joining us is Mona Mahajan, head of investment strategy at Edward Jones, where she helps shape the investment outlook and capital markets strategy for millions of individual investors.
Mona, welcome to the show.
Mona Mahajan: Great to be here. Thank you.
Joe Davis: Mona's not only are you a thought leader in industry, she's on TV and but for a good reason. When you're speaking, I listen and I read your team's research. We're peers in industry, but folks, views on the markets, thoughtful perspectives, where are the risks, where are the opportunities and Mona's not uncomfortable going against the grain if that's the correct assessment. And so, I'm really thrilled today to bring your perspective and the purview you have with nine million investors and counting to our listeners.
Rebecca: So, talk to us, is the investing playbook changing?
Mona: Well, maybe we start with what is the macroeconomic outlook given AI is now a huge factor. So, when we think about in the U.S. potential GDP growth, there are two factors that drive that. As many of us know, it's labor force growth, and it is productivity gains. And when we look forward maybe the next five or 10 years, the labor force growth component, especially in the U.S., but across a lot of developed world, is shrinking a bit.
And so labor force is coming in. We have immigration reform. We have an aging demographic. And so that component which historically by the way has been about 0.5% and the other productivity gain part of it has been about one, one and a half.
So, that gives you a total of 1 1/2 to 2% potential GDP growth. Now, where we are looking and monitoring carefully is the productivity side of this equation. So how does productivity gains factor in the next five to 10 years given this AI backdrop? And do we think on the margin we're moving higher than this one or 1 ½% or are we moving lower? So, our best guess would be we're probably inching higher, and productivity gains probably are going to be closer to 1 1/2 to 2%. If you're very bullish on AI, you can even get figures beyond that. But for argument's sake, if the labor force is shrinking a bit and you get back down to 0.3%, but productivity is making up more 1 1/2 to 2%, you can potential growth in the U.S. go from this 1 1/2 to 2% environment to maybe it's two-2 1/2% longer term.
And that has implications not only for economic growth, consumption, labor market, earnings growth as well.
Joe: Let's say, you know, we shorten horizon a little bit? So, say for the next year, what are the indicators that you're looking now to see where are the risks on the macro environment because the equity market is banking on a lot of generally good news.
Mona: Yeah. And you know, look, I think a lot of the risks that we see out there are probably similar to what many of our teams are watching right now. So, inflation is front center, and this is an inflation story that is driven not only by just higher prices, but supply shocks globally. And a lot of economies are thinking about how do we bring supply chains closer to home, how do we get alternative supply chains to some of the ones that have been established historically? And all of that does over time factor in and weigh on inflationary pressures.
We're also seeing the price of labor, you know, move higher and that has weighed on inflation. So, inflation is definitely front and center for us as a key risk. I'll also add there are a couple others. One of course is concentration risk from a market perspective. That continues to be one that we all grapple with
Rebecca: Feels like you really didn't need to diversify. You just need to hold a couple of stocks.
Mona: It's all about those few names. And that's not rare in history. We've seen that happen at other times when we've had, you know, industrial revolution or tech revolutions in the past, but we are watching that one closely as well. And then there's a geopolitical aspect, which, of course, all of that plays into what we're seeing on the inflation side as well.
Joe: That was very helpful, thank you, Mona, in terms of the economics. There's risk in both the inflation and growth side, right? That sounds like maybe near term it's the inflation, but longer term it's the growth could be the surprise.
So, let’s shift a little bit to the capital markets, right? So, I got my asset allocation. One of the key things I got to put in is what the expected return is, right? So, I'll leave it to you what the horizon is. Let's start maybe perhaps with stocks and we can move the fixed income. But what's your view? What's your vantage point and what are the sort of numbers you're starting to think about?
Mona: Yes, we spend a lot of time thinking about capital market assumptions. And what I will say to your point, the last 10 years and probably even since the ‘08-‘09 financial crisis, we've been in an amazing, unparalleled bull market. And the last five years alone, you know, we've seen since 2022 a tech-led bull market, and capital market assumptions have been mainly wrong on the equity side. Because on average if you look at it the last 10 years, the S&P 500 has returned actually about 15% whereas most models looked at 7-8, maybe 9%.1
Joe: Ours included.
Mona: Yeah, and vice versa. And we'll talk about fixed income, but fixed income last 10 years have returned about one to 2%.2 Now when we think about the next 10-year plus, we actually think there's a bit of mean reversion coming. And I think that's the direction you guys were talking about as well. Probably not going to see that 15% continue indefinitely into the future. There's a valuation component and earnings component to that, dividend component to that. But overall, we'd say yes, healthy return profile, especially in U.S., but also in non-U.S. parts of market from your equity returns.
What's more interesting is the fixed income side of the market, which by the way, we're seeing in recent history has started to yield a little bit more. And I think that's interesting for if you're in retirement, near retirement or looking for income opportunities.
Rebecca: So, how do should I as an individual investor think about positioning my portfolio knowing that maybe the future is not quite as rosy on the equity side?
Mona: Yeah. And you know, I would still argue that the future of equities is going to be driven by innovation, and we've seen huge amount of innovation come specifically from the U.S. market. All seven of the MAG 7 are housed here. For someone like yourself that is thinking about asset allocation, we look at it from probably three levels. One is where do you want to play in the market cap space? And we think still U.S. large cap and midcap are interesting places to be. The large cap will get you that exposure still to AI and technology. The midcap is where we see that catch up potential, the broadening of leadership. Now the other part we looked at is a regional perspective. So, we like the U.S. as we noted, but we also like emerging markets here. Still they've had a nice run, but they are an alternative we think to U.S. technology, a good earnings story emerging from emerging markets, and we are starting to like international value as a diversifier. So, keep that in mind as you're building a portfolio. Certainly, you can start with the U.S. large and mid, add some EM and international value. And then we think about it from a sector perspective, which we again like a cyclical and AI tech sector. So, industrials is an area that we like, as well as com services, which gives you that hyperscale or exposure. So, diversification is still the only free lunch you'll get. You'll want to do it. But if you think about it from those different layers, there's a great way to kind of establish a baseline.
Joe: So, what's the risk macro or market you most worry about to your baseline?
Mona: Yeah. And you know, I think it is probably an AI-driven risk. So, could we see whether it's a slow down beyond expectations? There are some risks in that there's some circular financing happening in some of these companies. There are also just a couple of big clients and players that have dominated the space. And finally, I'll add, there's competition coming from China and other parts of the world that could derail the story somewhat. Now all that being said, it does feel like we're still an environment where demand is outstripping supply and the demand for all of these tokens etc. is only moving higher. So, we don't see this getting derailed anytime soon. But as we think about, you know, we talked about the last time we really had a cycle, a downturn, a bear market prolonged and deep was back in 2008. So, as we think about the next, you know, whether it's 10 to 15 years, will we get another cycle in that that as well?
Rebecca: It’s a really pertinent question for individual investors who might have forgotten what it's like to go through a period of volatility like that.
Mona: So, in any given year, we tend to see one, two, or three corrections in the market in the 5, 10 to 15% range. And, historically, those bear markets do tend to occur once every four years or so. So, we want to make sure that one, investors know that volatility will happen. Two, though what we do know and as we are all long-term investors here, time in the market is so much more important than trying to time yourself in and out of the market. The other thing that we get a lot and we started to do some analysis on this is should I wait for a pullback before I add. Overall, the message seems to be if you're using a dollar cost averaging strategy, if you have a consistent approach to investing in the market, don't change that because we're back at an all-time high. Continue to use opportunities to get into the market. That's the power of compounding. That's really where the power of reaching your financial goals will come in.
Joe Davis: So, let's talk a little bit about diversification. We could go a number of directions with diversification, but has it changed? Again, AI is changing the playbook. I mean you go on the international side, you mentioned a little bit from a return outlook, perhaps a little better returns, but again we haven't had as much of the correction side. So, is it still the fixed income? Have you changed anything at all? What is that broad philosophy?
Mona: Yeah, absolutely. And you know, we are still very much believers in diversification, long-term quality. You know, the way we express that in our portfolios is one, and we talked through this as well, but we want to make sure that we have exposure to the U.S. But we do think as we think about the next 10 years or so, 5-10 years, we think international exposure will be important. If you invest in the S&P 500, you are investing in a very concentrated index.3 And so we want to make sure, yes, you have exposure to that theme. But as we talked about earlier, the sectors that will benefit eventually from AI, think about where we stand in international markets. There's a lot of banking, there's a lot of industrial companies, there's a lot of energy and cyclical parts of market that really may start to experience some catch up there. And so we think that's a good place.
Joe: So, AI usage is a global phenomenon, right? So, you're saying that's one way, that's one way to play offense and defense.
Mona: Exactly right.
Joe: If I'm hearing you right saying this is no, this is how technology cycle works. We're in a one phase, but that phase may not persist. So it's not a bearish on AI philosophy. I think it's quite profound and quite the opposite.
Mona: Yeah, absolutely right. And you know, and we look at two components of it, the emerging market theme, which by the way, has outperformed the S&P meaningfully in 2026 thus far.4 That is maybe more of a play on AI, but an alternative to U.S. technology. We think about the Korean market or the Taiwanese market. Semiconductors are huge, they are accelerating. China of course is innovating, but then there is the other part of developed non-U.S.
You think Europe, you think Japan, and those parts probably have lagged a little bit, but they have that catch up potential we think. And so, exposure to both. We're overweight EM, overweight international value right now. So, that we think is a good combination.
Joe: So, Mona, the fixed income side. But a lot of investors that we talked to maybe saying concerning the pressures in Washington, why should I own fixed income at all. I could hide out in cash. So, which one wins?
Mona: Yeah, absolutely. And you know, maybe a good starting point is investment grade bonds. You may know the best indicator of what their total return will be over their life of the bond is where the yield started at. And so when we're looking at these elevated yields, we're looking at better outcomes for clients in fixed income. So, that's the good news. I think there's a good starting point there, those that are in retirement, near retirement or you just like having a little more income in your portfolio, you're getting that.
Now the flip side of this is why are you getting that? And so those higher yields have been driven by a couple factors or a few factors. Yes, there's concern on U.S. fiscal debt and deficit rising. There's also concern that the AI bond issuance is crowding out a little bit of the IG yields. And then, there is this idea that global yields are also rising. And so, the U.S. is anchored a little bit higher.
Now on the other side, we're also seeing better economic growth that drives yields higher. So, better starting point from growth. But what we'd say overall is every now and then we see the yields move higher because these bond vigilantes come back out. They're worried about the debt and deficit situation. We know the U.S. overall fiscal situation, $40 trillion in debt.5
Joe: It’s a big number.
Mona: Now how do we think about this? Well, economic growth in fact has not slowed despite the spiraling levels of debt or the upward rise in in debt levels. Now we've seen a lot of good GDP, we've seen a lot of good consumption come out of this economy. Even with higher yields and higher debt levels, we still call it a yellow flag, not a red flag yet, but something we're watching. And you know, the best way if there are inflation concerns, the best way to combat inflation is to get yourself invested in a portfolio that outperforms inflation.
Joe: Which is not necessarily short in duration, it's actually maintaining bond exposure.
Mona: And you having that balanced portfolio, having that equity and having some bonds in there.
Rebecca: But you both spend a lot of time talking about portfolio construction. I, as a client, I'm coming to an advisor more for than just investments. It's more of a holistic wealth conversation. So, what does that look like and how important is that relative to the actual portfolio itself?
Mona: Yeah, we're finding more and more financial fulfillment. This idea that you feel comfortable with where you're going and you feel good about where you are in your monetary and financial situation. That is becoming more and more of a conversation we're seeing at Edward Jones amongst our advisors. We want to make sure there's what we call five stages of financial planning. One is you have your cash needs met. Two is you have your investment portfolio in place. The third is we want to make sure that you have things like your tax planning, intact, estate planning. And then there's things like insurance and making sure you have any liabilities covered, hedging, we call it in some ways. And so, all of that is part of a broader holistic financial plan. But more than anything, we'd say we want to first make sure we capture what are your needs, wants, and wishes. So what do you need out of, you know, the next 20-30 years? What do you want, and what do you really wish for? You know, how many trips or first class flights do you want to take?
Joe: What I have to mention that, you know, Mona, it resonates a lot with me and from my own personal situation, again, if my business, my line of work I was always focused on that. The investment you can tell of today, the investment conversation, I live and breathe it. But what I've come to really appreciate. I have an advisor and if you had asked me 10 years ago I would say well, I think I can do this myself. But then I started to realize I really don't know enough about estate planning or just enough to be dangerous taxes. The comfort recently for my wife and I of talking about the wishes, the needs, and desires. We had actually not done it even though we've been together for over 30 years. Whether we have an advisor or not, what you said resonated with me. I can tell you the anxiety of our portfolio, even though I have less worry about that because of what we had that recent conversation. It was profound for me, and I've been in the business for 30 years. I didn't appreciate it.
Mona: It's a good conversation to have.
Joe: So, we covered a lot of ground. I'm going to ask you for two potential listeners out there, someone who's roughly my age, let's call it 60, 50-sixties. What's the one single best thing you talk to investors, professionals all day long and have a perspective on the world. What's the one thing? It could be economic, could be investment, could be financial plan that you would leave with them. They'd say just please, if I could underscore one message what would it be and? And in the same thing but, for someone half their age.
Mona: I would say for someone older, your age although you're quite young relatively.
Joe: I'm no spring chicken!
Mona: I was going to say relative to policymakers, but at that age and you know exactly what we talked about, a lot of folks we've found in this generation have tried to do a lot themselves. And this is actually still a good time to think about that financial planning conversation. You're young enough where your estate needs haven't you know, hopefully you're still putting them together. You want to think about your legacy at this point. How do you want to leave money and assets to your children, to charities? What is you know, how are you think about where you're going to leave behind? And by the way, the tax conversation gets incrementally more and more important the older you get and the more gains you're sitting on. And so that conversation is huge we found in this generation. And so that financial planning conversation, we would urge folks in that age bracket to have.
The younger generation, however, that is one where we want to have the conversation of get invested, stay invested. Don't let the market shake you out. Don't make emotionally charged investing decisions. We want to make sure that they understand volatility is a norm and you might see some years more, some years less, get invested, stay invested. Make sure that you are spending that time in the market.
Rebecca: What I tell my 20-year olds all the time.
Mona: The other thing I'll say is a lot of people look at investing in themselves as a way to outpace inflation. So your wage growth should start looking better and better. Your gains, from that perspective, anything you can do to whether it's from education, training, taking that online course. And maybe get yourself to another level where you're actually making that wage gain that will outpace inflation. And so, I think that's an interesting one.
Rebecca: That's a great approach. Keep investing in the markets and keep investing in yourself.
Mona: I love that.
Rebecca: I think that's great advice. Thank you, Mona, so much for being here today.
Mona: It was great to be here, guys. Thank you.
Rebecca: Well, that's it for today's episode. Next time, we're diving into the great wealth transfer and whether families are ready for it. Join us for that conversation and all of our upcoming episodes.

Read more

In this episode of Better Vantage, Mona Mahajan, head of investment strategy and asset allocation at Edward Jones, argues that the investment playbook that worked over the last decade (leaning into U.S. technology and letting the markets do the work) may not be as successful in the next. AI disruption, shifting rates, and concentrated markets are raising questions every investor should ask.
The U.S. market's tech-driven run has been extraordinary, but history suggests such periods eventually broaden. Yet that concentration itself signals opportunity elsewhere — in U.S. value stocks, mid-caps, and international markets positioned to benefit as AI usage spreads globally.
Elevated yields also may offer better starting points for bond returns after a decade of minimal income. The combination of solid economic growth and persistent inflation suggests limited Fed rate cuts, keeping yields attractive for those seeking income or portfolio balance.
The takeaway: The future optimal portfolio may look different from the recent past — broader across market caps, more global, with fixed income reclaiming its role.

5 key takeaways from Wood Mackenzie’s CCUS Conference 2025

Opinion
3 October 2025
Is CCUS viable in power generation?

Opinion
6 March 2025
5 key ways to decarbonise cement production

View Tania Alvarez 's full profile

Carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) is entering a more selective phase.
As the industry matures, attention is shifting away from the scale of project announcements towards a more fundamental question: which CCUS projects can successfully reach final investment decision and commercial operation?
That question ran through discussions at Wood Mackenzie’s fourth annual CCUS Conference, held in Houston in October 2026. Nearly 300 participants from more than 150 organisations across the CCUS value chain joined the event, including energy companies, financial and insurance institutions, technology and engineering firms and project developers.
Three themes stood out: the growing importance of reliable power, the challenge of reducing the cost of proven capture technology, and the need to build durable revenue models.
How are energy security and rising power demand reshaping CCS?
Rapid growth in electricity demand from AI and data centres is putting the power sector increasingly at the centre of the CCS opportunity.
Hyperscalers are looking for reliable, lower-carbon power that can support expanding electricity requirements while meeting decarbonisation commitments. This creates an opportunity for CCS, but demand alone does not make projects investable.
Conference discussions highlighted that capital is increasingly concentrated around projects where development risk has already been reduced. Secured and permitted storage, experienced partners, proven capture technology, clear cost visibility and durable revenues are becoming important foundations for projects seeking to reach final investment decision.
For developers, this reinforces a wider shift across the CCUS market: execution is becoming as important as ambition.
If carbon capture technology is proven, what is holding deployment back?
For post-combustion capture, the central challenge is increasingly one of economics and scale rather than technological feasibility.
Amine-based capture is commercially established and remains a preferred option for many projects, but costs are high. Energy market volatility, inflation and higher raw-material prices are adding further pressure.
Alternative technologies could ultimately reduce capture costs, but many still require commercial-scale demonstration and policy support before developers and investors are comfortable deploying them widely. In the meantime, the industry is focusing on standardisation, project replication and greater supply-chain maturity to improve economics.
Yet these benefits depend on projects actually progressing. Permitting and regulatory hurdles, alongside retrofit and integration complexity, continue to constrain deployment. In harder-to-abate sectors, the economics can remain challenging even as project experience grows.
The result is that CCS is unlikely to become a fully market-driven industry in the near term. For many projects, policy support and multiple sources of revenue will remain important.
Can CCUS projects build durable long-term revenues?
This leads to perhaps the most important commercial question facing the sector: what happens as current incentives evolve or expire?
Support mechanisms such as the US 45Q tax credit have played an important role in project economics. But incentives are time limited, meaning developers have to consider how projects can remain viable over much longer operating lives. [
For many projects, the answer is likely to involve combining several sources of value rather than relying on one.

Expand

Carbon markets and environmental attribute certificates are among the mechanisms being explored alongside government and market-driven incentives. The voluntary carbon market could also provide a bridge towards more mature compliance and commercial markets, although questions remain around the depth and durability of demand.
What will determine the next phase of CCUS?
The next stage of CCUS development will not be defined simply by how many projects enter the pipeline, but by how effectively individual projects address risk across the value chain.
Access to transport and permitted storage, clear carbon-accounting frameworks, durable policy support and stronger demand signals will all matter. So will partnerships that bring together the expertise needed to manage increasingly complex projects.
The opportunity for CCUS remains significant. But as scrutiny increases, the projects best placed to progress will be those that can turn technical capability into commercially durable, executable business models.

articles.title: Better data first, then AI: Making aid work harder for people
articles.text:
Published on
Voices

Better data first, then AI: Making aid work harder for people

Gallina Andronova Vincelette

Hisham Abdo Kahin

Lisandro Martin

Haishan Fu

November 11, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Photo: Jonathan Ernst/World Bank

Imagine a minister of finance preparing for a budget review. They pick one line, say primary health care, in a single province, and see every activity financed there: a multilateral loan, two bilateral grants and a foundation-funded program. For each one, they can follow the money further: which donor or country provides it, which agency channels it, which ministry or NGO implements it, which districts receive it, and how much was already committed and spent. They notice that three funders are active in one district, while none in the neighboring, and take that evidence to the next donor coordination meeting.
Parts of that picture can already be assembled from open data and the aid management systems some governments run. But for most governments, the complete picture is still out of reach. Closing the gap matters now more than ever. Artificial intelligence (AI) is often pitched as the shortcut; and indeed, it could help, but only if the data underneath is good enough.
A crowded system with less money
Over the past two decades, the foreign aid system has become crowded and fragmented. Between 2002 and 2021, the number of official finance providers grew from 62 to 112, while the number of donor agencies more than doubled, from 215 to 565. Over a similar period, the average official development assistance (ODA) grant size halved, from US$1.7 million to US$0.8 million. For countries with limited capacity to carry out foreign-funded projects, that means more donors, more projects, more reporting and higher costs just to manage it all.
Now, the system is also shrinking. ODA from members of the OECD Development Assistance Committee fell by over 23 percent in real terms in 2025, according to preliminary data, the largest annual drop on record. A crowded system with less money leaves no room for duplication or waste.
Why the full picture matters
An integrated view of development financing helps governments identify synergies, overlaps, and gaps across programs, enabling better coordination and more effective allocation of resources, whether for skills development, rural roads, or support to small businesses.
With this fuller picture, governments can match projects to national priorities, plan investments in the right order, and negotiate with partners based on evidence rather than guesswork. That is where transparency meets jobs: aid that goes where it counts is more likely to fund the services, infrastructure, and businesses that create them.
This is work the World Bank has taken on. For the 2026 Aid Transparency Index, a biennial ranking by the independent organization Publish What You Fund of how openly aid organizations publish their data, we published the names of the organizations implementing our activities, along with transaction records showing who received each payment, so users could trace financing at both the project and the transaction level. We are also building shared reference lists with the governments we support. These are standard lists of codes for things like government ministries and agencies, so that each one is named the same way in every dataset, which makes data easier to connect. The results show: the International Development Association (IDA), the World Bank Group’s fund for low-income countries, ranked second among 34 organizations in the 2026 Aid Transparency Index. IDA scored 97.1 out of 100, up from 92.2 in 2024, with its biggest gain on networked data, meaning data that links funders, implementers and recipients. The ranking is not an end in itself, but it shows that openness can be put into practice.
Data comes first, then AI
Most ministries cannot build this picture on their own. Two things can help, and the order matters.
The first is networked data. Donors and financiers need to publish who they fund, who carries out the work, and who receives the money, using shared codes that link related activities. Then aid stops being a pile of separate files and becomes a trail that can be followed from start to finish.
The second is AI. Today’s tools can already query raw data, tell funders apart from implementers, and process large volumes with far less technical effort than in the past. They work best on open, machine-readable data. For ministries with limited capacity, this could turn a specialist task into a routine question: which partners are funding primary health care in this province, and how much have they spent?
But AI also has limits. It cannot compensate for missing, inaccurate, or outdated information, and it does not replace expertise. Given poor data, it can produce confident answers that are simply wrong, and decisions based on them affect real people. Experts still need to validate and interpret what it produces. So the sequence matters: better data first, followed by AI to make it usable.
The work still ahead
Better data is one part of making every dollar work harder; speed in implementation is the other. An approved project cannot help anyone until it is ready to start, and delays between approval and start-up are a cost of their own. Through its Development-Ready (D-Ready) initiative, the World Bank is putting legal, operational, and capacity conditions in place before projects are approved, with the aim of reducing the time from Board approval to effectiveness, so that jobs, services, and other benefits reach people faster.
And there is more work to be done. Closing that gap will require coordination among financiers, donors and partner governments. Once those identifiers are in place, a ministry’s own budget data will be able to connect to the World Bank’s published data and that of others. The minister in our budget review would no longer need to piece the picture together. They would simply see it. We will keep publishing in ways that help every country see, and steer, the aid it receives toward jobs and opportunities.

articles.title: Mandatory Fun? Suit Claims Ethereum Foundation Took Irony Too Far
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Mandatory Fun? Suit Claims Ethereum Foundation Took Irony Too Far

Written by:

Thaddeus Pinakiewicz
Vice President, Research

Topics

Ethereum

research • November 13, 2026

Mandatory Fun? Suit Claims Ethereum Foundation Took Irony Too Far

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.WHAT HAPPENEDA former Ethereum Foundation employee alleges she and a colleague were fired for organizing a written objection to a clause in its institutional mandate that, read plainly, asks violators to take their own lives with a sword. Kayleen Fulton, who led the Foundation’s protocol support team and facilitated All Core Developers, the open process through which the protocol is upgraded, filed a lawsuit last week against the Foundation and Vitalik Buterin, Ethereum’s creator. Her complaint, in the U.S. District Court for Colorado, describes a workplace where an inside joke from the Milady corner of crypto became a condition of employment, and where leadership passed up multiple opportunities to make the apparent suicide pledge optional, let alone remove it.According to the complaint, the foundation circulated the mandate on Feb. 25 with a “Source Seppuku License” attached, a bit of Remilia-flavored internet theater that names ritual suicide as the penalty for violating its terms. Within a week 79 employees had backed removing the language, some pointing to a colleague’s suicide the year before as the reason it was more than a matter of taste. Leadership responded by keeping it in an illustrated edition with anime art and cartoon cats, which is roughly what you would do if you had decided the problem was that the clause wasn’t whimsical enough.On March 20, employees were told to affirm the mandate or leave, and were reassured that the seppuku language was a cultural reference and not meant literally. Five days later, 53 of them signed a letter affirming Ethereum’s principles while rejecting the conditions under which they were being made to affirm them, which is about as polite and pro-institution as dissent gets. On April 6, the letter’s two organizers, Fulton and Trent Van Epps, were fired, according to the suit. Fulton’s suit alleges retaliation, disability discrimination, and medical-leave violations, and notes she had disclosed a cancer diagnosis shortly before her dismissal. These are still allegations, but it is hard to miss that the mandate itself describes Ethereum as liberating people from power relationships “where dissent imposes a heavy price.”According to the complaint, the EF’s lawyers denied in May that Ms. Fulton “was subjected to unlawful conduct, economic duress, retaliation, or termination in violation of public policy,” but did not state a reason for her termination. The EF has not made any public comments about her claims since they became public.OUR TAKEI put very little stock in the criticism the Ethereum Foundation usually gets, most of which comes from people wishing their bags were heavier. Crypto Twitter has blamed the EF for not doing enough, not promoting projects, and not pumping the token. Meanwhile Ethereum has the deepest DeFi ecosystem and the most TVL of any chain by a wide margin, and foundations that did pick winners, like Avalanche’s, got hammered when those memes went nowhere. The EF exists to steward a vision, not a price. It is a nonprofit foundation, not a corporation, a home for developers thinking decades ahead rather than for suits, and that is part of why the weirdness is a feature. When Vitalik gives a conference talk in a cape and a mask, I mostly think it’s fine.All of that said, the suit’s allegations are concerning. Imagine the HR department at a normal company hearing from 79 employees, some of them grieving a colleague, that a mandatory document was hurtful. It could have deleted the clause that afternoon without even consulting a lawyer, and it would certainly not have fired the people who asked nicely. Being esoteric is all well and good (especially when the work is mysterious, and important). But enforcing your esoterica by firing people, as the foundation allegedly did, is how you become Lumon, the fictional company in television’s “Severance,” an institution whose mission talks about care while its actions treat employees as disposable. Crypto Twitter may want the EF to start acting like a corporation, but it doesn’t need to. If the suit’s claims prove correct, the foundation needs to act like the organization its own mandate describes, one where disagreeing doesn’t cost you your job. Until then, please report to the Break Room.

articles.title: The AI Buildout Is Bigger Than the Chip | WisdomTree
articles.text: Back to BlogThe AI Buildout Is Bigger Than the ChipPublished November 5, 2026Christopher Gannatti, CFAGlobal Head of ResearchKey TakeawaysAI reasoning and continuously running software agents could broaden compute demand beyond the training budgets of a few large model developers.Power, land and advanced packaging could constrain AI infrastructure growth, widening the investment opportunity across utilities, electrical equipment, cooling and assembly suppliers.Nvidia’s platform strategy and deployment-focused AI safety measures highlight the potential importance of networking, software and security alongside chips.Four Ways Nvidia’s CEO Describes the AI Economy Differently from the Conventional FramingInvestors often reduce the AI infrastructure story to something simple. A handful of foundation model labs train ever-larger models, and one foundry’s wafer capacity decides how many accelerators can ship. Demand is cyclical, the supplier sells chips and the main question is how long the spending lasts.In a recent conversation of roughly 100 minutes on the BG2 podcast, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described a broader picture.1 This is useful as a statement of how the largest supplier in the ecosystem sees the next phase. We focus on four themes of the discussion.What drives compute demandWhere the constraints sitHow safety is being approachedWhat kind of business Nvidia says it isAt WisdomTree, if investors are looking deeply at artificial intelligence and seeking strategies with strong Nvidia exposure, they might consider:WisdomTree U.S. Quality Growth Fund (QGRW)2WisdomTree Artificial Intelligence and Innovation Fund (WTAI)3WisdomTree Physical AI, Humanoids, and Drones Fund (WDRN)41. Demand Is Shifting from Training to Reasoning and AgentsThe familiar framing treats AI compute as mostly a pre-training story, which is to say a small number of labs spending heavily to train large language models. Huang’s description gave pre-training a smaller share of the story. He pointed to inference-time reasoning, large populations of cooperating software agents (he referred to swarms of more than 10,000), and classical accelerated computing as demand drivers in their own right.The distinction matters because the two workloads behave differently.Training is a large, lumpy, project-style expense concentrated among a few buyers.Inference is closer to a utility. It scales with usage, and a model that reasons before answering uses more computation for each query than one that answers immediately.If software agents are running continuously, calling tools and checking one another’s work, the computation per task rises again. Demand then depends on how widely AI is used across an economy, which is a broader base than the spending plans of a few labs.The mention of classical accelerated computing is easy to overlook. Many workloads that never involved a chatbot, such as data processing, simulation and scientific computing, have been moving from general-purpose processors to accelerators for years. If that migration continues, it adds demand that does not depend on any single model release.Going forward, it may be worth watching how much of reported data center revenue comes from inference rather than training, and whether the growth of agent-based products shows up in usage data from the large cloud platforms. A broader demand base is a claim that can be tested against those numbers over the coming quarters.2. The Binding Constraints Are Moving DownstreamA second common assumption is that advanced chip manufacturing capacity is the main limit on how fast AI infrastructure can grow. Huang’s account moved the constraint further along the chain.His framing noted that the more critical constraints could include land, high-voltage power and the advanced packaging substrates that tie memory and processors together.This is a physical-world argument, and it fits what the industry has been saying more broadly. A data center needs a site, a grid connection and electrical equipment that can handle very large loads. Those items run on timelines of years, and they are not solved by building another fab. Packaging and substrates are a separate chokepoint. An accelerator is an assembly of logic, high-bandwidth memory and interconnect, and the final assembly step has its own capacity limits and its own suppliers.For investors, this widens the map of who benefits and who is exposed. If the limiting resource is power delivery, then utilities, electrical equipment makers, cooling specialists and developers of power-adjacent real estate sit closer to the center of the story. If packaging is the limit, substrate and assembly suppliers matter more than they have in past semiconductor cycles. It also suggests that the pace of the buildout may be set by the slowest link, and that the slowest link is probably not the one most headlines focus on.As we move forward from October 2026, it may make sense to watch lead times for transformers and switchgear, utility interconnection queues, and capacity announcements from packaging and substrate suppliers. If these constraints ease, the buildout can accelerate. If they tighten, delivery schedules may slip no matter how much chip supply exists.3. Safety as an Engineering Discipline, Not Only a Modeling ProblemPublic debate about AI safety often centers on alignment, which is to say whether a model’s weights and training produce behavior that matches human intent. Huang described a complementary approach built around how AI systems are deployed. As summarized, it relies on zero-trust isolation, containment and out-of-band telemetry.These terms come from cybersecurity practice. Zero trust means no component is assumed to be safe by default. Each one is given only the access it needs, and every request is verified. Containment means that when a system does something unexpected, the effects stay inside a boundary. Out-of-band telemetry means monitoring from outside the system being monitored, so that if the system fails or behaves badly, the record of what it did does not depend on the system’s own reporting.The logic is straightforward. A population of autonomous agents acting across company systems is difficult to certify as safe purely by inspecting a model. It is easier to limit what each agent can reach and to watch it from the outside. Organizations already use this approach for human users and conventional software, so applying it to agents extends existing practice instead of requiring new science.There is an investment angle as well. If this view holds, enterprise adoption of agents will depend on identity management, network segmentation, monitoring and security tooling, and not only on model quality. These are areas where established security and infrastructure software companies may have a role. It is also an area where reasonable people disagree. Engineering controls reduce risk, but they do not answer every question that alignment researchers raise, and the two approaches are best viewed as layers.4. Nvidia as a Platform, Not a PartThe conventional view treats Nvidia as a merchant silicon company, selling GPUs into a market that expands and contracts with customers’ capital spending. Huang described something broader, specifically, a full-stack infrastructure platform that spans chips, networking, software licensing and revenue-sharing arrangements.Each layer changes the economics in a different way. Networking is sold alongside the accelerators and affects how well large clusters perform as a whole. Software, including the libraries and tools developers build on, creates switching costs, because code written for one platform is costly to move. Licensing and revenue-sharing models, if they grow, would tie Nvidia’s income to the use of its platform and not only to the initial hardware sale.Whether the market should value such a company differently from a chip supplier depends on how much of its revenue actually comes from the non-hardware layers and how durable it proves to be. Huang’s description is a statement of intent and strategy. The company’s financial disclosures are the place to check how far the transition has gone, and the details of any revenue-sharing arrangements are worth reading in primary filings instead of relying on summaries.Putting It TogetherTaken together, the four themes describe an AI buildout whose demand is broader than a few training runs, whose limits are physical and located well beyond the foundry, whose risks are partly managed through familiar security architecture and whose largest supplier wants to be seen as a platform. None of this is settled. Each theme is a hypothesis that can be checked against data.For investors thinking about AI as a long-term theme, the practical implication is breadth. The opportunity set under this framing is not limited to chip designers. It extends to power, cooling, packaging, networking, software and security, and each of those areas has its own competitive dynamics and its own risks. A clear view of where the constraints are, and how they are changing, is likely to matter as much as a view on any single company.1 Source for the data, detail and inspiration of this piece, unless otherwise stated: Gerstner, B., & Tang, C. (Hosts). (2026, October 15). Jensen Huang | Does AI revenue justify capex, ’27 AI bottlenecks, singularity, open vs closed & more (No. 41) [Audio podcast episode]. articles.title: After Trump’s Rout, Will Global Trade Keep Defying Politics?
articles.text:
After Trump’s Rout, Will Global Trade Keep Defying Politics?

Tom Miller

Gavekal Research | 10 Nov 2026

War and tariffs have knocked President Donald Trump and the Republican Party off track, but global trade continues to defy these geopolitical headwinds. This is not simply an artifact of higher prices for oil and microchips: goods trade volume is growing at its fastest pace in 15 years, excluding the post-Covid rebound. The expansion is driven both by strong global appetite for artificial-intelligence equipment and by exporters finding alternative markets and adapting to supply-chain disruptions.The World Trade Organization forecasts that trade growth will accelerate further in 2027. The outlook is not without risks: if the AI boom turns to bust, trade growth will slow sharply in both volume and value terms. A political backlash against Chinese exports, which could reach a scarcely believable US$4.5trn in 2026, would compound the slowdown. Yet the world will struggle to break its addiction to Chinese goods, while a sustained AI investment boom would provide continued demand.

articles.text:

12 Nov 2026

The top cities in Central Asia and the South Caucasus in 2026

By Swayam Tanna

Often overlooked in favour of the rapidly growing cities in China and India, and far from matching the economic might of those in North America and Europe, Central Asia and the South Caucasus rarely feature in discussions of the world’s leading city economies. Yet, a closer look at the region’s major cities in our 2026 Global Cities Index reveals strengths that should not be ignored, including impressive standings across Human Capital and Economics metrics.

An overlooked region with strengths that should not be ignored

While rarely recognised as such, the major cities of Central Asia and the South Caucasus are among the most dynamic urban economies in the world. Over the next 25 years, we forecast real GDP growth across 10 of the region’s largest city economies to average 4.1% per year, well ahead of the 2.7% average across Asia Pacific’s cities. This growth is led by some of the fastest-expanding cities anywhere globally, with Tashkent (Uzbekistan) and Bishkek (Kyrgyzstan) both ranking among the top 10 of the 1,000 cities covered in our 2026 Global Cities Index. By 2050, we forecast the region’s combined city GDP to be more than two and a half times what it is today.

Yet, the region’s cities are far from matching the economic might of megacities in North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific, and have remained outside the upper reaches of our 2026 Global Cities Index, held back by weaker Governance and Environment scores. But with the region taking on a growing role as a key trade route between China and Europe, a closer look reveals strengths that should not be ignored. Robust economic growth is augmented by impressive standings across Human Capital, reflecting a large, growing, and increasingly skilled population that is set to underpin its rise in the decades ahead.

Human Capital: a young, growing, and skilled population sets the region apart

The strongest-performing category for the region’s cities is Human Capital, ranking highest of all five components for eight of the 10 cities we cover. In fact, four of these cities hold places among the top 150 cities for Human Capital globally, including Almaty and Astana in Kazakhstan at 66th and 98th, respectively, Tashkent (Uzbekistan) in 108th, and Ashgabat (Turkmenistan) at 146th.

For many of these cities, this strength rests on a solid educational foundation. Baku’s universities rank 57th globally, closely followed by Almaty’s at 67th, with the Kazakh city home to almost a third of the country’s university students. Kazakhstan has also moved to deepen its talent pool by attracting leading international institutions, with more than 30 foreign university branches now in operation, including Cardiff University’s Astana campus, the only Russell Group campus in Central Asia. Educational attainment is high across the region too, most notably in Tbilisi, which ranks 36th in the world for the mean years of schooling among its adult residents.

Crucially, the region’s highly educated labour force is also growing quickly. Unlike many advanced economies grappling with ageing populations and rapidly declining fertility rates, these cities are home to some of the fastest-growing populations in the world. Astana, Almaty, Dushanbe, and Bishkek all rank among the top 10% of cities globally for population growth, led by Astana in 16th, whose population is set to double by 2050. Over the next 25 years, we project that the region’s major cities will add more than 8 million residents. The pace of growth, however, is stronger in Central Asian cities than it is for those in the South Caucasus: Yerevan (Armenia), for example, is forecast to see its population decline, reflecting its more mature demographic profile.

This growing population is translating into rapidly expanding levels of employment. Employment growth across much of the region ranks among the fastest in the world, with Dushanbe (23rd) and Astana (25th) both in the global top 25. Combined with rising productivity, this trend is set to power the region’s rapid economic growth, increasing income level, and consumer appetite in the decades ahead.

Tashkent: Central Asia’s rising star and one of the world’s Cities to Watch

Tashkent offers one of the clearest examples of the region’s best strengths and overall potential, and features in the new Cities to Watch section of our 2026 report. While the Uzbek capital ranks 343rd overall, it posts the region’s highest Economics score (188th), underpinned by its fast economic growth forecast and favourable score for economic stability. We expect its economy to grow on average by 6.2% a year over the next 25 years, the seventh-fastest of any city globally, putting it on course to overtake Almaty as the region’s largest city economy within the next few years, and even to outgrow established European capitals such as Rome and Vienna by 2050.

Much of this momentum stems from Uzbekistan’s programme of economic liberalisation and opening to international markets, with construction- and investment-led expansions taking place across a range of sectors. The city is emerging as a regional leader in technology and finance, anchored by the Tashkent IT Park, while ‘New Tashkent’, a large-scale megaproject to build a modern city district, is fuelling construction activity. Its position along the Middle Corridor trade route connecting Europe and Asia is further cementing its role as a key regional logistics hub.

Tashkent’s skills base is another key attraction, with its universities among the best in the region and a growing pool of skilled labour drawing in businesses. As GDP per capita is still relatively low, the city has considerable room for catch-up growth, with productivity forecast to almost triple by 2050. However, this income gap also raises the risk of talent leaving for wealthier countries. Environmental pressures, particularly water stress (with Uzbekistan relying on external sources for 80% of its water) and high housing costs also weigh on its overall standing. How effectively these challenges are managed will shape whether Tashkent can sustain its momentum and growing regional leadership.

Challenges remain, but the region’s potential is clear

Indeed, sustaining the region’s urban growth momentum and ascent up our overall rankings will depend on addressing several key weaknesses. For most Central Asia and South Caucasus cities, Governance and Environment rank among their weakest categories. All 10 place outside the global top 500 for civil liberties and the global top 600 for temperature anomalies. High emissions intensities and poor air quality also weigh on Environment scores, particularly in Tashkent, Ashgabat, and Dushanbe. Strengthening institutions and addressing these environmental pressures will be key to ensuring the region’s growth translates into lasting prosperity and quality of life for residents.

Overall, the major cities of Central Asia and the South Caucasus are quietly emerging as a new frontier for growth, from the region’s highest-ranked cities Almaty and Astana to the rapid ascent of Tashkent. With a large, growing, and increasingly skilled population, the region is one that business decision makers would do well to watch closely in the years ahead.

articles.title: Daily: The risks reshaping global AI investment
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:The AI sell-off and US midterms: Live at the UBS Disruptive Tech Summit (6 mins)
CIO Live Replay: CIO Asia equity strategists on the AI sell-off and opportunities (30 mins)Thought of the dayNVIDIA’s shares fell more than 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday, helping to pull Nasdaq futures around 1% lower and putting pressure on technology-heavy markets in Taiwan and South Korea. The moves followed reports that NVIDIA’s board had met on Wednesday night to discuss whether CEO Jensen Huang should remain in his role, following news that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort and subsequent developments.These headlines come as investors are becoming more selective on the AI trade. Recent technology volatility reflects a shift from rewarding spending commitments toward assessing monetization, balance sheet strength, capacity utilization, and prospective returns. At the same time, underlying demand remains robust: Recent earnings have shown accelerating cloud revenue and expanding orders for computing capacity, and we forecast aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1.0tr in 2026 and USD 1.4tr in 2027.Without taking any views on individual companies, we see several lessons that investors across the technology sector should consider:Key-person risk warrants greater attention. The episode illustrates how leadership and governance can become material investment considerations when a company’s strategy, culture, and market standing are closely associated with an individual. This matters beyond any single company, particularly after several years in which AI-related equity gains have been concentrated in a relatively narrow group of businesses. As investors become more discerning about valuations and returns, governance and clarity around succession planning may play a larger role alongside earnings growth in determining performance.Chip restrictions look unlikely to ease. AI competition between the US and China already operates within tight restrictions on exports of advanced semiconductors. We believe recent developments reduce the likelihood of an easing in current restrictions on advanced AI-chip shipments to China, while scrutiny of where processors are ultimately deployed could increase. Greater restrictions could weigh on sales in certain overseas markets, though they would not necessarily alter underlying AI demand, with compute capacity remaining in short supply.AI is increasingly a geopolitical issue. As advanced computing becomes more strategically important, governments are paying closer attention to where chips are produced, sold, and deployed. This could result in greater tracking requirements, regulatory scrutiny, and friction around global AI supply chains, potentially raising costs and restricting access to some overseas markets. Greater geopolitical competition may also spur investment in alternative supply chains and domestic AI capacity, reinforcing the importance of distinguishing between strong underlying demand and the companies best positioned to capture it.So, while we retain our conviction in the structural AI opportunity, we think these events reinforce the case for greater selectivity and diversification as the tech investment cycle evolves. We continue to favor financially strong hyperscalers; tighter future compute capacity could increase the value of existing infrastructure, while lower future capital spending could support free cash flow. Within AI “picks and shovels” (semiconductors and hardware), we would stay selective and favor quality companies with less margin expansion to unwind, alongside defensive technology exposures such as payment networks and potential beneficiaries of lower memory costs within consumer electronics. For investors whose technology exposure has become overly concentrated, we would consider broadening exposure within technology and diversifying across sectors, asset classes, and geographies.

What you need to know
We place restrictions on the use of physical and digital images of Bank of England banknotes. This is to stop the creation of banknote copies that could accidentally be used for, or accepted as, payment and to avoid banknote images being used in an offensive or inappropriate context, including distortion to the monarch's image.
We give you consent to reproduce our banknotes, or a part of one, if you comply with our reproduction conditions (you do not need to contact us for permission). These conditions apply whether you are using our approved images or creating your own.
If you do not comply with our conditions, this may result in legal action.
Banknotes and the law
It is an offence to:

reproduce banknotes issued by us, or part of banknotes issued by us, on any substance or to any scale without our consent. For the avoidance of doubt, consent for items marketed as ‘Movie’, ‘Prop’ or ‘Training’ items can only be obtained if such items meet our reproduction conditions. We have described these in more detail in the FAQ below.
deface Bank of England banknotes (including printing, writing or impressing words, letters or figures on them).
without the Bank’s consent knowingly and in the course of a business make for sale or hire, import, offer, exhibit in public, or distribute a copyright work. Copyright in Bank of England banknotes is owned by the Bank of England and also contains works which the Bank uses under licence from public and private sector bodies.
without the Bank’s consent apply to goods or packaging, to sell, expose or distribute goods with the Bank’s registered trade mark (or a sign likely to be mistaken for it) with a view to gain for himself or another, or with intent to cause loss to another.
commit fraud by false representation and misuse the Bank’s name as an instrument of fraud.

Counterfeit banknotes
It is also an offence to:

make a counterfeit banknote without lawful excuse or with the intention of passing or tendering it as genuine.
pass or tender or deliver to another a counterfeit banknote knowingly or believing it to be counterfeit.
have custody or control of a counterfeit banknote intending to pass or tender or deliver it as genuine or have in custody or control without lawful excuse.
have custody or control of anything intending to or allowing any person to use it to make a counterfeit banknote intending to pass it as genuine or make or have anything designed or adapted to make a counterfeit banknote without lawful excuse.

Find more about counterfeit banknotes

These offences are covered under sections 14-17 and 18 of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981 Opens in a new window, section 12 of the Currency and Banknotes Act 1928 Opens in a new window, section 107 of the Copyright Designs and Patents Act 1988 Opens in a new window, section 92 of the Trade Marks Act 1994, and section 2 of the Fraud Act 2006.
In addition, civil liability attaches to infringement of the Bank’s copyright, moral rights, and trade mark rights.
The list is non-exhaustive. The content of this website is provided for general information purposes only and it does not constitute in any way legal advice. If you are seeking specific legal advice, you may wish to contact a qualified legal professional at your own expense.

Our banknote reproduction conditions
If you plan to use an image of one of our banknotes, you must meet our conditions. These are different depending on whether you plan to produce a physical or digital reproduction.
These conditions apply whether you are reproducing:

all or part of a banknote

Conditions for physical and digital reproductions
