articles.title: Why is Xi Jinping purging leaders of his own party? | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Podcast
Why is Xi Jinping purging leaders of his own party?

Listen on

Apple Podcasts

Spotify

YouTube

Pod.link

More

The Beijing Brief

The Beijing Brief

Hosts:
Jonathan A. Czin and

Jonathan A. Czin

Michael H. Armacost Chair in Foreign Policy Studies,

Fellow
- Foreign Policy, John L. Thornton China Center

Ryan Hass

Ryan Hass

Director
- John L. Thornton China Center,

Senior Fellow
- Foreign Policy, Center for Asia Policy Studies, John L. Thornton China Center,

Chen-Fu and Cecilia Yen Koo Chair in Taiwan Studies

Guest:
Joseph Torigian

Joseph Torigian

Assistant Professor, School of International Service
- American University

November 10, 2026

The fifth plenum of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) reveals the extent to which Xi Jinping cares about Party governance. He believes that the Party’s survival depends on putting the cause above oneself, so a lapse in Party discipline is an issue of political consciousness.
Mao Zedong rehabilitated purged members of the CCP, but for Xi, the consequence of inviting purged cadre back to the Party is too high of a risk. Analysts cannot know whether this reflects a reaction to his father Xi Zhongxun’s experience, an adaptation of his legacy, or no conscious distinction.
Xi Jinping’s purges in the PLA are about ensuring political loyalty and less about targeting corruption. Loyalty signifies to Xi whether the military will obey him during a power struggle with the elite, possible political unrest, or war with the U.S.
Xi Jinping himself may not even know whether he wants to designate an heir or continue in office until the end of his life. With no defined group to decide what comes next, succession will likely depend on who manipulates ambiguous rules and gets the jump on rivals.

Members of the Communist Party of China Central Committee attend a press conference following the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee in Beijing, China, October 30, 2026. REUTERS/Maxim Shemetov

40 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

The level of purges inside the Chinese Communist Party today is unprecedented in the post-Mao era, instilling a sense of fear amongst cadre at every level. On this episode, Joseph Torigian sits down with Ryan Hass and Jon Czin to unpack Xi Jinping’s approach to Party discipline and purges in the CCP, compare Xi’s outlook on Party politics to his father’s and Mao’s, and deliberate how Xi’s succession may look.

Listen to The Beijing Brief on Apple, Spotify, or wherever you like to get podcasts.
Watch episodes on YouTube.
Learn about other Brookings podcasts from the Brookings Podcast Network.
Sign up for the podcasts newsletter for occasional updates on featured episodes and new shows.
Send feedback email to podcasts@Brookings.edu.

Transcript

[music]
TORIGIAN: Xi Jinping really cares about this idea of Party governance. And that seems kind of boring and, like, a slogan or boilerplate to maybe people on the outside. But Xi Jinping believes that the Chinese Communist Party is the only way of organizing his nation to achieve the rejuvenation that it deserves.
HASS: Hello, you’re listening to The Beijing Brief from the John L. Thornton China Center at Brookings, part of the Brookings Podcast Network. I’m Ryan Hass, director and senior fellow at the China Center.
CZIN: And I’m Jon Czin, fellow and Michael H. Armacost Chair in the China Center. The Beijing Brief is a biweekly podcast focused on unpacking the forces shaping U.S.-China relations and China’s political, economic, and technological ambitions.
[0:42]
In late October, roughly 300 members of the Chinese Communist Party’s Central Committee met behind closed doors in Beijing for the Fifth Plenum, one of the last major party meetings before Xi is likely to start a new five-year term at next year’s Party Congress.
The meeting confirms the purges of several dozens Central Committee members, which only hammered home Xi’s key point during the meeting with rhetoric about the need for self-governance of the Party. Since his third term began in 2022, Xi has orchestrated the most brutal and thorough purge of the Party’s top ranks since the Mao era. He has purged every leader of the top military body, the Central Military Commission, leaving behind only him and the man who oversaw the investigations of his colleagues, General Zhang Shengmin.
In the last year alone, he has purged three members of the Politburo. This is not what many people would have expected at the start of Xi Jinping’s third term. He has pivoted from purging his enemies to purging his friends, including the military’s top officer.
Few China watchers would have expected these developments at the start of Xi’s third term when he stacked the party’s leadership with his old associates and muscled out any top official with ties to former bases of power in the Party.
All this turn is happening as Xi lays the groundwork to begin a fourth five-year term just about a year from now.
[1:56]
HASS: So, today we want to ask, what the hell is going on inside the Chinese Communist Party? And what does history tell us about the future direction of this party, particularly after Xi Jinping? There is no one better to help us read these tea leaves and understand the context of what is happening in Beijing than Professor Joseph Torigian. He is a professor at American University, as well as a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. He is the author of The Party’s Interests Come First, the first English language biography of Xi Jinping’s father, Xi Zhongxun. He’s also the author of Prestige, Manipulation, and Coercion: A Study of Elite Power Struggles in the Soviet Union and China After Stalin and Mao.
Joseph, welcome to the program
TORIGIAN: Huge fan of the podcast, huge fan of both of you. Look forward to learning from the two of you as well as we engage in conjecture about what this plenum means.
CZIN: Well, that’s very kind of you. We’re thrilled to have you on, Joseph.
[2:48]
So, we’ll start with something a little bit on the lighter side. What do you think is one common misconception that you hear, including among China watchers, about the thoroughgoing purges that have rocked the leadership over the last couple of years?
[3:02]
TORIGIAN: I think that the first sensibility that we should always bring to these purges is analytical humility. So, when you’re on social media, it’s amazing just how many rumors you see, and a sensitivity to what rumors are as a social phenomena I think is almost as useful as a sensitivity to how the party works.
And so, often what we see online is spread because people want to believe it, because they think that spreading it serves a particular goal, whether they believe in it or not. It gets a lot of attention. And then of course, nobody can really disprove these rumors because nobody actually knows what’s going on.
And so, a few times people have come to me and said, “Did you hear that blah, blah, blah happened?” And I say, “Well, that probably didn’t happen.” Occasionally it’s true that something did happen. In the case of Zhang Youxia, in this case, the rumors that immediately preceded his fall happened to be true, but a broken clock is right, you know, twice a day, so we should always be careful.
And I spend a lot of time going through U.S. archives, and you see all kinds of rumors that some leader died or there was a coup. And so, I think that what history allows us to do is to give us a little bit more of a sort of chronological horizon to contextualize the very limited evidence that we do have.
So, it gives us the ability to structure questions, come up with different hypotheses, ask what’s more or less likely, and then put what does come to light into a broader sort of mosaic that is a little bit more useful, I think, than trying to figure out whether one particular rumor is coming from a reliable source or not.
[4:49]
And also to say that, you know, it’s not just that Westerners are dumb and they don’t understand China. These people who are getting purged, these are pretty serious people. Right? These are people who have been around the block more than once.
And this plenum I think gives us a little bit of a hint into why this keeps happening. So Xi Jinping really cares about this idea of Party governance. Right? And that seems kind of boring and, like, a slogan or boilerplate to maybe people on the outside. But Xi Jinping believes that the Chinese Communist Party is the only way of organizing his nation to achieve the rejuvenation that it deserves.
And this is a plenum where he talks about why that’s the case. It’s a plenum, according to him, that the Party can take a lot of pride in because it’s accentuating that they have solved a problem that no other Communist Party has, and which Xi Jinping says Marx and Engels didn’t even think about, which is how do you ensure that a regime that has existed for a long time is able to endure and ensure that it is pure and has a sense of ideal and conviction.
And so he gets to decide who has it and who doesn’t, and when people get something wrong, it’s not because they made a simple mistake, it’s because there’s something wrong with their political consciousness, and because it’s so hard to look at these documents and figure out just exactly what you’re supposed to do because of these enduring dilemmas of the party that people who have looked at history have known have existed since the beginning, and how easy it is to get tripped up.
And so you see this like do this, but also do that all over this document. Right? And so on the one hand, it says, we need to have an institutional cage, but we shouldn’t create so many institutions that people are forced to go through the motions and engage in formalism and bureaucratism. articles.title: Corporate bonds: Finding alpha in an efficient market
articles.text:
PORTFOLIO PERSPECTIVES | PODCAST – 13:40 MIN
Corporate bonds: Finding alpha in an efficient market

By
ANTHONY DESROUSSEAUX, CHARLES CRESTEIL, DANIEL MORRIS 05.11.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

Corporate bond markets may be well researched, but that doesn’t mean opportunities for investors are hard to find. The key is knowing where to look. As Charles Cresteil, Investment Specialist, and Anthony Desrousseaux, Portfolio Manager, explain to Chief Market Strategist, Daniel Morris, active managers can uncover opportunities by identifying mispriced bonds, comparing securities from the same issuer and exploiting temporary market dislocations.

Differences in liquidity, investor behaviour and bond characteristics can create opportunities to generate additional returns without making big bets on the direction of interest rates or credit markets. A systematic, multi-factor approach can help investors avoid securities that appear cheap but may carry hidden risks.

Portfolio managers can pursue additional returns while keeping risk close to that of a benchmark through disciplined security selection, diversification and careful control of interest-rate sensitivity, credit exposure and issuer concentration. “A research-driven approach to corporate bond investing can seek modest but repeatable improvements in returns while keeping unintended risks in check.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast for insights into effective approaches when investing in corporate bonds.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Daniel Morris: Hello, and welcome to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing enhancing returns in corporate bond markets. I’m Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, and I’m joined today by Charles Cresteil, Investment Specialist and Anthony Desrousseaux, Portfolio Manager. Welcome, gentlemen, and thanks for joining me.

Charles Cresteil:

Happy to be here.

Anthony Desrousseaux:

Hello, Daniel.

DM: When we think about investing in corporate bonds, initially we think about what’s going on with central bank policy rates, with spreads, economic outlook and so on. But once you’ve taken that decision to invest in corporate bonds, what you’re really going to be looking for is how to generate the most alpha out of that investment. Where are the relative opportunities? What parts of the market do you want to invest in? And that is what you guys focus on.

If I could start with you, Charles, we think of corporate bond markets as fairly efficient. That makes the challenge of finding alpha all the more difficult. Where, for you, does the alpha come from?

CC: At first sight, corporate bond markets look highly efficient. They are widely researched, institutional investors dominate trading, and a great deal of information about issuers is available publicly. But that doesn’t mean that every bond is always perfectly priced. In fact, the structure of the market creates many small recurring opportunities. There are four main reasons for that.

The first is breadth. A large company may have five, 10 or even more bonds outstanding. Those securities were all issued by the same company but can differ in terms of maturity, seniority, currency liquidity, or even some ESG (environmental, social & governance) characteristics like green or social use of proceeds.

As a result, two bonds from the same issuer can offer different compensation for broadly the same fundamental risk. That gives us a much broader opportunity set than a market in which each company only has one listed security.

The second reason is fragmentation. Corporate bonds do not trade on a single central exchange as large-cap equities do. Liquidity varies significantly from one issue to another, and different investor groups may value the same bond differently. Insurance companies, pension funds, banks, ETFs (exchange-traded funds) and total return managers all operate with their own constraints, and their buying and selling can create temporary dislocations that are not necessarily linked to a change in the issuer[s[ long-term risk.

A third source of opportunity comes from the benchmark itself. A traditional corporate bond index is usually weighted by the amount of debt outstanding. In other words, the companies that borrow the most receive the largest index weights. That makes sense when the objective is to be representative of the overall market, but it doesn’t mean the index is optimal from an investor point of view in terms of expected risk-adjusted returns.

An active process can therefore be more selective about which issuers and which individual bonds provide good reward for their risks. And finally, prices do not always adjust at the same speed. A company’s fundamentals may improve before all its bonds fully reflect the change. A new issue may come with an attractive concession on the primary market. Or a bond may become temporarily cheap because a large investor needs to sell. These opportunities can occur repeatedly over a large investment universe.

Our objective is not to make calls on the direction of interest rates or credit markets as a whole; it is to identify a large number of small, relative value opportunities, referring one bond to another with comparable characteristics, avoiding securities where the reward looks poor compared to the credit risk and diversifying those decisions across the portfolio.

Each individual position should contribute only modestly, but together they can create a consistent source of excess return. That is the central idea: alpha in corporate bonds doesn’t have to come from big bets. It can come from a disciplined security selection approach applied across a broad market that remains fragmented and imperfectly efficient.

DM: Anthony, even though theoretically markets are supposed to be efficient, we know the reality is somewhat different. It’s nice to know there are these discrepancies in the market, but finding them is the real challenge. What are the signals you use to identify those opportunities?

AD: We use a multi-factor framework because there is no single indicator that can reliably identify attractive bonds in every market environment. A bond may look cheap, but it may be because the issuer is deteriorating. Another bond may have strong fundamentals but offer too little spread to compensate investors. The purpose of combining signals is to obtain a more balanced view of each security.

The first family of signals is valuation. How much compensation are we receiving for the risk we are taking? We compare bonds spread with those of relevant peers while adjusting for characteristics such as sector, rating, maturity and duration.

We may also compare different bonds from the same issuer. The objective is not simply to buy the bond with the wider spread, but to identify securities that appear attractively priced relative to their underlying risk.

The second family is quality. We examine the financial strength and resilience of the issuer using measures linked to profitability, leverage, cash flow, generation, balance sheet stability and the ability to service debt.

Quality is particularly important in credit because the return distribution is asymmetric. The upside on a bond is limited while the downside from a downgrade or default can be significant. A quality signal helps us avoid being paid a little more spread in exchange for a disproportionate deterioration risk.

The third family is momentum. Credit markets often adjust gradually as information is absorbed by different investors. Improving spread trends, supportive price behaviour or positive changes in market perception can indicate that a bond is moving in the right direction.

Conversely, a bond that looks statistically cheap but continues to underperform may be signalling that the market sees a problem not yet fully visible in accounting data. We also use technical and low risk indicators. Technical signals can capture elements such as issuance, liquidity, investors flows and supply demand imbalances.

Low-risk indicators help distinguish securities whose apparent return potential depends on taking excessive credit or market risk. These signals matter because a theoretically attractive valuation may not be investable. Once trading cost, liquidity and portfolio constraints are considered, we then combine the different signals into an overall assessment for each bond.

Importantly, the comparison is made within appropriate peer groups. We are generally not trying to forecast whether the entire credit market will rally or sell off. We are asking whether one bond is more attractive than another with broadly comparable characteristics.

The advantage of a systematic process is consistency and scale. The same questions can be asked across thousands of securities every time the data is updated. That does not eliminate judgement. The model, data, constraints and portfolio construction all require careful design and oversight. But it prevents the process from depending on a small number of subjective convictions.

In practice, the strongest opportunities are usually those where several independent signals agree [a] bond is reasonably valued, issued by a sound company, supported by market momentum and sufficiently liquid to trade. That combination is more robust than relying on any single factor alone.

DM: Anthony, you’ve talked about the different ways you can evaluate the markets to look for opportunities. But when it comes to portfolio management, there’s risk and return. How do you manage keeping tracking error low when you’re taking many active positions?

AD: The key is to separate active security selection from broad market exposure. We want the portfolio to remain close to its benchmark in the dimensions that investors expect, while using a limited risk budget to favour the bonds that our process finds more attractive.

Let us start with duration. If the portfolio has much more or much less interest-rate sensitivity than the benchmark, performance can be dominated by a view on government bond yields that may produce a positive result, but it’s not the type of alpha we are trying to deliver. We therefore keep duration tightly aligned with the benchmark, both at the portfolio level and, where relevant, across maturity segments.

We apply the same discipline to credit exposure. A portfolio could outperform simply by holding systematically lower-rated bonds or by taking more exposure to volatile sectors. Again, that would be a broad beta decision rather than evidence of successful security selection. We therefore control rating spread, duration, sector allocation and other measures of credit sensitivity. The objective is that the portfolio does not need a strong market rally to succeed.

Issuer concentration is another important control. Even when the model identifies a very attractive bond, we do not want the result to depend excessively on one company.

Corporate credit has an asymmetric risk profile. A single adverse event can have a meaningful impact, while the upside from any individual bond is naturally capped. Position limits help ensure that no single issuer or security dominates the portfolio.

Active risk portfolio construction then brings all these elements together. The process looks for the best combination of expected attractiveness and controlled risk. For example, if we overweight one bond in one sector, we may underweight a less attractive bond with similar duration and credit characteristics. The broad exposures largely offset one another, leaving the relative value preference as the main active decision. This is how we try to isolate alpha from beta.

Diversification is crucial. Instead of making a few large calls, we spread the risk budget across many modest positions. Each preference may have only a small impact on tracking error but the portfolio can contain a large number of such decisions. If those signals contain useful information and are sufficiently independent, their combined contribution can become meaningful while the effect of any individual error remains limited.

We also account for liquidity and turnover. A portfolio that looks attractive before cost may be much less compelling after bid/offer spreads and market impact. Trading therefore needs to be selective. We do not want to react to every small change. The expected benefit of a trade should exceed its likely cost. Low tracking error is not achieved by avoiding active positions. It is achieved by being precise about which risk we want to take and which we want to neutralise.

We accept diversified research-based security selection risk. We tightly constrain unintended duration. Market beta sector and concentration risk. The result is a portfolio designed to preserve the benchmark characteristics that matter to investors while seeking a modest but repeatable improvement in return.

DM: Well, Charles, Anthony, thank you very much for joining me.

CC: Thanks for having us.

AD: Thank you, Daniel.

DM: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you would like more information about our capabilities in investing in corporate bonds, please reach out to your asset management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website, for investment insights at viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com. The Talking Heads podcast is available on Spotify and on YouTube. For YouTube, visit YouTube.com bnppam playlist and tap or click on Talking Heads.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Daniel Morris, Charles Cresteil, Investment Specialist, and Anthony Desrousseaux, Portfolio Manager.

Please do join me next week. Until then, take care.

articles.title: Japan sees limited AI-driven productivity gains in the near term
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

05 Nov 2026

Japan sees limited AI-driven productivity gains in the near term

Generative AI should offer some support to Japan’s potential growth by boosting its total factor productivity, but less than in most other advanced economies in the near term. Slow adoption is likely to limit the gains.

We think Japan has significant potential to benefit from generative AI, given its relatively high exposure to and preparedness for AI technology. The recent acceleration in corporates’ software investment in response to Japan’s severe labour shortages appears to have laid some of the groundwork for AI utilisation, while the country’s ICT capital stock still lags far behind that of the US.

However, in practice, adoption of new tech is likely to be slow. Japan has lagged behind on digitalisation for many years. The shortage of IT personnel is a key bottleneck, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises. Its adoption rate is beginning to fall behind those of other advanced economies and China.

There’s high uncertainty around AI’s impact on productivity. Our optimistic ‘AI breakthrough’ scenario features faster adoption and stronger productivity gains than in our baseline, pushing GDP 7ppts above our forecast by 2035. But this still wouldn’t fully offset the drag from the labour supply’s decline on potential growth.

On the downside, there’s considerable risk that the AI boost to workplace efficiency won’t translate into higher productivity at the macro level, given Japan’s rigid corporate structures and labour market practices, particularly among permanent employees. In a scenario of lower pass-through of efficiency gains from workers to the economy, together with slower adoption of the tech, Japan’s potential growth rate would turn negative by the mid-2030s.

Technology & InnovationCustody+ and the Future of Market IntelligenceArticle • November 05, 2026Amit AgarwalGlobal Head of CustodyInvestor Services, CitiThe custody model is evolving. So are client expectations.Accelerated settlement cycles, continuous trading models, digital assets and AI are reshaping the post-trade landscape. Clients increasingly need faster access to information, greater transparency and more flexibility in how they consume custody services.That's the vision behind Custody+, Citi's next-generation custody platform. Moving beyond a traditional one-size-fits-all model, Custody+ provides a modular framework that allows clients to tailor custody solutions to their needs while leveraging the scale, resiliency and reach of Citi's global network.Eliminating friction starts with modern infrastructure and intelligent insights.At the core of Custody+ is Citi's patented Single Event Processing (SEP) technology for real-time asset servicing. By processing more than 80% of events only once across Citi's global and domestic custody layers, SEP significantly reduces operational touchpoints and accelerates the delivery of critical information.The results are tangible. In the U.S., SEP has reduced processing times for voluntary corporate actions by up to 92%, with 96% of events now processed in less than two hours. Combined with Citi's proprietary custody network of 62 branches, clients gain faster access to information, more time to make decisions and greater flexibility to redeploy capital.Custody+ is also applying AI to eliminate longstanding inefficiencies. In tax servicing, AI-powered automation has reduced document processing times by up to 70%, helping Citi process more than 100,000 withholding tax reclaims annually and enabling clients to recover and put capital back to work faster.But speed alone is not enough. As market structures, regulations and operating models become increasingly complex, clients need the ability to understand and act on change in real time. That is why a core component of Custody+ is the transformation of how market intelligence is delivered. The future of market intelligence is contextual, connected and AI-powered.As the custody landscape evolves, so must the way clients access and consume information.That's why Citi has reimagined Market Guide, a key component of the Custody+ ecosystem.Powered by Citi's network across more than 100 custody markets globally, Market Guide delivers timely and smarter insights into regulatory, tax, operational and market infrastructure developments, helping clients understand what changes mean for their business and prepare accordingly.Enhanced with AI, the platform provides faster access to relevant information through intelligent search, discovery and summarization capabilities. The authors have not purchased or sold any token for which the authors had material non-public information while researching or drafting this report. These disclosures are made consistent with Delphi’s commitment to transparency and should not be misconstrued as a recommendation to purchase or sell any token, or to use any protocol. The contents of each of these reports reflects the opinions of the respective authors of the given report and are presented for informational purposes only. Nothing contained in these reports is, and should not be construed to be, investment advice.
In addition to the disclosures provided for each report, our affiliated business, Delphi Ventures, may have investments in assets or protocols identified in this report. Please see here for Ventures’ investment disclosures. These disclosures are solely the responsibility of Delphi Ventures.
Summary
Hyperliquid has built a successful exchange, but its broader onchain economy remains underdeveloped. Kinetiq’s Elysium aims to address infrastructure constraints that make some financial applications difficult or uneconomical to operate. Its proposed capabilities and announced ecosystem support give the supply-side case credibility, while sustained demand remains unproven. If Elysium and Kinetiq’s social trading app, Markets, succeed, Kinetiq could become a core provider of infrastructure and distribution across Hyperliquid. That expansion beyond liquid staking makes Kinetiq a potentially asymmetric bet on the wider economy developing around an already successful exchange.
A Proven Exchange and an Unfinished Ecosystem
When the U.S.-Iran war began on Saturday, 28 February 2026, benchmark oil futures markets were closed. Hyperliquid’s HIP-3 oil markets kept trading.
Through HIP-3, independent operators can launch perpetual contracts using Hyperliquid’s trading infrastructure. On 9 March, TradeXYZ’s CL oil contract alone reached $1.69 billion in daily volume, 149 times its pre-war daily average. Bitcoin perpetual volume on Hyperliquid, meanwhile, remained broadly unchanged, averaging 0.98 times its pre-war level. The divergence suggests oil’s surge reflected real-world macro risk repricing rather than broader crypto momentum.

Oil illustrates a broader development: outside builders are expanding the business conducted on Hyperliquid. HIP-3 has opened its infrastructure to markets spanning equities, commodities, and other assets. By 8 November 2026, just over a year after launch, HIP-3 accounted for approximately 30.5% of Hyperliquid’s total perpetual open interest.

Hyperliquid’s expansion into traditional asset markets is also attracting established financial institutions. S&P Dow Jones Indices licensed the S&P 500 to TradeXYZ for an official perpetual contract. ICE, the NYSE’s parent, subsequently announced an investment in TradeXYZ and plans for a U.S. market and clearing structure, subject to regulatory approvals.
That institutional interest builds on a business that generated approximately $818 million in protocol revenue in 2025. Excluding Tether and Circle, Hyperliquid led onchain applications in revenue for six consecutive quarters, from Q2 2025 through Q3 2026.

Yet Hyperliquid’s ambition extends beyond a larger exchange: it aims to provide infrastructure that can “house all finance.”
HyperEVM was intended to support that ambition by providing a general-purpose environment for protocols. It operates alongside HyperCore, which runs Hyperliquid’s native spot and perpetual exchanges and staking for HYPE, the network’s token. Think of them as a catamaran’s two hulls: distinct execution environments within one blockchain, secured by the same validators through HyperBFT consensus.

Composability with HyperCore is a distinctive advantage for protocols building on Hyperliquid. HyperEVM contracts can read HyperCore prices, balances and positions, and submit orders or staking instructions through CoreWriter. Kinetiq already leverages this composability to stake HYPE on HyperCore and issue kHYPE on HyperEVM. Holders can then use the liquid-staking token across DeFi.
So far, HyperEVM has fallen short of delivering that broader application economy. Staking and lending have attracted substantial capital, but activity across the wider ecosystem remains limited.
Infrastructure is part of the problem. Limited execution capacity, fee spikes and complex integration with HyperCore make applications harder to build and operate economically. Such an environment can discourage builders and limit the range of products capable of attracting sustained activity.
Enter, Elysium.
Kinetiq aims to address this gap and is building Elysium, a general-purpose L2 for Hyperliquid, to provide more affordable execution and shared tools for integrating HyperCore. Just as HIP-3 opened Hyperliquid’s exchange infrastructure to outside operators, Elysium aims to make a broader range of EVM applications practical.
What Is Holding HyperEVM Back?
HyperEVM has given HYPE a financial ecosystem of its own. The challenge is extending that ecosystem beyond its native asset. Its lending markets show how concentrated the capital base remains.
As of date, WHYPE, kHYPE and wstHYPE accounted for 94% of HyperLend’s $320 million net TVL. These assets also represented 90% of Morpho’s $130 million HyperEVM TVL. By comparison, SOL and its staking derivatives accounted for approximately 43% of Kamino Lend’s net TVL on Solana.
Spot trading volumes also trail those of incumbent ecosystems. Year-to-date, HyperEVM DEXs and launchpads processed approximately $38 billion in spot volume, compared with $264 billion on Base and $777 billion on Solana.
But HyperEVM has not always been quiet, and August gave us a peek at what it could be. After Trump said the CFTC was working to bring Hyperliquid onshore on 19 August, HYPE rallied, and onchain trading surged alongside it. Average daily volume reached $286m that week, up from $58m the previous week. Average gas prices rose from 3.8 to 25.2 Gwei. Participation became more expensive just as activity accelerated.

August repeated a pattern seen during earlier activity surges in 2025. Keeping frequent activity economical has been a recurring challenge.
The rise in gas prices reflects competition for limited execution capacity. HyperEVM’s fast blocks provide a shared budget of 3 million gas roughly every second. Gas measures computational work, so swaps, deposits and other contract operations compete for that budget. When a block’s gas usage exceeds the network’s target, the base fee rises for subsequent blocks. This makes execution more expensive and discourages marginal transactions. Larger blocks provide roughly 30 million gas per minute. That slower capacity cannot replace fast execution for applications that trade or refresh quotes every second.
For comparison, Base’s configured maximum provides approximately 200 million gas per second, roughly 67 times HyperEVM’s maximum fast-block budget. Hyperliquid chose these conservative limits to protect HyperCore’s performance while gradually expanding HyperEVM’s capacity.
For a market maker, keeping quotes current means paying gas each time prices need adjusting. Cutting back on updates leaves outdated quotes that other traders can exploit. Wider spreads offer some protection, but customers get worse prices and less reason to trade. These recurring costs are especially difficult to absorb on small trades and thin margins.
For applications using HyperCore, execution costs are only part of the problem. Developers must also manage financial operations that cannot be completed together in one transaction.
Consider a vault that accepts wrapped BTC on HyperEVM and opens a Bitcoin short on HyperCore to offset its price exposure. Orders sent through CoreWriter face a deliberate delay of a few seconds. Prices and available liquidity can change during that interval, so the hedge may fill only partly or fail to execute.

If the vault accepts one BTC-equivalent deposit before confirming its hedge, a short that fills only 0.6 BTC leaves 0.4 BTC unhedged. Partial fills are a general trading risk. Here, the completed deposit does not automatically reverse if the hedge falls short. The application must manage that exposure until it completes the hedge or unwinds the position.
The vault must track outstanding orders and unhedged exposure, with rules for pausing deposits, retrying hedges, or unwinding positions. Existing libraries simplify HyperCore interactions and provide local testing tools, but developers still need to implement and test those application-specific decisions.
In our view, these constraints can reinforce one another. Expensive quote updates weaken market-making economics, while execution delays and integration work make some applications harder to operate reliably. Less competitive products can struggle to retain users, limiting the trading activity available to support liquidity providers and developers. Shallower liquidity and weaker application revenues can then discourage further investment. We see infrastructure as a key bottleneck for developers and users interacting with HyperEVM.
But better infrastructure does not guarantee demand. HyperEVM’s costs and constraints have made it a difficult environment for builders and traders to experiment. Limited activity under those conditions is an incomplete test of appetite for a broader application economy. Elysium could provide a more conducive environment. The test is whether better conditions translate into applications people keep using and sustained EVM activity on Hyperliquid.
Elysium and a Larger Hyperliquid Economy
Elysium is designed to give applications a separate execution environment while supporting composability with HyperCore. Built using Arbitrum Orbit, the general-purpose L2 will settle to HyperEVM and use HYPE for gas.
The network targets 300 million gas per second, roughly 100 times HyperEVM’s fast-block execution budget, with blocks every 100 milliseconds. Greater capacity gives applications more room to operate; shorter block intervals let them act more frequently.

For applications using HyperCore, Elysium also proposes richer market data and tools for submitting orders and returning execution results to application contracts. Mainnet was announced for 9 November, with these integration tools planned roughly four weeks later.

So, another L2 to make execution cheaper? Haven’t we been down this road before?
The familiar criticism is that L2s are parasitic: they can build thriving application economies while returning little direct fee revenue to their parent chains. Year-to-date, Base and Arbitrum’s payments to Ethereum each amounted to less than 1% of their chain revenue. Low settlement payments leave limited direct value accrual to ETH through fee burn.

articles.title: The Effect of Oil Prices on Core Inflation: Recent Evidence from the Advanced Economies
articles.text:
FEDS Notes

Twitter

Share

RSS

November 09, 2026
The Effect of Oil Prices on Core Inflation: Recent Evidence from the Advanced Economies
Andrea De Michelis, Musa Orak, Avani Pradhan, and Albert Queralto1
Elevated oil prices and heightened geopolitical uncertainty have renewed interest in a longstanding policy question: do supply shocks like oil-price increases pose a transitory or a persistent threat to price stability? This note sheds light on this question by providing new evidence on whether the inflation process has changed. In an earlier note, De Michelis et al. (2024) documented that core inflation had become more inertial after the pandemic, implying that supply shocks might be expected to have more persistent effects if this greater inertia continued. This note updates those results using a similar methodology with data extended through the middle of this year and documents a second change in the inflation process: an increase in the pass-through from oil prices to core inflation.

Because the post-pandemic period remains short, we estimate the model using a panel of five major advanced economies rather than data from a single country, which allows us to detect common shifts in persistence and pass-through more robustly. We find that the pass-through from oil prices to core inflation, which was statistically indistinguishable from zero before the pandemic, rose to an economically and statistically significant level afterwards. A horse race among nested specifications shows that allowing for stronger post-pandemic pass-through, on top of stronger persistence, delivers a marked improvement in our model's ability to track core inflation dynamics in recent years. Our estimated model implies that the recent rise in oil prices could significantly raise core inflation in the advanced economies over the next few years were the greater persistence and higher pass-through to continue. Finally, we use a structural global macroeconomic model to assess the broader implications of the changes in the inflation process, focusing on how these changes bear on the appropriate monetary policy response to supply shocks.

Admittedly, our empirical results are derived using a reduced-form approach that cannot distinguish a structural change in the underlying inflation process from the possibility that global supply shocks have become more frequent, more persistent, or both. The results presented here depend on our specification and set of controls, and different specifications might yield different results. Relatedly, while our panel approach expands the information set by pooling together data across the major advanced economies, it does not allow us to control for some specific factors that have seemingly contributed to persistently elevated inflation in the U.S. because of the lack of comparable data in other countries. In addition, even if our results stem from a structural change reflecting, for instance, a shift in behavior of price setters, we cannot say whether this change will endure or reverse. These caveats notwithstanding, we view our results as suggestive of an upside risk to inflation. We also stress that the results shown here do not represent any official forecasts of inflation in the U.S. or foreign economies.

Empirical framework: an augmented Phillips curve for core inflation

Our empirical strategy follows De Michelis et al. (2024) and relies on a backward-looking augmented Phillips curve for core inflation. In this reduced-form framework, inflation expectations depend on past inflation outcomes. More specifically, core inflation follows:

πi,t=αi+γ1πi,t−1+γ2πi,t−2+λxi,t+βst+∑j=04δjoi,t−j+εi,tπi,t=αi+γ1πi,t−1+γ2πi,t−2+λxi,t+βst+∑j=04δjoi,t−j+εi,t

where πi,tπi,t is core inflation in economy ii in quarter tt, xi,txi,t is the output gap, stst is a measure of supply-chain disruptions, and oi,toi,t is relative oil-price inflation.2 The specification includes four lags of oil-price inflation because energy price changes take time to pass through to core prices, and it controls for supply-chain disruptions through the Global Supply Chain Pressure Index (GSCPI).3 The sum γ1+γ2γ1+γ2 measures the degree of inertia, or persistence, in the inflation process, while the sum of the δjδj coefficients measures the cumulative pass-through from oil prices to core inflation.

To let the inflation process change after the pandemic, we augment this equation with two sets of interaction terms, one on the lags of core inflation and one on the lags of oil-price inflation, each interacted with a post-pandemic dummy DposttDtpost that equals one from 2021:Q1 onward and zero before:

πi,t=αi+γ1πi,t−1+γ2πi,t−2+η1πi,t−1Dpostt+η2πi,t−2Dpostt+λxi,t+βst+∑j=04δjoi,t−j+∑j=04ζjoi,t−jDpostt+εi,tπi,t=αi+γ1πi,t−1+γ2πi,t−2+η1πi,t−1Dtpost+η2πi,t−2Dtpost+λxi,t+βst+∑j=04δjoi,t−j+∑j=04ζjoi,t−jDtpost+εi,t

Here the persistence interaction terms η1η1 and η2η2 allow inflation inertia to shift after the pandemic, so that post-pandemic persistence is given by γ1+γ2+η1+η2γ1+γ2+η1+η2. Symmetrically, the pass-through interaction terms ζjζj allow the response of core inflation to oil prices to change, so that post-pandemic pass-through is given by ∑jδj+∑jζj∑jδj+∑jζj. A positive and significant sum of the ζjζj would indicate that a given oil-price shock transmits more strongly to core inflation than it did before the pandemic. This single specification therefore nests the two distinct questions we ask: has the core inflation process become more persistent, and has oil-price pass-through become stronger?

To answer these two questions, we estimate the equation on panel data for five major advanced economies: Canada, the euro area, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States, which improves our ability to more precisely identify common post-pandemic changes over a relatively short sample.4 The panel regression includes country fixed effects to absorb time-invariant differences across countries. The sample period spans from 2000:Q1 through 2026:Q2, with the post-pandemic period starting in 2021:Q1. Core inflation is measured using core PCE prices for the U.S. and core CPI prices for the other economies; oil inflation is measured from quarterly Brent prices in local currency and enters the model relative to core inflation.5 Supply-chain pressures are measured by the Global Supply Chain Pressure Index of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The estimates of the output gap—measured as percent of potential GDP—come from the Bank of Canada, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York (euro area), the Cabinet Office of Japan, Haver Analytics (U.K.), and the Congressional Budget Office (U.S.).

How well do the models track post-pandemic core inflation?

Before examining the estimated coefficients, it is useful to assess how much each of the additional post-pandemic effects improves the model's ability to track the data. Figure 1 plots four-quarter core inflation for the panel of advanced economies against the in-sample predictions of three progressively richer specifications, each of which is a restriction of the equation above:

No post-pandemic dummies (dashed black line). The most restrictive case, with constant coefficients and no dummies for the post-pandemic period (η=ζ=0η=ζ=0).
Stronger persistence (red line). Interacts the post-pandemic dummies with persistence coefficients but not with the pass-through coefficients (ζ=0ζ=0).
Stronger persistence and pass-through (blue line). The full specification, with interactions with both persistence and pass-through coefficients.

Figure 1. Average Advanced-Economy Core Inflation

Note: Advanced-economy core inflation is calculated as the simple average over Canada, the euro area, Japan, the U.K., and the U.S. Pre-COVID average is calculated over 2000:Q1–2019:Q4.

Source: Haver Analytics; Authors' calculations.

Accessible version

Of course, the specifications are nearly indistinguishable before 2021, when the post-pandemic dummies and interaction terms are inactive by construction. The horse race is therefore decided over the post-pandemic period. There, the differences are stark. The specification without post-pandemic interactions (the black dashed line) captures the broad contour of the inflation surge but noticeably underpredicts its peak and subsequent stickiness. Allowing persistence to rise (the red line) closes part of the gap, especially during the decline from the peak, when the model predicts inflation remaining elevated for longer. Adding stronger pass-through as well (the blue line) tracks both the climb and the peak of the surge most closely.

Table 1 makes this comparison precise by reporting the root-mean squared errors (RMSEs) of each specification relative to actual core inflation, both over the full charted sample and over the post-pandemic period. The results are consistent across the two windows: each additional layer of post-pandemic flexibility lowers the RMSE, and the full specification performs best by a wide margin. Over the post-pandemic period, moving from constant coefficients to stronger persistence and pass-through lowers the RMSE from 0.37 to 0.17, with the single largest improvement in fit coming from the pass-through interaction.

Table 1. Root-mean squared errors of core-inflation estimates by specification

Note: RMSE measures forecast accuracy against realized four-quarter advanced-economy core inflation, calculated as the simple average across five advanced economies: Canada, euro area, Japan, the U.K., and the U.S.

Source: Authors' calculations.

Rising persistence and stronger oil pass-through

Table 2 reports the panel estimates from the full specification. The persistence results confirm and extend De Michelis et al. (2024), which uses a similar framework. Pre-pandemic persistence—the sum of the coefficients on the first two lags of core inflation—is estimated at 0.35 and is highly significant. The post-pandemic increase in persistence is 0.30, also highly significant, implying that persistence roughly doubles to about 0.65 from 2021:Q1 onward. The result that core inflation has become substantially more inertial is therefore robust to extending the sample through 2026:Q2 and to allowing oil-price pass-through to change at the same time.

Pass-through is the sum of the coefficients on current and lagged relative oil-price inflation. The post-pandemic increases are the sums of the corresponding interaction coefficients. The lower bound and upper bound report 95 percent confidence intervals. *** p < 0.01, ** p < 0.05.

Source: Haver Analytics; Authors' calculations.

The pass-through results are the more novel contribution. Before the pandemic, the response of core inflation to oil prices was very small and statistically insignificant: the point estimates in Table 2, which are for one-unit changes, imply that a 10-percentage point increase in relative oil-price inflation raised core inflation by only about a statistically insignificant 0.01 percentage point. After the pandemic, the pass-through rises to a statistically significant 0.14 percentage point. Although still modest in absolute terms, this estimate represents a meaningful qualitative change: a channel that was effectively switched off before the pandemic became active afterwards. Together, the two panels of Table 2 imply that oil-price shocks now transmit to core inflation both more strongly and more durably than before.6

Figure 2 translates these coefficient changes into a cumulative response, tracing the effect on the core price level of a permanent 10 percent increase in oil prices under three specifications. Under pre-pandemic dynamics (the black line), the effect is very small, raising the core price level by only 0.05 percent after three years. Allowing persistence to rise (the red line) lifts the cumulative effect to just under 0.1 percent, because the same modest pass-through now decays more slowly. Allowing pass-through to strengthen as well (the blue line) raises the response much further, to 0.35 percent after 12 quarters, with most of the effect building over roughly eight quarters.7 The bulk of this increase comes from the stronger pass-through, amplified by higher intrinsic persistence of the core inflation process.

Figure 2. Effects on Core Prices of a Permanent 10 Percent Increase in Oil Prices

Note: Cumulative response of the core price level to a permanent 10 percent increase in oil prices, averaged across five advanced economies (Canada, euro area, Japan, U.K., and U.S.). All exogenous variables are held fixed; the response reflects only oil price pass-through and the intrinsic persistence of core inflation.

Source: Authors' calculations.

Accessible version

What does the model imply for the 2026 oil price shock?

We next use the estimated model to gauge how the recent rise in oil prices might affect core inflation over the next few years. We feed into the model three key inputs: core inflation data through 2026:Q2; the Brent futures curve (as of early August 2026) for the path of oil prices from 2026:Q3 onward; and the reading of the GSCPI through June 2026, at 1.63 standard deviations above its historical mean and projected forward at an estimated quarterly decay rate of 0.8.8 Figure 3 reports the resulting projections under our three specifications.

Figure 3. Advanced-Economy Core Inflation Forecasts

Note: Advanced-economy core inflation is calculated as the simple average across Canada, the euro area, Japan, the U.K., and the U.S. Forecasts are based on: (i) the Brent futures curve as of early August 2026; (ii) realized GSCPI through 2026:Q2, projected forward with a decay rate of 0.8; and (iii) average core inflation in 2026:Q1–Q2 as initial conditions. Shaded area indicates model forecasts.

Source: Haver Analytics; Bloomberg; Authors' estimates.

Accessible version

The three specifications imply materially different paths for core inflation. With no post-pandemic dynamics (the black line), core inflation edges up only modestly, peaking near 2.2 percent. Allowing for stronger persistence (the red line) raises the path to a plateau of about 2.5 percent. Adding stronger pass-through from oil prices as well (the blue line) produces the highest and most front-loaded response: core inflation climbs to nearly 2.8 percent around mid-2027, roughly 0.6 percentage point above the path implied by pre-pandemic dynamics, before receding toward about 2.2 percent by the end of 2028. The difference between the red and black lines—about 0.3 percentage point at the peak—reflects the stronger persistence; the additional difference between the blue and red lines—a further 0.3 to 0.35 percentage point—reflects the higher pass-through. The timing differs across channels: the higher pass-through dominates the near-term peak but fades as the oil impulse in the futures curve normalizes, so the blue path eventually falls back below the red one; the stronger persistence, by contrast, produces a more durable elevation that keeps core inflation above the no-persistence path well into 2028. The post-pandemic inflation process can thus turn even a temporary relative-price shock into a more lasting increase in underlying inflation.

These forecasts assume that the higher persistence of core inflation and stronger oil-price pass-through estimated for the post-pandemic period remain in place at least through 2028. We therefore view these paths for core inflation as an upper bound on the likely impact rather than a central prediction. There are several reasons why persistence and pass-through may prove lower than assumed. The post-pandemic surge in inflation was extraordinary and the result of a confluence of factors, including reopening demand, fiscal stimulus, labor-market tightness, supply-chain disruptions, and high energy prices (as argued, for instance, by Bernanke and Blanchard, 2024). As such, the post-pandemic interaction terms likely capture more than a pure structural oil-to-core channel and, in line with Kilian (2009), may partly reflect the co-movement of oil prices with broader global demand pressures. In a more normal environment, both persistence and pass-through could therefore be weaker than our post-pandemic estimates imply. To that extent, the estimated amplification may overstate the effect of an isolated oil shock and the extent of lasting structural change in the inflation process remains uncertain.

Consistent with this interpretation, second-round effects have not yet materialized; however, risks are mounting. Indeed, some advanced-economy central banks, including the European Central Bank and the Bank of England, have noted that measures of underlying inflation remain broadly stable but also highlighted that inflation risks have increased. The risk highlighted by our estimates is conditional: if oil prices remain elevated for longer than implied by futures pricing, stronger post-pandemic transmission could reassert itself and push core inflation closer to the path implied by our model.

Macroeconomic and monetary policy implications through a structural model

We conclude by assessing the macroeconomic and monetary policy implications of the estimated changes in the inflation process that we have documented above. We examine this issue using the GEMUS model, a structural open-economy macroeconomic framework developed by Federal Reserve Board staff. The model comprises the U.S. and a foreign block, which includes a small region of oil-producing countries. We generate an increase in oil prices through a reduction in that region's supply of oil to global markets. The model also incorporates trade in final consumption goods, intermediate inputs, and capital goods, as well as a broad set of features found to be important in accounting for the data, including nominal and real rigidities and financial frictions.9

The black lines in Figure 4 depict the effects on advanced economies of a 10 percent increase in oil prices under a model calibration corresponding to the pre-pandemic inflation process—with low intrinsic inflation persistence and low pass-through from oil prices to core inflation. Under these conditions, the effects of the oil price shock are manageable: activity declines a little over 0.1 percent, headline inflation rises noticeably but briefly, and core inflation increases only modestly. Monetary policy responds modestly, tightening slightly in response to higher core inflation.10 The red lines show the effects of the same shock under the higher inflation persistence indicated by our post-pandemic estimates. With greater persistence, the rise in core inflation is larger and longer lasting, and the contraction in activity is somewhat more severe, although the differences are not large. Monetary policy continues to respond only modestly.

Figure 4. Effects of a 10 Percent Rise in Oil Prices: Structural Model Simulations

Note: All variables are for an average advanced economy.

Source: Haver Analytics; Authors' calculations.

Accessible version

The picture differs, however, when higher persistence is accompanied by stronger pass-through, shown by the blue lines. Here we assume that firms' marginal costs respond more strongly to an increase in oil prices—engineered through a higher cost share of oil in production—and calibrate this increase to match the rise in pass-through estimated in our regressions.11 The increases in both headline and core inflation are now much larger and more persistent, and the GDP hit is about twice as large. Monetary policy is put in the uncomfortable position of having to tighten materially to contain inflation even as the economy weakens. The decline in activity reflects both supply-side forces, as firms face higher costs, and demand-side forces, as higher oil prices and tighter monetary policy restrain spending. The model exercises illustrate the structural mechanisms that might be embedded in the empirical estimates.

Conclusion

Our analysis suggests that oil-price shocks may now pose greater challenges to monetary policy. Oil-price shocks were relatively manageable before the pandemic, when intrinsic inflation persistence was lower and there was more limited oil prices-to-core prices pass-through. However, the post-pandemic data point to a shift in the inflation process that, if it continues, would amplify the response of core inflation to oil-price shocks: the stronger pass-through raises the initial core-inflation response, while higher persistence makes that response more durable. The evidence should be interpreted cautiously, because the post-pandemic interactions are estimated from a short and unusual period and so it is uncertain how long they may continue. Nevertheless, they illustrate an upside risk to inflation should oil prices remain elevated or supply-chain disruptions persist for an extended period.

2. This specification uses actual oil-price changes rather than attempting to isolate oil supply shocks using structural decomposition methods (e.g., Kilian, 2009). This choice reflects our focus on the issue that is relevant for policy: conditional on observed oil-price movements and cyclical conditions, how much do core prices respond? While oil prices rise for various reasons, our inclusion of the output gap controls for the state of economic activity, helping to isolate the cost-push component. Return to text

3. We also augmented the specification by controlling for relative core import price inflation but found no evidence of additional explanatory power for core inflation in the panel regression. While Peneva et al. (2025) showed that for the U.S. it is important to control for import prices excluding oil and other energy products, we lack a consistent measure for it across major advanced economies. Relatedly, there are no tariff-inclusive measures of import prices for the foreign advanced economies. We therefore did not include import prices in our baseline specification. Return to text

4. Country-specific OLS estimates deliver largely similar results, with the rise in core inflation persistence post-pandemic broad-based and significant across all five economies. The increase in oil pass-through shows more cross-country variation: it rose significantly in Canada, Japan, and the U.S., but was weaker and not statistically significant in the euro area and the U.K., possibly reflecting Europe's natural gas price shock following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Return to text

5. Using energy CPI in place of oil prices delivers similar, indeed somewhat larger, estimates of the post-pandemic increase in pass-through. We also test our specifications without contemporaneous oil prices, which delivers largely similar persistence and pass-through results. Return to text

6. As a robustness check, we replace the output gap with the vacancy-to-unemployment ratio (V/U), motivated by Benigno and Eggertsson (2024), who emphasize labor-market tightness and its nonlinear relationship with inflation in explaining the post-pandemic U.S. inflation surge. Canada is excluded from this analysis because its vacancy series only starts in 2015. The estimated post-pandemic increases in persistence and pass-through are 0.292 and 0.010, respectively, close to the baseline estimates of 0.298 and 0.013, and remain statistically significant. Given that results align for both measures, we retained the output gap in the baseline to preserve the five-economy sample. Return to text

7. These estimates can be compared to those of Alp et al. (2023), who found statistically significant but modest second-round effects of oil prices on inflation using data through 2022 from a large panel of advanced economies: a permanent 10 percent oil-price increase raises the core CPI level by about 0.1 percent over roughly eight quarters. That magnitude is close to what we estimate before allowing pass-through to strengthen, but our full specification implies a larger effect because it captures full oil-to-core pass-through and allows both pass-through and persistence to shift after the pandemic, rather than estimating a single average relationship over 2000–2022 with one COVID dummy. A further difference is country coverage: their estimates focus principally on the euro area, the United Kingdom, and Canada, whereas our panel also includes the United States and Japan. Return to text

8. The decay rate is obtained by regressing the GSCPI on one quarterly lag of itself over 2020:Q1–2024:Q4, which yields a slope of approximately 0.8; the GSCPI is measured in standard deviations from its historical mean, so this implies a return toward the mean with a half-life of roughly three quarters. Return to text

9. GEMUS stands for Global Economy Model for U.S. Policy Analysis. The version used here is an extension of the framework developed in Cuba-Borda et al. (2025). Return to text

10. Monetary policy in the model follows an inertial rule similar to that in Taylor (1999), with the policy rate responding to core inflation and the output gap. Return to text

11. The assumption of a higher cost share of oil in production proxies for the underlying reasons why oil pass-through could be stronger, like larger indirect effects on wages or on the prices of other inputs. For example, Erceg et al. (2024) find empirically that an exogenous oil price shock raises real wages in the euro area but lowers them in the U.S., while also generating a larger increase in core inflation in the euro area than in the U.S. We also experimented with generating higher pass-through by raising the frequency of price adjustment—which produces a larger increase in prices for a given rise in marginal cost—and found similar implications for the near-term effects on activity and the policy rate. articles.title: From AI Adoption to Enterprise Value with Agentic AI
articles.text:
How EY-Parthenon can help

EY-Parthenon Edge Platforms: AI-powered Tech for Strategy and M&A

Discover EY-Parthenon’s AI-powered deal technology platforms that drive real-world results across strategy, transactions and transformation.

Read more

Unlocking this trapped value requires activating cross-functional workflows at scale (we call these enterprise value streams) that will address decision-making friction, approval latency, coordination overhead, analysis duplication, rework loops and fragmented accountability.

These friction factors rarely appear clearly on organizational charts or financial statements, yet collectively they shape enterprise responsiveness, execution speed, operating cost, customer experience, and ultimately value creation.

This is the hidden “75% gap” and remains largely untouched by today's AI efforts. This mismatch explains why organizations are doing more AI every year but not seeing the compounding effect of AI in enterprise results.

A recent automotive original equipment manufacturer (OEM) transformation value estimation led by EY-Parthenon illustrates the scale of the opportunity. Total AI- and digital-enabled value creation potential exceeded US$2.4b, of which nearly US$2b came from enterprise value streams.

Why enterprise AI fails to compound value

The root cause lies in the architecture of the modern enterprise itself. Over decades, organizations and the systems supporting them evolved vertically around functions, reporting hierarchies and control structures. enterprise resource planning (ERP), customer relationship management (CRM), human resources information systems (HRIS), product lifecycle management (PLM) and workflow platforms were designed primarily to optimize functional execution, governance and control. But enterprise value does not flow vertically. It flows horizontally across customer journeys and product lifecycles through cross-functional operational value streams such as concept-to-launch, order-to-cash, procure-to-pay and service incident-to-resolution.

This creates a fundamental structural tension: people, systems, key performance indicators (KPIs) and governance are organized vertically, while value creation flows horizontally. Where these intersect, friction emerges. In most enterprises, a substantial proportion of effort is consumed not for value creation itself, but for managing the friction between silos.

In the recent automotive OEM example, the Incident-to-Resolution process spans across eight functions, touches a number of enterprise systems and requires significant human intervention, with 15-25% of the effort in warranty management spent on internal coordination activity rather than solving customer or operational problems directly.

articles.text:
Research & Insights

Pulitzer Prize Winner Dan Yergin on How the Iran War Is Reshaping the Energy Map, and the Race to Power AI

By Daniel Yergin, Atul Lele, CFA, Ian Singer, Jake Davidson

When we look at the major dynamics reshaping the world today—from modern mercantilism, to the rise of artificial intelligence, to the war in Iran—it’s striking how often the energy market sits at the center of them. In today’s podcast, we’re sharing the highlights from a recent discussion diving into each of these topics, featuring Daniel Yergin, one of the world’s leading energy experts, in conversation with Bridgewater’s Atul Lele, Head of Portfolio Strategists, and Ian Singer, Head of Commodities.Across the conversation, Dan, Atul, and Ian explore how energy producers are likely to respond to what Dan calls “the mother of all supply shocks,” the implications of a global push for energy security on markets and economies, how the race to power the AI build-out is playing out, the political debate around AI energy use, and more.Dan is Vice Chairman at S&P Global and the author of several books, including The Prize: The Epic Quest for Oil, Money, and Power, which won a Pulitzer Prize, and The New Map: Energy, Climate, and the Clash of Nations.Editor’s note: The views of external guests do not necessarily reflect the views of Bridgewater.
