articles.title: How states can organize themselves to build more housing near transit | Brookings
articles.text:
Research

How states can organize themselves to build more housing near transit

Tommy Wan,

TW

Tommy Wan

Former Research Intern
- Brookings Metro

Ben Swedberg, and

Ben Swedberg

Research Analyst
- Brookings Metro

Adie Tomer

Adie Tomer

Senior Fellow
- Brookings Metro

November 13, 2026

An Amtrak train departs Raleigh Union Station alongside new apartment buildings. Photo credit: Wileydoc / Shutterstock.com

25 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Editor's note:
This report is one component of a three-part series studying the barriers to transit-oriented development (TOD) in U.S. metropolitan areas. It’s accompanied by a statistical survey of over 70,000 roadway corridors owned by state governments and a report on how business groups can advance TOD in their regions.

There is a broad recognition among state leaders that they need to build more housing. The nation’s housing shortage is a key driver of the current affordability crisis, and state government’s fiscal and regulatory authority directly shapes development. States play a crucial role in determining whether and where housing is built, and many are looking to transit-oriented development (TOD) as they consider how to tackle their housing shortage.
TOD is a strategy that involves building more housing—as well as shops, schools, and offices—near transit stations. By building near transit, places can deliver housing units while also capturing co-benefits such as making life more affordable and lowering government costs per capita. State officials have responded to this opportunity by taking multiple steps to help their local partners accelerate TOD. For example, Texas state law lets the Dallas transit agency enter TOD public-private partnerships. Lawmakers in Utah allow localities to set up tax increment financing districts, which are able to generate revenue that can be reinvested in TOD. In Maryland, Governor Wes Moore issued an executive order creating a housing ombudsperson to streamline permitting for localities, meaning those places can realize TOD projects faster.
But there’s another tool that’s rarely been deployed: state-level TOD offices and programs. Few states have established designated offices or programs specifically designed to implement TOD policy and leverage state governments’ unique capabilities to advance TOD. Research on the states that have taken this step is just as rare, leaving motivated state leaders with little guidance.
For states that want to lead on TOD, there’s a script. We’ve learned that successful states often take similar and specific steps, which form a playbook any stakeholder can reference.1

Build the case for TOD internally and publicly.
Create or designate a TOD office and put it where it’s most likely to succeed.
Deploy the full suite of financial and regulatory tools at states’ disposal to accelerate TOD.
Share the success of TOD efforts early and often.

By centralizing knowledge and streamlining operational decisions, TOD offices and programs can expand the impact of related legislation and executive orders, enabling the state to more directly facilitate TOD projects. State leaders who want to accelerate TOD should look at these established offices and programs for inspiration.

Transit-oriented development helps cities, businesses, and people thrive
Transit-oriented development is a relatively straightforward real estate concept, although there are specific variations in the definition. At its core, TOD refers to land development around transit lines that is walkable and compact, includes a mix of real estate uses, and offers higher population and job densities than regional averages. Formal definitions often limit TOD’s extent to a quarter- or half-mile surrounding a transit station, but entire neighborhoods could still qualify as TOD across many square miles. Critically, TOD offers residents greater transportation choices to reach destinations, whether by transit, biking, walking, or driving.

Riders wait as an IndyGo Red Line bus arrives at Statehouse station in downtown Indianapolis.
Photo credit: Momoneymoproblemz / Wikimedia Commons

A Rapid Transit vehicle in Charlotte, North Carolina.
Photo credit: Harold Stiver / Shutterstock.com

Capital One Center in Tysons, Virginia, beside the Silver Line’s McLean station.
Photo credit: Duane Lempke / Wikimedia Commons

While exact definitions vary, what’s less variable are the types of benefits TOD can deliver:

TOD can support housing capacity at scale. The blocks surrounding transit stops are ideal for larger, multifamily residential developments. Recent evidence demonstrates numerous metro areas have built many new housing units near rail stations over the last few decades.
TOD promotes a more affordable cost of living. Overall affordability often does not come from reducing housing costs, but more so by enabling households to travel shorter distances and making it easier to own fewer vehicles.
TOD promotes lower costs for local and state governments. Greater density allows more people to use the same number of sidewalks, roadways, water pipes, and parks, effectively lowering service costs per capita.
TOD boosts transit ridership. Putting more households and businesses close to transit increases ridership demand, and those extra riders help cover greater shares of a transit agency’s operating costs.
TOD increases tax returns per developed acre. The more people who live and work in a given acre, the greater the number of tax returns and total revenues generated in that place. This is a well-established benefit of more compact development.
TOD promotes greater accessibility, which itself is an economic accelerant. Concentrating more people and jobs in various nodes—which TOD can do across cities and metro areas—increases job accessibility by transit, biking, walking, and even automobiles. That’s a benefit to businesses of all sizes that need their workers to be able to reliably get to work, and for residents who can access more job opportunities and other amenities. Such accessibility gains are a key feature of agglomeration, or the economic benefits derived from geographic proximity.

Why states should govern TOD themselves instead of just empowering their partners
While it’s true that land use and transit are mostly controlled by local governments, nearly every state (48 of 50) owns land near transit. The Center for Geospatial Solutions at the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy estimates that state-owned acreage within a quarter-mile of a transit station is over 33,500.2 Florida and Massachusetts top the list with 3,367 and 2,656 acres, respectively, and 14 states own more than 1,000 buildable acres. In general, states in the West, Mid-Atlantic, and New England tend to own more land near transit than states elsewhere.

Map 1

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

State-owned land has significant development potential. Under fairly conservative TOD density assumptions (7 units per acre), state-owned land near transit could deliver more than 235,000 housing units. Make those developments medium- or high-density (15 and 25 units per acre, respectively), and the estimates rise to more than 500,000 and 840,000 units, respectively.
In many states, that’s a huge opportunity. Take Massachusetts: Assuming a density of 15 units per acre, the state could build more than 39,800 units near transit just on its own land. High-density development could yield roughly 66,400 units. For reference, Massachusetts built only 34,500 units in 2025, and the state’s goal is to build 220,000 units by 2035; building new homes only on the state’s own land and only near transit could achieve 18% of that goal at a medium density and over 30% at a high density. Fewer acres may be available in other states, but the opportunity is still real. For example, medium-density development on state-owned land in Pennsylvania could reach 6% of the state’s goal of 450,000 new homes by 2035.
Several states also directly control transit agencies in their states, which can be a potent starting point for state-led TOD efforts (Map 2). Of those states, eight actively operate their own service and another seven appoint all or most of the leadership of a regional transit agency.3 CT Transit, for example, runs buses across all of Connecticut. Though the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) is a quasi-separate entity with trains and buses that serve 177 cities and towns (of 351 total across the whole state), it is technically a division of the state department of transportation (DOT). State leaders are responsible for governance and oversight of regional agencies in Indiana, Minnesota, New York, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, and Utah. For example, the Utah Transit Authority’s board and CEO are appointed by the governor and legislature, while TriMet in Portland, Ore., and Metro Transit in Minneapolis both have boards appointed by state officials.

Map 2

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Even more states run limited transit services, which are not displayed in Map 2.4 Many states operate some level of ferry service, including sophisticated systems such as those in Washington and Alaska. Others have intercity buses, such as Bustang in Colorado and Breeze in Virginia. Qualifying transit services don’t neatly fit into simple categorization, but the broader point is that multiple states directly operate transit services.
Even in states that don’t own transit and own relatively little land near stations, a TOD office or program can still effectively serve local partners. Such an entity can implement state laws regulating and incentivizing TOD at the local level, and the entity can better leverage state resources to provide technical assistance. A TOD office or program may also be effective at coordinating applications for federal funding from localities and regions.
Some states already have TOD offices or programs, especially those with their own transit service
Most states have no office or program dedicated to TOD; in fact, only 13 have set one up. What these offices are named, what they do, and where they’re situated within the broader organizational chart are all unique to each state.5
TOD offices and programs usually sit within state DOTs, state transit agencies, or agencies that implement housing policy. Connecticut, Maryland, and New Jersey all run TOD through their state DOT. State-owned transit agencies and state-controlled regional agencies in Massachusetts, Minnesota, New York, Oregon, and Utah also host TOD programs and offices. In New Jersey, NJ Transit complements the work of the state’s DOT. In three more states—California, Rhode Island, and Washington—TOD is managed by staff that implement housing policy. In Colorado and Hawaii, unique structures have taken on state-level TOD efforts.

Map 3

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

It may be easiest to establish state TOD offices where states control transit. Nine of the 13 states with a TOD office operate sizable transit service or control a regional agency. The fact that so many of the states with state-controlled transit systems have also adopted TOD offices underscores how interwoven these governance responsibilities can be in accelerating TOD—something experts routinely confirmed in interviews.6
Where states establish a TOD office or program depends on priorities and existing staff capacity. The Washington State Department of Commerce implements the state’s housing policy, so the TOD program landed there after legislation focused on housing supply was put into law. Hawaii took a collaborative approach, convening many state agencies in a concerted effort to meet the state’s housing goals. Maryland assigned the state DOT secretary’s office responsibility for TOD, since that staff already managed real estate responsibilities; the TOD office at the MBTA emerged from a similar organizational structure.7
The structure of these offices and programs affects the functions they perform. In Colorado, HB 24-1313 saw lawmakers apply specific requirements that some cities meet housing opportunity goals; the Colorado Department of Local Affairs is naturally situated to provide the technical assistance municipalities need to reach those goals and administer associated grants. Connecticut’s DOT owns many parcels of land near transit stations; putting the TOD office there lets the state more easily pursue its development goals.
How state governments can organize themselves to deliver TOD
Every state can accelerate transit-oriented development. Their fiscal and regulatory authorities affect the speed, quality, and cost of real estate development. Almost all own sizable amounts of developable land near transit, and some own and manage transit agencies too. Channeling those capabilities to accelerate TOD, however, requires multiple actions that most states have not yet begun.
Based on a series of expert interviews and background research, there are common steps that every state should consider to better support TOD within their borders.

Table 1

Visual checklist of steps state DOTs can take to accelerate TOD

Understand the TOD opportunity

Define TOD in state law, including what modes it applies to, and solicit stakeholder input.

Survey state-owned land near transit.

Create or designate the TOD office

Keep open and consistent communication across TOD implementers.

Release a request for information (RFI) to involve the developer community and build early interest.

Adequately fund the new TOD office or program.

Select a natural landing place for TOD implementation in state government.

Leverage the unique position of the TOD office or program to accelerate TOD

If not yet done, survey state-owned land.

Pursue value capture and joint development.

Let the TOD office or program implement new TOD-supportive incentives and regulations.

Communicate the successes of TOD.

Understand the transit-oriented development opportunity
States need to start by understanding the potential of TOD. Some states may use TOD to boost transit ridership, while others will focus on increasing housing supply to address the affordability crisis. In either case, state officials should seek to learn what assets are at their disposal.
State agencies in charge of transportation, housing, and commerce should survey state-owned land near transit. When Hawaii leaders did so, they learned they had 1,900 acres near the Skyline rail line. In Maryland, staff identified 134 acres of land in the Baltimore region alone that could generate over $1.4 billion; the state owns 300 developable acres statewide. For reference, that’s nearly as much as Maryland spends operating transit for an entire year: roughly $1.6 billion split across the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA) and the Maryland Transit Administration.8 Just having these numbers on hand can be crucial in building support for TOD. Top-line numbers may persuade the public, while more detailed estimates can act as the basis for conversations with developers.
Legislators, meanwhile, can immediately move to codify TOD in law. That includes deciding what kinds of transit the state will prioritize TOD near. For example, Washington state lawmakers used HB 1491 to help define development near transit stations. Those kinds of distinctions are an invaluable reference point for other decisions, such as permitting rules and qualifications for state-led housing incentives. Critically, legislators should solicit input from developers, state agencies, and regional and local officials; defining TOD right the first time can save agency staff from implementing foreseeable changes to those definitions down the line, and it can make projects successful by clarifying expectations and aligning stakeholders.
Create or designate a TOD office
Once state leaders have built a rationale for pursuing TOD and laid the groundwork for supporting it, they must decide what their approach to TOD will be and who should execute it. Those activities should be consolidated within a TOD office.
From the start, it’s up to governors to make sure lines of communication across state agencies stay open and let staff know that TOD is an executive priority. The TOD office should receive formal guidance to convene officials across multiple agencies and include touchpoints with the private sector. Then, it’s incumbent on TOD office leadership to regularly gather agency executives in a “council” format and meet frequently with the private sector. Experts said this may mean formal meetings with peers at other agencies, but they explained that a standing coffee or lunch with a counterpart can be just as valuable.9
The TOD office should also have clear responsibilities and goals. For example, it should manage a database of publicly developable land and have access to information around privately owned parcels.10 It should issue a request-for-information (RFI) or request-for-proposal (RFP), in part to build early interest among developers and to forge public-private relationships. The office can publish materials to make the case for the benefits of TOD and report on statewide progress. (The next subsection details more specific responsibilities that the legislature and governors would have to authorize.)
While state government staff ready themselves to accelerate TOD, legislators must appropriate administrative funds to support their work. Funding amounts should be closely aligned to agency capacity—and if it’s the legislature itself assigning state staff to pursue TOD, they should make sure that new legislation is accompanied by funding to support its implementation. Appropriators should fund technical assistance whenever possible, especially for smaller municipalities that may lack the capacity to interpret new legislation and execute new regulations and incentives around TOD.
Then, state leaders will have to choose which agency should lead the state’s TOD efforts. They may find the following questions useful:

Does the state own and operate its own transit?
Could any existing offices easily become a TOD office, such as the real estate arm of a department of transportation or commerce?
Does anyone in state government already do TOD work?

In states where a TOD office already exists, these questions have been decisive. That was true for all three questions in Massachusetts: The MBTA runs transit, and it had a real estate office already staffed, which state leaders helped transform into the agency’s TOD office.11 That office benefits from natural synergies between their work and the Office of Real Estate and Economic Development at the state DOT.
Hawaii, on the other hand, had no state-run transit and no office that could naturally rebrand to an “Office of TOD.” So, the state created an interagency TOD Council, co-chaired by the Office of Planning and Sustainable Development and the state housing authority, to align its membership on accelerating mixed-use development and boosting transit ridership.
Maryland runs its own transit agency, but leadership chose to convert the state DOT real estate office into its TOD office. Agency leaders knew that the staff’s land development expertise was crucial to executing TOD well, and the office’s central role in the DOT let it coordinate across modes and with other state agencies.
Maryland’s history illustrates a broader trend. Across the country, experts agreed: Offices managing state-owned land, those with relationships with developers, and those with experience implementing housing and land use legislation were best set up to excel as TOD offices.12
Leverage the unique position of the TOD office or program to accelerate TOD
States don’t need to own their own transit to accelerate TOD. Almost every state owns land near transit, but the value of those parcels is often unrealized. Surfacing parking lots near rail stations, for example, are often economically underproductive. For states that want to reap the benefits of TOD on their own land, these three strategies are key: understanding what the state owns, lifting regulatory barriers, and closing financing gaps.
In an ideal world, state agencies would have inventoried and prioritized their transit-adjacent land before a TOD office was set up. For those that haven’t, it’s a crucial first step. States can’t communicate the scale of opportunity to developers if they themselves don’t know what they own. And they can’t make targeted changes to regulations, nor spend funds effectively, without this knowledge. Leaders trying to figure out how to get started might look to California, where a 2019 executive order instructed two state departments to identify state-owned land available for housing development, or Massachusetts’ State Land for Homes program.
Once the state TOD office or program understands the state’s assets, it has two distinct responsibilities. First, the office or program should tackle value capture and joint development. Second, the office or program should take responsibility for implementing new TOD-supporting legislation and gubernatorial orders.
On the first responsibility, state TOD offices should pursue value capture and joint development policies. Value capture, which includes tools such as tax increment financing, can reinvest some of the taxable value developers generate through TOD into the system itself. Joint development is the private sector partnering with government to pay part of the cost of a transportation improvement while a complementary real estate development occurs. In the TOD context, the public entity usually owns the land and finds a private partner to develop it. Adopting formal guidelines around both practices can help incentivize TOD, and states should reach out to municipal officials who may have prior experience with both techniques.
Massachusetts has leveraged both strategies. The MBTA owns considerable land in the 177 communities it serves, and its real estate office is charged with using that land to generate non-fare revenue.13 The agency has taken a unique approach near major hubs such as South Station and Back Bay, where it leases air rights and ground space to private developers. The MBTA keeps the land and collects rent on it too.
Connecticut similarly focuses on building near state-run transit. The state DOT owns the vast majority of its bus service and a commuter line, and operates intercity rail. Taking a proactive approach, the DOT created a TOD officer role and scored almost 20 state-owned parcels along fixed rail and bus routes. The department is now executing joint development on those parcels: One of several new apartment buildings anchoring mixed-use development near Meriden station was on a state-owned parking lot, and there are plans underway to take on similar efforts at stations in New Haven and Stamford. All of this means that private developers have new, high-value land available to them, and the state has extra capital for station infrastructure improvements.
Aside from value capture strategies, the state TOD office or program should also implement new laws and gubernatorial orders.
Some states have sought to reduce regulatory barriers to building housing. That might include lifting statewide parking minimums and reducing curb set-back distances, or even preempting local zoning near transit stations. Zoning is a consistent sticking point between state and local officials, which means state leaders should be extra thoughtful before they take that step. If they pursue any such reforms, the TOD office or program should be responsible for assisting localities with their implementation and enforcing state implementation.
Other states are figuring out how to make development more likely to pencil out. Though developers have typically borne the cost of infrastructure supporting new developments, those costs are increasingly preventing projects from happening at all. State TOD offices and programs can examine this issue in their state, such as in Hawaii, where the TOD office showed how costly required infrastructure upgrades are. Brookings research has found that a statewide fund to pay for that infrastructure in infill locations—including TOD-ready areas—would help spur development. If such a fund is implemented, the state TOD office or program should administer it.
Though state offices and programs most aggressively pursuing TOD have found success by first using these strategies on their own land, many could also be applied to land they don’t own. This is especially important in states that don’t own lots of land near transit or where land ownership is so disparate across state agencies that it’s too difficult to assemble for development. Here, the state TOD office or program can play a crucial coordinating role between different land-owning agencies, private landholders, and private developers.
Communicate the successes of transit-oriented development
TOD projects can take years, if not decades, to deliver results. State leaders and local constituents, however, usually want to see benefits long before a ribbon is cut. To that end, TOD offices and programs should be thoughtful about how they measure their impact in the long and short term. For example, states may prioritize finishing a signature project to boost the visibility of TOD and garner goodwill, while measuring total units produced in the long term. In Connecticut, leaders are doing precisely that by focusing on the Stamford rail station and adjacent TOD corridor—particularly given its connection to neighboring New York City—to help build support for their TOD efforts.14
At the same time, state legislators and executives must understand how long implementation by a TOD office or program can take. Experts in some states reported that their legislature responded to slow progress, even in the first year or two after a TOD law was passed, by passing more legislation.15 In some cases, the added burden of interpreting and administering those new laws slowed delivery of the initial legislation.
The next generation of governors, legislators, and agency leaders must advance TOD at the state level
TOD can help add hundreds of thousands of housing units and address a host of challenges Americans and their governments face. State leaders know it too—over the coming years, even more states will pass laws and issue executive orders designed to accelerate TOD.
Before they do, they should take the step of setting up a TOD office or program in state government. That kind of entity can make sure that all future laws and executive orders have a place to land, staff to execute them, and a name associated with their implementation. As states experiment with the most cutting-edge strategies for accelerating TOD, something as basic as a TOD office or program will ensure their success.

articles.title: How are bottlenecks in the energy development pipeline reshaping the US market?
articles.text:
Observations
How are bottlenecks in the energy development pipeline reshaping the US market?

Macquarie expert: Ed Northam, Global Head of Green Investments, Macquarie Asset Management

12 November 2026

Grid congestion, equipment shortages and stalled permits have made achieving speed to power increasingly challenging. Buyers are paying a premium for it and the advantage is shifting to developers with scale and execution capability, creating consolidation opportunities.

Electricity demand growth by sector and end use in the United States, 2015 – 2030
Total incremental electricity demand over each five-year period (TWh)

Source: IEA 2026; Electricity demand growth by sector and end-use in the United States, 2015-2030, https://www.iea.org/, License: CC BY 4.0.
Energy demand is soaring, with 420 TWh of incremental electricity demand forecast to be added in the US over the next five years, as shown above.1 This is driven by a combination of diversified demand sources including the electrification of transport and industry, heating and cooling and data centre requirements.
Developers are racing to respond, but the development pipeline is clogged by:
Interconnection queues: the waiting lists for grid connection grew 116 per cent between 2020 and 2025.2
Equipment bottlenecks: lead times for generator step-up transformers, which link new generation to the grid, have reached 144 weeks.3
Permitting delays: more than 125 wind projects across 25 states are awaiting approval.4

Speed to market is now driving what gets built. Rapid growth in power demand is outpacing available supply, a challenge compounded by stalled wind approvals in the US. Against this backdrop, developers are increasingly prioritising technologies that can connect fastest. Solar and storage lead on deployment speed and storage is emerging as a way to unlock grid capacity directly. At Aligned Data Centers’ Hillsboro campus, an on-site battery system developed by Calibrant, a Macquarie Asset Management portfolio company, supports earlier energisation than would be possible through conventional grid upgrades that would otherwise have been required to connect the site.
It is also shaping prices. As demand outpaces available grid capacity, data centres, for example, are paying more for power that can be connected sooner. In PJM North Illinois, the US’ most congested data centre market, corporate Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) are pricing $US38 per megawatt-hour (MWh) above the 2027–2041 forward curve. In ERCOT West Hub, where supply connects faster, they sit $US14 per MWh below it.5
In other words, the harder it is to connect, the higher the premium available supply commands.
Why does it matter?
The bottlenecks are changing who can compete.
Holding queue positions, reserving equipment years ahead and financing longer development timelines require balance-sheet strength and specialist teams. In our view, this complexity can push smaller platforms out, while larger developers can spread risk, absorb delays and raise capital more cheaply.
We believe the next phase of energy delivery is an execution race that sophisticated, scaled players are positioned to lead, driving further consolidation across the sector.

What we’re watching next
A pipeline is only worth what a developer can actually deliver, which puts the larger, best-equipped developers in a strong position to lead.

Grid access reform
Whether interconnection reforms shorten queue times.

Equipment supply
Whether new transformer manufacturing capacity brings lead times down.

Permitting outcomes
Whether stalled wind projects win approval, or capital shifts toward solar, storage and gas.

articles.title: Supporting Australia’s fuel security infrastructure | Macquarie Group
articles.text:
Infrastructure
Supporting Australia’s fuel security infrastructure

Link copied to clipboard

Macquarie Capital advised Stonepeak on its acquisition of a 75 per cent interest in iOR, one of Australia’s key independent fuel providers

Swipe for more

SectorInfrastructureSub-sectorTransportLocationAustralia

Opportunity

Australia's liquid fuels market has undergone significant transformation over the past decade.
The closure of several domestic fuel refineries has driven Australia's reliance on diesel imports to approximately 90 per cent of total consumption.1
As the Australian Government seeks to strengthen fuel supply resilience, iOR has emerged as a critical player in the country's fuel infrastructure sector. The family-owned business operates a vertically integrated fuel import terminal and distribution platform, including special-purpose diesel import terminals in Queensland and South Australia and a network of more than 250 sites, making it one of Australia’s largest independent fuel distributors.2
The company also operates a network of highly reliable, unmanned diesel stops for heavy vehicles, while delivering bulk fuel, storage and monitoring solutions across Australia. It supplies fuel to customers across the mining, agriculture, transport, logistics and aviation sectors. By supplying businesses and transport hubs in industrial, rural and remote areas, iOR helps sustain critical sectors of Australia’s economy.

Approach

Macquarie Capital acted as sole financial adviser to Stonepeak on its acquisition of a 75 per cent interest in iOR, providing strategic financial advice and management of stakeholder engagement.
With few comparable assets in the Australian infrastructure sector, positioning iOR as a margin-per-litre business with cost pass-through characteristics was key to demonstrating its infrastructure-like earnings profile and maximising value for the founding shareholders. This strategy aligned with the growing trend of infrastructure investors expanding beyond traditional core infrastructure assets into adjacent core plus sectors, including fuel distribution.
Macquarie Capital brought together specialists from its Infrastructure, Critical Minerals and Energy, and Debt Capital Markets teams to provide Stonepeak with insight into operational dynamics, the competitive landscape and sector trends. Macquarie Capital also arranged an acquisition financing package, securing a new term loan facility and a right-sized trade finance facility.
The transaction was structured as a long-term partnership, with existing shareholders and management retaining a 25 per cent stake, ensuring continuity of operations and alignment.

Outcome

Stonepeak’s investment strengthens iOR’s capacity to support Australia’s growing fuel security requirements and reinforces fuel supply chains across regional and remote communities.3
The transaction highlights the important role private capital plays in essential and core plus infrastructure, helping distribution networks remain resilient, efficient and responsive to changing energy needs. It also reflects increasing institutional appetite for non-traditional, infrastructure-adjacent investments.
iOR’s unique assets and distribution network enabled it to play a role in supporting Australia’s fuel security during periods of heightened supply-chain volatility. The company entered partnerships with federal and state governments, including agreements with Export Finance Australia (EFA) to support the purchase of additional fuel to address regional shortages and a partnership with the South Australian Government to establish a strategic diesel reserve for industry and regional communities.4
Macquarie Capital navigated this complex transaction by aligning its diverse expertise across sectors to deliver integrated strategic advice, along with a commercial financing solution that supported Stonepeak to secure a high-quality asset with long-term national significance.

articles.title: Money and power: lessons from history for stablecoins and US dollar dominance – speech by Carolyn Wilkins
articles.text:
Money and power: lessons from history for stablecoins and US dollar dominance – speech by Carolyn Wilkins

Given at Queen’s University, Belfast

Published on
15 September 2026

In her speech, Carolyn Wilkins draws on historical experience of private money issuance to explore whether private digital money can operate safely at scale. She also considers what could happen if US dollar stablecoins become widely used, and what that could mean for the future of international monetary power.

Speech
Introduction
Thank you for inviting me. It is a pleasure to be here at Queen’s University in Belfast to talk about payment innovations, and what they mean for international money and power.
I’ll focus on stablecoins. They have some affinities with the local banknotes issued here. And while stablecoins are often presented in very dry terms - blockchains, tokens, settlement layers - the bigger questions are about money and power.
Payment means and systems are like electricity grids. When they are working, they are in the background, and when they are not, there can be widespread disruption. And, payment systems can be used by governments to enforce economic sanctions, as we saw after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. They can also be used to monitor financial flows and to project influence. That has made the infrastructure of money and payments an increasingly important part of economic statecraft.
The strategic issue here is what role stablecoins will play in a system where money, payments and geopolitical power are becoming increasingly intertwined. We want to know which forms of digital money will ultimately succeed, and which currencies and institutions will become embedded in the next generation of payment infrastructure. It is early days, so the answers are honestly unknown. But we can learn a lot by considering three questions.
First: can private digital money work safely at scale?
Second: what happens if US dollar stablecoins really do scale?
Third: what would that mean for international monetary power?
These questions are top of mind for me because the Bank of England recently published a framework for systemic sterling-denominated stablecoins.footnote [1]
1. Can private digital money work safely at scale?
Let me start with what a stablecoin is.
A fiat-backed payment stablecoin is a privately issued claim designed to maintain a fixed value against sovereign money - usually one stablecoin for one dollar.
There is a familiar analogue here in Northern Ireland. Private banks issue their own sterling banknotes, which circulate pound-for-pound with other sterling money and are fully backed by ring-fenced assets, but the basic monetary promise is familiar: a privately issued claim that people expect to maintain its value at par.
One way to see what stablecoins add is to compare them with Bitcoin. Bitcoin showed something fundamental: value can be transferred globally and continuously without a central intermediary. Bitcoin is not backed by reserve assets, and its value can move enormously.
In 2010, two pizzas were actually bought for 10,000 bitcoins - about $40 at the time. Today, 10,000 bitcoins would be worth about $770 million. Those are probably the most expensive pizzas in history.
Figure 1 shows the underlying problem more systematically. Bitcoin is far more volatile than the major payment stablecoins, making it poorly suited to everyday payments.
Stablecoins were designed to address that problem by backing the monetary promise of a stable value with reserve assets, while retaining some of the features of crypto technology. Transfers can take place continuously, often across borders, and transactions can be programmed using smart contracts.

Figure 1: Volatility of Bitcoin, USDT and USDC

Footnotes

Source: Defillama.

There is a real demand for this innovation, particularly where payments systems are slow, expensive and difficult to access.
For now, they are used mainly inside the crypto ecosystem, as a settlement asset for trading and lending, as collateral, to provide liquidity, and as a way of moving between crypto markets and conventional money.
The market has grown very quickly. Stablecoins in circulation reached roughly $300 billion by mid-2026, up from less than $5 billion at the beginning of 2020 (Figure 2).

Figure 2: Stablecoins in circulation by market capitalisation

Footnotes

Source: Defillama.

As much as the blockchain technology seems avant-garde, the economic structure of stablecoins is very familiar.
Private institutions have issued money-like claims for centuries. Those systems repeatedly had to solve the same basic problems: can the issuer make good on the promise to redeem; will claims issued by different institutions be accepted and settled at the same value; and what happens when many people want to redeem at once?
The nineteenth-century history of private money is a useful place to start.
In the United Kingdom, private banknotes circulated alongside Bank of England notes. Scotland developed a relatively stable system built around large branch networks, stronger shareholder liability and regular clearing among banks. If a bank issued too many notes, other banks returned them for settlement and it lost reserves. That imposed discipline in normal times.
England had a more fragile structure. Many country banks were small and poorly diversified. This weakness was reinforced by the Bank of England's monopoly on joint-stock banking within London, which limited the development of larger banking institutions. Dozens of banks failed in the crisis of 1825. Parliament responded by allowing larger joint-stock banks outside London.
But stronger banks did not solve the problem of liquidity in a crisis. Reserves and crisis management became increasingly concentrated around the Bank of England. The Bank Charter Act of 1844 tied note issuance more tightly to gold, yet crises followed in 1847, 1857 and 1866. Each time, the statutory limit on note issuance was temporarily relaxed so that the Bank could lend into the panic.
So the UK experience points to two conditions for success. Private money needs mechanisms that keep different claims trading at par in normal times. And it needs a way to provide liquidity when the system comes under stress.
The United States learned much the same lesson, but through a more turbulent route.
During the Free Banking era, banks issued their own notes, and those notes did not necessarily trade at face value. Their value depended on the assets backing them, the reputation of the issuing bank and even the distance from the place of redemption. There were catalogues telling people what different banknotes were worth.
So a dollar was not always simply a dollar.
The National Banking Acts of 1863 and 1864 tried to fix that problem by requiring national banknotes to be backed by US government bonds. The notes became more uniform and the collateral improved.
But another problem remained. The supply of currency could not expand easily when demand for liquidity rose. The panics of 1873, 1893 and 1907 exposed that weakness.
Private clearinghouses tried to fill the gap by providing emergency settlement liquidity. In 1907, J.P. Morgan and others also organized extraordinary support. But the system still depended on improvised private cooperation.
The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 eventually put those crisis-management functions on a permanent national footing.
Across these historical experiences, several conditions for success stand out.
Private money needs credible convertibility, so holders are confident they can redeem at par, and high-quality, transparent backing that makes that promise believable. It also needs a sufficiently uniform regulatory perimeter, so that similar monetary claims are subject to consistent standards, and clearing and settlement arrangements that keep those claims exchanging at par. Finally, there must be credible arrangements for crisis management and loss allocation when the system comes under stress.
Together, these conditions support what Gary Gorton and Jeffery Zhang call the “no questions asked” property of money.footnote [2] A monetary claim works well when people can accept it at face value without having to assess the issuer every time they use it.
Stablecoins have already provided a useful test of that principle.
When Silicon Valley Bank failed in March 2023, Circle - the issuer of the stablecoin called USDC - had about $3.3 billion of reserves deposited there.
Holders suddenly had reason to question whether USDC could still be converted into one dollar. Redemptions accelerated and USDC lost its peg (Figure 3). The peg recovered after US authorities guaranteed all of Silicon Valley Bank’s deposits.footnote [3]

Figure 3: USDC around the failure of Silicon Valley Bank
Deviation from par value (per cent)

Footnotes

Source: Defillama.

The episode showed how a weakness in the institutional structure behind a stablecoin can quickly affect confidence in the token itself.
Regulatory frameworks are now trying to address those weaknesses.
In the US, Congress passed the GENIUS Act in July 2025, creating a federal framework for all payment stablecoins.footnote [4] The Act sets rules for who can issue a stablecoin, what assets must stand behind it, and what happens when a holder wants their money back.
It requires at least one dollar of eligible reserves for every dollar of stablecoins issued. Those reserves can include Treasury securities, bank deposits and other short-term liquid assets. It also strengthens disclosure and gives stablecoin holders priority in insolvency. One implementation challenge will be maintaining consistent standards across its federal and state regulatory regimes.
That goes a long way toward answering one question: are the assets there? The trickier question is: can they be turned into cash quickly when everyone wants to redeem at once?
We saw why that distinction matters during the “dash for cash” at the onset of the pandemic in March 2020. Even the US Treasury market came under severe strain, and the Federal Reserve had to intervene on a very large scale. Assets that are safe and liquid in normal times can become much less liquid in a crisis.footnote [5]
The Federal Reserve has also proposed a new, limited form of account that would allow eligible firms to connect more directly to its payment system. That could make day-to-day settlement more reliable. But it would not allow them to borrow from the Fed, which means there is no pre-established source of emergency liquidity in a run.
The Bank of England’s framework for systemic sterling-denominated stablecoins, which will be finalised at the end of this year, goes further on some of these issues.footnote [6] It is more restrictive about reserve assets and puts more weight on liquidity contingency planning, payment-system access and arrangements for failure. It also allows for the possibility of central-bank liquidity under appropriate conditions.footnote [7]
This framework applies only to systemic stablecoins and is more demanding than the US framework. I think this is appropriate because it gives greater weight to the liquidity and crisis-management problems that recur in the historical record.
Let’s not forget that cross-border use makes these issues even harder. In some regimes, a stablecoin may be issued in one jurisdiction, hold its reserves in another, use a custodian in a third and serve holders in many more.footnote [8] Redemption rights, insolvency treatment, supervision and crisis-management responsibilities do not automatically travel with the token.footnote [9]
International banking spent decades developing home- and host-country responsibilities, common standards and supervisory cooperation. That said, stablecoins may become global much faster than the institutional framework around them.
So, my answer to the first question is a qualified yes. Private digital money can work at scale, but the historical record is clear about the conditions required to make that possible.
2. What happens if dollar stablecoins really do scale?
This brings me to the second question.
Today, about 98 percent of stablecoin value is denominated in US dollars.footnote [10] The dollar therefore has a considerable first-mover advantage as stablecoins move beyond their original role in crypto markets.
The US administration sees this as a strategic opportunity. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued explicitly that dollar stablecoins can reinforce the dollar’s international role and increase demand for US Treasury securities.
There are three main channels through which wider use could matter.
The first channel is settlement. Stablecoin transactions can take place around the clock and cross borders without passing through every link in a correspondent-banking chain. They do not eliminate intermediaries, but they can reduce reliance on traditional banking links. Recent work presented at Jackson Hole just a few weeks ago argues that this could make settlement faster or cheaper where cross-border banking is slow or costly.footnote [11] In 2024, sending a USD 200 remittance cost around 6.4% on average globally, while costs in Sub-Saharan Africa averaged about 8.5%.footnote [12]
The second channel is digital dollarisation. If your local currency is unstable or access to dollar banking is difficult, a dollar stablecoin can put a dollar-linked asset on your phone without requiring a US bank account. Recent work finds that the advantage can be significant in some emerging-market payment corridors with capital controls or segmented foreign-exchange markets, although limited liquidity still constrains scale.footnote [13] This could extend the use of the dollar into new digital markets.
The third channel is demand for US safe assets.
Stablecoin issuers hold reserves against their liabilities, and the GENIUS Act requires reserves to be held in specified highly liquid assets, including short-dated US Treasury securities.footnote [14]
USDT and USDC together held almost $150 billion in Treasury bills at the end of 2025. Their net purchases in that year were around $33 billion (Figure 4).footnote [15]

Figure 4: Holdings of US T-bills Q4 2025, US$ Billions

Footnotes

Source: Ahmed, R. and Aldasoro, I. (2025, revised 2026), Stablecoins and Safe Asset Prices, BIS Working Papers No. 1270; authors' calculations.

Those amounts remain small relative to the Treasury market as a whole, but they make the largest stablecoin issuers meaningful participants in the short-term market.
That additional demand can affect Treasury prices. Recent evidence suggests that stablecoin inflows put modest downward pressure on short-term Treasury yields, consistent with issuers adding to demand for safe and liquid assets.footnote [16]
Of course, the overall effect will depend on where the money comes from. If investors move from a Treasury money-market fund into a stablecoin whose issuer then buys Treasury bills, the net increase in demand for US safe assets is limited. If stablecoins attract funds that would otherwise be held in another currency or another asset class, the effect is larger. If stablecoins instead draw materially from bank deposits, they could also affect bank funding costs and credit supply.
At sufficient scale, these channels could reinforce one another – creating a positive feedback loop. Greater use of dollar stablecoins expands dollar settlement. Issuers hold more Treasury securities. Deep and liquid dollar markets make dollar stablecoins more attractive to users and platforms.

Figure 5: Positive feedback loop

But the same balance sheet can work in reverse. Inflows mean reserve purchases; redemptions mean asset sales.
Remember, like deposits or money market fund investments stablecoins are demandable claims. They can trade around the clock, and holders can seek redemption quickly. Issuers therefore need to turn reserve assets into cash when redemptions rise.
If several large issuers had to sell Treasury bills at the same time, particularly into an already stressed market, they could amplify moves in yields and market liquidity. We saw a similar feedback mechanism in the UK gilt market during the LDI episode in 2022.
And the stress need not begin with the stablecoin. Concerns about US inflation, fiscal sustainability or institutional credibility could weaken demand for dollar assets, with stablecoin redemptions adding to the selling pressure.

Figure 6: Negative feedback loop

The stablecoin sector is not currently large enough for this mechanism to pose a major threat to the Treasury market or a material financial stability risk in UK. However, a major de-pegging episode could also damage confidence in regulated stablecoins more broadly.
US policy is intended to provide space for the sector to grow substantially. If successful, the balance-sheet link between stablecoins and the rest of the dollar system will matter more over time.
Scale therefore brings both benefits and vulnerabilities. Dollar stablecoins could extend dollar settlement, support digital dollarisation and add to demand for safe US assets. At greater scale, they would also create a stronger link between confidence in privately issued money and conditions in the markets where the reserves are held.
3. What would that mean for monetary power?
That brings me to the third question.
When I talk about monetary power, I do not mean only the dollar’s share of reserves or international trade.
I mean control of the system itself. Who provides the monetary anchor, who provides liquidity in a crisis, who writes and enforces the rules, and who can control access to the financial network.
By conventional measures, the dollar remains in a strong position in global finance, although its share of global reserves has declined since the beginning of the century.footnote [17] Its share of disclosed foreign-exchange reserves has fallen from a little over 70 percent around 2000 to about 57 percent in the first quarter of 2026. The decline has been gradual and spread across a range of currencies. The euro remains near 20 percent, while the renminbi accounts for a much smaller share. At the same time, the dollar was on one side of 89.2 percent of over-the-counter foreign-exchange trades in April 2025.footnote [18]

Figure 7: Official Foreign Exchange Reserves by Currency

Footnotes

Source: IMF Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves (COFER) Survey.

Since the end of Bretton Woods in the early 1970s, there has been no promise to convert dollars into gold. The anchor instead has rested on confidence in the fiscal and monetary policies of the United States, as well as in its institutions and legal systems and judiciary.
The sheer economic and geopolitical weight of the US has traditionally reinforced those advantages.
Network effects have made the US more powerful. Firms tend to invoice in currencies widely used by their counterparties. Financial institutions value currencies with deep markets and liquid hedging instruments. US Treasuries provide a large stock of safe assets that are used as reserves, collateral, stores of value and pricing benchmarks.
That safe-asset advantage has historically been valuable to the United States. Investors have been willing to accept lower yields on Treasuries because they are safe and liquid; one influential estimate put that advantage at about 70 basis points.footnote [19] But recent evidence suggests it has weakened. The advantage attached specifically to Treasury securities has fallen sharply, even turning negative at longer maturities, while the broader international advantage of the dollar remains strong.footnote [20]
This financial infrastructure also gives the United States strategic leverage.
Because many international transactions depend on institutions subject to US jurisdiction or on access to dollar markets, US authorities can monitor financial flows, impose sanctions and restrict access to important parts of the financial network. Secondary sanctions can extend those effects beyond US institutions.
The sanctions imposed following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine made the strategic importance of financial infrastructure particularly visible. More broadly, the use of financial sanctions has strengthened the incentive for some governments to develop alternative channels for international payments.
China is the most important example. This is not because the renminbi is close to displacing the dollar, but because China has the economic scale to develop alternative infrastructure.
It has expanded the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, or CIPS, for renminbi-denominated international payments. China has also participated in mBridge, which has experimented with cross-border settlement using wholesale central-bank digital currencies.
These arrangements remain much smaller than the dollar-centred financial system. Their importance lies in the development of additional payment routes that rely less heavily on traditional dollar-based correspondent banking.
This points to an important distinction: the currency and the rails can change at different speeds.
The dollar could remain the leading reserve and financing currency while more cross-border payments move through regional or digital networks that are less centred on the United States. This form of monetary multipolarity does not require another currency to replace the dollar. But it could still reduce US direct control over the infrastructure through which some international payments are made.
Stablecoins can contribute to both sides of this process. Dollar stablecoins can extend dollar settlement into new digital networks. Other countries can use digital currencies, stablecoins or new payment platforms to develop alternative networks.
This competition can improve efficiency and encourage innovation. It can also create fragmentation if systems are not interoperable or if legal, regulatory and liquidity arrangements diverge sharply across jurisdictions.footnote [21]
The strategic question therefore concerns both the currency people choose to use and the infrastructure through which they use it.
The US position remains strong because no competitor currently offers the same combination of deep and liquid capital markets, a large supply of safe assets, convertibility, legal credibility and established global use.
History nevertheless shows that network advantages are persistent rather than permanent.footnote [22]
Sterling is the clearest example.
Before the First World War, sterling bills financed international trade far beyond transactions involving the UK. London was the leading international financial centre. Imperial trade links and the sterling area reinforced a powerful network even after the UK’s relative economic position had begun to weaken.
The transition away from sterling took decades.
War debts strained the UK’s fiscal capacity. The commitment to gold became harder to sustain. Britain’s relative economic weight declined, and its ability to provide international liquidity weakened. At the same time, the United States became a larger economic and financial power.
The shift reflected changing economic strength and changing confidence in the institutions supporting the currency.
That history matters for the current questions about stablecoins and US dollar dominance.
Network effects can reinforce an international currency for a very long time. But, ultimately, they sit on top of fundamentals.
For the dollar, as for any currency, those fundamentals are the same ones I mentioned earlier: sustainable fiscal capacity; credible institutions and policies, including monetary policy; predictable legal institutions and the rule of law; deep and liquid capital markets; and a demonstrated ability to provide liquidity when the financial system is under stress.footnote [23] General government gross as a percent of GDP has been on an upward trend and is projected to increase further, particularly in the US and China (Figure 8).
These are fairly old-fashioned foundations of monetary power. Digital technology does not make them less important.

Figure 8: General government gross debt (per cent of GDP)

Footnotes

Source: International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Economic Outlook Database, April 2026. Chart shows total gross general government debt on an internationally comparable basis. Separately published country measures can use different methodologies.

4. Conclusions
Let me close by returning to my three questions.
First, can private digital money work safely at scale? Yes. History shows that it can, but only when the institutions around it make redemption credible, support exchange at par and provide a way to deal with stress.
Second, what happens if dollar stablecoins really do scale? They could extend dollar settlement, deepen digital dollarisation and add to demand for US safe assets. But greater scale would also create stronger links between stablecoins and the markets in which their reserves are held. This could create financial stability risks that extend past US borders.
And third, what does this mean for international monetary power? History shows that network effects can sustain a dominant currency for a long time, so stablecoins could help reinforce the dollar. At the same time, global payments systems could become more multipolar. But technology cannot secure dollar dominance on its own. As sterling’s experience ultimately showed, that rests squarely on monetary credibility, fiscal capacity, deep capital markets and the rule of law.

Global Markets and EconomyIndustry Perspectives Episode 5GROWTH: Trade, Inflation and Balance SheetsIndustry Perspectives • Podcast • November 05, 2026View TranscriptIn continuing our Industry Perspectives podcast series, we remain focused on the topic of growth. We are joined again by Citi industry experts Rob Rowe and Nathan Sheets in discussing the recent performance of the global economy, looking at the real-world consequences for businesses, nations and individuals.Our latest episode of the Industry Perspectives series unpacks whether the world is really deglobalizing, why inflation may be a bigger threat to trade than politics, and whether surging government debt is a solvency problem or a governance one.Amanda Hale, Director & Head of Regulatory Services, Global Trustee & Fiduciary, CitiAmanda has over 40 years of experience in the investments industry and has been with Citi since 2008. Prior to joining Citi, Amanda worked in the CIS Policy Team at the Financial Services Authority (FSA), now the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) after having been with HSBC for 26 years in various areas such as Trustee and Depositary Services, Custody, Settlements, Corporate Actions and Income. Amanda currently represents Citi on external industry committees and panel discussions as well as chairing various internal Citi regulatory committees. She demonstrates an excellent understanding of the financial services’ regulatory environment. Andrew Newson, Senior Regulatory Technical Analyst, CitiAndrew has 27 years’ experience working in financial services. Joining Citi in 1999, Andrew worked as a Valuations Officer in the Citibank Private Bank before moving to Switzerland to become a Fund Management Support Manager in Zurich, where he managed a small team. On his return to London, Andrew joined Citibank Global Asset Management as Manager of the Fiduciary department, leading a team conducting post-trade compliance monitoring of private bank portfolios, institutional and sovereign wealth mandates, and Luxembourg Mutual Funds.In 2006, Andrew stepped into the funds business as a Fiduciary Relationship Manager, entrusted with managing key client relationships spanning both UK authorised and unauthorised fund structures. Since 2014, Andrew has been a driving force within Citi's Regulatory Services team, where he plays a pivotal role in preparing and delivering high-impact regulatory updates to clients, translating complex regulatory change into clear, actionable insight. Andrew has also represented Citi as its Technical representative at the UK Depositary Association.Rob Rowe, Interim Head of Research, CitiRob Rowe is the Global Head of Citi Research’s Global Strategy & Macro Group (GSMG) as well as Head of Research for the Americas. GSMG unites all of Citi’s Economists with Fixed Income, FX, Equity and Commodities strategists to create a common team providing research on the world’s major economies and asset classes. Rob has been with Citi for well over 30-years serving in various capacities within markets and research. He originally joined Smith Barney Harris Upham & Company in 1989 working in Investment Banking, Fixed Income sales and Research. He has worked in the past as a rates and agency debt strategist and continues to provide portfolio strategy for select clients as part of his previous role overseeing the Global Bond Portfolio Analysis team. He has written numerous articles and publications on fixed income and portfolio strategy.Nathan Sheets, Global Chief Economist, CitiNathan Sheets, Ph.D., is Global Chief Economist at Citi Research. In this role, Nathan leads Citi’s surveillance and forecasting of the global economy and directs the analysis of the firm’s economics team. He interacts closely with Citi’s major institutional clients and internal risk takers and publishes research on cross-cutting themes shaping the global economy and financial markets.Most recently, Nathan was Chief Economist and a member of the senior investment team at PGIM Fixed Income. He also has served as Under Secretary of the U.S. Treasury for International Affairs, representing the U.S. government on international economic issues. Previously, he held positions with Citigroup, as Global Head of International Economics, and with the Federal Reserve Board, as Director of the Division of International Finance and FOMC Economist. In addition, Nathan was a senior advisor to the U.S. Executive Director of the International Monetary Fund and a visiting fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. articles.title: Daily: Chip rout tests AI investment case
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:The AI sell-off and US midterms: Live at the UBS Disruptive Tech Summit (6 mins)
Video: Allocating Assets | Adding FX carry, hedging oil risks, managing volatility(6 mins)
Video: CIO Monthly | Mark Haefele on AI earnings, energy prices, interest rates (4 mins)Thought of the dayWhat happened?
US technology stocks led broader markets lower on Thursday, as the post-election relief rally reversed and investors reassessed the implications of the Democratic gains, especially at the state level, for AI infrastructure and data centers. The Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 fell by around 6.4% and 4.4%, respectively.Semiconductor and AI infrastructure companies were at the center of the decline, including Qualcomm, which fell sharply after its profit outlook disappointed investors. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.3%, extending its drawdown since June to around 38.3%.Pressure extended into Friday, with North Asia's tech-heavy indices leading declines. Japan's Nikkei 225 and South Korea's Kospi closed 6% lower, and Taiwan's benchmark index shed 4.5%. Major European stock indices all stand roughly 1% lower at the time of writing.The sharp risk-off move followed an initial post-election rally, when the removal of political uncertainty and the prospect of policy gridlock were seen as supportive for stocks. Investors now appear to be focusing more closely on how greater congressional oversight and changes in state governments might affect electricity consumption, water use, permitting, and development costs for data centers.Oil and geopolitical developments remained a secondary source of volatility, with Brent crude rebounding to around USD 100 per barrel before coming down to around USD 98 at the time of writing. US Treasuries and perceived safe havens have gained since the market close on Tuesday. The yield on 10-year US Treasuries has fallen by 12 basis points to near 4.84%, while gold is holding near USD 4,070/oz.What do we think?
In our view, the decline reflects uncertainty about the cost and pace of the data center buildout rather than a sudden deterioration in the outlook. It also appears to represent a de-risking event rather than a material change in fundamentals.Further technology volatility would not be surprising. The sector has delivered strong gains in recent years, leaving valuations, expectations, and investor positioning elevated in parts of the market. Investors are hence moving from rewarding spending commitments to demanding clearer evidence of monetization, capacity utilization, potential returns, and the ability to raise capital. The sensitivity of AI-linked stocks to company guidance, regulatory developments, and changes in risk appetite has increased.Greater congressional oversight may indeed increase scrutiny of data center construction and AI regulation. However, except in the event of a widespread AI security issue, we believe broad federal restrictions would likely face legislative and presidential constraints.And while political opposition at a state and local level may delay, relocate, or raise the cost of data center projects, it is unlikely to change underlying demand. Proposed US capacity of around 400 gigawatts already far exceeds our buildout assumption of roughly 90 gigawatts by 2030. We therefore see regulation as potentially redistributing and extending the investment cycle rather than derailing it, with power access, permitting, financing, and execution increasingly separating leaders from laggards.Underlying AI-related demand also remains strong. Recent earnings have shown accelerating cloud revenue and growing advance orders for computing capacity. Recent reports point to significant chip backlogs among Chinese buyers. We forecast aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1.0tr in 2026, USD 1.4tr in 2027, and USD 1.5tr in 2028.For the sell-off to signal a lasting downturn in the AI investment cycle, we think we would need to see evidence that AI-related revenue growth is slowing, cloud utilization is weakening, or lower AI costs are failing to generate sufficient new usage to absorb expanding capacity. We would also reassess the outlook if advances in algorithmic efficiency sharply reduced compute requirements, larger investments failed to produce commensurate gains in AI capabilities, or tighter financial conditions constrained spending by the largest technology platforms and frontier labs.How do we invest?
We see potential for gains in broad equity indices over the next six to 12 months and believe the sell-off looks overdone, given our base case for only modest changes to the outlook for the pace, timing, and cost of data center deployment. We believe the AI investment cycle remains intact, corporate earnings growth is resilient, and a positive global cyclical backdrop should support equities.Nevertheless, we acknowledge that investors may need more certainty about the data center policy environment before volatility fully abates, and we could see a period of market indigestion following the election results. This reinforces the importance of diversification and disciplined portfolio construction.Investors should decide in advance how they would respond to further market swings rather than making allocation decisions during periods of stress. This could include identifying target weights for equities, technology, fixed income, and alternative assets, then addressing allocation gaps progressively as markets move. Structured strategies may enable investors to respond in a disciplined way.Manage concentration risks. Although broad indices were down sharply on Thursday, volatility was even more elevated at the individual stock level. To prepare for potentially greater differentiation within the technology sector in the weeks and months ahead, investors should review portfolios and progressively reduce excessive single-stock concentration relative to technology and broad market benchmarks.Within AI, we prefer diversification over concentrated exposure to individual companies experiencing bottlenecks. We favor financially strong platform and application companies that can monetize growing AI adoption, together with infrastructure businesses that have durable pricing power, strong competitive positions, and access to capital. We are more selective toward highly valued companies whose investment case depends heavily on a single component, capacity constraint, customer, or stage of the data center buildout. Diversified exposure across foundry, compute, networking, power, and other enabling technologies can provide participation in structural growth while reducing dependence on any one bottleneck.Rebalance across sectors and regions. We reduced our sector preferences for US IT and US communication services to Neutral in February. Investors whose US tech exposure has risen materially in recent years and now stands in excess of benchmark weights should consider using opportunities to rebalance toward other sectors. Within equities, our preferred sectors include industrials, health care, and financials. Regionally, we have a relative preference for the Eurozone, emerging markets, and Asia ex-Japan.Build a strong core portfolio. To prepare for possible further equity market volatility ahead, investors with significant bond underweights should prepare for opportunities to rebuild allocations: We see attractive diversification and income potential in fixed income, particularly in high-quality bonds with short- to medium-term maturities and in emerging market bonds. Allocations to alternatives and commodities can also provide investors with exposure to a broader, differentiated range of return drivers beyond traditional asset classes.

Global growth is projected to slow to 2.5 percent in 2026, with emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) facing the weakest per capita income growth since the pandemic. The effects across EMDE regions differ based on direct impact of the conflict, energy exposure, and policy buffers. Risks to the outlook remain skewed to the downside and include escalating hostilities, further commodity market disruptions, and additional geopolitical strains, while broader adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) offers some upside. Policy action is critical: globally to safeguard energy and food security and advance the energy transition, and domestically to control inflation, strengthen fiscal sustainability, and support job creation through investment in physical, human, and digital capital. Compounding pressures from the energy shock, rising debt is driving up sovereign borrowing costs for EMDEs, particularly for those most indebted, underscoring the need for stronger revenue mobilization and improved debt management. Commodity-exporting EMDEs can improve their fiscal resilience by using credible fiscal rules, maintaining well-governed sovereign wealth funds, and diversifying revenue sources to better manage commodity price cycles.PublicationWorld Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2026-08-04) World BankThe World Development Report 2026 assesses what artificial intelligence (AI), as a general-purpose technology, means for 5.6 billion people living in low- and middle-income countries and how it could address development challenges that have resisted solutions for decades. Advancing the AI frontier that relies on semiconductors, data centers, AI-ready training data, and top-level research talent is out of reach for most developing countries in the near term. But adopting AI that is available in the market is not enough because AI’s effectiveness depends on the local context. Adapting AI to solve defined problems in developing countries can do in a decade what might have otherwise taken a century – diagnosing disease, growing small businesses, advising farmers, and delivering public services.

To seize AI’s potential, governments will need to keep strengthening the analog and digital complements that power AI solutions: electricity, internet connectivity, and foundational skills, but also access to compute infrastructure and local language data. Countries will also need to establish frameworks to procure, monitor and evaluate AI applications so that pilots that work well can be deployed on a larger scale. To manage the risks, countries can leverage voluntary standards to facilitate trustworthy AI and turn to existing regulations when markets fail to protect people against the harms of AI. This report urges policy makers in developing countries to be blinded by neither the hype nor the hysteria surrounding AI in the global headlines. It reminds them instead that adopting and adapting AI—with care but without delay—and eventually advancing AI could enable developing countries to solve problems that have resisted solutions for decades.PublicationMissing SDG Gender Indicators (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2023-08-15) Serajuddin, Umar; Beegle, Kathleen; Stacy, Brian; Wadhwa, DivyanshiThe Sustainable Development Goal

a population estimate also had a sex-disaggregated estimate
(which is almost always feasible), the Sustainable
Development Goal gender coverage rate would be 43 percent
instead of 31 percent. Second, better statistical systems
are a major part of the solution, as statistical system
strength is correlated with higher coverage. Third, poorer
countries are doing no worse in reporting on gender-related
Sustainable Development Goal indicators than high-income
countries, despite weaker statistical systems. Lastly,
sizable over (and under) performance in reporting,
conditional on statistical strength, suggests that
country-level advocacy and focus can yield wins in
