There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesTalks at GSHow Aaru Uses Advanced AI Simulations to Predict Human BehaviorNov 5, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyAppleYouTubeDownload TranscriptAaru, a two-and-a-half-year-old startup valued at $1 billion, is redefining market research and consumer intelligence by deploying multi-agent AI simulations to predict how humans will make decisions. Cam Fink, co-founder and CEO, and Ned Koh, co-founder and president, discuss Aaru's founding story and how advanced behavioral simulation overcomes the limitations of traditional consumer polling. In this conversation with Goldman Sachs Chief Information Officer Marco Argenti, they also explore the real-world enterprise applications of such predictive simulations across retail, financial services, and utilities, which are driving Aaru's rapid rise.
Transcript:
Cam Fink: We help you understand the composition of any population on the globe, and what decisions they make. What marketing campaigns they're going to click on, what subway lines they're going to ride.
Ned Koh: Our model is able to process how humans are able to think.
[MUSIC INTRO]
Marco Argenti: Welcome to Talks at GS. And also welcome to Ned and Cam from Aaru. Nowadays with AI almost like anything is possible, including being 19 and then, you know, having a $1 billion valuation startup, which is pretty incredible. So, since then, Aaru has become one of the most closely watched companies in the research and intelligence space. Thank you for being here.
Cam Fink: Thank you, Marco, for hosting us. We're really glad to have the opportunity today to talk a bit more about what we do.
Marco Argenti: The first question I'm going to ask you is, when was the first time you kind of realized that AI was something big?
Cam Fink: So, it's interesting you ask this because the ChatGPT moment was right in our senior year of high school. So, I remember, you know, having worked in the NLP space, in the computer vision space, where Ned and I were researchers before ChatGPT was released. You could tell that like AI was gaining a lot of capabilities very quickly.
But it wasn't until it became actually productized into something consumers could use that all of a sudden it felt like not only was AI going to gain capabilities, but actually that it would create serious change in how people work on, you know, ideas, on products. But even still, like I remember the most enterprising students were already using AI to evaluate their answers to papers or come up with new ideas or test new things.
And if you were even more enterprising before that, you would have been using the GPT-3 API to try and finish papers. So, you know, I think that was truly the moment that it became clear AI was going to be inevitable.
Marco Argenti: Was there another ah-ha moment recently? Because, you know, right now it feels like things are changing so fast. What's another inflection point that you've seen?
Ned Koh: The tools are incredibly powerful for being used for incredibly rudimentary application: note taking, you know, or summarization as like the key use cases or demonstrations of like how this can help you. And I still think in many businesses it is. It's easy to get behind. There's not really any friction to adopting those technologies. And so, I think that the larger change is this wave of product-first AI businesses. You saw that in health care. You saw that in, you know, financial services and beyond. But I think it was when it went beyond just those into more complex applications, for sure.
Marco Argenti: So, rolling back, like, kind of two basics. If you're in front of a CEO that doesn't know what Aaru is and you have a few seconds to explain, what would you say to them? What's your pitch? Like you're 30 second pitch.
Cam Fink: We predict human behavior. So, we help you understand the composition of any population on the globe and what decisions they make. We can help you understand how U.S. household purchase decision makers are going to purchase products, what marketing campaigns they're going to click on, what music they're going to stream, what subway lines they're going to ride. That's really the core of what we do: predicting behavior to make better business decisions.
Marco Argenti: And I think we met maybe two years ago for the first time. So, really early on. So, what have you learned in terms of sort of what kinds of decisions is AI really good at predicting and what others are not that good?
Ned Koh: Yeah, I think the first place that you look when you define what good means is understanding like the relative for how people make those decisions today. Right? So, let's take something that's like very simple - product launches. So, you have someone who's going in front of a survey, you're asking people questions. It's easy to benchmark. And that's a very interesting market. Product innovation is massive for us.
But when you think about like use cases and how that's kind of diverged across the board, the most relevant ones for us and where we offer the most amount of value, of course, are places where you may not traditionally have data. Right? And so, that may exist in a population who doesn't respond to surveys. The example I like to give is like everybody in this room is wearing a shirt. Did anyone tell someone how much they were willing to pay for it? Probably not. Right?
But then you get into like other categories. Right. You know this answer better than I do. But you know, there are four industries that make up about like 15% of the GDP of the U.S. Airlines, telecom, utilities, insurance. What are the times that matter to those companies about their behavior? When do you remember who your cell provider is? When your cell service goes out. When do you remember that you pay bills to Con Ed? When your power goes out. When do you remember that you fly a specific airline versus another? When your flight gets delayed. Right? And so, on and so forth. When do you remember who your insurance is? When you crash a car.
And so, those businesses, despite being massive, the most important place and time for them to understand the behavior of their customers is somewhere where it's fundamentally impossible to get inside their head inside that moment. Right? And so, the most interesting use cases to us have always been those areas that have the most challenging to reach groups. The time frames of traditional research, it can take weeks and weeks or months to get people in a room and ask them questions or show them a product. You don't have the ability to do that. Right?
So, things that are compressed in timeline are the use cases that are most relevant for simulation because human insight just doesn't reach that same level.
Marco Argenti: But why can't you just ask ChatGPT?
Cam Fink: Language models themselves alone can't understand human behavior with the depth and the capability that is required to actually allow a business to trust their decisions. There are a lot of startups out there now doing what you might call synthetic personas. That's sort of like the last generation of the technology we build. They can be useful. Those startups can help you get like a really quick read on marketing copy. But if you want a decision that you can trust, you need something that's grounded in real world outcomes. And that's where someone like Aaru would come in.
Everything we do is AI. Right? So, what underpins our capabilities to predict human behavior are models. Models that we train. Models that leverage LLMs but aren't LLMs alone. But through fusing kind of LLMs with statistical models and traditional mathematical models, we're able to be far more accurate and take advantage of all of LLMs’ advantages without falling into those kind of gaps with LLMs and predicting behavior.
Marco Argenti: And how do you verify the accuracy and the results? I mean, what is what's ground truth for you guys?
Ned Koh: At the end of the day, if you're trying to predict and make a decision better, what you should be aiming for is a better business outcome. That was very first principle to us, right? You want to benchmark it to the sales result, to the product selling better or selling worse or the limited time offer not flying off the shelves like you wanted it to.
The way that we've been able to grow our business so quickly is by making sure that people walk out of a pilot with us and don't just say, "Yes, we came to a decision faster," but rather we came to a decision better than we otherwise would have.
Marco Argenti: So, let's actually kind of bring it to life a little bit with some examples. What does the client actually get? Give us some examples of that.
Cam Fink: So, we do a lot of work with CPG companies. We do a lot of work with retail, beauty, apparel, kind of like anything that touches a consumer brand. And every kind of business ultimately sells a product. But for consumer brands, it's typically really linear. You can hold the product in your hand, right? A canned beverage, a carton of milk, whatever it might be.
So, we do a lot of product innovation work where we'll go work with, you know, a canned sparkling water company, for example. And that sparkling water company will come to us and say, "Hey, we've built this great business around this one core product. What is our next new product line, right? Is it still hydration? Is it a shelf-stable dairy product? Is it an energy drink? Is it--," you know, all of these things.
And we can use Aaru to do everything from the very core conceptual stage of what is the next frontier, right, all the way into figuring out who exactly is the purchasing audience. Then into the product concept itself specifically. So, say we pick out that it's an energy drink. We figure out who the energy drink purchaser is going to be from this brand. And then we figure out, okay, what flavors of energy drink do we want to put out in the world? And then we can do everything from getting as niche as optimizing the caffeine content to helping figure out the right pack size and carry that entire product innovation cycle from start to finish in just a few weeks.
And one of our clients we worked with, their product innovation cycle traditionally was nine months long, right? That's actually pretty quick for the CPG industry. A lot of the big global companies might be taking 12 months, 18 months, to go from product idea or, you know, new market entrant to ready for manufacturing. We managed to squeeze it down into eight weeks. That was a really, really, really powerful case study. And now the product ended up hitting the shelves earlier this year. And they saw more success than they had with any of their previous product launches before.
Marco Argenti: And if I remember, that you guys can decide the size of the core. Tell us a little bit about that spectrum.
Cam Fink: Yeah, we don't go down to individual-by-individual level, right? We're never processing PII or any kind of individual data. So, we can't recreate Tom Smith from Iowa or Cameron Fink from New York City, right? We can get down to audiences that in the real world might only be a couple hundred people.
I remember at one point doing hospitals that have to purchase this third-party risk management software. You're probably talking only a few hundred to low thousands of people nationwide. And yet we were still able to recreate that audience. And for the company that we did do that study for, they saw a massive impact from the work we could do together.
So, we're getting really niche. We can talk about very small groups of buyers or social media influencers or Gen Z in one particular city metro. And then we can go as wide as US household purchase decision-makers or British residents or, you know, even residents of the EU if you want it.
Marco Argenti: And where do you get your data?
Cam Fink: I mean, it's a massive wealth of data sources, right? So, when we talk about how we leverage that data, we have audience data and we have behavioral outcomes data. On the audience data component, that's what helps us understand who actually exists inside of a population. So, when you come to me and you say, "Hey, I want to talk to ultra high net worth individuals in, you know, the United States and Canada," we can actually tell you what the distribution of that population looks like.
And then we have behavioral outcome data. That helps us figure out what decisions are they going to make. So, that would, you know, be for each of these given value propositions, how will UHMW individuals react to them?
Now, when it comes to where that data actually comes from, you can think about three different buckets for each of the data sources that we leverage. The first would be publicly accessible data. We're leveraging tons of things like the census, academic research where there's license to train on top of it, you know, anything else available publicly that our model is able to use.
Then there's a lot of data we purchase. So, we buy data from everyone from credit card, you know, purchase history data providers to receipts, there are music streams, social media data. And then I would say really the final component is proprietary partnerships that we leverage. So, we do a lot of work with organizations that wouldn't fit the shape of traditional customers of ours but still want access to the impact of our software. We have done data sharing through those sorts of engagements before that's been incredibly powerful for what we do too.
Marco Argenti: How do you make your clients comfortable that they can share their most valuable data?
Cam Fink: Every client is sandboxed entirely. We're SOC 2 compliant. I didn't expect that I'd be saying that up on stage. But just in case anyone was worried, we have any InfoSec people in the room, we are SOC 2 compliant. We have all the compliance certifications we can. Most importantly, we do not train on customer data. And all of our clients are sandboxed.
So, we actually end up being trusted as one of the most secure places to store, you know, that data because you would never be able to leverage a traditional research provider for anything sensitive. Right? You wouldn't want to go survey people and then someone takes a screenshot and says, "Hey, you know, my favorite brand was polling me about this on the internet." Instead, when you're leveraging our software, it's kept entirely secure to, you know, the model that we train.
Marco Argenti: You just said the models that we train. So, has your attitude and approach shifted over the years with regards to kind of using your own models versus using frontier models versus using quasi frontier open-source models?
Cam Fink: Yeah, our approach has definitely changed. I mean, when we started the business, we were definitely more in this realm of like, hey, can you take an LLM and train it on top of survey results? We found some of our own issues with that, right? Historically, we found it wasn't extensible. And that's what really led us to the next generation of our technology.
So, those are all the models that we built ourselves. And that was really the big leap forward in terms of how our technology was able to reach the accuracy level that it is today.
And so, we've been on, you know, all of our own models ever since that point in time. LLMs help us write analysis. They help us do tons of tasks as part of the simulation pipeline. But LLMs aren't driving the fundamental underlying prediction and behavior themselves.
Now, when it comes to the LLMs we integrate, we use tons of different providers. We default to whatever is the best provider for each task that we have to do.
Marco Argenti: Which could be, you know, somehow maybe filtering all the data or explaining or prompt interpretation. But then the actual prediction machine or the simulation machine is your own. And that's your secret sauce.
Ned Koh: That is the secret sauce. Every single economist in the history of like behavioral science and everything else that you can go into has dreamed to be able to build a model off of something that's based on outcomes. You want to be able to remove as much bias as possible. Right? And so, not always is the magic and the data exclusively. It's much more in how our model is able to process things that are in many ways useless by their own right into something that can become a holistic view of how humans are able to think.
Marco Argenti: If every customer is protected and everything, how do you evolve the model?
Cam Fink: We're integrating new data sources all the time, right? So, the data that we have alone is enough that we are able to go out and make tons of valuable predictions. We can generate a lot of insight without having to integrate client data. Integrating client data for us is the key to unlock, you know, much deeper capabilities and integrations, both in terms of, you know, the simulation component and also in terms of how simulation results end up getting used.
Marco Argenti: I get that. But within, let's say, client engagement though, let's say we use it in private wealth in GS and then we want to kind of continue to learn, so do you allow your clients to continuously learn on the model that you provide and that stays theirs?
Cam Fink: It's actually interesting. A huge part of what we're talking about now is this idea of compounding intelligence. One of the biggest issues that our clients feel, one of their biggest pains, is this idea that traditional insight is very static, right? You run one survey, you run another survey, maybe you run a quarterly brand tracker, but it's not like those survey results are propelling forth the next survey that you run.
And when you think about simulation, what's really incredible about the difference with our platform is that it's not just the power to like access more accurate, faster results. Our simulations can also contain the insights from all the simulations before it. And what that means is that it actually builds and compounds in value over time.
You can imagine someone using our platform at the end of running nine projects about studying the Gen Z audience together, could come to us and say, "What are the insights, you know, we didn't even know we had about the Gen Z audience?" And that can go into helping build the next product that people might be interested in. So, a big focus for us is that compounding intelligence piece.
Marco Argenti: Are you guys mostly focused on the US, or do you have a lot of international customers?
Cam Fink: Yeah, we're a totally global business in terms of what we support. So, when you think about the range of Aaru today, it's over 130 countries across the globe. All of the EU, all of North America, much of South Asia, Southeast Asia, you know, and beyond. In the future, we are actually planning international expansion starting soon. But today, the bulk of our customers are based in North America.
Marco Argenti: And so, on that note, so do you think you need to tune sort of your models by culture and by countries?
Ned Koh: I think one of the best markets that is super relevant for a lot of the biggest enterprises that we work with today is expansion into Germany is really interesting, right? I've seen this across customers of ours in consumer electronics. I've seen this across customers of ours in financial services, right? Like it really goes across so many areas.
The amount of safety regulations that people care about in like South Florida versus in, you know, Central Germany are vastly different. I can tell you that, right? Like the reality is, you know, you talk about why do we train models within this time when you're actually in runtime? Why do we keep them updated? These sorts of elements. The news, the way they digest social media, the things that changed their environment is what we like to call it within a given sim. Absolutely do. The context of how you and I make decisions on today versus tomorrow, absolutely do change.
Does my race change? No, that's not the most important part to measure. So, we absolutely have to do that and have to do it on a hyper localized basis.
Marco Argenti: What's your biggest bottleneck at this point?
Cam Fink: 100% hiring. Like it's the best people in the world is the number one thing you need for any fast-growing business. And so, when we think about what is going to-- has defined the last six months, going to define the next six months, next six years of Aaru, it's all going to be about working with the best people in the world.
Marco Argenti: And what kind of people are you looking for?
Cam Fink: The first thing that we evaluate for is raw capability. We do look for people who are the best in the world at something. Right? People who are truly excellent at the craft or at their craft, so to speak, and represent the pinnacle of understanding knowledge capability in a given area. That's something that every person wants. Right? I'm sure Goldman wants people who are the best in their craft as well.
We also look for people who are really high slope. So, even if you're not the absolute best in the world at something today, do you have the potential to be that in the future? Can you learn quickly? Can you adapt is something that's really important to us as well.
And then finally, we look for people who are real collaborators. Every time someone joins our team, it's not just about whether or not they themselves are a really, really brilliant individual. Tons of people who are super smart and, you know, would be lucky to work at any incredible business on the globe. We spend a lot of time focusing on who is exactly right for Aaru and the people who have much to teach our team, much to teach myself, but we also have much to teach them and they can be, you know, leverage, exponential or multiplicative leverage to the people around them.
Ned Koh: Most of our research team, right, you'll have people who are pure math backgrounds. You'll have people who have done Alzheimer's and dementia research, right, who are able to tie in these really interesting areas. On the other side, we've recently brought on the head of research and data science from Qualtrics, who was there for over 13 years. Right? It's like you need some of those incredibly experienced perspectives to understand how to solve these problems. But you also need very fresh ones to think outside of the box to be able to do it as well. It's all about a combination and a balance.
Cam Fink: I think what we believed was true when we started this business is still true for the most part. Right? Like, we've always believed in being open communicators. We've always believed internally in, you know, the power of learning from each other, the power of collaboration. I think those are all important things. We've always believed in wanting people who are excellent at their craft.
When we started to think about it, it's that as a growing business, it's actually time to write that down for the first time and distill it into the things that matter most for us. And that is what led us to kind of starting to think more about culture and principles in the last few weeks than we had previously.
Ned Koh: To that point, a really interesting thing that we've been discussing, especially with some of the larger implications of being able to model behavior, is this idea of like trustworthiness of a model. There's a very big difference between being worthy of trust and being a trustworthy company. And we certainly try to stay on the prior, right? We define that as being worthy of trust to the people who work next to you, right? That you're going to do an incredible job. It's being worthy of trust of your investors. It's being worthy of trust of your customers. It's being worthy of trust of the world that you're using the technology for the biggest impacts you can.
Marco Argenti: Ned, Cam, thank you so much.
Ned Koh: Thank you so much for having us, Marco.
Marco Argenti: Was great. And good luck. Thank you so much.
Cam Fink: Thank you. Thank you.

articles.title: Get to know Vanguard Investor Choice
articles.text:
Vanguard Investor Choice

Get to know Vanguard Investor Choice

November 09, 2026

In early 2027, Vanguard Investor Choice will reach more investors than ever, as access extends to all Vanguard U.S. equity index funds, bringing the program to $8 trillion in eligible assets.1

Newly eligible funds will include Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market Index Fund and our full Target Retirement suite. This final expansion will achieve Vanguard’s goal of making Investor Choice available across its full U.S. equity index lineup and will add millions of additional investor voices to the proxy voting ecosystem.
In this article, we answer five key questions about Investor Choice to provide newly eligible and other interested investors with the information they need to know about the world’s largest retail proxy voting choice program.2

What is Vanguard Investor Choice?

Vanguard Investor Choice gives eligible investors an easy, accessible, and free way to have a voice in proxy voting. Investors can choose a proxy voting policy aligned with their perspectives on corporate governance. That policy then directs how their share of Vanguard U.S. equity index funds is voted at public company shareholder meetings on important questions, such as who should be elected to the board and how executive pay should be structured.3
Investors don’t need to select a policy for every issue at every company held in their funds. Through Investor Choice, a single policy selection enables investor voices to be heard on thousands of individual ballot items for the companies held in their eligible Vanguard funds.
How Investors Vote insight: For the 12 months ended June 30, 2026, Investor Choice policy options directed how eligible funds voted on nearly 30,000 unique ballot items across 3,300 company shareholder meetings.

Why does investor choice in proxy voting matter?

Investors hold different views on what proxy voting outcomes are most likely to maximize long-term shareholder returns. Investor Choice was created on the principles that investors deserve the opportunity to easily express those views and that a healthy corporate governance ecosystem benefits from having more investors’ voices heard. Investor Choice empowers investors to express their views by directing how their shares of Vanguard U.S. equity index funds are voted at company shareholder meetings, on votes held to reelect directors, approve compensation packages, and support shareholder rights proposals or not.
How Investors Vote insight: As of July 31, 2026, more than 70% of voting policy selections among eligible mutual fund and ETF holders were for policies other than the Fund Proxy Policy.

Who can participate in Investor Choice?

Effective in early 2027, investors across all Vanguard U.S. equity index funds will be eligible for Investor Choice. Individual investors, their financial advisors, and retirement and 529 plan sponsors can select a voting policy.
Participation is easy. Throughout 2026, Vanguard expanded access to Investor Choice through new technology integrations and industry partnerships, including with ProxyVote.com and BetaNXT, helping more investors to participate through the platforms they already know and trust.
Investors in eligible Vanguard funds can select a voting policy whether they hold their fund directly through Vanguard’s retail brokerage platform or through a third party.4
How Investors Vote insight: More than half a million participating fund shareholders have selected a voting policy for their eligible funds, representing $151 billion in participating assets under management. This includes nearly 80 retirement plan clients with more than one million underlying plan participants.5

Are investors interested in proxy voting choice programs?

Two years of survey data reveal that investors consistently value having their preferences considered and remain interested in participating in proxy choice programs. Among those surveyed, we found that:

Investors continued to place a high value on having their preferences considered by asset managers when casting votes, with a high level of interest holding year-over-year from 83% in 2025 to 85% in 2026.6

More than half of those surveyed expressed interest in participating in proxy voting programs (57% in 2025 versus 55% in 2026).6

The 2026 survey also asked a subset of Vanguard retail clients additional questions about proxy voting, yielding the following insights:

Nearly nine in 10 investors (85%) believed that their preferences should be considered when casting votes for their funds.7

More than half (59%) of self-directed Vanguard clients said they would participate in proxy voting.8

Among investors who work with a financial advisor, 82% said they would like some level of advisor involvement if they choose to participate in a proxy voting program.9

How Investors Vote insight: Participation in Vanguard Investor Choice increased sixfold to over 500,000 investors, and participating assets increased seventeenfold since 2025.

What voting policy options are available, and how can investors make an informed choice?

The current voting policy options available through Investor Choice include the Company Board-Aligned Policy, Egan-Jones Wealth-Focused Policy, Glass Lewis ESG Policy, Mirror Voting Policy, and Fund Proxy Policy.10
Different investors can have different views about governance. The Investor Choice menu is designed to provide investors with a range of straightforward, differentiated policy options that offer different approaches to proxy voting, enabling investors to select one that is aligned with their preferences.
How Investors Vote insight: In 2026, no single policy was selected by more than 38% of investors.
Voting policy descriptions can be found on the Investor Choice webpage, and selections can be made or updated at any time.
Learn more about Vanguard Investor Choice by visiting the webpage or discovering investor participation and policy preferences in our annual How Investors Vote report.

Notes:

1 As of September 30, 2026.
2 Based on eligible assets under management as of July 31, 2026.
3 Voting policies offered through Vanguard Investor Choice apply only to votes at shareholder meetings of public companies registered with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
4 Vanguard Investor Choice is a program offered by the Vanguard equity index funds and not by Vanguard Brokerage Services.
5 Vanguard, as of July 31, 2026.
6 Ipsos Investor Choice Survey: 2025 n=1,010, 2026 n=914 (sample weighted to reflect U.S. population). Investors were defined as respondents who indicated that they have any of the following types of accounts or funds: retirement funds (such as a 401(k), IRA, or Roth IRA); a high-yield savings account; a certificate of deposit (CD) account; a money market account; a brokerage account (such as one in which you choose the stocks, bonds, and mutual funds you invest in); or a managed investment account (such as one in which a financial advisor manages and chooses investments for you).
7 Vanguard Investor Choice Survey: 2026 n=845. Total investors reflect the retail and participant investor market, sourced from the Ipsos panel, and include prospects and natural fallout of survey self-identified Vanguard clients in the general investor population. The figure is the net percentage of respondents stating that it is extremely/very/moderately important for mutual fund/ETF managers to consider investor preferences when casting votes for their funds.
8 Vanguard Investor Choice Survey: 2026 n=232. Self-directed clients reflect Vanguard clients who are self-directed at Vanguard and sourced from Vanguard’s client database.
9 Vanguard Investor Choice Survey: 2026 n=471. Advised Vanguard clients reflect Vanguard clients who are advised at Vanguard and sourced from Vanguard’s client database.
10 The Fund Proxy Policy is the applicable proxy voting policy that has been adopted by either Vanguard Capital Management- or Vanguard Portfolio Management-aligned Funds’ Trustees.

articles.title: Daily: Dip buying lifts US stocks after tech sell-off
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:The AI sell-off and US midterms: Live at the UBS Disruptive Tech Summit (6 mins)
CIO Live Replay: CIO Asia equity strategists on the AI sell-off and opportunities (30 mins)
Circle One Jumpstart: What next for tech volatility, quality bonds, and oil prices? (4 mins)Thought of the dayWhat happened?
US stocks rose sharply on Monday as investors returned to technology and other growth shares after last week’s sell-off. The S&P 500 closed 2.4% higher and the tech-heavy Nasdaq gained 2.7%. The rebound has continued in Asia on Tuesday, with AI-heavy indices in South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan leading the rally, up between 2% and 5%.Semiconductor shares have led the rebound: The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 6.9%, although NVIDIA shares fell 4.3% following the start of an internal investigation into CEO Jensen Huang. The rally was also relatively broad, with most S&P 500 sectors advancing. Consumer discretionary and communication services were among the strongest performers, while airlines and cruise operators benefited from lower expected fuel costs.Oil prices have extended their decline as investors assessed the potential for progress in US-Iran diplomacy. Brent crude oil is down 8% this week to just below USD 90 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate has fallen toward USD 84/bbl. Lower energy costs have eased near-term inflation concerns ahead of Tuesday’s US consumer price report.What do we think?
In our view, the rebound this week primarily reflects dip buying and a reversal of some of last week’s sharp de-risking. The decline in semiconductor and AI infrastructure stocks had been amplified by elevated positioning, high expectations, and uncertainty surrounding data center development. Monday’s advance is consistent with our assessment that the sell-off represented a positioning reset rather than the beginning of a lasting downturn in the AI investment cycle.The breadth of the rally is also encouraging. Last week’s weakness was concentrated in chips, data center companies, and other highly valued growth stocks, while Monday’s gains extended across most sectors. This supports the view that investors are differentiating between companies and parts of the AI ecosystem rather than reassessing the broader outlook for economic growth and corporate earnings.Underlying AI demand also remains robust. Recent earnings have shown accelerating cloud revenue and growing advance orders for computing capacity. We forecast aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1.0tr in 2026, USD 1.4tr in 2027, and USD 1.5tr in 2028. Political and physical constraints may delay, relocate, or raise the cost of data center projects, but they are unlikely to eliminate underlying demand. Regulation may therefore redistribute and extend the investment cycle rather than derail it.But this week's rebound does not remove the risks that contributed to last week’s volatility. Investors are increasingly demanding evidence that rising AI spending will generate sustainable revenue, utilization, and returns. High expectations and concentrated positioning leave individual companies sensitive to changes in guidance, regulation, financing conditions, and market sentiment. Further technology volatility would therefore not be surprising.Lower oil prices provide an additional near-term tailwind by reducing pressure on inflation, consumers, and company costs. But the physical oil market also remains vulnerable following earlier supply disruptions and inventory drawdowns. Diplomatic progress could push prices lower, while renewed attacks or a breakdown in negotiations could quickly reverse the move.Tuesday’s US consumer price report is the next important test. Strong October employment data have kept alive expectations for a December Federal Reserve rate increase. A stronger-than-expected inflation reading could lift bond yields and challenge the equity rebound, while evidence of contained price pressures would support expectations for a measured tightening cycle.How do we invest?
We continue to see potential for gains in broad equity indices over the next six to 12 months. Resilient corporate earnings and economic growth provide a positive backdrop for equities. But the rapid reversal between last week’s sell-off and Monday’s rally reinforces the importance of diversification and disciplined portfolio construction. We highlight three practical ways to do so.First, manage concentration risks. Investors should consider retaining exposure to the structural AI opportunity rather than abandoning the theme after periods of volatility. That said, investors with excessive positions in individual technology companies should use periods of market strength to reduce concentration relative to technology and broad equity benchmarks. Diversified exposure across the AI ecosystem can potentially provide participation in growth while reducing dependence on any single company or bottleneck. We favor established technology platforms with existing computing capacity, visible AI revenues, strong balance sheets, and the ability to finance investment internally.Second, rebalance across sectors and regions. Investors whose technology sector exposure has grown beyond its intended portfolio weight should consider broadening into other sectors. Our preferred US sectors include industrials and health care, and our regional preferences include the Eurozone, where we expect similar 2027 earnings growth to the US but with lower valuations.Third, build a strong multi-asset core. Investors with significant bond underweights should consider rebuilding strategic allocations. High-quality short- and medium-term bonds offer attractive income and can potentially help diversify portfolios during periods of equity volatility. Alternatives and broad commodity exposure can also provide additional sources of potential return and hedge against geopolitical or inflation shocks for investors willing to tolerate the associated risks of investing in these asset classes.

Rising yields raise the portfolio appeal of bonds and diversified investing

articles.title: More than a change of address: Reflections from previous part VIII transfers − speech by Manuel Sales
articles.text:
More than a change of address: Reflections from previous part VIII transfers − speech by Manuel Sales

Given at Association of Financial Mutuals Annual Conference 2026

Published on
05 October 2026

Speech
Opening remarks
Thank you for inviting me to speak today.
Having been in my role for a few months, I have been reflecting on the insights it has given me into how firms operate. One thing that has stood out about mutuals is not just that they are owned by their members, but how that ownership shapes the decisions they make. We can see this in the important role they play in serving parts of the market that may otherwise be underserved.
Against this background, you can understand why the Mutuals Landscape Report sets out our ambition to support the sector’s sustainable long-term growth. What that means will differ from one mutual to another. Many mutuals will continue to operate sustainably. Some will grow organically, while others may pursue acquisitions.
For some mutuals, the strategic challenge is different. They have told us that their current business models may not be sustainable over the longer term. The reasons for this include high levels of competition, keeping pace with technological change, and responding to rapidly-changing economic pressures. Some of these firms are responding by adapting their strategies and exploring new opportunities. Others are considering whether a solvent exit, including through transferring some or all of their business to another firm, may provide the best outcome for their members.
Where the firm being acquired is a friendly society, the transaction will take place through the Part VIII transfer process under the Friendly Societies Act 1992, with the PRA being ultimately responsible for deciding whether a transfer should proceed. While that process is grounded in legislation, we heard feedback that firms would benefit from having a clearer understanding of both the process itself and the factors that inform our decisions. In the Mutuals Landscape Report, we committed to providing more clarity, and CP12/26 (the CP) fulfils that promise. It sets out proposals intended to make our approach clearer and gives firms a more structured sequence of steps to follow. And alongside that, we are also improving the way we manage these transactions internally.
With these initiatives, we aim to promote a dynamic market and support sustainable growth of the mutuals sector.
But the PRA is not the only one working to make this process more efficient. We have also observedfootnote [1] practical approaches developed by firms to improve how these transactions are managed. Today, I want to provide an overview of the Part VIII process. As I do so, I will weave practical insights on how we have seen firms successfully navigate that process, so that others can benefit from the experience of previous transactions.
Reflections from a recent mover
Before turning to those insights, let me take a step back and explain why the process matters.
A Part VIII transfer can offer significant strategic benefits, such as realising economies of scale, improving service standards, and becoming more resilient. All of these improve outcomes for members. But it also requires firms to commit considerable time and resources, with the costs ultimately borne by members. At the PRA, we are very conscious that if a transfer cannot be confirmed, those costs may still have been incurred without the expected benefits being realised. That’s why we work with firms to try to help them build the evidence needed to demonstrate that the legislative requirements have been met.
Meeting those requirements is not just about ticking a legal box. Members rely on the safeguards built into the Part VIII process, including scrutiny by the PRA and FCA, to protect their interests.
So, how should firms approach the Part VIII process?
While no analogy can fully capture the significance of a Part VIII transfer, particularly for mutuals with long histories and strong member communities, it may be helpful in illustrating the process itself, especially for those who are less familiar with Part VIII transfers. The decisions surrounding a transfer are often complex and significant. But when it comes to the process, it has some parallels with moving house. Driving the moving van into your new driveway may feel like the culmination of the journey, but a successful move depends on everything that happened beforehand. You need to understand why you are moving, weigh up the options, complete the necessary checks, and prepare carefully for what follows.
The same is true of a Part VIII transfer.
As the slide shows, we have split that journey into five parts. Let me take each in turn.

Chart 1: Part VIII Transfer Process

Part A: Planning and preparation
Let me start with planning and preparation.
Every house move begins with a reason for moving. When my wife and I bought our home, we spent as much time discussing why we wanted to move as we spent choosing the house. Did we need more space? Or a shorter commute? Once we were clear about our objectives, many of the decisions that followed became easier.
A1: Intention to transfer, A4: Details of transfer plans
When similar questions are considered in the context of a Part VIII transfer, firms may have many avenues to explore. To help firms navigate these factors, the CP highlights the matters the PRA is likely to focus on early in the process, including members' interests.
Of course, firms will generally pursue a transfer because they believe it will deliver better outcomes for members. However, those benefits may not be shared equally between all members, and they may emerge at different times. It is possible that in some circumstances, particular groups of members could be worse off. The key question then is whether the transfer is in the interests of the members of each friendly society participating in the transfer.
Part of answering that question comes from how the benefits are expected to arise. Where a proposal relies on cost savings, operational changes, or integration programmes, those assumptions help explain how the combined business is expected to operate after the transfer. They can provide an important indication of whether there is a credible strategy and a realistic plan to deliver the expected benefits to members.
We have also found it helpful to consider the proposal from another perspective: in what circumstances might some members be worse off? Firms often undertake careful analysis of that question to understand whether potentially adverse impacts have been appropriately considered.
We can work with you as you develop your thinking in this area, which will help with later stages of the transfer. For example, some benefits may depend on integrating the two firms and could take several years to emerge. Whilst there are different ways to ensure that members will be protected in the meantime, the PRA can work with firms to establish what evidence could help show that the legal test has been met. These discussions could inform the transfer documentation, actuarial analysis, and communications with members.
A2: Preparations, updating rules, and applying for permission
Moving on to the preparations step, we have seen firms take a careful and considered approach to the practical aspects of the process. That includes considering whether the acquirer has the necessary regulatory permissions. This matters because permissions do not transfer with the business.
As an extra check, some firms have used the FCA’s register to compare the transferring society’s permission with the acquirer’s permission. This has allowed the acquirer to confirm whether it has identified and addressed any gaps in its permission.
This has also helped firms explain why a permission will no longer be required to cover specific regulated activities and, in doing so, show that the relevant statutory test has been met. These checks may appear relatively small. But when carried out early, they help the wider process run more efficiently.
A3: Considerations of overseas members and regulators
Turning to overseas members, this relates to one of the statutory tests, where the PRA must assess whether there is a substantial risk that the acquirer will be unable legally to carry on the business being transferred. This is usually relatively straightforward for members in the UK, but firms have found it more challenging for members based overseas.
Much of that work begins with a simple question: where are your members based? Maintaining up-to-date member records has helped firms with this work. There are other useful ways of checking those records. Some firms may find it helpful to consider payments to and from non-UK bank accounts to identify any other overseas members.
With that information in hand, firms can consider their overseas members in the context of the legal test and develop a reasoned explanation of why the legal test is met. There is a range of different forms of evidence to consider, from local legal advice to the relevant EIOPA recommendationfootnote [2]. The CP highlights engagement with overseas regulators, which firms may find to be a practical and cost-effective way of exploring the position.
While these steps should help, we recognise that firms continue to face challenges in this area. Indeed, we engaged with the Law Commission on the issue ahead of its recently published proposals. At our recent roundtablefootnote [3], firms also suggested ways in which the PRA could help firms with the overseas member part of the process. We are considering if we can further clarify what information we might need from firms in order for the PRA to assess the legal test under the existing legislation. We will, of course, consider this feedback alongside any responses we receive to the CP.
A5: PRA’s approach to special resolution: consent for Part VIII transfers
Let me turn to the final part of planning and preparation: what many firms call the dispensation process. This is where the acquiring society can seek the PRA's consent for the transfer to be approved by its board, rather than through a special resolution voted on by its members.
Giving the acquirer’s members the opportunity to vote is an important safeguard, so it is not a requirement the PRA will dispense with lightly. But we also recognise that holding a vote comes at a cost, which is ultimately borne by members.
In the past, firms have told us that this is one of the less predictable parts of the process, so we have added more clarity on our approach in the CP. It provides some reference points for how the PRA is likely to consider whether to consent to a dispensation. One of these is that firms will also need to show that the transfer is in the interests of the acquirer’s members and that there are no factors likely to lead a material number of them to vote against it. Firms are likely to benefit from discussing this with their transfer partner and considering this point together.
For example, that collaboration may bring to light a history of tension between the societies that could influence how members would vote if they were given the opportunity. Factors like this don’t necessarily mean that consent couldn’t be granted. But open discussions on such matters can help the PRA understand the position more quickly and reduce the need for further questions.
Part B: Recording and analysing the transfer
Let me move on to recording and analysing the transfer.
Once my family had decided which house to buy, our attention turned to the practicalities. The paperwork began, surveys were commissioned and the important decisions had to be documented.
The same is true of a Part VIII transfer. Once firms have developed their proposal, the focus shifts to documenting the terms of the transfer and analysing its effects.
B1: Instrument of Transfer
Once firms are clear about the purpose and structure of the transaction, that understanding must be captured in the Instrument of Transfer. Producing the Instrument is a statutory requirement, but it can also provide important protections for the members of both firms.
The Instrument can cover a wide range of matters, from service standards to membership rights. We have seen firms benefit from bringing together legal, risk, and actuarial specialists to develop it. It has also helped firms consider not only what is needed to give effect to the transfer, but what additional protections could be provided to members, both now and over the long-term.
Those protections will depend on the circumstances of each transfer. We have seen firms consider important safeguards for the management of transferred funds, appropriate governance arrangements, and commitments about the future treatment of policyholders.
Where with-profits policies are involved, firms have found it helpful to specify the fund to which those policies will be allocated and how expenses will be apportioned. They have also considered what support may be available from other funds, particularly where this could affect the receiving fund’s investment strategy. Setting out these details in the draft Instrument can then provide a clear basis for the actuarial analysis supporting the transfer.
B2: Internal actuarial reports, B3: Independent actuary report and supplementary report(s)
The actuarial analysis is an important part of the process. Internal actuarial reports help boards and regulators understand how a proposed transfer is expected to affect members. Clear and balanced reports can also provide a strong foundation for communications with members, particularly where outcomes are uncertain or depend on judgement. The more useful reports explain the assumptions, evidence, and reasoning behind the conclusions they reach.
In our experience, the more complete internal actuarial reports consider how members are expected to be affected before the transfer, immediately after the transfer, as well as after any integration of the two businesses. This helps all of us – including members – understand both the destination and the journey to get there.
The firms’ own analysis is important. However, in some cases, the process also requires an independent perspective. Much as an independent surveyor provides an objective assessment when someone is purchasing a property, the Independent Actuary provides independent scrutiny of the firms’ analysis. The CP provides greater clarity on when we are likely to require a report from an Independent Actuary. We hope this will help firms better understand the likely costs of a transfer.
Where an Independent Actuary provides a report, the legislation requires it to address the likely effects of the transfer on members who are long-term policyholders. We have found that reports are most useful when they explain both the positive and adverse effects, how those effects may differ between groups of policyholders, and the basis for any conclusions about materiality. Of course, this balanced analysis helps members understand the proposal. But it also supports the PRA’s assessment of whether the transfer is in members’ interests, alongside the FCA’s consideration of fairness.
As an aside, we have found that it is often a good idea for firms to also consider any FCA requirements that apply to the transaction (for example, if the FCA's reattribution rules for with-profits business apply).
There is also an important relationship between the internal actuarial reports and the Independent Actuary’s report. If an internal report contains material information that is not reflected in the summary of the Independent Actuary’s report included in communications sent to members, firms will need to consider whether members have received all the information they need to understand the proposal and make an informed decision. This is one of the statutory tests the PRA must assess. In previous transfers, we have worked with firms to understand how they have met it.
Even where an Independent Actuary is not appointed, another form of independent review may still be valuable. We have seen firms benefit from independent peer review of their internal actuarial analysis and key judgements. This can strengthen the overall assessment and give members greater confidence in the analysis, particularly where they are considering whether to make representations about the proposed transfer.
Part C: Member engagement and member vote(s)
Having considered the key documents supporting a transfer, the next stage is to translate them into communications that members can understand and engage with.
When my family moved house, it wasn’t enough for me to know the plan. Everyone needed to understand what was happening, why it was happening and what it means for them (or, in our case, who was getting the biggest bedroom). Member engagement is similar. The technical analysis may be robust, but it only serves its purpose if members can understand what the transfer means for them.
C1: Member engagement: general approach, C2: Member engagement: Schedule 15 statement, C3: Resolutions
Member communications play an important role in informing how members vote. So, as you would expect, the FCA considers them through the lens of the Consumer Duty, with a focus on ensuring that they are clear and easy to understand. What makes the Part VIII transfer process slightly different is that the PRA also has a statutory role in reviewing one of the key communications sent to members: the Schedule 15 statement.
The CP provides more details on what the PRA considers as part of that review. I want to reflect on some practical approaches that we have seen work well in previous transfers.
The more developed Schedule 15 statements are those that clearly explain what the transfer means for members. They present the key considerations fairly and help members reach their own view. One approach that could work well is testing communications before they are finalised. We have read documents that include all the relevant technical details, but it is not always clear whether these messages are framed in the best way for members to fully understand them. To ensure that the proposed messages can be understood, it may be helpful to run the proposed communications past a colleague who has not been involved in the transfer or seek feedback from a small group of members.
We have also seen the value of careful and balanced drafting. The stronger summaries of the Independent Actuary’s conclusions tend to be those that faithfully reflect the full report while focusing on the matters most relevant to members’ decisions.
Of course, even the clearest communication is only effective if it reaches the people for whom it is intended. The legislation requires the Schedule 15 statement to be sent to all eligible voting members. Where firms have faced challenges contacting members, we have seen a range of practical approaches, including tracing exercises, updating records, using alternative contact methods, and contacting members directly to confirm their details. Firms have also used press notices and other engagement channels to raise awareness of the transfer and the voting process. In some cases, firms have supplemented this with dedicated webpages containing information about the transfer.
Although I have focused on the Schedule 15 statement, we have seen firms engage with their members in different ways. This includes with letters, frequently asked questions, presentations, webinars, and online material. The aim is to help members understand the proposed transfer and give them a genuine opportunity to engage with the proposal before casting their vote. Where members are effectively engaged, it helps firms address issues and reduce the likelihood of unexpected representations arising later in the transfer process.
Part D: Formal application, public notices, and representations
When buying a house, arguably the most important stage is the period leading up to the exchange of contracts. During that stage, surveyors, solicitors, mortgage brokers, and banks can all raise questions, identify risks or challenge assumptions underlying the proposed purchase.
D1: Formal notice of the application
The formal notice of the application plays an important role in the period leading up to the transaction, bringing it to the attention of interested parties and ensuring that those affected have an opportunity to engage with the process.
Firms will submit the formal notice after the member vote. So, whilst the progression of these tasks remains subject to member approval, there is preparatory work we can do ahead of that. In previous transfers, firms have provided draft notices for our review.
The PRA will also direct firms to publish the notice in the London, Edinburgh, or Belfast Gazettes as well as other newspapers where appropriate. However, firms can suggest which Gazette(s) and newspapers they feel would be the most appropriate.
D2: Approach to representations, D3: Representations Hearing
Once the formal notice has been published, the representations period begins. It gives members and other stakeholders an opportunity to raise concerns about the transfer.
But the representations process is about more than formal representations submitted directly to the PRA. Firms also consider whether concerns, complaints, or queries received through their own channels raise issues that are similar in nature to a formal representation. These interactions can provide valuable insight into the matters that are most important to members.
Part E: Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s) and related processes
The final stage of buying a house is exchanging contracts and moving into the property. By that point, much of the hard work has already been done. The legal issues have been addressed and the financing agreed. What remains is to finalise the purchase arrangements. The same principle applies to the final stage of a Part VIII transfer.
E1: Preparations for the Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s), E2: Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s)
The Preclusion Grounds Analysis sits at the heart of this stage. It explains why none of the statutory grounds that would prevent the PRA from confirming the transfer have been met. The stronger submissions tend to be balanced and leverage the evidence already generated throughout the transfer process and present it in a thorough and structured way.
Let me give you an example. When looking at the solvency ground, some firms carefully consider whether the acquiring society will maintain an adequate margin of solvency after the transfer. They bring together the evidence supporting that conclusion, such as post-transfer financial projections, actuarial analysis, audited financial information, and any material changes since the latest valuation date.
We have seen a similar approach taken when considering whether the members’ vote was representative. Firms’ analysis usually explains why the requirements of the legislation and the relevant society rules have been met. The more developed analyses also consider factors such as how voting turnout compares with previous member votes and whether the outcome would have changed under different assumptions. For example, where some members could not be traced despite reasonable efforts being made to contact them, firms could consider whether the outcome of the member vote would have been different if those members had voted against the transfer.
Perhaps the area where we have seen the greatest variation is the assessment of whether the proposed transfer is in the interests of the members of both societies. The more developed analyses bring together actuarial, risk, and legal evidence to consider factors such as benefit security, benefit expectations, service standards, and membership rights. They also identify situations in which some members may be disadvantaged and explain how those risks have been assessed and mitigated.
In considering firms’ post-transfer target operating models, we have taken a proportionate approach, with discussions often centred on three related questions.

How will the enlarged business operate immediately after the transfer?
What is the target operating model?
How does the firm intend to move from one to the other?

E3: The PRA’s decision, E4: Processes after the Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s)
After the PRA has reached its decision, it is not the end of the journey. There are a few procedural steps left including issuing the decision notice and registering the Instrument of Transfer.
Firms will also continue implementing aspects of their target operating model after the transfer has completed. Boards should continue to satisfy themselves that members are seeing the expected benefits from the transfer.
Closing remarks
I appreciate that this statutory process may feel a long and complex journey. But members rely on the safeguards built into the Part VIII process, including scrutiny by the PRA and FCA, so it’s right that we approach the statutory requirements with care.
At the same time, we recognise that members ultimately benefit from an efficient process. CP12/26 sets out our proposals to make our approach clearer, more transparent, and easier to navigate. Your engagement has already informed those proposals, and I would encourage you to respond to the consultation so that we can continue refining our approach together.
I don’t want to close without recognising the important work being undertaken by the Law Commission to modernise the legislative framework for friendly societies. We have engaged with the Law Commission as it has developed its final report and draft bill Opens in a new window. Should any legislative changes be made, the PRA stands ready to update its approach and guidance as necessary.
I hope that what I’ve shared today will highlight that a successful transfer is not simply about completing a transaction or changing an address. It’s about finding the right long-term home for a friendly society’s members.
I am grateful to Hannah-Kousar Rashid for preparing these remarks. I am also grateful to Abi Batchelor, Alex Tapp, Giles Woodruff, Nozipho Gazi, Robert Kipling, Robyn Dwyer, Sanjeev Chandran, and Wayne Snow for their support and comments.

The observations shared in this speech are based on a range of firms and transfers at different times. They are illustrative of the general approach taken. Some details may have been changed or combined from different transfers to ensure confidentiality. As such, the information included should not be considered attributable to any one firm or transfer.
