articles.title: New Bank Start-Up Unit
articles.text:
New Bank Start-up Unit

The New Bank Start-up Unit provides information and support for those thinking of setting up a new bank in the UK.

On this pageIntroductionThinking of becoming a bank in the UK?Engaging with the NBSUNew Bank Pre-application engagementSubmitting the applicationThe application feeThe authorisation (including decision making) processRegulatory expectations as part of the assessment approachThe assessment – authorisation with restrictions (mobilisation)Life as an authorised bank (with restrictions - mobilisation)Life as an authorised bank (without restrictions)Resource links, new banks authorised since 2013 and contact details

Introduction
Firms that want to operate as banks in the UK (see ‘thinking of becoming a bank’ section) must be authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), with the consent of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).
International banks seeking to establish a banking subsidiary and/or branch in the UK should, in parallel with referring to the NBSU website, consult SS5/21 (International banks: The PRA’s approach to branch and subsidiary supervision), as well as the FCA’s Approach to international firms publication Opens in a new window.
The New Bank Start-up Unit (NBSU) is a joint initiative set up by the UK financial regulators, the PRA and the FCA, to provide information and support for firms interested in, or currently applying for, authorisation as a bank in the UK.
To advance the PRA and FCA’s primary and secondary objectives (information on the PRA’s objectives, goals and latest business plan. Information on the FCA objectives Opens in a new window, both regulators will assess whether a firm meets the Threshold Conditions, which are the minimum standards that all firms must meet at their point of authorisation, and on an ongoing basis while operating as a bank.
The Threshold Conditions for the PRA and FCA (below) are set out in Schedule 6 to the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 Opens in a new window.

Legal status: Deposit-takers must be corporates or partnerships;
Location of offices: A UK incorporated corporate body must maintain their head offices and, if one exists, their registered office in the UK;
Prudent conduct of business: The firm must conduct their business in a prudent manner, which includes having appropriate financial and non-financial resources;
Suitability: The firm must satisfy the PRA that they are a ‘fit and proper’ person with regard to all circumstances to conduct a regulated activity; and
Effective supervision: The firm must be capable of being effectively supervised by the PRA.

Effective supervision: The firm must be capable of being effectively supervised by the FCA;
Appropriate non-financial resources: The firm’s non-financial resources must be appropriate in relation to the regulated activities they seek to carry on, having regard to the FCA’s operational objectives;
Suitability: The firm must be a fit and proper person. The firm’s management must have adequate skills and experience and act with integrity (fitness and propriety). The firm must have appropriate policies and procedures in place, and it must appropriately manage conflicts of interest; and
Business model: The firm’s strategy for doing business must be suitable for a person carrying on the regulated activities it undertakes or seeks to carry on and must not pose a risk to the FCA’s objectives.

Thinking of becoming a bank in the UK?A ‘bank’ is an entity that carries out deposit-taking business. The PRA and the FCA glossaries define a ‘bank’ as a firm with a Part 4A permission, which includes accepting deposits and is a credit institution, but is not a credit union, friendly society, or building society.The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 Opens in a new window defines the regulated activity of accepting deposits (see Chapter II Accepting Deposits) and stipulates that, to accept deposits, one of the following statements must be true:a) Money received by way of deposit is lent to others or;
b) A firm uses deposits to materially fund a business line.Firms must consider if their proposed business satisfies the definition of accepting deposits and be able to justify this assessment to regulators. You should also consider the following:

Firms should consider their options for accessing payment systems as early as possible and adequately reflect this in their plans. Payment systems are critical to allow the transfer of funds between people, businesses and financial institutions – new banks are unlikely to be able to operate without access to a payment system. The NBSU encourages firms to consider the guidance on payment systems access.
New banks can access a payment system in the following ways:
Full direct access – where the new bank will have a direct technical and settlement relationship with the payment system provider (PSP);
Direct technical access – where the new bank will have a direct technical relationship with the PSP but use a sponsor for settlement; or,
Indirect access – where an Indirect Access Provider (IAP) acts as the new bank’s sponsor for both technical and settlement sponsorship.
There are a variety of software vendors with products and services that may reduce the cost and complexity of the direct access option, as well as several IAPs providing indirect access offerings. Further information about direct and indirect access can be found on the Payments Systems Regulator Opens in a new window and Payment System Operators’ websites, and in the Code of Conduct for Indirect Access Providers Opens in a new window.

If the firm is already FCA solo-authorised (for example an investment firm seeking to broaden their funding base to take on retail deposits), they will need to apply to vary their permissions to add deposit-taking. Whilst this is a different regulatory transaction, the firm should follow the same authorisation process as fully unauthorised firms. In this instance, the NBSU recommends that, like unauthorised firms, the solo-regulated firm should follow the pre-application stages before applying to become authorised. In addition, the NBSU encourages FCA solo-authorised firms seeking dual authorisation to consider their capital and ownership structures and ensure that those are as simple as possible.

The use of certain sensitive words such as ‘bank’ and ‘banking’ in registered company names is controlled by legislation to prevent the public from being misled. Firms cannot call themselves a ‘bank’ until they have been authorised by the PRA. Prospective firms must take care when liaising with press, prospective investors, and posting on social media, prior to obtaining authorisation.
Firms may begin the application process as ‘Example Ltd’ but only once they are authorised as a bank can they call themselves ‘Example Bank Ltd’.
Firms must seek the FCA’s consent before using domain names that include sensitive words including ‘bank’ and ‘banking’. Further information can be found on the FCA’s sensitive business name Opens in a new window page.

Please refer to ‘Should I become a bank Opens in a new window’ guide to help firms understand whether being a bank is the appropriate model for them.
Are there alternatives to being a bank?
Yes, please refer to the ‘alternatives to being a bank Opens in a new window’ guide for further information on some of the alternatives.

The NBSU is open to listening to proposals and answering any questions you may have - before any significant work has been undertaken towards becoming a bank in the UK. If you have a proposal that you would like to raise or discuss, please email NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk with your proposal/enquiry – someone from the team will get back to you within five working days.

Engaging with the NBSUTo navigate the authorisation process as efficiently as possible and achieve their objective of setting up a bank, firms should be ready, willing and organised. We have provided below some examples of how firms can demonstrate this. Please note that this is not an exhaustive list:
Ready and thinking ahead – Firms should ensure that they have a well thought through proposition which has undergone robust challenge and consideration of the inherent risks (this should also be appropriately reflected into their key documents). Firms should ensure that they will have in place appropriately skilled staff and operational infrastructure to commence trading at the point of being authorised. This includes a robust IT framework, a robust governance framework, risk management framework, premises, and finances;
Willing – Firms should demonstrate that they have done their research, understanding not only the activities that they will be undertaking but the rules and regulations which their business will be governed by; and
Organised – Firms should ensure that they are operationally ready to carry out the regulated activities at the time of their authorisation (if successful).
We aim to have positive regulatory relationships with firms along their journey, from pre-authorisation to becoming authorised and later becoming established banks. We do this by keeping an open and constructive dialogue:

Be open and honest;
Have considered the guidance provided on this website
Provide all the necessary information to undertake our assessments
Notify us of any changes, challenges or concerns as soon as possible
Develop plans, complete the necessary work, and prepare and send materials in good time for meetings with us;
Fully consider and address the feedback we provide on key documents such as the Regulatory Business Plan (RBP)/the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP)/the Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process (ILAAP) documents
Understand, consider and demonstrate how they will meet the required standards at authorisation and on an ongoing basis.

To clearly set out the process and requirements for setting up a bank;
To host pre-application meetings to discuss the firm’s proposals and highlight any concerns;
To provide firms with clear feedback on their proposals including formal written feedback;
We will end our pre-application engagement with firms if our feedback is not adequately addressed in the development of their proposition and key documents
To help firms understand the standards required of being an authorised bank.

New Bank Pre-application engagement
(Optional but recommended)
The NBSU offers firms a ‘complimentary service’, which includes enhanced engagement and support as firms build out their proposals before applying for a banking licence.
Although pre-application engagement is optional and not part of the statutory authorisation process, it is something that the NBSU encourages firms to take advantage of at an early stage (feedback from previous applicant banks has shown how valuable they have found it).
Early engagement allows the NBSU to provide input into the development of regulatory business plans, by guiding potential applicants towards what the PRA and FCA are most interested in, as well as helping them understand regulatory requirements. It also allows the NBSU to identify any significant issues or showstoppers at an early stage.
Pre-application engagement with the NBSU is usually focussed around three stages (although this is flexible and all three stages might not be necessary):
i. business proposition;
ii. draft regulatory business plan; and
iii. technical sessions.
If you would like to take advantage of this complimentary pre-application engagement service, then please contact NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.

Although still early in a firm’s preparations, you will have reached the stage where you can present (usually as a PowerPoint presentation) high level information on your business model, financial forecasts, governance, source of funding, ownership, controllers and risks. You should also provide an indication of the timeframes that you are working towards and indicate whether you will be applying for full authorisation or authorisation with restrictions (also known as mobilisation), as this will impact your planning, as well as the information requirements for your application.
Upon receipt of your business proposition, the NBSU will review and schedule a meeting, typically within three weeks from date of receipt (this meeting may be over MS Teams so progress can be made as efficiently as possible). You will also receive written feedback within three weeks of the meeting.

The RBP forms a critical component of the assessment of a potential application, and therefore the NBSU expects your RBP to already be at a detailed stage prior to submission and should include the following:

Business model and financials covering business strategy, route to profitability, financial projections;
Market analysis and research that underpins the business model assumptions;
Corporate governance setting out board and committee structure as well as proposed approach for recruiting senior managers;
Risk register and stress testing;
Risk management and control framework;
Funding plans, which includes details around the owners and controllers. Where funding is still being sought, you should provide details of your plan to bring in investors;
Conduct risk of harm and consumer duty (if applicable);
Financial Crime Risk Management Framework;
Operational resilience covering outsourcing, IT infrastructure timescales to implement/test and business continuity;
Details of the regulated activities you wish to undertake (please refer to the application form for further information on the regulated activities that can be applied for);
Mobilisation plan (if applicable);

Please refer to the Regulatory Business Plan guide for further information on why an RBP is important, what should be included and the common challenges.
Once you have submitted your RBP (it is useful to be notified of the planned RBP submission date two weeks in advance), the NBSU will review and schedule a face-to-face or hybrid MS Teams meeting, typically within three weeks from date of receipt. You will also receive written feedback within the three weeks following the meeting.

At this stage, the expectation is that you have addressed all the feedback provided and can submit a fully developed RBP. For UK start-ups and subsidiaries of international banks, you will also have drafted and submitted your ICAAP and ILAAP documents by this stage.
The firm’s management team should own ICAAP and ILAAP and be able to discuss these in detail at the technical session. The ICAAP and ILAAP should have gone through a full review and challenge by someone other than the author (the Board or the key guiding minds of the firm), before they are submitted to the NBSU.
At this stage, the PRA will assess the ICAAP and ILAAP, which includes engagement with the relevant technical specialists. The assessment will focus on whether the ICAAP and ILAAP meet the relevant regulatory expectations and consider whether the documents would be sufficient to set capital and liquidity requirements during an application.
The NBSU will also consider the latest RBP to assess if there is any further feedback prior to the firm submitting the application. Further, depending on the nature of the proposed business model and operational design, the FCA may also look to hold focused technical sessions on the financial crime control framework.
Following the submission of the near final RBP, ICAAP and ILAAP, the NBSU will schedule a face to face or hybrid MS Teams meeting. Typically, this will be within six weeks from date of receipt. As this review involves technical specialists, it is important to give both the PRA and FCA as much notice as possible prior to submitting, and to provide at least two weeks' notice, so that both regulators can line up the necessary resource and avoid delays. You will also receive written feedback within three weeks of the meeting.

Submitting the application
The application process commences with the submission of the New Firm Authorisation application (and supporting documentation), and the payment of the PRA and FCA’s non-refundable application fee. It is entirely up to the firm to decide when it should submit its application, but this should be at a point where the firm can demonstrate that their business is ready, willing and organised to be authorised as a bank.
There are two routes available for applying to be a bank in the UK:

Full authorisation; or
Authorisation with restrictions (mobilisation) – this route is primarily targeted at UK start-ups. Although the Threshold Conditions still need to be met, the NBSU’s approach to the information requirements will be proportionate to the restrictions that will be put in place, and therefore will likely result in a quicker authorisation (the information instead will be required during the mobilisation period and will be assessed as part of the application to remove the restrictions). Please refer to the further information on mobilisation.

The application forms
Please note, firms will need to send an email with an electronic copy of their application (and supporting documentation) to the PRA at the following mailbox: NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.
If the file size exceeds 25 MB, please use multiple emails to accommodate your submission.

Full authorisation application form (doc)

Authorisation with restriction (mobilisation) application form (doc)

Branch application form (doc)

Corporate controller form (doc)

Individual controller form (doc)

Partnership controller form (doc)
Trust controller form (doc)

Please refer to Senior Managers Regime where the Long Form A, Short Form A and Form M can be downloaded.

Please refer to Holding company approvals.

Please refer to Banking capital instruments - pre/post-issuance notification (PIN).

This form can be downloaded from the FCA website: FCA IT Controls Form Opens in a new window.

The application fee
The PRA and the FCA Regulatory Transaction fees for applications for new authorisations are payable in accordance with PRA Rulebook Opens in a new window and FCA Handbook Opens in a new window.
The total fee payable (covers both PRA and FCA fees) to seek permission to accept deposits (other than a credit union) is £56,300.
The preferred method for payment is via BACS to the FCA, who will provide a single invoice covering both the PRA and FCA fees.
Please make the payment to the FCA using the details below:
Account name: FCA Collection account
Bank name: Lloyds Bank
Account number: 00828179
Sort code: 30-00-02
Swift code: LOYD GB 2LCTY
Iban code: GB68 LOYD 3000 0200 8281 79.
When you make the payment, please reference it with the following: Title: ‘New authorisation application’ and the ‘firm name’ (name of the firm applying for authorisation).
Please then email your remittance advice and payment details to: fcafees@fca.org.uk and NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.
Information on how to pay the fee is also contained within the application form.
Please note that in the case of a firm withdrawing its application, and later re-submitting another application, they would likely need to pay the full fee again.

The authorisation (including decision making) process
The NBSU will acknowledge receipt of your application within two working days.
Usually, the NBSU will communicate whether your application is complete or incomplete within three weeks of receiving it (if incomplete, the regulators will inform you of any missing information).

For complete applications (i.e., the NBSU has received the application fee and all the necessary applications and supporting documents, which should be of sufficient quality and detail for completion of the assessment) – the PRA targets four months to determine the application (with a statutory timeframe of within six months).
For incomplete applications – the PRA targets 10 months to determine the application (with a statutory timeframe of within twelve months).

During the assessment period the NBSU welcomes regular dialogue and encourages you to reach out as and when you need. The NBSU will keep you informed on the progress of any reviews and proactively highlight any significant risks or issues identified. In addition, the NBSU will typically meet monthly with the firm’s senior management.
The PRA aim to issue a decision as quickly as possible, but this depends on how complete your application is and how promptly you respond to our requests for information. We may have questions or need more details from you during our assessment. Responding quickly and thoroughly will help speed up the process.
The decision-making process:

Both the PRA and FCA will independently decide whether to authorise your bank.
Without FCA consent, the PRA cannot authorise your bank

If authorised, you'll receive:

An authorisation letter
A Scope of Permission Notice detailing your permissions and any requirements
A welcome pack

Your bank’s details will be added to the Financial Services Register on the date shown in the authorisation letter.

Initial notification
If during our assessment of the application we think there are grounds for refusing your application, we'll inform you both verbally and in writing where you'll have time to address our concerns.

Minded to refuse letter
If you can't address the concerns, we'll send you a letter explaining why and which rules or threshold conditions haven't been met.

At this point you can either withdraw your application (and reapply later when issues have been addressed) or, if you want to proceed, the PRA and FCA will follow its decision-making process
Issuing statutory notices (Warning Notices and Decision Notices)
Please refer to SoP1/24 - The Prudential Regulation Authority’s allocation of decision making and approach to supervisory decisions, which sets out

the PRA’s allocation of decision-making regarding statutory notices (Warning Notices, Decision Notices, and Supervisory Notices);
the PRA’s approach to decision-making on statutory notices in relation to supervisory decisions under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000; and
the PRA’s approach to publication of decisions in supervisory cases.

Regulatory expectations as part of the assessment approachThe assessment – full authorisationThe areas that the NBSU assess as part of a new bank application are set out below but should not be considered an exhaustive list. Firms are responsible for considering in detail all relevant laws, rules and regulatory policies, and ensuring that they understand and can fully comply with them.

Read information on ‘regulatory expectations’ (including where expectations are different for branches)
The assessment – authorisation with restrictions (mobilisation)
It is up to firms to propose to the NBSU which activities they complete in mobilisation (please refer to the application form for details of the activities that can be applies for). Therefore, the key for the NBSU’s assessment is that all the design work is complete with a clear plan to deliver everything with a plausible timeframe.
Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

Life as an authorised bank (with restrictions - mobilisation)
Once a new bank is authorised with restrictions, it enters a mobilisation period, which typically lasts no longer than 12 months. During this time, the bank's deposit-taking permission is restricted to a total of £50,000, while it completes the remaining build-out of its operations. This period allows new banks to secure further investment, recruit staff, invest in IT systems, and commit to third-party suppliers, as they are now an authorised bank.
Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

The PRA and FCA anticipate that new banks will want to progress quickly through the mobilisation phase. This could take as little as a few months but cannot continue indefinitely and should take no longer than 12 months. For a new bank to exit mobilisation, they should submit a Variation of Permission (VoP) application via Connect.
Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

Life as an authorised bank (without restrictions)
At this stage, the firm should be fully operational and in a position to fulfil its business proposition as agreed with the PRA and FCA.

Authorisation is only the start of the journey towards becoming an established bank.
New banks must always meet their capital and liquidity regulatory requirements and the Threshold Conditions.
New banks must ensure that they submit their regulatory returns on time and keep up to date with the latest regulatory information.
New banks must ensure that risk management frameworks and controls evolve commensurately with the scale of business growth.
The PRA and FCA will assess how new banks are managing the key prudential and conduct risks, respectively, to their businesses through supervisory engagement.

What could RED IV mean for Europe’s renewable hydrogen market?
A leaked draft of the EU’s post-2030 renewable energy framework points towards a significant change in how renewable hydrogen demand could be supported. If adopted, the proposals could shift the market away from binding EU-level quotas and towards greater national flexibility, wider eligibility and an indicative long-term target

06 November 2026
5 minute read

Email
Share by email

Monica Trilho, Research Analyst – Hydrogen & Derivatives
Mónica is a hydrogen-focused research analyst for the Power & Renewables department.

Close

Monica Trilho
Research Analyst – Hydrogen & Derivatives

Europe’s approach to supporting renewable hydrogen could change significantly after 2030.
The European Commission is developing the fourth Renewable Energy Directive (RED IV), which will shape the EU’s post-2030 renewable energy framework. A draft impact assessment leaked in September 2026 suggests policymakers are considering a different approach to hydrogen from that established under RED III.
The document is not adopted policy. The Commission is expected to publish its legislative proposal before the final framework is negotiated by the European Parliament and Council.
But the direction under consideration raises an important question for the hydrogen industry: if binding EU-level targets become less prominent, what will drive demand after 2030?
How could RED IV change renewable hydrogen requirements?
The leaked assessment points towards a more flexible framework for renewable and low-carbon hydrogen.
In transport, obligations on fuel suppliers could remain, but implementation would increasingly sit at member-state level rather than being driven by a standalone EU-wide quota. The proposals also contemplate broadening the types of hydrogen and electricity sources eligible for compliance.
For industry and refining, the change could be greater still. Instead of continuing the current model of binding national RFNBO requirements, the draft considers moving towards an indicative EU-level hydrogen target for 2040.
That distinction matters. A binding mandate creates a clearer compliance-driven source of demand. An indicative target may give governments and companies more flexibility, but it also puts greater emphasis on the policies, incentives and market mechanisms used to translate ambition into actual hydrogen consumption.
Why is the EU considering a different approach?
The proposals reflect a difficult reality for Europe’s emerging hydrogen market.
Renewable hydrogen has faced persistent challenges around production economics, infrastructure development and demand creation. These conditions have made the pace of market development slower and more uncertain than earlier European ambitions implied.
Broadening eligibility to include additional forms of low-carbon hydrogen could therefore give policymakers another way to support hydrogen deployment while maintaining decarbonisation objectives.
For developers and producers, however, the important issue is not simply the size or structure of a future target. It is whether the framework creates sufficiently predictable demand to support projects and investment decisions.
What would the changes mean for hydrogen producers and developers?
If the framework develops along the lines set out in the leaked assessment, hydrogen producers could face a more varied European market after 2030.
National implementation may become more important, while a broader range of hydrogen production pathways could compete to meet demand. That could create opportunities for some producers, including suppliers outside the EU, while changing the competitive environment for projects developed around the existing RFNBO framework.
The assessment also considers mechanisms intended to connect hydrogen use across different sectors. Depending on their eventual design, these could give producers greater flexibility in how they participate in European compliance markets.
Much will depend on the detail, however. The way targets are translated into national policy, the treatment of different hydrogen pathways and the interaction between industrial and transport demand could all materially affect project economics.
Could removing binding quotas weaken hydrogen demand?
This is arguably the central question raised by the draft.
Replacing binding requirements with a more flexible framework could help address some of the challenges policymakers have encountered in scaling renewable hydrogen. But greater flexibility can also mean less certainty over where demand will emerge and how quickly.
Parts of the hydrogen industry have already argued for continued binding RFNBO requirements beyond 2030, highlighting the tension facing policymakers: balancing achievable decarbonisation rules with enough long-term visibility to support investment.
From Wood Mackenzie’s perspective, the crucial issue will therefore be how policy ambition translates into bankable demand.
The headline targets matter, but so do the mechanisms beneath them: national implementation, incentives, compliance rules and the interaction between transport, industrial and refining demand.
Why does refinery hydrogen matter under RED IV?
One area requiring particular clarification is the treatment of refineries.
Under the existing framework, refinery hydrogen can interact with transport-fuel compliance requirements. The leaked proposals also bring refining into the scope of the future industrial framework.
How policymakers reconcile those two routes will have implications for member states that have developed hydrogen strategies around refinery demand, as well as for producers assessing where future European demand could emerge.
This illustrates a wider issue with the draft: the direction of travel may be becoming clearer, but many of the rules that will ultimately determine commercial outcomes are not.
What should the hydrogen industry watch next?
Three questions will be particularly important as RED IV develops:

How will Europe create durable hydrogen demand if binding EU-level mandates are reduced?

How will industrial, refining and transport demand interact under the new framework?

Will the eventual incentives and compliance mechanisms provide enough certainty to support project development?

The Commission’s eventual proposal will be only the next step. The European Parliament and Council will then shape the legislation before the framework is finalised.
For hydrogen producers, developers and buyers, the significance of RED IV will therefore extend beyond any single target. The bigger question is what type of European hydrogen market the post-2030 rules are designed to create, and whether that framework can provide the demand certainty needed for the sector to scale.
Wood Mackenzie will continue to assess how the evolving RED IV framework could affect hydrogen demand, project economics and market development across Europe and the wider global hydrogen value chain.

Written by:

Will Owens

Topics

research • November 13, 2026

Chart of the Week: How Polymarket Priced Odds of Huang’s Exit

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning. Find our past reports and newsletters at galaxy.com/research. Send feedback to research@galaxy.com. Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia was a slow-building story before it became a fast one. As they say: gradually, then suddenly. The New York Times first reported his close relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, on Oct. 29. On Nov. 8, Huang admitted infidelity in a letter to employees and the company said the board had opened an investigation. At the time, Nvidia said he remained committed to continuing as CEO.

Nevertheless, observers began speculating (in the armchair sense) whether he was on his way out, and financial speculation followed as prediction markets spun up. Initially, they gave low odds for a Huang departure. Then, on Nov. 11, the Times reported Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Within about two hours, Polymarket contracts on whether Huang would leave had repriced from ~17-30% to ~90%. About 12 hours later, Nvidia announced his ouster.Data note: Prices are Polymarket CLOB price history (1-minute fidelity) for each contract’s YES token, with token IDs pulled from the Gamma API. articles.title: Operational resilience of the financial sector
articles.text:
Operational resilience of the financial sector

We make sure banks and financial services firms in the UK can overcome disruption

Related links

Co-ordinating the response to disruption of financial services

On this pageOverviewStrategic outcomesFirm-level outputsSystem-level outputs

Overview
Operational resilience is the ability of firms and the entire financial sector to prevent, adapt, respond to, recover from and learn from disruptions.
Financial firms and financial market infrastructures (FMIs) must have robust plans to deliver important services, no matter the disruption. This includes man-made threats such as physical and cyberattacks, IT system outages and third-party supplier failure. It also includes natural hazards such as fire, flood, severe weather and pandemic. These can affect firms’ safety and soundness, undermine policyholder protection and, in some cases, affect financial stability.
The Bank of England and our Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) carry out this work with the UK's two other financial authorities: the Treasury and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).
Our approach assumes that sometimes disruptions that prevent firms from operating as usual will occur and mean they cannot provide their services for a period.

External links

Operational Resilience - Financial Conduct Authority Opens in a new window
The National Cyber Security Centre Opens in a new window

Prudential and Resolution Policy Index related links

Banking - Operational resilience
Insurance - Operational resilience

Strategic outcomes

Build firms' resilience: when severe but plausible disruption occurs, it should not affect financial stability, safety and soundness or policyholder protection. Firms must ensure high standards of IT and cyber resilience, third-party dependency risks.
Build systemic operational resilience: firms and the Bank work to ensure that when systemic operational risks crystallise, they do not impact the UK's financial stability. Third parties must be sufficiently resilient to support this outcome. It is important that firms can contribute to sector-wide incident response and can learn and evolve from failures.
Manage risks: limit the likelihood and impact of losses. Firms must set aside capital so that the crystallisation of risks is unlikely to affect firm safety and soundness.

The following outputs are designed with these outcomes in mind:

Monetary Policy Committee voting history

Firm-level outputs

Operational resilience policy
Our Financial Policy Committee (FPC) looks at the entire system. Our Prudential Regulation Committee (PRC) and Financial Market Infrastructure Committee (FMIC) focus on the firms and FMIs we regulate.
In summary, we ask firms to:

identify important business services: boards and senior management must prioritise services that, if disrupted, would affect our objectives and the public interest;
set impact tolerances: firms must say to what extent they could continue important business services after severe but plausible disruptions; and
make sure they can stay within impact tolerances: firms must map their important business services and test their capacity to continue to the agreed extent – they should address any vulnerabilities they have identified.

The operational resilience policy SS1/21 requires firms to prepare a written operational resilience self-assessment of compliance. The aim is to document a firms’ resilience journey, identifying risks that could prevent them from delivering important business services within tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios. It helps the firms’ boards and senior management make informed investment decisions to address resilience gaps.
We assess the status of a firm’s implementation of our policy. This includes reviewing:

their important business services, impact tolerances and additional metrics
scenario testing details, results and assurance that the firm can remain within impact tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios
firms’ identification of risks, threats, and vulnerabilities through mapping, testing and live incidents
response and recovery actions, remediation plans and timelines

Self-assessments allow us to identify good practices at an individual firm level while also facilitating thematic comparisons, helping us build a clearer picture of the wider systemic operational resilience picture across the industry.
Incident management and reporting
The PRA has published a policy that details requirements for reporting certain operational incidents, and notification and reporting of material third-party arrangements. It sets out expectations for regulatory reporting, which aim to enhance the PRA’s understanding of firm and sector threats and vulnerabilities.

CP17/24 – Operational resilience: Operational incident and outsourcing and third-party reporting

Third-party management
The PRA’s current policy is set out primarily in Supervisory Statement (SS) 2/21: Outsourcing and third party risk management, which was published in March 2021. The Bank has a near-identical set of policies for FMIs, such as clearing houses and payment systems.
Operational risk framework
Our role is to assess whether a firm's operational risk management framework allows them to effectively identify, assess, monitor, report and manage material operational risks to which it is or might be exposed, in line with board-approved strategy and risk appetite.
We are also responsible for assessing whether firms hold sufficient capital to mitigate the impact when operational risks crystallise.
This supports the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Rules, which require us to assess whether firms’ own funds and internal capital is adequate to cover the level of the risks to which it is or might be exposed and is reflective of the firm’s operational risk profile.
Cyber resilience
Firms and FMIs should assess their cyber risk and build adequate resilience capabilities to prepare for, and respond to, potentially disruptive cyber incidents. To maintain the financial sector's cyber resilience and to support our supervisory oversight, we have developed cyber assessment tools. They include CBEST, STAR-FS and CQUEST.
CBEST
This provides a framework for regulators to work with firms using a simulated cyberattack. This allows firms to explore how to counteract an attack on the people, processes and technology of cyber security controls. We base the simulated attacks on present threats.
The aim is to test:

a firm's defences
its threat intelligence capability
its ability to detect and respond to external and internal attackers

Firms use the assessment to plan how they can strengthen their resilience.
An accredited service provider carries out the simulation, acting within legal, ethical and moral constraints. It aims to get through a firm's defences using the cyber kill chain. They also assess if the confidentiality, integrity or availability of systems and processes that deliver a firm's important business services can be compromised.

CBEST Threat Intelligence-Led Assessments

CBEST thematic review
The annual CBEST thematic is intended to inform the sector on the findings and lessons learned from our CBEST programme, which assesses the cyber resilience of key financial institutions through security testing performed in ‘live’ corporate environments.

2023 CBEST thematic findings
2024 CBEST thematic findings
2025 CBEST thematic findings

STAR-FS
STAR-FS (simulated targeted attack and response assessments for financial services) is part of the PRA and FCA supervisory toolkit, to assess the cyber resilience of firms' important business services. This allows regulators and firms to better understand vulnerabilities and take remedial actions, thereby improving their resilience and, by extension, the wider financial system.
It promotes a threat-led penetration testing approach that mimics the actions of actors' intent on compromising an organisation's important business services as well as the technology assets and people supporting them.
An implementation guide and supporting templates are available. If your firm is interested in conducting a STAR-FS please contact your supervisor. It aims to provide:

an outcome-based assessment of financial institutions' protection, detection and response technical capabilities against cyber-attacks;
an approach, conducted through a firm-led delivery model, that can identify cyber resilience vulnerabilities within systems, people and processes;
reduced regulatory and firm effort relative to other supervisory technical assessments such as CBEST;
levels of independent technical assurance beyond those ordinarily included in firms' own penetration testing programmes; and
a testing approach accessible by a larger number of financial institutions to experience and learn from.

STAR-FS Implementation guide – Threat Intelligence Led Penetration Testing for Financial Services (PDF 2.1MB) Opens in a new window

STAR-FS Detection & Response Assessment Guide (PDF 0.7MB) Opens in a new window

CQUEST
We use the CQUEST (Cyber resilience questionnaire) to gauge the cyber risk and resilience capabilities of the sector. Firms can also use it as a self-assessment tool to consider their own cyber risk and resilience maturity. It comprises 50 questions with multiple-choice answers across six domains:

governance and leadership
identify
protect
detect
respond
recover

To achieve a reliable outcome, an organisation should identify and direct a competent party with appropriate knowledge of the business to complete the CQUEST. When it is used to inform regulatory activities, supervisors might provide additional guidance and/or they could request evidence or clarifying information in response to the answers.
The latest version of CQUEST builds upon the previous one, and encompasses lessons learned from good practice frameworks and feedback from supervisors and firms.

Download the CQUEST

System-level outputs

Collective action and incident response
The Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG) leads sector-wide collective action on operational resilience. It comprises about 25 members: firms across retail, wholesale, FMIs, insurance, the financial authorities and the National Cyber Security Centre. Its co-chairs are senior executives of the PRA and UK Finance.
CMORG has three core objectives:

identify risks to the resilience of the financial sector.
develop solutions to improve the operational resilience of the sector.
share knowledge

Industry has developed CMORG-endorsed capabilities (including good practice guidance, response frameworks and contingency tools) to support the operational resilience of the UK's financial sector. The financial authorities support the development of these capabilities and efforts to improve resilience. However, their use is optional and they do not constitute regulatory rules or supervisory expectations. As such, they may not necessarily represent formal endorsement by the authorities.
Specialist subgroups support CMORG. They design, manage and deliver operational resilience improvements for the sector. Their work is voluntary. Their chairs meet regularly to discuss CMORG's activities and identify areas for more collaboration. A project management office (PMO) also supports CMORG. It is jointly resourced by us and UK Finance.

Find out more about CMORG Opens in a new window

The Financial Services Cyber Collaboration Centre (FSCCC) is a CMORG-led partnership. It aims to help identify, investigate and co-ordinate the response to incidents that may have consequences for the financial sector. It analyses and distributes information to produce timely outputs for the sector's benefit.

The Financial Services Cyber Collaboration Centre (FSCCC)

What happens if there is a disruption?
Firms should get in touch with their usual business or supervisory contacts at the Bank or the FCA. The sector's response is facilitated by the Sector Response Framework (SRF). It sets out how organisations across the sector and government are connected. It also explains how they may respond to incidents when the impact becomes broader than a single firm or FMI and requires co-ordination, information-sharing or collective action.
Its purpose is to:

allow firms, FMIs and the sector to make collective, timely and informed decisions in response to incidents
provide a reference to good practice, contingency tools and plans, which may be invoked as part of a sector response
include decision makers and subject matter experts
be organised on a modular basis, so that components of the SRF can respond
be recognised by the financial authorities as the principal structure by which the sector will respond to incidents
support collaborative engagement between the sector and the UK's financial authorities (see below)
be able to engage with frameworks in other jurisdictions, if required

The UK's three financial authorities are the Bank (including the PRA), the FCA and the Treasury. If disruptions could affect the whole sector, these authorities act together.

Find out about how we co-ordinate our response to the disruption of financial services

Sector exercising
The Bank works with the sector to co-ordinate and deliver exercises to strengthen the operational resilience of the UK's financial system.
The most prominent is SIMEX – a biennial, market-wide simulation conducted through a public-private partnership between industry participants and financial authorities. SIMEX performs a unique role in bringing the sector together to address the most challenging and complex risks that individual firms cannot manage alone.
These sector-wide exercises are based on our collective approach to resilience, working together with industry to identify emerging risks and build capabilities to enhance the system’s overall resilience.

SIMEX 24 – A major market-wide simulation exercise to test the UK's financial sector’s resilience to a major operational disruption
SIMEX 22 – A two-day market-wide simulation exercise to test the UK's financial sector’s resilience to a major operational disruption

Critical third-party oversight
The Bank, the PRA and the FCA (the regulators) are responsible for overseeing critical third parties (CTPs) to the UK's financial sector, following their designation by HMT.
Regulated firms and FMIs are increasingly dependent on a small number of third parties for the delivery of functions and services that are essential to the stability of, or confidence in, the UK's financial system. In some cases, third parties can become so critical that no single firm can adequately monitor or manage the systemic risks they pose.
The aim of oversight is to reduce systemic risks arising from the failure of, or disruption to the systemic services they provide to firms. The regulators will assess CTPs against outcomes-focused rules and expectations with the aim of ensuring the systemic services CTPs provide to the financial sector are resilient and therefore any failure of, or disruption to, those services does not threaten the stability of the UK's financial system.
The CTP regime complements, and does not replace, the existing requirements and expectations for firms on SS1/21 operational resilience and SS2/21 outsourcing and third-party risk management policy.

SS6/24 – Critical third parties to the UK financial sector
PS16/24 – Operational resilience: Critical third parties to the UK financial sector
Approach to the oversight of critical third parties

Find out more about the CTP regime:

Critical Third Parties

Cyber and operational resilience stress test (CORST)
The cyber and operational resilience stress test (formerly the Cyber Stress Test or 'CST') is a key part of the Bank’s toolkit on macroprudential operational resilience. The outcomes of cyber and operational resilience stress testing inform the FPC's monitoring of sector operational resilience and its articulation of its tolerance for disruption to vital services. The objectives of testing are to:

provide insight into sector vulnerabilities and the financial stability impacts and residual risk of severe but plausible operational disruption to vital services
explore firm and sector capabilities to respond to, and recover from operational disruption, and to mitigate its impact on financial stability
share lessons to support firms in maturing their approach to operational resilience and financial stability, including firms' roles as systemic risk managers

We invite firms to participate in CORST on a voluntary basis and they identify their own lessons and remediation actions. Actions that require cross-firm co-operation are often progressed through established collective action forums or voluntary groups.
The test aims, over time to explore all systemically important firms and provide insight into not just the impacts of disruption to the services they provide, but also the impacts to their customer firms and from their third parties. Participation may be direct, indirect through co-operation with a direct participant, or through engagement at cross-firm workshops.
The CST24 thematic letter, which provides thematic findings from the 2024 test, also provides resources to support firms’ role in mitigating potential financial stability impacts of disruption to their services.

Thematic findings from the 2024 cyber stress test
Thematic findings from the 2022 cyber stress test

FPC impact tolerance for financial stability
The FPC updated its impact tolerance for payments and settlements after CST22. This was published in the March 2023 FPC Record:

it expected the financial system to be able to complete critical payments by the end of the value date in severe but plausible scenarios; timely recovery of service delivery was the first best way firms could prevent adverse material economic impacts;
in such instances where restoring services would be harmful for financial stability, or impossible, alternative mitigating actions might be appropriate; firms should, therefore plan, prepare and test for such situations and invest so that their response could effectively mitigate any impact on financial stability until service delivery was restored; and
an example of mitigation may be providing an overdraft to a retail Banking customer, so that they can still make purchases, despite a disruption to the payment systems which may have prevented the normal 'payment' being completed

Financial Policy Summary and Record – March 2023 (see paragraphs 101-108)

In Financial Stability in Focus (FSIF), the FPC noted it would regularly review the operational resilience policy toolkit and will explore ways to continue to build system-wide resilience to operational disruption.
In addition to the tools mentioned above, the FPC does this, for example, through:

assessing potential system-wide gaps in, or risks to, operational resilience which are not adequately covered by firm-level or microprudential policies
considering whether to set impact tolerances for additional vital services beyond payments.

The committee has published its macroprudential approach to operational resilience in FSIF and sets out its priorities twice a year in its Financial Stability Report.

articles.title: What's behind young workers’ job struggles?
articles.text:
Expert insight

What’s behind young workers’ job struggles?

November 05, 2026

Adam Schickling, CFA

Vanguard Senior Economist

Get Vanguard's insights delivered straight to your inbox. Subscribe now

Get Vanguard's insights delivered straight to your inbox. Subscribe now

Entry-level workers often support more experienced colleagues by gathering information, conducting initial research, and handling routine client communications—work that firms can increasingly accomplish with AI. With recent college graduates struggling to find jobs, it’s easy to view AI as the culprit.

The logic is intuitive, but labor market data tell a different story. Our research finds little evidence that AI is the main reason why recent college graduates are struggling to find jobs. In particular:

Employment among recent college graduates in occupations highly exposed to AI remains relatively close to its prepandemic level.

Firms positioned to benefit from AI adoption have hired younger workers at a greater pace than firms less exposed to AI.

In other words, the evidence points elsewhere for the source of young job seekers’ struggles.

Stagnant job environment constrains young workers

To be sure, the current “low-fire, low-hire” labor market, where both new employment and job termination are down, is particularly challenging for young workers. While established workers are benefitting from historically low layoffs, those just entering the workforce depend on hiring to get their start. When companies pull back on hiring, young workers are the first to feel it.
But our research suggests that AI isn’t to blame. Employment of 22- to 26-year-old college graduates in occupations with high AI exposure is only modestly below its benchmark trend, as the chart that follows shows.

Occupations highly exposed to AI persevere

Notes: AI exposure is measured using a task-level framework, mapping AI capabilities identified in the Stanford AI Index to the task composition of roughly 800 occupations and grouping occupations into exposure terciles. Current Population Survey employment estimates cover 22- to 26-year-old college graduates. Employment is X-13 seasonally adjusted with COVID intervention controls and shown as annual averages. Benchmarks extrapolate 2015–2019 employment trends, adjusted after 2019 for slower college-graduate population growth.
Sources: Vanguard calculations, based on data as of September 30, 2026, from O*NET, the Stanford University 2026 AI Index Report, and the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics

We mapped AI capabilities to roughly 800 occupations and grouped them into high, medium, and low AI-exposure categories, then specifically examined activity among 22- to 26-year-old college graduates in each group. The patterns we found don’t line up with an AI-displacement story.
Recent college graduates frequently enter professional and cognitive occupations in which generative AI has relatively high task exposure. If AI were an important driver of recent labor market weakness, that weakness would be expected to be particularly pronounced in occupations highly exposed to AI.
Employment among recent graduates in occupations with high AI exposure is only modestly below its prepandemic trend. The bigger shortfall shows up in occupations with medium AI exposure, and that weakness started before the 2022 introduction of ChatGPT marked the public arrival of AI.
Meanwhile, low-AI-exposure employment has bounced back more strongly, helped along by teenagers leaving the labor force after a pandemic-era surge, freeing up leisure and hospitality positions for older recent graduates.

Employer behavior tells a similar story

Notes: The chart shows the change in the difference between AI-beneficiary and AI-agnostic firms in the measures of gross hires, work separations, and net hires pre-AI (February 2016 through February 2020) and in the AI era (November 2022 through June 2026). AI-beneficiary employers are firms where analyst review identifies clear, material, near-term upside from AI. Benefits may come from AI-related demand, such as compute and infrastructure buildout, or from firms’ own adoption through lower costs, automation, and improved products. Classifications cover large Vanguard plan sponsors across nine industries. Workforce outcomes come from Vanguard 401(k) recordkeeping data.
Sources: Vanguard data, as of September 12, 2026.

A separate Vanguard analysis classifies firms based on how AI is expected to affect their businesses, including firms positioned to benefit from AI-related investment and expected productivity gains.
If the AI displacement narrative were right, AI-beneficiary firms would likely be pulling back hardest on young workers. Instead, since the release of ChatGPT, AI-beneficiary employers have outhired AI-agnostic employers overall. And the net hiring advantage is largest among workers ages 22 to 26. The firms best positioned to leverage AI are hiring more young people, not fewer.

The first step of the talent management ladder

Companies hire young workers for many reasons. For one, given aging demographics, companies expect elevated retirements; those that don’t hire entry-level workers may find their workforce shrinking.
Companies also benefit from representation across the career spectrum. Today’s entry-level workers are the more experienced midcareer workers of tomorrow.
And younger workers are more likely forward-thinking on technology, such as the AI that we foresee automating some tasks, augmenting others, and creating an array of products, services, industries, and occupations that the technology will make possible.

articles.title: On My Mind: Out of the Blue | Franklin Templeton
articles.text:
The US midterm elections have brought about a major political realignment, with the Democratic Party taking decisive control of both the House and the Senate. What are the most likely implications for the economic outlook and financial markets?

Many analysts and commentators have argued that the two most likely consequences are (1) gridlock between the administration and the new Congress, which will narrow the budget deficit, and (2) a slowdown in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investment, which will reduce growth and force the Federal Reserve (Fed) to a less hawkish stance.

I disagree with both.

The best place to start is to understand what voters rejected, what they voted for, and what political parties are willing and likely to deliver. Judging by the exit polls, as well as opinion polls before the ballots were cast, voters were especially dissatisfied with the state of the economy, the Iran war (which also contributed to a higher cost of living), tariffs (ditto) and an immigration policy that went well beyond popular support for greater border control. Voters also expressed a strong dislike for the massive development of AI data centers.

Let’s start with AI. The election outcome will likely lead to several key states, such as Texas and Ohio, adopting a less-welcoming attitude to data centers. While projects that have already secured permits and power will likely go ahead without trouble, the bar for the rest will be higher, and the hyperscalers have already signaled they will be more sensitive to local concerns. In my view, this will probably make the AI infrastructure buildout slower after next year and more expensive: Data centers are less likely to benefit from fiscal incentives and more likely to have to contribute to build new power generation, or pay subsidies to help defray the higher cost of power due to their additional demand, and maybe commit to boosting local employment. These challenges are not insurmountable, but they could increase the cost of the build out.

The adverse fallout on economic activity, however, will likely be moderate. The often-repeated argument that US growth is now almost entirely dependent on AI investment is vastly overstated.

The contribution of AI capital expenditures (capex) to gross domestic product (GDP) growth peaked in the third quarter of this year, when it accounted for 1.4 percentage points out of an annual growth rate of 2.1%. What we and other analysts can measure as AI capex, however, captures more than just AI investment. National accounts statistics provide data on information processing equipment, software, research and development, and data centers as the categories most closely associated with AI. This is the combined measure of capex that peaked at 1.4 percentage points last quarter. Between 2015 and 2022, before generative-AI came onto the scene, this same measure averaged about 0.5 percentage points. The excess attributable to AI is therefore short of one percentage point. Moreover, a lot of the related hardware is imported and therefore needs to be subtracted to get the net contribution to growth. This adjustment would at least halve the contribution of AI capex to growth, bringing it to a more realistic 0.4 to 0.5 percentage points, somewhat less than one-quarter of the US economy's growth rate. Clearly this is a meaningful contribution, but far from the only driver of US growth.

Gross AI Capex Contribution to Year/Year GDP is 1.4 Percentage Points

2018-2026
Percent Y/Y, Y/Y Percentage-Point Contribution

Sources: BEA, Macrobond. Analysis by Franklin Templeton Fixed Income. As of November 10, 2026.

AI capex will not disappear, and these estimates show that even if it were cut in half, it would reduce US GDP growth by less than a quarter of a percentage point, which would still leave the US economy running at about potential. Since AI capex accounts for just over 7% of nominal GDP, the fallout would be modest, including in terms of employment (the same sectors account for about 5% of private payrolls). Finally, some of the slowing AI capex would plausibly be made up by an acceleration in other areas that have more recently been crowded out by the AI boom. The bottom line for me is that the shift in the political wind will make the AI infrastructure buildout slower and more expensive, but without major implications for growth and inflation.

If concerns about the growth impact of AI slowdowns are overblown, I think the idea that a divided government will narrow the fiscal deficit is wishful thinking. If there is one thing that unites the two political sides, it is their desire to spend more. Democratic election campaign featured multiple spending promises, and after the election result prominent Democratic leaders have reiterated their determination to reverse Medicaid cuts, extend Affordable Care Act tax credits, raise the federal minimum wage; reverse cuts to child care tax credits and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and eliminate the State and Local Tax deduction cap. The Republicans for their part have shown little support for fiscal restraint, and if anything are likely to want to spend more in areas like defense.

It seems likely, therefore, that any dealmaking between the two parties will lead to an even wider fiscal deficit. To get a sense of the potential implications, a rough accounting of the measures mentioned above would cost between US$250-US$330 billion on an annual basis over the next 10 years. Repudation of the Trump tariffs would add another US$140 billion per year to the bill. The total of US$390-US$470 billion would be more than one-fifth of the current estimated US$2 trillion budget deficit. This is obviously unrealistic, and the numbers are simply intended to illustrate the scale of the problem—noting also that we are not including here any of the increase in defense spending that the Administration is likely to demand. A divided house will not spend less. It will likely spend more.

The Iran war has proved unpopular on both sides of the spectrum. Leading Democratic politicians have been calling for a cessation of hostilities since before the elections, and after the midterm victory have vowed “we are going to end the war,” in the words of Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer. On this issue, Democrats might find support in the Republican camp, where some have viewed the attack on Iran as a betrayal of the president’s promise not to get embroiled in more “endless wars.” Last September, four Republican senators supported a Democratic-led resolution to end the war or require congressional authorization.

A similar argument holds for tariffs. As noted above, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries identified reversing US President Trump’s tariffs as one of the priorities for the new Congress. Here again, Democrats might find some sympathetic ears on the other side of the aisle. Trump's unpredictable use of high tariffs has increased prices for consumers, raised costs for industries, and made the business environment more volatile and unpredictable. While the relationship with China will remain contentious, there will be a strong push to eliminate or drastically reduce tariffs on our key longstanding trade partners such as Canada and European countries.

Putting this all together, the growth outlook remains healthy, in my view. Looser fiscal policy and potentially lower energy prices, if the Iran crisis is resolved, would be positive for economic activity and would outweigh the limited headwind from a potentially slower pace of AI infrastructure investment. As far as the Fed is concerned, a resilient economy, a strong labor market, and entrenched inflationary pressures will matter more than a potential marginal reduction in price pressures from energy and tariffs. I therefore think the Fed remains on track to deliver another two to three rate hikes, starting most likely in December.

I also think pressure on bond yields will remain to the upside. As I have argued in past articles, I think real yields are not rich yet. The neutral nominal fed funds rate is around 4%-4.50%, in my view, and adding about 1 percentage point of term and risk premium would give us a fair value of 5%-5.50% for 10-year US Treasuries. I expect continued loose fiscal policy will keep generating substantial funding requirements for the government. And as I mentioned above, I think any slack in funding demand created by a potential slowdown in AI infrastructure is likely to be taken up by investment in other sectors of the economy. Upward pressure on yields is therefore likely to persist.

In credit, attractive yields do not necessarily translate into adequate compensation for risk. Despite recent moderate widening, quality-adjusted high-yield spreads sit near the 29th percentile of their range over the past three decades, compared with the 60th percentile over the past five years. Dispersion is significant, however, with CCC spreads near the 99th percentile of their five-year range, signaling material distress among weaker borrowers. While I do not see evidence of broad deterioration in corporate fundamentals, refinancing risks are increasingly important. I favor durable cash flows, manageable refinancing needs and sufficient compensation for downgrade and default risk. The opportunity is to earn income without underwriting a refinancing problem. Follow Sonal Desai, Ph.D. Executive Vice President, Portfolio Manager
Chief Investment Officer

articles.title: Solana Alpenglow
articles.text:
Insights / Perspectives / Alpenglow: What We Learned Running Solana's Biggest Consensus Change

Written by:

Nitish Manivannan
Solana Engineer

Theo Bolognini
Solana Engineer

Will Campbell
Solana Engineer

Products & Services

Staking

perspectives • October 20, 2026

Alpenglow: What We Learned Running Solana's Biggest Consensus Change

TL;DR: Alpenglow, scheduled to go live on Solana mainnet on Wednesday, October 21, changes how validators agree on blocks. Votes move off the chain, finality is designed to drop from seconds to around 150 milliseconds, and a flat 0.8 SOL per-epoch fee replaces per-vote costs. Nothing changes in how stake earns rewards. Galaxy has run Alpenglow on the community test cluster since June 2026, through six re-geneses and the first successful migration, and our validators are ready.Galaxy has operated a validator on Solana's Alpenglow test cluster since June 2026, through six re-geneses (each wiped the chain and restarted it from a fresh genesis block), a migration that failed network-wide, and a rollback. This is what that taught us.Alpenglow is the largest change to Solana's core protocol since the network launched. Designed by Anza, Solana's core development team, it replaces the way validators vote on and finalize blocks, and it is scheduled to activate on mainnet on Wednesday, October 21, at the start of epoch 1064.
How Galaxy Took PartA consensus rewrite cannot be validated on paper. It has to be started, broken, restarted and broken again. That is what Solana's Alpenglow community cluster exists for.It launched in early May 2026 with around 50 independent operators and has since grown to roughly 100 validators. Everyone taking part is a volunteer, running their own hardware across different datacenters and time zones, which surfaces problems that no controlled environment produces.Along the way, we rehearsed failovers between machines in both directions under Alpenglow's stricter rules on double voting.

Figure 1. Galaxy's validator on the Alpenglow community cluster, from joining on June 18, 2026, through six re-geneses, the first successful migration and the first rollback.
What ChangesSince launch, Solana has used TowerBFT, where validators vote by submitting transactions to the chain itself. Vote transactions account for roughly three quarters of everything the network processes and before the recent slot-time reductions, a block took about 12.8 seconds to reach full finality, about 6 seconds at today's 200ms slots. Alpenglow changes both, with a finality target of around 150 milliseconds.Votes leave the chain. Validators exchange votes directly with each other rather than submitting them as transactions. The votes are signed with BLS, so many signatures aggregate into one compact certificate proving that enough stake voted, and that certificate goes into the next block in place of hundreds of individual vote transactions. If 80% of stake votes to notarize a block, it finalizes in a single round; if participation is lower, a second round finalizes it once a 60% notarization certificate and a separate 60% finalization certificate both exist. Both paths run concurrently, and whichever completes first decides.Proof of History retires once the migration completes, because votes now arrive in a single network hop and the chain no longer needs a shared cryptographic clock.A flat fee replaces per-vote fees. Each validator burns a Validator Admission Ticket from its vote account every epoch. SIMD-0357 sets it at the commonly quoted 1.6 SOL, a figure specified against the original 400ms slot and 48-hour epoch. Because the charge scales with slot time, it works out to roughly 0.8 SOL per day at every step, and now that mainnet has reached 200ms, the ticket at activation will be 0.8 SOL per epoch against an epoch of about 24 hours.The fault model changes. Alpenglow is built for what its designers call “20 plus 20”: fewer than 20% of stake actively misbehaving, plus a further 20% simply crashed or offline.TowerBFTAlpenglowByzantine stake tolerated (safety)up to 33%up to 20%Offline stake tolerated on top (liveness)none; the chain can stall above 33% unresponsivea further 20%, so 40% combinedThe total budget rises from 33% to 40%, but the share that may be actively hostile falls from 33% to 20%. That is the tradeoff: less stake is needed to threaten safety, in exchange for tolerating more stake going offline. The designers accepted it because Solana's outages have come from bugs, congestion and correlated crashes rather than coordinated attacks.
Is Voting Cheaper?It helps to separate Alpenglow from the slot-time cuts that finished on October 9. Faster blocks and shorter epochs came from those; Alpenglow brings faster finality, votes off the chain and the flat admission ticket.For the vote itself, the answer is yes. Under TowerBFT, a validator pays a fee on every vote, once per slot, so the slot-time cuts pushed that bill up: about 1 SOL a day at 400ms and about 2 SOL a day at 200ms. The admission ticket replaces it with a flat 0.8 SOL per epoch, roughly 0.8 SOL a day, which is less than half of what validators pay to vote today. Anyone reading the rising vote costs of the last two months as an Alpenglow effect has it the wrong way around: the slot-time cuts raised the cost, and Alpenglow brings it back down.

Figure 2. What a validator pays per day to vote at each slot-time step, against the flat admission ticket that replaces it. Each step is labeled with the date and epoch it took effect on mainnet.The saving is not the whole picture. Half of every vote fee went to the leader of the block that included it, so validators that produce many blocks also collected vote fees, and that income goes away along with vote transactions. The net effect for any one validator depends on how many blocks it produces. And this upgrade is about the cost of voting; the larger costs of running a validator, such as hardware, bandwidth and hosting, are a separate matter.SIMD-0326 does not change how vote rewards are earned. What changes is the accounting: vote credits are now derived from BLS certificates rather than from vote transactions on chain, and on the cost side the admission ticket replaces per-vote fees and is charged to the vote account.
What It Means in PracticeFor anyone building on or settling through Solana, the change that matters is not the headline number but how quickly a transaction becomes safe to rely on. Applications that waited seconds for finality can treat a transaction as final in a fraction of that. For stakers, nothing changes in how stake earns rewards. For validator operators, the cost of voting moves to the vote account.Moving votes off the chain also returns a large share of block space to user activity, and the flat admission ticket gives validators a predictable cost in place of a fee that scaled with how often they voted. A vote account that cannot cover the ticket at an epoch boundary is excluded from consensus for that entire epoch, so the funding operators used to keep in their identity accounts will now belong in the vote account.At Galaxy, an automated top-up service refills each vote account well before it approaches the admission threshold, and balances are continuously alerted on.
The Migration Itself Runs on AgaveValidators have been asked to run an Agave-based client through the migration. Operators on Firedancer can fail over to Agave beforehand and return afterwards, since Firedancer's 26.10 release supports Alpenglow. Frankendancer will not be supported once Alpenglow is active. Galaxy's validators will run Agave through the migration and return to Firedancer once it completes.
What Comes NextAlpenglow is arriving in phases:Phase 1: Votor, the voting change described here.Phase 2: A fast leader handover, letting the next leader start building optimistically rather than waiting for the previous window's decision.Phase 3: Rotor, which flattens block propagation into fewer hops.Slashing for validators that vote twice for conflicting blocks is well defined but deliberately not enabled in the first iteration.Galaxy is one of the largest Solana validator infrastructure operators globally and has tested Alpenglow on the community cluster since June 2026. Our staking and infrastructure solutions give institutions secure, high-performance access to Solana. Get in touch here .
