articles.title: Interest rates and Bank Rate: our latest decision
articles.text:
Interest rates and Bank Rate: our latest decision

Bank Rate affects other interest rates in the economy – we use this as a tool to keep inflation stable

Related links

Borrowing calculator

Savings calculator

Monetary Policy Reports

On this pageOur latest decision: Bank Rate raised to 4%What are interest rates?What is Bank Rate?How do interest rates affect inflation?

Current Bank Rate
4%

Next due: 17 December 2026

Current inflation rate
3.5%

Target: 2%

Our latest decision: Bank Rate raised to 4%

Energy prices have stayed high and volatile due to conflict in the Middle East

Inflation is expected to reach about 5% by mid-2027

We’ve raised Bank Rate to reduce how much rising energy costs affect other prices

Published on 5 November 2026
The Monetary Policy Committee is responsible for maintaining monetary stability by keeping inflation low and stable. It meets eight times a year to decide what level of Bank Rate is needed to return inflation to – or keep it at – the 2% target over time.
Key points:

we have raised Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4%
conflict in the Middle East has disrupted the transportation and supply of energy, raising its price and pushing up households’ motor fuel costs and utility bills
inflation has risen to 3.5% and we expect it to rise even further to about 5% by mid-2027 as higher energy prices have their knock-on effects; higher bills could force businesses to increase their prices to cover the cost, for example
so far, there is little evidence of significant knock-on effects on other prices and wages; but energy costs have been high for long enough now that we expect those knock-on effects to eventually kick in
the economy has been more resilient and activity has been stronger than expected – this is good news, but it adds to the risk that higher energy prices affect other prices; so, we must act now to reduce their impact
raising Bank Rate should help limit how far higher energy costs feed into prices in the economy more generally

Find out more
Read the latest Monetary Policy Summary and Minutes
Read the latest Monetary Policy Report
Read our explainer on interest rates

This video requires third-party analytical cookies to play. Read our cookie policy Opens in a new window for more information.

There is now enough inflationary pressure in the pipeline caused by the rise in energy prices that an increase in Bank Rate is warranted.
Today’s increase shouldn’t be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. But, unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase. The MPC will judge the outlook at each meeting, responding as necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to our 2% target.
Andrew Bailey, Governor

What are interest rates?
Interest is what you pay for borrowing money and what banks pay you for saving money with them.
If you are borrowing money, the interest rate (or lending rate) is the amount you are charged for doing so. If you are a saver, the interest rate (or savings rate) tells you how much money will be paid into your account.
Both are expressed as a percentage of the total amount you have borrowed or saved.
So, if you borrowed £100 with a 1% lending rate, you’d have to pay £101 a year later. If you put £100 into a savings account with a 1% interest rate, you’d have £101 a year later.

Latest and upcoming MPC dates

What is Bank Rate?
It is the core interest rate in the UK and it is our job to set it.
It is the rate of interest we pay to commercial banks, building societies and financial institutions that hold money with us. It is also the rate we charge on loans we may make to them. It, therefore, affects their own lending and savings rates. For example, when we raise the Bank Rate, banks will usually increase how much they charge their customers on loans and the interest they offer on savings. And the reverse if we lower it.

Monetary Policy Committee voting history

Bank Rate over time

Official Bank Rate history data from 1694

How do interest rates affect inflation?
Interest rates influence how much people spend, and that affects how shops and businesses set their prices.
Higher interest rates mean higher payments on many mortgages and loans, meaning people must spend more on them and less on other things. Saving becomes more attractive because the returns are higher and it becomes more expensive to take out a loan. These things all discourage consumers and businesses from spending.
When customers spend less, businesses are less willing or able to raise their prices. When prices don’t go up so quickly, inflation falls.
Lower interest rates can have the reverse effect. If payments on mortgages and loans go down, people will have more money to spend on other things. Savers will get a smaller return and, therefore, may feel less motivated to put their money away. It will be also cheaper for potential borrowers to take out a loan – and use that money to make big purchases.
All of these factors encourage spending. When people spend more, this means demand is high. And when demand is high, businesses often raise their prices, pushing up inflation.

Security and Fraud Awareness
KKR prioritizes the security of our clients’ information and assets and is committed to ensuring that clients and employees are made aware of fraudulent schemes and activities when communicating with KKR. Fraud is an issue that companies may face regardless of size, industry, or country.
While we maintain robust cybersecurity measures, cyber criminals may seek to impersonate or claim affiliation with KKR and create fraudulent websites, email domains, applications, and social media accounts. Fraudsters may pose as legitimate organizations and send emails or make phone calls to extract personal data that can be manipulated for the use of financial crimes. These scams are complex as the perpetrators may use real employee names and replicate proprietary documentation.
KKR encourages clients to be aware of the different types of fraud and to exercise caution when disclosing personal information. To help improve awareness and knowledge, we offer the following information about cyber threats and guidance to help protect from falling victim to a cyber-attack or scam.
When communicating with KKR please note:
KKR does not engage in cold calling or in sending unsolicited messages or emails to clients. KKR only contacts people from official kkr.com e-mail addresses. Confirm you are visiting a KKR authorized website.Do not share your password and login ID with anyone, including anyone from KKR.Do not communicate or deal with personnel who are not affiliated with an authorized KKR office. articles.title: US Data center real estate outperforms as development expands into new markets
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

12 Nov 2026

US Data center real estate outperforms as development expands into new markets

The US data center sector continues to expand as cloud computing and AI drive demand for compute.

US data centers have defied the broader commercial real estate slowdown, delivering an annualized 7.1% return over the past three years, more than triple the 2.1% for all commercial properties, according to NCREIF.

More recently, data center returns have moderated, reaching just 0.4% in Q3 2026 and 2.4% over the past 12 months, as an elevated construction pipeline and higher costs to build, upgrade, and power facilities likely weighed on property valuations despite relatively stable income.

The Bloomberg consensus projects capital spending of the five major hyperscalers will reach $1.17tn in 2027, nearly three times its 2025 level of $412bn, reflecting accelerated investment in AI infrastructure.

Secondary markets in the Midwest, Southeast, and Mountain West are gaining importance for data center supply as power constraints, high costs, and local permitting hurdles limit expansion in established hubs. Less latency-sensitive AI training can occur farther from population centers, reinforcing this shift.

Rising development, equipment, and property improvement costs are putting greater pressure on data center investors. Property capital expenditures nearly doubled to $161 per square foot in 2025, highlighting the expense of maintaining and upgrading existing facilities.

Institutional interest has strengthened in recent years, with large portfolio and entity acquisitions lifting data centers’ share of US commercial real estate transaction volume to nearly 10%, compared with less than 2% historically, according to MSCI.

articles.title: Who holds stablecoins? New evidence on euro area consumer holdings
articles.text: Who holds stablecoins? New evidence on euro area consumer holdingsPrepared by Alexandra Born, Johanne Evrard, Dimitris Georgarakos, Geoff Kenny, Claudia Lambert, Justus Meyer, Trixi Pairan and Luca ZannierPublished as part of the ECB Economic Bulletin, Issue 7/2026.The expanding stablecoin market, its increasing interlinkages with the financial sector and growing consumer holdings could affect financial stability in the euro area. The global stablecoin market has grown rapidly since 2020 but has recently plateaued (Chart A, panel a). At the same time, stablecoins have become increasingly interlinked with the traditional financial sector, particularly through reserve asset holdings.[1] See Ferrari Minesso and Habib (2022). While the euro-denominated stablecoin market has grown, it remains relatively small (Chart A, panel b). Stablecoins are mainly used for crypto trading, although they could potentially also serve as cross-border payment instruments. This box uses unique household-level evidence from a topical module of the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey (CES), carried out in August and November 2025, to assess the extent and composition of euro area consumers’ stablecoin holdings.[2] The CES covers the 11 largest euro area countries. For further information, see Bańkowska et al. (2021), Georgarakos and Kenny (2022) and the ECB’s CES web page. Current exposures in the euro area appear limited, but the concentration of holdings among crypto investors and the prominence of US dollar-backed tokens could amplify shocks. Wider stablecoin use in the euro area, especially outside the crypto ecosystem, could increase the risks to traditional finance over time.[3] A stablecoin’s primary vulnerability is that holders may lose confidence that it can be redeemed at par value, triggering a run. A run on a stablecoin could trigger a fire sale of its reserve assets, which could have an impact on traditional financial markets. See Aerts et al. (2025a) and Aerts et al. (2025b) for further details on the linkages and transmission channels between stablecoins and traditional financial markets. Chart AEvolution of the global stablecoin marketa) Size of US dollar-denominated stablecoins in the crypto-asset ecosystem(USD billions, percentages)b) Market capitalisation of MiCAR-authorised euro-denominated stablecoins(EUR millions)Sources: CoinDesk, CoinMarketCap and ECB calculations.Notes: Market capitalisation is based on the circulating supply of stablecoins. This includes EURC, EURCV, EURAU, EURØP, EURR, EURI, EURe and EURQ. Fluctuations in the share of stablecoins in total crypto market capitalisation are driven mainly by changes in the valuation of other crypto-assets. The latest observations are for September 2026.The use of stablecoins to facilitate transactions in the crypto ecosystem may carry a risk for consumers, as it could affect the traditional financial system.[4] See Bertsch (2023). While the EU has enacted a regulatory framework for stablecoin issuers with the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, which addresses risks from stablecoins for consumers and for financial stability, stablecoins that are not authorised under the Regulation may still pose these risks; see European Systemic Risk Board (2025). Stablecoins enable the trading and exchange of fiat currencies for non-stablecoin crypto-assets and vice versa.[5] See Chart A.6 in Aerts et al. (2025a). The reserve assets that back stablecoins link them to the traditional financial system, which can potentially lead to spillover effects.[6] Runs on stablecoins could force issuers to liquidate assets in order to satisfy redemption demands. See European Systemic Risk Board (2025) and Aerts et al. (2025a). Stablecoins may also enable low-cost cross-border payments, which could be an option for consumers sending money outside the euro area, though evidence on this use case is mixed.[7] See, for example, Di Iorio et al. (2026) or Vlaicu (2026). Euro area consumers are slowly increasing their direct exposure to crypto-assets, from low levels.[8] We rely on experimental data from the August and November 2025 waves of the CES. Data cover both consumer ownership of stablecoins and the approximate value of consumer holdings. Responses are subject to measurement uncertainty reflecting the experimental nature of the data, including sensitivity to questionnaire design and small samples given the small percentage of consumers that own crypto-assets. Respondents may also misreport asset types and their holdings owing to a perceived sensitivity of such information. The share of consumers owning crypto-assets increased from 9.8% in November 2024 to 13% in August 2025 (Chart B, panel a), a period in which crypto markets and stablecoins were growing rapidly (Chart A). The 2025 CES results distinguish stablecoin holdings within consumer crypto-asset exposures: in August 5% of consumers reported holding stablecoins, which was over a third of all consumers that held crypto-assets. The estimated distribution of stablecoin holdings in terms of amounts invested is skewed towards smaller amounts (Chart B, panel b). However, close to 10% of stablecoin owners are estimated to have had holdings of €10,000 or more in November, pointing to a substantial range.Chart BConsumer holdings of crypto-assetsa) Stablecoin and crypto-asset ownership(percentages of consumers)b) Estimates of stablecoin holdings(percentages of consumers with stablecoin holdings)Sources: ECB Consumer Expectations Survey and ECB calculations.Notes: Population-weighted data from 11 euro area countries. Panel a): experimental data from the August 2025 CES topical module. Consumers were asked: “Do you or any members of your household currently own crypto-assets?”, and as a separate follow-up: “Which of the following do you or someone of your household currently own?” Panel b): experimental data from the November 2025 CES topical module. Consumers who reported any investment in crypto-assets (including stablecoins) were asked: “To the best of your knowledge, what is the main type of crypto-assets you and your household currently own?” and could choose on a five-point scale from “fully invested in crypto-assets other than stablecoins” to “fully invested in stablecoins”. We assign weights in 0.25 steps, ranging from 0 (only crypto other than stablecoins) to 1 (only stablecoins) and calculate the stablecoin investment on the basis of self-reported crypto investments.Dollar-denominated stablecoins dominate euro area consumer exposure, as consumers tend to hold the crypto-assets with the largest market capitalisation. Around 63% of consumers with a crypto exposure hold bitcoin, followed by ether (36%) and XRP (22%) (Chart C, panel a). Among stablecoins, USDT is the most widely held (17% of consumers with crypto holdings), ahead of USDC (12%) and the euro-denominated EURC (10%). Other euro-denominated and non-euro-denominated stablecoins combined account for less than 9% of reported holdings. Although the survey does not directly report how assets are used, preliminary evidence shows higher usage among respondents born either in another EU country or outside the EU. Foreign-born respondents were found to be 2.1 percentage points more likely to hold stablecoins than domestic consumers after taking into account other characteristics. This pattern is consistent with the possibility that stablecoins are being used for cross-border payments or remittances.Chart CComposition of consumer crypto-asset investmentsa) Composition of crypto-asset and stablecoin investmentsb) Stablecoins as a share of financial assets(percentages of consumers with crypto-asset holdings)(percentages of portfolio)Sources: ECB Consumer Expectations Survey and ECB calculations.Notes: Data from 11 euro area countries. Panel a): experimental data from the August 2025 CES topical module. The panel shows the types of crypto-asset and stablecoin held by respondents who reported owning crypto-assets. Given the small percentage of respondents that owned crypto-assets, observations are also limited (1,286 respondents). As respondents could select multiple assets, shares do not add up to 100%. “Other” captures holdings not listed separately in the questionnaire. Panel b): experimental data from the November 2025 CES topical module. The panel shows average stablecoin portfolio shares based on the estimated amounts shown in Chart B, panel b and the total value of consumers’ financial assets (e.g. in bank accounts, stocks and mutual funds). Estimates are weighted using population weights.The use of stablecoins as transactional assets could have broader implications for financial stability if adoption continues to grow. Stablecoins account for a small share of consumers’ financial assets and are mostly held alongside other crypto-assets. This is consistent with their main use as transactional assets within the crypto-asset ecosystem (Chart C). While the relatively low usage of stablecoins in the euro area limits immediate risks to bank funding, it points to three vulnerabilities for the future if stablecoins were to become significantly more widely used: (i) exposure to runs on stablecoins and “de-pegging” events, when stablecoins deviate significantly from their par value; (ii) potential spillovers from a liquidation of US dollar stablecoin reserves; and (iii) a possible currency substitution channel. If the use of dollar-denominated stablecoins by euro area consumers begins to extend beyond crypto-asset transactions, their holdings of non-euro stablecoins could grow. Depending on the scale of adoption, this could affect deposit funding, monetary transmission and the role of euro-denominated payment instruments.[9] See Altavilla et al. (2026). Given the importance of stablecoins in the crypto ecosystem, a large shock to a stablecoin (e.g. a de-pegging event) could be detrimental.[10] See Du et al. (2025). As most stablecoin holders also own other crypto-assets, their wider portfolio would be affected. Conversely, an adverse shock to crypto-asset prices could trigger a stablecoin sell-off, potentially de-pegging stablecoins and causing additional wealth effects. The dual holdings suggest that stablecoin usage acts as a two-way channel between crypto-assets and investor wealth. Shocks may also harm investors’ trust in stablecoins, further contributing to crypto market instability.[11] See Vidal-Tomás (2025). Volatile crypto-asset valuations may pose a risk to investor confidence through stablecoins.The CES data suggest that while current holdings pose limited risks to euro area financial stability, this could change if stablecoin adoption were to broaden significantly. As the market continues to develop, euro area consumers may increasingly hold private, non-bank and non-euro stablecoins – especially as younger, more crypto-inclined cohorts enter these markets. While spillover risks from cross-border regulatory arbitrage may persist, the EU has implemented a robust regulatory framework through the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation which reduces many of the risks discussed. Monitoring consumer exposures and contagion channels remains essential to support consumer confidence and limit risks to consumer wealth.ReferencesAerts, S., Born, A., Gati, Z., Kochanska, U., Lambert, C., Reinhold, E. and van der Kraaij, A. (2025a), “Just another crypto boom? Mind the blind spots”, Financial Stability Review, ECB, May.Aerts, S., Lambert, C. and Reinhold, E. articles.title: The AI Boom's Two Engines
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

The AI Boom's Two Engines

Jason Furman (PIIE)

Date
November 9, 2026 1:48 PM

This blog post was originally published on PIIE senior fellow Jason Furman's Econvitals.org(link is external) website and republished here with permission. Furman wrote the blog post with assistance from AI (see his website(link is external) for details).

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
Econvitals just added a Macroeconomic Simulator(link is external) that lets you use the Federal Reserve's FRB/US model to simulate policies like Fed rate hikes and tax cuts, as well as shocks like an oil price spike or a fall in stock prices. Much of this post uses the same model to do a "what if" analysis of the data center buildout. The full analysis, along with many more "what if" counterfactuals for economic events from the financial crisis to the present, is on my personal webpage(link is external).

The data center buildout is set to be among the largest investment expansions in peacetime American history. How different is our economy today because of it? The answer, based on a simulation using the large-scale macroeconomic model used by the Federal Reserve (FRB/US), is not much. The buildout by itself has raised GDP by only about 0.3 percent, because most of the investment is imported, and imports do not add to U.S. GDP or lower the unemployment rate. The stock market boom that came with it matters more—together they have raised GDP by about 0.6 percent and lowered the unemployment rate by about 0.3 percentage point. If the stock market gains go away, they could take much of that growth with them.
To date, the AI boom has shown up in a large and clear manner on the demand side of the economy, through both the AI buildout itself and the associated stock market boom—which in turn is fueling demand. I believe we are also beginning to see a small increase in supply due to the higher productivity associated with AI. If you squint, you can see signs of it, but they are debatable and not large, and they are not included in this analysis—nor are any direct productivity benefits of the capital spending on the AI buildout.
These demand shocks are hitting an economy that was already at what the Federal Reserve considers full employment, with inflation above the Fed's target. Some of the extra demand can bleed through to the overall economy, but in a situation like this, effectively managed monetary policy will try to make sure that not too much of it does—so interest rates go up, which creates a headwind for interest-sensitive investment in areas like housing, and some of it shows up as output temporarily exceeding potential.
The table below summarizes the main results of the simulations. I should say at the outset that this is just one model, not the definitive truth. A full answer to this question should be based on multiple ways of approaching the problem. But at least the Fed's model is internally consistent and plausible, a big improvement over many of the other answers floating around in the discussion.

The Fed's macroeconomic model is basically symmetric, so if the data center boom ends and the AI stock gains disappear, the result would be roughly the negative of this, only faster—shaving about half a percentage point off growth next year and a quarter point the year after, but nothing resembling a recession. Toward the end of this post I'll come back to the question of whether or not that is the correct prediction.
A historic buildout, and a stock market boom to match
A recent paper(link is external) by Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh estimated that the data center buildout will be even bigger than the most historic capital expenditure booms, like building the railroads or the telecom and fiber buildout of the late 1990s:

Already the buildout of data centers and the computers and communications equipment that fill them—about 2½ percent of GDP, or roughly $840 billion a year—has surpassed what we saw during the telecom and fiber buildout, and analyst forecasts for future buildout keep rising and rising (although we will see if recent events change that).

And, of course, the stock market has boomed—and a disproportionate share of that boom is in AI buildout stocks: just seven companies account for about two-fifths of the increase in the value of U.S. public companies since ChatGPT launched, with their value more than tripling while the rest of the market rose by about half.

A few other facts about the economy worth noting: business investment has risen as a share of GDP to its highest level since 1982. Excluding computers, communications equipment and data centers, private investment has actually fallen, from 16.8 percent of GDP in 2023–24 to 16.1 percent. And construction outside of data centers is falling almost across the board: over the past year, adjusted for construction costs, spending on nonresidential construction other than data centers and power is down 13 percent, led by factories (down 22 percent), offices (13 percent) and warehouses (13 percent). The main exception is power (including oil and gas), up 6 percent, likely some of it to serve data centers.

Much of this investment has come from abroad. While the overall trade balance has been roughly unchanged, the portion due to the AI buildout has surged while the rest has shrunk.

The impact of the buildout on GDP has been limited by how much of it is imported
To get a plausible quantification of how the boom has changed the economy, I will use the Federal Reserve's large-scale macroeconomic model, FRB/US(link is external), which the Fed helpfully provides to the public in Python code(link is external)—something I worked with interactively using Claude Code. FRB/US is the model the Fed's staff has used for forecasting and policy analysis since 1996. It has 284 equations, with about 60 of them estimated from decades of data, covering households, businesses, government, trade and financial markets. The model is not truth, and over time more perspectives and evidence will help improve our understanding. But it's a pretty good baseline to start from.
The first step in this simulation is to take the economy and shock it with the increase in investment in data centers—spending on computers, communication equipment and data center construction above its 2015–2022 trend—which started in mid-2024 and ramped up to 1.3 percent of GDP by the third quarter of 2026. I assume 75 percent of it is imported (closer to 90 percent for computers and 80 percent for communication equipment, but only about 10 percent for construction), and the rest is domestically produced investment. The trade data suggests the import share could be even higher, which would make the effect smaller still. For now I will not incorporate the stronger stock market—that is covered in the next section. All of the simulations assume the Fed follows the inertial policy rule that is the default in the public model, responding to the output gap and inflation, and that these changes plus other sources of changes in long-term interest rates affect interest-rate-sensitive sectors of the economy. People update their expectations based on patterns in the data rather than anticipating where the economy is headed from observations like seeing the potential capabilities of AI. (You can change any of these assumptions on the website(link is external).)
The short answer is that the data center boom by itself has lifted GDP a little and lowered the unemployment rate a little—but neither effect was that large. By the third quarter of 2026, GDP is about 0.3 percent higher than it would have been, and the unemployment rate about 0.1 percentage point lower. If the data center boom continues at the 1.6 percent of GDP it is on track to reach by the end of this year, these effects would build a bit further and then level off, with GDP about 0.45 percent higher and the unemployment rate about 0.25 percentage point lower by the end of 2028 (the dotted lines). If it keeps growing—say, by another half a percent of GDP a year—the effects by the end of 2028 would be larger: about 0.7 percent on GDP and 0.35 percentage point on unemployment. A fuller set of results is in the appendix.

The effect on GDP has been much more muted than the direct spending. The reason is almost entirely imports. Data center spending above trend reached 1.3 percent of GDP, but about 1 percentage point of that was imported equipment. Imports matter because they do not directly enter GDP: imported equipment shows up as positive investment and as negative imports, which cancel out.
Crowding out of other spending barely shows up: because most of the spending leaks abroad, the Fed's rule raises rates only about a tenth of a percentage point, so housing is a touch lower while the extra income slightly raises consumer spending and other business investment. That is not to say there is no crowding out: residential investment is below its trajectory, and if the buildout continues that gap will grow. It's just that the change is not large enough—especially since residential investment is only about 3½ percent of GDP—to lower overall GDP by much.

The stock market boom is even more important than the buildout itself
The stock market boom associated with the data center buildout is a bigger deal. The stocks of seven AI-related companies (Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Broadcom and Oracle) are up about $11 trillion more than they would have been had they kept pace with the rest of the market since ChatGPT came out, and American households own about $7.6 trillion of that. If 3 percent of that is spent (a plausible estimate of the wealth effect), that would be about $230 billion in higher consumer spending, or 0.7 percent of GDP. A big deal. (These numbers are as of September 30, matching the focus on the economy through the third quarter; measured through November 5, the gain is only about $9 trillion.)
FRB/US gives a noticeably smaller number than this back-of-the-envelope math. In the model, the stock gain raises consumer spending by about 0.4 percent of GDP by the third quarter of 2026. I treat the stock gain as investors expecting higher earnings from these companies, not as investors accepting lower returns on stocks in general, so it works through household wealth rather than by making it cheaper for businesses to raise money; other business investment rises only a little, from the extra demand. Together, the buildout and the stock gain raise GDP by about 0.6 percent and lower the unemployment rate by about 0.3 percentage point, and the Fed's rule responds with a funds rate about 0.35 percentage point higher. These graphs show the effect on GDP and unemployment of the stock gain on top of the data center buildout. If the buildout holds at its end-of-year share of GDP and the stock gain stays at its early-November level, but does not keep increasing, the effects build further, with GDP leveling off in 2028: by the end of 2028, GDP would be about 0.75 percent higher and the unemployment rate about 0.45 percentage point lower, with the funds rate about 0.7 percentage point higher.

Overall, adding the stock market boom to the buildout raises consumer spending by about 0.4 percent of GDP and other business investment by less than a tenth of a percent, while pulling in more imports from abroad; with backward-looking expectations, housing falls by about 0.3 percent from where it would otherwise be—with the effect potentially tripling over the next few years as the lagged effect of interest rates continues to work its way through the economy.

The AI boom kept the trade deficit from narrowing
One of the biggest effects of the boom has been to keep the trade deficit roughly constant as a share of GDP rather than falling meaningfully, which is what would have happened absent the boom. That fall could have been the result of the tariff increases, although tariffs have complex and ambiguous impacts on trade deficits, so other factors could be at play too. It would have brought the trade deficit to the lowest share of GDP since 1998.
The figure below shows net exports with and without the AI boom (the stock market part of it barely matters here).

There are two ways to think about why the boom increased the trade deficit. The first is that it raised the imports of data-center-related stuff from its average over the years prior to the data center boom (note, these imports include items like computers used by consumers) of about 1¼ percent of GDP to about 3 percent of GDP so far this year. Absent a big depreciation in the exchange rate, this would not lead to any offsetting effects like lower imports of non-data-center stuff or higher exports. In fact, based on historical experience, investment booms often come with a stronger dollar(link is external), as foreign capital flows in(link is external)—which itself would reduce net exports by even more than the naïve counterfactual of simply buying more foreign chips and other material. In these FRB/US simulations, though, the dollar barely moves, so this effect is not in the results shown here.
The other way to think about the expansion of the trade deficit is that the AI boom has added about 1.4 percentage points of GDP to investment while saving has risen only about a tenth of a percentage point of GDP. And the current account balance (or basically net exports) is the difference between saving and investment, so it has gotten about 1¼ percentage points of GDP lower as a result.
How much to trust this: a reasonable baseline, with expectations the big unknown
This analysis is based on the FRB/US model. Most of the effects are smaller than much of the discussion would suggest—and smaller than the historic scale of the investment. That is usually true in this and other macro models: huge tariff changes, oil shocks or departures from Fed policy tend to move the growth rate by tenths of a percentage point.
Sometimes the estimates in macro models are small because FRB/US and other models miss or minimize complexities like supply chains, the financial system and the liquidity constraints many households face. And the Fed's model in particular was estimated largely on data from a relatively calm period, which is one reason it moves inflation so little—the Fed's staff forecasts, which lean on FRB/US but add judgment and other models, famously failed to predict the inflation surge in 2021. Moreover, it assumes monetary policy responds effectively—without the serially correlated errors that often plague policymaking in the real world. These shortcomings can be especially severe in some cases, as in the financial crisis, whose full damage the model did not capture.
In the case of the AI buildout, the disadvantages of the model are less obviously serious, and its advantage of being able to track a sprawling and interconnected set of identities and empirical relationships is compelling. Still, there may be some limitations. For example, a model with a richer industrial structure would capture some of the bottlenecks that have added to surging prices of chips and other hardware—potentially adding more to inflation than this model shows.
Even more important is the role of expectations. The results I have presented assume backward-looking expectations. If you assume forward-looking expectations, it can change the results a lot. For example, in FRB/US if people expect the buildout to continue through 2031 and also for productivity growth to rise by 0.5 percentage point annually starting in 2027, that would raise the 10-year Treasury yield by about 75 basis points, compared with about 13 basis points with backward-looking expectations. This would, in aggregate, more than offset the gains from the stock market boom—although it would change the composition, with somewhat more consumer spending and much less housing—and leave GDP slightly lower and unemployment slightly higher than they would have been with no boom at all. The truth is probably somewhere in between the two cases. (In fact, if financial markets and wage setters turned forward-looking only this year, we would have much of the added interest rate increase without enough time for it to show up in the macroeconomic data in a large way—you can see these results and others on the website(link is external).)
Overall, I believe the smaller results are probably correct—and the model does not have the same incentives that public discussion has to exaggerate effects. That said, each tenth of a percent of GDP is about $30 billion—a big deal.
The future: a smaller buildout would be fine, a stock market fall less so, and broader financial risks are the unknown unknown
The two biggest questions for the future are whether the building boom will continue and whether productivity will eventually show up. These are related. AI meaningfully increasing productivity—which I am optimistic will happen—is probably a necessary condition for the boom to continue. If I am wrong and AI does not add to the economy, it would be hard to monetize.
AI showing up in productivity, however, is not a sufficient condition for the boom to continue. Public policy changes or the inability to monetize the investments—the latter is what I am really worried about—could stop the AI boom and associated stock market increase.
This analysis suggests that the economy could survive less data center buildout just fine. Investment would fall, but so would imports and interest rates, and GDP would be little changed. A broader fall in the stock market would be a bigger deal: if the buildout ended and the whole market fell by something like 30 percent, then the FRB/US model would predict that growth would slow to about 1½ percent—still not even a shallow recession.
Largely absent from this model (as we found out at our peril in the financial crisis) are the complexities of the financial system, including the unwinding of leverage. I hope to return to those another time and explain why I see them as a tail risk—at worst more like 2001 (a short, shallow recession) than 2007–09 (a financial crisis), and even that is only a risk.
The bottom line: so far the AI economy is less a story about data centers than about the stock market—and that is also where the risk is.
Note: This post was written by Jason with title, copyedits and fact checks by Claude. The data work was done interactively with Claude. A replication package(link is external) is available on Econvitals.
APPENDIX: FULL SET OF RESULTS
Each panel traces out the economic changes that have resulted, and will result, from the data center buildout alone (blue) and the buildout plus the AI stock gain (orange). Solid lines run through the third quarter of 2026, the last quarter of actual data. The dotted lines assume the buildout rises to 1.6 percent of GDP in the fourth quarter and stays there, and that the stock gains stay at their early-November level, without further extraordinary growth. The simulations assume backward-looking expectations and the Fed's inertial policy rule—you can set other assumptions on the website(link is external).

articles.text:
Gavekal Technologies: New Energy

Most recent

Gavekal Technologies: Chips

The Nvidia Blast Zone

Laila Khawaja, Arthur Kroeber
12 Nov 2026

The Nvidia scandal looks sure to topple CEO Jensen Huang and put the company on a very rocky course for a few months. The headlines have focused on the romantic and spy stories, but the crucial issues lie elsewhere. The big risk for Huang and Nvidia is that they might be found guilty of breaking US export control rules by colluding in the illegal transshipment of AI chips from Singapore to China. The Chinese AI industry, which already has a tough time getting enough advanced chips, could soon find it even tougher, as there is a good chance that the US Congress will soon act to tighten up export controls.

Gavekal Technologies: New Energy

Permitting Reform’s Big Chance

AJ Cortese
10 Nov 2026

Efforts to clean up the US’s sclerotic system for approving energy infrastructure have failed twice before. The third time may be the charm, as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act or BAAJA cleared its first procedural hurdle in the Senate on Monday. If it passes despite last-ditch opposition by environmental groups, it will massively boost America’s ability to scale up its electricity grid, on a three to-five year horizon. This will remove an important constraint on both AI data centers and manufacturing.

More research

How Wuxi AppTec Stayed Sanction-Proof

2 Nov 2026

China’s two “Wuxi” biotech firms—AppTec and Biologics—are key partners for the US pharmaceutical industry, as contract developers and manufacturers of hundreds of thousands of chemical compounds. Washington lawmakers are increasingly uneasy about rising American reliance on the Wuxi firms. But their efforts to curb Wuxi’s access to the US market have been blocked, thanks to strong lobbying by the US pharma and biotech industries.

Power Lessons From China

26 Oct 2026

The US data center boom is facing a power crunch. So far, delays and cancellations due to electricity shortages have been sporadic but by some point in 2028, they could force a significant slowdown in data center construction. It will be important for the US to figure out how to better use batteries and distributed renewables generation to make power demand and supply more flexible. China is already ahead in this effort.

The State Of Chinese AI

19 Oct 2026

The AI world suffered tremors last week, as doubts began to surface about the frontier labs’ revenue growth and the rising amount of high-priced debt used to finance the US’s data center building binge. The risks raise a question: when and if the American AI bubble pops, can China race ahead? Probably not.

Can China Export Its Nuclear Boom?

12 Oct 2026

China is the world’s biggest builder of nuclear power plants, but unlike in other energy sectors it has not become a significant exporter of reactors. While Chinese nuclear firms have figured out how to make reactors relatively cheaply, the complexity and safety needs of nuclear projects mean they will never be able to gobble up world markets through ultralow prices, as Chinese solar, EV and battery firms have done. But over the next decade it is likely China will become an important nuclear exporter.

Great Tech In Search Of Profits

5 Oct 2026

On September 6-11, Gavekal Technologies held its inaugural China Tech Tour with 19 institutional-investor clients. Through a dozen site visits and in-depth conversations with senior executives, we examined China’s semiconductor, AI, new energy, robotics and biotechnology industries. This week’s China Tech Brief explores some of the key findings. By far the biggest theme was the gap between technological capabilities and corporate returns. China has plenty of globally competitive tech companies, but few that generate really attractive earnings.

GavekalTech On The Ground: 2026 China Tech Trip Takeaways

1 Oct 2026

On September 6-11, Gavekal Technologies made its inaugural China Tech Trip with 19 institutional investor clients. The trip offered a close-up view of China’s tech ecosystem, including semiconductors, AI, new energy, robotics, and biotech, via a dozen site visits and in-depth conversations with senior executives. This week’s Chips report summarizes our observations in the semiconductor and AI sectors.

articles.title: Data and analytics transformation at the Bank of England to enable, equip and empower − speech by Ben Martin
articles.text:
Data and analytics transformation at the Bank of England to enable, equip and empower − speech by Ben Martin

Speech to be given at DAMA Data and AI Conference Europe 2026

Published on
04 November 2026

In this speech Ben Martin explores how the Bank is transforming its use of data, analytics and AI. From building stronger data foundations to safely adopting new AI capabilities, he explains how the Bank is enabling, equipping and empowering colleagues to make the most of these tools.

Speech
Good morning. It is a great pleasure to be here today at the DAMA Data & AI Conference. This event is about sharing practical experience of building trusted, responsible and effective data and AI capabilities, so I thought it would be a good opportunity to share some of the work we are doing on this at the Bank of England.
In recent years, my colleagues at the Bank have spoken publicly about the implications of AI on the wider economyfootnote [1] footnote [2]. Today, I want to talk about this from a slightly different perspective: what data and analytics transformation means for the Bank of England itself, as an organisation.
But first, let me introduce myself: my name is Ben Martin and I am the Bank’s Chief Data Officer. I took up this role just under a year ago, following a career across the Bank’s economics, markets and supervision areas. This experience gave me a deep understanding of the Bank’s data needs. Taking on the CDO role has allowed me to bring those perspectives together at an enterprise level. It has been encouraging to see how much progress we have made – and continue to make – in improving our data, analytics and AI capabilities. Even though we are making good progress, this is by no means job done. The pace of change in this field is rapid, and our ambitions need to keep pace with it. So today, I want to reflect on the journey we have been on, where we are now, and some of the opportunities and challenges that lie ahead.
Our mission at the Bank of England is to promote the good of the people of the United Kingdom, by maintaining monetary and financial stability. Across our offices in London and Leeds, our people are working to deliver that mission. Central to this is our ability to make the best possible decisions using the most effective data and analytics to achieve our public policy objectives. Data and analytics are integral to our work. They support our understanding of the economy, our supervision of the financial firms within it, and the operations through which we fulfil our responsibilities.
A couple of years ago, we published our Data & Analytics Strategyfootnote [3]. Our overarching aim is to make the best use of data and analytics to fulfil the Bank’s mission. Our ambitions are summarised by three missions.

First, making it easy for people in the Bank to work with and analyse data.
Second, bridging data gaps to increase the value of what we collect and share.
Third, enabling safe and effective innovation, including artificial intelligence.

Those missions rest on two foundations: a modern enterprise data platform on the cloud; and investment in business change, skills and culture to embed this.
That combination is important. We are not simply replacing systems. We are seeking to change how people find and use data, how they collaborate on it with each other, and how they develop new analytical tools and techniques to gain the best insights to make good decisions.
Today I want to focus on how we are enabling, equipping and empowering our organisation to deliver this strategy. Let me give a quick overview before we dive into each in more detail later on.
First, what do I mean by enablement? This covers the work we are doing to build solid foundations by providing transformed systems and high-quality data for our colleagues.
Second, we are equipping our colleagues with new capabilities including AI, with effective guardrails and associated training, so they can safely achieve new insights.
Last, but by no means least, I will cover empowerment – our approach to supporting colleagues to make the most of the investment we have made and to have the confidence to explore these new tools.
I am a big fan of the television programme Grand Designs, watching people use exciting, modern solutions in an innovative way to build something truly special – not just special on paper or to look at, but special for the people who live there. I sometimes think about our strategy in the same way. We are using modern techniques and the latest thinking on how to use data, but not as an end in itself or to wow anyone. Instead, the point is to deliver the Bank’s mission effectively and to make sure our colleagues can flourish. We are enabling colleagues by putting the foundations in place, equipping them with new capabilities to continue building on those foundations and empowering them to make the most of those new capabilities. Thankfully, the one thing we don’t have is Kevin McCloud turning up every few months to see how we’re getting on!
I will say a bit more about the work we are doing on these three Es – enable, equip and empower – at the Bank of England.
Enable – by building solid foundations
As I have said, we are building solid foundations, so we can enable our colleagues by providing effective systems and high-quality data as the bedrock of good analysis. At the Bank, we are part way through a multi-year investment programme to build solid data foundations. This includes investing in new systems and technology, but also continuing to invest in the ‘bread and butter’ of good data management: quality, governance and trust. AI may be grabbing the headlines, but AI runs on data. This audience knows well enough that without high-quality, well-governed and trusted data, even the most sophisticated AI will struggle to deliver. So I will share some reflections on how we are bringing together the new systems and the good old basics to ensure solid foundations.
New systems
At the foundation of our Data & Analytics Strategy is a new Enterprise Data Platform, or EDP. This is our central, cloud-based data and analytics ecosystem. It will bring together a wide range of data needed across the Bank’s responsibilities, including macroeconomic and financial market data we bring in from partners, and the regulatory and statistical returns we collect directly from the financial sector. But the EDP is about much more than storing data. It provides a structured and governed way of bringing data into the Bank, and transforming it into trusted, reusable data that can be readily used for analysis. Alongside this, the EDP provides modern analytical tools and capabilities, including access to approved AI models, helping colleagues to work with data more effectively and strengthening analysis and decision-making across the Bank.
Earlier this year, we deployed the core of the platform. We are now migrating data services and data systems onto that foundation in stages. Those new data systems are being completely transformed from the legacy systems we are retiring. Alongside this technology, we are building the operating model needed to support it. Together, the platform and its operating model are intended to help us move beyond data silos, establish a shared foundation for future data initiatives, and make greater use of cloud-native capabilities to develop new products and services.
The word ‘enterprise’ really matters here. The Bank of England brings together a number of different responsibilities within one institution, in part because of the connections and synergies between them. Our approach to data should reflect that same principle. Data collected or created for one purpose can often have value elsewhere, and insights can be richer when we are able to connect information from across the organisation. So rather than recreating a collection of separate systems, we are building shared data and analytical capabilities that can be used right across the organisation to support delivery of the Bank’s mission.
Good basics
Now, there is no point in building new systems but immediately filling them with poorly managed data. I know that data management is familiar territory for this audience. DAMA gives us a useful way of thinking about it: not as a standalone control, but as the coordinating mechanism that connects ownership, quality, metadata, architecture and use. For us, the real test is whether those disciplines show up in the everyday experience of colleagues working with data. That is why, since launching our Data & Analytics Strategy, we have focused on putting those practical data management foundations in place.
We have an organisation-wide data management policy and an ownership and stewardship framework, alongside data management learning within our wider data fluency programme.
We have numerous Data Owners and Stewards across all areas of the Bank who support over 2,000 registered data assets. These arrangements combine accountability for data with the day-to-day work needed to manage it.
These are important foundations helping us improve consistency, transparency and trust across an increasingly complex data estate. But the existence of a policy, a register, or an assigned owner, is far from being the end of the task. Our objective is that data can be found, accessed, trusted, understood and used, where data management acts as an enabler, not a barrier.
That is the practical test of data management. Does it help someone coming with fresh eyes establish what a dataset contains? Or understand whether it is appropriate for their purpose? Do they know who can answer their questions about it? And can they use it with confidence?
Like other long-established institutions, we face particular challenges in modernising our data estate. The Bank has a long history and with that comes years of accumulated data, systems and processes. Recent independent reviews by the Independent Evaluation Officefootnote [4] and Dr Ben Bernankefootnote [5] have reinforced the importance of tackling these challenges. It is clear we cannot simply build something new and expect all that complexity to disappear. Our Enterprise Data Platform is a good example – as we move datasets across, we are ensuring we look carefully at what we are bringing with us, to improve our data quality and embed those enduring data management basics from the outset. To stick with the theme of houses, this is a bit like moving house. If you live somewhere for a long time, you inevitably accumulate things along the way, which get shoved in drawers or the loft. Moving gives you the opportunity to decide what you really need, tidy things up and organise them better, rather than simply packing everything into boxes and recreating the same clutter in your new home.
Equip – by providing new capabilities
Next, we want to equip our colleagues to safely achieve new insights by using new capabilities including AI, with effective guardrails, and by providing the right training.
New capabilities
Much of the focus on data tooling over the past couple of years has been around the opportunities from new AI capabilities. We have been open about our approach to using AI at the Bank of England, which we outlined in our AI strategy that was published last yearfootnote [6]. To support a consistent and coherent approach to AI across the Bank, our AI strategy rests on a set of principles that set the tone for how we approach AI. Although frontier AI models and their capabilities have advanced rapidly over the past year, these principles are enduring. The principles are embodied in the ‘TRUSTED’ framework, which is for our AI solutions to be:

Targeted on tightly defined use cases that have a clear business purpose.
Reliable with high performance standards and grounded in high-quality data.
Understood in the context of their intended purpose.
Secure so we protect ourselves from risks such as unauthorised access.
Tested thoroughly for their technology standards and impact on behaviour.
Ethical including being beneficial and scientifically rigorous, fair and inclusive, transparent and secure, and compliant and accountable.
Durable so they remain effective despite changing conditions and usage patterns.

To bring this to life, I thought I would share some examples of how we have implemented this framework in practice. Our approach combines broad access to general purpose tools across the Bank with a more tailored applications for specific business needs.
A significant milestone has been the organisation-wide rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot. Nearly all colleagues at the Bank use it each week. Some colleagues also use GitHub Copilot to support code development. As colleagues have become more confident, this has extended to the creation of many custom Copilot agents over the past year, typically to improve personal productivity in day-to-day tasks or to help navigate internal services. Many began as experiments, but some are now being used more widely across the organisation. For example, our ‘AskHR’ agent provides answers to questions on leave, pay and our people policies. Another agent, called ‘AskTech’, helps with technology-related questions and can direct colleagues to further support where needed. As you can see, our approach to naming them has been slightly less experimental!
Alongside these general-purpose tools, we are also developing bespoke AI applications for important business processes.
One example is our Agency Retrieval and Insights App, known as ARIA. The Bank’s regional Agents, based in 12 agencies across the nations and regions in the UK, maintain close relationships with businesses of all sizes, providing the Monetary Policy Committee with real-time insight into economic conditions and perspectives from across the country. Those relationships and the judgements of our Agents remain at the heart of that work, but ARIA complements this by helping them make sense of this wealth of intelligence they gather, using capabilities such as theme detection and quantitative analysis to identify patterns and draw out insights. It is a good example of technology augmenting human expertise and strengthening one part of the evidence base that supports the MPC in making its policy decisions.
Another example is called GRACE, which provides retrieval-augmented AI to enable colleagues to draw deep insights from large and trusted internal knowledge repositories. But what I particularly like is that it does this through an email interface, a tool colleagues already know how to use every day. They can send off a query, get on with something else and come back to the response when it arrives. The interaction is also captured naturally in the email chain. It is a simple example of designing AI around people and the way they work, rather than the other way round. These applications address different needs. What connects them is the effort to make technology useful within the work people already do.
Effective training
The pace of technology change can be dizzying, and with new capabilities emerging all the time, it can be difficult to know where to start. That is why we need to equip colleagues not just with the access to these tools, but to also equip them with the confidence and skills to use them safely and effectively. We want to help them feel confident navigating that change and so we have maintained a focus on training which is one of the two foundations of our Data & Analytics Strategy. It focuses on business change, skills and culture, recognising that successful adoption requires practical support, as colleagues move to new services and learning that goes beyond narrow technical training.
To put this in practice, we have a dedicated data and analytics learning function. To date, I am proud to say it has delivered more than 250 courses to many colleagues across our data science and analytical toolset.
Our aim is not simply to provide more training. It is to make learning more relevant to the work people need to do. On Copilot, we began with introductory learning to establish a common baseline for everyone. Many colleagues then attended application-based deep dives. We have subsequently introduced clinics offering more personalised support for local and role-specific use cases.
That progression from training course to back at the desk matters. General awareness can help people get started. Practical support helps them move from experimenting with a tool, to using it effectively and achieving results.
But formal learning is only part of the picture. We have a thriving Data Community, with almost 2,000 members. It actively supports collaboration, sharing and peer-to-peer learning. During our ‘Data & Analytics Fortnight’ in June, over 1,000 colleagues turned out to one of our events, which included a wide range of internal and external presenters sharing their expertise. Beyond this, the community also organises regular hackathons which have turned out some brilliant solutions.
Bringing people together is incredibly important but the value of a community is not only in the events it organises. It is in the opportunities it creates as a place for people to ask questions, share experience, and learn from colleagues who have faced and overcome similar challenges.
Beyond catalysing an organic approach to building capacity, we are also developing more structured pathways for embedding data skills professionally.
We launched the Data Profession last November, bringing together colleagues from across the Bank whose work involves data into a single professional community. It covers disciplines including data science, data analytics and data governance, helping us take a more joined-up approach to the data skills we need, how we recruit and develop people, and the career pathways and support available to them.
Building our capabilities also means broadening access to opportunities. I am pleased to say that our recently established partnership with Women in Data helps this through a range of initiatives supporting our commitment to greater representation and inclusivity in the workplace.
Like our data tools and technology, our learning approach must also keep evolving. We are working to understand shifting skills requirements across different time horizons, using a role-based approach to assessing skills profiles to help us to map the work different colleagues need to do, against the skills required to do it effectively, and the most appropriate ways to support them in addressing any gaps.
So, we are equipping colleagues to safely achieve new insights by using new capabilities including AI, with effective guardrails, and by providing the right training.
Empower – by supporting colleagues to innovate
Investing in equipping and enabling our people is important, but to unlock its full potential, we need to empower colleagues to try innovative new approaches in their roles. This is not just about doing what we already do more efficiently. It is also about opening up new possibilities, helping colleagues work differently and undertake types of analysis that simply were not possible before. Ultimately, it is about giving people the tools and confidence to evolve with the world around us.
Support
Like many organisations, we want to reduce the costs to trying new innovative approaches and to avoid the risks of this happening in siloes. To do so, we are bringing together a dedicated team of experts from both our data and technology functions to act as an innovation hub for the Bank as a whole. The aim is to support colleagues to understand the range of tools available to facilitate innovative work and to support them to bring insights from across different teams. The idea is not that we try to do the innovative analytical work centrally, but instead to be a centre of excellence and smooth the way for the innovative work that the various business functions of the Bank want to achieve. This includes a forum where local business and central support functions’ representatives can meet, share developments, and to prioritise work to achieve the biggest benefits.
Culture
Finally, we need a culture that gives colleagues the confidence to try something new. Sometimes trying something new feels daunting. We want colleagues to feel that innovation is part of their role – that they are empowered to question how something is done today, explore whether there might be a better way, and have a safe environment in which to test new approaches, which can be supported by the innovation hub. It gives colleagues somewhere to experiment with the right support and safeguards around them, reducing some of the barriers to trying something new. Of course, the design of this needs to be appropriate for the evolving culture of the Bank, just like a well-designed house needs to work in the place where it’s built and for the people who live there.
Senior leaders have an important role here too. We need to visibly take the lead in encouraging people across the organisation to innovate, make space for them to do it, and celebrate the examples that demonstrate what is possible. Over time, that is how we make innovation feel more like a natural part of how we work, and why we are launching in the coming months a new leadership programme focused on leading in an increasingly digital, data and AI enabled world.

Conclusion
Let me conclude by returning to the main theme of my remarks today. Data and analytics transformation is not primarily about technology for its own sake. It is about making sure the Bank of England can continue to fulfil its mission effectively in a world where the volume of data, the sophistication of analytical tools, and the pace of technological change are all increasing rapidly.
For us, that means doing three things together. First, we need to enable colleagues by putting the right foundations in place: modern platforms, well-managed data, clear ownership and the enduring disciplines of data management. Those foundations matter because high-quality analysis, effective decision-making and responsible AI all depend on trusted and accessible data.
Second, we need to equip people with new capabilities and the confidence to use them safely. That includes making general-purpose tools such as Copilot available at scale, developing more tailored applications where there are specific business needs, and applying clear guardrails through our AI framework. But it also means investing in training, communities and professional pathways, so that people can use these tools well and understand their limits.
Third, we need to empower colleagues to innovate. The opportunities from data, analytics and AI will not be realised by a central team alone. They will come from colleagues across the organisation identifying better ways to do their work, experimenting responsibly, sharing experience, and building on each other’s successes. Our role centrally is to reduce the friction, provide expertise and make it easier for good ideas to move from the drawing board to practical use.
We cannot stand still and our job is not done. At the Bank, our ambition is to build on the progress we have made and keep moving forward: enabling colleagues with trusted foundations, equipping them with safe and effective capabilities, and empowering them to innovate in support of the public good.
The technology around us will continue to evolve and expectations of what is possible will continue to rise in the era of AI. But keeping pace is not just about technology. It is also about continuing to learn from one another. The work of communities such as DAMA has a vital role to play in bringing people together, sharing practical experience as we are today, and ensuring that even as technology moves quickly, the standards underpinning our data remain strong. Thank you.
And if Kevin McCloud is in the audience, ignore what I said earlier – you're welcome to come to the Bank any time you want!

Global webinar: Key themes for 2027

online

In this webinar, we’ll explore the key themes shaping the global economy in 2027.

Despite a year of surprises, we see considerable resilience in global growth heading into 2027, with key factors shaping the outlook such as the AI boom, persistent inflation, and fiscal worries. In this webinar, we’ll cover our core expectations for the global economy next year and take extensive audience questions with a panel of Oxford Economics experts representing all major economies.

This webinar is being held on our new platform, ON24. If you do not receive your confirmation email, please check your junk and spam folders.

Speakers

Ryan Sweet

Ryan Sweet is the Chief Economist | Managing Director at Oxford Economics where he helps shape and coordinate the team’s global economic analysis and forecasting. Previously, Ryan was the Chief US Economist and led a team that was among the most accurate high-frequency forecasters of the economy.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Ryan spent 17 years at Moody’s Analytics as a member of the U.S. macroeconomics team and was also a co-host of the Inside Economics podcast. Ryan has also been an adjunct professor in the Economics and Finance Department at West Chester University of Pennsylvania.

Ryan received a master’s degree in finance from Johns Hopkins University, a master’s degree in economics from the University of Delaware, and a bachelor’s degree in economics from Washington College.

Chief Global Economist

Louise Loo

Louise Loo is the Head of Asia Economics at Oxford Economics. She leads the firm’s macroeconomic research and forecasting efforts on Greater China.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, she was a senior economist at Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs. At Goldman Sachs, she was also a long-term advisor to China Ministry of Finance and the China-based Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) with regards to their sovereign credit ratings.

Louise is a regular contributor to various international financial news outlets and has earned Economics and public policy degrees with Sheffield University and Columbia University.

Head of Asia Economics

Ben May

Ben May is a Director of Global Macroeconomic Research at Oxford Economics and is involved in the production and presentation of the company’s global macroeconomic views, with a leading role in our coverage of the advanced economies. Ben joined Oxford Economics in April 2014. He has over 15 years’ experience as a macro economist in the public and private sector and has over a decade’s expertise covering the Eurozone economy.

Before joining the Global Macro team, Ben worked on the Eurozone team at Oxford Economics. In addition to his working covering broad Eurozone issues he was also responsible for research on the ECB and Germany. Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Ben spent over six years at Capital Economics and was responsible for the coverage of the southern Eurozone economies throughout the Eurozone crisis. Before that, he spent seven years at the Bank of England, working in three divisions of the Monetary Analysis area of the Bank, which provides research and analysis for the Monetary Policy Committee. Ben has a BSc in Economics with Statistics from the University of Bristol and an MSc in Economics from University College London.

Director, Macro Forecasting & Analysis

Bernard Yaros

Bernard is a Deputy Chief US Economist at Oxford Economics, where he focuses on fiscal policy, inflation trends, and business investment. His past work on US elections and major policy proposals has been widely cited by the media, Congressional lawmakers, and even the White House. Previously, Bernard was an assistant director at Moody’s Analytics.

Bernard holds a Master’s degree in Economics from the Barcelona School of Economics and a B.A. in Political Economy from Williams College.

Deputy Chief US Economist

Angel Talavera

Ángel Talavera is Chief European Economist and is responsible for developing Oxford Economics’ macro view on the region, as well as producing macroeconomic forecasts for Spain. He manages a team of 12 economists producing regional and country-specific thematic research on over 30 countries, as well as contributing to the editorial line of Oxford Economics globally. Angel’s work also involves presenting the outlook to clients around the world and he is frequently quoted in international media.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Ángel spent over five years in two different stints as an economist at FocusEconomics, a Barcelona-based macroeconomic consulting firm. In between, he worked at Beazley Group, an insurance firm based in London, where he focused on country risk.
