articles.title: Daily: Gridlock and diplomatic hopes lift US stocks
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: CIO Monthly | Mark Haefele on AI earnings, energy prices, interest rates (4 mins)
Video: Why China's equity markets have lagged (6 mins)Thought of the dayWhat happened?
The S&P 500 closed 1.6% higher on Wednesday, reversing the initial negative reaction in futures markets to the Democrats taking control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the US.The Nasdaq Composite gained 1.4%, while the 10-year US Treasury yield fell 8bps from its level before the election result. The US dollar weakened against most other major currencies, with the DXY dollar index down 0.5%.Hopes for progress toward ending the US-Iran conflict also supported market sentiment. Qatar has stepped up mediation efforts following signs that Washington and Tehran are seeking to resume talks. Iranian officials, however, sounded less optimistic about a deal, reiterating that an agreement would only be possible if the US accepts Iran’s seven points. Brent crude oil fell 8.2% overnight, and has since stabilized around 95/bbl, as investors assess whether diplomacy could reduce the risk of further disruption to energy supplies.Still, overall risk sentiment remains fragile in early Thursday trading, with AI-heavy indices in South Korea and Taiwan down 5.3% and 3.2%, respectively, and Nasdaq futures pricing a 0.5% decline at the time of writing.What do we think?
The election result has removed a source of uncertainty. With Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress and President Donald Trump retaining the presidency and veto power, abrupt changes to tax and spending policy should be more difficult to enact.While this is not a forecast of future performance, the S&P 500 gained an average of 15.5% in the six months following the previous 14 midterm elections since 1970. This pattern may partly reflect the removal of election uncertainty and investors’ tendency to refocus on the economic and earnings outlook.Political risks remain, however. The next Congress will need to address government funding and the debt ceiling, potentially increasing bond market volatility. Democratic gains in key data center states could also delay projects, raise development costs, or influence capacity location. Trump retains broad executive authority over tariffs, foreign policy, and regulation.Individual stock performance is already beginning to reflect these differences in exposure. On Wednesday, large technology platforms performed strongly, while some companies linked to data center construction declined. Investors were concerned that Democratic gains in states including Texas and Georgia could lead to greater scrutiny of electricity consumption, water use, and permitting.Investors appear to favor financially strong platforms that can fund investment flexibly from existing cash flow. They are becoming more cautious about businesses exposed to financing, construction, permitting, or execution risks. This suggests that broad equity gains may be accompanied by greater dispersion in technology sector performance.Overall, the election does not change our view that economic growth, corporate earnings, inflation, and interest rates should remain the primary market drivers. Earnings remain supportive, with recent corporate results providing further evidence of robust demand

across parts of the technology sector and the broader economy.Prospects for US-Iran diplomatic progress offer another potential source of stability. Both sides have incentives to avoid a prolonged conflict that keeps energy prices elevated and increases economic pressure. However, global inventories have fallen sharply, and pledged releases from strategic oil reserves are largely complete. Continued undersupply could further deplete commercial stocks and support oil prices. Record freight costs, constrained tanker capacity, and recovering Chinese imports are also likely to keep prices elevated.Comments from Trump that no military strike is imminent have helped weigh on prices, but the risk of renewed military action leaves markets vulnerable to further energy price volatility, while open questions remain on how long the US will support energy flows with military escorts.How do we invest?
We remain constructive on global equities, but the uneven rally and uncertainty surrounding US-Iran negotiations reinforce the importance of diversification.Stay invested in diversified equities. Strong earnings, resilient economic growth, and robust demand for AI infrastructure continue to support our constructive view. Our preferred sectors include industrials, health care, and financials. Regionally, we prefer the Eurozone, emerging markets, and Asia ex-Japan.Rebalance concentrated technology exposure. Greater scrutiny of data centers, alongside existing questions about AI monetization, could increase single-stock volatility. Investors with oversized positions in individual securities should use periods of strength to reduce concentration and diversify across the AI value chain. We favor financially strong platforms and high-quality infrastructure providers over businesses that rely more heavily on external funding or the rapid completion of individual projects.Maintain protection against geopolitical disruption. Diplomatic progress could push down oil prices further, but renewed attacks or a breakdown in negotiations could trigger another rise. Broad commodity exposure can help diversify portfolios when geopolitical disruption weighs on both stocks and bonds. Investors should consider exposure across energy, precious metals, industrial metals, and agriculture, rather than rely on a single commodity or geopolitical outcome.

Rising yields raise the portfolio appeal of bonds and diversified investing

articles.title: Weekly Market View
articles.text:
13 November 2026
Weekly Market View

Download Report

Tactical plays within a diversified allocation
Our calls to dial down risk since early October have helped mitigate a bear market in semiconductors and the sharpest single-day post-mid-term election downturn in US equities in over three decades.
Volatility has eased after the post-election spike, helping the IT sector partly recover. We see further upside in our opportunistic US IT and healthcare sector equity ideas.
A strong job market is likely to keep the Fed focused on lowering inflation, cementing the prospect of a December rate hike, potentially followed by another in Q1 2027. A strong economy and elevated interest rates support our overweight allocation to US financial sector equities.
In bonds, we lock in gains on US inflation-protected bonds as inflation nears a peak.

Where do you see the most favourable risk-reward within the US tech sector?

How do falling oil prices and hot US inflation data impact your Fed and bonds outlook?

Does the USD rally have further to run?

Charts of the week: Volatility drops, reviving tactical plays

US equity volatility has dropped after a spike; we stay bullish on US IT equities and lock in gains in inflation-linked bonds

US S&P500 volatility (VIX) and volatility of volatility (VVIX) indices

US IT sector equities total return index

US government inflation-linked 1-10 years total return index*

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered. *Initiated on 11 April 2025.
Editorial

Tactical plays within a diversified allocation

Strategy summary: Our calls to dial down risk since early October have helped mitigate a bear market in semiconductors and the sharpest single-day post-mid-term election downturn in US equities in over three decades. Volatility has eased after the post-election spike, helping the IT sector partly recover. We see further upside in our opportunistic US IT and healthcare sector equity ideas. In bonds, we lock in gains on US inflation-protected bonds as inflation nears a peak.
Navigating volatility. Almost five weeks ago, we cut our semiconductor segment equity exposure as market breadth narrowed ahead of the US election. Two weeks ago, we cut equities from Overweight to a core allocation, positioning for mid-cycle market dynamics. Last week, as the US equity market volatility index VIX surged above 25, we partially dialled up risk with a tactical idea on the more diversified US IT sector.
Staying tactical within a diversified allocation. Equity volatility following last week’s Democratic clean sweep in the US elections has subsided. Questions about the pace of AI data centre buildout are likely to linger until Democrats take office in in January. Nvidia’s turmoil adds uncertainty. We remain broadly diversified and balanced in our core allocation across assets, sector and regions, while seeking tactical opportunities. History suggests sharp selloffs are followed by near-term volatility, particularly during macroeconomic stress. However, the balance of historical outcomes has typically shifted strongly to the upside over a three- to six-month horizon. Besides, historically, US equity markets have delivered the strongest 12-month returns after opposition clean sweeps in the mid-terms.
Rotation driving US IT sector recovery: As volatility eases, our opportunistic US IT equities idea, launched a week ago, has performed well, despite some significantly negative company specific developments. Attractive valuations support further upside. Investors are rotating within IT from semiconductors, affected by concerns over the pace of AI data centre buildout and Nvidia’s troubles, towards software and hardware providers. The latter have strong cash flows and balance sheets and are likely to benefit from AI monetisation. Together, they account for more than 60% of the IT sector (see page 4).
.

Remain constructive on US healthcare. US healthcare earnings are projected to grow almost 23% in 2027, the second-fastest among MSCI US sectors. We see scope for further upside in the sector as innovation underpins long-term earnings growth. With the market rotating away from concentrated AI exposure, healthcare’s stable, non-cyclical demand profile offers a compelling exposure as a diversifier (see page 5).
Outside the US, Switzerland and India offer diversified returns. The Swiss equity market consists of 41% healthcare, 19% financial services and 14% consumer staples, providing a defensive alternative to investors seeking to diversify away from tech-heavy exposure. The Indian equity market has been classified as an “anti-AI” trade. Historically narrow valuation premiums vs. EMs, low foreign investor positioning and c. 15% expected 2027 earnings growth make it an attractive diversifier.
Strong jobs and inflation reports cement December Fed rate hike. The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, more than twice the 70,000 consensus estimate. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. Meanwhile, headline and core inflation in October, at 0.4% and 0.3% m/m, respectively, exceeded expectations as elevated fuel prices, ‘techflation’ and earlier tariffs fed into directly exposed sectors, including food, utilities and transportation services. A healthy job market keeps the Fed focused on lowering inflation, cementing the prospect of a December rate hike, potentially followed by another in Q1 2027. A strong economy and elevated interest rates support our overweight allocation to US financial sector equities.
Locking in gains from our bullish US inflation-protected bonds idea. While near-term price pressures remain elevated, we expect inflation to ease with energy costs over the coming year. Republicans’ heavy losses in the US mid-term elections increase pressure on the Trump administration to end the Iran conflict. One-year US inflation expectations have slumped alongside oil prices. A potential slowdown in the pace of AI buildout is also likely to ease techflation. Meanwhile, Fed rate hikes should further tighten financial conditions, tempering price pressures. This disinflationary outlook makes the risk-reward for US inflation-protected bonds less compelling. We close the idea, locking in a 4.4% gain (page 6).
— Rajat Bhattacharya

The weekly macro balance sheet

Our weekly net assessment: On balance, we see the past week’s data and policy as neutral for risk assets in the near-term
(+) factors: Strong US job market; improving US consumer sentiment(-)factors: Hotter-than-expected US inflation; rising odds of Fed hikes

US job creation surged in October, with non-farm payrolls beating expectations, and the unemployment rate falling back to 4.1%

Quarterly US non-farm payrolls, unemployment rate and underemployment rate

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered.*Q4 2026 represents October data only

US headline and core consumer prices rose more than expected by 0.4% m/m and 0.3% m/m in October respectively, raising odds of Fed hikes

US headline and core consumer price inflation

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

China’s consumer inflation eased further, while factory-gate prices accelerated in October
China consumer and producer price inflation

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions

What does history tell us about the aftermath of a single-day sell-off of 4% or more in the S&P500 index?

Our view: The S&P500 fell 4.36% on 5 November 2026, a rare daily move of 3.8 standard deviations. Since 2009, there have been only 24 occasions when the index declined by 4% or more in a single session. The immediate aftermath of such sell-offs has historically been mixed. One-month returns ranged from around -15% to +23%, with positive returns in 70% of cases. The weaker outcomes were concentrated around periods of significant macro stress, including the tail end of the 2008 Global Financial Crisis (GFC), the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic and the 2022 monetary policy tightening cycle.
The historical picture becomes considerably more constructive beyond the first month. All 24 episodes generated positive three-month returns, ranging from roughly +0.5% to +38%, while six-month returns were positive in 96% of cases, with gains reaching as much as +49%. Overall, history suggests sharp sell-offs can be followed by near-term volatility, particularly during periods of broader macro stress. However, the balance of historical outcomes has shifted strongly to the upside over a 3-6-month horizon.
— Maggie Au Yeung, Quantitative Analyst— Francis Lim, Senior Quantitative Strategist

S&P500 forward returns following large sell-offs
Average forward returns for S&P500 index following sharp sell-offs

Source: Bloomberg, Standard CharteredNote: 1. Since 2009 • 23 completed events • November 2026 excluded. 2. Hit rate refers to % of positive returns

Where do you see the most favourable risk-reward within the US technology sector?

Our view: We favour high-quality Big Tech companies with strong balance sheets and prefer diversified exposure through our US Information Technology (IT) opportunistic idea.
Rationale: The recent pullback in US semiconductor stocks has improved their risk-reward profile. Earnings for these companies are forecast to grow by 65% in 2027, the fastest rate among technology subsectors. Despite this outlook, recent regulatory and corporate governance concerns are weighing on sentiment. Potential state-level restrictions on data centre development following the recent US mid-term election results could weigh on semiconductor demand growth. However, we believe these risks are manageable and continued AI adoption should support demand for AI inference. We prefer diversified exposure to quality semiconductor companies with durable demand and strong volume growth.
To navigate volatility in the US technology sector, we favour Big Tech companies with strong balance sheets and resilient cash generation, as they are better positioned to sustain AI investments without relying heavily on external financing. Our US IT opportunistic idea combines these preferences through exposure to semiconductors, software and hardware, allowing investors to participate in a potential recovery across a broader range of earnings drivers.
— Ryan Goh, Investment Strategist

The semiconductor segment is expected to continue to lead US technology earnings growth in 2027
Consensus earnings growth (y/y) by US technology subsector, 2025-27 (%)

Source: FactSet, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

Do fundamental drivers support a constructive view on the US healthcare sector?

Our view: We remain constructive on US healthcare, supported by its defensive characteristics and robust earnings growth.
Rationale: US healthcare earnings are projected to grow by 22.5% in 2027, the second-fastest among MSCI US sectors, driven by improving biopharma earnings. The US healthcare sector’s valuation gap against the broader market has been recovering from a steep historical discount a year ago. The sector’s forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of c. 20x now exceeds the broader US market’s c. 18.4x, but we see scope for the valuation to be supported amid investor demand for defensive growth. The sector’s broad legislative policy overhang has materially faded following the US election cycle, while targeted regulatory and oversight risks remain on the watchlist.
Healthcare innovation also underpins structural growth. Wider adoption of obesity and diabetes treatments, alongside advances in oncology treatments, medical devices and robotic surgery, should support long-term earnings growth. With the market rotating away from concentrated AI exposure, healthcare’s stable, non-cyclical demand profile presents compelling opportunities for investors seeking both defensiveness and growth in the near term.
— Jason Wong, Senior Equity Analyst

US healthcare sector earnings are projected to grow 22.5% in 2027 – the second-fastest among MSCI US sectors

Consensus 2027 earnings growth by sector in the S&P500 Index

Source: LSEG I/B/E/S, Standard Chartered

What is your outlook for China’s Big Tech sector?

Our view: We remain positive on China’s Big Tech sector, consistent with our Overweight stance on the country’s IT and communication services sector.
Rationale: Valuations across China’s technology sector remain inexpensive at 14.2x, with investor attention centred on whether AI-driven revenue can offset elevated AI-related spending, which is currently compressing margins. Elevated AI capex and negative free cash flow remain key investor concerns in the Q3 earnings season. Top-line momentum also remains uneven: soft domestic consumption continues to weigh on e-commerce, advertising and local services, whereas gaming and cloud computing are delivering resilient growth. The broader narrative is steadily transitioning towards commercialisation, with rapid enterprise penetration by AI workplace agents and upcoming AI model launches shifting the market focus towards active deployment and conversion to paid usage. Evolving regulatory frameworks covering AI governance, agent self-regulation, tax scrutiny and compliance requirements remain important variables influencing medium-term margin trajectories. Ultimately, valuation support, gradual monetisation of AI capabilities and resilient core segments support our Overweight positioning.
— Cindy Lam, CFA, Senior Investment Strategist

China’s technology sector valuations remain inexpensive at 14.2x, nearly 1 standard deviation below the mean
Hang Seng Technology (HSTECH Index) 12-month forward P/E ratio

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

Why are you closing your US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) opportunistic idea?

Our view: We are closing our opportunistic bullish US TIPS position, as the risk-reward profile has become less compelling. The trade returned 4.4% since its initiation on 11 April 2025.
Rationale: We initiated an opportunistic bullish position in US TIPS on 11 April 2025 as an oil and inflation hedge, expecting geopolitical uncertainty to keep inflation expectations elevated. The risk-reward, however, has since become less compelling, as hawkish Fed commentary, easing geopolitical risks and a potential slowdown in the pace of AI buildout are now likely to ease broader inflation and ‘techflation’ pressures. We have therefore closed the opportunistic idea, realising a gain of 4.4%.
— Cedric Lam, Senior Investment Strategist

While real (net-of-inflation) yields remain elevated, the inflation-protection function of US TIPS has diminished as inflation expectations ease
One-year USD inflation swap, 10-year US real yield

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

How do falling oil prices and October’s US inflation data affect your Fed and bond market outlook?

Our view: Our base case envisages two further 25bps Fed hikes by mid-2027, with scope for cuts in H2 2027 if energy prices remain consistently lower and growth trajectory normalises. We favour income over chasing duration gains, focusing on higher-quality corporate bonds with 3-7-year maturities.
Rationale: Lower oil prices have a two-sided effect: they ease inflationary pressures and support growth by boosting purchasing power and lowering business costs. Cheaper energy, therefore, does not automatically justify Fed easing. Our base case envisages two further 25bps hikes by mid-2027, with scope for cuts in H2 2027 if energy prices remain consistently lower. Sustained moderation in core inflation would challenge the near-term tightening path. However, October’s US consumer inflation print reinforced our assessment that each Fed meeting now remains a ‘live’ decision.
With the US 10-year government bond yield already within our 5.0-5.25% 3-month range, we favour income over chasing duration gains. Credit performance has diverged: Developed Market high-yield bonds have outperformed both investment-grade credit and government bonds. Credit still offers attractive income, and we retain our preference for 3-7-year maturities, although heavy primary issuance remains a counterweight. We favour selective carry, with a preference for higher-quality corporate bonds. These include bonds issued by leading AI hyperscalers, where risk-reward has become more attractive. Our emphasis is on generating steady income, rather than relying on further declines in bond yields or spreads.
— Cedric Lam, Senior Investment Strategist

Corporate bonds still offer attractive income, but fundamental quality matters
Total returns of Bloomberg US government, US investment-grade corporate, US BB-rated high-yield and US CCC-rated high-yield indices over the last 12 months

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

Does the USD’s rally have further to run?

Our view: Further upside appears limited. Stronger-than-expected US core inflation in October and hawkish Fed comments have pushed the US Dollar Index (DXY) above 103. However, markets already price in more Fed tightening than we expect. We see the DXY returning to its 101.00-102.95 range in the near term, before gradually weakening towards our 12-month forecast of 98.5.
Rationale: US core consumer prices rose 0.3% m/m in October, above the 0.2% m/m expected, meeting Fed Governor Waller’s threshold for considering a 50bps December rate hike. This pushed US government bond yields higher, supporting the USD rally. However, futures now imply a Fed rate peak of 4.50-4.75% by mid-2027, compared with our expectation of 4.25-4.50% following two 25bps hikes, one in December and the second in H1 2027. We expect the Fed to begin easing in H2 2027. As market expectations gradually converge towards our view, USD support from US bond yields should weaken.
Meanwhile, falling oil and petrol prices should help ease headline inflation in the coming months, reducing pressure for further Fed tightening. This reinforces our expectation of limited USD upside, although persistent services inflation remains a key risk.
— Vincent Tan, Senior Investment Strategist

US dollar index’s rally above 103 looks stretched

USD index (DXY) and technicals

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Do you expect USD/JPY to sustainably break out above 160 in the near term?

Our view: We see USD/JPY rangebound with a downside bias, as growing BoJ tightening expectations and potential policy convergence will support gradual JPY appreciation.
Rationale: Renewed tech optimism has encouraged the re-establishment of carry trades, providing support to the pair lately. Meanwhile, US core inflation beat expectations for a third consecutive month in October, reinforcing expectations for a December Fed hike. Further upside inflation surprises could widen the US-Japan interest rate differential and push USD/JPY higher.
However, the risk of intervention by Japan’s Ministry of Finance is likely to rise materially around 160, limiting the scope for sustained upside. On the downside, a 25bps BoJ hike to 1.50%, accompanied by clear signals of consecutive hikes in March and June 2027, would be a significant yen-positive catalyst. A more non-linear downside scenario would be a disorderly equity sell-off, which could trigger rapid JPY appreciation through carry-trade unwinding. We see scope for the pair to test support towards 156 in the coming weeks.
— Iris Yuen, Investment Strategist

articles.title: Tokenised stocks: what the SEC exemption really approved
articles.text: On 17 September 2026, the SEC allowed certain platforms to trade US shares as blockchain tokens under a temporary set of rules. But following a share’s price is not enough. Investors must receive the same shareholder rights, including dividends and voting rights, as buyers of the original shares.The announcement was not approval for every product sold as a “tokenised stock”. The distinction is between owning a share and buying a separate product whose price follows a share.Platforms meeting the SEC’s conditions can trade eligible tokens without registering as traditional stock exchanges. Some firms providing tokens for buyers and sellers also receive relief from dealer registration requirements.Automated market makers are software allowing participants admitted by the platform to trade against a pool of assets, rather than matching buyers with sellers. Order, page 33The SEC also limits the scale of trading:For shares in the S&P 500 and Russell 1000, plus certain other exchange-traded investments: a platform can offer up to 75 securities. Its average daily trading in each token cannot exceed 0.25% of the underlying investment’s average daily trading volume during the previous month.For other eligible listed investments: a platform can offer up to 250 securities, with a higher limit of 2.5%.For how long: the permission lasts from 17 September 2026 to 17 September 2031, unless the SEC changes the dates. Order, Section VAffiliated platforms must combine trading volumes when applying the limits.The limits do not apply to the token market as a whole.Before offering a token, a platform must check whether the token carries the same shareholder rights as the original share. If an unrelated business creates a token representing a company’s shares, the company must receive notice and a chance to object.The US exemption relieves trading venues and liquidity providers; it does not approve individual products. Nor does it replace the permissions providers need to offer products in the EU.Is a tokenised stock the same as owning the share, and do you get dividends and voting rights?A tokenised stock can represent the share itself, an ownership interest held through a custodian, or a separate instrument linked to its price. Dividend treatment and voting rights depend on the structure. For the SEC exemption, the holder must receive the rights of the equivalent traditional share class.Tokenisation represents an asset digitally on a shared ledger. CoinShares' tokenisation guide explains the process.SEC staff explained the different types of tokenised securities in January 2026.A transfer agent keeps track of who owns a company’s shares. A security entitlement gives an investor rights to shares held through a broker or another financial firm, rather than directly in the investor’s name.The order excludes synthetic exposure and requires equivalent company interests and liquidation rights. The standard is not 1:1 backing or 1:1 redeemability: the test is whether the holder receives the same shareholder rights, dividends and votes included.Who issues tokenised equities and how do their structures differ?Tokenised equities do not all give investors the same ownership rights. Ondo and xStocks offer claims against an issuer, while Superstate describes recording actual company shares. Backpack separates its tokens from shares held in a brokerage account. The table compares the products and what investors receive.According to Token Terminal, the tokenised equity market reached $4.68B on 2 November 2026, up from $407.5M a year earlier, with growth recorded every month.Backpack's brokerage explanation describes a property interest under New York's Uniform Commercial Code, Article 8. The token is a claim on a special purpose vehicle, a separate company holding the assets. Compare token rights with the rights attached to the brokerage holding received on redemption.Securitize's 8 October 2026 entitlement-token launch describes dividend and applicable voting rights, separately from issuer-sponsored SECZ.Beyond the table, Figure describes OPEN as a network for blockchain-registered equities. Dinari describes its Financial Network as infrastructure for securities liquidity and settlement. DTCC launched tokenised DTC entitlements on 28 October 2026, including through Canton Network.The ranking is led by certificates and notes offering broad distribution. Native share offerings are smaller. Whether equivalent-rights structures gain market share over the following year is the comparison to revisit.Why do tokenised stocks trade at a different price to the real share?A token and its referenced share can trade in separate markets. Creation and redemption help keep the token’s price close to the share price, but access, inventory and trading hours can limit the process. When the stock market is closed, token demand can push the price far from the share’s last traded price.Tram Doman, of Bullish, a backer of issuer-sponsored tokenisation, writing in CoinDesk opinion on 24 September 2026, reports Robinhood's AMC token moving from $2.55 to $23.16 late on 3 September, then back to $3.26 within the hour, on $10.5M of pool volume. The peak was 9.1 times AMC's $2.54 NYSE close seven hours earlier.Doman links the move to demand for a memecoin quoted in tokenised AMC and reports a median closing-price deviation of 0.9% across seven sessions from 31 August to 9 September. Tram Doman column identifies one authorised participant, no minting or burning during the spike, and 47 mints on 4 September. The account suggests constrained arbitrage; causation remains Doman's interpretation.An authorised participant creates or redeems through an issuer. Minting creates tokens; burning cancels tokens. Creation and redemption align depositary receipts with shares and ETPs with net asset value, but require access, inventory or borrowing, and executable conversion.Robinhood's prospectus page 60, warns the issuer may be unable to trade collateral "outside of exchange market hours, or in the necessary quantities, or at all". The NYSE's regular session occupies 32.5 hours of a normal week, or 19.3% of 168 hours. Inventory and extended-hours trading can help, but continuous token trading cannot guarantee continuous underlying liquidity.The wrapper serves investors seeking price exposure. Robinhood's EU KID pages 1 and 2, describes a derivative linked to a US-listed asset and identifies Robinhood Europe as the sole counterparty. As with a participating note, access comes through another party's obligation, bringing counterparty risk rather than shareholder ownership.Before allocating, ask four questions: what rights does the token itself carry? Who is the issuer, and which jurisdiction governs the claim? Can more than one participant create and redeem? What happens to pricing when the underlying market closes?FAQsWhat did the SEC's tokenised stock exemption approve?Conditional relief for qualifying venues and liquidity providers, not blanket product approval.Is a tokenised stock the same as owning the share, and do you get dividends and voting rights?Only some structures carry shareholder rights; backing alone is insufficient.Who issues tokenised equities and how do their structures differ?Companies and intermediaries issue shares, custodial interests or separate price-linked instruments.Why do tokenised stocks trade at a different price to the real share?Separate liquidity and constrained creation or redemption can prevent price alignment.

articles.title: Response to CSA Consultation Paper 51-406 Modernizing the Regulation of Public Companies | Norges Bank Investment Management
articles.text:
We refer to the Canadian Securities Administrators (CSA)’s consultation on modernizing the regulation of public companies. We appreciate the opportunity to contribute our perspective.
Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) is the investment management division of the Norwegian Central Bank that manages the Norwegian Government Pension Fund Global. We work to safeguard and build financial wealth for future generations. As of 30 June 2026, we managed approximately CAD 3.3 trillion (USD 2.3 trillion) in assets, with CAD 106 billion invested in Canada. We held shares in 149 Canadian public companies with a combined value of about CAD 54 billion.
As a long-term, diversified financial investor, we rely on companies' disclosures to inform our investment decisions, risk management and shareholder voting. We have an interest in disclosure regimes that surface material, investor-relevant information in a consistent and comparable format, without imposing undue cost or duplication on reporting companies. We support the CSA's aim of a balanced and responsive regime that maintains strong investor protection and disclosure quality.
We highlight four points from our response. First, we support removing undue cost or duplication while retaining the material, consistent and comparable disclosures investors rely on for their decision-making wherever relief is applied. Second, consistent with our view on optimizing corporate reporting frequency, we support giving companies the option to report semi-annually, but suggest a measured approach, with appropriate safeguards to retain disclosure quality in and between filings. Third, we stress the importance of maintaining strong shareholder protections and regulatory stability through any modernization process to support a competitive Canadian market. Finally, we encourage the publication of a roadmap for aligning with the standards of the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) for reporting financially material sustainability-related information.
Our responses to selected consultation questions are set out in Annex 1. They draw on our published positions and refer to our submissions to other regulators and standard-setters where relevant. We thank the CSA for considering our perspectives and remain at your disposal should you wish to discuss these matters further.
Yours sincerely,

Snorre GjerdePolicy Lead

}Source: GettyCommentaryStrategic EuropeIs Russia Winning the Perception War in Germany?In Germany, competing perceptions of Russia are highlighting a tension between public opinion and government policy. In the country’s east, where division is widespread, populist parties are taking advantage.Link CopiedBy Gwendolyn SassePublished on Nov 5, 2026The electoral results of parties like the Alternative for Germany (AfD), Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), and The Left in recent state elections in Germany have demonstrated the potency of pro-Russian policies and narratives for the country’s electorate. The platforms of all three parties prominently featured rhetoric that was notably positively inclined toward Russia.The election program of the AfD in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt went furthest, demanding a revival of Russian-language teaching and school exchanges in addition to an end to sanctions and the resumption of close energy relations. It also reduced Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine to the status of “simmering.” All three parties loudly called for peace and diplomacy—without any indication of how to open a meaningful diplomatic channel.The strategy here is not to deliver on these objectives but to tap into uncertainty, fear, and anger in order to mobilize voters. The varying successes of the three parties are, of course, not only the result of prominent references to Russia, but also of a now-embedded contestation over Germany’s support for Ukraine and future relations with Moscow acting as a new political cleavage.It seems paradoxical that pro-Russian views have such popular appeal at a time when Moscow’s hybrid attacks on Germany and other European countries have been on the rise. After all, the explosive-laden drone found at Leipzig airport in August, 2026, had marked a new stage in the confrontation. For the first time, Berlin clearly attributed the attack to Russia and the head of the German foreign intelligence service subsequently spoke of an ongoing “shadow war.”The paradox is part of a new iteration of Germany’s Russia complex, which has historically seen Berlin waver between the extremes of enmity and cooperation. This time around, views on appeasing Moscow are not only rooted in a fear of military escalation but also tied to the assumption that military spending and support for Ukraine undermine social policy and long-overdue structural reforms. This despite the government separating the budgetary logics for both types of spending in order not to pit one against the other.Germany is not the only European country where support for Ukraine and an increase in military spending have become contested, but the framing of Russia-friendly views in terms of history and culture has a specific salience in the country’s discourse. Moreover, it is wrapped up in a continued juxtaposition between eastern and western regions, despite the fact that these regional and political denominations have become fuzzy as a result of mobility as well as structural and generational change. A softer reinterpretation of the Soviet-controlled German Democratic Republic functions as an instrument to build distance to western Germany and an idea of closeness to Russia. Such arguments create a space for projections which have little to do with eastern Germany’s Soviet past or Russia’s political actions today.Instead, different historical paths led to Russia-friendly or Russia-blind attitudes in east and west. A shared positive memory of rapprochement under former Soviet premier Mikhail Gorbachev continues to cloud current assessments of Russia. He remains a prominent reference point in discussions about Russia across Germany. The experience of post-1989 transformation provides convenient building blocks for an image of alleged closeness to or expertise on Russia—although citizen-level contact was and is extremely limited. The fact that the populist and extremist parties using such narratives are, for the time being, more successful in eastern Germany can be explained by the higher level of alienation and resentment there that is linked to the memory of that transformation—but it is, above all, a difference in scale and timing.In Germany, the debate about Russia has become a vehicle to position oneself against the national government and the traditional parties. It is a particularly striking proof that in politics, perceptions matter and can develop their own dynamics. Recognizing this is critical to understanding the presence and simultaneous absence of the real Russia in the public debate. Even Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pointed to widespread misconceptions about Russia in Germany. At the level of the national government, perceptions and policies have changed since 2022, but a significant gap remains between the national government and society at large. Opinion polls, focus groups, and in-depth interviews with citizens provide ample evidence of this.Germany’s Russia policy over the last decades has been critically examined by a number of studies and several political actors have called for an official investigation. However, government policy is not formulated in a vacuum but in close interaction with society. Therefore, a bottom-up view focusing on perceptions of Russia deserves more attention. An explicitly positive image of the country’s President Vladmir Putin has been drowned out by his full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and an ambivalent image of his country has taken its place. There is not only a widespread self-reported lack of knowledge about Russia but also a tangible lack of interest in—even outright avoidance of—its domestic politics and foreign policy. Against this backdrop, populist and extremist parties manage to mobilize voters on the basis of emotions and vague calls for peace or better living standards through normalization with Russia. This gap between perceptions, wishful thinking, and an attitude of burying your head in the sand on the one hand and political reality on the other makes Germany a prime target for Russian disinformation campaigns and poses a risk to democracy. It is also a significant obstacle to developing a whole-of-society understanding of security that goes beyond the military dimension.Get more news and analysis fromStrategic EuropeSubscribe to Strategic Europe, delivered every Tuesday and Thursday!About the AuthorGwendolyn SasseNonresident Senior Fellow, Carnegie EuropeGwendolyn Sasse is a nonresident senior fellow at Carnegie Europe. Her research focuses on Eastern Europe, with a particular focus on Ukrainian politics and society, EU enlargement, and comparative democratization.Recent WorkCommentaryUkraine: Between a Rock and a Hard PlaceGwendolyn SasseCommentaryThe Power of Language on War and PeaceGwendolyn SasseEUDemocracyDisinformationCivil SocietyEuropeRussiaGermanyCarnegie does not take institutional positions on public policy issues; the views represented herein are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of Carnegie, its staff, or its trustees.More Work from Strategic EuropeCommentaryStrategic EuropeTaking the Pulse: Can Europe Fund Ukraine Without Russian Assets?A sizeable funding shortfall looks increasingly likely to hit Ukraine in 2027. articles.title: Digital asset fund manager survey – October 2026
articles.text: Digital asset allocations rise as diversification eclipses speculationDigital asset allocations rose to 1.3%, from 1.2% in July, as investors shifted from equities and bonds towards alternatives rather than cash.Diversification now accounts for 40% of investment motivations, while speculation has fallen to fifth place, representing less than 9%.Bitcoin retains the strongest growth outlook by a wide margin, while Bitcoin and Ethereum remain core holdings, accounting for 47% of positioning responses.Altcoin preferences are shifting towards newer tokens, including Hyperliquid, SUI and Uniswap, alongside improving sentiment towards Ethereum and Solana.The survey highlighted slightly improving outlook for Ethereum and Solana and a wide selection on new age altcoins such as Hyperliquid, Uniswap and SUI. This improved outlook for these altcoins came at the expense of multi-asset, Cardano and Bitcoin. Although the latter retained the top spot as the asset with the most compelling growth outlook by a significant margin.Allocation to digital assets in the average survey portfolio rose to 1.3%, having risen from 1.2% in the July survey, having risen since July 2025. We can see a trend of investors having re-allocated out of equities and bonds, in favour of a broad set of alternative assets such as commodities and digital assets rather than the perceived safe haven of cash.The largest positions remain those with the most flexible mandates, such as family offices and individual investors.This survey saw a large swing out of the “old guard” altcoins, with the exception of Ethereum, and in to newer tokens such as SUI, Near, AAVE, Hype, Uniswap and Link commonly mentioned.Bitcoin and Ethereum remain core positions in portfolios, comprising 47% of survey responses. Multi-asset also remains popular despite a rise in the stock picking approach we have seen over the last year.Diversification remains the prominent reason for investing in digital assets, and has risen significantly from the last survey to be 40% of all responses, and has been steadily rising since the survey began in 2021. Speculation, once the most prominent reason, has fallen to 5th on the list, now representing less than 9% of responses.Interestingly, since the price rises over the last quarter, we have seen an increase in those who see it as good value, although client demand has fallen significantly.Among survey respondents who have yet to invest, regulatory concerns and corporate restrictions stubbornly remain the main barriers.A perceived lack of fundamentals also featured regularly among the leading concerns, although this has fallen sharply over the past year. Reputational risk, meanwhile, is cited half as often as in last quarter’s survey.Concerns over volatility have also eased, which we believe is understandable given Bitcoin’s volatility is now comparable to that of gold.Of those who have invested, puzzlingly, volatility remains the greatest risk. This is perhaps due to the 50% drawdowns in Bitcoin experienced over the last 12 months.Others concerns over regulations being high are not surprising given the continual stalling of the passing of the Clarity Act in the US.Given recent rise in inflation and consequent rate hikes in the US, it isn’t surprising the those who believe the US Federal Reserve is making a policy error has fallen. Policy expectations are now an important driver of Bitcoin prices, therefore, recent hawkishness from the FED has had a detrimental impact.ABOUT OUR SURVEY: The October 2026 Survey drew 28 responses from investors who cover ~US$642 billion of assets under management.

articles.title: Stalling the production line:  How late arrivals hold up production, and why firms tolerate it. Guest post by Shreya Chandra
articles.text:
Published on
Development Impact

Stalling the production line: How late arrivals hold up production, and why firms tolerate it. Guest post by Shreya Chandra

Development Impact Guest Blogger

November 12, 2026

This page in:

English

English

This is the 6th in this year’s job market series
In the narrow, residential streets of Tiruppur, South India, nearly every other door opens to a small garment factory. At 9 am, when these factories open, many sewing machines remain idle. Their tailors haven’t arrived yet.
Tiruppur is not unusual: worker absences and lateness are common across the developing world. This matters more as firms grow, because moving from individual production to assembly lines requires worker coordination. I study whether late arrivals reduce worker and firm output, and why firms tolerate this behavior.
Factories in Tiruppur are organized as production lines which need coordination
My job market paper focuses on small garment factories in Tiruppur, located inside residential neighborhoods. These factories typically employ 6 workers, 85% of whom live within a 15-minute commute of their firm. Production in these firms is organized in batch processing lines where each worker performs one operation (e.g., joining shoulder seams) and passes bundles of garments to the next worker. This organization of production requires coordination between workers. For example, if the worker who joins shoulder seams arrives late, workers performing later tasks sit idle. This can delay order completion.
However, workers commonly arrive late. Using novel, high-frequency data on the internal functioning of these firms, I show that workers arrive late at work on 43% of worker-days, and arrival times range from 3 hours before to 3 hours after firms’ start time. (Figure 1) These late arrivals reflect workers exercising their preference for flexible arrival times: workers are on average 37 years of age, 45% are female, 94% are married, and 84% have at least one child younger than 14 years of age. Thus, these workers are at a stage of life with substantial care responsibilities at home. Even though owners can learn which workers tend to be late, this unpredictability makes it harder to plan production around worker arrival times.
Figure 1: Distribution of Arrival Times Showing Lateness is Common

The puzzle: firms allow lateness even when production lines require coordination
This setting presents a puzzle. The production line setup implies gains from workers arriving on time, but workers arrive late and unpredictably. This may imply either (1) there are no gains from timely worker arrival, or (2) firms cannot enforce timings or provide large-enough incentives given workers’ value for flexibility.
Firm owners believe that late arrivals hurt their firm and would like workers to arrive at the same time. Yet, they do little to coordinate arrival times. First, most pay workers operation-specific piece-rates with no direct incentives for finished garments. This contract does not provide explicit incentives to arrive on time. Second, firms neither reward punctuality with bonuses nor penalize lateness.
An experiment to test the puzzle
I designed an experiment with 92 firms comprising 600 workers to test whether reducing lateness affects worker and firm outcomes. To do so, I offered workers in 46 randomly selected treatment firms a daily incentive worth 20% of their average daily earnings if they arrived before the start time for four weeks. Control workers received unconditional transfers equivalent to realized incentive payments in treatment firms, so comparisons between treatment and control outcomes don’t reflect income effects. The experiment lasted 6 weeks with 2 pre-incentive weeks and 4 incentive weeks.
Small, informal firms in developing countries often do not maintain any personnel or production records. Over six weeks, I collected daily data on worker attendance, arrival times, work hours, along with weekly firm output, quantity of new orders procured, and their delivery timelines. Uniquely, I recorded each worker’s output for each operation stitched in the day. This helps study the precise mechanisms behind the relationship between worker lateness and firm outcomes.
Comparing production outcomes between treatment and control firms tests whether there are gains from coordinating worker arrival times. Since the bonus was offered as a choice to workers, their decision to arrive on time reveals how much they value flexibility. Workers who forgo the incentive reveal that they value flexibility at more than 20% of their current earnings.
Incentives induced late workers to arrive on time, but output increased for everyone
Workers in treatment firms are nearly 40% more likely to arrive on or before time (21 p.p., compared to a control mean of 58%). This implies that 4 out of 5 arrive on time during incentives compared to 3 out of 5 workers during pre-incentive weeks, conditional on being present. This increase is driven by workers who typically arrived late before the experiment (henceforth, “late”). Workers who were early at baseline (“early” workers) did not change their arrival times. There is no change in whether workers show up to work at all, and a small increase in daily work hours which approximately offsets how late workers were before the incentives.
As a result, workers in treatment firms produce 24% more output per week, equivalent to ~930 additional pieces per week. Output rose by a similar amount for all workers, including “early” workers who did not change their arrival times. This suggests treatment generated positive spillovers within the firm.
Spillovers are concentrated in firms where late arrivals created bottlenecks in production lines
These spillovers could either reflect a better coordinated production line, or other potential mechanisms such as team morale. I use the positioning of “late” workers on the production line to identify firms where lateness is more likely to create bottlenecks along the line. I classify firms as ‘Bottleneck’ firms if any worker who performs upstream tasks in the production line at baseline is a “late” worker. In remaining firms, “late” workers perform downstream tasks (‘Non-Bottleneck’ firms). Incentives improve timely arrival for “late” workers in both sets of firms, while “early” workers don’t change their arrival times.
Effects on worker output are larger in Bottleneck firms (Figure 2). Relative to control, workers in these firms produce 32% more in weekly output, compared to 12% more in Non-Bottleneck firms. Strikingly, spillovers to “early” workers are only present in Bottleneck firms: both “early” and “late” workers gain ~33% in weekly output. In Non-Bottleneck firms, gains are concentrated among “late” workers only. Therefore, spillovers reflect gains from a better coordinated production line.
Figure 2: Treatment effects and spillovers

Incentives increase firm output and reduce delivery delays, but are too costly to implement
Increases in worker output translate to overall firm output. Treatment firms produce 29% more in total output, procure 21% more new orders, and reduce delivery delays by 40%.
Profit estimates suggest that, excluding incentive payments, weekly profits would rise 8%. However, paying the 20% incentives I offered reduces weekly profits by 5%. Despite the large incentive, about a quarter of the workers in treatment firms continue arriving late, suggesting strong preference for flexibility. Thus, incentivizing timely arrival requires large incentives. This finding is suggestive and does not rule out other cost-effective mechanisms or contract designs that can reduce lateness.
Why do workers need flexibility? Workers report limited access to market alternatives for household and care services, and a high degree of volatility in daily lives due to unreliable public services (electricity, water supply, lack of school buses), as key reasons behind the need for flexible work schedules. Women and workers caring for children or elderly demonstrate a stronger preference for flexibility.
Owners are aware of the costs of lateness, but continue to allow it
Treatment firm owners acknowledged the benefits from the experiment but were only willing to pay incentives worth 5% of workers’ daily earnings. A year later, treatment firms reported little effort in enforcing timely arrivals beyond verbal encouragement.
Why can’t firms enforce timely arrival through disciplinary measures? These small firms operate in dense clusters where most other firms pay similar piece-rates and allow workers to be more than 30 minutes late. This reflects a segmented labor market: large firms enforce strict schedules and hire younger, less experienced migrant workers, while small firms compete for more experienced local workers by offering flexibility. Given workers' strong preference for flexibility, half of firm owners (52%) believe that strict rules without extra pay would increase worker attrition. Therefore, no single firm can easily enforce strict work timings.
Addressing factors that drive preference for flexibility can serve as effective industrial policy
Overall, the findings suggest that returns to coordination within the firm are economically meaningful. However, workers have a strong need for flexible work schedules and neighboring firms tolerate lateness. This makes it difficult for firms to enforce or incentivize timely arrival.
The need for flexibility appears to stem from poor quality of public infrastructure and missing markets for household services and childcare, disproportionately affecting women. Policies aimed at improving public services and infrastructure could reduce worker lateness and consequently accelerate firm growth.
Shreya Chandra is a PhD student at University of California, Berkeley.

articles.title: Active ETFs: broadening the sources of portfolio returns - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
Are traditional equity and bond allocations still enough to diversify portfolios? With correlations between the two asset classes rising again in 2026, investors are increasingly looking beyond conventional approaches for new sources of returns.

Vincent Bérard, BNPP AM’s Head of Product Strategy, explores with Chief Market Strategist, Daniel Morris, how active exchange-traded funds (ETFs) can potentially help investors diversify and manage risk. Among the approaches they discuss are equity long-short strategies that seek to capture differences in company fundamentals and option-based income strategies that seek to generate regular cash flow from option premiums.

Each approach comes with its own risks and trade-offs. “Understanding how these strategies work, what drives their returns and how they behave across different market environments is essential to assessing their potential role in a diversified portfolio.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast for more detailed insights into how investing in active ETFs can potentially provide effective solutions in different market conditions.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Talking Heads with Vincent Bérard

Daniel Morris: Hello, and welcome to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing active ETFs (exchange-traded funds). I’m Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, and I’m joined today by Vincent Bérard, Head of Product Strategy.

Welcome, Vincent. Thanks for joining me.

Vincent Bérard: It’s great to be here.

DM: One of the more sustained trends we’ve seen in investing over the years is the increasing popularity ETFs. Alongside that, we’re seeing a lot of innovation, and we’ll be talking about that around active ETFs today. In your view, Vincent, why are investors looking beyond traditional equity bond portfolios?

VB: For a long time, the default to build a portfolio was a balance between equities and bonds, whether 60% bonds and 40% equities or 70/30. The logic was that when shares fell, high-quality bonds would usually hold up. But that relationship is not a ‘law of nature’.

In 2022, global equities and bonds both fell at the same time and by more than 15% following inflation and rising interest rates that hit both asset classes.

That was a reminder that diversification depends on where returns come from. To put this into perspective, the correlation between US bonds and equities reached almost 50% that year and remained at around 40% in 2023. After two years of correlation around zero percent in 2024 and 2025, we are now observing, in 2026, a correlation of returns around 40%.

Investors are increasingly asking, “Where does my return come from? How independent is it from the rest of my portfolio, and how can I truly diversify further my returns?” There are two broad answers, in my view.

The first is liquid alternatives – strategies that seek to earn returns from assets or portfolios that behave differently from the broad market, so they can add a new source of returns. They are typically accessed through a discipline[d] and quantitative model. Popular examples are managed futures and equity long-short factor investing.

The second is income or outcome-orientated strategies to generate regular cash flow but from a different source of returns, typically from option premiums. Outcome-orientated strategies aim to shape the range of possible returns over a set period. For example, they can absorb an initial part of losses in exchange for capping gains. Both come with trade-offs, and we can speak about these in a moment.

The common thread is a shift from “how many asset classes do I own?” into “what drives each part of my portfolio?”

DM: One of the topics that you mentioned – managed futures strategies – can you tell us more about them and why some investors see it as an interesting option?

VB: A managed futures strategy or portfolio aims to follow trends in a systematic way by investing in a model-driven dynamic portfolio of liquid futures. What this means is, rather than predicting what may happen in the markets based on macro or fundamental analysis, it follows price.

If the market has been rising for a sustained period, the model tends to go long. If it has been falling, the model tends to go short. It’s applied through futures across many markets – equities, bonds, currencies and commodities, typically. Why do investors value it?

First, diversification: it draws on many markets and does not depend on the forecast. It can behave differently from a traditional portfolio.

Second, convexity: trends can develop in both directions, including during sharp sell-offs, so the strategy can benefit when markets move sharply up, but also down. In periods of pronounced trends such as inflation-driven or rate-hike cycles, trend strategies have historically been an important contributor.

Going back to the example of 2022, managed future strategies did very well that year, keeping typically long commodities position and short bond exposures. I think the average return of managed future strategies that year was north of 20%. And the first nine months of 2026 showed a similar environment of pressures on bonds and oil markets.

Managed futures also help in investor portfolios. The average is up 14% this year. When markets move sideways, however, the models can be whipsawed by repeated reversals and lack of direction, so you can have drawdowns and that can potentially last a long time.

This is why managed futures is best judged as a diversifier over full market cycles rather than in any single quarter.

DM: One of the other strategies you mentioned was long-short, which I think for a lot of people brings to mind hedge funds, which is not what we’re discussing today.

VB: Long-short strategies originate from the world of hedge funds, as you mentioned, but it is now being implemented and popularised in more liquid and transparent ways.

It’s anchored into what we call factor investing. Even though not all long-short strategies would be following these type of models, it remains quite a prominent way to do it. Factor investing starts from a simple observation. Some characteristics of companies – such as their valuation, quality, momentum and volatility – have been associated with differences in returns over long periods.

Researchers have studied this effect since the ’70s and they are now widely used by practitioners. A long-short approach builds on this. It buys companies typically with stronger characteristics in these factors and sells those with weaker ones. The attraction is that the return comes from the difference between the two rather than relying only on the market rising.

That can be useful in environments where investors are paying close attention to company fundamentals – as they were during the higher rate periods of ’22 and over the last 18 months. The approach is not without risk. Factors can underperform for years. The environmentalsub-factors can underperform for years, and the environment matters.

For example, when interest rates are very low or even negative, fundamental stock picking criteria is a lot less efficient and can struggle to add value simply because investors do not really look much into the leverage of a company, for example, when rates are near zero.

Short positions also carry their own risks, including the possibility that a shorter stock rises sharply. For investors, the useful question is: What is the rationale behind the construction of such [a] portfolio? What is the approach? And how [does] it behave across different market conditions?

DM: Another innovation you mentioned was defined outcome or buffer strategies. What do they offer?

VB: Buffer or defined outcome strategies are designed to shape the range of possible results. A buffer structure, for example, combines an equity exposure with options so that a minuscule portion of losses will be absorbed, and in exchange gains are capped at a predetermined level.

The main benefit is predictability. A large fall just before or early in retirement, for example, can do lasting damage even if markets recover later because the withdrawals that will be taken are taken from a smaller base. A buffer can help manage this risk of drawdown and can also support capital preservation during an accumulation phase, not only when you’re really close to retirement.

This is because the result is a clear range of outcomes for the given period. The trade-offs need to be clear. The upside is capped. The outcomes depend on when you enter and exit this type of product. Two investors in the same fund or ETF can have different experiences.

The level of the cap above which you give up upside and the protection are also set usually at each period. I would tell investors to read carefully the documentation, understand the products, speak to a professional advisor. But it is a powerful tool to give clarity in potential outcomes and mitigate some potential losses in your portfolio.

DM: Finally, let’s talk about option-based income strategies. What do they offer?

VB: Option-based in-income strategies are quite a broad category. Generally, they aim to earn a premium that option buyers pay. Buyers pay for protection or for exposure through options, and the sellers of these options collect the premium. For investors, this can create a regular cash flow that is a distinct source of return alongside capital growth.

And because it depends on equity options rather than interest rates or bonds, this source of return is less sensitive to rates movements than traditional income solutions.

There’s been quite a strong interest over the last few years on very short-dated options, which expire within days or a week. This market has grown significantly, partly because demand for short-term protection by market participants has increased, so the liquidity of the market has deepened. Because more and more participants use these instruments to hedge short-term risk, they are happy to pay a higher price and a higher premium.

If you are able to benefit from this premium, it’s an interesting way to generate income. Again, fairly de-correlated, fairly diversifying compared to the usual source of return.

Now, with any income strategy, there are scenarios in which this income can be offset by capital losses. The seller typically takes the risk of sudden large market moves, sometimes called gap risk, where the losses can exceed the premiums you collect. So, income can be steady in calm markets and may reverse in stressed ones.

Then again, these instruments are interesting tools in the portfolios, but the details matter, and it is important to look at scenarios and how it fits in in one’s portfolio.

DM: Well, Vincent, thank you very much for joining me.

VB: It was my pleasure.

DM: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you would like more information about our capabilities in active ETFs, please reach out to your asset management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website for investment insights at viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com.

Viewpoint brings commentary and analysis in a variety of formats, from investment outlooks to asset allocation videos and podcasts, to help investors make better-informed decisions.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Daniel Morris, and Vincent Berard, Head of Product Strategy.

Please do join me next week. Until then, take care.

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesEuropeWhy European Companies Are Forecast to Have Robust Earnings GrowthNov 13, 2026Share Strong earnings growth has helped European stocks absorb higher bond yields, elevated energy prices, and subdued domestic economic growth over the last year. European earnings are growing significantly faster than the euro area’s economic growth rate: Goldman Sachs Research forecasts STOXX 600 EPS to grow 18% in 2026. The equity market is a “distorted mirror” of the economy, with some sectors representing a higher proportion of earnings in the stock index compared with their contribution to overall economic activity. Listed companies now generate most of their revenues outside their country of domicile, and the euro area’s share of STOXX 600 sales has fallen from more than 60% in 1990 to about one-third today.European company earnings are growing rapidly—and at a faster pace than the euro area economy. The strong earnings have helped the stock market absorb higher bond yields, elevated energy prices, and subdued domestic economic growth, writes Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist for Goldman Sachs Research, in a report.
What is the forecast for STOXX 600 index earnings?

Our analysts expect earnings per share for the STOXX 600 index of European stocks to grow 18% in 2026 and 7% in 2027. Meanwhile, euro area nominal GDP is forecast to grow 3.3% in 2026 and 2.8% in 2027.
“This raises an important question,” Bell writes. “Why are European earnings proving more resilient than the domestic economy would suggest?”
Are listed companies an accurate representation of the economy?

Investors often use domestic GDP growth to gauge company earnings growth, Bell observes. “But this relationship is far from mechanical and can vary significantly over time,” she adds.
For example, the two were roughly aligned in 2025 when euro area nominal GDP grew around 3.7% while STOXX 600 earnings growth was 2.4%. This year, though, earnings are expected to considerably outpace economic growth. (The STOXX 600 benchmark reflects a broader European footprint than the euro area, spanning companies domiciled in the UK, Switzerland, and Denmark, among others.)
One possible reason why earnings of listed European companies appear to be decoupling from domestic economic growth could be the composition of sectors represented among Europe’s biggest stocks.
“The equity market is a distorted mirror of the economy,” Bell writes. GDP measures value across the entire domestic economy, whereas aggregate market earnings reflect the profits of a concentrated group of large listed companies.
For example, companies in the financial sector account for more than 30% of EURO STOXX earnings (an index of euro area stocks), but only 10% of euro area economic activity. Energy and technology are also more important to listed earnings, while real estate, retail, and industrials have much larger weights in the economy relative to the European stock market.
Why does global growth matter more than domestic growth for European companies?

Country exposure also helps to explain the divergence between European earnings and the domestic economy. Listed companies now generate most of their revenues outside their country of domicile, and the euro area’s share of STOXX 600 sales has fallen from more than 60% in 1990 to about one-third today.
At the same time, exposure to the US, Asia, and emerging markets has increased steadily, Bell observes.
“With more than half of STOXX 600 revenues now generated outside Europe, global rather than domestic growth is increasingly more relevant for listed companies.”
Goldman Sachs Research captures this with sales-weighted GDP growth, which weights regional growth by the geographic breakdown of companies’ revenues in the prior year. This measure has exceeded euro area growth in most years since the early 2000s. It is also the dominant driver of earnings: A 1 percentage point acceleration is associated with roughly 10 percentage points of higher STOXX 600 EPS growth.
Currency also matters. A weaker euro raises the translated value of overseas profits, a meaningful share of which is denominated in US dollars, and improves the competitiveness of European companies.
Can higher energy prices support company earnings?

Europe is a net energy importer, so higher prices squeeze households and raise corporate costs. But the economy's sensitivity to oil prices has declined as the euro area economy has become less dependent on oil.
The market's composition also provides a cushion: companies involved in energy and basic resources benefit directly from higher commodity prices, while chemicals companies and many industrial companies can pass costs on to customers.
The cushion may not last. Sustained high energy costs can weaken company profit margins as growth and pricing power fade. The negative impact of higher costs can take time to appear in margins: After the 2022 energy shock, earnings for energy companies rose quickly while easing supply bottlenecks supported autos and chemicals companies; six to 12 months later, earnings estimates for energy and chemicals companies began to fall as commodity prices normalized and cost pressure became more visible.
The current Middle East shock could follow a similar sequence, with margins outside financials and commodities coming under pressure if demand slows and pricing power fades.
Given that our economists do not expect significant changes in euro area economic growth momentum, Bell’s team is more cautious than the consensus of financial analysts when it comes to European companies’ profit margins. Goldman Sachs Research forecasts broadly flat margins for STOXX 600 companies until 2028 after financials and commodities are excluded. On the other hand, the consensus of analysts expects margins to expand by more than 100 basis points to 10.1% from 8.7%.
