We should be careful not to overstate precision here. Some of the post-2022 evidence is based on short samples, and it is difficult to separate cleanly the effects of inflation itself, media attention, energy prices and broader uncertainty. But the broad direction of travel is clear enough to matter for policy: today’s shocks may now have larger effects on expectations than similar shocks would have had before 2022.
I would not call this de-anchoring. But I would call it a change in the environment in which expectations are formed. A central bank that could previously assume a high degree of inattention among households and firms may no longer be able to do so.
That observation cuts both ways. Greater attention means that clear and credible central bank communication may have more traction. But it may also allow adverse price news to travel more quickly into beliefs. Louder noise is not necessarily offset by louder signals, especially if attention to recent inflation crowds out the forward-looking information policymakers seek to convey.
The conclusion I draw is deliberately cautious. Household and firm expectations may now respond more strongly to inflation shocks than before 2022. We should not treat every rise in those expectations as evidence of a wage-price spiral, but neither should we dismiss them simply because they are noisy or imperfectly measured.
But expectations are only the first stage of the mechanism. Whether they ultimately matter for inflation depends on whether they feed through into behaviour. I turn to that second stage next.
Stage 2: The importance of inflation expectations in generating persistent inflation
Survey expectations are not behaviour. They are an input into behaviour. For monetary policy, the crucial question is whether they feed into wage bargaining, price setting, consumption and investment and, ultimately, inflation itself.
That is Stage 2, and it is harder to establish empirically.
In theory, the mechanisms are straightforward. On the nominal side, households expecting higher inflation may seek higher nominal wages to protect real incomes; and firms may raise prices. In the extreme, as Lorenzoni and Werning (2023) Opens in a new window formalise, when workers’ real-wage aspirations and firms’ desired margins are jointly inconsistent with the real income available, attempts to protect those positions through wage and price setting can generate persistent inflation.
On the real side, expectations may also affect household spending decisions, with two competing effects: higher expected prices can bring consumption forward, while concern about future real incomes can push households in the opposite direction (Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, 2005) Opens in a new window. For firms, the effect on employment and investment depends not only on price expectations but also on what they expect to happen to demand.
Identification is difficult because inflation influences expectations, as we saw in Stage 1, while expectations may also influence inflation, and both respond to wider economic conditions. As a result, the evidence base is thinner than the importance of the question might suggest.
I would organise the evidence in two buckets: microeconomic studies that ask whether changing expectations changes behaviour; and aggregate evidence on whether expectations help explain or predict inflation dynamics. Considered as signposts, neither bucket is perfect. But together they help us assess which expectations matter most, and why.
Micro evidence
The micro evidence is strongest for firms’ price setting. Experimental and survey studies find that higher inflation expectations lead to higher intended price increases. Estimated pass-through is not one-for-one, but economically meaningful at around 20 to 30 per cent in (Abberger Opens in a new window et al., 2025 Opens in a new window; Coibion, Gorodnichenko, Ropele, 2019 Opens in a new window), and larger in some UK survey evidence (Ghassibe et al., 2025; Yotzov et al., 2025 Opens in a new window). Expectations are therefore not merely epiphenomenal: in at least some settings, they enter directly into decisions that matter for inflation.
The wage evidence is positive but weaker, and much of it predates the recent inflation surge (Guerreiro et al., 2024 Opens in a new window; Jain et al.,2024 Opens in a new window; Savignac et al., 2024 Opens in a new window; Hajdini et al., 2023 Opens in a new window). Crucially, the ability to translate an increase in inflation expectations into wage outcomes is likely to depend on labour-market conditions, institutional arrangements and bargaining power.
Evidence on real decisions is more mixed. Higher expected inflation can bring some households purchases forward (D’Acunto et al., 2022a Opens in a new window; D’Acunto et al., 2022b Opens in a new window),footnote [3] but it can also make them more cautious if they associate inflation with weaker real income or greater uncertainty (Coibion Opens in a new window, et al., 2023 Opens in a new window; D’Acunto et al., 2023 Opens in a new window; Coibion et al., 2022 Opens in a new window),footnote [4] as growing evidence suggest they do (Zhang Opens in a new window, 2026 Opens in a new window, Debortoli & Iovino, 2025 Opens in a new window). Similarly, firms’ employment and investment decisions similarly depend on whether higher inflation is interpreted as stronger demand or as a cost shock squeezing margins (Coibion Opens in a new window et al., 2019 Opens in a new window; Coibion et al., 2018 Opens in a new window). That ambiguity is not a nuisance in the data; it is part of the economics.
Aggregate evidence
The aggregate evidence begins with a deliberately simple question: do expectations predict inflation? Using UK data, we can look at the relationship between headline inflation and the one-year-ahead expectations reported one year earlier by different groups. We focus short-horizon expectations, which evidence suggests matter more for transmission to aggregate dynamics (Reis, 2026 Opens in a new window; Coibion & Gorodnichenko, 2025 Opens in a new window; Werning, 2022 Opens in a new window).
Chart 12 summarises the results. Financial-market expectations have the strongest correlation with future headline inflation and explain the largest share of the variation. Firms come next, followed by households. Among households, those with more accurate perceptions of current inflation have relatively greater predictive power, as one might expect.

But forecasting performance is not the same thing as policy relevance. A forecasting regression cannot tell us whether an agent matters because their expectations influence inflation, or because they are good at forecasting inflation that would have happened anyway. That distinction is central. Financial-market participants are paid to process macroeconomic information, and they incorporate forward-looking signals quickly. It may not be surprising that their expectations look like better forecasts, even if they have no direct part to play in setting goods prices and wages.

Put another way, an expectations measure can matter for two different reasons. It may contain useful information about inflation that would occur anyway, or it may influence the decisions that determine inflation. A measure can therefore be a good forecast without being causally important, or a poor forecast in levels while still affecting the direction of wage and price-setting. Policymakers need to distinguish between those roles.
We can get closer to the hypothesised mechanism by focusing on inflation measures that households and firms are more likely to influence, such as domestic, underlying and wage-sensitive inflation, rather than imported energy prices or agricultural shocks. The results are more consistent with a behavioural channel operating through domestic price-setting, although they do not identify such a channel causally.

Whether expectations influence inflation is also likely to depend on the state of the economy. Households have more scope to translate inflation expectations into wage outcomes when labour markets are tight. Firms have more scope to translate them into prices when demand is strong, and pricing power is greater. A given movement in expectations may therefore have considerably more traction in some economic conditions than in others.
One suggestive test of that state-dependence is to compare the periods before and after 2022 (Chart 15). The later period combined high inflation and elevated attention with a tight labour market and pressure on firms’ margins. During that period, the predictive power of household and firm expectations appeared to have increased.

Again, I would not claim that this proves a causal mechanism. The stronger relationship could reflect greater inflation persistence or improved forecasting, rather than a greater influence of expectations on wage and price setting. Causal proof is a high bar, but this evidence is at least consistent with the hypothesis that household and firm expectations gained traction during the high-inflation episode.
Structural US evidence points in the same direction. Coibion & Gorodnichenko (2025) Opens in a new window find that short-horizon household expectations help explain inflation dynamics in a New Keynesian Phillips Curve, while professional expectations play a smaller role. That result clearly depends on details of the model specification, especially its inertial pieces, and it should not be imported mechanically to the UK setting; but it cautions against focusing only on the most sophisticated forecasters.
To sum up, financial-market expectations are timely, forward-looking and often informative at the policy-relevant horizon. For the questions we face, they would be the first place I would look. But household and firm expectations matter for a different reason: they are closer to the decisions that can make inflation persistent. They need not be superior forecasts and are often biased. But in the wrong state of the economy, however, they can become part of the propagation mechanism itself.
That brings us to the current juncture. Stage 1 showed that households and firms may now respond more strongly to shocks; Stage 2 suggests that this matters only if those expectations gain traction in wages, prices and demand.
A broader historical perspective is also useful. After the experience of the 1970s, the lesson was not simply that inflation expectations could rise, but that they could become embedded in wage bargains, price-setting rules and contracts, and thereby become part of the inflation process itself (Taylor, 2026a; Taylor, 2026b)
The lesson of 2011 is almost the mirror image. Headline inflation rose well above target and household expectations moved with it, but weak demand and a softer labour market limited the transmission into wages and domestically generated inflation.
Indeed, one of the achievements of the modern monetary framework is precisely to weaken that second-stage transmission: credibility does not mean that near-term expectations never respond to shocks, but that temporary shocks are less likely to be built mechanically into wage claims and pricing plans, and so less likely to persist.
The question as to what happened in 2022 and later is whether a very different transmission environment — tighter labour markets, stronger nominal wage growth, disrupted supply and greater pricing flexibility — temporarily gave expectations more traction than they had in earlier episodes, and whether we are still in that regime now.
That is where the final part of my discussion begins, on the policy problem we face today. Higher attentiveness means that shocks can still move expectations. But whether those movements matter for policy depends on the state of the economy. It is that configuration of risks, rather than expectations in isolation, that I now turn to.
Where do we go from here?
There are many signposts and they can often conflict. Some of them are true signs, an informative picture of the road ahead; others are ghost signs, a fading image of past structures.
Expectations remain central to monetary policy, but not all expectation measures answer the same question. Some are better forecasts. Some are closer to behaviour. Some are more sensitive to recent inflation. And the importance of each depends on the wider economic environment.
The task for policymakers is not to follow any single measure mechanically, but to understand what each measure is telling us, whether it is signalling information, influence, or both, and how that signal should shape the risk calculation for inflation persistence.
Recap of Stages 1 and 2
The argument so far can be summarised briefly. Inflation expectations are indispensable signposts for monetary policy, but they are not straightforward guides. Large and salient shocks can move the expectations of households and firms, perhaps more readily now than before 2022. But those movements become inflationary only if they affect wage bargaining, price-setting and other economic decisions. Their policy significance therefore depends not only on the expectations measure itself, but on whether it is influencing behaviour and on the economic conditions governing that transmission.
The policy problem is therefore not to follow any one expectation measure mechanically, but to judge whether it is signalling information, behavioural influence, or both.
Second round effects = State x Shock
Second-round effects depend on the interaction between the shock and the state into which it arrives. A large or persistent energy shock is more likely to generate enduring domestic inflation when expectations, bargaining conditions and pricing behaviour allow it to propagate. That is why the difficult interpretive work around expectations is not merely academic: it is central to judging whether today’s shock will fade, or whether it may start to reproduce the dynamics that made the 2022 episode so persistent.
Chart 16 provides direct evidence of state-dependence. The cumulative inflation response to an oil price shock is larger when the labour market is tight and, more strikingly, when firms adjust prices frequently. The confidence intervals are wide, so the precise magnitudes should be treated cautiously. But both exercises point in the same direction: energy shocks propagate more strongly when workers have greater bargaining power and firms have more scope to adjust prices.

Shock
The shock side of the equation is unusually hard to pin down at present. Since March, spot Brent has moved sharply, ranging from roughly $70 to around $110, and we should be humble about what comes next. Geopolitics is now driving economic outcomes — and therefore monetary policy — to an unusual degree, and remains highly unpredictable.
But the task is not to forecast the next tick in energy markets; rather it is to judge the distribution of risks and the conditions under which those risks would generate persistent inflation.
The central scenario, in my view, is likely one of oscillation, as in the last six months, a continued stalemate followed by modest de-escalation later in the autumn. Under this outcome, Persian Gulf exports gradually recover, oil prices remain elevated but manageable, and the global economy avoids a major energy shock. A more optimistic scenario assumes some form of a resolution in the near term, allowing energy flows to normalise by year-end and easing inflationary pressures. By contrast, a pessimistic scenario involves further escalation and renewed disruption to shipping and production, substantially reducing energy flows and generating another sharp rise in oil prices and energy-driven inflation.
For the UK, it is also important not to look only at the crude oil curve. UK inflation risks can also come through other energy-market channels. Crack spreads have risen, pointing to tightness in refined products such as diesel and petrol, as well as jet fuel, which matter directly for transport costs and indirectly for distribution and production costs. LNG is another risk factor, as it is central to UK electricity pricing and costlier to arbitrage across locations. Even if oil markets stabilise, relatively low inventories mean gas prices could remain sensitive to cold weather, stronger demand or further supply disruptions.
The overall message is that energy risks into winter are two-sided but asymmetric. The downside for prices appears limited in the near term, while the potential for renewed upward pressure remains significant. That does not mean the shock must inevitably become macroeconomically large enough to generate second-round effects. But it does mean the first part of the risk calculation — the size, duration, salience and breadth of the energy shock — cannot be dismissed. But that brings us to the next point.
Implications for second-round effects
We can see some signposts about the state and the shock. But what do we know about the risk of transmission?
The Bank is monitoring a broad set of signposts, including inflation expectations, wage settlements, firms’ pricing behaviour and margins, alongside demand conditions and labour-market slack. The key is to distinguish between a temporary rise in inflation and genuine transmission into prices, wages and persistent inflation. High-frequency indicators can help us trace that process in real time, but no single measure is decisive, so we need to assess whether these indicators collectively show that the energy shock is spreading beyond its direct effects and becoming embedded in domestic inflation.
The sectoral evidence suggests that some propagation beyond direct energy costs may already be present (Chart 19). Since the 2026 shock, prices have risen somewhat faster in sectors historically associated with quicker second-round effects than in sectors where those effects have been weaker. But the overall increases remain much smaller than after the 2022 shock and closer, so far, to the 2011 episode. This is consistent with second-round effects that are present but more limited in magnitude, reflecting both a smaller shock and a less permissive economic environment.

Chart 19: Cumulative price growth relative to pre-shock level for sector groups associated with fast and slow second-round effects.

Footnotes

Notes: The figure shows cumulative price growth relative to the pre-shock level for sector groups associated with fast and slow second-round effects (2RE). Fast 2RE sectors are those where second-round effects are strongest within the first year following an oil price shock (0–11 months), while slow 2RE sectors are those where second-round effects peak later (24–36 months after the shock). This classification is based on estimated sector-level responses to historical oil shocks. Source: Bank of England staff estimates

The DMP evidence gives a similar message (Chart 20). Realised own-price growth among energy-intensive firms has so far responded less strongly than during the 2021–22 episode, even though expected own-price growth has risen. That gap is consistent with firms intending to raise prices but facing greater constraints on their ability to do so. The comparison remains provisional because the follow-up period is much shorter.

Chart 20: Sensitivity of realised and expected own-price growth to energy intensity less pronounced in 2026 vs 2022

Footnotes

Notes: Event-study estimates of the relationship between firms’ energy intensity and own-price growth around each energy-price shock. Error bars show 90% confidence intervals. Source: Bank staff calculations. Latest observation: June 2026

Policy
To conclude, the recent surge in gas and oil prices has clearly increased near-term inflation risks and could push headline inflation considerably higher over the winter. But the key policy question is not the current level of energy prices alone. It is whether those prices remain elevated for long enough, and become broad enough, to generate more persistent inflationary pressure.
On the evidence so far, higher energy costs still appear largely concentrated within the energy complex itself rather than spreading widely through the economy. Monetary policy should respond to the risk that a relative-price shock becomes a general inflation process, not mechanically to every movement in the relative price itself. This is about judgements on propagation, not about denying the shock.
Evidence for significant second-round effects remains scant at present. Inflation in many energy-intensive goods and services categories has not accelerated as one might have expected after such a visible energy shock; food inflation has in fact fallen markedly and unexpectedly, though could rebound; and survey and producer-price indicators point to only modest pass-through so far. The labour market tells a similar story. Underlying wage growth appears broadly consistent with inflation returning to target over the medium term, and there is little sign of an emerging wage-price spiral.
Taken together, these developments suggest that the economy is proving less susceptible, at least so far, to a repeat of the inflation dynamics seen in 2022.
Nevertheless, there remains a nontrivial risk. Where views may differ on the Committee is on the extent to which we lean against these risks. Now, by holding Bank Rate fixed while financial conditions have tightened, policy has already become materially more restrictive relative to the outlook, and especially compared to the pre-war configuration in February. My view is that the current stance is also sufficiently restrictive, given the initial conditions of the economy in which the shock is hitting.
Against that backdrop, the case for further rate increases is not compelling to me unless energy prices remain high for an extended period and also generate clearer signals of a transmission into broader inflation persistence, as revealed by the signposts that we are actively monitoring.
The central judgement, then, must be whether the current energy shock remains a relative-price shock or evolves into a more general inflation process. That judgement has to combine both sides of the framework: the magnitude, duration and salience of the shock, and the initial conditions that determine whether it transmits. The available evidence currently points more toward the former interpretation.
That does not remove the need to stay alert. However, it does suggest, to me, that the burden of proof for additional tightening should rest on evidence that second-round effects are actually gaining traction, rather than on the existence of the energy shock alone.
That judgement, as ever, is conditional: if pressure builds and second-round effects begin to gain traction, the policy assessment would have to change. But symmetrically, if the economy evolves broadly as expected, with demand weakening and underlying domestic inflationary pressures continuing to moderate, then at some point, once energy risks abate, policy will need to move in the other direction — not because the risk has disappeared, but because maintaining an unnecessarily restrictive stance would itself carry costs.
The right policy response is therefore vigilant but disciplined. We should not deny the shock, nor dismiss the risk that it could propagate. But neither should monetary policy react mechanically to movements in energy prices if those movements remain primarily relative-price shocks.
The views expressed in this speech are not necessarily those of the Bank of England or the Monetary Policy Committee.

articles.title: Municipal Bonds: Are They Having A Moment?
articles.text:
Municipal Bonds: Are They Having A Moment?

Despite its size and quality, the $4.4 trillion municipal bond market is often
overlooked in core fixed income portfolios.

October 2026

KEY TAKEAWAYS

Municipal (muni) bonds may
present attractive after-tax income opportunities, particularly for investors in the
highest tax bracket.1
In our view, the scale and complexity of munis can create opportunities for active managers to generate value
beyond income.
Munis are generally considered
to be high quality, with
historically low default rates
compared to corporate bonds.

Despite its size and quality, the $4.4 trillion municipal bond market is often overlooked in core fixed income portfolios. However, at certain maturities, the highest-quality AAA municipal bonds can sometimes offer higher after-tax yields than high yield corporates. In our view, the market’s size and complexity can create opportunities for active managers to add value.
Municipal bonds currently offer their highest yields since 2008, climbing close to 7.9% on a calculated tax-equivalent yield basis for investors in the highest tax bracket.2
Longer-dated AAA municipal yields are even higher and may surpass equivalent BB high yield corporate yields on a tax-equivalent basis for the highest taxpayers, potentially reflecting material relative value and inefficient pricing.3

These yields indicate that municipal bonds may be able to deliver compelling income potential through their coupon payments.
Additionally, municipal bonds may benefit from price appreciation over time. Because the municipal yield curve is steeper than those of Treasury and corporate bonds, investors may benefit from the “roll-down” effect, where a bond’s yield falls over time (and thus its price rises) if the yield curve remains steep and credit conditions are stable.
Further, we believe that if wider macroeconomic and global interest rate volatility subsides, high grade municipal bonds could be favorably positioned to rebound from their current levels.
Municipals’ High Credit Quality May Offer Stability
72% of the tax-efficient municipal bond market is rated AA or above, versus only 10% of the U.S. investment grade corporate bond market. In addition, 10-year historical municipal bond default rates have been 0.15%, compared to 10.82% for global corporates.4

We believe munis could provide diversification benefits to a core fixed income allocation. They also present a direct opportunity to invest in local communities, financing infrastructure such as hospitals, schools, transportation, and utilities.
Potential Opportunities for Active Managers
The scope of municipal bonds is vast, with over 65,000 investment grade taxexempt municipal bonds available – far surpassing the total available in related bond markets.5
California and New York account for about a third of the tax-exempt municipal bond market. As a result, national municipal strategies may hold bonds issued outside an investor’s home state, and depending on the applicable tax rules, income from such bonds may be subject to state or local taxes.

Many municipal bonds are small issues spread across local governments throughout the U.S. As a result, comprehensively covering the full market can be difficult, particularly for investors without significant resources.
We believe credit spread pricing is inefficient and there are mispricing opportunities across the universe. In many cases, our internal credit assessments differ from those of the rating agencies.
In our view, active managers can seek significant value through independent credit research and opportunistic trading.

Outcomes Matter
Learn more about Insight Investment’s capabilities, philosophies & solutions:
Getting to Know Insight Investment

ABOUT INSIGHT INVESTMENT
BNY Investments’ fixed income platform can deliver a wide range of solutions, and leverages Insight Investment’s deep active fixed income expertise across traditional, specialized, municipal bond, and absolute return strategies.

Endnotes
Municipal bonds currently offer attractive tax-equivalent yields for investors in the highest federal tax bracket; at certain maturities, AAA municipal taxequivalent yields may exceed yields on certain below-investment-grade corporate bonds.Bloomberg (Bloomberg Municipal Bond Index), September 28, 2026. The municipal tax-equivalent yield (TEY) is calculated using an assumed 40.8% tax bracket, which includes a 37.0% top federal marginal income tax rate and a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT).At certain longer maturities, AAA municipal tax-equivalent yields may exceed yields on comparable BB-rated corporate bonds for investors subject to the assumed 40.8% federal tax rate.Moody’s, 1970-2024, July 2025.Source: Insight Investment, Bloomberg Municipal Bond Index, October 2026.

Risks
All investments involve risk including loss of principal. Certain investments involve greater or unique risks that should be considered along with the objectives, fees, and expenses before investing.
Bonds are subject to interest rate, credit, liquidity, call and market risks, to varying degrees. Generally, all other factors being equal, bond prices are inversely related to interest-rate changes and rate increases can cause price declines. The amount of public information available about municipal securities is generally less than that for corporate equities or bonds. Legislative changes, state and local economic and business developments, may adversely affect the yield and/ or value of municipal securities. Other factors include the general conditions of the municipal securities market, the size of the particular offering, maturity of the obligation, and the rating of the issue. Income for national municipal funds may be subject to state and local taxes. Income may be subject to state and local taxes for out-of-state residents. Some income may be subject to the federal alternative minimum tax for certain investors. Capital gains, if any, are taxable.
Appendix
Asset-Backed Securities (ABS) are financial securities such as a bond or note collateralized by a pool of assets such as loans, leases, credit card debt, royalties, or receivables. Mortgage-Backed Securities (MBS) are investments made up of a bundle of home loans bought from the banks that issued them. Investors in MBS receive periodic payments similar to bond coupon payments. Commercial Mortgage-Backed Securities (CMBS) are fixed-income investment products that are backed by mortgages on commercial properties rather than residential real estate. Bond ratings are an evaluation of a bond’s credit quality and the issuer’s ability to meet scheduled interest and principal payments, assigned by NRSROs on a scale from AAA (highest) to D (default). Ratings of BBB- and above are investment grade; BB+ and below are non-investment grade (speculative/high-yield), with BB, B, and CCC representing progressively higher credit risk. Tax-equivalent yield (TEY) calculates the pre-tax yield a taxable bond needs to offer to match the after-tax return of a tax-free investment. Roll-down return is the potential price appreciation a bond may experience as it approaches maturity. Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) is an additional federal tax that applies to investment income above certain income thresholds.
Bloomberg Municipal Bond Index tracks the performance of the USD-denominated long-term tax-exempt bond market in the United States. Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index is a broad-based flagship benchmark that measures the investment grade, U.S. dollar-denominated, fixed-rate taxable bond market. Bloomberg U.S. High Yield Corporate Bond Index tracks the performance of U.S. dollar-denominated below-investment-grade-rated corporate debt publicly issued in the U.S. domestic market. Bloomberg U.S. MBS Index tracks fixed-rate agency mortgage-backed pass-through securities guaranteed by Ginnie Mae (GNMA), Fannie Mae (FNMA), and Freddie Mac (FHLMC). articles.title: Industrial policy in the EU: new opportunities, old risks?
articles.text:
Industrial policy in the EU: new opportunities, old risks?

Prepared by Sam Langfield, Daphne Momferatou and Ralph SetzerPublished as part of the ECB Economic Bulletin, Issue 7/2026.1 Definition and relevance for central banksIndustrial policy can be defined as government intervention that targets the structural transformation of economic activity in pursuit of a public goal. Industrial policy deliberately directs factors of production to specific sectors. Conceptually, this distinguishes industrial policy from macroeconomic stabilisation measures and structural policies that aim to improve the general business environment (Juhász et al., 2024). While structural policies can also have uneven effects – for example, a research and development (R&D) tax credit would favour R&D-intensive industries – the conceptual distinction is useful for identifying policies explicitly designed for sectoral reallocation.While market failures can be the rationale for industrial policy, its selectivity creates efficiency and governance risks. Industrial policy can help address coordination failures, knowledge externalities and vulnerabilities (International Monetary Fund, 2025). However, because interventions selectively promote specific sectors or activities, opportunity costs are implicit. Shifting resources away from potentially more productive uses risks allocative inefficiency owing to the bounded knowledge of policymakers and the potential for rent-seeking behaviour, especially in environments with weak institutional quality. Historically, this has often led governments to support politically influential incumbents rather than address genuine market failures (Grossman and Helpman, 1994). The open question is whether modern industrial policy can overcome informational frictions, resist undue influence from vested interests and avoid institutional inefficiencies in a contemporary European Union (EU) context.Governments implement industrial policy, the macroeconomic effects of which can affect monetary policy transmission. Sector-specific interventions alter relative prices, for example by subsidising factor costs. Other general equilibrium effects emerge from cross-border spillovers, policy responses by other governments and fiscal implications. Effective interventions can raise potential growth or dampen the inflationary impact of price shocks. Poorly designed measures, however, can subsidise capacity-constrained sectors and distort economic decisions. Nationally differentiated industrial policies can also affect cross-country competitiveness and financial fragmentation, with implications for monetary policy transmission. For these reasons, it is important for central banks to assess the design and macroeconomic effects of industrial policy.Industrial policy has re-emerged worldwide in response to geoeconomic fragmentation, rapid technological change and the climate transition. The remainder of this article documents the resurgence of industrial policy, reviews the evidence of its effectiveness and examines the specific opportunities and risks it presents in the EU context. It then identifies key principles for the design of industrial policy in Europe.2 Resurgence of industrial policyThe use of industrial policy has expanded across major economies. Governments deploy targeted grants, equity and credit support, trade measures and localisation requirements to promote selected sectors. There has been an increase in the number of such measures in the EU and its Member States, with similar patterns in the United States and China (Chart 1, panel a). Panel b) plots the yearly time series of all research publications referencing “industrial policy” as a percentage of those referencing “economic policy”.Three structural trends – geoeconomic fragmentation, technological progress and climate change – underpin this renewed attention to industrial policy.First, geoeconomic fragmentation exposes supply chain vulnerabilities and raises concerns about resilience. The pandemic and recent conflicts have highlighted the macroeconomic risks associated with external dependencies. The more interventionist trade policy stance in the United States and technological upgrading in China, partly supported by domestic industrial policy, are further reshaping global production networks. While lower import prices improve the terms of trade, reliance on foreign capacity increases exposure to supply disruptions and geoeconomic coercion, motivating policymakers to intervene as insurance against price and quantity shocks.Second, rapid technological change generates discrete outward shifts in potential output. Breakthroughs in general-purpose technologies, including artificial intelligence and robotics, raise the opportunity cost of operating behind the global productivity frontier. Technological dynamism can motivate intervention in specific sectors to stimulate domestic innovation (by addressing knowledge spillovers and financing constraints) or accelerate adoption (by targeting coordination failures and network externalities). Effective implementation of innovation-oriented industrial policy means overcoming informational constraints so that market failures can be targeted precisely.Third, the climate transition requires large-scale investment in physical capital. Carbon pricing is the primary policy used to incentivise necessary capital formation, by correcting the underlying environmental externalities. However, price signals may be weakened by barriers to investment, including coordination failures in infrastructure deployment, network effects in green technologies and financial frictions. This could provide a rationale for climate-motivated industrial policy to complement carbon pricing through sectoral interventions.Stated reasons for intervention broadly align with these structural trends, but the emphasis differs across economies. EU measures are more often climate-related, US measures place greater weight on resilience, and Chinese measures are more often framed around competitiveness.[1] According to New Industrial Policy Observatory data, 40% of measures were motivated by climate, 39% by competitiveness and 21% by resilience. Climate accounts for 49% of EU and Member State interventions, compared with 12% for resilience; resilience accounts for 39% of US interventions, while competitiveness accounts for 73% of Chinese interventions. 3 Policy instruments and empirical effectivenessSurveying the range and targets of policy instrumentsModern industrial policy draws on an established policy toolkit. Based on Evenett et al. (2024, 2025), this article focuses on sector-specific instruments that can be classified in terms of whether they provide financial support or restrict market access.[2] This narrower classification excludes broader macro-financial tools sometimes associated with industrial policy, such as financial repression, foreign reserve accumulation and capital controls (Gourinchas et al., 2026). This classification is necessary because outcomes may diverge from stated policy intentions.Grants: non-repayable grants, tax and social insurance relief, production subsidies, in-kind transfers and price stabilisation measures alter firms’ cost structures. Similar effects can also arise indirectly, for example when public procurement or defence contracts support related civilian technologies or firms. These tools provide immediate support but carry fiscal costs. If deployed without strict conditionality and exit criteria, subsidies are vulnerable to pressures from vested interests, leading to resource misallocation by shielding supported firms from market discipline.Equity and credit: state-sponsored loans, guarantees, interest payment subsidies and equity capital injections transfer risk from private balance sheets to the public sector. These interventions can support targeted sectors by lowering the cost of capital for recipient firms, especially those developing new technologies (see Box 1). Their effectiveness, however, depends on careful design: poorly designed measures can generate fiscal liabilities, crowd out private investment and sustain unproductive firms.Trade policy: governments implement import tariffs, quotas, anti-dumping duties and export controls to influence the prices and quantities of foreign goods relative to domestic goods in specific sectors. Such measures can insulate domestic production capacity from external competition and secure supply. However, they can raise downstream costs and interfere with comparative advantage, disrupting global supply chains and increasing retaliation risk. From a fiscal perspective, the net impact of trade measures is ambiguous; while tariffs can generate revenue, outcomes depend on import elasticities.Localisation: local content requirements, procurement preferences, restrictions on foreign direct investment and sector-specific regulations limit market access. While these interventions can coordinate technological standards and establish domestic capacity without significant fiscal implications, they serve as implicit protectionism. Compliance costs distort firm-level decisions, and barriers to cross-border investment and competition risk fragmenting markets, with the magnitude of these effects depending on the coverage of the measures.The industrial policy mix varies across major economies. Measured by the number of recorded interventions between 2020 and 2024, the EU and its Member States together rank highest in the G20, with equity and credit support the most frequently used instrument, partly reflecting the deployment of measures related to the pandemic and the energy crisis (Chart 2, panel a). Intervention counts, however, do not capture fiscal scale and are affected by differences in transparency: the EU’s State aid framework makes its measures particularly visible. China records fewer interventions but relies on larger-scale fiscal and quasi-fiscal support, including grants, support for state-owned enterprises and state-directed finance (Garcia-Macia et al., 2025 and Attinasi et al., 2026). The United States exhibits a more uniform policy mix, with a notable use of localisation requirements. Other G20 countries deploy industrial policy on a smaller scale and tend to rely more on trade-related measures.Macroeconomic effects also depend on the specific sectors targeted for intervention. Natural targets for intervention include sectors responsible for supply chain bottlenecks and emerging R&D-intensive sectors. Jakubik and Langfield (2026) find some evidence of policy targeting bottlenecks, but little evidence of R&D targeting. Instead, industrial policy interventions are more common for products that already account for a large share of exports (Chart 2, panel b). Fund-of-funds approaches mitigate capture risk and support venture capital market development, while direct intervention allows portfolio allocation to be fine-tuned to policy priorities (Moretti, 2025). Furthermore, an institution’s stage orientation affects whether public funds complement or crowd out private capital, with later-stage intervention in particular facing three constraints. First, fiscal space is insufficient relative to the aggregate financing needs of scale-ups. Second, later-stage intervention risks crowding out private investment: while moderate government participation can be complementary, more significant involvement displaces private capital (Brander et al., 2015). Venture capital stimulates patent activity when directed towards early-stage ventures (Popov and Roosenboom, 2012). To achieve successful market exits, capital needs to be managed by autonomous institutions with project selection and management expertise (Bottazzi et al., 2008). Joint public-private investment rounds allow public institutions to absorb early-stage risk while maintaining private-sector discipline (Çamoğlu, 2026). At later stages, public involvement faces a trade-off between supporting firm expansion and displacing private investors. To resolve this tension, deep pools of patient private capital must be mobilised, particularly from pension funds and insurance companies (Kukies and Noyer, 2026). This underscores the necessity of deepening capital markets to complement innovation-oriented industrial policies.Empirical assessments of effectivenessAssessing the effectiveness of industrial policy requires an economy-wide approach. Welfare assessments must consider whether factor displacement effects are justified by gains in productivity or resilience. While any evaluation requires a counterfactual, resilience is harder to observe and quantify, especially if an adverse shock does not materialise. Consequently, the empirical literature focuses mainly on observable outcomes such as investment, employment and productivity. Yet the same economy-wide trade-offs apply to resilience objectives: even if targeted interventions build resilience at sector level, they can reduce it on aggregate, for example by diverting resources from other critical activities or entrenching protected incumbents.Early empirical evaluations found that sectoral interventions tended to channel resources to declining industries, contributing to depressed productivity growth. Cross-country panel evidence suggested that support was often misdirected (Pack, 2000), a finding echoed by studies of East Asia, including Japan (Beason and Weinstein, 1996) and South Korea (Lee, 1996), and by early European evidence on State aid allocation (Neven and Röller, 2000). Informational constraints and vested interests caused policymakers to support incumbents rather than high-potential sectors facing market failures (Pack and Saggi, 2006). This literature gave rise to a long-standing presumption that industrial policies are unlikely to improve total factor productivity.More recent literature identifies specific contexts in which industrial policy can resolve sector-specific market failures in emerging economies. By exploiting firm-level data and improved identification strategies, these studies distinguish policy effects from underlying sectoral trends. Successful interventions rely less on open-ended protection than on conditional support and continued competition, allowing unproductive firms to exit (Aghion et al., 2015 and Lane, 2020). However, when institutions are weak, the same tools can sustain inefficient incumbents and generate overcapacity (Barwick et al., 2025 and Fang et al., 2025). Consistent with these concerns, recent evidence links industrial policy in China to lower aggregate productivity through factor misallocation (Garcia-Macia et al., 2025).In mature economies, policy justification extends beyond coordination failures to include underinvestment in knowledge, as well as resilience and security objectives. Public research and procurement agencies in the United States have been shown to accelerate technological development by targeting early-stage innovation and promoting knowledge spillovers (Gross and Sampat, 2023 and Gazzani et al., 2025). The evidence on production subsidies is more mixed: expanding capacity in targeted sectors diverts resources from non-subsidised competitors while incurring fiscal costs (Goldberg et al., 2024). The literature therefore suggests that the benefits to industrial policy in mature economies are more clearly established for foundational research than downstream production.Assessments of interventions in Europe demonstrate the difficulty of translating targeted support into aggregate productivity growth. Brandão-Marques and Toprak (2024) find that EU State aid has positive effects on employment and revenues in recipient firms, but no effect on investment or productivity. They also find adverse spillovers to competing non-recipient firms, which can offset the direct benefits of support within the Single Market. Evidence from regional interventions in the United Kingdom is consistent with this pattern, showing that support increased recipient employment without improving total factor productivity (Criscuolo et al., 2019).Constraints on industrial policy are tighter in open economies. Across integrated markets, uncoordinated national subsidies can alter relative prices and distort comparative advantage (Hodge et al., 2024). Likewise, import tariffs intended to shield domestic capacity raise input costs for downstream manufacturing, dampening sector employment (Flaaen and Pierce, 2026). To address these challenges, industrial policy should preserve a level playing field and limit the influence of vested interests.4 A new industrial policy strategy for EuropeFeatures specific to the EU contextIn the EU, governments pursue industrial policy across a partially integrated Single Market. Decentralised industrial policy risks distorting competition by allocating resources according to countries’ differing abilities to intervene and preferences as to where to do so, risking subsidy races. Limiting this distortive effect is a key underlying principle for State aid rules: while these rules constrain the provision of selective economic advantages to firms or sectors, Member States still provide substantial fiscal support through industrial policy, the overall scale of which is subject to measurement challenges (see Box 2). More intensive use of fiscally costly industrial policies may require further EU-level coordination and, where appropriate, common decision-making or centralisation of policy instruments. This could help mitigate local capture risks, safeguard competition across the Single Market and reduce the scope for local maladministration.Fragmentation risk is compounded by uneven institutional quality across Member States. Discretionary intervention demands “embedded autonomy”: the state must be informed on the sources of friction while resisting rent-seeking and withdrawing support according to predefined exit criteria (Rodrik, 2004). Yet institutions vary across Europe. At national level, regulatory quality and control of corruption differ significantly across country groups (Chart 3, panel a). At regional level, weaker quality of government is associated with lower labour productivity (Chart 3, panel b). In the EU, support is largely provided through credit and guarantees channelled via national banking sectors, which favour domestic capital-intensive firms with established bank relationships. The EU economy exhibits greater openness to external trade than the United States or China. Deploying trade-restrictive measures such as tariffs or local content requirements can trigger retaliation and geoeconomic fragmentation (Baba et al., 2023 and Rotunno et al., 2026). These constraints are particularly relevant for climate-related industrial policy, where the EU faces trade-offs between climate ambition, trade openness and preserving the Single Market (Wunsch and Langenus, 2026). Fragmentation can weigh on economic growth and reduce resilience by weakening the diversified trade networks that help economies absorb external shocks. For export-oriented EU manufacturing, these costs may outweigh the shorter-term benefits of shielding domestic industries. Preserving competitive neutrality and multilateral trade frameworks is therefore still important.Europe’s distinct institutional, financial and macroeconomic features limit the scope for direct replication of foreign industrial policies. The Draghi report calls for EU action to be refocused on policy priorities, supported by stronger coordination, simplified rules and better targeted financing (Draghi, 2024). The EU has introduced several legislative initiatives, including the Net-Zero Industry Act, the Critical Raw Materials Act, the European Chips Act and the Tech Sovereignty Package. Furthermore, the Industrial Accelerator Act proposal aims to introduce targeted public procurement and foreign direct investment rules. The Commission’s proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework would reorient spending towards EU-wide priorities, alongside a transition from a programme-based budget to a policy-based framework intended to better target EU funds and a move from cost-based payments to performance-based disbursements. EU-level industrial policy can help limit the fragmentation and subsidy races associated with uncoordinated national interventions, while pooling resources to achieve scale in targeted activities or sectors. The EU can build on existing frameworks, including State aid control and performance-based instruments such as the Recovery and Resilience Facility, which offer relevant experience in linking funding to results. At the same time, differences in institutional quality and national regulatory frameworks, together with Europe’s bank-based financial system, can amplify risks of resource misallocation. Five design principles are therefore relevant to strengthen governance, safeguard cross-border competition and ensure that industrial policy complements structural reform.First, industrial policy benefits from clearly defined objectives in order to inform instrument selection and define criteria for ex-post evaluation. Productivity and resilience-related objectives ought to be differentiated, and broad motivations should be translated into operational targets. Interventions aimed at economic resilience require particularly narrow targeting to prevent mandate expansion. A lack of precision risks shielding incumbents rather than resolving specific dependencies and improving economy-wide resilience.Second, the targeting of specific sectors depends on linking interventions to well-identified market failures. Where the objective is productivity growth, interventions are most efficient when directed at activities with knowledge spillovers, such as frontier technologies in areas where the EU is lagging behind. This avoids using scarce fiscal resources to subsidise incremental innovation by financially unconstrained incumbents. Where the objective is resilience, targeting should be based on empirical identification of critical dependencies and supply chain vulnerabilities. Labelling a sector “strategic” is insufficient; designation must be accompanied by economic analysis and clear identification of the public interest objective, whether related to market failures, resilience, or security concerns.Third, preservation of the Single Market calls for mechanisms that account for cross-border externalities. National subsidies can distort competition and create negative cross-border spillovers. To avoid subsidy races and capture economies of scale, interventions should prioritise common EU instruments. While operating at EU level mitigates concerns regarding Single Market fragmentation, it does not eliminate the need for safeguards against resource misallocation.Fourth, predefined exit mechanisms are key to enforcing market discipline. Governments cannot reliably predict winners, so some interventions will fail. Policy implementation should incorporate sunset clauses to ensure that support is withdrawn from underperforming projects or projects for which the reasons for intervention no longer hold. Without credible termination mechanisms, temporary interventions risk becoming permanent, trapping resources in unproductive uses.Fifth, industrial policy underscores the importance of structural reforms. With finite institutional capacity, industrial policy risks crowding out structural reform. Yet without structural improvements, interventions will underperform. For example, subsidising high-tech sectors will fail if fragmentation prevents firms from reaching minimum efficient scale. Advancing the savings and investments union, easing labour market rigidities and reducing burdensome administrative work would help mobilise private risk capital across borders. These conditions enable capital and labour to be reallocated from declining firms to productive sectors – a market mechanism industrial policy cannot replace.5 ConclusionIndustrial policy can play a role within the broader policy framework, provided interventions are well designed, targeted and time limited. The macroeconomic impact of interventions is context dependent. In the EU’s multi-country Single Market, with its heterogenous institutions and bank-based financial structures, uncoordinated national measures risk fragmenting competition and triggering subsidy races. To be effective, industrial policy needs a clear mandate, robust governance, market-based incentives and mechanisms for continuous evaluation. Interventions should be time limited by design, with support for capital-intensive activities conditional on predefined milestones, targets and exit criteria.Even with institutional safeguards, industrial policy entails macroeconomic trade-offs. Where the goal is productivity, industrial policy can be most effective when fostering innovation and supporting the adoption of frontier technologies rather than shielding incumbents from competition. Where the goal is resilience, policymakers need to weigh the insurance value of reducing dependencies against the costs of allocative inefficiency. articles.title: The strategic role of the EU fuel manufacturing and refining sector
articles.text:
Consulting Report

13 Nov 2026

The strategic role of the EU fuel manufacturing and refining sector

The EU fuel manufacturing and refining industry remains a strategic pillar of Europe’s economy and industrial base.

Our report explores the industry’s strategic importance to the EU, the role it can play in enabling industrial transformation, and the economic risks that could emerge if refining capacity contracts faster than the transition can be delivered.

In 2025, the sector supported €200 billion in GDP, 1.8 million jobs, and €83 billion in tax revenues across the EU, while supplying the fuels and feedstocks that underpin transport, manufacturing, petrochemicals, agriculture, and household activity. However, the analysis also highlights the risks of a continued decline in refining capacity. A faster-than-expected contraction could reduce EU GDP by almost €25 billion, eliminate around 120,000 jobs, lower government revenues by €14 billion, and increase the EU’s reliance on imported fuels by 2035, with implications for competitiveness, energy security, and the transition to low-carbon fuels.

articles.text:
Managing our Environmental Impact. Our Commitment. Our Targets. Our Progress.

Man Group is committed to reducing its absolute carbon footprint and to being consistent and transparent about the progress we are making. As a key part of our Corporate Sustainability strategy, you can read more about how we manage our environmental impact in our Corporate Sustainability Brochure.

We continue to implement changes to our operations to ensure we are on track to meet our emissions reduction target set for 2026 and are on the strategic pathway to net zero carbon in our global workplaces by 2030.

Environmental Policy

Our Environmental Sustainability Policy Statement focuses on: using natural resources responsibly; minimising the environmental impact of our activities through maximising energy efficiency; reducing greenhouse gas emissions and; recycling and / or minimising waste. We also commit to at least annual reporting of our environmental targets, data and any issues we encounter. In 2024, we achieved ISO 14001:2018 for our London office.

Board Oversight of Environmental Matters

Our Man Group Board has responsibility for Man Group's environmental impact and ensures that Man’s Environmental Sustainability Policy Statement is implemented and reviewed. The Board has a collective role in providing environmental leadership throughout Man's global operations and is committed to continual improvement in environmental performance.

Environmental Risk Management

Man Group considers operational climate risks 15+ years into the future. It does this through multi-disciplinary company-wide risk identification, assessment and management processes. The types of risks considered include current and emerging regulation, technological changes and upgrades, market risks, reputational risks, acute and chronic physical operational impacts as well as upstream and downstream risks.

Green Buildings

Minimising our environmental impact is at the centre of our real estate strategy. We occupy eight buildings certified by LEED (Leadership in Energy Efficiency and Design), one by Energy Star and one by NABERS (National Australian Built Environment Rating System), accounting for 92% of our global headcount. Man Group’s largest office, Riverbank House (RBH) in London, has a Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method (BREEAM) ‘Excellent’ rating.

Riverbank House - London

Riverbank House is rated “Excellent” via the Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method (BREEAM). The building has a green roof, rainwater harvesting and solar power generation.

Pfäffikon - Switzerland

Our Pfäffikon office is a short walk from Lake Zurich and is powered by renewable hydro-electric energy.

Environmental data compilation systems

We strive to deliver clear and transparent reporting that captures the measurable elements within our control. We monitor and track our global environmental impact using specialist specialist tracking software and an energy services consultancy which help us to mitigate risk, maximise opportunities and reduce our carbon footprint.

Responsible Procurement

Man Group’s offices procure goods and services that are in line with our environmental objectives. We utilise ISO standards and ratings systems (such as energy star for IT equipment and green star for paper supplies) to assist us in choosing sustainable products. We also ensure all our equipment complies with the Restriction of Hazardous Substances EU Directive.

Man Group’s Supplier Code of Conduct

As a condition of supplying services to Man Group, our suppliers are directed to adhere to our Supplier Code of Conduct. This code outlines the minimum standards Man Group expects of its suppliers, regarding economic activity, impact on the environment, as well as engagement with wider communities.

Man Group intends to lead by example, and we endeavour to work closely with our suppliers to rise to the opportunity of addressing the global, social and environmental challenges that we all currently face.

Environmental Improvements

Man Group’s largest office, Riverbank House, is continually assessed for energy and air-conditioning efficiency. The recommendations inform our investments.

During 2024, we achieved ISO14001:2018 for our Riverbank House office.

Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD)

Man Group is a supporter and signatory of the TCFD, and is committed to taking action against climate change. The Board oversees the development of our climate-related financial disclosures which cover governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets, as described in our Annual Report.

Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change (IIGCC)

Man Group is a signatory to the Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change, the European membership body for investor collaboration on climate change.

UN Global Compact

We are also proud, active signatories of the UN Global Compact, supporting the Ten Principles on human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption.

Environmental Training and Awareness

Environmental awareness campaigns are run in offices focusing on areas such as increasing recycling, reducing energy use, cycling to work and removing single use plastics.

We have run a number of sustainable volunteering activities across our offices including litter pick-ups, local garden and park maintenance as well as educational awareness events.

articles.title: Proactive Monitoring of Markets and Institutions
articles.text:
Financial Stability

What Is Financial StabilityTypes of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks Monitoring Risk Across the Financial System Proactive Monitoring of Markets and InstitutionsFinancial Stability and Stress Testing

Proactive Monitoring of Markets and Institutions

Related Content

Federal Reserve Board finalizes rules that tailor its regulations for domestic and foreign banks to more closely match their risk profiles

Calibrating the GSIB Surcharge

The changing nature of risks and fluctuations in financial markets and the broader economy require timely monitoring of domestic and foreign financial markets and their effect on financial institutions. They even require monitoring of the nonfinancial sector to identify buildups of vulnerabilities that might require further study or policy action.

To this end, the Federal Reserve maintains a flexible, forward-looking financial stability monitoring program to help inform policymakers of the financial system’s vulnerabilities to a range of potential adverse events or shocks. Such a monitoring program is a critical part of a broader Federal Reserve System effort to assess and address vulnerabilities in the U.S. financial system. In the case of individual institutions, the Federal Reserve may take more direct action and in various ways.

Research Examining Causes, Effects, and Remedies for Financial Instability

A macroprudential approach to ensuring financial stability builds on a substantial and growing body of research on the factors that lead to vulnerabilities in the financial system and how government policies can mitigate such risks.

The Federal Reserve actively engages in financial stability research to improve understanding of issues related to financial stability and to engage with the broader research community on crucial policy matters. This engagement often involves collaboration with researchers at other domestic and international institutions.

Macroprudential Supervision and Regulation of Large, Complex Financial Institutions

Large, complex financial institutions interact with financial markets and the broader economy in a manner that may—during times of stress and in the absence of an appropriate regulatory framework and effective supervision—lead to financial instability.

The Federal Reserve promotes the safety and soundness of Systemically Important Financial Institutions (SIFIs)—including large bank holding companies and financial market utilities—through robust supervision and regulation programs that are informed by the macroprudential monitoring programs. In addition, the Federal Reserve serves as a “consolidated supervisor” of nonbank financial companies that the Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC) has determined should be supervised by the Federal Reserve Board and subject to prudential standards. Currently, there are no such firms that have been designated by the FSOC.

Monitoring Systemically Important Financial Institutions

The Federal Reserve actively monitors indicators of the riskiness of Systemically Important Financial Institions (SIFIs), both individually as well as through interlinkages in the broader network of financial institutions, to help identify vulnerabilities. It also imposes certain regulatory requirements on SIFIs in order to ensure that these large and interconnected institutions properly manage potentially risky activities and to mitigate spillover of distress into the broader economy. If a SIFI were to become distressed, disruptions in the financial system could arise from direct losses imposed on SIFI counterparties, contagion, fire sales effects, or a loss of critical services.

Recovery and Resolution Framework

During the 2007–09 financial crisis, the lack of effective resolution strategies contributed to the damaging spillovers of distress at or between individual institutions and from those institutions to the broader economy. The Federal Reserve, in collaboration with other U.S. agencies, has continued to work with large financial institutions to develop a range of recovery and resolution strategies in the event of their distress or failure. Improvements in resolution planning are intended to, among other things, diminish adverse effects from perceptions of certain institutions as “too big to fail” and contribute to more orderly conditions in the financial system if institutions face strains or fail.

International Financial Stability Monitoring

The U.S. dollar is the leading global funding and investment currency and is used widely for trade and other international transactions, and well-functioning dollar funding markets in the United States and abroad are critical in supporting these roles. Strains in these markets can adversely affect U.S. and foreign businesses, governments, households, and NBFIs that borrow in dollars. The Federal Reserve actively monitors the functioning and health of dollar funding markets and, in cooperation with foreign central banks, has worked to mitigate strains in these markets through the use of the Federal Reserve’s dollar liquidity swap arrangements.

The Federal Reserve actively monitors the resilience of foreign financial systems and potential transmission channels of foreign financial stress. An understanding of financial vulnerabilities abroad and how foreign shocks are transmitted to the United States is important for gauging the significant risks to the U.S. financial system.

articles.title: Adaptation and financing for smallholder farmers
articles.text:
Published on
Development and a Changing Climate

Adaptation and financing for smallholder farmers

Ana Luiza Dutra

Thea Louise Jung

Tatiana Nenova

November 11, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Lake Market, Kolkata. Photo credit: Suprabhat Dutta/iStock.

Family farmers and smallholders produce 80 percent of the world’s food. Among them are half a billion small producers, the majority women, who form the backbone of the food sector across low- and middle-income countries.
Yet, smallholder farmers – and the agricultural firms they own – are disproportionately impacted by climate change. Extreme weather events have almost doubled in frequency over the past 40 years, contributing to declining productivity, new pests and diseases, and volatility in prices and supply. By 2050, this is expected to result in a 94–111 percent price increase for wheat alone. Adapting to these risks requires changes in farming practices and investment, but smallholder farmers face a $172 billion funding gap, making them arguably the world’s largest group of financially underserved people. Initiatives like AgriConnect aims to help 300 million smallholder and family farmers access services, markets, and finance.
Finance is needed to help farmers adapt and invest in resilience. Our recent World Bank Group report, Silent Adapters: Uncovering the Resilience of Smaller Firms in Developing Countries, examines how smaller firms are adapting to climate change and how they are paying for it. Adaptation can involve changes in processes or the introduction of climate-resilient products and inputs. Examples include crop diversification, drip irrigation, cold chain storage, resilient seeds, mist cooling, or changes in animal feed, fertilizers, equipment use, and livestock breeds. This is smart development in action: these investments can improve yields, create jobs and drive growth while also building resilience and reducing emissions.
Access to credit is necessary for adaptation in agriculture, yet agricultural firms in emerging markets and developing economies face barriers to accessing finance. Their cash flows are limited and seasonal, collateral is scarce, and agricultural production is exposed to weather-related risks, pests and diseases, and price volatility. These factors increase their risk profile. About 60 percent of farmers are not commercial or integrated into supply chains and rely on informal and social lending. For lenders, serving small, remote, and often informal borrowers also entails higher transaction costs. In lower-income regions, underdeveloped payments markets and the prevalence of cash transactions can further impede agricultural value-chain finance.
Given the scarcity of long-term adaptation finance, innovative short-term financing can help smaller firms fund climate-smart agriculture. Smaller agricultural firms often combine different lending approaches, including trade finance, asset-based finance like factoring and warehouse receipts, or a mix of both—such as contract farming or buyer-backed equipment leasing. Pay-as-you-go financing models have allowed millions to acquire solar home systems, water heaters, and irrigation pumps, paying flexibly according to usage. In some sectors, such as livestock and agroforestry, carbon markets are also emerging as a source of finance for adaptation investments.
Aggregation and bundled services can improve access to finance. Grouping smaller agricultural firms can lower lending costs, while combining finance with non-financial services such as training increases adaptation effectiveness. Digital technology can also connect farmers directly with markets, service providers, and aggregators, increasing profitability and efficiency.
Financial products can help farmers and lenders manage climate risk. Lines of credit, first-loss schemes, and partial credit guarantees have been used to manage risk and crowd in private finance. In Bangladesh, BRAC offered farmers guaranteed access to emergency loans, triggered automatically by climate index data. Farmers had no upfront payment and only paid if they borrowed after a flood. The added security encouraged them to expand their crop production despite climate risks. Most farmers suffered no flooding and never needed the credit but saw 36 percent higher yields because of the higher investment. Those affected by floods were better able to cope with the shock.
Insurance can complement short-term crop finance for smaller agricultural firms by reducing risks for both farmers and lenders. It supports access to credit, boosts technology adoption, and increases productive investment and can drive adaptation, provided it is integrated into a broader risk-reduction strategy. In Haiti, for example, natural-disaster insurance has been bundled with microcredit, providing borrowers with loan-balance reimbursement and access to new credit after a covered shock. Shocks can disrupt lending to farmers after a disaster, increasing losses, and delaying recovery. But risk can also discourage lending and investment before disasters even happen. Insurance can help address both problems by reducing systemic weather-related risks for lenders. However, the use of insurance against climate and disaster risks in developing countries remains limited. High costs, low take-up, limited distribution networks, poor product design, and a lack of products tailored to smaller agricultural firms continue to constrain the market.
Closing the adaptation financing gap will require more than expanding the supply of conventional credit. Financial products need to be designed around the realities smaller agricultural firms face – seasonal cash flows, compounding risks – while reducing the cost of reaching them. Done well, finance can help farmers invest in resilience before the next shock hits, rather than scrambling to recover after it.
