articles.title: Inside Western Europe’s $2 Trillion Crypto Economy
articles.text:
Summary
Western Europe’s $2.08 trillion crypto economy held firm despite a global downturn. The region grew 1.2% between July 2025 and June 2026, making it the world’s second-largest crypto economy. The EU grew 2.2%, while the UK contracted 8% but remained the region’s largest crypto market.
Stablecoins and cross-border activity are reshaping Europe’s crypto economy. Regional stablecoin holdings surged 131%, compared with 52% globally, lifting Western Europe’s share of global stablecoin balances from 3.4% to 5.1%. The UK led in domestic stablecoin transfers, while Spanish exchanges attracted growing activity from across Europe, with cross-border inflows rising 79.1%.
Regulatory shifts and financial uncertainty are driving new patterns of crypto activity. MiCA is helping create a more integrated EU market, while the euro is gaining ground in crypto trading. Meanwhile, rising bond yields coincided with increased euro-denominated trading in Bitcoin and tokenized gold, and French users increasingly turned to self-custodied stablecoins, with balances surging 192% amid mounting fiscal pressures.

The 2026 Geography of Crypto Report

Reserve your copy
As the global crypto market faced a downturn, Western Europe proved relatively resilient. Between July 2025 and June 2026, the reporting period, the region’s all-in crypto economy totaled $2.08 trillion, making it the second-largest worldwide. Activity grew by a modest 1.2%, placing Western Europe among just three regions to record positive growth over the period, after Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America.New regulation, rising institutional investment, and closer ties to traditional finance are reshaping the region’s crypto market, though what this looks like varies from country to country. Stablecoins are gaining traction, the euro is playing a bigger role in global crypto trading, and exchanges are building cross-regional user bases.For Christopher Beck, co-CEO of Boerse Stuttgart Digital, a leading European crypto infrastructure provider, these developments are part of a broader shift in how crypto is viewed and used: “Institutional adoption is accelerating, marking a shift from crypto being an emerging asset class to becoming an increasingly mainstream financial product.”But this is playing out as the region deals with rising economic uncertainty and changing user preferences, which greatly impacts how crypto is adopted and where activity is concentrated.Six markets account for two-thirds of Western Europe’s crypto economyThe UK retained its position as Western Europe’s largest crypto economy, at $424.5 billion, and accounted for 20% of the regional total. As a longstanding global financial hub with deep capital markets and a well-established banking sector, the UK’s crypto market has evolved as a natural extension of its financial services landscape. Yet activity declined 8% over the reporting period, largely due to a drop in decentralized exchange (DEX) activity.Germany’s crypto economy was second at $288.8 billion, followed by France at $215.8 billion. Germany experienced another modest contraction, largely driven again by declining DEX activity, while France’s crypto economy remained broadly flat. Elsewhere in the region, Spain ($156.1 billion) and Switzerland ($132.8 billion) both saw growth, fueled by increased activity on centralized exchanges (CEXs).Together with the Netherlands ($207.8 billion), these six markets accounted for roughly two-thirds of Western Europe’s crypto economy, highlighting the concentration of activity within the region’s leading markets. Broadly, the experts we spoke with pointed to a maturing crypto economy entering a new phase of growth.As Faustine Fleuret, Global Head of Public Affairs at Morpho, the decentralized credit infrastructure provider, notes: “We are seeing a clear move from experimentation with crypto toward the integration of blockchain into core financial activities. Banks, asset managers and Fintech companies increasingly recognize that on-chain finance is not a parallel system competing with traditional finance, but a new technological infrastructure on which they can build.”The euro’s growing role in crypto reflects its strength in traditional FX marketsOne indicator of the region’s expanding crypto economy is the euro’s growing role as a bridge asset, mirroring its longstanding position in global foreign exchange markets.According to the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the euro was involved in 28.9% of global FX turnover in April 2025. To ensure comparability with crypto order-book data, which captures one-sided trading pairs (such as EUR-to-token trades) rather than both sides of an FX transaction, we use half this figure, or 14.5%, as our benchmark.Our data suggest the euro is increasingly serving as a gateway into crypto markets. By the end of our study period, euro-denominated trading accounted for 11.8% of crypto volume across the 33 leading government-issued currencies. This represents a substantial increase from previous periods, bringing the euro’s share of crypto trading closer to its adjusted FX benchmark.This growth coincides with when the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation’s implementation took effect. MiCA establishes a harmonized framework for crypto-asset issuers and service providers across the bloc, which in turn can help reduce uncertainty for investors and make it easier for new providers to enter multiple EU markets at once.While our data cannot establish a direct link, the euro’s growing share of crypto trading volume may be one result of having a more regulated, uniform sector, as well as the growth in the EU’s overall crypto economy, which will be discussed in more detail.Laurynas Spangevičius, General Manager at Robinhood Europe, points to the significance of MiCA more broadly: “The single most impactful regulatory shift for European crypto has been the complete rollout and enforcement of the EU’s MiCA framework. The resulting market clarity has replaced regulatory uncertainty with mainstream, long-term investor confidence across Europe.”Western Europe’s stablecoin holdings outpaced global growthOur research finds that stablecoins are playing a growing role in how people across Western Europe hold digital assets. Stablecoin holdings in personal wallets increased across every country measured.The shift matters: as stablecoins become more widely held, Europe faces a bigger question about how these digital currencies should fit into its financial system.Stablecoin holdings across the region surged 131%, far outpacing global growth of 52%, with Austria and France recording the strongest gains in 2026. This rapid expansion also lifted the region’s share of global stablecoin balances from 3.4% to 5.1%.Several factors may be contributing to this, including rising interest among Europeans in alternative ways to store and transfer value. The expansion of the euro-backed stablecoin market is another potential factor, driven by MiCA’s framework for stablecoin issuer authorization. As stablecoins gain traction across Europe, their potential impact on the region’s financial system is becoming harder to ignore.And debate over their potential impact is already taking shape: in September 2026, the ECB and EU national central banks called for changes to MiCA’s requirements on how stablecoin issuers hold their reserves, arguing that the current minimum threshold of 30% (or 60% for significant issuers) of reserves held in deposits at European banks could create vulnerabilities for these banks if large-scale redemptions triggered sudden withdrawals.Meanwhile, traditional financial institutions are beginning to impact the market more directly as well. Jan-Oliver Sell, CEO of Qivalis, a consortium backed MiCA-regulated stablecoin, points to several emerging use cases for regulated euro stablecoins, including serving “as the on-chain cash leg for tokenised assets” and enabling “conditional and programmable payments between businesses, such as payment on delivery.”A spokesperson for CaixaBank, the Spanish multinational bank, also points out that such efforts are part of Europe “trying to avoid becoming solely dependent on USD-denominated stablecoins.”Taken together, these developments suggest that euro-backed stablecoins could play an increasingly important role in Europe’s digital financial infrastructure, even as regulators and banks weigh the risks to financial stability and monetary sovereignty.How changing Euro bond yields are shaping Bitcoin and tokenized gold trading in the EUOur research also points to rising euro-area government bond yields relative to US yields coinciding with increased euro-denominated trading in Bitcoin and tokenized gold.This relationship is emerging amid growing concerns over Europe’s public finances, as mounting fiscal pressures fuel questions about sovereign debt risks. While these concerns have reached a boiling point in recent months, they are the result of years of high public debt, successive economic shocks, and persistently weak growth in the region.France has emerged as a key flashpoint in these mounting fiscal concerns. Rising sovereign debt and political gridlock have unsettled bond markets, with French 10-year government bond yields climbing above 5.14% in October — the highest level in over 20 years — reflecting mounting investor concern over the country’s fiscal and political outlook.Against this backdrop, we examined whether shifts in sovereign risk perceptions coincided with changes in demand for alternative assets during the report period. Using weekly data from July 2025 to June 2026, we compared yields on the highest-rated euro-area government bonds, based on ECB data, with US government bond yields and trading activity in Bitcoin and tokenized gold.We found a clear pattern: as euro-area yields rose relative to US yields, euro-denominated trading in Bitcoin and tokenized gold increased relative to dollar-denominated trading. When the yield gap narrowed, euro trading weakened by comparison.The larger the rise in yields, the stronger the increase in euro trading. When euro yields rose by around 2 basis points (0.02 percentage points) relative to US yields, euro trading was about 7.5% higher relative to dollar trading. When yields rose by around 7 basis points, it was about 12% higher. When euro yields fell relative to US yields, euro trading was 8–10% lower.One possible interpretation is that traders are broadening their portfolios to include Bitcoin and tokenized gold as confidence in the euro area’s fiscal outlook comes under pressure. French data discussed later in this report point to related shifts, suggesting that crypto usage may shift with mounting debt concerns, although our data cannot establish direct links.How Europeans use crypto to trade on global eventsPrediction markets are extending crypto’s reach beyond digital assets, allowing users to speculate on real-world events, from geopolitics to economic outcomes. To examine this trend in Europe, we analysed European wallet activity involving geopolitical bets.Our findings predate ESMA’s July 2026 classification of certain event contracts as falling under existing EU restrictions on retail binary options, which effectively banned prediction markets in the EU. Other Western European countries, such as the UK, have bans on the markets. Our analysis accounts for this evolving regulatory landscape.Our research found that wallets in the region put almost twice as large a share of their prediction market volume (74% compared to 49%) into negative outcomes of US-Iran binary markets in the 2026 period. These bets delivered weaker returns, on average, than the positive side of the bet.This suggests that prediction markets may be serving not only as venues for forecasting real-world outcomes, but also as outlets for expressing views on geopolitical developments. However, the gap between the share of volume and returns highlights a potential disconnect between what users expect to happen and where they can profitably position themselves.After years of higher growth, the UK contracts as the EU continues to expandThe UK’s crypto economy has outgrown the rest of Western Europe in recent years, but that growth advantage has now reversed. While the UK remains Western Europe’s largest crypto economy, its crypto economy contracted by 8% during the 2026 period, while the rest of Western Europe grew by 3.8% (the EU specifically grew by 2.2%).This divergence raises two questions: what drove the UK’s stronger growth in recent years, and why is the EU now holding up better?MiCA may be at play here again. The initial implementation period starting in December 2024 may have constrained growth at first, as providers faced new compliance costs and uncertainty. But as existing regional domestic providers approached a final July 2026 transition deadline, this may have actually spurred a final push for authorisation. Moreover, once MiCA licensed, all providers have passporting rights to expand across the bloc without seeking separate licences in each member state.MiCA may therefore have initially held back growth, while then helping set the stage for even greater expansion. This expansion also came as the international crypto market was seeing a downturn, with total market cap falling 50%.The UK on the other hand didn’t have a MiCA build up to potentially help offset the global bear market. Moreover, the slowdown in the UK could also reflect a wait-and-see approach ahead of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) finalising its rules and opening its authorisation gateway on in September.Our data cannot establish a direct link, and no story is ever purely regulatory. Other market dynamics were also at play over the last few years, making it impossible to isolate MiCA’s specific impact, though the timing of these shifts remains notable.The UK now leads region in domestic stablecoin activityOur research finds stablecoins are gaining traction in the UK, where domestic stablecoin value (UK wallet to UK wallet) surged during the 2026 reporting period. The UK now leads Western Europe in this measurement, with domestic transfers outpacing cross-border activity. This shift suggests stablecoins are expanding beyond cross-border payments to play a growing role in moving value within the UK.UK domestic stablecoin wallet-to-wallet transfers surged to $2.09 billion during the 2026 period, up from $109 million in the previous 12 months. The UK also outpaced the rest of Western Europe combined, which recorded $1.41 billion, accounting for 65.2% of the region’s growth and 60% of total domestic transfer value.The UK also stands apart in how stablecoins are used. Domestic transfers were 1.32 times the value of cross-border P2P and service-to-wallet transfers, while the rest of Western Europe saw cross-border activity outweigh domestic transfers by 4.38 times. This divergence suggests stablecoins may be taking on a more prominent role in the UK’s domestic financial activity, beyond their traditional use in cross-border payments.This shift comes as UK regulators increasingly focus on stablecoin payments. The FCA identified stablecoins as a priority area in its 2026 plans, reflecting a broader push to support their development and use in payments.In June 2026, the Bank of England published a policy statement and draft rules for regulating systemic stablecoins, outlining a framework that could shape how they are issued and used at scale, including in domestic payments.UK retail holders are switching more of their crypto into stablecoinsThe Bank of England has also proposed a £20,000 per-coin holding limit for individuals in systemic sterling stablecoins, reflecting again how the use of stablecoins has been a key policy question in the UK in recent years.These rules will help decide what role stablecoins play in household finances. On-chain data offer an early indication of where that role is heading, with our data suggesting that a growing share of UK retail holders already see stablecoins as somewhere to keep their money, not just as a medium of exchange.In the 2026 period, 1.03% of eligible UK retail personal wallets converted at least 80% of their crypto holdings into stablecoins, up from 0.66% a year earlier. Among the top six Western European markets in this measurement, the UK recorded the highest conversion rate in both periods. It was ahead of the Netherlands (0.54%), Italy (0.52%), Finland (0.46%), Sweden (0.38%) and Germany (0.20%).Conversion rates rose in all six markets, and more quickly elsewhere. Italy’s rate rose 2.5 times and Germany’s 2.3 times, compared with 1.6 times in the UK. Even so, the UK’s lead widened in absolute terms, from 0.40 to 0.49 percentage points over the Netherlands. This points to a broad shift toward stablecoins across Western Europe, with UK holders further along than their peers.Notably, the shift does not appear to be a reaction to the recent downturn. UK conversions peaked between July and September 2025, before bitcoin reached its October high. That is more consistent with a gradual change in how UK holders use stablecoins than with a response to a single sell-off. It also raises a related question: once UK holders had moved into stablecoins, did they keep them when prices fell? Following the same wallets through the 2025–26 drawdown offers an answer.Amidst fiscal pressures, French users turned towards self-custodied stablecoinsAs explored earlier, France has become a focal point for concerns over global and regional economic pressure. Rising public debt and a fragmented parliament have complicated efforts to rein in spending and reduce deficits, fuelling protests over austerity and the cost of living. With successive governments struggling to secure budget support, questions over how France will restore its public finances have weighed on confidence.Against a backdrop of heightened economic and political uncertainty in France, our data reveal three signs that users may be turning to self-custodied stablecoins to manage their assets: a rising share of withdrawals from centralised exchanges, more self-custody wallets holding stablecoins, and growing balances in those wallets. These shifts may reflect users making greater use of alternative financial tools to manage their savings and navigate changing market conditions.France climbed from 10th place in 2023 to first by 2026 among Western Europe’s largest crypto markets by the share of stablecoin-related withdrawals from centralised exchanges. By 2026, these withdrawals accounted for 54.2% of French service withdrawals, surpassing Germany as number one.The value transferred from exchanges to France rose 12%, compared with 7% across the rest of Western Europe. As these withdrawals move assets on-chain, where users can hold them in personal wallets or transfer them elsewhere, the trend suggests growing user control over crypto assets in France.At the same time, the number of French personal wallets holding stablecoins rose every month of the 2026 period, from 3,577 in June 2025 to 12,255 in June 2026, a 3.4-fold increase. Across the rest of Western Europe, the count rose 1.7-fold.This timing also follows the bond market. Growth in French wallets sped up from about 6% a month in mid-2025 to 18% by end of 2025, after an autumn bout of bond market stress, then slowed to 5% by June 2026 as markets calmed. Since our reporting period ended in June 2026, before this October’s sharpest stress, we cannot yet show whether the latest turmoil is spilling into crypto even further.French self-custody stablecoin balances also grew 192% during the reporting period. While the sum is still small next to traditional savings, it stands out in the direct and the pace of growth. For comparison, French bank deposits grew 2% over the same period.Together, these trends suggest that French users may be making greater use of self-custodied stablecoins amid economic uncertainty. This by no means signals a broader loss of confidence in the euro or regional crypto markets, but may instead reflect users diversifying how they hold and access their funds.Spanish exchanges now draw more from the rest of Europe than from SpainSpain’s crypto market is increasingly attracting users from beyond its borders, pointing to the growing importance of Spain as a destination for crypto activity across the wider European market.While inflows to Spanish-registered exchanges from both domestic users and the rest of Europe have grown since 2024, cross-border activity has accelerated more sharply. By the 2026 period, inflows from users elsewhere in Europe had overtaken those from Spanish users, making international customers the larger source of funds flowing into Spain’s registered exchanges.The acceleration in cross-border flows was broad-based. Among countries that sent at least $0.1 million to Spain-registered exchanges in the preceding year, average growth in the 2026 period reached 198%, nearly double the 100% recorded in 2025. The median growth rate also jumped from 82% to 162%, indicating that the surge extended across a wide range of source markets.Italy and Portugal, Spain’s two biggest sources of inflows, led the charge. Growth in flows from Italy accelerated from 22% to 329%, while Portugal saw an even sharper increase, from 36% to 751%. These gains helped propel the broader trend.Inflows to Spanish exchanges grew more than three times as fast as Spain’s crypto economy overall. Inflows from Western European users to Spain-registered exchanges rose 79.1%, compared with 24.6% growth across Spain’s broader crypto economy. A year earlier, both grew at the same pace. Since July 2023, Western European users have sent $984 million to Spain-registered exchanges, including $521 million during the 2026 period.Why are pan-European inflows to Spanish crypto exchanges on the rise? One possible explanation lies in the structure of neighboring markets. According to Gabriel Ayala, Director of API & Banks at Bit2Me, Spain’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, the absence of large, consolidated domestic operators in some countries has created openings for established European platforms to attract users across borders.“In Portugal, the size of the market and linguistic particularities may have limited the emergence of local platforms with sufficient scale. In Italy, regulatory complexity and sector fragmentation have historically made it difficult to consolidate certain operators,” Ayala said.For platforms such as Bit2Me, these gaps create an opportunity to compete beyond their home markets by combining competitive offerings with regulatory expertise, operational scale and the capacity to expand internationally.The evolving regulatory landscape may provide a further tailwind. The representative pointed to MiCA as opening up new opportunities for pan-European growth, as it has helped facilitate expansion within a single European market.Spain’s exchange story reflects a broader trend across Europe: the interplay between national markets and European integration.Defining the next chapter of crypto in EuropeFrom rising use of stablecoins to declining DEX activity in some markets and established exchanges attracting users from across Europe, Western Europe’s crypto economy is being reshaped by a mix of evolving user behavior, investor and market dynamics, and broader external forces. As Robinhood’s Spangevičius notes: “Europe’s crypto landscape has shifted from regional speculation into structural maturity.”Financial uncertainty, geopolitical developments and regulatory shifts are reshaping digital asset activity worldwide, with Europe offering a particularly clear illustration of how these forces are playing out. As the region’s crypto economy matures, its trajectory will depend not only on evolving user behavior and institutional participation, but also on how market participants adapt to changing financial conditions and regulatory frameworks.As institutional participation deepens, consumer protection, regulatory consistency and the links between crypto markets and traditional banking will become increasingly important to the sector’s development.FAQsHow large is Western Europe’s crypto economy?Western Europe’s crypto economy totaled $2.08 trillion between July 2025 and June 2026, making it the second-largest crypto economy globally. Despite a downturn in the global crypto market, the region grew 1.2% during the reporting period.Which countries have the largest crypto economies in Western Europe?The UK had the largest crypto economy in Western Europe at $424.5 billion, followed by Germany at $288.8 billion, France at $215.8 billion, the Netherlands at $207.8 billion, Spain at $156.1 billion, and Switzerland at $132.8 billion. Together, these six markets accounted for roughly two-thirds of the region’s crypto economy.How is MiCA affecting crypto adoption in Europe?The EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation establishes a harmonized framework for crypto-asset issuers and service providers across the bloc. Its implementation coincided with growing euro-denominated crypto trading and expansion across EU markets. MiCA also gives authorized providers passporting rights to operate across the bloc. However, the data cannot establish that MiCA directly caused the region’s growth.Why are stablecoins becoming more popular in Western Europe?Western Europe’s stablecoin holdings increased 131% between July 2025 and June 2026, compared with 52% globally. Potential factors include growing interest in alternative ways to store and transfer value, the expansion of euro-backed stablecoins, and a more developed regulatory framework. The data also show different patterns across countries, including increased domestic transfers in the UK and greater self-custody in France.How is the UK crypto market changing compared with the EU?The UK remained Western Europe’s largest crypto economy, but its activity contracted 8% during the reporting period. The rest of Western Europe grew 3.8%, while the EU grew 2.2%. The UK also recorded substantial growth in domestic stablecoin transfers and had the highest share of retail wallets converting at least 80% of their crypto holdings into stablecoins among the six largest markets measured. articles.title: The Commodity ETF Tax Surprise: When a Big Rally Doesn’t Mean a Big Return for Investors | WisdomTree
articles.text: Back to BlogThe Commodity ETF Tax Surprise: When a Big Rally Doesn’t Mean a Big Return for InvestorsPublished November 10, 2026Jonathan FlynnDirector of Market StrategyKey TakeawaysThree commodity exchange-traded funds posted approximately 32%–51% year-to-date price returns, while estimated flow-weighted buyer returns were roughly 9%–16% through October 30, 2026.Investors buying shortly before a taxable distribution may receive income reflecting earlier fund activity, even if their own shares have barely appreciated.The WisdomTree Enhanced Commodity Strategy Fund (GCC) completed its substantial October distribution and uses contract selection and portfolio construction to seek enhanced returns.A strong year for commodities has created a new question for investors: How much of the rally did they capture, and what taxable distributions might still be coming?A Big Rally, but Not Necessarily for Every InvestorCommodities have attracted renewed attention in 2026, as investors seek diversification, inflation protection and exposure to real assets. Yet an ETF’s headline return and the return earned by investors who bought it are not necessarily the same. Our analysis of three major commodity ETFs through October 30, 2026, illustrates the disconnect. Although the funds’ year-to-date price returns ranged from approximately 32% to 51%, estimated flow-weighted returns on dollars entering during the year ranged from roughly 9% to 16%. In one fund, approximately $976 million of $1.36 billion in gross inflows had earned 10% or less by October 30. These estimates reflect the timing of weekly inflows, not actual investor-account performance.Figure 1: Commodity ETF Price Returns vs. Estimated Buyers’ ReturnsSource: WisdomTree Market Strategy analysis; ETF.com weekly net flows and daily closing prices. Each inflow week assigned estimated return from average daily price in that week to October 30, 2026; flow-weighted estimate, not actual investor trades or account returns. Funds anonymized.The explanation is straightforward: many investors arrived after substantial appreciation had already occurred. Now, as year-end approaches, those investors have another reason to pay attention: taxable fund distributions.The Question Advisors Should Ask Before BuyingHas the commodity ETF already made its major taxable distribution for the year, or could one still be coming? That question matters because taxable distributions are generally determined by income and gains realized within a fund, not by how long a particular shareholder has owned it. An investor purchasing shares late in the year may receive a distribution reflecting activity that occurred before the purchase. Imagine an investor buys $100,000 of a fund shortly before a taxable distribution equal to 20% of its share price. Even if the investor has earned little or no appreciation, the distribution may generate taxable income. The fund’s share price would ordinarily decline by approximately the distribution amount on the ex-dividend date, so the payment is not an additional 20% investment return. Nor does a 20% distribution mean a 20% tax rate. But it can accelerate a tax obligation for a recent buyer. For investors who already missed much of a rally, that can be an unwelcome combination: modest personal gains and a meaningful taxable distribution.Why Commodity ETF Structures MatterNot all commodity ETFs are taxed alike. Some futures-based products are structured as partnerships, while others are registered investment companies that may obtain futures exposure directly or through subsidiaries. Certain regulated futures contracts can receive so-called 60/40 treatment: 60% of eligible gains or losses are treated as long-term and 40% as short-term, regardless of holding period. That rule does not describe the tax treatment of every commodity ETF shareholder or every fund distribution. Traditional equity ETFs often use in-kind redemptions to help manage embedded capital gains. Futures-based strategies may not be able to use that mechanism in the same way for all exposures. Contract rolls, portfolio adjustments and the fund’s legal structure can influence realized income, gains and eventual distributions. The lesson is not to avoid commodities. It is to look beyond performance charts and understand how a fund’s investment process and distribution calendar may affect the shareholder experience.GCC: A Distribution Already Behind It, and an Enhanced Process AheadThe WisdomTree Enhanced Commodity Strategy Fund (GCC) made a substantial distribution with an ex-dividend date of October 27, 2026, and payment date of October 29. The reported amount was $6.45254 per share, classified on WisdomTree’s recent-distributions page as ordinary income, with no short- or long-term capital gains reported in that listing. For an investor evaluating GCC in November, that specific October distribution is already behind the fund. This does not guarantee that GCC will make no additional distributions, or that it is categorically more tax-efficient than other commodity ETFs. It does, however, demonstrate why the timing of a new allocation deserves consideration. GCC also offers a differentiated reason to consider commodity exposure. Rather than simply tracking a traditional front-month futures benchmark, the strategy seeks to enhance returns through contract selection and portfolio construction. WisdomTree’s Research Team sets longer-term strategic allocations, evaluates eligible futures maturities for liquidity, and generally favors contracts with attractive expected carry. The team also reviews supply-and-demand conditions, sentiment and technical factors for potential tactical adjustments. The approach seeks to manage an important component of futures returns: the benefit or cost of rolling contracts along the futures curve. The fund provides broad exposure across energy, agriculture, precious and industrial metals, along with a limited allocation to bitcoin futures exposure. Its enhanced roll process is designed to offer a different investment experience from a conventional commodity benchmark, although it cannot eliminate market or futures-related risks.What Investors Keep MattersStrong commodity returns have drawn significant investor interest. But headline performance does not tell advisors what their clients earned, and it certainly does not tell them what their clients may owe in taxes. As investors assess commodity allocations heading into 2027, three questions belong together: What has the fund earned? What have its shareholders actually experienced? And what taxable distributions could lie ahead? For those considering a new allocation, we believe GCC merits a closer look, not only because its substantial October distribution has already occurred, but because its enhanced futures process offers a differentiated approach to commodity investing.Sources for this blog: WisdomTree Market Strategy analysis of weekly ETF flows and daily prices through October 30, 2026; WisdomTree GCC recent-distributions page (user-provided screenshot); WisdomTree Enhanced Commodity Strategy Fund presentation, June 2026. Flow-weighted buyer returns are estimates and exclude investor-specific taxes and trading costs.Important Risks Related to this ArticleThere are risks associated with investing including possible loss of principal. An investment in this Fund is speculative, involves a substantial degree of risk, and should not constitute an investor's entire portfolio. One of the risks associated with the Fund is the complexity of the different factors which contribute to the Fund's performance. These factors include use of commodity futures contracts. In addition, bitcoin exchange-traded products (ETPs) and bitcoin futures are relatively new and the markets may be less developed. They are subject to unique and substantial risks, and historically, have been subject to significant price volatility. As a result, the markets for bitcoin futures and bitcoin ETPs may be less developed, and at times, potentially less liquid and more volatile, than more established commodity futures and ETP markets. While the bitcoin futures market has grown substantially since bitcoin futures commenced trading, there can be no assurance that this growth will continue. In addition, derivatives can be volatile and may be less liquid than other securities and more sensitive to the effects of varied economic conditions. The value of the shares of the Fund relate directly to the value of the futures contracts and other assets held by the Fund and any fluctuation in the value of these assets could adversely affect an investment in the Fund's shares. Because of the frequency with which the Fund expects to roll futures contracts, the price of futures contracts further from expiration may be higher (a condition known as “contango”) or lower (a condition known as “backwardation”) and the impact of such contango or backwardation may be greater than the impact would be if the Fund experienced less portfolio turnover. The Fund will not invest in bitcoin directly. Please read the Fund’s prospectus for specific details regarding the Fund’s risk profile.CategoriesCommoditiesAlternativeRelated ProductsGCCEnhanced Commodity Strategy FundLearn moreRelated articlesThree Alternative Strategies to Consider When Volatility ResurfacesNovember 5, 2026A New Chapter in Systematic Alpha: Introducing WSLS and WTALOctober 8, 2026Four Markets, One Basket: A Mental Model for Commodities into 2027September 9, 2026When Markets Zigzag, Trend-Followers Can ShineSeptember 1, 2026Register to get insights from WisdomTreeIndividual investors who register can access daily blog posts, latest videos, podcasts and stay current with industry insights. On top of that, Financial Professionals get additional access to the tools, technology, resources and support they need to take the business to the next level.RegisterSign inAbout the contributorJonathan FlynnDirector of Market StrategyJonathan Flynn serves as Director of Market Strategy at WisdomTree, helping bridge research, product strategy, distribution and investor engagement through data-driven market insights and thematic storytelling.He brings more than 25 years of experience working with leading wealth management teams and advisors, with deep expertise in investor behavior, ETF trends, market flows and behavioral finance. Jonathan specializes in identifying emerging themes early, translating complex ideas into compelling investment narratives and helping investors better understand the intersection of sentiment, positioning and long-term opportunity.His work is grounded in the belief that understanding investor behavior and crowd dynamics can help uncover tomorrow’s investment opportunities before they become consensus.READ ALL INSIGHTS

articles.title: Financial conditions: what’s priced in? − speech by Catherine L. Mann
articles.text:
Financial conditions: what’s priced in? − speech by Catherine L. Mann

Given at the Nomura London Macro Forum

Published on
01 October 2026

Catherine L. Mann discusses how UK financial markets have priced in greater risk premia since the Middle East conflict intensified. She uses several models to uncover their sources and considers how monetary policy and communication can help reduce premia to ensure inflation returns to target.

Speech
Introduction
The conflict in the Middle East has generated significant volatility and financial market repricing in the UK, relating to uncertainty around the evolution of the conflict, the outlook for UK inflation, and our monetary policy response. Financial conditions are an essential mechanism through which monetary policy transmits and therefore form an important input into my monetary policy decisions. In this speech, I will evaluate the information that financial conditions provide about the current monetary policy stance and transmission, and carefully examine what they reveal about the types of risks driving recent moves.
Financial conditions
Let me start with a headline indicator of financial conditions, which summarizes how a broad range of asset price movements contribute to changes in nominal and real financial conditions. The effect of policy tightening since 2022 on nominal financial conditions in the UK is clearly visible, as the pink line in Chart 1 shows. Despite a modest loosening over 2025, this measure of nominal financial conditions resumed a slight tightening since the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East on account of higher short and long-term nominal interest rates.

Chart 1: Changes in UK financial conditions since 2020
Index points

Footnotes

Source: Burr (2023) Opens in a new window using Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb and LSEG.
Notes: The real financial conditions index uses real interest rate variables, exchange rate and equity prices – that is, net of inflation compensation. Latest observation: August 2026.

Nominal financial conditions incorporate inflation expectations and inflation risk premia, which may distort the signal about real tightness, particularly following an inflationary shock. The real financial conditions index in Chart 1 (white line) strips out the effects of rising inflation compensation following the start of the conflict in the Middle East at the end of February. This index suggests that real financial conditions loosened around the beginning of the conflict (consistent with inflation compensation measures rising significantly in March), some of which have since retraced, albeit with a notable compression in spreads.
Given that inflation has been well-above target for five years already and the conflict in the Middle East has contributed to further upside risks to inflation, real and nominal financial conditions need to remain tight. There are two mechanisms through which I can tighten real financial conditions: reducing measures of inflation compensation, and/or, raising nominal yields (and expectations), both of which can be achieved through an increase in Bank Rate. In my view, our current monetary policy stance is not sufficiently tight, which is why I voted in the last two meetings for a 25 basis point increase in Bank Rate.
As financial conditions indices summarize a range of underlying market dynamics, I will unpack some of their key drivers and explore what they reveal about what is priced in. This assessment concludes that the MPC cannot simply rely on policy restrictiveness coming from an upward shift in the nominal yield curve. At some point, we need to follow-through with Bank Rate rises – to maintain credibility, and to avoid policy expectations repricing downwards and inflation expectations repricing further upwards.
What does the gap between markets and participants imply?
Overall nominal financial conditions have remained relatively tight, but what are financial market expectations for the future path of monetary policy? We can gauge market expectations of the policy rate path from a variety of sources. For the UK, these are the yield curve, such as the overnight index swap (OIS) curve, and the Bank of England Market Participants Survey (MaPS).footnote [1]
Chart 2 plots the OIS curve across the UK, US and euro area (EA), and survey-based policy rate expectations from the respective central banks’ latest surveys of market participants. The survey-based measures should offer a cleaner read on policy rate expectations than the OIS curve, because they do not include risk premia or other market-based technical factors. As the differences between the light and dark solid lines in Chart 2 show, there are gaps between the two measures for all three jurisdictions, but the difference is largest for the UK.
If the OIS curve only reflected expectations for policy rate changes, it would imply almost 75 basis points of tightening in Bank Rate over the next 12 months, in contrast to a prolonged hold (and subsequent cuts) implied by the MaPS. I have plotted the OIS curve at the respective dates of survey closure. Since then, the gap has widened further, implying over 100 basis points of tightening in Bank Rate over the coming 12 months. The swathes indicate the interquartile ranges of the survey-based distributions; however, taking that into account does only a little to explain the gap in the UK.

Chart 2: OIS curves and survey-implied expectations for policy rates
Percent

Footnotes

Notes: UK survey data shows the median response (solid light aqua line) and the 25th-75th percentile of responses (shaded aqua area) to the September 2026 Market Participants Survey. US survey data shows the median response (solid light purple line) and the 25th-75th percentile of responses (shaded purple area) to the July 2026 Survey of Market Expectations Opens in a new window. OIS curves (dark solid lines) on the respective dates of survey closure (4th September, 20th July and 26th August). Survey measures typically ask for policy rate expectations (Bank Rate, Federal Funds Rate/Range and Deposit Rate Facility) for UK, US and EA respectively. These do not exactly match the interest rate underlying the OIS (SONIA, SOFR and €STR).

The UK seems to be an outlier internationally, but is the current gap also large by historical standards? Chart 3 shows how the average difference between the OIS curve and market participants’ median expectations for Bank Rate has evolved over a 3-year horizon (left panel). There has been a material increase in the gap since the beginning of the conflict in the Middle East, to levels last seen following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Because the survey-based measure only captures market participants’ expectations for Bank Rate, movements in the gap can be a crude measure of risk premia. The widening observed this year therefore suggests that investors are demanding greater compensation for UK risk.

Chart 3: Average gap between market-based and survey-implied expectations for policy rates over a 3-year horizon
Basis points

Footnotes

Sources: Bank of England, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, European Central Bank, Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.
Notes: The height of the bar reflects the average gap between the respective survey’s median ‘most likely’ (modal) profile for the policy rate and the average OIS curve observed across the survey window over a 3-year horizon.

What risks are investors demanding greater compensation for? There is no single model that allows us to decompose this risk premium into its various sources and drivers. In the remainder of this speech, I will go through various hypotheses, using a variety of different models and data, to pinpoint the types of risks relevant to driving this gap.
The role of the term premium
Movements in nominal government bond yields can be decomposed into contributions from changes in expected interest rates and a term premium. The term premium is the additional compensation required by investors (above and beyond their interest rate expectations) to hold interest rate risk. Before discussing what the charts show, it is worth noting that the term premium, and risk premia in general, are unobservable. We rely on a suite of models to estimate them.
Chart 4 shows a model-implied structural decomposition of a 3-year nominal yield into these two categories across the UK, US and Germany. The model decomposition is an average of three term structure models: Malik and Meldrum (2016) Opens in a new window, Vlieghe (2016) and Andreasen and Meldrum (2015). For the UK, this structural model-based decomposition complements the survey-based evidence from MaPS on policy expectations.footnote [2] In both the UK and Germany, 3-year government bond yields have risen by around 100 basis points over the past year, but the drivers appear to be different.
According to this term structure model, higher term premia account for around 24 basis points of the increase in the UK, compared with just 4 basis points in Germany. This contribution has been increasingly positive in the UK throughout the year. In the US, a positive contribution from the term premium is only visible more recently, accounting for around 25 basis points of the 140 basis points rise in yields.

Chart 4: Decomposition of UK, US and German 3-year nominal yields
Cumulative differences since January 2026

Footnotes

Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb, Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Bank calculations.
Note: The expected rates and term premium contributions may not sum exactly to the observed nominal yield because they are averages of model-implied decompositions and contain residuals that reflect model fitting error. Latest observation: 25th September 2026.

To compare results across different models I show, in Chart 5, a decomposition from a different model (Lengyel and Walker, 2026) that adapts a standard affine term structure framework to identify near-term risk premia more cleanly. Relative to classic models, which are typically calibrated to fit the yield curve as a whole, this approach uses OIS instead of government bond yields, allows for a richer factor structure, and directly incorporates survey-based expectations for Bank Rate. While term premia make a larger contribution to yields overall across the UK, US and EA, the result that its contribution is largest for the UK is robust.

Chart 5: Decomposition of UK, US and German 3-year OIS yields
Cumulative differences since January 2026

Footnotes

Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.
Note: The expected rates and term premium contributions may not sum exactly to the observed nominal yield because they are averages of model-implied decompositions and contain residuals that reflect model fitting error. Latest observation: 25th September 2026.

In a historical and international context, it is somewhat unusual that the term premium has contributed significantly to the rise in short-term yields. The term premium is often defined as the additional compensation investors demand to hold a longer-term bond relative to a series of shorter-term bonds (Kaminska, Meldrum and Young, 2015 Opens in a new window). It is therefore common for the term premium to show up at the longer end of the yield curve. That is, the further into the future you go, the more uncertain the future path of interest rates is. So why is the UK term premium such an outlier, and such a significant driver of short-term yields?
Chart 6 plots the model-implied 1-year and 3-year term premium between 2009 and today. Over this period, the 1-year and 3-year term premium have been negative throughout the 2010s and after the Russia-Ukraine shock. A negative term premium is not unusual. Joyce, Kaminska and Lildholdt (2008) discuss various drivers for the UK, including regulatory changes, excess liquidity, and “flight to quality” dynamics away from risky assets in times of uncertainty. This could also be explained by a negative inflation risk premium (Cieslak and Pflueger, 2023 Opens in a new window).

Chart 6: UK model-implied 1-year and 3-year term premium
Percent

Footnotes

Source: Lengyel and Walker (2026) using Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb and Bank calculations.
Note: Latest observation: 25th September 2026.

However, term premia rose at the start of the conflict in the Middle East and have recently turned positive. That is also true for the 3-year term premium, which stands out as particularly high in recent history, and was only exceeded during the post-GFC period and when Russia invaded Ukraine. The Middle East energy shock is notable, but not as large as the Russia-Ukraine energy shock.
Staff work finds that the UK term premium, especially at the short end, has become more volatile and responsive to news about economic and financial market developments. In part, this reflects higher sensitivity of (international) investors (Mann, 2026) and a different composition of demand for government debt, including a reduced role of preferred habitat investors such as insurance companies and pension funds, as Beltran and Li (2026) Opens in a new window also find for the US.
Lengyel and Walker (2026) argue that risk premia at the short end of the curve reflect the compensation investors require for uncertainty around the policy rate path. It is therefore important for monetary policymakers to understand whether changes in nominal yields reflect changing policy expectations or uncertainty around them – distinguishing between the two has important consequences on how to interpret the moves in financial conditions.footnote [3]
I explore the role of near-term policy uncertainty in the next section.
What is the role of uncertainty?
Chart 7 shows the option-implied distributions of SONIA (the risk-free overnight interest rate for sterling markets, and the rate underlying the overnight index swap) 12 months ahead, and its equivalents for the US (SOFR) and the euro area (€STR) based on the methodology of Clews et al. (2000).footnote [4] While the OIS rate shown in the earlier Chart 2 reflects a summary statistic of the underlying distribution, the full distribution in Chart 7 contains additional information. Prior to the conflict (orange), the distributions for all three jurisdictions are tight – implying little uncertainty, and high conviction, about the future path of policy rates. Since the conflict began, the distributions for all three have shifted to the right and widened. The UK distribution, however, has widened slightly more, implying that perceived risks and uncertainty about the future policy rate have increasingly been priced in by markets, and particularly more so for the UK.

Chart 7: Option-implied distribution of interest rates, 12 months ahead
For SONIA, SOFR and €STR

Footnotes

Source: ICE, CME and Bank calculations
Note: The underlying rate for the UK distribution is the 3-month SONIA rate 12 months ahead. Latest observation: 25th September 2026

Furthermore, the skewness of SONIA has turned sharply positive following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, which implies that upside risks to interest rates are perceived to be materially larger than downside risks. This degree of positive skewness was last observed following the post-Covid supply chain disruptions in 2021 and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The increase in uncertainty and the positive skewness could simply reflect a repricing of the outlook for the economy – reflecting uncertainty about how the conflict in the Middle East could play out, how the resulting supply shock will affect the UK economy going forward, and how it is passed through to broader pricing dynamics. However, such trade-off inducing shocks (shocks that are inflationary but have contractionary effects on activity) also make it more challenging for monetary policymakers to set policy, and uncertainty about the policy rate path could also be higher.
Financial markets are trying to price in both: uncertainty about the economic outlook and uncertainty about the monetary policy response. There is no “textbook” monetary policy response to supply shocks, and therefore, the market’s understanding of how members of the MPC might respond (that is, our reaction function) could be incomplete or unclear. Given that inflation has remained above target for five years and is expected to increase further as the energy shock propagates, the market might be pricing in a reaction function that is not consistent with bringing inflation back to the 2% target sustainably in the medium-term.
Is there a monetary policy uncertainty premium?
Could uncertainty about the monetary policy response to the conflict in the Middle East have also contributed to the gap between the OIS curve and market participants’ expectations for Bank Rate? Research about the effects of monetary policy has generally focused on the effect of changes in the level of Bank Rate on the UK economy (see for instance Brandt et al., 2026 Opens in a new window; Braun et al., 2025 Opens in a new window; Di Pace et al., 2025 Opens in a new window). Uncertainty about future interest rates and its effects on financial markets and the real economy has received less attention.
Based on a methodology developed by Bauer et al. (2022) Opens in a new window, Raviraj (forthcoming) constructs a financial market-based measure of UK monetary policy uncertaintyfootnote [5] surprises that uses changes in the standard deviation of the option-implied distribution of SONIA around MPC announcement dates. Using the surprise series as an instrument for a monetary policy uncertainty shock in a structural VAR allows the author to causally identify the effects of monetary policy uncertainty on a set of outcome variables.
Let me start by showing what this monetary policy uncertainty variable looks like and how it relates to MPC announcements. On average across the sample period (1997 to 2026), a monetary policy announcement leads to a resolution of uncertainty about short-term interest rates, as the decrease in the aqua line following the day of an MPC announcement in the left panel of Chart 8 shows. Monetary policy and communications around MPC decisions have acted as a stabilizing force in the economy, resolving uncertainty around the future path of interest rates.

Chart 8: Changes in monetary policy uncertainty around MPC announcementdates
Percent (LHS) and factor score (RHS)

Footnotes

Source: Raviraj (forthcoming).
Note: The solid aqua line in the left chart shows the average change in short-rate uncertainty on trading days around MPC announcements from June 1997 until July 2026. The pink line shows the change in short-rate uncertainty around the March 2026 MPC announcement. The shaded area represents the 95% confidence interval. In the right chart, monetary policy uncertainty factors are constructed by applying Varimax rotation to principal components of changes in short-rate uncertainty and first moment interest rates around MPC announcements.

However, there is one notable meeting where our decision and communications do not seem to have played that role. In the left panel of Chart 8, I also plot (in pink) changes in uncertainty around the March 2026 decision – the first monetary policy meeting after the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East. One may argue that this simply reflects elevated levels of uncertainty following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East. However, the identification strategy for the monetary policy uncertainty shock isolates changes in uncertainty on MPC announcement days – these changes should therefore largely reflect news associated with the monetary policy decision and associated communications. It strips out any first moment, level effects of monetary policy and captures shocks associated with MPC announcements beyond what markets had already priced in. I plot the estimated monetary policy uncertainty factor in the right panel of Chart 8, which shows that monetary policy uncertainty increased significantly following the March decision, which cannot simply be attributed to uncertainty around the economic outlook resulting from the conflict.footnote [6]
What are the implications of an increase in monetary policy uncertainty? Using the monetary policy uncertainty shock series, we can evaluate the impact of such a shock on financial market variables. The left panel of Chart 9 shows the impulse response function of short rate uncertaintyfootnote [7] to a one standard deviation increase in monetary policy uncertainty. An increase in monetary policy uncertainty also leads to a rise in the 1-year OIS rate, driven by both a higher term premium and higher interest rate expectations. An increase in monetary policy uncertainty tightens financial conditions.

Chart 9: Impulse response functions of short rate uncertainty, term premium and expected interest rates to a monetary policy uncertainty shock
Percentage points

Footnotes

Source: Raviraj (forthcoming).
Note: Impulse response functions to a one standard deviation structural monetary policy uncertainty shock, proxied by the monetary policy uncertainty factor presented in the right panel of Chart 8. Shaded areas represent 68% and 90% confidence intervals.

Yet, why did such a clear signal, a unanimous decision to hold Bank Rate, result in higher uncertainty? It could be because our communication about the outlook for the economy, beyond what was already priced in by markets, was too focused on the uncertainty resulting from the conflict in the Middle East, rather than the underlying dynamics of the economy. Or our reaction function to the shock – the balance between looking through the shock and responding to signs of propagation – was not clearly articulated.
What does this mean for the role of monetary policy uncertainty in driving current risk premia? The committee’s vote splits in the past have revealed differences in views about both the economic outlook and the appropriate monetary policy response. The unanimous vote at the March meeting deviated from these previously communicated reaction functions in light of the conflict in the Middle East. Central bank communication – including our Monetary Policy Report, Monetary Policy Summary and minutes, press conferences, and speeches – is an important tool to explain past monetary policy decisions and to manage expectations about the economy and potential Bank Rate paths. Communication should provide clarity about our reaction function and reduce uncertainty around the future interest rate path (Blinder et al., 2008 Opens in a new window; Gebauer et al., 2024 Opens in a new window), even without having to provide explicit forward guidance.
Our communications in March highlighted larger uncertainties. Perhaps they were not clear on how the MPC’s reaction function would evolve with new information – it appeared we were in “wait mode”, which discounted our assurance to the markets that we would “act as necessary” to reach the inflation target. And, as discussed by my colleague Alan Taylor (Taylor, 2026), not publishing a baseline forecast in April most likely did not help either.
The March announcement and the uncertainty it reflected did trigger a strong upward shift in the OIS curve, contributing to the gap between OIS and MaPS. My concern is that this gap has continued to increase, and that one spike in monetary policy uncertainty may have had lasting effects, particularly in an environment with a higher sensitivity of term premia to shocks.
What about risk premia in other assets?
Risk premia and term premia are not synonymous. Term premia specifically refer to the additional compensation required for interest rate risk on risk-free bonds. Risk premia is a general term referring to the additional compensation required by investors for holding risky over risk-free assets.
One would expect uncertainty about the economic outlook arising from geopolitical and energy shocks to be reflected in risk premia for a range of assets. For example, the equity risk premium is the additional compensation for risk associated with holding stocks. Chart 10 plots model estimates of this risk premium (Kontoghiorghes et al., 2025). While there is a temporary spike following the conflict in the Middle East, equity risk premia do not appear elevated in historical context (other than in the US since 2020), likely driven by a robust demand for equities as an asset class in general, or reflecting lower perceived (relative) risk across asset classes.

Chart 10: Equity risk premium
Percent

Footnotes

Source: Kontoghiorghes et al. (2025).
Note: The measure used follows the lower-bound ERP estimate of Chabi-Yo and Loudis (2020) Opens in a new window over a one-year time horizon, and uses options on the FTSE 100, S&P 500, and EUROSTOXX 50 for the UK, US, and euro area, respectively. Latest observation: 16th September 2026.

But there is another source of risk premia that is of particular concern for an inflation-targeting central bank – the inflation risk premium. Chart 11 (left-hand panel) shows cumulative changes in the 3-year inflation swap since February, decomposed into contributions from changes in inflation expectations and inflation risk premia. It shows that the inflation risk premium has contributed significantly to the rise in the 3-year inflation swap this year. Rising CPI inflation expectations have also played a considerable role. This reduced slightly in June and July, when the Memorandum of Understanding between the US and Iran was in place, but subsequently rose again following re-escalation of the conflict.

Chart 11: Decomposition of UK 3-year inflation swap rate (LHS) and 3-yearnominal yield (RHS)
Cumulative differences

Footnotes

Source: Kaminska et al. (2018) Opens in a new window for LHS, and Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb and Bank calculations for RHS.
Note: The left panel is estimated using a model proposed in Kaminska et al. (2018) Opens in a new window. Latest observation: September 2026 (LHS) and 25th September 2026 (RHS).

The right-hand side panel shows that the contribution to the rise in 3-year nominal yields has been almost entirely accounted for by a rise in inflation compensation, which is a combination of inflation expectations and the inflation risk premium. This brings me back to my very first chart where I showed that while nominal financial conditions have tightened following the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East, real financial conditions remained looser.
Monetary policy strategy
What does all this mean for my monetary policy strategy?
The supply shock resulting from the conflict hit at a time when the disinflationary process from previous supply shocks was still incomplete, with nominal rigidities limiting the speed of normalization. Inflation has been above target for the last five years and the Bank’s updated short-term inflation forecast from September projects inflation to increase to over 4% in Q1 2027. This raises inflation above the attentiveness threshold of households and firms ahead of wage negotiations next spring.
Given rising upside risks to inflation, a risk management strategy to monetary policy is appropriate. When there is uncertainty about inflation dynamics and second-round effects, raising Bank Rate to commit to the inflation target can help ensure a sustainable return of inflation to the 2% target, with smaller losses to economic activity.
With the ‘sporadic continuance’ of the conflict in the Middle East, uncertainty around the outlook for the economy and inflation risks have remained elevated. Uncertainty about the MPC reaction function should not compound the problem. Ensuring that this communication is clear and that the reaction function is well understood is the purpose of collective communications. When a policy decision deviates from the collective, speeches such as this can provide additional clarity on the outlook, risks, and decisions.
Against this backdrop, as a monetary policymaker, I cannot take comfort from tighter nominal financial conditions when much of that tightening reflects a higher inflation risk premium and, possibly, a monetary policy uncertainty premium that our own decisions and communications may have contributed to. These premia raise nominal yields without necessarily tightening the real financial conditions that matter for demand and inflation. In my view, real financial conditions are insufficiently tight. The appropriate response therefore is not to rely on risk premia to do the work of policy, but to reduce inflation risk and policy uncertainty through a clearly communicated reaction function and a sufficiently restrictive path for Bank Rate.
The views expressed in this speech are not necessarily those of the Bank of England or the Monetary Policy Committee.
Acknowledgments
I would like to thank Natalie Burr and Christoph Herler for their help in the preparation of this speech.

Protecting Our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity

Protecting Our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity
Across the industry, we are seeing an increase in bad actors impersonating and misusing corporate brands to get access to personal information and funds from unsuspecting individuals. These activities may involve individuals acting as company representatives and may include fake websites, social media inquiries, or communications that closely resemble official channels.
Please read the below for important reminders that can help protect you from potentially fraudulent activity.
We strongly caution against providing personal data or transferring funds in response to unsolicited requests. For your safety, always verify the authenticity of communications claiming to be from Lazard by contacting us through our official website or known contact points.
Specifically, Lazard will never engage in the following activities:

Sending unsolicited investment proposals or requests for personal information from nonverified persons.
Requesting payments to bank accounts in the names of individuals, third parties, unknown company names, or through payment intermediaries.
Offering unrealistically attractive returns that seem too good to be true.
Expressing urgency to complete an investment or make a payment.
Requesting additional payments to release investments that have already been made.
Requesting money to be sent via social media messaging apps and/or platforms.

If you believe that you have fallen victim to fraud, please contact your bank immediately. Additionally, you should report the incident to law enforcement in your jurisdiction as soon as possible.
The safety and protection of data and information is a priority for Lazard, and we appreciate your careful attention and diligence.
***
Lazard cannot accept any responsibility for any loss, damage, or claims arising from fraudulent activities. Please fully read account disclosures and related policies.

articles.title: Behind Australia’s building material import boom
articles.text:
Webinar

Behind Australia’s building material import boom

Register Now

3 December 2026 – 1.00pm AEDT (Sydney / 10AM HKT)

online

Imported building and construction materials are taking a bigger share of the Australian market. Steel, aluminium and timber are where the pressure shows most, but pressure is building in most segments. In this webinar, Harry Murphy Cruise will use Oxford Economics’ detailed trade data to look at:

Import volumes and market share: how much material is coming in, and what that means for sizing the domestic market accurately.

Price competitiveness: how import prices compare by product and country of origin, and where the cost gap is widening.

Trade remedies: what recent anti-dumping activity tells us about shifting supply sources.

Emerging segments: an early look at prefabricated and modular construction, a fast-growing area where reliable data is still scarce.

This webinar is being held on our new platform, ON24. If you do not receive your confirmation email, please check your junk and spam folders.

Speakers

Harry Murphy Cruise

Harry Murphy Cruise is the Head of Economic Research and Global Trade at Oxford Economics Australia. He leads the Australian Macroeconomic Service and global trade initiatives, including TradePrism. Harry frequently provides insights to major media outlets, including CNBC, BBC, Reuters, and the Wall Street Journal. His research primarily focuses on global trade and investment flows, with particular interest in the challenges and opportunities of economic decoupling.

Harry holds a master’s degree in international and development economics from the Australian National University and a bachelor’s degree in arts and commerce from Monash University. He is a PhD candidate at ANU, exploring the role of China’s diverse households and firms in the country’s economic transition.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Harry was the Head of China and Australia Economics at Moody’s Analytics. He was previously responsible for Australian state and territory analysis at Deloitte Access Economics.
