articles.title: Euro Tax Flash from KPMG's EU Tax Centre: 04 November 2026
articles.text:
Go back to the Euro Tax Flash homepage.

KPMG feedback on the European Commission Tax Omnibus proposal

At a glance: KPMG member firms in the EU have submitted feedbackopens in a new tab on the European Commission’s Tax Omnibus proposal, broadly welcoming its simplification measures while identifying areas where further changes or clarifications may needed.Taxpayer impact: The Tax Omnibus could reduce tax-related costs and compliance burdens for businesses operating across the EU, although the extent of these benefits will depend on the outcome of Council negotiations.

European Commission – Tax Omnibus – Direct taxation – Withholding taxes – Parent-Subsidiary Directive – Interest and Royalties Directive - ATAD – CFC rules – Interest limitation – R&D tax incentives – Merger Directive – Tax dispute resolution

Background

On September 10, 2026, the European Commission (EC) launched a public consultation on its Tax Omnibus proposalopens in a new tab, inviting interested parties to submit comments by November 5, 2026.The consultation follows the publication, on June 24, 2026, of the Commission’s Tax Omnibus proposal, which forms part of its broader agenda to simplify the EU direct tax framework, reduce administrative and compliance burdens and support the competitiveness of the EU internal market.The proposal would amend several key EU direct tax Directives, including the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD), the Parent-Subsidiary Directive (PSD), the Interest and Royalties Directive (IRD), the Merger Directive and the Directive on Tax Dispute Resolution Mechanisms (DRM). Key measures include:removing withholding taxes on qualifying intra-EU dividends, interest and royalties and introducing a simplified procedure for accessing withholding tax relief;introducing a carve-out from EU Controlled Foreign Company (CFC) rules for groups within the scope of Pillar Two;further harmonizing the ATAD interest limitation rules, including by making certain currently optional relief provisions mandatory and introducing additional carve-outs;introducing a common minimum standard for R&D tax incentives;extending the Merger Directive to certain cross-border conversions; andamending the DRM with the aim of facilitating access to dispute resolution procedures and strengthening taxpayers’ procedural rights.KPMG member firms1 in the EU have submitted feedbackopens in a new tab on the Commission’s Tax Omnibus proposal. The submission builds on recommendations made by KPMG member firms in response to the Commission’s earlier call for evidence and provides comments on the specific measures included in the Tax Omnibus proposal.The proposal is currently being discussed by Member States in the Council, with a political commitment to reach agreement by the end of 2027. As amendments to EU direct tax legislation require unanimous agreement, the final scope and timing of the package will depend on the outcome of those negotiations.For more information on the Tax Omnibus proposal and KPMG’s earlier recommendations, please refer to Euro Tax Flash Issue 582 and Issue 577.

KPMG feedback

We welcome the ambition of the Tax Omnibus proposal and its focus on simplifying the EU direct tax framework, reducing compliance burdens and supporting the competitiveness of the EU internal market.In particular, we welcome the proposed removal of withholding tax barriers on intra-EU payments, the CFC carve-out for groups subject to Pillar Two, targeted changes to the ATAD interest limitation rules and the proposed common minimum standard for R&D tax incentives and we believe that they send the right signal to enhance the EU's attractiveness as a place to invest.In the submission, we acknowledge Member States’ concerns regarding the potential budgetary impact of certain measures but consider that the potential short-term revenue impact should be weighed against the longer-term benefits of reducing barriers to cross-border investment, lowering compliance costs and supporting the competitiveness of the EU internal market.As Council discussions progress, we encourage Member States to preserve the overall ambition of the Commission’s proposals and to ensure that additional anti-abuse safeguards or conditions do not significantly reduce the practical benefits of the proposed simplification measures.In our submission, we also highlight areas where further changes or clarification could help ensure that the proposals deliver meaningful simplification in practice. Key observations with respect to the different Tax Omnibus building blocks include:Withholding tax relief for intra-EU paymentsWe welcome the proposed removal of withholding taxes on qualifying intra-EU dividends, interest and royalties and the move to a common and simplified relief procedure based on self-assessment, which could reduce compliance costs and cash-flow constraints for businesses. We also welcome the proposed extension of the dividend withholding tax exemption to EU pension funds and suggest considering similar treatment for certain investment funds and other entities that are tax-exempt for genuine public-policy reasons. We consider that the current participation thresholds create an arbitrary distinction between economically comparable investments, rather than serve as an effective anti-abuse filter. Potential abuse can instead be addressed through existing anti-abuse rules and targeted ex-post controls.The submission therefore stresses that any notification, documentation, anti-abuse or ex-post review requirements should be clear and administrable and operate within appropriate deadlines. We also recommend greater clarity on the proposed safeguard for interest and royalty payments to recipients in zero-tax jurisdictions, including a common EU approach to identifying the jurisdictions concerned and clarification of its application where the income is effectively taxed elsewhere in the ownership chain.CFC rules and overlaps with Pillar TwoWe welcome the proposed carve-out from EU CFC rules for groups within the scope of Pillar Two as an important step towards reducing overlapping anti-avoidance rules and associated compliance obligations. We also suggest considering whether similar simplification could be extended to the ATAD anti-hybrid mismatch rules. The submission notes, however, that the proposed carve-out includes specific limitations for groups headquartered in jurisdictions operating a qualified Side-by-Side regime and calls for these provisions to be clarified to avoid uncertainty and differences in implementation across Member States. At the same time, we consider that the existing flexibility for Member States to apply either Model A or Model B under the ATAD CFC rules should be retained.GAARWith respect to the proposed extension of the ATAD General Anti-Abuse Rule (GAAR) to Pillar Two Top-up Taxes, we recommend taking into account the ongoing OECD work on Pillar Two integrity measures to ensure that the two sets of rules are compatible and do not overlap.ATAD interest limitation rulesWe support the proposed changes to the interest limitation rules, including making the 30 percent EBITDA threshold, the indexed EUR 3 million de minimis threshold, the group escape clause and the carry-forward of non-deductible interest mandatory across Member States. We also welcome the proposed additional carve-outs, including for qualifying third-party debt and significant reductions in EBITDA. However, the conditions attached to the third-party debt carve-out could limit its practical benefit, particularly where groups borrow externally through centralized treasury functions. We also suggest reconsidering the proposed removal of Alternative Investment Funds from the carve-out for financial undertakings.R&D tax incentivesWe welcome the proposed introduction of a common minimum standard for R&D tax incentives, while allowing Member States to maintain or introduce more favorable domestic incentives. We note, however, that the proposed allowance may provide limited benefit to loss-making businesses, including early-stage innovative companies, where domestic rules restrict the use of tax losses. We therefore suggest considering additional mechanisms, including the possibility of allowing losses generated by the R&D allowance to be surrendered in exchange for cash tax credits. We also recommend considering whether the EU State aid framework should be updated to facilitate incentives that qualify for favorable treatment under the Pillar Two Substance-based Tax Incentive Safe Harbour.Cross-border reorganizationsWe welcome the proposed alignment of the Merger Directive with developments in EU company law, including the extension of tax neutrality to cross-border conversions. We consider that further attention should be given to the treatment of carry-forward losses and other tax attributes, particularly where losses could remain trapped in the departure jurisdiction or be lost following a reorganization. The submission also calls for further guidance on divisions by separation and the interaction between cross-border conversions and EU exit taxation rules.Dispute resolution proceduresWe welcome the proposed clarifications to the scope of the Directive on Tax Dispute Resolution Mechanisms, including changes that would make it easier for taxpayers to access the procedures and reduce the risk of complaints being rejected on procedural grounds. We note, however, that taxpayers may continue to incur late-payment interest even where double taxation is ultimately eliminated and that differences between Member States in the treatment of penalties may affect access to the procedure. The submission also calls for greater clarity where a complaint is accepted by one Member State but rejected by another.

ETC Comment:

Following the release of the Tax Omnibus proposal end of June, Member States subsequently submitted initial questions and comments to the European Commission. In addition, several discussions covering the individual elements of the package have been held at Council level (in the so-called Antici Group composed of foreign affairs ambassadors with tax experts contributing to the discussion where appropriate).The public comments from Member States, dated July 27opens in a new tab and July 31opens in a new tab, indicate that several elements of the proposal remain under debate based on a number of concerns that can be grouped as follows:Sovereignty: Several Member States consider in their comments that parts of the package go beyond administrative simplification and amount to substantive harmonization of direct tax policy (e.g., through the proposed introduction of anti-derogation clause). This is particularly relevant in relation to ATAD, which was originally designed as a minimum standard and currently allows Member States to apply stricter domestic anti-avoidance rules.Budgetary concerns: According to the comments from some Member States, the proposed withholding tax changes, amendments to the interest limitation rules and the common R&D allowance could all have potentially significant budgetary effects. Some countries have therefore requested country-by-country impact assessments from the EC, or have commissioned local assessments, rather than relying only on EU-wide estimates of compliance savings and economic benefits.Tax avoidance concerns: According to some Member States’ comments, simplification should not weaken enforcement or existing anti-abuse protections. This concern arises, for example, in relation to the removal of ex-ante WHT relief controls, proposed new carve outs from the interest limitation rules, and the suggested exclusion of Pillar Two groups from the EU CFC rules.It will therefore be important for stakeholders to engage with the process to ensure the final rules are workable in practice and achieve their intended objectives without being diluted during the Council negotiations.This is similarly true for the public consultation on the Directive on Administrative Cooperation (DAC) recast proposal, which is being conducted by the EC in parallel and that closes on December 1, 2026 – see E-News Issue 237 for more details.

Should you have any queries, please do not hesitate to contact KPMG’s EU Tax Centre or, as appropriate, your local KPMG tax advisor.

Technology & InnovationIntelligence Delivered for the Real-Time WorldArticle • November 06, 2026Sonat BayatliGlobal Head of Network ManagementInvestor Services, CitiThe Challenge: Keeping Pace with Constant ChangeIn today's markets, the challenge is no longer access to information. It is identifying what matters, understanding its implications and acting with confidence. As decision-making windows continue to narrow, institutional investors must navigate a constant flow of macroeconomic events, geopolitical developments, regulatory change, market infrastructure updates and evolving tax regimes that can directly affect liquidity, collateral mobility and settlement activity.That's where Market Guide comes in.Market Guide, Citi Investor Services' flagship market intelligence platform, helps clients navigate the complexities of global custody and clearing through a single destination for trusted post-trade insights. As part of Citi's Custody+ strategy, the enhanced platform combines Citi's global market expertise with AI-powered capabilities to deliver timely, actionable intelligence across local market practices, settlement information, infrastructure guidance, regulatory developments and Citi service insights. With coverage across more than 100 custody markets globally, including 62 proprietary branches and access to approximately 99% of global market capitalization, Market Guide transforms Citi's global network into a centralized source of intelligence, helping clients assess change, manage risk and make informed decisions with greater confidence.A More Intelligent Way to Access and Use Market IntelligenceThe enhanced Market Guide platform combines a redesigned user experience with AI-powered search and summarization capabilities, making it easier for clients to discover, consume and act on critical market intelligence. Designed for increasingly always-on capital markets, the platform helps make trusted information more accessible and actionable, enabling clients to quickly identify relevant developments, assess potential impacts and make more informed decisions with confidence.Rather than navigating lengthy reports or searching across multiple sources, users can ask questions in natural language and receive concise, synthesized answers generated from Citi's verified market intelligence content. Each response includes source citations, providing transparency and traceability while helping users quickly understand the context and implications of market developments.Built within Citi's established risk, compliance and data governance framework, the platform's AI capabilities operate exclusively on trusted content, enabling clients to access information with confidence. At the same time, Market Guide is designed to integrate seamlessly into the way clients work. articles.title: View from the markets: Asia may not follow US rate hikes
articles.text:
FRONT OF MIND | ARTICLE – 3 min read
View from the markets: Asia may not follow US rate hikes

By
CHI LO 13.11.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article
US inflationary pressures remainAsia is differentExchange rate is paramount in AsiaThe bottom lines

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

By Chi Lo, Senior Market Strategist, Asia Pacific, Hong Kong

The forces keeping the US Federal Reserve in monetary tightening mode have not faded. Diesel and petrol prices remain high, artificial intelligence-driven inflation has not eased, and the labour market remains resilient. Housing market weakness and the recent wobble in AI optimism may make the Fed cautious, but core inflation is still skewed to the upside.

Asian central banks have typically followed the Fed’s rate increases. However, it may be different this time unless the Fed’s hikes cause significant exchange rate depreciation in the region.

US inflationary pressures remain

The underlying inflation dynamics in the US have not changed much since the Fed’s rate increase in September. Global energy prices have remained high and tight diesel markets have boosted diesel price inflation (see Exhibit 1). Diesel prices are pivotal to the pass-through to broader inflationary pressures due to the fuel’s widespread use in transport, manufacturing and farming.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh acknowledged recently that tighter financial conditions (due to the rise in bond yields) had helped the Fed to contain inflationary pressures. However, he also stressed that the Fed’s job was to ensure that sector-specific price shocks do not broaden out and that inflation expectations would not be unanchored. So, rising bond yields do not necessarily stand in the way of further rate hikes.

Asia is different

The Fed has already raised rates once in September. October’s stronger-than-expected consumer price index inflation has increased the markets’ conviction of another Fed rate hike in December. Headline inflation came in at 0.4% month-on-month versus the consensus forecast of 0.3% and core CPI was 0.3% versus consensus expectations of 0.2%.

The European Central Bank, the Bank of Japan, the Bank of England and the Bank of Canada have also hiked their rates since September. In Asia (excluding Japan), the picture is more diverse. While a couple of central banks have hiked rates, most have stood pat.

Recent monetary policy cycle experience shows that Asia has not always followed the Fed’s rate moves in lock-step or has followed them with a lag unless the Fed’s hikes triggered sharp exchange rate depreciation. Why is that?

Firstly, Asian central banks have a wider set of policy targets than the Fed. They do not follow the Fed if its moves are inconsistent with their own domestic policy needs. Both market experience and Bank for International Settlements research1 show that Asia’s regional central banks have ‘unwritten targets’ including the exchange rate, economic growth and bond yields.

These factors, in turn, affect domestic inflation. Furthermore, the regional authorities also target headline inflation alongside core inflation. All these are different from the Fed-style dual mandates that put core inflation and maximum employment on an equal footing.

Exchange rate is paramount in Asia

Among these policy targets, the exchange rate is of primary importance for Asian authorities. Fed rate hikes widen the interest-rate differential between Asia and the US and if exchange rates depreciate markedly, this could amplify the inflationary effects on the region’s economies and financial conditions. To contain that potentially greater impact, the regional central banks will follow the Fed or even react more strongly than the Fed’s original move.

However, other than Indonesia and the Philippines, most of Asia’s economies have large current account surpluses (see Exhibit 2) that provide strong support for the region’s exchange rates, thus lessening the pressure to follow the Fed’s rate hikes. The recent downward pressures on Asia’s exchange rates mostly reflect a risk-off sentiment arising from the speed and breadth of the global rates sell-off rather than poor fundamentals and wider interest-rate differentials.

Secondly, despite nine months of high oil prices, core inflation has remained close to, or even lower than, target in most Asian economies, with the notable exceptions of Vietnam and the Philippines (see Exhibit 3). Subsidies have so far helped Asia to contain oil price-induced inflation and the region’s central banks to stay put at low fiscal costs to their treasuries.

However, if the oil shock lasts longer, fiscal pressure will increase and eventually prompt Asian governments to let fuel prices adjust accordingly, unleashing inflationary pressures. This would, in turn, likely prompt regional rate hikes in the wake of those by the Fed.

The bottom lines

The macroeconomic backdrop suggests that Asia is far from being in a broad-based interest-rate hike cycle. Policy rates are currently being driven by the impact of rising oil prices on domestic inflation.

A hawkish Fed may lead to a potential tightening bias in Asia, but it will not likely prompt widespread rate hikes unless interest-rate differentials between Asia and the US result in large and persistent regional exchange-rate depreciation.

Data sources: CEIC, Trading Economics, as of 10 November 2026 (unless otherwise stated). Past performance should not be seen as a guide to future returns.

[1] The Expansionary Lower Bound: Contractionary Monetary Easing and the Trilemma, Bank for International Settlements, 2019.

articles.title: The AI Supply Chain Post Elections
articles.text:
The AI Supply Chain Post Elections

Tan Kai Xian, Will Denyer

Gavekal Research | 11 Nov 2026

The US midterm elections have strengthened political support for restrictions on data center construction. The question, now being debated within Gavekal and elsewhere, is whether these will merely slow the artificial intelligence investment boom or bring it to a halt. This piece explores both scenarios and their impacts on the AI supply chain—from semiconductor companies and data center operators to frontier AI labs.Federal legislation is not the concern. President Donald Trump has reiterated his support for the AI industry since the election and is therefore likely to veto any bills that undermine the boom. In fact, the next big change to federal legislation could be positive for AI capital spending. The current Congress appears to be moving toward passing permitting reform through the Bipartisan American Affordability And Jobs Act during the lame-duck session. If passed, this should shorten approval times for new power infrastructure projects and make existing infrastructure more efficient, removing one potential constraint on future data center growth (see Permitting Reform’s Big Chance).

articles.title: What Jensen Huang’s Exit Could Mean for Open-Weight AI
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Open-Weight AI Loses Its Best Advocate at the Worst Possible Time

Written by:

Alex Thorn
Head of Firmwide Research

Topics

AI

Regulation

research • November 13, 2026

Open-Weight AI Loses Its Best Advocate at the Worst Possible Time

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.WHAT HAPPENEDJensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO after admitting marital infidelity and following news reports he had multiple affairs, including one with a woman suspected by the U.S. government to be an asset of Chinese intelligence.Nvidia said Thursday that Huang, 63, stepped down as president, CEO and board member effective immediately, ending a 33-year run atop the company he co-founded in 1993. CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO while the board weighs internal and external successors, and former Synopsys chief Harvey C. Jones became Nvidia's first-ever chairman. The company gave no reason for the shake-up. The exit came four days after Huang told employees he had been unfaithful to his wife, and after the board opened a probe into whether he had been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort" while initially saying it retained confidence in him.The woman at the center of the story is Alice Huang (a.k.a. Huang Le, no relation), a Chinese citizen and former top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company. It was spun out of a Chinese gaming firm in 2023, shortly after Biden-era chip export controls tightened. Megaspeed became an official Nvidia cloud partner, buying Nvidia GPUs and renting the compute to Chinese firms including Alibaba. U.S. authorities have reportedly investigated Megaspeed since 2024 over suspected diversion of chips into China, and Singapore opened its own probe in October. The Information has reported, citing two people who know her, that Alice Huang helped arrange at least $7.5 billion of Nvidia chip shipments that moved roughly 240,000 restricted chips into China.The New York Times reported on Oct. 29 that U.S. intelligence, surveilling Alice Huang during the Megaspeed investigation, concluded she had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) and was passing information to Beijing, and that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Her alleged objectives were to gather intelligence on Nvidia's plans and on Huang's lobbying of the Trump administration to loosen export controls, and potentially to push him to advocate for selling Nvidia's most advanced chips into China. Officials reportedly did not believe Huang knew about her alleged role, and he reportedly never received a defensive briefing. On Nov. 6, the Financial Times reported that a U.S. intelligence memo, circulated among senior officials before President Trump's May trip to Beijing, described Jensen's relationship with Alice as romantic. Nvidia has said it does not share classified information with customers, Beijing has called the allegations smears, and no public reporting shows Jensen Huang knowingly passed anything along. The chairs of the House China, Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees have asked him to testify in a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18.The second shoe dropped Wednesday night. The Times reported, citing video evidence its reporters had heard descriptions of from unnamed sources but not seen, that Huang also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care and a subordinate. Nvidia's code of conduct cites personal relationships as a conflict of interest, and the board met that night to discuss whether to oust him. Hours after Thursday's resignation announcement, Reuters reported a third relationship, with another Nvidia employee it did not name, citing two unnamed sources (neither Huang nor the employee has confirmed it). Shareholders have already filed a potential class action alleging Nvidia failed to disclose the relationship, and the company says it will still report quarterly results on Nov. 17 as scheduled.Nvidia shares fell as much as 14.4% at Thursday's open, to $148.80 from Wednesday's $173.73 close, the stock's steepest intraday drop since the DeepSeek selloff of January 2025. Buyers stepped in quickly, and by midday the stock had pared losses to roughly 5%, around $165. That still leaves Nvidia more than 30% below its October all-time high, and the Wall Street Journal estimated the slide has erased close to $750 billion in market value since the scandal broke. Bernstein halved its price target from $400 to $200, and Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at the brokerage, noted that an affair with a direct report made it far harder for the board to keep Huang in place.The broader market wobbled but held. Nvidia is roughly 6% of the S&P 500, and both the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite opened lower as the S&P tech sector fell 1.3%. By midday both had turned modestly positive, helped by rallies in AMD and Broadcom that picked up the slack from Nvidia, along with strength in energy as oil rose. Investors appear to be treating this episode as a Nvidia governance shock rather than a referendum on AI demand, at least until the company reports results on Nov. 17.OUR TAKEThe speed at which this story unfolded was striking. The FT published its memo report on Friday, Nov. 6. By Sunday, Huang had admitted infidelity and the board had opened a probe while publicly backing him. By Thursday morning, the founder who ran Nvidia for 33 years and built it into one of the world's most valuable companies was gone, with no named successor. Founder-CEOs of that stature have historically been close to untouchable. Notably, the intelligence concern had reportedly been known to senior U.S. officials for about a year without consequence. What likely broke the board's posture was the Powell report: a relationship with a direct report is a plain code-of-conduct breach, and since similar indiscretions by Intel's Brian Krzanich in 2018 and McDonald's Steve Easterbrook in 2019, boards have treated it as disqualifying regardless of stature. Layer on a securities class action, a Congressional summons and a national-security overlay, and it’s understandable that the board's tolerance collapsed in roughly 48 hours.In the longer run, we are watching for potential consequences for open-weight AI. Huang was the most important corporate champion of open models in the U.S., and he backed it with the balance sheet: a five-year, $26 billion commitment to open-weight model development disclosed in an SEC filing; the Nemotron family, including a 550-billion-parameter open-weight Ultra model; a coalition of eight labs building frontier open models; stakes in Reflection AI and Thinking Machines; and a pending $12.9 billion acquisition of Hugging Face, the default distribution layer for open models. He also led a July open letter from about 25 companies urging Washington not to broadly restrict open-weight models, many of which are Chinese. With Meta retreating from fully open releases, Nvidia had become the primary U.S. counterweight to the Chinese labs that now lead in open weights.Founder priorities rarely survive leadership transitions intact, and an interim CEO coming from the CFO seat, a stock down more than 30% from its high and a board in damage-control mode make discretionary spending a natural target. Multibillion-dollar open-model programs and a Hugging Face deal that has not closed (it is targeted for the first half of 2027, and the DOJ has begun asking questions) are the type of line items that could come under review. The long-term viability of the open-weight movement in the U.S. is also at risk. The open-weight coalition just lost its best-resourced advocate in Washington at the worst possible moment, and the manner of his exit hands restrictionists a narrative: the executive most associated with both loosening China chip controls and defending open weights is now tied to an alleged asset of the Ministry of State Security. The two issues are distinct on the merits, but we expect them to become conflated, starting with the Nov. 18 Congressional briefing.To be fair, Nvidia's incentive to support open weights does not leave with Huang. Every downloaded model is a GPU workload, and spreading AI beyond a handful of frontier labs that are designing their own silicon is core to Nvidia's moat. Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue has vowed to keep fighting for open source, and the open-weight coalition includes Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Palantir. Our base case is erosion rather than reversal, but erosion matters. For crypto, open weights are the substrate for decentralized and privacy-preserving AI, local inference, and permissionless agents. A thinner U.S. open-weight frontier would leave builders more dependent on closed APIs, or on Chinese models that face growing political and regulatory risk in the U.S. We will be watching whether Kress addresses Nemotron and Hugging Face on the Nov. 17 earnings call, whether the Hugging Face timeline holds, and how hard Capitol Hill leans on the open-weight question in its China hearings.

articles.title: Global Annual Review 2026 | PwC
articles.text:
15 min read

Transform Today, Build Tomorrow

Global Annual Review 2026

Publication

19 October 2026

Chairman’s letter

Chairman’s letterMohamed Kande, Global Chairman

The world is changing quickly, reshaping how businesses compete, how people work, and where new opportunities for growth will come from. At PwC, we are changing with it, while staying focused on what matters most: helping our clients navigate what is happening today and prepare for what comes next.

The environment our clients operate in is shifting rapidly, and the pace of change is not going to slow. AI has moved beyond experimentation. The harder question now is how it can create new sources of value and growth. Geopolitical shifts are reshaping investment decisions. And supply chains continue to adjust to shifts in trade flows, costs, consumer demand, energy markets, and physical risks.These issues can appear separate. They are not.Technology choices affect energy demand. Geopolitics influences supply chains and capital flows. AI changes how work gets done and what skills people need. A decision in one part of the economy creates consequences across several others.For our clients, this makes transformation more complex, but also more urgent. And it is changing what they need from PwC and how we work together to deliver it.

Transformation starts with our people. As technology takes on more routine tasks, our people are learning new skills, expanding what they can do, and finding new ways to apply their expertise.Knowing how to use AI effectively is now essential. More than 330,000 people have taken part in AI training at PwC.AI skills alone are not enough. As AI becomes more capable, distinctly human skills become even more important: judgment, creativity, curiosity, adaptability, leadership, and the ability to connect insight across disciplines. Our AI Jobs Barometer found that roles where AI automates routine tasks and increases the emphasis on human-intensive work are growing twice as fast. These findings reinforce why we are investing at scale to help our people thrive in an AI-enabled world.Our AI-powered learning platform gives our people more personalized opportunities to learn and grow, whether that means deepening their industry expertise, understanding geopolitical shifts, or strengthening their leadership skills. We are also using technology and data to better understand the skills across our network and where we need to invest for the future.The aim is not simply to do yesterday’s work faster. It is to expand what our people can contribute.

As we invest in the skills of our people, we are strengthening our technology and capabilities. This year, we invested US$3 billion to expand these capabilities, with a particular focus on AI and technology.Our strategic alliances bring together PwC’s industry and business expertise with leading technology capabilities to help clients turn new ideas into results. This year, we were ranked as a leader across seven premier AI industry analyst reports.We are working in a more connected and multidisciplinary way across our network of firms with over 360,000 professionals. This means bringing together people with different capabilities and perspectives, across businesses and borders, around the issues our clients are trying to solve.We are investing in new ways of delivering our work and value to our clients. This includes our tax data aggregation and project management platform; our AI-native assurance platform; and PwC One, our AI-enabled platform bringing together PwC’s knowledge, standards, and expertise across lines of service.

Our financial results show the strength and resilience of our business. We achieved robust growth in the face of geopolitical and economic uncertainty. PwC firms reported aggregate gross revenues of US$60.2 billion for the fiscal year ended 30 June 2026, representing growth of 5.7% in US dollars and 3.5% in local currency.Underpinning this performance is something that does not change: our commitment to quality and to earning the trust of our clients and stakeholders. That means delivering high-quality work for our clients, understanding the expectations of those we serve, and maintaining a robust approach to ethics and governance.

The year ahead is unlikely to offer simple answers. But what I see and hear from leaders around the world gives me reason for confidence.Companies are adapting. They are making choices amid uncertainty and finding ways to keep moving forward. Resilience is not about knowing what comes next. It is about having the ability to respond when change arrives.We will keep listening to our clients, evolving with their needs, and protecting the trust that gives our work its value. We will keep investing in the development of our people, using AI to expand what they can do, and evolving how they respond to what the market demands. We will continue to connect our capabilities across disciplines and borders.To our clients, thank you for the trust you place in PwC.To our people across the PwC network, thank you for the care and commitment you bring to your work and to one another.Transforming today and building tomorrow is ultimately about the choices we make now: how we invest, how we work together, and how we prepare for what comes next. Those choices will shape the PwC we build together.Mohamed Kande

Note to readers: In this Global Annual Review, the terms PricewaterhouseCoopers, PwC, our, we, and us are used to refer to the network of member firms of PricewaterhouseCoopers International Limited, or, as the context requires, to one or more PwC member firms. PricewaterhouseCoopers International Limited and its member firms collectively comprise the PwC network.Unless otherwise noted, all snapshot data reflects the position on the final day of the financial year: 30 June 2026.

PwC at a glance

PwC at a glance

Financial performance

Financial performance

For the 12 months ending 30 June 2026, PwC firms around the world recorded gross revenues of US$60.2 billion, an increase of 5.7% in US dollars and 3.5% in local currency. This is a robust performance in a complex operating environment often characterised by geopolitical and economic uncertainty. The equivalent growth figures for the previous year are 2.9% and 2.7%.PwC firms invested US$3 billion across the network to expand capabilities in key areas, particularly AI and technology. This year saw the initial roll-out of PwC One, our AI-enabled platform that brings together PwC’s knowledge, standards, and expertise. At the same time, firms continued to invest in our AI-native assurance platform, our tax data aggregation and project management platform, and other agentic and data-driven delivery models. These technology investments complement ongoing investment in the skills of PwC people, including the ongoing roll-out of our AI-powered learning platform.

Revenue by regionRevenue increased[1] by 4.6% across the Americas to US$26.8 billion, with particularly strong revenue growth in countries including the US and Brazil.Revenue increased by 0.7% in Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA) to US$23.9 billion, despite challenging operating environments in the region, with particularly strong growth in countries including Germany, Greece, and Spain.In Asia Pacific, revenue increased by 7.7% to US$9.4 billion, with particularly strong growth in countries including India, Japan, and South Korea.

[1] References to growth rates refer to growth in local currency terms unless otherwise stated.

Revenue by line of service Revenue grew in all our lines of service.

Important note on revenue growth by line of service During the year, within our member firms there were a number of business sales and changes in business structures and categories which involved the movement of revenue between our lines of service. In the table above, no adjustments have been made to the FY25 comparative numbers to reflect these changes in FY26. If adjustments are made to the FY25 comparative numbers to ensure a “like for like” comparison of revenues, the growth rates for each line of service in FY26 would be as follows:

Revenues from our Advisory operations grew by 4.2% to US$25.8 billion or 3.0% when adjusted for changes in business structures. We entered the fiscal year with strong momentum, although growth moderated towards year-end as geopolitical and economic uncertainty affected client investment and demand in several key markets.PwC’s strength is grounded in the trust we build with clients and our firms’ ability to bring together deep industry knowledge and a broad range of multidisciplinary capabilities across strategy, consulting, managed services, deals, and risk. We continued to strengthen how these capabilities connect across markets and territories, in ways that help clients address increasingly complex challenges.PwC firms continued to invest in strategic, market-driven alliances that expand capabilities and accelerate sector-led and AI-enabled innovation. Wins through the PwC alliance ecosystem grew strongly in FY26, reinforcing the important role these relationships play in bringing differentiated capabilities to clients and driving growth across our business.We are redefining Managed Services, moving past traditional outsourcing to deliver what clients actually need: continuous transformation and measurable business outcomes. PwC’s Managed Services 2.0 unites our deep multidisciplinary strength across industries, domains, risk, regulatory, tax, and cybersecurity, and powers it with advanced AI from the world’s leading technology alliance partners. The result sets a new standard for the market: sharper operational efficiency, relentless innovation, and lasting business value.

Revenues from member firm assurance practices grew by 0.7% to US$20.5 billion without adjusting for changes in business structures, or 2.6% adjusting for changes in business structures. Our work remains grounded in quality and trust. Growth is accelerating particularly rapidly across new areas of assurance, including trust and transformation services and digital and AI capabilities. Across Assurance, our services, including audit, risk, capital markets, and accounting advisory offerings, enable us to support clients ranging from the world’s largest organisations to emerging innovators, all with the same commitment to building trust in society. Our audit businesses continue to grow, supported by talent development, investments in technology, and a sustained focus on quality.In FY26, PwC firms continued to advance their collective US$1 billion investment in the next generation audit programme, driving a fundamental transformation in how PwC delivers audits across technology, methodology, processes, and ways of working. At the heart of this transformation is our AI-native assurance platform and its ecosystem of integrated digital tools, built from the ground up with AI at their core, integrating human judgement, technology, and AI to deliver a more digitised and seamless assurance experience for our clients. This completed its internal development phase in FY26, with the first clients onboarded for the initial use cases in July 2026.

Revenues from our Tax and Legal Services businesses were up by 6.5% to US$13.8 billion or 6.3% when adjusted for changes in business structures, reflecting continued demand for technology-enabled tax, legal, and workforce solutions as clients responded to an increasingly complex business and regulatory environment.Demand was particularly strong in areas impacted by increasing regulatory and reporting complexity, including Pillar Two, multiple other areas of cross-border tax, and around our clients’ tax operating models. This reflected client organisations’ work to manage cross-border reporting requirements, global trade developments, and evolving tax regulations while maintaining operational efficiency and governance. Importantly, we are seeing increased recognition and related demand around broad areas of business decision-making where tax elements impact operational and/or financial value generation.To help clients meet these challenges, we continued to expand technology-enabled capabilities, including client data aggregation and project management platforms, AI-enabled tax research agents, and data-driven delivery models. Our strong results reflect our continued focus on helping organisations address and enhance their tax compliance, improve governance, generate deeper insights, and create greater value from their tax and legal functions.

Governance, quality, and risk

Governance, quality, and risk

PwC is a global network of separate firms, delivering assurance, advisory, tax and legal services in 136 countries. We combine deep local expertise with global capability to help clients create and protect value.PwC firms operating under the PwC brand are referred to as the PwC network, which includes, and is coordinated by, PricewaterhouseCoopers International Limited (PwCIL), a private company limited by guarantee in England and Wales.The firms in our network are committed to working together to provide quality services on a global scale to international and local clients, while remaining local businesses with deep knowledge of local laws, regulations, and standards.As members of the PwC network, PwC firms benefit from access to network methodologies, technologies, and resources. PwC firms agree to abide by certain common policies and standards, to further the network’s vision and values, and to conduct themselves in a way that protects the reputation of the PwC network.PwCIL’s purpose in the PwC network is to facilitate coordination between PwC firms. Focusing on key areas such as strategy, brand, and risk and quality, the Network Leadership Team and Global Board of PwCIL develop and implement policies and initiatives to achieve a common and coordinated approach among individual firms where appropriate. PwCIL is not an audit firm and does not provide services to clients or practice public accountancy.Our legal structure and the relationship between PwCIL and its member firms can be found here.

Strong governance enables us to uphold our commitment to integrity, build trust with our stakeholders, and deliver value for our clients.Our Network Leadership Team (NLT) develops the overall strategy for the PwC network and the standards to which firms agree to adhere. PwCIL’s Global Board is responsible for the governance of PwCIL and the PwC network. Among other things, the Global Board approves strategy, oversees strategy activation by the NLT, and approves network standards. The standards are designed to support consistently high performance across the PwC network. The composition and role of the NLT and the Global Board are described on our governance structures page, available here. During the last financial year, two additional external directors were appointed to the Global Board, taking the total to three. Each PwC firm is required to have a separate local governance body, independent from management, to provide effective and continuing oversight of the firm's leadership, strategy, and operations.

At PwC, robust risk management is fundamental to sustaining the trust and confidence of our clients, regulators, and other stakeholders. Our network Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) programme draws on a wide range of network information to develop a connected and forward-looking view of the risks facing the PwC network. This supports earlier identification of changing risk exposures and more informed decisions about where network-wide attention and action are most needed.Our governance and oversight structure supports firms’ risk awareness, decision-making, and accountability across the network:Global Board of PricewaterhouseCoopers International Limited (PwCIL): Approves the network’s ERM approach and oversees the Priority Network Risks identified under it.Risk Committee: The Global Board Risk Committee provides continuing oversight of risk and quality across the network, including the operation of the ERM framework and compliance with network standards, policies, and legal and regulatory requirements.Network Leadership Team: Develops the network’s strategy and sets the standards that PwC firms agree to adhere to, including matters related to ERM and Priority Network Risks.We identify Priority Network Risks (PNRs) from the broader network risk landscape. PNRs are the risks requiring the greatest network-wide focus at a point in time because of their potential impact, interconnected nature, or ability to escalate across PwC firms. They provide a common focus for understanding how significant risks may develop and for coordinating appropriate responses across the network.

The PwC Global Code of Conduct (the Code) and PwC purpose and values describe the values and behaviours that guide how we conduct ourselves. We are all responsible for maintaining high standards of ethical behaviour and acting with integrity to maintain the trust that our clients, communities, and people place in us.The Code reinforces the importance of how we conduct business within professional standards, laws, and regulations.The Code has five major sections:Speaking up. We prioritise speaking up as foundational to our ethical culture. It enables our people, clients, and third parties to feel comfortable and safe raising a question or concern. Speaking up when something doesn’t seem right shows our integrity and courage to do the right thing. We explore when and how to express concerns and report situations that don’t seem right. There are many channels of reporting, including a confidential PwC Ethics Helpline within each PwC firm. Reports are investigated in an appropriate, timely, and objective manner, and we have a strict non-retaliation policy.We build trust in how we do business. We define what’s expected of us as professionals and uphold our reputation by maintaining professional standards, adhering to laws and regulations, and fulfilling ethical obligations—all while delivering high-quality, innovative work.We build trust in how we use information. We respect the privacy and confidentiality of information of our clients, our people, and others we do business with. We protect personal and confidential information in all forms, and we don’t misuse it. We exercise good judgement on social media.We build trust in our communities. We focus on how we present ourselves to the world and markets we operate in. We aim to earn the trust of our stakeholders by demonstrating care, openness, and honesty, and by maintaining a strong focus on ethics and quality.We build trust with each other. Trust is essential to working effectively with our colleagues and serving our clients. It begins with each of us treating each other with care, courtesy, dignity, fairness, and respect.The Code and our ethical framework are based on the fundamental principles set out by the International Ethics Standards Board for Accountants (IESBA).PwC firms must comply with our network standards, which cover areas related to ethics and compliance, including business conduct, independence, anti-money laundering, antitrust and fair competition, anti-corruption, information protection, sanctions laws, and insider trading.Partners and staff are required to complete mandatory training that covers the ethics and compliance standards as part of new hire training when they join their local firm and on an annual basis thereafter. They must also submit an annual compliance confirmation covering applicable network and territory policies, regulations, and compliance requirements.In order to monitor and reinforce our ethics and compliance requirements, each PwC firm has an accountability framework that sets out consequences for behaviour that is inconsistent with our policies and procedures.

PwC member firms must comply with the PwC Global Independence Policy, which aligns with the IESBA International Independence Standards and additional jurisdictional requirements, such as the SEC, PCAOB, and EU Audit Regulation requirements. The policy sets minimum requirements, including prohibitions, for maintaining independence from assurance clients, addressing the interests and relationships of PwC firms and their partners and staff, including financial interests and arrangements, employment, the provision of services, use of technology, and business relationships with assurance clients.In accordance with Global Independence Policy, PwC firms identify and evaluate threats to independence arising from services and relationships with assurance clients. Where threats to independence cannot be addressed through designing and implementing safeguards that either eliminate the threat or reduce it to an acceptable level, firms must decline the relationship or services giving rise to the threat. Such threats include self-interest such as acting in a management capacity or having business relationships with shared risks and rewards, acting as an advocate for an audit or assurance client, or providing assurance over the results of other services the PwC firm has provided.Local regulation may add further restrictions, which vary by country and may include additional prohibition of certain services or caps on the revenue a PwC firm may earn from them as a proportion of audit fees. Where local requirements include additional restrictions, those are applied.As a member of the PwC network, each PwC firm has access to systems and tools that support firms, and their partners and staff, in executing and complying with our independence policies and procedures.PwC firms implement Independence Accountability Requirements and Guidelines, which put independence standards into practice at the level of the individual partner or staff member—translating the firm’s policy on financial interests, employment, service provision, and business relationships into personal compliance obligations.

Delivering quality work is the foundation of trust in the network and forms the basis of our reputation.Quality is a benchmark by which we measure our own performance. Our focus on quality influences every aspect of our work—from the way we engage with clients to the solutions we develop. This includes how we develop, deploy, and use AI. Our Network AI Policy establishes shared principles for responsible AI, including human accountability and review, testing and validation, and appropriate governance to support quality, reliability, and responsible innovation.PwC invests, and monitors performance in, areas critical to delivering quality, including:GovernanceOrganisational culture and accountabilityEthics, integrity, and objectivity/independenceReporting and compliance with both external requirements and internal policiesCertified and experienced professionalsFrameworks for quality managementControls, policies, processes, and monitoringTechnologiesLeaders throughout the PwC network are expected to reinforce PwC's focus on quality through setting the right tone at the top, communicating expectations to PwC people, proactively investing in and monitoring quality, learning from any mistakes, and holding themselves and PwC people accountable as appropriate.PwC’s values and the behaviours we expect of our people—in particular our commitment to quality and integrity—set clear expectations for how people carry out their work. By embedding these values into leadership, culture, and everyday conduct, PwC aims to consistently deliver quality for clients and stakeholders.The section that follows sets out how each line of service delivers quality.

To find out more about our approach to quality within each line of service, see Approach to quality by line of service.

articles.title: China's undervalued currency is driving its trade surplus higher
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

China's undervalued currency is driving its trade surplus higher

Joseph E. Gagnon (PIIE) and

Nishtha Agrawal (PIIE)

Date
November 9, 2026 9:00 AM

Photo Credit: Sipa via Reuters/CFOTO

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
As Europe prepares to discuss exchange rates(link is external) with China (while the United States is curiously silent), Chinese officials publicly downplay(link is external) any connection between China's currency and its trade surplus. This is a repeat of Chinese arguments back in 2006–07, the last time China's currency was weak and its trade surplus on the rise. The data reject the Chinese position, both then and now. China's currency is undervalued by around 20 percent. Relative to the size of the world economy, China's trade surplus already exceeds the value reached during the "China Shock" of the 2000s, and it continues to rise, grabbing sales from manufacturers outside China and contributing to rising international tensions.
To get sustainable growth both in China and the rest of the world, China needs to consume a lot more of the goods and services it produces and more goods and services from abroad. That requires major domestic reforms, including to the social safety net, as well as making it easier for foreign firms to serve the Chinese market. It will also require a substantial appreciation of China's currency to level the playing field between Chinese and foreign producers. Despite some liberalization of China's foreign exchange market over the past 20 years, the government maintains multiple levers of control and any appreciation would require the active support of policymakers, explaining why European policymakers are keen to discuss the exchange rate with their Chinese counterparts.
In assessing the valuation of China's currency, it is important to control for inflation in China and in the rest of the world by using a real effective exchange rate (REER).[1] China's nominal exchange rate in US dollars has not changed much lately, but most of its trading partners had a burst of inflation, whereas China has been struggling with deflation. The result is a sharp decline in the REER since 2022, as shown in figure 1. This decline is especially significant when set against the trend increase in the REER over the past 30 years because of faster productivity growth in China than elsewhere, shown as the trend line (figure 1).[2]
In 2026, the REER is estimated to be about 8 percent below trend. But China's currency is undervalued by more than 8 percent because the trend value of the REER is historically associated with large trade surpluses, and thus the trend itself is undervalued. In order to gauge the true undervaluation, we need to measure how much the REER would have to rise to eliminate China's trade surplus.

Before we take that measurement, we must grapple with the rapid rise of nonmonetary gold imports in recent years. Although these imports are included as a negative in the trade balance (current account),[3] they are primarily used as a financial asset and arguably should be classified with the financial account. (Monetary gold is included as a reserve asset in the financial account.) The spread between the lines in figure 2 shows that net nonmonetary gold imports are on track to reach a record 1.0 percent of China's GDP in 2026.

The following simple equation explains 88 percent of the movements in China's current account balance excluding gold (CABXG, in percent of GDP) over the past 32 years. OPEN is the openness to trade of China's economy, defined as the sum of exports and imports of goods and services divided by GDP. REERGAP is the ratio of China's REER to its trend level. To allow for a lag in the effects of exchange rate changes, the regression uses the average of the 2-year and 3-year lagged values of REERGAP. The equation implies that movements in REERGAP have a larger effect on CABXG when trade is a larger share of China's economy. RELGDPGAP is the share of China's GDP in world GDP on a purchasing power parity (PPP)adjusted basis divided by its trend level.[4] Fluctuations in RELGDPGAP reflect different stages of the business cycle in China and the rest of the world. A high value of RELGDPGAP means activity is relatively stronger in China, pulling in imports and pushing down CABXG. The coefficients are all highly significant, both economically and statistically. (Coefficient standard errors are shown in parentheses.)
CABXG(t)=2.8(0.1)−62.9(5.0)∗OPEN(t)∗log(REERGAP(t−2,t−3))−57.9(7.4)∗log(RELGDPGAP(t))R2=0.88Observations=321994–2025
This equation can be used to estimate what sustained level of REERGAP is required to set CABXG=0.[5] We note that OPEN=0.38 in 2025 and assume it remains at that level in 2026. We set log(RELGDPGAP)=0.0 because we want to measure the equilibrium value of REER.[6] Under these assumptions, the value of log(REERGAP) that sets CABXG=0 is 0.12. Given that log(REERGAP) in 2026 is estimated to be -0.08, the total undervaluation is thus around 20 percent.[7] This assessment is in accord with that of the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) 2026 External Sector Report(link is external), which finds that China's REER was undervalued by 21 percent in 2025. Other economists also find a significant undervaluation, including Brad Setser(link is external) and economists at Goldman Sachs(link is external).
This analysis is similar in spirit to the longstanding work by our former PIIE colleagues William R. Cline and John Williamson on fundamental equilibrium exchange rates. Applying their framework to China's estimated 2026 CABXG and assuming a target CABXG of 0 yields an estimated undervaluation of roughly 20 percent.[8]
As important as currency appreciation is for rebalancing between China and the rest of the world, it is not a silver bullet. Policies to boost consumption inside China are an essential element for strong and balanced future growth.
Notes
1. "Real" means inflation adjusted. "Effective" means an average across trading partners.
2. Fast-growing economies typically have rising REERs. The trend growth rate of the REER is around 1 percent in the 1990s, rising to 1.5 percent in the 2000s and then falling to 0.5 percent after 2020 as China's growth slowed relative to growth in the rest of the world.
3. This post focuses on the current account, which is the broadest measure of the trade balance.
4. The trend is based on a Hodrick-Prescott filter with a smoothing parameter of 100 over the period 1990–2030, using IMF projections for values in 2026–30. Similar results are obtained using a centered 11-year moving average. Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook October 2026 and authors' calculations.
5. We believe 0 is a reasonable benchmark for China. As a fast-growing developing economy, it might be expected to have a trade deficit. But its rapidly aging population pushes up saving and thus the trade balance. The IMF 2026 External Sector Report sets a norm of 0.6 percent of GDP, but this is distorted upward by China's excessive official reserves, an issue that IMF staff plan to address in the next Report.
6. RELGDPGAP was reportedly very close to equilibrium in 2025. But there are strong reasons to doubt that measurement(link is external) given the collapsing property prices and substantial undershooting of China's inflation target since 2023. If the true value of RELGDPGAP is deeply negative, that would be another factor pushing up China's trade surplus. The goods trade surplus in January–September 2026 came in notably higher than expected(link is external) (link accessed on October 31, 2026), suggesting that the IMF projection for 2026 is likely to be too low.
7. The value of log(REERGAP) that sets CABXG=0 is robust to alternative specifications. We estimated eight versions of the equation based on the following assumptions: (1) the average of one-year and two-year lags or the average of two-year and three-year lags of REERGAP; (2) including or excluding the lagged value of CABXG; and (3) including or excluding OPEN. In each case, the equilibrium value of log(REERGAP) lies between 0.11 and 0.14.
8. We thank Bill Cline for providing us with this result from his model.

articles.title: Debt sustainability and the range of multiple equilibria
articles.text:
Publication Type
Working Papers

Debt sustainability and the range of multiple equilibria

Olivier Blanchard (PIIE), Gonzalo Huertas (International Monetary Fund; former PIIE) and Pedro Martínez-Bruera (International Monetary Fund)

Working Paper 26-17

November 2026

Photo Credit: IMAGO/Westlight via Reuters

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
The authors characterize the size of the range of multiple equilibria in sovereign debt markets. They show that the nature of the equilibrium depends crucially on the degree of uncertainty, which they formalize first as uncertainty about primary balances and later as uncertainty about the fiscal feedback rule. For low uncertainty, the range can be large, but it becomes smaller as uncertainty becomes larger. If uncertainty is large enough, the multiplicity disappears. The interest rate is then unique and becomes a continuous function of the debt level. Interpreting the source of an increase in the interest rate in actual situations is difficult and complicates the use of intervention by central banks.
