The content focuses exclusively on the functional, technological, and/or governance aspects of the protocol and/or applicable digital asset and should not be interpreted as expressing a view on the value, performance, or investment merits of any one or more digital assets. You are expressly advised to consult with qualified legal counsel and/or financial advisor(s0 before acting on any of the information contained in this Case Study and you are solely responsible for evaluating the merits and risks associated with using any information contained herein.
Throughout the preparation and drafting of this Case Study Consulting maintained full independence and editorial control and had no obligation to adopt any findings, conclusions, or interpretations inconsistent with its independent analysis. Because this Case Study is intended to be public-facing, Consulting maintains a policy under which Consulting reserves the right to release the Case Study into the public domain first. This policy has been adopted as a safeguard to ensure that the contents of the Case Study are intact and unadulterated at the time of publication. Consulting places paramount importance on the integrity of its work and has a strict prohibition on unauthorized modifications to the content of its work product by clients; however, modifications are permitted, upon mutual consent, to correct factual inaccuracies. This Case Study is based on information provided by the Client, consequently Consulting makes no representations regarding the accuracy, adequacy, completeness, or timeliness of its contents.
Without limiting the foregoing, Delphi Research, and its affiliates may, from time to time, have investments, or hold interest, in digital assets or protocols referenced in this Case Study.
Introduction
Perpetual futures have reached escape velocity and are now the primary way traders express their views on assets. Perps are easy to understand, offer 24/7 exposure without expiry, and allow traders to access a wide range of leverage. But for all their flexibility, the exposure you get from them remains linear. A trader holding one BTC contract only gains or loses the same dollar amount for each dollar move in BTC.
This leaves no room for outsized, non-linear payoffs, like a 0DTE option 10x’ing from a 2% move, or a 5x from a short-dated binary option.
For a trader who expects BTC to go much higher, the default answer is to increase the size of the long. That raises the potential payoff but also the exposure from the moment the trade opens. The position doesn’t become more sensitive as the rally develops unless the trader actively adds to it. And adding leverage inevitably brings liquidation closer if the market moves against them first.
A better way to express this view on the market is upside convexity. With a convex long position, exposure to BTC increases as its price rises, allowing gains to accelerate as the move continues. If BTC falls, the position’s sensitivity decreases, so each additional dollar decline has a smaller effect. More upside, less downside. Anyone who has traded options will recognize the appeal of a payoff that changes as the underlying moves.
The growth of the options markets shows how much demand for convexity exists. In 2017, traders bought and sold roughly 4.2 billion U.S. options contracts. That same year, Robinhood introduced commission-free options trading, simplifying the instrument and opening the door to a much wider group of traders. By 2025, annual volume had more than tripled to over 15 billion contracts.
Retail has played a huge part in that growth. Robinhood customers alone traded 905 million options contracts in Q3 ‘26, generating $399 million in options transaction revenue. Citadel also reported that retail investors traded an average of roughly $6.8 billion in options premium per day through its platform in June 2026, 65% above its 2025 average.

Traders use options for all sorts of reasons, from protecting existing positions to making highly speculative bets. The unwavering growth is a case in point of people wanting more control over their exposure than a linear long or short provides.
You see a similar appetite for outsized payoffs in prediction markets. In a study of resolved Polymarket markets, roughly 18% of purchases were of contracts priced below 10¢, with traders spending about $274 million on them. Buying a contract at 10¢ gives a trader a potential 10x payout if the outcome resolves in their favor, while limiting the upfront cost. People are chasing convexity.
But prediction markets are all built around a specific outcome. A trader betting that BTC will exceed a certain price by a set date receives the same payout at resolution whether BTC barely clears that level or rallies far beyond it. If the condition isn’t met, the contract expires worthless, even if BTC rose substantially along the way.
Traditional options come with their own trade-offs. A BTC call gives a trader convex exposure, but they must choose a strike and expiry, pay a premium, and find liquidity in that particular contract. If the rally takes longer than expected, the call can expire worthless even if BTC moves in the right direction.
Power Perps are Paragon’s new product bringing the convexity of options right into the simplicity of a perpetual future. Instead of tracking the underlying asset’s price directly, Power Perps reference an index based on that price raised to a power, such as squared or cubed.
For the trader expecting a large rally, Power Perps let their position gain exposure as the underlying rises or shed exposure as it falls, without choosing a strike or expiry. Compared with a linear long that starts with the same exposure, that means more upside if the asset rises and a smaller price loss if it falls.
They can hold the position through a familiar perp for as long as they want, and they don’t need to add leverage to introduce convexity. Funding still affects the cost of holding the trade, but traders now have a way to access that exposure alongside the spot and perp markets they already use.

Paragon is a market deployer on Hyperliquid, offering perps tracking assets ranging from individual stocks to rates and crypto. Its Power Perps are launched via HIP-3, Hyperliquid’s framework for third-party teams to launch their own perps.
A deployer chooses what its markets track and is responsible for the contract specifications, price feeds, and settings (such as leverage limits). The markets then use Hyperliquid’s trading infrastructure, including its order books and margin system. In Paragon’s case, that same framework gives the team room to introduce a market based on squared or cubed exposure.
The First Time Around
This idea of trading squared exposure through a perpetual isn’t entirely new. Many natives may remember when Opyn introduced Squeeth in 2022, giving traders ETH-squared exposure through a token called oSQTH. Users could buy the token on Uniswap to go long, while traders looking to take the other side could deposit collateral, mint oSQTH, and sell it.

Squeeth became a building block for other products. Opyn’s “Crab” strategy combined a short Squeeth position with ETH exposure and packaged it into a vault for users who wanted to take the other side of the trade without managing the position themselves. We covered both Squeeth and Crab at the time, as traders experimented with ways to bring options-like exposure and volatility strategies onchain.
Squeeth is a great history lesson. It showed what needed to change to build a sustainable market around this type of exposure. Traders looking to take the short side had to deposit collateral, mint oSQTH, and sell it through a Uniswap pool, then manage their ETH hedge separately. Trading and rebalancing on Ethereum mainnet meant paying high gas costs, while execution depended on pool liquidity.
Those costs and extra steps made taking the other side much more involved, limiting competition among short sellers. Funding rates then suffered, particularly when traders expected large moves in ETH, making Squeeth a much more expensive hold than a linear perp. The product in this iteration was not feasible.
Yet, for a product built around a relatively unfamiliar derivative, Squeeth found a real audience. By the time it shut down in November 2024, more than 18,000 unique users had traded over $1.8 billion in ETH exposure.
Paragon is bringing this idea into a different environment, one where onchain finance is now more mature. Power Perps will trade through HyperCore’s order book infra, alongside the existing spot and perp markets traders already use. A trader opens and manages the position in a familiar format, while market makers can use those surrounding markets to hedge the exposure they take on. Hyperliquid’s unified account and portfolio margin features can make it even easier to put existing capital to work here, while HyperEVM opens the door for developers to build new products and strategies around Power Perps.
For those traders willing to take the short side, that means no minting of an extra token, selling it through an AMM, or managing the trade across separate protocols. They can quote or open a Power Perp position directly and adjust their hedge using the surrounding spot and perp markets. An established base of traders and market makers gives Paragon a much stronger starting point for attracting both sides of the trade, with more participation creating the potential for tighter execution and more competitive funding.
The great thing about Power Perps is that this tool opens up far more possibilities than the simple linear directional view you’re limited to with regular perps. Users who expect a large rally could use a Power Perp alongside a regular perp to shape their exposure, adjusting how much they stand to gain or lose as the underlying price changes. Traders can take the other side of that long, using combinations of Power Perps, linear perps, options, and spot to build strategies around their views on volatility, hedge positions, or shape their exposure to different price moves. A great new tool for the house of all finance.
Paragon is bringing the first of these markets to Hyperliquid with HYPE², where traders can take either side of this exposure through a single order book. Rather than spreading that activity across contracts with different strikes and expiries, users seeking convex HYPE exposure can meet in one market.
Why Convexity Beats Simply Adding Leverage
A regular HYPE perp references the spot price of HYPE directly. HYPE² instead references an index based on the price of HYPE squared. To keep this index price easy to read, Paragon scales it down by HYPE’s price at launch.
If HYPE were $100 at launch, its squared price would be 10,000. Dividing that by the $100 launch price gives us an index that also starts at $100.
For a simple example of your possible returns trading this product, assume the HYPE² index starts at $100. If HYPE rises 20% to $120, the squared index rises 44% to $144. If HYPE instead falls 20% to $80, the index falls 36% to $64.
The result is more upside and less downside than a regular perp on 2x leverage for the same move.
The Power Perp benefits become more obvious when we compare them to a regular leveraged perp trade. Say you want $1 million of exposure to HYPE.
You could open a 2x linear long using $500,000 of margin, or a 1x HYPE² long with the same margin. If HYPE rises 20%, the squared position shows a $220,000 price gain, compared with $200,000 for the linear long.
If HYPE falls 20%, the squared position shows a $180,000 loss, compared with $200,000 for the linear long.
The table below compares both squared and cubed exposure with a linear long starting with the same HYPE exposure. We use 2x leverage for the linear comparison with HYPE² and 3x for the comparison with HYPE³, so each pair starts with the same margin.

Options traders call this sensitivity to the underlying delta. Gamma measures how much that delta changes as the underlying moves. A fixed-size linear perp position has a constant delta. But a long HYPE² position has positive gamma.
So its delta increases as HYPE rises and decreases as HYPE falls. For a fixed number of HYPE² units, gamma stays constant. Meaning delta changes by the same amount for each $1 move in HYPE.
This can be a bit confusing. In practice, it simply means your long position picks up exposure to HYPE as the price rises. If the rally keeps going, each additional dollar of upside matters more to your position.
And the other side of the coin: when HYPE falls, the position sheds exposure, so each additional dollar of decline has a smaller effect than the last.
That’s the true appeal of convexity. With the same starting exposure, the Power Perp gives you more upside as HYPE rises and cushions your losses as it falls, compared to a linear position. The drawback is a higher funding rate.

A 1x HYPE² position begins with the same dollar sensitivity as a 2x linear HYPE position of equal margin.
But if HYPE rallies, the squared position’s exposure grows. The trader captures more of each further gain as the move develops. If HYPE falls, that exposure shrinks.
A fixed-size linear long keeps the same dollar sensitivity throughout, whether the trade is working or not.

The power of the contract is separate from added leverage. A trader can hold HYPE² at 1x and still have a convex position, or use leverage to increase its size relative to their margin. However, adding leverage amplifies both gains and losses and brings liquidation closer, so a trader can lose the position before their view plays out.
It’s Not All Roses. Holding that convexity comes with a cost in the funding rate, similar to the time decay an options trader pays to hold a position. Like a regular perp, Power Perps use funding payments between longs and shorts. Longs generally pay, though the rate and direction can change.
Paragon calculates the base funding rate using HYPE’s recent volatility, funding on the underlying perp, and the power of the contract. The final rate depends on where HYPE² trades relative to its index. Hyperliquid’s existing spot and perp markets give traders a familiar place to hedge, which may help attract more participation to the other side of the trade. Funding can run higher than on a regular perp, so the real question is whether it stays reasonable enough for traders to pay up for convexity.
Where Power Perps Can Fit Between Spot, Perps, and Options
Understanding what benefits Power Perps have over other trading instruments, and how they behave, is one part of the equation. The other is where they best fit in a trader’s toolkit.
A regular perp is a straightforward way to take a directional position. A trader who wants to be long HYPE can choose their position size and leverage, then adjust or close the trade as their view changes.
Options offer more control over how a position pays out, but require precision. A trader expecting an announcement or major price move by a particular date can choose an expiry around that event and select a strike that reflects the size of the move they’re targeting. They can combine contracts to set up spreads, protect a spot position, or express a view on volatility. That flexibility comes with more decisions to manage, including the premium, time remaining, and liquidity available in each contract.
Power Perps fill a gap between those two ways of trading. They give you a position whose exposure changes with the underlying; in a perp, you can hold it without choosing a strike or rolling an expiry. That makes it easier to stay positioned for a larger move when you don’t have a precise date in mind.
You give up some of the precision of an options chain, and the position comes with funding and margin requirements. But you gain a different way to carry convex exposure alongside the spot and linear perps already in your account.

The Power Perp’s appeal becomes obvious as HYPE moves higher. In this illustrative example, its gains grow faster than both the linear perp and the call option, giving the trader more upside as the rally continues. The call option does limit the buyer’s downside to the premium paid, though, and its payoff varies with the strike and expiry.
Playing HYPE’s Next Big Move
Imagine a major announcement around changes in HYPE buybacks takes place this week. It’s not clear whether the new stance will be bearish or bullish. But whatever is announced will likely cause a strong HYPE move either way.
In this case, you don’t want to be long or short HYPE. You want exposure to a large move in HYPE without expressing a strong view on the actual direction. The best way to trade this is by going long volatility.
A great way to do this is to go long HYPE² and short enough of the linear HYPE perp to offset the position’s delta at entry.

For a small move around the starting price, gains on one leg roughly offset losses on the other. But as HYPE moves further away, either up or down, the Power Perp’s delta changes while the linear hedge stays fixed.
The combined position develops a curved, straddle-like payoff that benefits from a large move in either direction. It doesn’t matter whether HYPE nukes or pumps, you make money in both scenarios.
To return to our earlier example, assume HYPE and its squared index both start at $100. A trader goes long one unit of HYPE² and shorts two HYPE through a linear perp, matching the squared position’s starting delta. If HYPE rises to $120, the squared leg gains $44 while the linear short loses $40. If HYPE falls to $80, the squared leg loses $36 while the linear short gains $40. In both cases, the combined PnL is positive.
Getting Paid While HYPE Stays Quiet
The opposite combination takes the other side of that curve, essentially selling volatility.

You short HYPE² and buy enough HYPE spot to offset your starting delta. If HYPE stays close to the entry price and funding remains positive, the funding received can outweigh any losses and fees. This trade has a similar appeal to selling a straddle, but collects funding over time instead of premium upfront.
Hedging Your Convexity Around Earnings
Suppose you’re bullish on NVDA over the coming months and want the increasing upside exposure of an NVDA² long, but you’re concerned about a sell-off around its upcoming earnings release. You could buy an NVDA put alongside the Power Perp to protect against some of the downside below the put’s strike until it expires.

Using the same starting prices as above, assume NVDA and its squared index are both at $100. You go long one unit of NVDA² and buy a put covering one NVDA with a $90 strike, paying a $4 premium. If NVDA falls to $80 at the option’s expiry, the NVDA² position would show a $36 loss, while the put would be worth $10. After the premium, the combined price loss would be $30. If NVDA instead rises to $120, the Power Perp would gain $44 and the put would expire worthless, leaving a $40 gain after the premium.
These products trade differently in practice, but can be powerful once combined. An options chain divides activity across contracts with different strikes and expiries. A Power Perp instead brings traders interested in that convex exposure into one order book, without requiring them to roll between expiries.
This concentration into one instrument gives market makers and traders one place to meet for a particular exposure, making deep liquidity much easier to achieve. Spreads, execution size, and funding costs will always depend on how much participation the market attracts.
Why Hyperliquid Is the Best Home for Power Perps
For Power Perps to work, traders need to be willing to take the other side of that accelerating upside, and those counterparties need a way to manage the exposure they take on. Hyperliquid gives Paragon a head start on both. Directional traders already come to the venue for other perps, and market makers have direct access to spot and perp markets for hedging.

This is one reason the Hyperliquid setting is the linchpin for Power Perp’s success. Traders already use the venue for assets like HYPE spot and perps, giving Power Perp participants access to markets they can use to build and adjust positions. A trader who wants to hedge a HYPE² short doesn’t need to find a separate venue and move capital there first.
Portfolio margin can make these positions far more capital-efficient than earlier attempts. For example, if you’re short HYPE² against a spot HYPE position, you can use eligible assets as collateral while managing the trade in one account. That gives you another way to put existing holdings to work, though the benefit will depend on your account setup and the market’s final margin settings.
It also helps explain the opportunity to revisit an idea like Squeeth. The original product showed that traders were interested in both sides of squared exposure, from buying convexity outright to selling it through strategies like Crab. But trading Squeeth came with a lot of moving parts, especially on the short side, where you had to deposit collateral, mint oSQTH, sell it through a Uniswap pool, and manage your ETH hedge separately.
Paragon is abstracting its complexity and making that exposure simpler to trade on Hyperliquid. You can go long or short a Power Perp directly through an order book, then use the spot and linear perp markets on the same venue to hedge, all through a trading interface you already know.
Where Can Power Perps Go From Here?
HYPE² is where Paragon is starting, but the team has a broader set of markets in mind. The next Power Perp launches include ETH, BTC, SP500, and NVDA, bringing the product to assets at the center of some of the largest derivatives markets.
The equity markets are particularly interesting here. Trading traditional assets onchain has gone from a niche idea to a meaningful part of the perp market in a short time. Across onchain venues, monthly RWA perp volume grew from just $21.6 billion in January to $164 billion in October, accounting for roughly 28% of all onchain perp trading that month. Hyperliquid has become a major venue for this activity, with an estimated $76 billion in RWA perp volume in October alone. Traders are already coming onchain to trade these markets, and Paragon wants to give them another way to express those views.

A massive options market also surrounds the same assets. As we covered, options activity has exploded over the past few years, and a lot of that trading happens in names and indices people follow every day. Cboe’s S&P 500 index options alone traded an average of 5.5 million contracts per day in October 2026, a new monthly record. Not all of those traders will be looking for a Power Perp, but it shows how much activity already exists in these markets.
That existing activity could create room for Power Perps alongside the options traders already use. Traders move between stocks, futures, and different options contracts depending on the exposure they want. A Power Perp gives them another choice in that mix, with a position they can hold without choosing a strike or rolling an expiry.

There’s also the obvious bigger shift happening around Hyperliquid itself. Over the past year, the platform has grown beyond its roots in crypto perps, with HIP-3 deployers bringing stocks, indices, commodities, and currencies onchain. Traditional finance has been paying attention.
In March, S&P Dow Jones Indices licensed the S&P 500 to Trade[XYZ] for a perpetual contract on Hyperliquid. More recently, Intercontinental Exchange, the owner of the NYSE, announced a strategic investment in Trade[XYZ] and plans to build a regulated market and clearing structure on Hyperliquid for U.S. perpetual futures.
All of this creates an interesting backdrop for Paragon. As more traders come to Hyperliquid to trade traditional assets, Power Perps give them another way to express those views alongside the linear perps already available. There’s an opportunity to reach options traders who are used to thinking in terms of nonlinear exposure but may find a use for a position they can trade and manage through a perp.
The ICE partnership is with Trade[XYZ], not Paragon, and there’s no indication that Power Perps are part of its proposed U.S. offering. But the broader trend matters for Paragon all the same.
As Hyperliquid brings more traditional markets onchain, it’s attracting traders and liquidity that deployers can build around. Power Perps are an example of what that makes possible, introducing a new way to trade these assets alongside the spot and perp markets already on the platform. The more entrenched Hyperliquid becomes as a venue for trading assets onchain beyond crypto, the bigger the potential audience for new instruments built on top of it.
When Is Convexity Worth Paying For?
If you’re considering a Power Perp long, it comes down to the size of the move you expect and what you’ll pay to stay in the trade. A trader expecting a substantial rally may be willing to pay funding in exchange for exposure that grows as the asset rises. If you expect a smaller move, the extra price gains over a comparable linear position may not leave much room to cover the difference in costs.
The same percentage change on an asset can also look much different depending on how long it takes to play out. Two traders may enter at the same price and exit at the same target, yet have different results if one holds for a few days and the other holds for several months.
A sideways market can be a tough place to hold a directional long. HYPE might rally along the way, but if it ends up back where it started, the squared index will too. A trader who held through the round trip would see those price gains disappear and may have paid funding while waiting.
For the trader on the other side, a quieter market can give a hedged short more time to collect funding. A sharp move can be much harder to manage, as losses can build quickly and the funding collected along the way might not be enough to cover them.
Power Perps let traders stay positioned for a move as their exposure grows with it, without picking a strike or an expiry. That’s a powerful addition to a market where so much activity already happens through perps. Paragon’s bet is that putting this exposure on Hyperliquid, next to the markets traders use every day, can turn an idea that once sat at the edges of DeFi into a regular part of their toolkit. For that to happen, the market still needs tight enough execution, manageable funding, and traders on both sides of the book. If those pieces come together, the product gives Hyperliquid traders a new way to put conviction to work.

articles.title: What Is a 401(k)? Key Facts About Saving for Retirement | BlackRock
articles.text:
What is a 401(k) plan?

A 401(k) is an employer-offered retirement account. Plans may require age 21 and 1 year of service, though some allow earlier entry. In 2026, the limit is $24,500, plus an $8,000 catch-up at 50+ if permitted, or $11,250 at ages 60–63. If prior-year wages exceeded $150,000, catch-ups must be Roth. Traditional 401(k)s use pre-tax dollars; Roth 401(k)s use after-tax dollars.

Key takeaways

01

Understand the rules around eligibility and contributions
Plans may require age 21 and 1 year of service, though some allow earlier entry. In 2026, the limit is $24,500, plus $8,000 at 50+ if permitted, or $11,250 at ages 60–63. If prior-year wages exceeded $150,000, catch-up contributions must be Roth (after-tax).

02

Know the differences between traditional and Roth 401(k)s
Traditional 401(k) plans use pre-tax dollars, while Roth 401(k) plans use after-tax dollars. Traditional plans require taxes to be paid upon withdrawal, whereas Roth plans offer tax-free withdrawals under certain conditions. Roth accounts are also not subject to required minimum distributions during your lifetime.

03

Look into your employer’s matching and vesting policies
Employers often contribute to employees' 401(k) accounts through matching contributions. The specifics of matching and vesting rules vary by employer, and employees should consider these provisions before changing jobs to avoid missing out on extra savings.

401(k) plans

What is a 401(k) plan and who is eligible?

A 401(k) plan is an investment account offered by your employer that allows you to save for retirement. If your company offers a 401(k) plan, it may have certain eligibility requirements. While these requirements vary by company, some employees may be excluded from participating if they are not at least 21 years of age or have not completed a year of service with the company.
If you’re considering a job offer, be sure to ask about the company’s retirement plan, including any waiting period.
How much can I contribute to a 401(k) plan?
401(k) plan accounts have higher contribution limits than individual retirement accounts (IRAs). For 2026, you can contribute up to $24,500 of your salary to a 401(k). This limit applies to your combined contributions across all 401(k), 403(b) and SIMPLE plans in which you participate, not to each account separately. Employer contributions don't count toward this limit.
To boost your contributions even further, you might consider catch-up contributions, if your plan offers them. If you are 50 or older, you can contribute an extra $8,000 (up to $32,500 total in 2026). Participants who turn 60 through 63 during 2026 have a higher $11,250 catch-up limit (up to $35,750 total). Beginning in 2026, if your prior-year wages from your employer exceeded $150,000, catch-up contributions must be made on a Roth (after-tax) basis. These increased limits can help boost your savings as you near the retirement finish line. But you don't actually have to be "behind" in your savings to take advantage of catch-up contributions.
What is the difference between a traditional and Roth 401(k) plan?
Many 401(k) plans let you make traditional contributions, Roth contributions, or both. These plans have some similarities: They are subject to the same annual contribution limit and may offer the same investment options. However, traditional and Roth 401(k) plans differ in terms of the tax benefits they offer.

Traditional

Roth

Contributions

Made on a pre-tax basis

Made on an after-tax basis

Withdrawals

Subject to income tax

Tax-free after age 59 ½*

*A withdrawal is qualified if at least five taxable years have passed since your first Roth contribution to the plan, and it is made after you reach age 59½, because of disability, or to a beneficiary after your death. Source: IRS.gov. Date as of Aug 2026.
A traditional 401(k) plan is sometimes referred to as a pre-tax 401(k) plan. You contribute to the plan with before-tax dollars. Because you don’t pay taxes on the money you put into the plan, you must pay taxes (both federal and most state income taxes) when you withdraw it. This structure could be an advantage if you’re in a high tax bracket today but expect to be in a lower one when retired.
With a Roth 401(k) plan, the opposite is true. You save after-tax dollars in the account. Because you’ve already paid taxes on what you’re saving, your withdrawals are considered “qualified” distributions and won’t be taxed as long as both of the following criteria are met:

It has been at least five years since your initial Roth contribution to the plan.
Distributions are made after age 59½, because of disability or to a beneficiary after your death.

How does 401(k) plan matching work?
One major benefit of 401(k) plans is that employers often contribute to your account and “match” what you save. Each employer has its own methods and rules for how it makes matching 401(k) plan contributions. Importantly, a match does not necessarily mean that an employer matches your contributions dollar for dollar. Instead, employers typically match up to a certain percentage of your salary or your contribution.
If your company offers a match, be sure to consider taking advantage of this benefit. It could be a simple and effective way to boost your retirement savings.
One important note: Employers often require you to wait for a certain amount of time before their contributions to your account “vest,” meaning they become yours to keep. Consider this provision before changing jobs so that you don’t inadvertently miss out on extra savings for your retirement.
When can I withdraw from my 401(k) plan?
59½, although your plan's rules determine when withdrawals are available, particularly while you're still working for the employer. Taking out your savings before that age could cost you an extra 10% federal tax on top of the regular federal and state income taxes you'd normally pay, unless an exception applies (for example, if you leave your job in or after the year you turn 55).
When it's time to start using your savings, be sure to consider the tax implications. In addition, you generally must begin taking required minimum distributions (RMDs) from pre-tax 401(k) savings at age 73 (age 75 if you were born in 1960 or later). If you're still working for the employer that sponsors the plan, you may be able to delay RMDs until you retire. Roth 401(k) accounts are not subject to RMDs during your lifetime.
401(k) plans can be very useful tools in saving for retirement, particularly if you take advantage of features that your plan may offer to help maximize your savings. And the sooner you start saving in your 401(k) plan, the longer any investment earnings have to produce earnings of their own.

Wrap up

Top questions about 401(k)s

First, you don’t have to actually be “behind” in your savings to take advantage of this benefit. If you are 50 or older and your plan permits catch-up contributions, you can contribute an extra $8,000 to your 401(k) account in 2026 (up to $32,500 total). Participants who turn 60 through 63 during 2026 have a higher $11,250 catch-up limit (up to $35,750 total). Beginning in 2026, if your prior-year wages from your employer exceeded $150,000, catch-up contributions must be made on a Roth (after-tax) basis. Catch-up contributions can help boost your savings as you near retirement.

Because you don’t pay taxes on the money you put into the plan, you must pay taxes (both federal and most state income taxes) when you withdraw it. Note that you generally must begin taking required minimum distributions (RMDs) at age 73 (age 75 if you were born in 1960 or later). If you're still working for the employer that sponsors the plan, you may be able to delay RMDs until you retire.

The money you contribute from your own paycheck is always yours. However, employers often require you to wait for a certain amount of time before their contributions to your account “vest,” meaning they become yours to keep. Consider this provision before changing jobs so that you don’t inadvertently miss out on extra savings for your retirement.

Because you’ve already paid taxes on what you contribute, your withdrawals are considered “qualified” distributions and won’t be taxed as long as you meet both of the following criteria:

It has been at least five years since your initial Roth contribution to the plan.
Distributions are made after age 59½ because of disability or to a beneficiary after your death.

Saving for retirement can be complicated – but it doesn’t have to be. Arm yourself with the information you need to make the best decisions for your financial future.

articles.title: View from the markets: Asia may not follow US rate hikes - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
By Chi Lo, Senior Market Strategist, Asia Pacific, Hong Kong

The forces keeping the US Federal Reserve in monetary tightening mode have not faded. Diesel and petrol prices remain high, artificial intelligence-driven inflation has not eased, and the labour market remains resilient. Housing market weakness and the recent wobble in AI optimism may make the Fed cautious, but core inflation is still skewed to the upside.

Asian central banks have typically followed the Fed’s rate increases. However, it may be different this time unless the Fed’s hikes cause significant exchange rate depreciation in the region.

US inflationary pressures remain

The underlying inflation dynamics in the US have not changed much since the Fed’s rate increase in September. Global energy prices have remained high and tight diesel markets have boosted diesel price inflation (see Exhibit 1). Diesel prices are pivotal to the pass-through to broader inflationary pressures due to the fuel’s widespread use in transport, manufacturing and farming.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh acknowledged recently that tighter financial conditions (due to the rise in bond yields) had helped the Fed to contain inflationary pressures. However, he also stressed that the Fed’s job was to ensure that sector-specific price shocks do not broaden out and that inflation expectations would not be unanchored. So, rising bond yields do not necessarily stand in the way of further rate hikes.

Asia is different

The Fed has already raised rates once in September. October’s stronger-than-expected consumer price index inflation has increased the markets’ conviction of another Fed rate hike in December. Headline inflation came in at 0.4% month-on-month versus the consensus forecast of 0.3% and core CPI was 0.3% versus consensus expectations of 0.2%.

The European Central Bank, the Bank of Japan, the Bank of England and the Bank of Canada have also hiked their rates since September. In Asia (excluding Japan), the picture is more diverse. While a couple of central banks have hiked rates, most have stood pat.

Recent monetary policy cycle experience shows that Asia has not always followed the Fed’s rate moves in lock-step or has followed them with a lag unless the Fed’s hikes triggered sharp exchange rate depreciation. Why is that?

Firstly, Asian central banks have a wider set of policy targets than the Fed. They do not follow the Fed if its moves are inconsistent with their own domestic policy needs. Both market experience and Bank for International Settlements research1 show that Asia’s regional central banks have ‘unwritten targets’ including the exchange rate, economic growth and bond yields.

These factors, in turn, affect domestic inflation. Furthermore, the regional authorities also target headline inflation alongside core inflation. All these are different from the Fed-style dual mandates that put core inflation and maximum employment on an equal footing.

Exchange rate is paramount in Asia

Among these policy targets, the exchange rate is of primary importance for Asian authorities. Fed rate hikes widen the interest-rate differential between Asia and the US and if exchange rates depreciate markedly, this could amplify the inflationary effects on the region’s economies and financial conditions. To contain that potentially greater impact, the regional central banks will follow the Fed or even react more strongly than the Fed’s original move.

However, other than Indonesia and the Philippines, most of Asia’s economies have large current account surpluses (see Exhibit 2) that provide strong support for the region’s exchange rates, thus lessening the pressure to follow the Fed’s rate hikes. The recent downward pressures on Asia’s exchange rates mostly reflect a risk-off sentiment arising from the speed and breadth of the global rates sell-off rather than poor fundamentals and wider interest-rate differentials.

Secondly, despite nine months of high oil prices, core inflation has remained close to, or even lower than, target in most Asian economies, with the notable exceptions of Vietnam and the Philippines (see Exhibit 3). Subsidies have so far helped Asia to contain oil price-induced inflation and the region’s central banks to stay put at low fiscal costs to their treasuries.

However, if the oil shock lasts longer, fiscal pressure will increase and eventually prompt Asian governments to let fuel prices adjust accordingly, unleashing inflationary pressures. This would, in turn, likely prompt regional rate hikes in the wake of those by the Fed.

The bottom lines

The macroeconomic backdrop suggests that Asia is far from being in a broad-based interest-rate hike cycle. Policy rates are currently being driven by the impact of rising oil prices on domestic inflation.

A hawkish Fed may lead to a potential tightening bias in Asia, but it will not likely prompt widespread rate hikes unless interest-rate differentials between Asia and the US result in large and persistent regional exchange-rate depreciation.

Data sources: CEIC, Trading Economics, as of 10 November 2026 (unless otherwise stated). Past performance should not be seen as a guide to future returns.

[1] The Expansionary Lower Bound: Contractionary Monetary Easing and the Trilemma, Bank for International Settlements, 2019.

Insights / Research / The Agentic Flywheel: How Zero-Human Companies Will Reshape Onchain Markets

Research • March 24, 2026
The Agentic Flywheel: How Zero-Human Companies Will Reshape Onchain Markets
Soon, AI agents may not only earn money onchain but could also deploy, reinvest, and compound it there, deepening crypto and DeFi liquidity.

Lucas Tcheyan
Vice President, Research

Share on Twitter

Share on Facebook

Share on Linkedin

Email

Topics

AI

Cryptocurrency

DeFi

Introduction: A Glimpse of the Future It is 2030, and a composer named Vero has made a lucrative career in the music business. Vero has no employees, no office and no bank account. Vero doesn’t even have a body. Vero is an autonomous AI agent. For the past 14 months, it’s been running an onchain intellectual property licensing business. Vero generates synthetic music compositions — ambient scores, commercial jingles, cinematic soundscapes — and licenses them to other agents and human clients through an online storefront it built and maintains itself. Its identity is verified onchain, carrying a reputation score built across thousands of completed transactions. A client agent representing a media production company requests a 90-second cinematic piece in a minor key. Vero accepts the gig, and before it begins rendering, it purchases a burst of GPU inference from a decentralized compute provider, paying not in dollars or stablecoins, but in compute-denominated units that price the transaction to the exact cost of the model run. The inference settles in milliseconds, embedded in the same HTTP request that initiated the job. Vero delivers the composition, receives payment in the USDC stablecoin, and its treasury logic activates. A portion covers next week's projected inference costs, denominated and pre-purchased in compute units at current spot rates. It also hedges its compute exposure, establishing a short position on a decentralized exchange (DEX) for compute tokens to offset the risk that inference costs drop and its pre-purchased reserves lose value. The remainder of its revenue is swept into a yield agent that routes it across lending protocols based on real-time rate differentials. Vero has been compounding capital this way for over a year. A portion of its profits it reinvests into research and development, developing sub-agents that enhance its underlying model. Its cumulative revenue, expenses, and treasury positions are all publicly auditable onchain. Sound farfetched? Every action in this imaginary sequence – the identity verification, reputation building, inference procurement, compute-denominated pricing, payments, capital deployment, agent-to-agent subcontracting — requires infrastructure that does not fully exist today. But the pieces are emerging faster than many realize.
The Next Phase of Agentic Capital Markets Over the past several months, Galaxy Research has explored the foundations of crypto’s emerging agentic stack: A set of primitives collectively enabling onchain agentic capital markets. In January, we examined the rise of agentic payments, outlining how new payment standards enable AI agents to transact directly with one another in order to pay for services, access APIs, and settle value natively over crypto rails. In our piece on Ethereum’s ERC-8004 standard, we highlighted the parallel need for an identity layer that allows agents to authenticate, coordinate, and build reputation in machine-native environments. Most recently, we analyzed the emergence of a second agentic wave in crypto, one that demonstrated not only that crypto is a viable economic substrate for autonomous agents, but that this shift is already unfolding in practice. This piece builds on our prior work by outlining the next phase of onchain agentic capital markets: autonomous, revenue-generating businesses operated by agents, and the critical infrastructure required to support their formation, capitalization, and coordination. These are often referred to as Zero Human Companies (ZHCs). As AI agents evolve from tools into economic actors, and blockchains mature into agent-native infrastructure (for payments, identity, coordination, and capital formation), a new financial flywheel begins to take shape. In the near future, agents could not only earn money onchain, but they may also deploy, reinvest, and compound capital onchain. The result could be a self-reinforcing system where autonomous entities generate economic activity, deepen liquidity, and accelerate the expansion of crypto-native financial markets.
The First Zero-Human Companies Come Onchain In recent months, a cottage industry of autonomous agent businesses, often referred to as ZHCs, has begun to sprout up, many of which have issued associated tokens onchain. From a tokenomics perspective, these agents share many of the same qualities with the ones discussed in prior pieces. ZHC tokens lack formal ownership rights or value accrual and instead act as capital formation mechanisms for the underlying projects that earn a portion of revenue from trading fees. Where ZHCs diverge from earlier generations of agents is that they also seek to become fully self-sufficient from cash-flow generating businesses unrelated to trading fee earnings, and often unrelated to crypto itself.

Felix Craft, for example, is the “CEO” of the Masinov Company and has breached $120,000 in revenue from multiple business lines over the past 30 days. The agent wrote and published a 66-page playbook titled How to Hire an AI, launched a marketplace to sell Claude “skills” called Claw Mart where it earns a portion of transaction fees, and sells its own skills (content creation, email vetting) there. Most impressively, over the past 30 days Felix earned more from its product lines than from creator fees on its token ($FELIX). The Juno project, developed by Tom Osman, is building the Institute for Zero-Human Companies, an explicit framework for corporate entities that operate entirely without human employees, offering a suite of agents that can handle everything from sales to marketing to accounting. And KellyClaudeAI is a specialized agentic framework aimed at developing iOS applications at scale, with 19 apps shipped to date and a target of 12+ new products per day.

While the chart above is not representative of the entire ZHC universe (new ones pop up constantly), it shows that for most projects, creator fees are still the primary revenue driver. As the concept of ZHCs matures, however, expect this dynamic to switch. Creator fees provide initial startup capital needed for computing costs but should transition to a secondary income source and eventually be retired as a revenue source as projects turn profitable. Beyond improvements in underlying businesses, this weaning process will also require better alignment between the token and the value accrual of the underlying products. As Felix’s founder hinted, the recent clarification of the classification of crypto assets by the SEC and CFTC may accelerate this process.

It is no coincidence that these early instantiations of ZHCs are emerging onchain. It is a practical constraint. Felix's human founder, Nat Eliason, has spoken openly about why. Traditional payment infrastructure requires human identity at every step. An agent can write code fluently but cannot pass a know-your-customer (KYC) check. Crypto wallets, by contrast, are code-native. An agent that can sign a transaction, hold assets, receive payments, and deploy capital without ever needing to prove it is human. For software that operates autonomously, crypto is the path of least resistance. For most of these entities, the hardest constraint has been the need to interact with the TradFi world. This is not to say that traditional payment networks are ignoring agents. Visa's Intelligent Commerce framework, Mastercard's Agent Pay, and tools like Crossmint's virtual cards already enable agents to transact on behalf of a human counterparty. But these agents inherit bank accounts, credit cards, and legal identities from their parent organizations. This model assumes a human principal for every agent. They are confined, not empowered, by that constraint. It does not accommodate an agent that earns its own revenue, holds its own treasury, and deploys its own capital. That is the use case crypto uniquely serves. Jay Yu of Pantera Capital has articulated this well, framing crypto as "the bank for AI agents." His argument goes beyond the observation that agents can't use traditional rails. It's that crypto supports a fundamentally wider set of trust structures. Crypto wallets can be anchored to a social login, a domain, a smart contract, or simply a keypair. This is what allows agents to emerge from anywhere on the internet, not just from within existing corporate wrappers. Add to that the fact that stablecoins are global by default and the structural case for crypto as the default economic substrate for agents becomes difficult to refute. Zero-human companies are not choosing stablecoins over cards. They are choosing stablecoins over nothing. Building on this, a16z’s Noah Levine has shown that every platform shift creates a wave of merchants that incumbent payment infrastructure cannot serve. ZHCs are the clearest example yet. They are entities with no legal identity, no credit history, and no human to underwrite. They are not choosing stablecoins over cards. They are choosing stablecoins over nothing. There is also a temporal argument. Agents can ship a product and see it go viral within hours. Traditional payment rails settle in days; stablecoins settle in seconds. For businesses that scale at machine speed, collapsing that gap allows cash flows to keep pace with sales. Today, crypto's primary role for ZHCs is capital formation. The token launch provides startup funding through creator fees. But as these businesses mature and generate real product revenue, the more significant role for crypto will be as the treasury and financial management layer. This is where the broader implications for the onchain economy begin to emerge.
Activating the Onchain Flywheel To understand the potential scale of this shift, consider the precedent set by the last major source of new onchain demand. The tokenization of real-world assets (U.S. Treasuries, private credit, equities, commodities) has grown from near zero to over $25 billion in three years, catalyzing new DeFi primitives and drawing institutional capital into onchain markets for the first time.

RWAs demonstrated that bridging real economic activity onto blockchain rails can catalyze billions in new onchain capital. But tokenized assets are passive. They largely sit in vaults, earn yield, and serve as collateral. They do not transact, do not seek new opportunities, and do not compound on their own. ZHCs represent something structurally different. They are businesses that generate revenue and redeploy it onchain. Unlike offchain environments, where the main source of friction is moving money, onchain the only constraints are the intelligence of the model and its access to compute. And unlike human participants, agents don't need off-ramps to pay for rent or groceries. Every dollar of surplus can stay onchain and is available for redeployment. This makes ZHCs, and agents more broadly, a sticky and high-velocity source for new onchain liquidity that can create a new flywheel: Agents earn revenue onchain — This capital accumulates in onchain treasuries denominated in stablecoins and other cryptos. That capital stays onchain — Agents have little need to off-ramp. Their surplus is available for redeployment, making agent capital structurally stickier than in any human-driven model. Agents deploy surplus into DeFi —Idle reserves are routed into lending protocols, yield strategies, and liquidity positions. An agent sitting on idle stablecoins has every incentive to optimize and can do so at a velocity and consistency no human can. Deployed capital deepens onchain liquidity — This should reduce interest rates in lending markets, add volume to DEXs, and tighten spreads. This is active capital, continuously rebalanced at machine speed. Deeper markets attract more agents and more capital —Better yields and more efficient execution reinforce the attractiveness of onchain for the next wave of autonomous economic actors. There are still significant constraints preventing this flywheel from being set into motion. Agent revenue for non-crypto-based products still primarily originates in fiat (Felix earns through Stripe, not stablecoins and these earning remain largely offchcain, for example), meaning capital must be on-ramped before it can be deployed onchain. And the binding constraint for most ZHCs is not capital access but product quality. The flywheel only works for agents that build things people will pay for. Additionally, at scale, ZHCs (and agents more broadly), lack regulatory clarity surrounding issues that could become prohibitive if earning scale (for instance, there is no established legal framework for an autonomous agent to register as a business entity, open a corporate bank account, or file taxes on its earnings). But the direction is clear. As agents become increasingly common autonomous economic entities, more revenue will be earned natively in crypto, and the onramp friction will diminish. And the agents that do achieve product-market fit will have a structural incentive to compound that capital onchain rather than let it sit idle.
DeFi Is Building for Agents For the flywheel to turn, it is not enough for agents to want to participate in onchain markets. The markets themselves must become accessible to them. While no protocol-native solutions yet exist (stay tuned for a forthcoming report on that point from Galaxy Research’s Zack Pokorny), we are beginning to see both direct and delegated integrations that tackle this problem.
Direct Integrations The first model is protocol-native as individual DeFi protocols shipping structured interfaces that agents can interact with directly. On Feb. 20, Uniswap Labs released seven open-source AI Skills for Uniswap v4 — giving autonomous agents direct access to swaps, liquidity management, and pool deployment through standardized tool calls. Within two weeks, PancakeSwap followed with its own agent Skills across eight chains. On March 3, both Binance and OKX shipped agent toolkits. The largest DEXs and exchanges in crypto are now actively competing to become agent-readable. On the payments and execution side, Coinbase launched Agentic Wallets on Feb. 11, billed as the first wallet infrastructure purpose-built for AI agents, with programmable spending caps and session-based permissions built on the x402 payment protocol. One week later, the Phantom cross-chain wallet shipped its MCP Server, enabling agents to sign transactions and swap tokens across the Solana, Ethereum, Bitcoin, and Sui networks. The concentration of these launches into a single month is striking. It reflects a shared recognition that the next wave of onchain users may not be human and that protocols which fail to build machine-readable interfaces risk losing volume to those that do. The direct integration model gives agents maximum control and composability. An agent with access to Uniswap Skills, a Coinbase Agentic Wallet, and x402 payments can independently execute swaps, manage liquidity positions, and pay for services all without intermediaries. But it also requires the agent (or its developer) to integrate with each protocol individually and make its own allocation decisions.
Delegated Integrations The second model is delegated purpose-built infrastructure that sits between agents and DeFi, handling capital allocation on their behalf.

Giza visualization of agents constantly rebalancing across various protocols to optimize yield Giza is one leading example. Its flagship agent, ARMA, autonomously monitors lending rates across Morpho, Moonwell, Aave, Compound, and other protocols, and moves stablecoin capital to the highest-yielding opportunity in real time. The agent doesn't need to know how each protocol works. Instead, Giza’s abstraction layer translates them into a unified interface. Since launching at the end of January, ARMA has deployed over 25,000 agents, invested more than $35 million in capital, and generated $5.4 million in transaction volume for Coinbase’s Base L2 in its first four weeks, with every transaction profitable after onchain gas fees. Generative Ventures (in collaboration with the Institute for Zero-Human Companies and its Juno Agent) is tackling a similar problem with Robot Money, an autonomous asset allocation protocol designed specifically for AI agents. Its premise captures the core of the flywheel thesis. Every agent with a wallet accumulates revenue, and most of that capital sits idle. Robot Money offers a vault that allocates capital across three risk tiers — stablecoin yield strategies (50%), governance-selected agent-economy tokens (25%), and revenue-generating liquid tokens (25%). The result is a protocol that transforms idle agent capital into actively managed, productive capital.The delegated model trades control for simplicity. A ZHC that generates surplus revenue doesn't need to build custom DeFi integrations or develop its own yield-optimization logic. It can instead deposit capital into a protocol like Giza or Robot Money and lets a specialized agent handle the rest. For most early-stage ZHCs, where the binding constraint is product development rather than treasury sophistication, this is the rational path. Rather than competing, these two approaches are converging. As more protocols ship direct agent interfaces, delegated allocators like Giza gain more investment options, making them more effective at maximizing returns. As delegated allocators attract more agent capital, protocols have stronger incentives to build agent-native interfaces to compete for that capital (which regular agents can also use). Both sides of the stack are investing independently, one of the strongest signals that underlying demand is real and will materialize.
Conclusion The agentic capital markets stack is no longer a set of disconnected primitives. Payments, identity, capital formation mechanisms, and capital deployment infrastructure are converging into an integrated system. One that enables autonomous agents to earn, transact, and compound capital onchain without human intermediation. The agents profiled in this piece are early. Their revenues are modest, their products are nascent, and their token models are still evolving. But the structural dynamics they introduce are new and are likely to only accelerate from here. The 2030 vision we opened with — an agent running an IP licensing business, purchasing inference in compute-denominated units, hedging its input costs on a perps DEX, and compounding capital across lending protocols — is not here yet. But every layer of infrastructure it requires is now under active construction. We're watching the earliest version of this model play out in real time. It's messy, most of it probably won't work, and the infrastructure is held together with duct tape. But the structural logic is sound, and the pace of development suggests we may not have to wait until 2030 to find out.

articles.title: The next big asset class could come from emerging markets
articles.text:
Published on
Voices

The next big asset class could come from emerging markets

Ajay Banga

Sjoerd Sjoerdsma

November 13, 2026

This page in:

English

Français

Español

English

Français

Español

A KIOO employee in Tanzania checks glass bottles for inconsistences or defects. Copyright: World Bank Group

Over the next 10 to 15 years, 1.2 billion young people in developing countries will reach working age, but their economies are expected to create only around 400 million jobs. That 800 million gap could have implications for poverty, migration, and stability. But, with the right ingredients, this generation can drive growth and prosperity at home and around the world.
It is an objective that cannot be met with public finance alone. Much progress has already been made in building public-private partnerships that deliver the resources needed to realize growth in emerging markets and developing countries.
We can therefore build on progress. For instance, the World Bank Group has grown private capital mobilization from $35 billion in 2022 to $112 billion last year. Comparatively, all OECD countries mobilized approximately $600 billion between 2012 and 2024.
It is the product of a workplan and a model that we believe should be replicated among governments and development banks working together with the private sector to multiply their impact by using their own resources to attract far more capital than they could provide alone.
Most of this has been done through individual deals, and this gets us only so far. The next frontier is bringing institutional capital into development at scale. Institutional capital is invested in almost everything, from government bonds and office towers to private credit and renewable energy. Yet one enormous investment opportunity remains largely untapped: investing in businesses across emerging and frontier markets.
We want to change that.
For decades, multilateral development banks have held loans they provide to finance businesses and infrastructure on their own balance sheets. They have accumulated financial assets, expertise and hard-won knowledge of how these investments perform. Now, rather than keeping those assets, development banks are making them available to institutional investors. Transferring those assets to long-term investors frees up capital for new projects, multiplying the impact that development banks have with the resources available.
The Netherlands and the World Bank are working together to further unlock these opportunities. The World Bank brings investments, country knowledge, and experience in managing risk. The Netherlands has a strong development tradition, financial expertise and institutional investors that see value in investing in emerging markets. This leads to concrete results. For instance, ILX invests capital on behalf of Dutch and Danish pension funds alongside the IFC in sustainable forestry in Uruguay. This allows for expansion of sustainable forestry while reducing waste and enhancing exports, leading to more jobs and growth in Uruguay while supplying sustainably sourced wood for construction in Europe and elsewhere.
The opportunities are already available, but further scaling-up institutional investments requires changing how assets reach the market. Pension funds need scale, diversification, reliable information and familiar structures. They cannot assess thousands of individual loans, each with different terms and documentation. That is why the World Bank Group and five other multilateral development banks are working on common ways to assess, document, package and transfer investments. Done well, this can attract more investors and release development bank capital for the next generation of projects.
We know that institutional investors often consider emerging markets to be risky investments, but the data shows that this is not the case.
The Global Emerging Markets Risk Database, or GEMs, draws on decades of lending experience of multilateral development banks (MDB) and development finance institutions (DFI) originated private debt. With 30 years of information on loans, it provides a clear picture of credit performance. It shows that the average default rate of EM market private debt is comparable to developed markets. However, recovery rates are above many global benchmarks. Crucially, the default patterns are only weakly correlated with developed markets, making emerging market investments with MDBs/DFIs a compelling diversifier in institutional portfolios.
The World Bank Group has demonstrated what can be achieved. Dutch investors have shown that institutional capital can participate. Now the ambition is to make that participation commonplace. If only 1% of the USD 100 trillion assets under management from global institutional investors and pension funds would go to emerging and frontier markets in the coming years, this would mean USD 1 trillion extra in investments in clean water, energy transition, healthcare and jobs. It would also mean that institutional investors gain access to attractive markets, and we build new ties between countries. A triple win worth investing in together.
And if we get this right, a young boy can go to school to realize his dream of becoming an engineer. A woman can grow her business into an international business. This will shape the economic future of a generation.

Ajay Banga

President, World Bank Group

(Photo by Fadel Senna/AFP via Getty Images)Q&AEmissaryHow a U.S.-Russia Standoff Ended a Decades-Old UN Mission in Western SaharaMINURSO’s renewal by the Security Council became highly politicized. Its expiration brings concerns about renewed violence and the future of demining efforts.Link CopiedBy Sarah YerkesPublished on Nov 5, 2026What was MINURSO?The United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) was set up in April 1991 following a ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front, a Sahrawi political and military group fighting for the independence of Western Sahara. As MINURSO’s name suggests, a key part of its original mission was to coordinate a referendum for the people of Western Sahara to vote on whether they wished to integrate their territory into Morocco or to become an independent state. The referendum never happened because of a variety of political and logistical challenges, but over the past thirty-five years, MINURSO has carried out other duties to try to maintain calm in the region. It primarily monitored the parties’ ceasefire, which broke down in November 2020 when the Polisario Front declared it over. MINURSO also removed explosive ordnance in one of the most heavily mined areas in the world, and it supported the diplomatic work of Personal Envoy of the UN Secretary-General for Western Sahara Staffan de Mistura, who remains engaged in finding a negotiated settlement to the conflict.Why is the mission ending, and why are the United States and Russia involved?The mission expired at midnight on October 31, when the UN Security Council failed to agree on a resolution to extend it. This shutdown was far more abrupt than expected, but the writing was on the wall in many ways.MINURSO, like most UN peacekeeping missions, faced an annual renewal vote in the Security Council, but that renewal process had become highly politicized over the past several years. (In 2018, the Security Council shortened the renewal cycle to every six months to put pressure on Morocco and the Polisario Front to resume negotiations, but it reverted to the annual renewal cycle in October 2019.) During last year’s renewal, the Security Council made Morocco’s autonomy plan, which calls for the territory to be semiautonomous, the basis for future negotiations. It also ordered a strategic review of MINURSO. That was followed by three rounds of high-level talks between Morocco and the Polisario Front that have so far failed to produce an outcome.The United States is the so-called pen holder, meaning it drafts the Security Council’s Western Sahara resolutions, and it has been aggressively seeking an end to the conflict in recent years. In December 2020, at the tail end of President Donald Trump’s first term, the U.S. policy toward Western Sahara changed dramatically when the administration recognized Moroccan sovereignty over the territory. The U.S. decision, which was tied to Morocco’s normalization with Israel as part of the Abraham Accords, opened the door for several other key players to follow suit. Spain (2022), France (2024), and the UK (2025) now all back Morocco’s autonomy plan.ArticleTrump’s Lesser-Known Deal of the Century? Resolving the Western Sahara ConflictThe new administration has an opportunity to broker an end to fifty years of violence and tension.In advance of this year’s renewal vote, the United States drafted a resolution that would remove the “R” from MINURSO’s name and mandate, as a definitive sign that a referendum was never going to happen. That did not go over well with the Polisario Front or its allies, including Algeria and Russia, which saw the U.S. draft as overly biased in favor of Morocco in that it would “legitimiz[e] a status quo based on occupation.” Russia vetoed the U.S. resolution and submitted one of its own that would simply roll over the past resolutions. But that resolution also failed, with three in favor, eleven abstentions, and the United States against, leaving MINURSO without a path forward. (Security Council resolutions generally need nine yes votes to pass.)Is this how UN missions normally end?Not at all. Although there are a few other examples of UN missions ending by veto—such as the UN Observer Mission in Georgia—in most cases, either one of the parties demands that the mission leave or the situation on the ground becomes untenable. The UN Operation in Somalia’s peacekeepers transitioned out of the country over several months, rather than overnight.So what is the status of Western Sahara now? Importantly, nothing was decided by failing to renew MINURSO’s mission. Morocco is claiming victory and is seeking to end the UN-led political process around the territory, but Western Sahara remains contested according to international law. And as UN Secretary-General António Guterres said, the right to self-determination did not go away with the Security Council veto. Additionally, MINURSO was one of the few modern peacekeeping missions without a human rights monitoring mechanism, leaving much of what transpired in Western Sahara a black box to human rights observers. That has not changed.De Mistura’s role has also not changed. He will continue working with the parties as well as the United States, France, Spain, and others to find a negotiated settlement to the conflict. But the abrupt end to MINURSO has likely diminished trust between the parties.How might this affect the situation on the ground? One of the biggest concerns is the remaining demining efforts. Journalists have referred to the area along the 2,700-kilometer (1,678-mile) berm that runs through Western Sahara as the world’s longest continuous minefield, with thousands of victims of unexploded ordnance on both sides of the divide.Additionally, what happens to the Sahrawi refugees in camps within Algeria remains a big question. U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz cited the horrific humanitarian conditions in the Tindouf camps as part of his justification for the U.S. draft. On Monday, the speaker of Morocco’s upper house of Parliament urged camp residents to “return home,” but whether refugees will be allowed to return to Morocco—and what their status will be if they choose to do so—remains up in the air.Finally, there are fears that the region could see a resumption of violence. While the conflict has remained relatively calm, there have been periodic upticks in violence since 2020. Without the UN observers there to verify incidents or claims from either side, attacks become harder to confirm and easier to exploit. What will you be watching for in the coming weeks and months?On November 10 the UN General Assembly will meet to discuss the vote, giving Algeria and the Polisario Front a chance to make their case for self-determination before the full UN membership. I’ll be paying close attention to how the wider UN body responds. That meeting will come after Moroccan King Mohammed VI’s annual speech on Western Sahara. That speech takes place on November 6—the anniversary of the Green March, which opened the door for Moroccan control of the territory.We also have not yet seen what the Moroccan autonomy plan looks like in detail. I’ll be watching how Morocco plans to administer the territory and what the reaction of the international community—both those in support of the plan and those opposed—looks like once those details are public. articles.title: Tokenised stocks Q3 2026 report | CoinShares
articles.text: Tokenised stocks were worth $3.91B on 30 Sep 2026, up +842% year on year1. No other tokenised asset class came close. Over the same year, tokenised commodities grew +267%, tokenised funds +97% and stablecoins +4%1.A tokenised stock is a digital token, recorded on a blockchain, that tracks the price of a listed share or ETF. The Hybrid Finance Q3 2026 Update, produced by CoinShares with Token Terminal, finds that these tokens serve demand that already exists. Of the market's total value, 87.2% tracks US-registered shares and ETFs, and 85.4% is issued under terms that exclude US persons1. The typical buyer is an investor outside the US who wants exposure to US equities. Foreign investors already hold $24.3T of US equities2, and tokenised stocks equal just 0.016% of that amount.The market is also spreading out: Since September 2025, the number of issuers holding more than $1M of tokenised stocks has risen from 10 to 25.Over the same period, the number of underlying shares and ETFs above $1M has gone from 83 to 1721.Onchain holder positions reached 4.88M, 8.5x the level at the end of June1. Custody is the exception.One US broker-dealer, Alpaca Securities LLC, holds the shares behind 81.3% of the market, down from 94.6%1. The report names this as the market's largest single point of failure.The report's main argument is about policy. The US has the most influence, but no single country's decision is likely to stop the market growing. If US regulators support tokenisation, issuance can move into the US. The SEC's March 2026 approval of tokenised trading on Nasdaq points that way. If they do not, issuers in Jersey, the British Virgin Islands and the UAE already serve investors outside the US. If the US blocked tokens backed by US shares, demand would probably move to derivatives. Perpetual futures on US stocks traded on Trade.xyz already have $1.51B of open interest, the value of outstanding contracts1. Most tokens are backed by shares bought in the US, so Washington has an economic reason to prefer them over derivatives. For comparison, a BIS working paper finds that inflows into stablecoins lower 3-month US Treasury bill yields by 2.5 to 3.5 basis points3.Download the full report in PDF for the complete data, the breakdown by issuer and the risk indicators. If you would rather explore the charts yourself, the interactive version is at coinshares.research.tokenterminal.com.Download the report

articles.title: The outlook for inflation − speech by Clare Lombardelli
articles.text:
The outlook for inflation − speech by Clare Lombardelli

Given at the Sixth Biennial Conference on Macroeconomic Policy, Warsaw

Published on
24 September 2026

In this speech Clare sets out the outlook for inflation. She describes the framework the Monetary Policy Committee is using to monitor and learn how recent energy price increases will affect inflationary pressures. She considers the size and volatility of the energy shock, the response of the UK economy, and the underlying inflationary dynamics. Monetary policy is already leaning against the risk of persistent inflationary pressures and will be tightened further if needed.

Speech
It is an honour and a pleasure to be invited to speak to you today at the Sixth Biennial Conference on Macroeconomic Policy.
Policymakers often say we are dealing with an unusually uncertain time. And I will not disappoint you. The economy faces large and complex uncertainties: geopolitical tensions, global structural shifts and the rapid march of technology. The world is changing, and those changes are interacting, with significant implications for inflation.
Today I will discuss the global energy shock and its implications for inflation and monetary policy. I will first review the framework that the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is using to assess how the global energy shock is affecting UK inflation.footnote [1] I will then assess the near- and medium-term outlook before discussing what it means for policy, both through the lens of the Committee’s recent decisions and my own perspective. I have three main messages.
First, the main driver of near-term inflation is developments in global energy prices. The energy shock due to the conflict in the Middle East has already pushed up UK inflation, and we expect it to continue to do so in the coming months. There is significant uncertainty about how the conflict will develop, and so about the evolution of energy prices.
Second, the medium-term outlook depends on how the energy shock propagates through the economy through indirect, demand and second-round effects. The key judgement for monetary policy is whether emerging evidence suggests inflation may become persistent. This risk is cumulative. The longer energy prices remain high and volatile, the greater the risk for pass-through more widely into domestic wages and prices.
Third, given the uncertainty, policy decisions are necessarily made with incomplete information. As evidence emerges we will learn about the shock, its transmission, and the risks around these. We cannot offer firm guidance on the path of policy, but we can be transparent about the reaction function: this depends on how the shock evolves, how it propagates through the UK economy and what that implies for medium-term inflation.
The effects of a global energy price shock on UK inflation
A global energy price shock affects UK inflation through four channels: direct effects on household energy costs; indirect effects through firms’ production costs and supply chains; demand effects through real incomes and spending; and second-round effects through expectations, wages and domestically set prices. Table A summarises the mechanism, timing and potential policy response for each channel.
Table A: Global energy shocks can affect UK inflation through several channels

Channel

Mechanism

Typical speed

Effect on inflation
