articles.title: The PRA’s second decade − speech by Katharine Braddick
articles.text:
The PRA’s second decade − speech by Katharine Braddick

Given at Mansion House

Published on
22 October 2026

In her first Mansion House speech as Chief Executive Officer of the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), Katharine Braddick sets out her vision for the PRA's second decade. She outlines plans for a new five-year strategy centred on four priorities: resilience, growth, innovation and transparency, alongside a series of reforms to strengthen operational resilience, streamline regulation and improve regulatory processes for firms.

Speech
Lady Mayor, thank you for inviting me to speak this evening. It is an honour to address you and your guests and a pleasure to be speaking alongside Nikhil, who I have known for many years and who I look forward to working with in this new role.
When I joined the PRA in July I joined an organisation that in a little over a decade had succeeded decisively in its initial core mission, a mission that is vital to the success of the United Kingdom and its economy: to restore the resilience of the financial sector, so that it can properly support businesses and households across the nation.
Thanks to the work of the PRA, and significant effort by industry, that resilience has not only been restored but significantly strengthened. This hard-won stability is a source of advantage for our financial sector and this country, and it underpins our position as a leading and trusted financial centre. It is also the principal legacy of my predecessor Sam Woods: we might all wish to say we had achieved such a thing in our careers.
In that decade or so the world has also, of course, changed. Security threats increase, exacerbated by a more fractured geopolitical landscape. Interconnected financial vulnerabilities are arising from stretched sectoral valuations, rising sovereign debt levels and increased market leverage. Technology presents extraordinary opportunities and material and novel risks. And society demands accountability and transparency from its public institutions to maintain their legitimacy.
A new long-term PRA strategy
In this context, then, our task is to determine what the PRA must deliver in its second decade and how to create the regulator the UK will need for the future. Next year I will publish for the first time a five-year strategy for the PRA. The strategy will set out how we intend to deliver four priorities I believe are central for the PRA’s future success:
Resilience
The first priority is resilience. Maintaining the resilience of the UK’s banking and insurance sectors is the foundation of our mission; the PRA identified early on that the need to address operational resilience as well as financial resilience is a prudential matter. Addressing non-financial resilience is an ever wider and more complex task, not least as the frequency and materiality of cyber incidents grows. Firms need to continue to invest in their capabilities, not only to prevent incidents, but to ensure they can respond to and recover from severe disruption.
The PRA similarly needs to evolve. We will significantly increase our focus on firms’ operational and cyber resilience. The cyber challenge, in particular, is an area where we can and do partner effectively with industry and our international counterparts to progress our understanding of both risks and mitigants. We will create a new PRA directorate, reporting directly to me, to act as a centre of excellence for operational and cyber resilience. We will also consult jointly with the FCA on a new supervisory statement by the end of the year, clarifying our expectations of firms as we develop our experience and understanding.
Growth
Our second theme is growth. Achieving sustained and sustainable growth is the key economic policy question of this moment and regulation has its part to play, even if it is rarely the determinative factor.
In the coming period we will further develop our framework for the secondary competitiveness and growth objective. It will address not only the costs and benefits of regulation, but how our work influences the investment environment, the availability of capital for the firms we regulate and the pricing of the services they provide. We will set out how that framework is embedded in our day-to-day decision-making, and how we will track the effect our work is having on the growth and international competitiveness of the UK.
This framework will help ensure our regime remains relevant, effective, and proportionate. We will engage industry and Parliament as we shape, use and learn from it. It will enable us to be clear and confident about our role, and articulate a well-founded understanding of our contribution to the economy. This is not just a means to deliver against the secondary objective but is ultimately a foundation for good regulation.
Of course, the PRA has already taken steps to keep our regime up to date, most recently working with our FCA colleagues to devise a new captive insurance regime to enable innovation and growth in the insurance market. And to remove barriers to growth and provide predictability, we consulted earlier this month on a framework to automatically index our regulatory thresholds with nominal growth, a first among major financial regulators.
As a next step, we have today set out with the FCA a second set of significant reforms to streamline the Senior Managers and Certification Regime. These proposals reduce the number of senior management functions requiring pre-approval and remove requirements relating to the certification regime, halving its regulatory burden on firms whilst retaining clear accountability of their senior leaders.
Innovation
Our third priority is innovation. The PRA is a world-class regulator. To continue to be so, we must become a world leading technologically enabled regulator. Working with industry, we will go further in refining the data we collect and how we collect it to ensure we can react to emerging issues and risks in a timely manner, while shrinking the need for ad hoc collections and removing collections whose benefits are not justified. We will take feedback from you on this as we go, refining our approach and prioritising the changes that add the most value.
We will accelerate our deployment of data analytics and new technologies, enabling supervisors to rapidly identify emerging themes and trends in risks. Working with industry, we will make it easier and more efficient to work with us by taking innovative approaches to data collection and enhancing the clarity and accessibility of our rulebook and supervisory guidance, streamlining communications so that firms can quickly and easily understand what we expect.
Transparency
And our fourth priority is transparency. A sound understanding of the intentions and priorities of the regulator is crucial for firms to be able to effectively plan and manage their risks. And a stable and predictable business environment is essential to enable investors to deploy capital in the UK economy. So we will provide a clear and transparent line of sight to firms, Parliament and society about our plans and priorities, not least through the publication of and reporting on the new strategy. That will provide the means for us to be held accountable for meeting our commitments and demonstrate that we are a listening and learning organisation.
As an early example of this approach, we will take decisive steps to improve the experience of banks and building societies in relation to internal models for residential mortgages. This has been a source of particular difficulty for many firms, and we need to learn the lessons of this experience.
The PRA has already improved the approval process for firms, and we will go further by providing additional transparency about our operational performance. We will consult in Spring next year on material policy changes to improve firms’ access to a modelled approach. These proposals will be subject to challenge by an independent panel of industry and regulatory experts to ensure their feasibility, learning the lessons of the past to ensure our future policy is grounded in operational realities. Working with our colleagues in the wider Bank, we will also examine the interactions between hybrid mortgage models and stressed buffer requirements.
And we will conduct an independent review of the UK’s implementation of hybrid mortgage model requirements to identify tangible ways to assist firms as they maintain and develop their models. The work of that review will be sequenced to ensure it does not jeopardise the delivery of ongoing model approval and policy work.
Delivering the strategy
The delivery of our strategy will rely on the considerable strengths that characterise the PRA: our deeply expert and purpose-driven people; our comprehensive knowledge of the firms we regulate; and our established approach to supervision – judgement-led, forward-looking and focussed on key risks to safety and soundness. That work has underpinned the success of the PRA’s first twelve years and must never be taken for granted.
As we take the PRA into its second decade, we will build on our strengths and track record by evolving our approach to meet the challenges of today and of tomorrow. We will ensure the financial sector remains resilient to the increasingly volatile environment we now face. We will set out clearly and confidently how we contribute to growth. We will exploit technology to retain our position as a world-leading regulator and supervisor. And we will operate transparently to underpin confidence in our work and thereby in our financial sector and economy.
The PRA in 2032 will be a forward-looking regulator that is respected and trusted. A regulator that is recognised for its work supporting a resilient, competitive and innovative financial system that in turn supports a thriving UK economy. I look forward to working with my PRA colleagues, and importantly also with you all, to deliver that vision.
Now, would you please join me in raising a toast to the Lady Mayor and the Mayoral Consort.

Katharine Braddick
Deputy Governor for Prudential Regulation and Chief Executive Officer of the Prudential Regulation Authority

articles.text:
RETIRE WITH CONFIDENCE

CONFIDENT CONVERSATIONS®on Retirement

Get the retirement insights you need from the retirement leader who millions trust every day. This award-winning podcast1 equips you with knowledge, tools, and confidence to create the future you imagine. For over 50 years, T. Rowe Price has been asking questions to gain a deep understanding of investors’ retirement challenges and goals. See where our curiosity can take you.

Listen on Spotify

Listen on Apple Podcasts

Browse by season

Season 5

Season 4

Season 3

Season 2

Season 1

How can you set and reach both your short- and long-term financial goals? Determine the right time to claim Social Security, especially as a woman? Learn how ETFs can power up your portfolio? Discover a 360° view of tax planning in retirement? And find balance while caring for multiple generations?
Host Jessica Sclafani and our financial experts have you covered. Tune in to our fifth season, because your financial future deserves clarity. And you deserve to feel confident in every decision.

Episode 8

Staying Safe in a Digital World: How AI is Changing Financial Security and How to Respond

Host Jessica Sclafani talks with T. Rowe Price Chief Information Security Officer, Tom Quinn, and CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professional Lindsay Theodore, about how the malicious use of artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the world of financial fraud—and the tools to fight back. They discuss emerging threats such as deepfakes and AI-generated scams, the most common risks retirees may face, and how to recognize red flags before it's too late. The conversation also explores how AI is being used to strengthen fraud prevention, helping investors stay confident and secure in a rapidly evolving digital world.

Episode 1

How to Connect Your Savings With Your Life Goals –Now and in the Future

Balancing your desire to live fully today with the need to plan for tomorrow can feel overwhelming —but it doesn’t have to be. In this episode, host Jessica Sclafani sits down with CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professional, Stuart Ritter, and Retirement Strategist Rachel Weker to explore how to confidently save for short- to long-term financial goals. Whether you're setting aside money for a vacation, building an emergency fund, or planning for retirement, this conversation offers a practical and inspiring roadmap.

Episode 2

Social Security Planning for Women: Timing, Benefits, and More

Navigating Social Security can feel complicated—especially for women, who often face unique challenges like longer life expectancy, career breaks, and lower lifetime earnings. But with the right knowledge, it becomes a powerful tool for retirement planning. In this episode, host Jessica Sclafani sits down with CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professionals Stuart Ritter and Judith Ward, for a practical and encouraging discussion on how women—and their spouse if they have one—can make informed, confident Social Security decisions. From understanding benefit basics to timing strategies and coordinating with other income sources, this conversation is designed to help women feel more empowered about their financial future.

Episode 3

How ETFs Help You Defer Taxes - and Boost Long-Term Growth Potential

ETFs offer unique structural benefits that can help investors better manage taxes—especially in taxable accounts. In this episode, we break down how in-kind redemptions work, what makes some ETFs more tax-efficient than others, and what to look for when building a portfolio. You’ll hear practical guidance on how ETFs can support retirement income strategies.

Episode 4

Strategies to Balance Retirement Savings with Multigenerational Care

Caring for both children and aging parents—while planning for your own retirement— takes strategy and intention. In this episode, host Jessica Sclafani joins CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professionals Mycha Marshall and Emily Herstein to unpack the unique financial and emotional dynamics of the “sandwich generation.” From setting boundaries with adult children to planning for long-term care costs, this discussion provides practical strategies to help you stay in control and confident as you manage multigenerational caregiving and your own future.

Episode 5

360° Retirement Tax Planning: Minimize Lifetime Taxes and Extend Your Portfolio

Host Jessica Sclafani sits down with CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professionals Mycha Marshall and Roger Young for a 360° look at tax planning before and during retirement. Learn how to optimize withdrawals across different account types, tackle the Social Security “tax torpedo,” time Roth conversions, and manage RMDs. Plus, explore advanced strategies like Qualified Charitable Distributions and tax-loss harvesting, and walk away with practical steps to help minimize lifetime taxes and extend your portfolio.

Episode 6

Finding a Financial Advisor Who Shares Your Vision and Goals

Host Jessica Sclafani is joined by CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professionals Emily Herstein and Matt Spratt to discuss practical steps for finding the right financial professional. Building on our earlier conversation in Season 3 about the value of financial advice, they share what to look for when hiring an advisor, from credentials and communication style to trust and compatibility. Listeners will learn how a financial professional can help set clear goals, personalize your plan, and give you confidence in your financial decisions.

Episode 7

How Global Diversification Helps Manage Risk and Capture Opportunity

Host Jessica Sclafani talks with Som Priestley, CFA®, and CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professional Roger Young, about why international investing continues to play a vital role in a diversified portfolio. They discuss how global diversification can help manage risk, how global markets offer access to many of the world’s leading companies, and how behavioral biases like home-country and recency bias can affect decisions. The conversation also explores tariffs, currency effects, and how to stay globally balanced through market shifts.

Podcast Host

Jessica Sclafani

Jessica Sclafani is a global retirement strategist for the Global Retirement Strategy team. The team leads an enterprise retirement strategy, advises on new product development, and helps amplify the firm’s voice in retirement policy and thought leadership domains. Jessica is responsible for authoring original thought leadership that is designed to support the retirement objectives of retirement plan sponsors, consultants, and intermediaries in the U.S. and around the world. She is a vice president of T. Rowe Price Group, Inc., and T. Rowe Price Associates, Inc.

How can you protect your portfolio from inflation and uncertain markets? Unlock the power of your Social Security benefits? Prepare for housing and care in the second half of retirement? Or determine a drawdown strategy to fit your personal retirement income needs?
Host Kim Zook and our financial experts have you covered. Catch our fourth season now for insights to help you make confident decisions.

Episode 8

Common Retirement Savings Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

Retirement planning can be complex, and it's easy to make mistakes along the way. But with the right information, you can steer clear of these common pitfalls. Host Kim Zook is joined by CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professionals Judith Ward and Lindsay Theodore to discuss our experiences with retirement savings mistakes and how to avoid them.

Episode 1

Taking Advantage of 50 Years of Retirement Innovation Inspired by ERISA

401(k) plans are tax-advantaged accounts that remain the backbone of a retirement savings strategy. Host Kim Zook is joined by Michael Davis, Head of Global Retirement Strategy, and CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professional Roger Young to discuss the evolution, benefits, criticisms, and the future of 401(k) plans. 

Episode 2

Living and Long-Term Care Considerations for the Second Half of Retirement

Host Kim Zook is joined by CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professionals Molly Burton and Lindsay Theodore to discuss an essential topic for anyone approaching or already in retirement: planning for the mid-to-later years of retirement. This period, often filled with unique challenges and opportunities, requires thoughtful preparation and a clear understanding of your options. 

Episode 3

Navigating Inflation and Market Volatility: How to Help Manage Your Portfolio

When prices are rising and markets feel uncertain, making sound investment decisions may be overwhelming. In this podcast, we’ll discuss inflation and market volatility and provide you with practical strategies that can help you weather the storm. Host Kim Zook is joined by CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professionals Emily Herstein and Matt Spratt to discuss navigating inflation and market volatility. 

Episode 4

Don't Miss Out: Unlock the Power of Your Social Security Benefits

Host Kim Zook is joined by CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professionals Stuart Ritter and Lindsay Theodore to discuss Social Security and how it works overall, using some examples based on specific situations. The goal of this episode is to truly simplify the core of Social Security by focusing on what you need to know about the power and importance of Social Security as part of a retirement income strategy. 

Episode 5

Innovative Approaches to Tailoring Your Retirement Income Plan

Host Kim Zook is joined by CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professional Roger Young and Global Retirement Strategist Jessica Sclafani to discuss a critical topic for retirees: Personalizing your retirement income needs, solutions, and drawdown strategies. Whether you're gearing up for retirement, already retired, or simply interested in the current trends in retirement income planning, this episode is filled with valuable and insightful information you won't want to miss.

Episode 6

Adapting Your Spending Habits in Retirement: Why to Plan Ahead

Research shows that spending tends to decrease in retirement, but this decline isn't always steady and predictable. To prepare, you must adapt and develop plans to manage both essential and non-essential expenses. Host Kim Zook is joined by CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professional Lindsay Theodore and Sudipto Banerjee, Ph.D., Global Retirement Strategist at T. Rowe Price to discuss how thoughtful spending plans can lead to a more assured and satisfying retirement.

Episode 7

Traditional and Alternative Investments for Retirement Savings: The Unique Benefits of Each

Host Kim Zook is joined by Multi-Asset Portfolio Specialist Kathryn Farrell and CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professional Stuart Ritter to discuss the differences between traditional and alternative investments for your retirement, including what they are, how they work, and which might be right for your investment goals.

Podcast Host

Kim Zook

Kimberly Zook is the head of U.S. Intermediaries (USI) Retirement, leading the overall vision, strategy, and execution for defined contribution investment-only (DCIO) and insurance businesses. She is a member of the USI Executive team and the firm’s Retirement Leadership Council. She also is an active member of the business resource groups PRIDE, WAVE, and VALOR. Kim is a vice president of T. Rowe Price Group, Inc., T. Rowe Price Investment Services, Inc., and T. Rowe Price Trust Company.

Tune in to our third season for insights on the psychology of money, strategies to help you manage income in retirement, and the value of financial advice in your savings journey. Plus, the growing trend of unretirement: are you already retired but thinking about going back to work? Host Francisco Negrón and our financial experts break it down with clear perspectives and takeaways.
Explore all episodes here.

The Best of CONFIDENT CONVERSATIONS® on Retirement: Highlights and Insights Over the Years

Host Michael Davis takes listeners for a walk down memory lane with this “best of” episode, where we revisit some of the most impactful and inspiring clips from the past three seasons of T. Rowe Price's CONFIDENT CONVERSATIONS® on Retirement podcast.

How the Psychology of Money Influences Your Financial Behavior

How do our beliefs and attitudes toward money shape our financial behaviors, impact our financial well-being, and influence our retirement planning? Host Francisco Negrón is joined by T. Rowe Price experts—CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professionals Stuart Ritter and Matt Spratt—to discuss how the psychology of money influences our financial behavior and ways investors can cultivate a healthier and more empowered relationship with money on their journey to and through retirement.

“Unretirement”: Why Recent Retirees Are Going Back to Work

Have you already retired but are considering returning to work? You aren’t alone. Host Francisco Negrón is joined by T. Rowe Price experts—CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professional Stuart Ritter and Global Retirement Strategist Sudipto Banerjee—to discuss the unretirement phenomenon, along with factors to consider before transitioning back into the workforce.

The Value of Financial Advice: Is it Right for Your Savings Goals?

Are you considering soliciting financial advice but unsure if it’s worth the cost? Host Francisco Negrón is joined by T. Rowe Price experts – CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professionals Emily Herstein and Matt Spratt – to discuss the different ways that financial professionals can add value to your savings journey and how these benefits can outweigh the fees associated with their services.

Tax Planning Strategies to Help Maximize Savings To and Through Retirement

Taxes can be a complex and often overwhelming subject. In this episode, we will review the simplest and most accessible options that investors have in order to be more tax savvy. Our experts from T. Rowe Price discuss how the right knowledge and planning can help you make informed decisions to minimize your tax burden and maximize your retirement savings and financial well-being. Host Francisco Negrón is joined by Roger Young, CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professional and thought leadership director.

Women & Money: Aligning Your Financial Strategy With Your Motivation

Women face unique challenges when it comes to saving and investing. Host Francisco Negrón receives multi-generational insights from four T. Rowe Price financial experts to delve into actional steps and valuable advice to help guide women to determine what motivates them in life and how they can connect that with their financial strategy.

Retirement Income Planning: Building Financial Stability & Freedom

When it comes to planning for income in retirement, there is incremental value in developing a plan customized for your personal financial situation, because there is no one size fits all solution. Host Francisco Negrón is joined by T. Rowe Price CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professional Emily Herstein and Bill Meyer, head of Retiree Inc. to discuss how well-planned withdrawal strategies can help investors build financial security and enjoy their golden years.

Practicing Retirement: Maintaining Purpose & Thriving

Is the thought of transitioning into retirement overwhelming to you? It can help to think of retirement not as an end, but as a new beginning. Host Francisco Negrón is joined by CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professionals Sam Smith and Judith Ward to discuss strategies for setting goals and exploring new interests, insights, and inspiration to make the most of your retirement years and create a fulfilling and joyful post-work life.

Retire Early: Embrace Financial Freedom and Design Your Ideal Lifestyle

Retiring early is a dream for many, but it requires careful planning and a commitment to financial independence. Host Francisco Negrón is joined by CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professional Lindsay Theodore to discuss strategies, mindset, and financial considerations that can help you retire years ahead of the traditional timeline.

The Evolution & Impact of Target Date Solutions on Modern Investing

How much do you know about target date solutions? Host Francisco Negrón is joined by Head of Target Date Strategies at T. Rowe Price, Wyatt Lee, and CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER® professional, Stuart Ritter. Together, they unpack the world of target date solutions, one of the most popular investment vehicles designed to simplify the path to retirement. Topics covered will include the history of target date solutions, along with their purpose and benefits.

Desmintiendo los mitos sobre la jubilación

In this special Spanish episode of our CONFIDENT CONVERSATIONS® on Retirement podcast, host Francisco Negrón and T. Rowe Price financial professionals Natalia Garayoa and Pedro Rodriguez explore retirement and saving myths that are sometimes present among the Hispanic community.

As the war in Iran has sent shock waves through energy markets and the global economy, national oil companies (NOCs) in the Middle East have been in the eye of the storm. Neivan Bouroujerdi, Director, Corporate Strategy and Analytics Service, analyses Saudi Aramco, ADNOC and QatarEnergy, three of the giant NOCs in the region.
I asked him how they have fared through the turmoil, how the war is changing their strategies and the future appeal of Gulf resources to international oil companies (IOCs).
How has the war affected Middle East NOCs’ performance?
All Gulf-based NOCs took a production hit from export constraints over the past nine months, caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and damage to infrastructure. Alternative oil export routes that circumvent the Strait, however, have proved invaluable for some, effectively acting as an insurance policy. By getting their oil to market and capturing high prevailing prices, Saudi Aramco and ADNOC have generated US$35 billion more operating cash flow (OCF) in 2026 than we forecast at the start of the year.
That option was not available to producers further north, including Kuwait and Iraq. Nor is there any alternative shipping route for LNG. QatarEnergy (QE), the world’s biggest LNG producer, lost 17% of its liquefaction capacity to war damage and, with the Strait effectively closed since February, has exported only minimal cargoes to its customers. Its OCF is US$10 billion lower than we forecast at the start of the year, despite the start-up of its new 18-mmtpa liquefaction facility on the US Gulf Coast, Golden Pass.
What lessons have we learned from the crisis?
Building resilience into the system has leapt to the top of the agenda, with access to alternative export routes now a must for these export-dependent economies. The UAE is adding 1.5 million b/d to the capacity of its 1.8-million b/d pipeline to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. Saudi Arabia’s alternative export pipeline capacity could rise from 7 million b/d to up to 10 million b/d by 2030 – technically sufficient for all of its exports.
Geography, though, is (almost) everything. Qatar, Kuwait and Iraq face stiffer challenges to develop alternative liquids export capacity at scale. Gas presents additional complexity. Alternative routes for Qatar LNG exports would realistically involve cross border arrangements for gas pipelines and liquefaction infrastructure. Ceding sovereign control of critical parts of the value chain will come with significant risks and costs.
Will Middle East NOCs look to diversify overseas?
A strategy for some time, the rationale has been strengthened by the war, with gas and LNG at the forefront of their efforts. Government-to-government relationships are providing an increasingly important route to overseas opportunities. Leveraging existing partnerships with IOCs that operate with an NOC domestically, notably in the UAE and Qatar, has also proved to be another useful option.
• ADNOC: the strategy for XRG, ADNOC’s vehicle for international growth, is bold. Launched in December 2024, XRG has already built positions in the Americas, Africa and the Caspian. It is reportedly targeting a US$15 billion-plus US shale gas position and exploring a stake in LNG Canada. The announcement of XRG’s acquisition of Shell’s North West Shelf LNG stake earlier this month bulks up the overall portfolio to 22 mmtpa. If the ambitious goal of 47 mmtpa by 2035 is achieved, ADNOC would become the fifth-largest LNG supplier globally. And we could see further deals both upstream and downstream of these positions to support integration.
• Saudi Aramco: Aramco has been pursuing multiple international LNG opportunities, both independently and through its (now reduced) stake in MidOcean Energy, targeting 10 to 20 mmtpa of supply by 2030. To date, it’s secured two LNG sales and purchase agreements with US LNG projects, Rio Grande and Commonwealth LNG, and has ambitions to build further.
However, the biggest opportunity in LNG might be domestic. We estimate Aramco could have 6 bcfd of surplus domestic gas production early next decade, sufficient to support up to 40 mmtpa of LNG exports. At present, foreign participation in Saudi oil and gas production is not permitted, though domestic funding requirements and ambitions in gas may open up parts of the country’s upstream sector to strategic partners.
• QatarEnergy: QE recently signed up for 7 mmtpa of US LNG via deals with Cheniere and Woodside Energy – undoubtedly a response to events in the Gulf – and more deals are likely. Combining these deals with its 70% stake in Golden Pass makes QE the largest offtaker of US LNG, shoring up its LNG marketing position and playing to an existing strategy to diversify the LNG portfolio and build LNG trading capabilities.
QE has also leveraged its relationships with its domestic partners to build an exploration-led international upstream portfolio, one that could produce over 200,000 boed next decade. We expect organic investment and perhaps even M&A deals.
• KUFPEC: Kuwait Petroleum’s international business, KUFPEC, has been investing overseas for decades and produces around 80,000 boed. Even after recent deals to enter offshore Brazil and progress on the Lang Lebah gas project in Malaysia, more business development is needed to reach its target of 200,000 boed.
Do IOCs still want to invest in the Middle East?
Undoubtedly. Recent deals struck by ExxonMobil, BP and ConocoPhillips in Iraq, and BP and TotalEnergies' Bab Gas Cap deal in the UAE show the appetite is still there. Kuwait’s extension of enhanced technical service agreements to BP and Shell may be a precursor to offshore investment opportunities for IOCs.
Big Oil faces a longevity challenge, with declining production over the next decade. Discovered resource opportunities in the Middle East can help address at least part of the problem, offering access to significant long-life and low-cost reserves. And while returns are typically modest, we expect Middle East governments will be increasingly keen to attract investment in a competitive environment for capital.

BulletShares are a suite of defined maturity exchange-traded funds (ETFs) designed to help investors build targeted fixed income portfolios. Each fund holds a diversified basket of bonds that all mature in the same calendar year, helping investors target specific maturity timelines, risk preferences, and investment objectives. By combining the precision of individual bonds with the structural benefits of ETFs, BulletShares offer diversification, transparency, and liquidity. The funds typically distribute income monthly.

A bond ladder is built with individual bonds of varying maturities. As the bonds mature, the anticipated proceeds can be used for income needs or reinvested in new bonds that mature in subsequent years. Investors may use bond ladders to help create some predictability and stability regardless of market volatility and interest rate environments. Since they have specific maturity dates, investors can use BulletShares to build bond ladders without the time and expense of using individual bonds.

BulletShares can provide investors with an efficient way to establish potential protection from rising rates because the duration of the fund slowly rolls down to zero over the life of the ETF. Most traditional fixed income mutual funds and ETFs typically have a perpetual duration target, making them more sensitive to rising interest rates. Investors using BulletShares in bond ladders can also take advantage of rising interest rates by reinvesting the proceeds at maturity into BulletShares that mature in subsequent years and invest in bonds with higher interest rates.

BulletShares provide targeted exposure to investment-grade corporate bonds, high-yield corporate bonds, corporate bonds, municipal bonds and treasury bonds.

BulletShares have defined maturities to simulate the investor experience of buying and holding individual bonds to maturity for use in bond ladders and other strategies. BulletShares have designated years of maturities that are included in the fund’s name. Each BulletShares is designed to terminate in December of the designated year and make a final distribution at maturity. At each fund’s expected termination, the net asset value (NAV) of its assets is distributed to investors without any action on their part.

As BulletShares approach maturity, their durations decrease. In the last six months of the ETF’s maturity year, it is anticipated that the bonds in the portfolio will either mature or be called. Proceeds for these events will then be held either in cash or in cash equivalents such as US Treasury bills or commercial paper.

As your BulletShares mature, you may want to consult with an investment professional and explore having the distribution proceeds invested in a BulletShares ETF in a subsequent maturity year.

Title: Why build a bond ladder with BulletShares ETFs
Description: Our BulletShares ETFs offer a flexible and cost-effective solution to help you achieve your income goals now and — and in the future. Our Head of Fixed Income and Alternatives ETF Product Strategy Jason Bloom explains why.
Hello, I’m Jason Bloom head of the Fixed Income ETF Product Strategy team.
Having a flexible and resilient income strategy is crucial because markets are everchanging. Bond ladders are a solution and our BulletShares ETFs offer a convenient and cost-effective solution to implement a ladder to help you achieve your income objectives now — and in the future.
Here’s how.
Think of a bond ladder as a series of bonds on rungs on a ladder with each bond maturing at a different time. As each bond matures, you can use the proceeds to either meet specific financial needs — such as college tuition or an upcoming tax bill — or reinvest the proceeds into new bonds with longer maturities and maintain the ladder.
There are two key reasons why bond ladders can be advantageous:
First, they can provide a predictable and steady income.
Second, you have the flexibility to tailor your portfolio’s maturity and duration profiles and adjust for interest rate changes. If interest rates increase, you can reinvest any proceeds from maturing bonds at higher future interest rates. If interest rates decrease, only a segment of your laddered portfolio has to be reinvested during the low-rate period.
BulletShares ETFs can help make building bond ladders easier and more efficient. They have designated maturity years and cover a range of bond types, including investment-grade corporate, high-yield corporate, and municipal bonds. This allows you to build a bond ladder that matches with your financial goals.
They also combine the best of both worlds ­— the benefits of individual bonds and the advantages of exchange-traded funds.
Like individual bonds, BulletShares offer the potential for monthly income and a final distribution at maturity. You choose your portfolio’s maturity, yield, and credit quality.
As ETFs, BulletShares provide enhanced diversification, liquidity, transparency, convenience, and cost-effectiveness.
Whether you’re looking to generate steady income, customize your portfolio, or insulate against interest rate fluctuations, BulletShares ETFs provide a robust and versatile tool for building bond ladders.

Global Investment Views

9 November, 2026

16 minutes

Global Investment Views - November 2026

EDM

Global Investment ViewsEN

Global Investment Views - November 2026

16 minutes

EDM

Global Investment ViewsEN

Summary

Shifts to quality and scarcity

Recent weeks have seen a reassessment of risks across energy markets, fiscal space, artificial intelligence-related (AI) stocks and emerging markets. Investors are increasingly favouring businesses with strong balance sheets, pricing power and exposure to structural supply constraints. In energy markets, the geopolitical premium appears more apparent, reflecting tighter and more expensive supply routes, rather than a temporary disruption. Although energy prices have retraced, this premium is likely to stay for some time. In equities, we are witnessing a rotation out of AI-related stocks. Markets are scrutinising the earnings potential and cash flows from the massive capital expenditure on AI. In addition, the Democratic sweep in the mid-term elections has raised concerns about closer examination of AI, Big Tech and data-centre development.Government bond yields initially rose to levels not seen in years, but Treasuries eventually regained their safe-haven appeal. Core European bonds also benefited from a flight to quality.This could, however, change, particularly amid a growing market focus on energy prices, monetary and fiscal policy, and the evolution of the AI narrative. We discuss these points below:The second round of energy shock and inflation risk. Oil markets have shifted materially, with rerouting implying that effective supply is currently around 80% of pre-Iran-war levels. We expect prices to remain elevated through year-end before gradually easing over H1 2027, as transport conditions normalise. Gas markets face tighter constraints, as rerouting options are more limited. The inflation pass-through is becoming increasingly evident, and this second wave of energy price increases could prove more persistent. The key risk to monitor is second-round effects via wages and services inflation.

While AI remains a compelling long-term productivity theme, markets are now seeking clearer evidence of cash generation and are differentiating more carefully between likely winners and losers.

Higher-for-longer rates. This remains the dominant narrative across yield curves. The short end continues to reflect central bank policy tightening, or signals of further action. As inflation is expected to remain above target across most developed countries, the Fed will likely hike once in December and possibly again in early 2027, before staying on hold for the rest of 2027. We also expect the ECB to raise rates once in December and again in early 2027. The long end of the curve in most developed countries is likely to remain under pressure from fiscal deficit concerns. Additionally, competition for capital may weigh on long-dated bonds, primarily via real rates, as investment and issuance may continue to outpace savings.Fiscal policy in Euro Area. Europe’s fiscal framework is facing its toughest test since the post-pandemic overhaul of the Stability and Growth Pact. Policymakers face an increasingly difficult trade-off between public backlash and the need for fiscal consolidation, creating an incentive to delay the latter. The broader risk is credibility erosion, with widening European sovereign spreads suggesting that investors are scrutinising debt trajectories more closely. Looking ahead, the key question is whether the institutional framework can hold under the combined pressure of monetary tightening and fiscal strain.AI trade dispersion amid higher rates and power bottlenecks. AI-related investments are becoming increasingly differentiated. Investors are becoming more cautious about higher interest rates, power constraints and the lack of near-term returns from large capital outlays. Weak IPO performance, project delays and rising credit default swap costs for AI-linked companies all point to cooling sentiment.Emerging market fragmentation. We believe the developing world is becoming increasingly fragmented, with a split between commodity exporters and importers. Some idiosyncratic risks are also emerging and we continue to monitor events in Brazil and Indonesia.

Amundi Investment Institute: Building portfolios that adapt to a changing world Portfolio construction guidelines: In a supply-driven environment, where supply constraints matter more than demand, investors should focus on scarce assets. Many commodities markets are likely to remain structurally undersupplied. In equities, this includes scarce resources such as rare earths, as well as sectors linked to supply constraints, such as AI infrastructure, defence, aerospace and energy. In bonds, preference should be given to countries with low debt-to-GDP ratios, given the risk of oversupply in more indebted economies.

Image

Monica DEFEND

Head of Amundi Investment Institute & Chief Strategist

In a multipolar world, where supply chains are being rewired for security rather than efficiency, careful selection and diversification are increasingly important.

Below we have outlined our views on asset classes: In fixed income, we have marginally raised our constructive stance on Eurozone duration, favouring peripherals over core and retaining a steepening bias. We are also positive on the UK. However, in the US and Japan, we remain close to neutral. EM bonds remain attractive, and we are increasingly selective, favouring countries with strong external finances. In credit, we prefer global and EU IG as well as higher-quality yield opportunities.In equities, we maintain a balanced approach, combining defensive sectors with quality cyclical stocks and a focus on balance sheet strength. We remain positive on Europe and Japan over the long term, and constructive on EM, where earnings remain supportive, despite widening divergence. From a multi-asset perspective, we see rotation opportunities emerging in favour of the US and Japan. At the lower-risk end of the spectrum, we are positive on US and European duration, as well as euro investment-grade credit. Secondly, in EM, we have become more constructive on both local-currency and hard-currency EM debt. In FX, we raised our tactical view on the BRL. Overall, our stance is well diversified through gold while we also see a need for bond hedges.Overall, we maintain a mildly risk-on stance, with an emphasis on diversification and selectivity amid volatility, while paying close attention to portfolio construction.

Rising geopolitical competition is likely to tighten supply chains, create scarcity and, over time, generate opportunities across economies, reinforcing the case for a global, diversified investment approach.

FIXED INCOME

Constructive and flexible amid high rates

Amaury D’ORSAYHead of Fixed Income

Resilient economic data on both sides of the Atlantic keep the macro backdrop constructive, but sticky inflation and elevated energy prices make the path of oil and gas the key variable for rates. In the US, the Fed remained on hold in October but still has accommodation to withdraw. The central bank’s patience should not be mistaken for complacency. The ECB also held rates steady amid higher energy prices, and tighter financial conditions, leaving the door open to further action.Looking ahead, we remain constructive on duration, albeit selectively, and continue to prefer short- to medium-maturity bonds over the long end.

In the US, we remain close to neutral on duration, with a preference for intermediate maturities. Long-end yields look attractive, but we would only reduce our cautious stance gradually, given persistent fiscal risks.In the Eurozone, we are marginally more positive on duration, while retaining a preference for curve steepening and peripheral debt. We remain positive on UK duration, supported by Budget reassurance and QE adjustments.In Japan, we are neutral, with a flattening bias.

Although credit spreads have widened recently, they remain range-bound at low levels, with demand for high-quality fixed income continuing to offset heavy supply. Dispersion is increasing across sectors, making selectivity more important. We remain positive on global and EU investment-grade credit. Within the latter, we favour subordinated bonds, short-dated maturities and corporate hybrid debt.At sector level, we prefer financials, telecoms, technology and pharmaceuticals.

Tactically, we have marginally upgraded our view on the USD due to Fed policy and higher US real yields. Long term concerns over debt and deficit remain. On the euro, we are less cautious than before owing to improved economic activity. In EM, we stay positive on corporate and sovereign HC debt, with a regional preference for LatAm and commodity exporters. Brazil stands out in HY credit. In LC bonds, we see selective opportunities in Hungary and South Africa, while EM FX is attractive in LatAm and Central and Eastern Europe.

EQUITIES

A balanced approach in volatile times

Barry GLAVINHead of Equity Platform

Global economic momentum has remained resilient, but fragilities persist. Concerns over heavy AI spending, sticky inflation and persistent geopolitical risks are some factors likely to shape trends in corporate earnings. This has led to higher volatility in rates and is affecting equities. In this environment, we aim to generate higher long-term returns through fundamental, bottom-up analysis. We are avoiding expensive tech mega-caps, preferring to remain balanced. We favour markets such as Europe and Japan, which offer better risk-adjusted returns. While we favour EM over DM, returns are becoming increasingly selective, supporting the case for idiosyncratic opportunities.

Globally, we maintain a balanced approach, combining defensive sectors with industrials and materials. Europe is attractive in terms of valuations, and we are focusing domestically. But we remain alert to the risk of an energy shockIn Europe, the AI theme is broadening. Industrials and utilities are benefiting from capex in power infrastructure and rising AI-driven electricity demand. The tight supply of critical minerals needed for grids and networks is supporting higher mineral prices and benefiting the metals and mining sector. We are also exploring structural winners, such as selected French industrials, where current share prices do not reflect the true earnings potential.In Japan, we like industrials exposed to supply-chain resilience, infrastructure and AI. Regional banks are attractive, as consolidation could act as a catalyst.

While we favour EM over DM, we recognise that US AI capex is becoming increasingly important for companies in some countries, leading us to be selective.Over the long term, the digitalisation of global economies should benefit North Asia and South Korea also stands to benefit from expectations of strong dividend growth under the “Corporate Value-Up” initiative.In China, where we are neutral, earnings remain uncertain due to overcapacity in many industries. If exports weaken, the government may adopt a more proactive fiscal policy. In Latin America, we are positive on Brazil, although President Lula’s victory was a surprise. We are now closely monitoring any early signs of pragmatism from the political leadership.

MULTI-ASSET

Rotation supported by earnings strength

Francesco SANDRINICIO Italy & Global Head of Multi-Asset John O’TOOLEGlobal Head - CIO Solutions

The economic backdrop remains resilient, with growth holding up despite higher rates, sticky inflation and geopolitical uncertainty. Markets have repriced aggressively, particularly in rates, while credit spreads have widened. Although liquidity conditions have modestly deteriorated, they remain benign. We maintain a moderately pro-risk stance by remaining selective and seizing tactical opportunities created by excessive market moves. We have balanced this by adding protection in asset classes such as European bonds, which may be more susceptible to near-term newsflow.In equities, while our overall views have not changed, we see opportunities to rotate away from Europe (downgraded to neutral) toward the US (upgraded) and Japan (upgraded). We believe the US could continue to perform if earnings and capex remain supportive, while Japan offers a more diversified sector mix than Europe, with less direct exposure to financials. We see a strong long-term case for Europe. while in EM, our stance is positive on LatAm.We retain a constructive duration view in the US and Europe (Schatz and Bunds). We also like Italian BTPs, given the country’s fiscal deficit trajectory and strong domestic demand. EU IG credit is another area where underlying fundamentals remain strong. Elsewhere, EM bonds offer attractive carry and, we have upgraded our view. We are now constructive on a select group of local bonds following recent market moves and have turned more optimistic on EM spreads.In FX, we are slightly cautious on the USD, but constructive on select EM FX, which offer attractive carry. In particular, we have turned more positive on BRL in the near term after the recent repricing. Finally, we now see potential for hedges in euro bonds and remain positive on gold.

VIEWS

articles.title: Food prices climb as conflicts and El Niño tighten grain supplies
articles.text:
Published on
Data Blog

Food prices climb as conflicts and El Niño tighten grain supplies

John Baffes

Dawit Mekonnen

Kaltrina Temaj

November 12, 2026

This page in:

English

English

According to our latest Commodity Markets Outlook, global grain supplies are projected to decline in 2026-27 while inventories tighten, increasing the risk of higher food prices and food insecurity. / Image: Shutterstock

This blog post is part of a special series based on the October 2026 Commodity Markets Outlook, a report published by the World Bank Group. This series features concise summaries of commodity-specific sections extracted from the report. Explore the full report here.

The World Bank Group's food price index eased in October after reaching a three-year high in September but remained 15 percent above its year-earlier level. Grain prices surged 9 percent in 2026Q3 (q/q), driven by attacks on Black Sea shipping and ports, dry weather in major grain-exporting countries, and the early effects of a very strong El Niño. Maize and wheat prices rose 8 and 13 percent, respectively. Oils and meals edged down in the third quarter but remained 17 percent higher than a year earlier, supported by biofuel demand. The World Bank Group’s food price index is projected to rise by 10 percent in 2026 and 7 percent in 2027, with risks tilted to the upside.

Global grain supplies are set to shrink for the first time in four years. According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s November update, global grain supply, including production and beginning stocks, is projected to fall by about 20 million metric tons (mmt) in 2026–27. Even so, supplies would remain the second highest on record, limiting upward pressure on prices. Wheat faces the strongest headwinds, with global output projected to decline by 2 percent. U.S. output is projected to drop by 23 percent to its lowest since 1970–71, and Ukraine’s exports are expected to fall by 18 percent. Global maize and rice production are also expected to decline, by 3 and 2 percent, respectively, with rice posting its first drop in a decade as El Niño weighs on Asian harvests.

Edible oil supply growth is slowing just as biofuel demand surges. Global edible oil supply is projected to grow by 2.7 mmt in 2026–27, well below the long-term average annual increase of 5.7 mmt, partly because of the ongoing very strong El Niño. Meanwhile, demand for soybean and palm oil as biofuel feedstocks continues to rise, supported by elevated energy prices, record U.S. biofuel volume requirements, and Indonesia's increase in the palm oil share of biodiesel blends from 40 to 50 percent. The World Bank Group’s oils and meals index changed little in 2026Q3 (q/q) but was still 17 percent higher than a year earlier.

Declining global inventories leave markets more exposed to shocks. The global stocks-to-use ratio for maize (a measure of inventories relative to consumption) is projected to fall to 21.5 percent in 2026–27, its lowest level since 2012–13, though still well above its 2010–11 low of 13.2 percent. Ratios for wheat and rice are expected to edge down to 34 and 37.2 percent, respectively, while the ratio for edible oils is set to fall to 12.5 percent, its lowest since 2009–10. These tight buffers could amplify the price effect of weather or trade shocks.

Food price inflation is picking up, threatening recent gains against hunger. Median food price inflation in emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) rose to 3.9 percent (y/y) in 2026Q3 from 3.5 percent in 2026Q2. It reached 7.4 percent in the World Bank’s Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan region, and reached 122 percent in the Islamic Republic of Iran. Meanwhile, severe food insecurity fell from 837 million people in 2021 to 779 million people in 2025, aided by a 21 percent drop in global food commodity prices during this period. With prices projected to rise a cumulative 18 percent in 2026–27, that tailwind is set to become a headwind.

Food prices are set to keep rising, with risks tilted to the upside. The World Bank Group’s food price index is projected to rise by 10 percent in 2026 and 7 percent in 2027, before easing by 5 percent in 2028. Grains are forecast to rise by 14 and 9 percent and oils and meals by 17 and 8 percent in 2026 and 2027, respectively. Prices for other food items are expected to remain broadly stable in 2026 and edge up in 2027. Risks remain tilted to the upside: stronger-than-expected effects of El Niño, prolonged Black Sea hostilities, export restrictions, higher energy prices, and stronger biofuel demand. Under a scenario of prolonged conflicts and stronger El Niño effects, the food price index would exceed the 2027 baseline by 12 percent and would also surpass its 2022 level.

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesThe MarketsHow Will Higher-than-Expected Inflation Data Impact the Fed's Next Rate Decisions? Nov 13, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyYouTubeAppleDownload TranscriptWhile a smaller hike remains more likely, October’s hotter-than-expected inflation data may open the door to a 50-basis point rate hike at the Fed’s December meeting, says Muhammad Qubbaj, co-head of North America Interest Rate Product Sales and Trading in Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities. A recent drop in oil prices is unlikely to give the Fed cover to look past the CPI number without becoming more aggressive in the inflation fight, Qubbaj says on this episode of The Markets podcast. He also explains why his base case is for the 10-Year Treasury yield to remain below recent highs.
Transcript:
Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Thursday, November 12th, and we're here on the Goldman Sachs trading floor with Muhammad Qubbaj, who is co-head of North American Interest Rate Sales and Trading within FICC and Equities. And today, we're going to talk about how a hot CPI print this week is impacting rates and bonds markets, and how that has a carryover effect to other markets around the world.
Q, thanks so much for joining us.
Muhammad Qubbaj: Thanks for having me.
Chris Hussey: Okay, Q, let's start with the CPI print. It came in hot this week. What did you make of the market's reaction? How do you think the Fed is going to respond?
Muhammad Qubbaj: Well, there's no rest for the wicked when you look at the sources of volatility in the market, whether it's geopolitics, whether it's the Fed, whether it's AI.
We felt we almost had a little bit of a respite, maybe for five minutes, and all of a sudden CPI comes to the forefront and changes the board a little bit, too, and the Fed walks right back into the building. CPI affected us in three ways. First, I would say that it was unacceptable number, .3, third time in a row.
Strong across all categories. The Fed has to reckon with that number, and the market priced that accordingly. Two, it wasn't just about the CPI level, it was about the Fed reaction function. We woke up that morning, Waller had made a speech and put 50s back on the table. He basically asked a question, and CPI answered.
He said, "Contingent on .3, 50s could be on the table." And-
Chris Hussey: And by 50s on the table, what you mean is that we could do a hike of 50 basis points, not 25.
Muhammad Qubbaj: Exactly. So it just, again, underscored a hawkishness to the Fed and opened up the distribution to 50s, which was definitely a surprise that morning, before we even walked in and got the CPI number.
The third thing was we spent almost a month executing a hike compression. We took out almost 50 basis points of hikes in the next one year, and some of this is a give back. So in terms of the market reaction, unwind of positioning and the high compression, a reaction to the strength of the CPI, the third one in a row and a re-understanding of the Fed's reaction function and opening up the distribution for 50s.
Chris Hussey: All right, so it wasn't trivial. That's interesting. But you also talk about a Fed reaction function, and one of the things they have to react to is oil, I would imagine, because, this was an October report, but for the month of November, oil prices are now down 15%. How does oil factor into the rates market?
Muhammad Qubbaj: We can't basically say that the causality between oil and rates is a one-for-one thing. They're definitely a participant. They definitely have a feed through to CPI, and they definitely show up into, basically, core CPI and how the Fed takes that number so that they can adjust policy.
But, the sell-off wasn't just about oil when we had the big sell-off in the year. At one point it was about corporate earnings and growth. At another point it was a debate on the Fed reaction function uncertainty because they removed forward guidance term premium on the back of bond supply and CapEx supply, convexity hedging or the convexity profile of the market where we saw a lot of selling and positioning.
Oil coming off in the last couple of weeks is definitely affects the level of rates, but you can't expect a full refund just based on the oil movement.
Chris Hussey: Okay. Another thing that's changed since that October CPI print was the midterms. We got the midterms in early November. How does a change in Congress, if at all, have any impact on the rates market?
Muhammad Qubbaj: I think a couple of things. One is the Fed's not a political body. It should not affect the Fed path, first order. It affects oil, obviously, based on the vote on the geopolitical outlook of the Iran war. Midterms affect oil, CPI affects the Fed. We've had almost triple the move based on the CPI morning print that we did in rates for the entire of midterms week. So I think that's where the focus is.
Chris Hussey: Okay, Q, let's expand the conversation to 10-year bond yields. They have such an impact across markets. We were up at 5.3% not too long ago. They've come back to 5%. Are the conditions still in place, though, for us to eclipse the recent highs?
Muhammad Qubbaj: You have to look at basically what took us to the peak in rates. There were several different factors. One, we had this new reaction function from the Fed, no forward guidance, the debate on how the Fed's reaction function will evolve under a Warsh leadership.
You had the debate on term premium. You had the debate on Government issuance compounded by AI CapEx-related supply. You had a positioning situation in the market. You also had convexity selling in the market. All of those things contributed to the sell-off. So, I don't think that you're going to have that same set of circumstances reassert itself on the market again and push yields to the high, high level that we saw in October.
Furthermore, you have two new breaks in the system: a Fed that is actively hiking, a hike lands in the front end but flattens the curve. Two, we had some sort of reflexivity that's been put onto the market in Warsh's last speech. He specifically tied the level of rates to the level of AI CapEx financing.
So what happens when you do that is basically saying that you have a self-balancing system. If rates go up too much, then it can slow down the AI CapEx build-out, and it will almost have a self-balancing system from that perspective. But let us remember that if -- Do I think it's going to be a rate sell-off can happen again driven by positioning or term premium or supply worries or convexity selling?
No. If we have a reassertion of strong earnings and I think that can give us some room.
Chris Hussey: Yeah, a little bit of a growth-driven thing. Can I ask you to define one thing? Convexity selling, what is that?
Muhammad Qubbaj: Convexity selling is a situation where, as the market sells off, people have more to sell.
At its core, it means as things are getting worse, your flows are going to make it even worse.
Chris Hussey: Right. It's a little technical factor. All right, let's talk about the competition between stocks, bonds, and credit.
Cause that's always part of the equation here, I would imagine. How do you see that shaping up here? You talked about the growth equation being such a big one for where yields go from here.
Muhammad Qubbaj: When we look at yields as it pertains to credit and as it pertains to equities, we have to look at it from a couple of lenses.
What drives higher yields? Is it growth? Is it earnings? Then that should be good for the credit complex, and should be good for the equity complex. Is it driven by term premium worries and a supply absorption worries? Then you have a capital markets problem, and that's where they could be negative for equities, and it could be negative for credit.
That's one factor. The other factor is the amount of leverage that we're talking about. When you're looking at a bond that is a corporation that is on the lower side of the spectrum of leverage, then higher rates affects the discount factor. When you look at a bond that's on the other side of the leverage spectrum, higher rates is a funding bill.
It's a funding problem. So you can't... You have to be a little bit more nuanced when you say how do higher rates affect the equity market or credit market. It's a function of how did we get there, and how levered are the companies that we're talking about? And that's basically where you get your answer.
Chris Hussey: All right, lot to digest. Let's put a bow on it. What's the trade?
Muhammad Qubbaj: I like to think of it from a serenity prayer perspective.
Chris Hussey: Ah, the serenity prayer.
Muhammad Qubbaj: Accept the things you cannot change. It is a one-factor market.
It's all about mega-cap tech. Once you accept that, you realize that's the bet you're going to be making. Now, where do you have control? Where can you make some changes on the edges? One is how much of a size of a position you're going to take. It depends on how you hedge your portfolio. Two, the amount of leverage and what's the expression you take on mega cap to see basically how much exposure you have and how much factor risk you have.
So we have discussed the risk. Now let's discuss the hedges. When you look at the hedges, you basically have out-of-the-money dollar puts. You have out-of-the-money equity puts. Delta one is favorable in the level of rates. A combination of those, you can build a carry neutral or positive carry hedge portfolio, and you can size it up and down depending on the amount of risk and leverage you're taking on the mega-cap tech.
Now, you wanna own the factor, and you wanna rent the insurance.
Chris Hussey: And by owning the factor, you want to own stocks.
Muhammad Qubbaj: Yes.
Chris Hussey: And by renting the insurance, you wanna maybe own some puts as well.
Muhammad Qubbaj: Exactly.
Chris Hussey: All right, what are you looking for in the weeks ahead?
Muhammad Qubbaj: Three sources of volatility we mentioned in the market. Oil, let's continue to see how the geopolitical, situation unfolds. The Fed, we are going to look at Fed speak and the Fed minutes and basically try to read the tea leaves and to see how hawkish the Fed is right now so we can get a feeling for the size.
While, we're confident on the direction of which way the Fed is going. It's about size and timing right now. And the third factor is the AI economy. Anything, whether it's a capital market situation or an earning situation, anything that can continue to give us confidence or allow us to re-rate the level of risk in the market as it pertains to the AI economy.
Chris Hussey: That's terrific. Q, you're always just a fountain of knowledge for us. Really appreciate you joining us.
Muhammad Qubbaj: Thank you for having me.
Chris Hussey: That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: Daily Navigator
articles.text:
13 November 2026
Daily Navigator

Download Report

Key highlights
Overbought USD signals suggest gains may slow: The USD index (DXY) rose 0.3% to 103.17, its highest since April 2025, as markets priced a more hawkish Fed path. October consumer inflation beat expectations. Markets fully price a 25bps December hike, with slim but growing odds of a 50bps increase. The 10-year US government bond yield rose above 5.10%, while the 2-year yield reached 4.87%. President Trump said Washington “does not need a deal with Iran”, sending oil sharply higher and adding to inflation concerns. DXY is nearing overbought territory, with resistance at 103.5. We open a bullish XAU/USD idea at USD 3,910/oz, expecting central bank demand and geopolitical hedging to limit downside.
A support break opens the way for EUR/USD to reach 1.0873: EUR/USD fell to a 19-month low of 1.1046, extending its slide from above 1.16 in late August. The widening US–Euro area rate gap has weighed on the pair as Fed hike expectations have outpaced ECB repricing. EUR/USD broke below the 1.1065–1.1105 support zone, and momentum remains bearish. Next major support is at 1.0873. We close our bullish EUR/USD idea after it reached the neutral level of 1.1080.
Intervention risk is likely to cap near-term USD/JPY gains near 160: USD/JPY hit 159.95, its highest since 2 September, amid broad USD strength. Japan’s top currency official Mimura warned that “the currency moves over the past few days have been too fast” and “it’s too early to forget what happened this summer”, likely referring to summer intervention. BoJ board member Asada pushed back against early tightening, warning that premature hikes could hurt growth. We initiate a conditional bearish USD/JPY idea with a target of 155.2. The idea would be triggered if the pair rises to 160.40.

articles.title: KPMG 2026 Technology and Telecommunications CEO Outlook
articles.text:
Boardroom questions

Growth outlook

Leader perspective

Our insights

As AI accelerates, the stakes are rising

Technology, media and telecoms CEOs remain confident about the growth prospects for their businesses. But beneath that confidence, the forces shaping the next phase of growth are becoming more complex. AI is moving rapidly from experimentation into the heart of business strategy. But greater adoption is also increasing the pressure to prove returns, strengthen cyber resilience, navigate a changing regulatory environment, manage growing infrastructure and energy demands, and rethink how people and AI will work together.The KPMG 2026 Technology, Media & Telecoms CEO Outlook explores how leaders are responding to this new reality, and where they are planning on capitalizing on growth opportunities. The findings show technology CEOs pursuing the economics of AI, media CEOs navigating changes in how content is created and distributed, and telecoms CEOs considering how connectivity, data and customer relationships can support higher-value services.

Where TMT growth is taking shape

Technology CEOs have the strongest growth expectations and 28% expect to see AI returns within six months. But as the capital required to scale AI rises, the bigger question is whether that investment can translate into sustainable returns.

AI is changing content creation and discovery and the relationship with audiences, while raising questions around IP, provenance and trust. With 62% of media CEOs calling for greater AI regulation, protecting the value and credibility of content is becoming a commercial imperative.

Seventy percent of telecoms CEOs already report significant or transformational measurable value from AI, even though most expect returns over a one-to-three-year horizon. The opportunity now is increasingly about translating that value.

The findings point to a new phase for TMT. AI ambition is clear. The question now is whether companies can prove the economics, secure the infrastructure, strengthen resilience, manage energy demand and build the workforce required to turn technological change into sustained growth.

articles.title: Can good management keep primary health centers open in crises?
articles.text:
Published on
Let's Talk Development

When Crises Hit, Can Good Management Keep Primary Health Centers Running?

Kathryn Andrews

Fabiano Dal Ri

Roberta Gatti

Renata Lemos

Mario Macis

November 12, 2026

This page in:

English

English

When crises hit, management quality, specifically operational practices that keep a facility organized and responsive, can help private primary health centers continue to provide services. | © Shutterstock.com

In low- and middle-income countries, primary health centers (PHCs) are often people's first point of contact with the health system. They provide everything from treatment for common illnesses to chronic disease care, immunization, family planning, and maternal and child health services. When a pandemic hits or health workers strike, some facilities stay open and others close. For the communities they serve, that can mean the difference between getting care and going without. A World Bank Policy Research Working Paper asks whether better management helps public and private PHCs keep services running during major disruptions.

How the Question Was Studied
The study adapted the World Management Survey for use in a low-resource health care setting. The survey measures structured management practices on a scale from 1 to 5, covering areas such as patient flow, inventory management, use of standardized protocols, performance tracking, review of goals, and staff management. In 2021, 429 PHCs and 73 hospitals across Kenya were surveyed, covering both public and private providers. At around the same time, Kenya faced two major shocks in quick succession—the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020 and a national public health workers' strike between December 2020 and January 2021.
To assess whether management quality affected facility performance during these shocks, the survey data was linked to administrative records from Kenya's Health Management Information System, which tracks monthly outpatient attendance at health facilities. This made it possible to compare how attendance diverged over time—before, during, and after the disruptions—across facilities with different management scores and different ownership types.

What the Research Found

PHC’s adoption of structured management practices is limited in both public and private sectors. Kenya's PHCs averaged a management score of just 1.61, well below comparable benchmarks in India (1.87), Brazil (2.20), and the United States (3.11)—and most were clustered near the bottom of the scale.

Figure 1. Distribution of Management Scores in the Health Care Sector

Ridgeline chart of management score distributions for 11 groups. Averages range from 3.11 in the US down to 1.87 in India. Kenya's primary health care facilities (average 1.61) and hospitals (1.59) sit below every other country, and their scores are tightly bunched, with standard deviations of 0.17 and 0.14, compared with 0.41 to 0.66 elsewhere. Kenya's density curves peak at 2.6 and 3.1, against 0.6 to 0.9 for the other countries.

Note: Management scores on a scale of 1 to 5. Management scores are calculated with a comparable set of dimensions across surveys (Layout of the Patient Pathway; Standardization and Protocols; Continuous Improvement; Performance Tracking; Performance Review; Balance of Goals; Interconnection of Goals; Clarity and Comparability; High-Performance Evaluation; Removing Poor Performers). Facility-level management scores are a simple average of included dimensions. SD = standard deviation; N = number of facilities; PHC = primary health care facility.

Private PHCs were better able to maintain services than public ones during disruptions. Both public and private PHCs experienced attendance declines during the first year of COVID-19. During the public health workers' strike, however, the gap widened: public PHC attendance fell while private PHCs remained comparatively stable, consistent with patients shifting toward private providers when public facilities were disrupted.

Within the private sector, better-managed PHCs maintained services more effectively. A one standard deviation increase in management score was associated with 6.5 percentage points higher outpatient attendance during disruptions, relative to the period before. The practices that mattered most were operational ones—managing patient flow, tracking supplies, following protocols, and using data to spot problems early. These systems help managers respond before disruptions translate into missed care. People-management practices, such as hiring, performance evaluation, and staff incentives, were less strongly associated with attendance differences during crises.

In public PHCs, better management did not translate into the same ability to maintain services. This does not mean management is irrelevant in the public sector. It suggests that management practices may be less useful when managers lack the autonomy, tools, or resources to act on them when crises hit.

Figure 2. During disruptions, better management is associated with higher outpatient attendance in private PHCs—but not in public PHCs

Two-panel chart of quarterly coefficients, 2019 Q2 to 2021 Q4, relative to t minus 1 (2019 Q4). In private primary health care facilities, better management is associated with higher outpatient attendance from 2020 Q3 through 2021 Q1, peaking at about 0.065 in 2021 Q1 during the health workers' strike, with confidence intervals above zero in those quarters. In public facilities, coefficients after the start of COVID-19 stay close to zero, between about minus 0.01 and 0.02, with confidence intervals that include zero.

Number of PHCs: Public = 260. Private = 91. The analysis is restricted to a shorter time period to alleviate data availability constraints and improve statistical power.

Three Lessons for Policymakers
1. Management is not a "soft" issue. In essential service delivery, operations management—tracking supplies, managing patient flow, having data-driven meetings—can determine whether a PHC continues to deliver services when crises hit.
2. Institutional context matters. Strengthening management in public PHCs needs to consider the institutional context, such as whether managers have real authority, adequate resources, and flexibility to respond.
3. The private sector needs to be part of the strategy. Rather than treating public and private health care as separate, mixed health systems should account for the complementary role private facilities already play during disruptions and consider how to regulate and integrate this role more deliberately.

The Bottom Line
When crises hit, management quality – and specifically the operational systems that keep a facility organized and responsive – can help PHCs continue to provide services.
Private PHCs can absorb patients when public systems are unable to do so, and so health planners can no longer afford to treat the two sectors as unrelated. Building primary health care systems that are able to maintain services during crises means investing in management, reforming institutions, and integrating the private sector—ideally well before the next disruption arrives.

The authors would like to thank Lydia Nakhone, a co-author of the research paper on which this blog post is based, for her contributions to the project, particularly her collaboration on the fieldwork, insights into the Kenyan context, and efforts to facilitate engagement with local agencies.
