articles.title: First Meeting with a Financial Advisor | Wells Fargo Advisors
articles.text:
Day One With Your Financial Advisor

Preparing for your first meeting

Your first meeting with your Financial Advisor marks the beginning of an important professional relationship. Just as you rely on your doctor with your health and your mechanic with your car, you’ll be entrusting your Financial Advisor with something of great value too — your financial goals.

call out

Your Financial Advisor will want to know you as a person — not just as a client.

end call out

Our Financial Advisors work with many types of investors and value their diversity. Your Financial Advisor will want to know you as a person — not just as a client — so he or she can understand the best way to help you with your investment needs and life goals.

The right fit

Meeting with a Financial Advisor for the first time, you should expect a friendly, casual conversation — you’re just getting to know each other. There’s no obligation, no pressure, no judgment — and no cost for your first meeting. You should be candid about your level of investing experience, overall financial situation, and financial goals. You should also feel comfortable asking as many questions as you’d like.
It’s important you choose a Financial Advisor who listens to your concerns, understands your financial needs, and values your input. The relationship between you and your Financial Advisor is a critical one — through the years, you should have many sensitive, private conversations. The relationship may even expand to include friends and future generations of your family.

Getting ready

Before the meeting, your Financial Advisor should send you a checklist of items to bring. Your privacy is a top priority, and your Financial Advisor is committed to maintaining strict confidentiality.
A good Financial Advisor will want the right fit for you as much you seek the right fit in him or her. Before your first consultation, you’ll want to reflect on and be prepared to discuss:

Your values about money and your vision for your future
What life events are happening or could potentially happen
Short- and long-term life and financial goals
Investment questions
Your current financial situation
Preferred account management style

Remember, the more you share about your financial picture, investment goals, and risk tolerance, the better your Financial Advisor will be able to recommend strategies and create an investment plan. You’ll find the initial meeting with your Financial Advisor will set the stage for many conversations to come.

Next steps

Think about how you prefer to work with your advisor and what types of investments you’re interested in.
Gather the necessary documentation for your initial meeting and prepare answers to questions your advisor may ask.

Prime money market funds are a type of mutual fund that invests primarily in corporate debt and other taxable short-term securities, such as commercial paper, certificates of deposit, and asset-backed commercial paper.

Ultrashort and short-term bond funds are investments that hold debt securities with short maturities, typically less than one year for ultrashort funds and one to three years for short-term funds. (Photo by Orhan Cicek/Anadolu via Getty Images)CommentaryEmissaryCOP31 and the Future of Climate ClubsAs the United States exits UN climate efforts, these smaller and less formal groupings will take on greater significance in global climate governance.Link CopiedBy Theodore Zaritsky and Stewart PatrickPublished on Nov 5, 2026On November 9, delegates from nearly 200 nations will meet in Antalya, Türkiye, for the annual UN climate conference, COP31. They will gather for the last time before the United States becomes the first country to leave the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)—the 1992 treaty that underpins climate diplomacy—and the only one left outside. Previous U.S. presidents have denounced landmark accords, notably the Kyoto Protocol in 2001, but none abandoned the convention beneath them. Now, the country that has polluted the atmosphere more than any other, and that produces more oil and gas than any other, is backing out of not just a deal but the multilateral framework for making any deal at all.This refusal of even the premise of global cooperation comes at a perilous moment. In October, UN experts judged that breaching the 1.5 degree Celsius threshold set under the Paris Agreement in 2015 is now “imminent and unavoidable.” Few governments are rallying, and in January 2025 the United States repudiated the Paris Agreement altogether. Warming at this pace will push some 2 billion people beyond the temperatures in which humans have historically lived, expose tens of millions to coastal flooding, and force tens of millions more from their homes.Even so, little may be lost from this untimely departure. No one else is following America out of the convention, and some argue that a future president could rejoin as easily as President Donald Trump withdrew, because the Senate’s original consent still stands. Until then, the burden falls on a vanguard of nations to do what the lumbering United Nations cannot: to pioneer ambitious action. The success of such coalitions and clubs depends on how well they withstand duress, as the United States moves from politely shirking its duty to brashly spoiling their endeavors. Already GoneDeserting the UNFCCC, set for February 2027, is a formality. Last year, the United States sent no delegation to COP30 in Belém, Brazil; stopped paying its dues, about a fifth of the convention’s core budget; and rescinded $4 billion in pledges to the largest multilateral fund for climate projects in developing countries. The intent was clear even earlier: In 2017, during his first term, Trump considered withdrawal from the UNFCCC before he announced the first U.S. exit from the Paris Agreement, and Project 2025, the blueprint for a second Trump term, called for junking the convention as “inimical to the prosperity of the United States.”The standard model of climate cooperation, which treats emissions cuts as a global public good, predicts that when one party’s cheating goes unpunished, others will realize that they, too, can free ride. Yet no other country has taken the Trump administration’s dumping of “radical climate policies” as a cue to do the same. In fact, neither the UNFCCC nor the Paris Agreement enforces any cuts, so quitting them frees a country from almost no obligation while forfeiting a seat at the table where the targets are set. The one leader tempted, President Javier Milei of Argentina, has so far held back, as the cost of leaving would come due under a trade deal with a strong club of climate-committed countries: the European Union tied its agreement with Mercosur, Argentina’s South American bloc, to staying in the Paris Agreement.Forum of All, Groups of SomeWhile the annual COP summit still draws the lion’s share of media attention and commentary, governing increasingly happens in focused, minilateral groups, alongside or entirely apart from that universal forum—comprising a “varied array of narrowly-focused regulatory regimes.” There are two main types of groupings: coalitions, where countries are each better off contributing on their own, so agreement is loose and informal, and clubs, where at least one member is better off withholding their contribution, so agreement requires binding commitments tied to receiving the benefits of cooperation. In the eight years after Paris, such small groups multiplied fivefold.Most are coalitions, setting goals and sharing lessons, such as the Global Methane Pledge, the Powering Past Coal Alliance, and, among private actors, the now-defunct Net-Zero Banking Alliance. The G7’s hollow Climate Club, like these, has no punitive measures after Germany’s pitch for a common carbon price and border tax collapsed. A few, however, are clubs in more than name, punishing defectors or outsiders with fines or trade restrictions, such as in the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol and, among subnational actors across borders, California and Québec’s cap-and-trade system, which Washington state is set to join. The clearest example is the European Union, whose market now comes with a charge on carbon-heavy imports.The choice between coalition and club comes with trade-offs. To ensure legitimacy, coalitions are open, often decide by unanimity, and ask little of their members, which makes them easy to form but easy to block—a flaw the UNFCCC shares. To act boldly, clubs are closed, often decide by majority, and ask much of their members, which makes them hard to block but hard to form. COP30 President André Corrêa do Lago acknowledged the virtues of each form of cooperation, advising countries to work at “two complementary speeds,” through broad consensus that is “deliberative and slow by design” to set a legitimate target, and through narrow groups to get there.A country’s commitment to a coalition or club lasts only as long as its support at home. In democracies, that support depends on a contest between those who profit from pollution, such as oil and gas producers, and those who gain from cutting emissions or suffer from them, such as clean-energy manufacturers and coastal property owners. That contest explains the Trump administration’s strategy: by backing the polluters abroad, it can unmake climate commitments where they were made.From Shirker to SpoilerThe United States increasingly prefers spoiling, preventing others from paying their share, to shirking, merely refusing to pay its own. The de facto U.S. exit from the UN climate regime last year removed a member that sometimes haggled to shirk its share, but it did not ease talks. Rather, the next holdouts in line just stepped up, exploiting consensus rules to obstruct cuts even without the United States. Seeing little point in scuttling a ship already aground, the Trump administration is turning to press the clubs whose commitments actually bind American corporations.The U.S. government is intervening in the strongest climate club, the EU, by “cultivating resistance to Europe’s current trajectory within European nations,” as outlined in the 2025 National Security Strategy. This year, the State Department offered nearly $5 million in grants to European groups contesting “supranational bureaucratic overreach,” which covers climate regulation. Leaning on European governments is neither new nor partisan, but no recent presidency has done so as broadly or as brazenly as this one. In 2012, President Barack Obama’s administration urged the EU to suspend carbon charges on international flights and channeled the dispute toward a multilateral deal. Now, the Trump administration is holding up multilateral deals, including a carbon price on shipping, by threatening sanctions, visa restrictions, and port fees. The White House found ready allies in Greece and Cyprus, home to two of Europe’s largest shipping fleets, in a vote last year to postpone any deal. Headlines about American retreat from multilateralism are a sideshow to the United States’s spoiling from within.Clubs Bend, Coalitions BreakBrandishing Europe’s reliance on U.S. energy, the Trump administration has bent but not broken the EU as a climate club. The August 2025 U.S.-EU trade framework tied a European pledge to buy $750 billion of U.S. energy to promises to address American concerns about the carbon-border adjustment mechanism, deforestation regulation, and corporate sustainability due-diligence directive (CSDDD). Those rules have given way only where domestic lobbying strained them before U.S. interference stressed them further.Against the CSDDD, the United States worked alongside American companies operating within EU member states. A European Commission official described “direct calls from the American ambassador and other U.S. agencies” intent “on killing the directive.” In 2025, a handful of firms, including Chevron, ExxonMobil, and Koch, assigned themselves to lobby specific governments in order to “divide and conquer in the Council” and kept “close ties” with U.S. diplomats. In February 2026, the EU adopted a revised, much narrower CSDDD. “The wish list of American oil majors has been copy-pasted by the Commission,” said Lara Wolters, the European parliamentarian who led the original law.Against the EU’s methane rule for imports, the United States worked through the EU members leading the resistance. As one U.S. oil executive explained: “It’s only when we couldn’t make any progress there that we turned more towards the [Trump] administration to say, ‘Can you help us?’” In the spring, U.S. cabinet officials discussed the rule with ministers from Czechia and Slovakia, and over the summer, U.S. diplomats raised the issue with senior officials from Austria and Germany, which then joined the opposition. In July, a German nonprofit reported that every U.S. embassy in Europe had been instructed to lobby for the rule’s abolition. In October, the European Parliament voted to delay the import requirements by three years, “bowing to pressure from the fossil fuel lobby and blackmailing from the Trump administration,” according to Jutta Paulus, a lead negotiator on the rule.Under U.S. pressure, the club’s rules have only bent—being diluted or delayed. Coalitions, in contrast, break easily because defection costs little. Private coalitions are the extreme case: nothing binds members, and U.S. legal reach lets opponents raise the cost of staying for any firm with large American operations. In 2022, nineteen state attorneys general began investigating the six U.S. banks in the Net-Zero Banking Alliance. All six quit after Trump’s reelection, and the remaining members dropped the alliance’s 1.5 degree Celsius requirement to stem the exodus, but the coalition disbanded in October 2025 anyway. The Global Methane Pledge, another fragile coalition, launched by the United States and the EU in 2021, will likely outlast a White House that dismantles its own methane rules, but not one that turns to spoil the pledge itself.This is the paradox of club cooperation: enforcement makes a group strong but also creates internal losers that external spoilers can employ. A binding rule is most at risk when it concentrates costs on organized groups and spreads benefits thinly, and safest when the winners are organized too.After AntalyaCOP31, and the annual conferences that follow, will likely reinforce the centrality of coalitions and clubs in global climate governance. The EU will be among the most central, making rules its trading partners must accept to access its market. But any group of countries able to commit credibly, despite opposition at home, can form a club to hold one another to those commitments. The growing agency of “middle powers” in Europe and across the Global South may sustain multilateralism despite superpower abdication or obstruction, but their clubs remain assailable by divide-and-conquer tactics.What makes clubs resilient—their binding rules—also makes them vulnerable. International regimes rarely collapse when a great power defects, as the UNFCCC shows, but they do erode when one plays spoiler. Clubs will persist only where the winners of climate policy compensate its losers, across the club and within its members, and they need to pay up before the United States starts funding their opponents.Get more news and analysis fromEmissaryThe latest from Carnegie scholars on the world’s most pressing challenges, delivered to your inbox.About the AuthorsTheodore ZaritskyJames C. articles.title: Consumer resilience
articles.text:
Weekly UpdatesAs the Gulf war drags on, wage growth is struggling to match the pace of inflation. US civilian wages rose 3.1% y/y in the third quarter. Consumer prices are currently rising by 3.7%. European wages are growing faster than inflation, but not by much. Consumers have reduced how much they save each month to help cover higher prices.However, alternative income streams have been growing in importance. In 2025, the used clothing website Vinted sold EUR 10.8bn of second-hand goods. That is the same as what Belgians spent on clothing last year. Income from such side hustles add to consumers’ spending power and are a mitigating factor that labor market data overlooks.Aging populations also change the importance of wage growth. In the US, the contribution of paid employment to household income fell below 60%—the only time it has done so, aside from the pandemic. Pension income is more significant. The rise of self-employment means that proprietors’ profits, rather than wages, play a larger role in supporting spending power.The resilience of consumer spending in the face of rising prices owes much to changing savings behavior. But some of the resilience comes from the fact that wages matter less than they used to as a driver of spending power.

articles.title: What share of public services employment is contributed by the private sector?
articles.text: What share of public services employment is contributed by the private sector?Prepared by Afonso S. MouraPublished as part of the ECB Economic Bulletin, Issue 7/2026.Public services have been a notable contributor to aggregate employment growth in the euro area in recent years. Since the COVID-19 pandemic employment has grown faster in the public services sector than most others, increasing this sector’s share in overall euro area employment. By the end of 2025 its share was around 0.8 percentage points higher than in 2019 and almost as high as when it peaked in 2021.[1] See Consolo and Dias da Silva (2022) for a detailed characterisation of public services employment during the pandemic and other previous recessions. ,[2] The 2021 peak was largely mechanical. While other sectors experienced significant declines in early 2020, public services employment held relatively steady, before returning to strong growth following the pandemic. Over the last three years public services have contributed disproportionally to employment growth in the euro area, accounting for more than one-third, despite representing less than one-quarter of total workers (Chart A, panel a). This box analyses that contribution from two perspectives. First, it identifies health as the dominant driver within public services and argues that this reflects a structural trend. Second, it shows that a significant share of employment in public services, particularly in health and social work activities, is in fact provided by the non-public sector, as ageing demographics are fuelling demand for residential care and social work. The importance of the private sector in providing public services puts the increasing contribution of public services to employment growth – and the associated perception of a growing public sector – into perspective. At the same time many of the public services jobs in the private sector may be partly funded by the state, for example through social transfers in kind or long-term care insurance. Therefore the findings concern who employs these workers, rather than the overall fiscal footprint of public services.Chart ASectoral breakdown of employment growtha) Total employment growth and sectoral contributions(percentage changes in total, percentage point contributions by sector)b) Total growth in public services workers and sectoral contributions(millions of workers)Sources: Eurostat, Eurostat’s EU Labour Force Survey and ECB staff calculations.Notes: Panel a) shows cumulative growth in total employment relative to the fourth quarter of 2022. Public services includes the NACE one-digit statistical classification for the sectors “human health and social work activities”, “education” and “public administration and defence”. “Market services” is defined as all other sectors not included in “public services”, “agriculture” or “industry”. Panel b) shows cumulative growth in total public services employment relative to 2008. Sectoral contributions follow the NACE one-digit classification.Health has been the dominant driver of growth in public services employment, reflecting a structural trend rather than a cyclical factor. Within public services, the category “human health and social work activities” has been the largest contributor to employment growth in recent years. Its average annual growth of around 2% over the last three years is well above the 0.8% recorded for “public administration and defence” and 1.2% for “education”. This is not a recent phenomenon. From 2008 to 2025, the number of workers employed in public services grew by around 6.9 million, of whom 4.8 million – nearly 70% – were engaged in “human health and social work activities”.[3] Over the period 2008-19 the average annual growth rates for employment in health, education and public administration stood at around 1.8%, 1.0% and -0.3% respectively, confirming that the stronger employment growth in the health sector predates the pandemic. “Education” contributed more modestly, while employment in “public administration and defence” remained virtually flat (Chart A, panel b). This trend was repeated across the OECD countries, in which employment in the health and social work sector grew at roughly twice the pace of the rest of the economy over a similar period and amounted to some 11% of total employment in 2023.[4] See OECD (2025b) for the latest trends among OECD economies. It is far more common for health services to be privately provided than services in public administration or education. Public services are not necessarily publicly provided – a distinction that matters for how we interpret employment trends in the sector. Drawing on the ECB Consumer Expectations Survey, around 85% of respondents working in “education” or “public administration and defence” report having the public sector as their institutional employer (Chart B, panel a). This stands in sharp contrast with “human health and social work activities”, where fewer than 40% report working for a public employer (Chart B, panel b). Since these shares are relatively stable over time, they can be used to approximate the public sector contribution to overall growth in public services employment.[5] The questions on employer type were included in the ECB Consumer Expectations Survey from 2022 onwards. We compute the average public sector share within public services sub-sectors for the period 2022-26 and apply these shares to labour force survey employment data going back to 2008. It is worth noting that this exercise assumes that the public-private split for new jobs is similar to that of the existing stock of employment and that the mix of public and private provision has remained broadly unchanged since 2008. Applying the respective shares to each sub-sector, only around half of the 6.9 million public services jobs created since 2008 can be attributed to the public sector, with the remainder attributable to other types of providers (both private and non-profit making). Within health and social work alone, this suggests only around 1.9 million of the 4.8 million jobs created are likely to be on the public payroll. As many new jobs were on the payrolls of private and non-profit making entities, the number of public sector workers relative to total employment has broadly stabilised after falling from its 2021 peak. There is, however, significant variation across countries: the public sector share among those employed in human health and social work activities ranges from roughly 64% in Finland to around 30% in Germany and Belgium. This suggests that the share of the public sector in health-related employment growth varies considerably across the euro area.[6] The evidence for Finland is consistent with the high share of general government employment in Nordic countries, see OECD (2025a). ,[7] The country differences are also corroborated by expenditure data as broken down according to the Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG). In Germany, for instance, health expenditure – comparable across countries as a share of GDP – relies predominantly on social transfers in kind rather than compensation of employees, which is consistent with hospitals being mainly market-based providers. Chart BEmployer types – respondents to the ECB Consumer Expectations Surveya) “Education” and “public administration and defence”b) “Human health and social work activities”(percentage contributions)(percentage contributions)Sources: ECB Consumer Expectations Survey and ECB staff calculations.Notes: Results are weighted to represent the full population rather than only the survey sample. The relevant survey question asks respondents: “In which sector do you currently work? If you have more than one job, please consider the job in which you work the most hours per week.” This survey question is asked annually in the May topical module on the labour market.Residential care and social work for the elderly and disabled have been growing considerably, reflecting an ageing society. Within the category “human health and social work activities”, growth since 2008 has not been evenly spread. It has been more concentrated in residential care and social work, which gained over 2.6 million workers, than in human health, which covers more traditional areas of medical activity and gained around 2.1 million workers. Looking at the data in more detail – specifically at the three-digit NACE level – reveals that the bulk of the growth in residential care and social work is accounted for by activities directly connected with ageing – i.e. those activities related to care of the elderly and disabled (Chart C, panel a).[8] The elderly and disability-related care sectors are defined by the sum of the sub-sectors Q873 (“residential care for the elderly and disabled”) and Q881 (“social work without accommodation for the elderly and disabled”). Cross-country evidence is broadly consistent with the finding that economies with larger increases in the share of the population aged 65 and above tend to record stronger employment growth in these activities (Chart C, panel b).[9] It is worth noting that this is a conservative characterisation, since societal ageing may also be partially driving employment growth in other health activities not included here. Ageing societies are therefore not only reshaping the demand for health services, but also seeing this increase, to a large extent, take place outside the public sector. Private providers are absorbing a large share of the demographically driven demand for these workers.Chart CEmployment related to elderly and disabled carea) Residential care and social work employment growth and contributions(percentage changes in total, percentage point contributions by sector)b) Change in elderly and disabled care-related employment and share of older population(x-axis: percentage points; y-axis: percentage change)Sources: Eurostat, Eurostat’s EU Labour Force Survey and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel a) shows cumulative growth since 2008. As NACE three-digit statistical classification data are not available for some countries as of 2008, their contribution is allocated to “Other” when unavailable, effectively making the orange and yellow bars conservative estimates. In Panel b), changes are calculated from the first year for which elderly and disabled care-related employment information is available and up to 2025. The pattern holds when including only those countries with data available from 2008 onwards. “Share of older population” is defined as the percentage of the population that is aged 65 or older.Societal ageing is driving lasting growth in public services employment, much of it outside the public sector. Not all employment in public services should be attributed to the public sector: a considerable share of the jobs created in health and social work – the main driver of the growth observed in public services employment – are, in fact, in the private sector. Taken together, only around half of the 6.9 million public services jobs created since 2008 can be directly attributed to the public sector. Moreover, the increase in this type of employment appears to be a long-run structural trend, closely linked to societal ageing, and one that is expected to continue.ReferencesConsolo, A. and Dias da Silva, A. (2022), “The role of public employment during the COVID-19 crisis”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 6, ECB.OECD (2025a), “Government at a Glance 2025”, OECD Publishing, Paris.OECD (2025b), “Health at a Glance 2025”, OECD Publishing, Paris. See Consolo and Dias da Silva (2022) for a detailed characterisation of public services employment during the pandemic and other previous recessions. The 2021 peak was largely mechanical. While other sectors experienced significant declines in early 2020, public services employment held relatively steady, before returning to strong growth following the pandemic. Over the period 2008-19 the average annual growth rates for employment in health, education and public administration stood at around 1.8%, 1.0% and -0.3% respectively, confirming that the stronger employment growth in the health sector predates the pandemic. See OECD (2025b) for the latest trends among OECD economies. The questions on employer type were included in the ECB Consumer Expectations Survey from 2022 onwards. We compute the average public sector share within public services sub-sectors for the period 2022-26 and apply these shares to labour force survey employment data going back to 2008. It is worth noting that this exercise assumes that the public-private split for new jobs is similar to that of the existing stock of employment and that the mix of public and private provision has remained broadly unchanged since 2008. The evidence for Finland is consistent with the high share of general government employment in Nordic countries, see OECD (2025a). The country differences are also corroborated by expenditure data as broken down according to the Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG). In Germany, for instance, health expenditure – comparable across countries as a share of GDP – relies predominantly on social transfers in kind rather than compensation of employees, which is consistent with hospitals being mainly market-based providers. The elderly and disability-related care sectors are defined by the sum of the sub-sectors Q873 (“residential care for the elderly and disabled”) and Q881 (“social work without accommodation for the elderly and disabled”). It is worth noting that this is a conservative characterisation, since societal ageing may also be partially driving employment growth in other health activities not included here.

articles.title: Daily: Using structures to stay invested in stocks while limiting risk of loss
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:The AI sell-off and US midterms: Live at the UBS Disruptive Tech Summit (6 mins)
CIO Live Replay: CIO Asia equity strategists on the AI sell-off and opportunities (30 mins)
Circle One Jumpstart: What next for tech volatility, quality bonds, and oil prices? (4 mins)Thought of the dayAsian stocks started the week on a stronger footing as concerns over artificial intelligence investment and Middle East risks eased. The MSCI Asia-Pacific index excluding Japan rose 2%, Japan’s Nikkei 225 gained 3.5%, and Taiwan’s benchmark rallied more than 6%. The moves followed Friday’s recovery on Wall Street and a decline in oil prices as prospects for progress in US-Iran negotiations improved.The rebound should be viewed in the context of last week’s declines. Selling was centered on semiconductors and other AI-linked companies as investors reassessed the profitability of infrastructure investment, the funding of data center expansion, and the potential for greater regulatory scrutiny following the US midterm elections.We believe the recent technology sell-off represents a positioning reset rather than the start of a structural downturn in the AI investment cycle. But the rebound does not remove the risks created by concentrated positioning and elevated expectations. Investors whose technology exposure has grown beyond its intended portfolio weight may therefore wish to use periods of market strength to rebalance, lock in some gains, and diversify across sectors and regions.But certain types of structured strategies, sometimes known as capital preservation strategies, may provide a middle path for those who believe stocks can rise further but want greater peace of mind against an adverse outcome.They combine potential loss limitation with participation in potential equity gains. Such approaches typically combine a zero-coupon bond with call options on an equity index or another underlying asset. The bond component is designed to return the predefined investment amount at maturity, subject to the issuer meeting its obligations, while the options provide participation in potential market gains. This can help investors retain equity exposure without assuming the full potential losses of a direct investment.They can be tailored to an investor’s objectives and risk tolerance. The maturity, level of capital preservation, underlying asset, and participation rate can be adjusted. Investors may therefore replace part of a concentrated or linear equity position with a structure that more closely matches their tolerance for losses, investment horizon, and future spending needs. A blend of notes with different maturities and underlying assets can also help balance capital preservation and growth.Predefined outcomes may make it easier to remain invested through volatility. Sharp market swings can encourage investors to sell after prices have fallen or remain in cash while waiting for a more attractive entry point. By defining the loss limit and potential participation in advance, capital preservation notes can reduce the temptation to react to short-term market moves. They may be especially useful for investors with concentrated portfolios, substantial accumulated gains, lower drawdown tolerance, or a desire to add equity exposure more cautiously.These potential benefits come with important trade-offs. Capital preservation generally applies only at maturity, and an early sale may generate a mark-to-market loss. Participation in gains may be limited, investors do not receive dividends from the underlying equities, and repayment depends on the creditworthiness of the issuer. Liquidity, product complexity, and the effect of interest rates and option prices on the participation rate also require careful consideration.So, we expect further gains for broad equity markets over the next six to 12 months, supported by resilient economic activity and broadening earnings growth. We recommend maintaining diversified core equity exposure while reducing concentrated single-stock positions.

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesGoldman Sachs Chief Economist Jan Hatzius Joins CNBC to Discuss the US Jobs Report and the Economic OutlookNov 6, 2026ShareThe recent stronger-than-expected employment report indicates a stable labor market, according to Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Jan Hatzius. He joined CNBC to discuss his views on the data and his outlook for the year ahead.
Transcript:
Host: Welcome back. The October jobs number came in hotter than expected: nonfarm payrolls rose by 165,000, above nearly every forecast. Joining us is Jan Hatzius, Goldman Sachs Chief Economist, to discuss the report, the midterms, markets, data centers, and more. Jan, it is great to have you.
Jan Hatzius: It is great to be here.
Host: There is nothing wrong with this number, I assume you agree. Do you think it marks the beginning of something new?
Jan Hatzius: Definitely nothing wrong with it. It is a very solid report, certainly as far as payrolls are concerned. There is some month-to-month volatility, but we think the underlying trend in job growth is probably back above 100,000. That is more solid than it was earlier in the year.
What we are not seeing is sustained downward pressure on the unemployment rate. It edged down a little, but it has remained in the 4.1% to 4.2% range. To me, this still looks like a labor market that is stable at about full employment. We think it will probably stay roughly in that range over time, which remains consistent with relatively subdued wage growth and low inflation.
Host: How low can claims get? Are we scraping the bottom of that historic range?
Jan Hatzius: It is the lowest we have seen in a series that goes back more than five decades. Layoffs are at extremely low levels, which is consistent with what we see in other indicators.
Hiring continues to be relatively subdued as well, so we have not really seen a major pickup in hiring. It is still a more stagnant environment, but at a very solid level.
Host: The markets this week have been rethinking the possibility of a more elongated buildout cycle. Does that lead you to lower your nominal GDP estimates for next year?
Jan Hatzius: We are growing at a very rapid pace right now. GDP numbers fluctuate, but we are talking about growth with a three-handle in the second and third quarters, and likely in the fourth quarter as well.
I do think growth will be softer next year. We have thought that before, but we have not made a change to our underlying growth estimate. We think it is probably in the 2% to 2.5% range, which should keep the unemployment rate roughly stable.
There are some downside risks to that growth outlook. We have seen tightening in financial conditions of about 50 basis points according to our index. There are also questions around energy prices, the war with Iran and its implications for real income growth, as well as the AI buildout and its effects on both GDP and the labor market.
But our baseline remains relatively stable growth.
Host: Goldman also closely monitors increases in enterprise efficiency from AI use, or at least expected productivity gains. Where are we now, and what are your expectations for 2027?
Jan Hatzius: We have seen some effects on the labor market, mainly in the technology sector. That has been worth roughly 10,000 to 15,000 fewer jobs per month in employment growth.
There are some indications that this is broadening into the service sector. For example, we have begun to see a correlation across service-sector industries between employment growth and unemployment rates on one hand, and AI adoption on the other.
But the relationship is still not particularly strong, and you would not expect it to be if you looked at overall labor-market outcomes. Over the next year or two, I think that relationship will probably strengthen. By 2028, it is likely to become somewhat more of a headwind for employment growth.
I have a fair amount of conviction that AI will be more of a macroeconomic story by 2027, though the timing remains one of the open questions.
Host: That could also affect profit margins.
Jan Hatzius: Yes, although at the moment it is clearly still a tailwind.
Once we get into 2028, you would expect the volume of investment to flatten out, and eventually investment spending will come down. That is what tends to happen in historical investment booms: infrastructure is built out, the necessary capital stock is achieved, and investment then begins to decline.
That is probably still some way off, but there is, of course, substantial uncertainty around the path.
Host: We are glad we will have you around for 2027 and 2028. I hope we will speak many times.

articles.title: FinCEN Bars U.S. Institutions From Moving Funds for MEXC Global
articles.text:
Summary
Under Operation Economic Outcast, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) issued an order blocking U.S. financial institutions from sending funds to or receiving funds from MEXC Global, a centralized exchange ranked among the world’s twenty biggest.
The activity spans Russian sanctions workarounds, dealings connected to Iran’s IRGC-Qods Force, North Korean laundering, and cybercrime.
FinCEN determined that MEXC Global poses a primary money laundering concern tied to Russia’s illicit finance networks. The order starts December 10, 2026, and has no expiration date.
On November 6, FinCEN ordered U.S. financial institutions to stop sending funds to or receiving funds from MEXC Global, a move that will shut the exchange out of American payment channels, with no end date, when it takes effect on December 10, 2026.Launched in 2018, MEXC Global handled over $1 billion in trades each day and held roughly $5 billion in reserves, per FinCEN. The platform’s rules ban customers in Iran and North Korea, but FinCEN says gaps in its compliance program meant that sanctioned parties still got through.Russia was the central focus. For the five years ending in May 2026, FinCEN found close to $1.5 billion in exposure to Russian sanctions-evasion activity, including $232 million exchanged directly with designated parties. As late as June 2026, the platform was still dealing with Garantex and its successor, Grinex. It also handled at least $26 million that benefited the sanctioned A7 Network, along with nearly $200 million connected to the network’s ruble-backed A7A5 token.The exposure extended well beyond Russia. FinCEN says about $1 billion moved straight to or from more than 40 Iran-based exchanges, and roughly $22 million was tied to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC-Qods Force. Another $36 million was linked to the Al-Qassam Brigades and other Iranian proxy groups. On the North Korean side, approximately $350,000 reached Sim Hyon Sop, a sanctioned money launderer, more than two years after he was designated.What happens nextWhen the order kicks in, U.S. institutions will have to stop routing funds to and from MEXC Global. Reporting duties under the Bank Secrecy Act, including filing Suspicious Activity Reports, remain as they were. FinCEN also concedes that some firms could receive crypto from the exchange that they have no technical means to refuse, and it lets them decline or return those transfers depending on the circumstances.FAQsWhat is Operation Economic Outcast? It’s a Treasury effort to choke off financing for the Iranian regime, including its use of crypto to get around sanctions.Does the order apply to MEXC Global’s U.S. operations?No. Any MEXC Global entity based in the United States falls outside its scope. articles.title: The Nvidia Blast Zone
articles.text:
The Nvidia Blast Zone

Laila Khawaja, Arthur Kroeber

Gavekal Technologies: Chips | 12 Nov 2026

The Nvidia scandal now looks certain to topple CEO Jensen Huang, who had affairs with a woman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset, and with one of his subordinates. The questions now are what the longer-term impacts will be both on Nvidia and the US and Chinese AI ecosystems. Understandably, much coverage has focused on the spying and sex angles, but the crucial issues lie elsewhere.The biggest risk to Nvidia is if it or Huang is found to have knowingly colluded in the diversion of export-controlled chips from a Singapore datacenter to unauthorized end-users in China. The biggest risk to China’s AI industry is that the scandal leads to a tightening of US export controls on advanced chips and chip-making equipment, possibly by the end of this year. And while the US AI industry can probably weather the tumult inside Nvidia—especially if the board swiftly ousts Huang and installs credible new leadership—the scandal raises the chance that the incoming Democratic Congress will push for much tougher regulation of the sector.

articles.title: Daily: Hotter US inflation keeps the Fed on course to hike
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioPodcast:What next for tech after the sell-off? Plus the US midterms arrive (5 mins)
Video:The AI sell-off and US midterms: Live at the UBS Disruptive Tech Summit (6 mins)
CIO Live Replay: CIO Asia equity strategists on the AI sell-off and opportunities (30 mins)Thought of the dayUS inflation came in stronger than expected in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its December meeting. Headline consumer prices rose 0.4% month over month, above the 0.3% consensus forecast, while core prices increased 0.3%, versus expectations for 0.2%. Price pressures were relatively broad, with increases in food, housing, recreation, medical care, electricity, airfares, and delivery services. The yield on 10-year US Treasuries rose 11bps to 4.99% and the S&P 500 fell 0.4% on Tuesday.Before the inflation print, Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said a core CPI reading of around 0.3% or higher could warrant considering a 50-basis-point hike in December. Separately, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan called for at least two more 25bps hikes, and suggested the Fed could raise rates more rapidly this winter. Federal funds futures markets now price 28bps of hikes for December.But, we still think FOMC support for a 50bps hike is limited because it could signal a need for more aggressive monetary policy recalibration. For now, our base case remains for 25bps Fed hikes in December and March, with the latest developments bolstering the case for higher rates and raising the risk of more or faster tightening than currently expected.Underlying core inflation showed only limited improvement. The monthly core reading slowed to 0.30% from 0.33%, but short-term momentum continued to deteriorate. The three-month annualized rate rose to 3.75%, having been below 2% as recently as August. This was the second consecutive disappointing report and strengthens the possibility that the Fed will deliver at least two further rate increases, in our view.Core goods inflation remained firm beneath the surface. A 1.2% decline in used-car prices obscured broader price pressures, with core goods excluding food, energy, and used vehicles rising by around 0.4% over the month. Tariff-sensitive categories were notable and consistent with a lingering tariff pass-through, including greater than 1% month-over-month increases in toy, furniture and bedding, and appliance prices. AI-sensitive technology prices also remained firm, with the broader IT commodities group rising 0.4% m/m, extending recent gains across many hardware items. These categories carry relatively small consumer price index weights, so the direct contribution to aggregate core inflation remains limited, but their personal consumption expenditures weights are substantially larger. The persistence of digital goods-price increases, alongside broader tariff-sensitive goods firmness, suggests that goods disinflation is becoming a less reliable theme going into 2027.Shelter inflation cooled, but remained sticky, while energy added further pressure. Shelter inflation slowed to 0.30% from 0.39%, including a moderation in owners’ equivalent rent. Still, the three-month annualized rate for the latter moved back toward 3.5% after falling below 3% in August. Energy remained an inflationary impulse but faded dramatically from September, rising another 0.7% and contributing only about 5bps to headline CPI.So, we think the October report increases confidence that at least two further Fed hikes are likely and raises the risk of a faster sequence of quarter-point moves. We continue to think support for a 50bps adjustment is limited, given it could signal that policy is materially below its appropriate level and make the recalibration appear more open-ended.For investors, the repricing in bond markets has restored meaningful return potential for high-quality fixed income. We favor quality short- and medium-maturity bonds, where elevated starting yields should support returns, while remaining cautious on the longest maturities amid persistent fiscal deficits and heavy Treasury issuance.We continue to expect equity markets to be volatile in the near term. Investors should consider maintaining diversified exposure across sectors and regions and managing excessive single-stock and technology concentration. We also favor broad commodity exposure as a diversifier, particularly through an actively managed approach.

articles.title: Market update - November 6th 2026 | CoinShares
articles.text: Bitcoin, the AI sell-off and October payrolls Bitcoin had initially taken the Democratic sweep relatively calmly, which is perhaps unsurprising given markets had been rehearsing the outcome for weeks. The more disruptive move came yesterday, when the AI trade finally wobbled hard enough to drag almost everything else with it. The Nasdaq fell 5.5%, the Nasdaq 100 6.4% and semiconductors 12%, while Bitcoin fell just over 5%. More than US$1B of leveraged crypto positions were liquidated in the process. The weakness was particularly acute among Bitcoin miners that have increasingly repositioned themselves as AI and data-centre plays, with several falling by double digits. Highlighting that this looks less like a crypto-specific deterioration and more like Bitcoin becoming collateral damage in a broader de-risking of the technology trade.The election itself still looks more relevant for the pace of crypto reform rather than specifically for Bitcoin’s medium-term direction. The CLARITY Act now faces a harder path, while Democratic control gives the party greater influence over committee agendas, appointments and investigations into Trump-linked crypto ventures. But The CLARITY Act is also becoming less important than it once was. The GENIUS Act is already law, while the SEC and CFTC have continued to provide regulatory pathways within their existing powers. Congress is therefore no longer the only route to progress. The CLARITY Act would still provide more durable statutory certainty, particularly for Ethereum, DeFi and token issuers, but its absence no longer amounts to regulatory paralysis.The consequences should vary considerably across the market. Bitcoin is relatively insulated because its regulatory status is already well established. US exchanges, token issuers and businesses dependent on new permissions have more at stake. Established, compliant operators could even benefit if political scrutiny falls disproportionately on weaker competitors. Among listed crypto equities, miners remain more complicated. Their existing power and data-centre infrastructure makes them attractive to AI hyperscalers, but that same exposure now leaves them vulnerable when the AI trade itself comes under pressure.Oil has also fallen sharply as hopes for progress in US-Iran talks have improved, taking some pressure off inflation expectations. That looked supportive for rates yesterday, especially as the equity sell-off drove demand into Treasuries and pulled expectations for a December hike lower. The relief did not last long. Today’s October payroll report came in at 165,000, massively above the roughly 65,000 consensus, while unemployment edged down to 4.1%. Professional and business services, healthcare and transportation all added jobs. The labour market is clearly stronger than the market had assumed.The latest payrolls data reinforces the Fed’s hawkish stanceThat is an awkward result for Bitcoin with yesterday’s tech rout briefly giving markets reason to think the Fed might be able to soften its stance, particularly with oil falling and financial conditions tightening through equities. Today’s payroll beat pushes back in the opposite direction. With inflation still elevated, a labour market adding 165,000 jobs gives the Fed considerably less reason to worry about growth and more room to focus on price stability. Bitcoin remains highly sensitive to precisely this sort of repricing in short-term rate expectations.For crypto policy, the election result is not game over, there was bipartisan support for The CLARITY Act before the vote, and stablecoins still provide a useful additional source of demand for US Treasuries at a time when fiscal pressures remain uncomfortable. The administration also retains substantial executive authority. Less legislative freedom does not necessarily mean less policy influence, and a frustrated president may lean more heavily on foreign policy and executive action, hardly a recipe for lower market volatility.So the picture is more complicated than it looked immediately after the election. Political uncertainty has fallen, oil is moving in the right direction and regulatory progress can continue without The CLARITY Act. Against that, yesterday’s AI sell-off exposed how intertwined crypto has become with the broader technology and data-centre trade, while today’s payroll number has restored some of the hawkish macro pressure. For Bitcoin, real yields, dollar liquidity and ETP flows still matter more than the composition of Congress. The election changes the political backdrop, but the Fed still holds the more important cards.SourcesUS Bureau of Labor Statistics, Employment Situation, October 2026, released 6 Nov 2026CoinDesk, AI-led technology and crypto sell-off, 5-6 Nov 2026Federal Reserve / CME FedWatch, December rate expectations, 5-6 Nov 2026US Bureau of Labor Statistics, JOLTS, September 2026S&P Global, US PMI, October 2026

articles.title: The importance of public engagement in maintaining trust in banknotes - Speech by Victoria Cleland
articles.text:
The importance of public engagement in maintaining trust in banknotes - Speech by Victoria Cleland

Speech at the Intergraf Currency & Identity Conference, Denmark

Published on
15 October 2026

Maintaining trust in banknotes is crucial to their continued demand and relevance. This requires more than robust security features and resilient infrastructure. Victoria Cleland explores how communications and public engagement can help build and maintain confidence and trust in cash.

Speech
Trust is essential to everything the Bank of England (the Bank) does. It underpins all our activities, from setting Bank Rate to operating payment settlement systems and much in between. And banknotes are among the most visible manifestations of that trust.
The Bank is the second oldest central bank in the world and issuing banknotes (originally promissory notes) was one of its earliest functions. Historically, confidence in banknotes was linked to their convertibility into gold. You can still see the words ‘I promise to pay the bearer on demand’ on our banknotes. While the nature of that promise has evolved over time and our notes are now indirectly backed by UK government bonds,footnote [1] the principle remains the same: banknotes derive their value from trust, and that trust must be maintained.
Every time someone accepts a banknote, they trust that it is authentic and worth the value stated. They have to be confident that it can be used again in the future: whether to spend it, save it or bank it. Without that trust, a banknote is simply an object, albeit with a beautiful design. With it, households spend, businesses trade and economies function.
Central banks play a crucial role in maintaining this trust in banknotes. We do so by ensuring banknotes are available, that the cash industry remains effective, resilient and sustainable, and that banknotes remain a secure method of payment.
Communicating openly with businesses and the public so that they can recognise and easily authenticate banknotes is also an essential part of maintaining this security. The Bank has engaged extensively with the UK public on the imagery for our next series of banknotes to ensure our banknotes remain recognisable as national symbols. This culminated in last week’s announcement that the Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will feature as the central imagery on our next series of banknotes.
I will now dive deeper into the Bank’s work to ensure this essential trust in our banknotes through availability, secure design and public engagement.
Ensuring trust through availability
The public need to trust that banknotes will be available when required. The Bank does not, and cannot, do this in isolation. Just as a beehive depends on its community of different bees performing complementary roles, maintaining trust in banknotes requires organisations across the cash ecosystem to work together.
Central banks, printers, cash centre operators, cash-in-transit companies, financial institutions and retailers are all important members of this ecosystem. They all play crucial and complementary roles in ensuring that the public can continue to access and use banknotes so that cash remains a trusted source of payments. At the Banknote Conference earlier this year,footnote [2] I spoke about the importance of preserving choice in payments and the role of cash in preserving choice. Ensuring that choice remains requires the whole industry to work together like an efficient beehive.
For the Bank, this includes issuing banknotes to meet public demand. The use of cash for transactions has declined over recent years, accounting for 8% of all transactions in the UK in 2025, down from 45% a decade earlier.footnote [3] But according to our research, cash is still the preferred payment method for one in seven people and, is used at least once a week by almost a quarter of the public. It is essential for some people and is seen as an important contingency by many.
And the value of Bank of England notes in circulation has continued to increase, reaching £91.5 billion at the end of February 2026. This demonstrates the enduring importance of cash to our economy and our society.
We are committed to meet the demand for our banknotes and to ensure that the right banknotes are available, in the right places at the right time. It is important to us that people and businesses who want to use cash can continue to do so. We do this by monitoring payment trends and a range of economic factors to inform demand forecasts and contingency requirements, and to help us decide how many banknotes we need our printer De La Rue to produce.
Authorities and industry must work closely together to ensure the cash cycle as a whole remains effective, resilient and sustainable. The wholesale cash distribution market is the underlying “plumbing” that gets cash to where it is needed, via cash centres through to ATMs and retailers. Last year, the Bank took on a new role to supervise firms in the wholesale cash industry who operate cash centres and their backing FIs.footnote [4] In addition, the Financial Conduct Authority has powers to protect retail access to cash for consumers. Together, these regimes will help ensure that cash will be available and accessible.
Ensuring trust through design
Another key component of trust in banknotes is counterfeit resilience: the public and businesses must be confident that the banknotes they receive are genuine. We do this by incorporating sophisticated security features into the design: these need to be both hard to counterfeit and easy to authenticate. For trust in the security of banknotes to endure, it is important that central banks change the design from time to time to incorporate the latest security features. This requires suppliers and manufacturers to innovate and invest in developing new technology and more resilient features. To maintain trust in banknotes, it is essential that this innovation continues.
When you picture a puffin, you may think of its distinct colouring including its bright orange beak. Did you know their beaks glow under UV light, just like our banknotes? These markings and photoluminescence are not purely about aesthetic appeal but also serve a functional purpose in helping puffins lure prey, deter predators and attract mates. Similarly, at the Bank, we need to design banknotes that are not only attractive but also designed with function, particularly security, at their heart.
Our next series of banknotes (Series H) is currently being designed. The driver, as with any new series, is to further enhance counterfeit resilience. And following public consultation, the new notes will celebrate UK wildlife. Images of wildlife will also support resilience, enabling us to incorporate intuitive movements into the security features which are engaging and easy for the public to recognise and distinguish.
Trust also stems from our notes being accessible to all. We are continuing to invest in banknote accessibility, running research on how people with disabilities use cash today and including tactile features to help people with visual impairments differentiate between denominations.
Ensuring trust through communication and engagement
Trust in banknotes is founded on availability and effective design, but sustaining it requires engagement – with businesses, law enforcement and the public. Even the most sophisticated security feature is only effective if people know how to use it to verify a banknote. And so public engagement and communication are a pivotal part of our anticounterfeiting strategy.
The Bank provides free educational materials, such as booklets and posters to help businesses and the public to authenticate banknotes. We also provide online training and run a free Banknote Checking Scheme to help businesses keep a watchful eye out for counterfeits: a vigilance one could compare to the barn owl which will feature on our next series. This Scheme has grown considerably, now covering over 50,000 business locations.
Recently, we have supplemented this by launching a communications campaign aimed at businesses. This campaign shows business owners talking about their own experiences and how using best practice banknote checking has enhanced their trust in banknotes. We also engage closely with law enforcement, including the National Crime Agency and local police forces, to help them investigate and prosecute potential counterfeiters.
Incorporating images that resonate strongly with the public and which they can easily recognise is also a key part of banknote authentication and maintaining trust. So last year, we launched a two-stage process to engage the public in the choice of imagery for the next series of banknotes.
In July 2025, we announced that we would introduce a new series of banknotes with even more robust security features. A new series necessitates changes to the imagery, so we launched a consultation asking the UK public which theme they wanted to see featured in the design. The Bank has been celebrating historic figures on our banknotes since 1970. However there are many ways to represent the UK so we wanted to hear the views of the public, the users of our banknotes.
Around 60% of respondents chose nature as one of the themes they wanted to see featured with many nominating specific native animals. And this March, we announced that in the light of feedback from the consultation, images of UK wildlife would feature on the next series of our banknotes. We worked closely with a panel of wildlife experts to create a shortlist of native UK animals and in June we launched a second consultation asking the public to help us choose which of the shortlisted animals to feature as the central imagery on the next series. We were delighted by the scale of the response, with almost half a million people participating.
The Bank’s overarching objective is to increase counterfeit resilience through secure design, and for this to be effective, it is also important that the new series represents the UK and resonates with the users. After all, banknotes are not just a means of payment, but also a shared symbol of national identity. This helps to promote trust and security, as familiar imagery which resonates with the public will mean they look more closely at their banknotes.
The importance of awareness and familiarity is not new. In 1797, when the Bank rushed to issue new £1 and £2 banknotes following gold shortages, counterfeiting surged as counterfeiters took advantage of people’s unfamiliarity with new banknotes. The lesson remains relevant today: when introducing a new series, issuers must bring the public along on the journey to ensure they can recognise and authenticate the notes.
To do this successfully and inclusively, central banks need to engage people through different methods including the platforms they use every day. To help publicise our most recent consultation, the Bank used an integrated communication strategy which included press, social media, engagement with schools and visiting local communities around the UK. We also collaborated with influencers to help us reach young people and audiences who may not have engaged with the Bank’s work in the past.
We opened the consultation with a launch event at the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) London Wetland Centre to celebrate the shortlisted animals and give journalists an opportunity to ask questions – both to me and the wildlife Expert Panel who helped us develop the shortlist of animals. This provided an engaging backdrop to create content about wildlife to help raise awareness and encourage participation in the consultation.
To sustain momentum, we produced a variety of engaging and accessible content with the aim to appeal to different audience groups and help convey our broader message. This included factsheets on each of the animals and educational posts showing how banknotes have evolved over time, as well as some more fun posts.
Alongside the formal consultation, we also visited schools and ran a design challenge for children across the country to give young people a voice in shaping our next generation of banknotes. And we held a number of in-person Youth and Citizens’ panels in communities including Llandudno and Devon. These were a great opportunity for the Bank to learn directly from people about the role that cash continues to play in society as well as their views on the shortlisted wildlife.
Conclusion
Trust in banknotes begins with secure design but only endures if banknotes are available and recognised. Keeping banknotes trusted and relevant requires innovation and strong collaboration across the whole of the cash industry. And this must be coupled with communication and engagement to enable businesses and the public to understand, recognise and trust the banknotes they use.
Our recent consultation gave people a voice, helping them connect with the banknotes they use and have a meaningful say about their future design. There will now be a quieter period in our communications about the next series, while our design work continues in the background, with security at its heart. Like the hedgehog emerging after its winter retreat, we will return when we are ready to unveil the first denomination.
I would like to thank Elijah Lee, Zahra Damji, Nick McLaren, Ellen Caswell, Stuart Cooper, Lauren Murphy, Kiran Keer, Millie Rettie and Lisa Young.

articles.text: Back to BlogIt’s Good to, Still, Be #1Published November 11, 2026Christopher Gannatti, CFAGlobal Head of ResearchKey TakeawaysThe WisdomTree Japan Opportunities Fund (OPPJ) ranked first among 43 managers in the Morningstar Japan Stock category for the year ended September 30, 2026.OPPJ’s four sleeves target trading conglomerates, high shareholder yield, corporate governance improvers and companies positioned to benefit from geopolitical and economic shifts.Following its July 2025 strategy change, OPPJ combines these equity exposures with a currency overlay that adjusts yen hedging monthly between 0% and 100%.Ranking first in a category is the kind of result that speaks for itself. Over the one-year period ended September 30, 2026, the WisdomTree Japan Opportunities Fund (OPPJ) ranked #1 in the Morningstar Japan Stock category. The specific data is presented in Figure 1b.Figure 1a: Standardized PerformanceFigure 1b: Morningstar Japan Stock Category Rankings (as of September 30, 2026)Sources: For Figure 1a: Morningstar, FactSet and WisdomTree, with data from the PATH Fund Comparison Tool, accessed as of October 23, 2026, but showing returns for the period ended September 30, 2026. Prior to July 1, 2025, the Fund was known as the WisdomTree Japan Hedged SmallCap Equity Fund (DXJS). On that date, the Fund’s investment policy changed. Current performance may be lower or higher than the performance data quoted. For the most recent month-end and standardized performance, click here.Happy One-Year+ AnniversaryThat result did not happen by accident. It reflects a deliberate strategic repositioning made more than one year ago, and an investment thesis on Japan that has, so far, proven correct.What ChangedPrior to July 1, 2025, OPPJ operated under a different investment policy as the WisdomTree Japan Hedged SmallCap Equity Fund (DXJS). On that date, the Fund transitioned to track the WisdomTree Japan Opportunities Index, which is a meaningfully different approach designed to capture the full complexity of Japan’s evolving equity opportunity rather than a single factor or market-cap segment.The new strategy is built around four distinct sleeves.The Sogo ShoshaThe first targets the five trading conglomerates, the sogo shosha, in which Berkshire Hathaway holds strategic stakes:1Mitsubishi CorporationMitsui & Co.Marubeni CorporationItochu CorporationSumitomo CorporationThese firms are themselves broadly diversified across the Japanese industrial economy, and they have delivered shareholder yields that compare favorably to both the MSCI Japan Index and the S&P 500 Index.2 Buffett’s entry into these names in 2019 reinvigorated foreign investor attention to Japan, and the positions have compounded well since.3High Shareholder YieldThe second sleeve focuses on high shareholder yield, meaning companies returning capital through dividends and net buybacks at above-average rates. Two-plus decades of data show that the highest shareholder yield quintile within Japan has outperformed the lowest by a wide margin, with lower volatility.4 As Japanese companies increasingly deploy buybacks alongside dividends, the signal becomes more powerful:Over 90% of MSCI Japan constituents now carry a positive net buyback yield, up from nearly zero in the mid-1990s.5Corporate Governance ImproversThe third sleeve targets corporate governance improvers, companies with low valuations, such as low price-to-book ratios, that are also demonstrating earnings and dividend growth. This is a systematic way to capture companies mid-reform, before their transformation is fully priced in.GeoAlphaThe fourth, and most distinctive, sleeve is the Geopolitical-Alpha (GeoAlpha) component. This provides exposure to companies positioned to benefit from geopolitical events, fiscal and monetary policy shifts, technological innovation and shifting consumer preferences. It is where the AI infrastructure, defense spending and domestic capital expenditure themes enter the portfolio in a rules-based way.The strategy also applies a dynamic currency hedging overlay, managing yen exposure monthly across a 0% to 100% hedged range.Conclusion: Why the Approach Has Fit the MomentThe Japan investment story in 2025–2026 has not been a single-factor trade. It has been a convergence:An exit from deflation that is changing corporate behaviorA governance reform wave driven by Tokyo Stock Exchange pressureAn AI and defense capex cycle running through Japan’s upstream industrial sectorA domestic savings rotation beginning to redirect household assets from cash toward equitiesNo single sleeve or factor captures all of that, but OPPJ was designed around that complexity.The #1 ranking in the Morningstar Japan Stock category over one year reflects both the strength of the underlying Japan thesis and the quality of the strategic design.1 As of July 13, 2026, OPPJ held 7.45% in Sumitomo Corp., 7.18% in Marubeni Corp., 7.06% in Mitsubishi Corp., 6.40% in Mitsui & Co. articles.title: KPMG M&A Outlook 2027: From market resilience to renewed deal activity
articles.text:
Consulting Report

11 Nov 2026

KPMG M&A Outlook 2027: From market resilience to renewed deal activity

Discover how international investment and AI are shaping Germany’s M&A outlook through 2030.

In collaboration with KPMG Germany, Oxford Economics surveyed over 200 M&A decision-makers from German corporates, private equity funds, and family offices. We combined their insights with transaction data and economic forecasts to examine the forces shaping German dealmaking.

German M&A proved resilient in 2026 despite weak domestic growth, higher borrowing costs, and geopolitical disruption. International interest was particularly strong, led by US investors seeking German industrial and technology assets.

The outlook for 2027 is cautiously positive. Nearly half of respondents expect German M&A activity to increase. Our modelling forecasts deal counts to rise through 2028, supported by SMEs succession, international investment, and the gradual effect of public spending.

AI is also changing how and why deals are pursued. Adoption in M&A processes has doubled, although most firms still rely on general-purpose tools.

Money Markets Committee and UK Money Markets Code

The Bank of England chairs the Money Markets Committee, which has endorsed the voluntary UK Money Markets Code setting out best practice for participants in the deposit, repo and securities lending markets.

In this section

Fair and Effective Markets

Market intelligence

Settlement and collateral management

Transition from LIBOR to risk-free rates

On this pageMoney Markets CommitteeUK Money Markets Code CommitteeSecurities Lending CommitteeMoney Markets Liaison Committee and Securities Lending and Repo CommitteeUK Money Markets Code

Money Markets Committee
The Money Markets Committee (MMC) is a senior-level forum for market participants and the relevant UK public authorities to discuss issues concerning the UK unsecured deposits and funding market, the securities lending market and the repo market.
The MMC is chaired by the Bank of England.
The committee meets quarterly and also has two permanent sub-committees: the UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee and the Securities Lending Committee.
Objectives of the Money Markets Committee

To discuss important domestic and global market or structural developments affecting the UK money, repo and securities lending markets.
Where appropriate, to propose responses to any issues identified.
To aid understanding and enhance monitoring of the functioning of the UK money markets.
To endorse and facilitate continuing market-wide adoption of the UK Money Markets Code, a voluntary code of good practice for the money and securities financing markets.
To identify and address any high-level issues concerning contingency planning in the UK money markets and payment systems, having regard to international developments.

Increasing diversity in our committees
The UK Money Markets Code includes an expectation that market participants will promote the development of a diverse and inclusive within their money market teams. This includes working to create a diverse pipeline of potential future Committee members.
We also aim for diversity within the Money Markets Committee and its Sub-committees, in order that they can best represent the people of the United Kingdom. Diverse membership means that these Committees benefit from diversity of thought, which bring different viewpoints and help to ensure well-informed decision-making.
We work with members from the Money Markets Committee to diversify its membership. As part of this, we provide opportunities for members to bring observers to Committee meetings, in order that these observers can gain a better understanding of the Committee, and to help identify potential future diverse candidates.
You can find out more about ‘Meeting Varied People’ – our initiative to increase the diversity of the market contacts that we engage with – on the Market intelligence page.

The UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee is a permanent sub-committee of the MMC, and is co-chaired by, and made up of, senior market participants. The sub-committee meets regularly to ensure that the code remains relevant and up to date as markets evolve.

Securities Lending Committee
The Securities Lending Committee (SLC) is a sub-committee of the Money Markets Committee. The SLC is chaired by a market participant. It is a forum for market participants and the relevant UK public authorities to meet to discuss issues concerning the UK securities lending market, including all collateral activities.
Objectives of the Securities Lending Committee

To discuss important domestic and global market or structural developments affecting the UK securities lending market.
To discuss legal, regulatory, trading, settlement, infrastructure, tax, disclosure and other related developments in this market.
Where appropriate, it will propose responses to these issues.
To aid the understanding and enhance the monitoring of the functioning of this market.

Working Group on Settlement Efficiency
The Bank of England Securities Lending Committee has established a Working Group to examine the issue of settlement failure in the UK securities lending market. It provides a senior-level forum for market participants to meet to identify root causes for settlement issues in the UK securities lending market and suggest best practices.
The Working Group will examine drivers and impact of fails and determine potential solutions to settlement failure in the UK securities lending market. Part of this work will be to advocate best practice in the securities lending market.
Membership of the group will reflect a diverse group of market participants with relevant expertise, perspective and knowledge. It is chaired by Tim McLeod (Blackrock, Inc.). The Bank of England will participate as Ex-Officio members and provide administrative support.
Please note that views and outputs of the Working Group do not constitute guidance or legal advice from, and are not necessarily endorsed by, the Bank of England (including the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA)).
