Money Markets Liaison Committee and Securities Lending and Repo Committee
The Money Markets Committee was formed in March 2017 to replace previous markets committees, the Money Markets Liaison Committee (MMLC) and Securities Lending and Repo Committee (SLRC).
Please see the National Archives for historic MMLC and SLRC minutes.
The National Archives Opens in a new window
UK Money Markets Code
The UK Money Markets Code is a voluntary code written by market participants. It incorporates revised relevant sections of the Non-Investment Products (NIPs) Code, and also a revision and update of the Gilt Repo Code and Securities Borrowing and Lending Code.
The UK Money Markets Code was published on 26 April 2017.

The UK Money Markets Code
The UK Money Markets Code: explanatory notes

Voluntary codes of best practice can help to establish the basis on which financial markets function, ensuring trust between participants. This in turn creates an environment so that a fair, effective and transparent market can flourish and in which, by adhering to such codes, high standards of behaviour can be assured.
The code sets out such standards and the best practice expected from participants in the deposit, repo and securities lending markets in the UK. It supersedes previous guidance for participants in these markets provided by the NIPs Code, the Gilt Repo Code and the Securities Borrowing and Lending Code. By bringing these together it will more clearly establish the framework for transacting in UK money markets. The code is endorsed by the Money Markets Committee and will be updated regularly.
The Money Markets Committee has also established a Public Register of Institutions who have signed a Statement of Commitment or a Statement of Support to the Code. The purpose of the Register is to further restore trust in financial markets by making it easier to see which institutions have taken the important step of committing to the principles set out in the Code.
UK Money Markets Code: Public Register
The UK Money Markets Code Committee and the Association of Corporate Treasurers have produced this guide to promote and encourage wider adherence to the Code among the Corporate sector.

The future of tech infrastructure is being built now

Featured topic

This three-part research series from the Deloitte Center for Integrated Research examines how enterprise technology infrastructure is being reshaped by simultaneous shifts across computing, coordination, interaction, and trust. Drawing on interviews with more than 30 technology leaders alongside Deloitte's published research and market-signal analysis, the series traces how piecemeal modernization can quietly lock organizations into constraints they didn't intend to build — what the research calls "architected disadvantage." It maps where that risk shows up today, models four plausible futures for the tech stack by 2032, and lays out the architecture, orchestration, and security capabilities leaders can start building now to stay adaptable no matter which future arrives.

4 shifts are shaping technology infrastructure. How can leaders avoid creating systems they can’t change?

Technology architecture choices made today could become tomorrow’s constraints. The future of enterprise IT may depend on understanding these 4 shifts.

articles.text: Source: GettyArticleCarnegie IndiaWill a UN Treaty on Autonomous Weapons Arrive Too Late?The final report by the Group of Governmental Experts is a key milestone toward a potential instrument regulating Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems and has garnered both accolades and criticism.Link CopiedBy Charukeshi BhattPublished on Nov 12, 2026On September 4, 2026, the Group of Governmental Experts (GGE) on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS), constituted under the United Nations’ Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), concluded discussions under its three-year mandate. The group has met twice every year since 2017, deliberating one of the most consequential and topical issues at the intersection of technology and security: the regulation of weapons that can identify and engage targets, and use lethal force, without human intervention.The group’s current mandate, as decided in the 2023 meeting of the High Contracting Parties (HCP) to the CCW, was to develop, by consensus, a set of elements for an instrument to address the issue of emerging technologies in the area of LAWS. The group produced a final report based on discussions held from 2023 to 2026, building on past work since 2017. The report will be tabled at the upcoming Seventh Review Conference of the HCPs to the CCW in November this year, making it the foundational text for any future discussion on regulation and governance of LAWS. As the primary UN body entrusted with implementing treaties to regulate the use of certain kinds of weapons, the CCW’s role is significant in shaping the instrument of regulation that the GGE has spent its mandate deliberating.The final report is a key milestone toward a potential instrument regulating LAWS and has garnered both accolades and criticism. The criticism is in part due to how long it took to conclude and the possibility that it may move to yet another round of such consultations when the Seventh Review Conference picks it up this month. Even so, it is useful to examine what the report was able to achieve. Examining the report will provide a clear sense of the threshold with which the CCW will begin its discussion on regulating the use of LAWS.The report is also important for national policymakers, as it sets the fencing around which future guardrails on LAWS will likely be built, notwithstanding discussions and subsequent modifications to the normative structure as the CCW process itself takes place. But there is a caveat: How long the subsequent process takes could impact the effectiveness of any future guardrails. The road toward this potential instrument could be as long as that of the final report. There is a need to be mindful of how a delay in this process could affect the governance of such technologies, and a stretched timeline leaves little room for negotiation.This article looks at the final report produced by the GGE, examines key tenets of the set of elements for an instrument on LAWS, and identifies gaps that remain unaddressed. It then looks at what’s next in the process toward an instrument of regulation and what the time delta between ongoing multilateral discussions and the eventual adoption of an international instrument could mean for the global governance of LAWS. As these weapons are increasingly used in combat, the risk is that an international instrument seeking to regulate their use might arrive too late.The Final Report: What Was Discussed and What Remains?Under its 2023 mandate, the GGE’s task can be broadly understood as the following:defining what constitutes as LAWS and what does notdetermining the scope of the application of international humanitarian law (IHL), among other various aspects of governing a kind of weapon systemascertaining where responsibility and accountability would lie in the context of human-machine interactionclarifying what obligations these tenets place on contracting partiesDiscussions and negotiations within the GGE since 2017 have contributed to the final report. This article compares the advance copy of the final report to the rolling text circulated in December 2025, which was the basis for discussions held under the two sessions of the GGE this year. This comparison might be helpful in understanding the changes introduced in the final draft.Characterization of LAWSIn the rolling text from December 2025, LAWS were described as a “functionally integrated combination of weapons and technological components capable of identifying, selecting and engaging a target without intervention by a human operator.” The text also clarified that humans setting target parameters did not exclude a system from the definition of LAWS. Meanwhile, the September 2026 report defined LAWS as systems capable of identifying, selecting, and engaging a target in a way that “results in loss of life,” without human intervention. The main change here was the emphasis on the weapon’s autonomous capability to cause loss of life, whereas the previous definition focused on the autonomous capability of a weapon to identify, select, and engage targets. This could narrow the scope of what constitutes LAWS, potentially excluding autonomous weapons that injure but do not kill.Application of IHLThe two documents maintain significant continuity when it comes to this tenet. Both maintain that IHL applies to international and non-international armed conflicts and governs “all weapons, means and methods of warfare.” The text also states that IHL applies fully to the development and use of LAWS and that obligations rest on states, parties to armed conflicts, and individuals, and not on machines. The rolling text from December 2025 however, placed stronger restrictions on states in that it specifically “prohibited certain LAWS whose effects could not be anticipated and limited as required by IHL and required states to refrain from manufacturing, acquiring, stockpiling and transferring such LAWS that did not comply with IHL.” The report of September 2026, while maintaining the applicability of the IHL to all LAWS, removes the restrictions placed on states with regards to manufacturing and stockpiling.Human-Machine InteractionWhile the two documents retain the central idea that human control and judgement are necessary for compliance with IHL, there is considerable weakening of the language when thinking of human-machine interaction and the transparency of a weapons system. As mentioned above, the obligations of IHL compliance rest on individuals and states. The December 2025 text mentioned “context-appropriate human judgement and control” and listed measures, including “responsible chain of command and control, human assessment of legal obligations and limits of the scale, types, duration and geographical scope of operations.” This rolling text was subsequently modified and shared in the first session of the GGE conducted in June 2026, where, in addition to the aspects of human control and judgement, the states’ responsibility to ensure that LAWS were “adequately predictable, reliable, traceable and explainable” to those responsible for their use was also added. The report of 2026 retains “human control (over LAWS) directly or indirectly, before and during use,” but it does away with “predictability, reliability, explainability and traceability” as a requirement for LAWS to comply with IHL. These requirements for AI systems are crucial for assigning human agency and accountability. Being able to ascertain why AI systems prefer certain outputs over others is key to identify where biases originate. In the context of weapons systems, such explainability is critical to ensure compliance with IHL principles of distinction and proportionality. In the absence of explainability requirements, there will be no consequence to a weapon system misidentifying a target group.How Far Are We From a Binding Instrument?The GGE’s recommendations will be taken up by the Seventh Review Conference of the HCPs scheduled for November 2026. The CCW convenes these conferences every five years as forums to review the different protocols, each of which ban or regulate specific kinds of weapons, asses their implementation, and make amendments. To keep the convention flexible and responsive to the changing nature of conflicts, weapons, and their technologies, Review Conferences also consider and discuss the creation of new protocols—as in the case of the Protocol on Blinding Laser Weapons (Protocol IV) that was deliberated and drafted at the Review Conference concluded between 1995 and 1996, or the expansion of their existing scope of implementation.To be clear, the creation of a protocol will not automatically forbid the use of a kind of weapon. Protocols only apply to state parties to the Convention that have ratified them. Further, states also can denunciate their association with the Convention and its protocols via Article 9. The CCW remains important however, because it provides a framework for developing shared norms that prevent military interests from overriding humanitarian norms during times of conflict. Its value is in creating a moral and political suasion for states. It has also, in the past, addressed the risks of weapons before their full-fledged deployment. For example, Protocol IV prohibited blinding lasers before they became widely used. This preventive role is especially relevant when thinking of weapons powered by emerging technologies whose full effects are unknown as they continue to evolve. CCW can help establish norms for the use, transfer, and proliferation for such weapons before their harmful effects become entrenched.The final report of the GGE was endorsed by seventy-six members, seventy of which are HCPs of the CCW, meaning that they will likely participate in the proceedings of the review conference. This majority could make it easy to carry on the momentum of the GGE into the review conference, and for the set of elements of an instrument to be seriously considered for a draft text for a potential instrument.Possible PathwaysWith regard to the GGE’s final report, the Review Conference has a few possible ways forward. It may continue the GGE’s mandate to further discuss the issue of LAWS. Proposals being submitted to the Seventh Review Conference are already advocating for the need for more discussions on LAWS. However, the UN Secretary General’s 2026 deadline to conclude negotiations on a treaty on LAWS might pressure states to move toward the next steps.Alternatively, the Review Conference could begin formal proceedings toward negotiating a binding instrument. This seems likely because a majority of endorsers of the GGE report are HCPs participating in the Review Conference. Moreover, a cohort of countries represented by Brazil have extended support for the work done by the GGE and called the December 2025 rolling text sufficient to negotiate an instrument for LAWS. The urgency of beginning the process of negotiations is also echoed in the joint appeal made by the UN and ICRC in August this year to “establish specific prohibitions and restrictions on the use of autonomous weapons systems.” Strong support for a binding instrument is already visible both at the Seventh Review Conference, with proposals submitted for negotiating a protocol, and at the UNGA, with 163 states voting in favor of the resolution “to advance to negotiations on an instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems.”The CCW may also exercise the option of abandoning the work concluded under the GGE. This could stem from disagreements over the necessity of a binding instrument that persisted within the GGE and reportedly even continued in the culminating session. It was in response to these differences that forums outside the GGE formed to address emerging technologies in the military domain. For example, the Responsible use of AI in the Military Domain (REAIM Process) was launched in 2023 by the Netherlands and the Republic of Korea. As part of the REAIM Process, a Global Commission was set up which concluded its mandate in September 2025. Its report, titled Responsible by Design, consists of guiding principles and recommendations for states, militaries, and industry when thinking of AI use in the military domain.The U.S.-led Political Declaration on the Responsible use of AI and Autonomy was the second track that emerged in 2023. It set out voluntary guidelines for the development and use of AI in the military. While the declaration did garner over fifty endorsements at the time of its launch, it was not a legally binding document. It was also launched during the Joe Biden administration and the current policy toward AI in and for the military domain seems to be more permissive. The Pentagon’s dispute with Anthropic over the use of its models for fully autonomous weapons points more directly to the shift in this policy and toward a more permissive stance.Moreover, these processes and platforms were only forums for discussions, seeking convergence around voluntary principles and responsible use-practices. None of them had the power to enforce a binding treaty.What Happens in the Duration of the Treaty’s Negotiation?As modern day conflicts witness increased deployment of AI-assisted weapons, with some being associated with autonomous behaviors, the governance process will become complicated. Longer negotiations will increase the risk of the final instrument reflecting the lowest common denominator among states. This is so because, as AI-assisted weaponry capabilities get more distributed among states, they will be more inclined to interpret concepts such as “human control,” meaningful human judgment, and acceptable levels of autonomy according to their interests. The draft report is already being dubbed by some experts as a weaker version of previous texts by the GGE.In the interval between the current deployment of AI-assisted technologies in conflict and the implementation of any binding instrument, companies building AI systems are setting their own red lines through contracts, deployment restrictions, and technical safeguards. These voluntary red lines, however, will be hard to maintain as companies try to balance market competition and ethical commitments. The Anthropic case is an example to consider in this regard. The U.S. Department of Defense’s subsequent contract with another AI firm points to the limitations of such redlines.First, these do not reflect universally agreed upon rules that bind other states or companies. And what could emerge is a fragmented regulatory space where acceptable military AI use and deployment vary according to the supplier.Secondly, market competition among rival technology providers will ultimately weaken the leverage of even one company willing to adhere to voluntary checks. In active conflicts, where procurement needs to happen quickly, states might look for comparable alternatives launching a race where suppliers might be disincentivized to even build voluntary guardrails for themselves. Over time, this could also weaken the incentives for states themselves to exercise restraint. If the state can secure technological capability through different vendors, then voluntary adherence to normative guardrails might be seen as bearing an unjustified strategic cost. Conflict and competition will reward vendors willing to maintain lower thresholds of regulation, and this may further pressurize other states and companies to reduce restrictions.ConclusionThe final report of the GGE is a result of a consensus-driven process and was able to bring together multifaceted differences across the technical, legal, ethical and the aspects of a potential instrument to govern LAWS. With the UN Secretary General re-iterating the need for an instrument of governance, the urgency of the matter is well established. The Seventh Review Conference is also likely to approach the report with some momentum since most of the states that endorsed the report are also HCPs to the CCW and will sit at the Review Conference.Still, a few concerns must stay in view. First, the timeline for an instrument cannot be stretched too far. A drawn-out negotiation will leave little room for effective control, especially as technology keeps advancing. Second, there is also the need to think about how to keep companies committed to voluntary guardrails, whether through incentives or reputational benefits. While this does not fall under the purview of the work that the Review Conference will undertake, engagement with industry will be critical to the designing of an instrument, specifically aspects of assigning human responsibility and the extent of control and judgement. This would help instill more trust and create moral suasion for industries to devise guardrails for technologies they build.About the AuthorCharukeshi BhattResearch Analyst, Technology and Society ProgramCharukeshi Bhatt is a research analyst with the Technology and Society program at Carnegie India. articles.title: UK Retail Payments Infrastructure: moving from vision to design − speech by Victoria Cleland
articles.text:
UK Retail Payments Infrastructure: moving from vision to design − speech by Victoria Cleland

Given at the FTT Fintech Festival

Published on
11 November 2026

The UK’s next-generation retail payments infrastructure is being designed to meet evolving needs of the whole ecosystem. It must enable different payment journeys and forms of money and provide a platform for innovation. Victoria Cleland explains how industry inputs are shaping the Blueprint for the new core infrastructure. She also explains why collaboration remains essential, throughout the process.

Speech
It is a pleasure to join you this morning at the FTT Fintech Festival, with an exciting update on our journey to create a next generation retail payments infrastructure for the UK. And when I say “our journey”, I do not just mean the Bank of England. I do not just mean the other authorities. I mean everyone in this room, and the whole payments ecosystem. To design and deliver an infrastructure that is well used, trusted and truly valued requires strong collaboration between the public and the private sectors, between incumbents and fintechs, and between providers and users.
Payments are a key part of all our lives, and the lifeblood of the economy and of the financial system. And we need to keep them relevant in an ever-changing landscape. Technology, about which we are hearing so much at today’s Festival, is reshaping how payments are initiated and authorised. And demand is changing, with expectations of speed and functionality increasing as payments respond to our "always on" world.
So, what is our destination?
Last year the Payments Vision Delivery Committee (PVDC) footnote [1] outlined five key outcomes for a next generation infrastructure:

greater choice of innovative and cost-effective payment options;
interoperability across a multi-money ecosystem;
protection from fraud and wider financial crime;
fair and transparent access that supports competition and innovation; and
an operationally and financially resilient payments ecosystem.

Together these will make a real difference for consumers and businesses, enhance resilience and support competition and innovation.
To help realise this ambition, the Retail Payments Infrastructure Board (RPIB) was established. I chair the RPIB, which brings together a range of industry experts, with the FCA/PSR participating as an observer, to translate these PVDC outcomes into a high-level design for the core clearing and messaging infrastructure. Next Spring the Blueprint will be handed over to the industry led Delivery Company to deliver the new infrastructure.
We took an important step towards this in June this year when the RPIB issued a public consultation inviting respondents to help shape the design of the new infrastructure. The consultation asked what payment journeys the infrastructure should support; the principles and characteristics that should guide its design; and the role of the core infrastructure as a platform for innovation across the wider payments ecosystem.
Today, I want to explain what we heard, how that feedback is helping us on our journey from vision to design, and the next steps.
Respondents
First, I would like to say an enormous thank you to everyone who contributed to the consultation. I was really encouraged by the diversity of organisations responding and by the insightful feedback in the 121 responses. We received responses from: financial institutions, payment firms, technology firms, merchants, consumers as well as trade bodies, consultants and individuals. This feedback has been supplemented by a variety of roundtables, forums and discussions, with the high level of engagement underlining how important payments are to so many players.
Feedback demonstrated broad support for the direction of travel, and for moving at pace. Respondents saw the payment journeys, design principles and conceptual architecture as a strong basis for the next stage.
Of course, broad support does not mean that every detail has been agreed and every question has been answered. Important choices remain: where the boundary of the core should sit, how interoperability should work in practice, and how migration should be managed safely. But we have strong buy-in for the overall destination and we know the big questions that need to be addressed.
From feedback to design
I cannot do justice to all of the feedback this morning - there is far more detail in our published consultation response - but I would like to focus on a few of the key points that will be front of my mind as we move into the co-creation phase.
There was strong support for the proposed payment journeys: both the existing journeys and the new and emerging journeys including A2A at point of sale, payments between different forms of money, instant payments using aliases, advanced delegated payments, programmable and deferred payments. This endorsement was very good news, as ultimately payments need to meet users’ needs. And importantly the new infrastructure will enable not just different types of payments but also different types of money, with a core infrastructure that can support many different products. I sometimes refer to this as being able to plug and play products, be they faster payments, stablecoins, programmable payments and much more, into an infrastructure that supports future developments such as those being discussed at the Festival today.
Interoperability between these different forms of money, allowing a payer to initiate a payment in one form of money and a payee to receive it in another form of money frictionlessly and at par, was welcomed. This will be a crucial feature of the new infrastructure and will greatly enhance choice for consumers and scope for Fintechs to develop new solutions.
An ecosystem that prevents fraud and financial crime was a priority for respondents. While some features will be included in layers above the core, it is essential that the new infrastructure can support and enable effective controls across the ecosystem. They need to be designed in from the start.
Respondents were supportive of a ‘layered’ architecture footnote [2] for the wider payments ecosystem where the core infrastructure can act as a platform for innovation. They also welcomed the proposed modular and extensible approach, footnote [3] designed around common capabilities, rather than around each product in isolation. This should support existing payment journeys and provide a foundation to enable new products and forms of money to be included in the future. And extensibility will be key as the new infrastructure will need to be able to scale as payment volumes grow.
As we reflect on these responses, we will be considering that there was a preference for a relatively thin core, footnote [4] that is the element that will be common to all products. However, there was a range of views as to precisely how thin the core should be, and where certain capabilities should sit. Respondents placed varying levels of emphasis on the role shared services and common capabilities should play, and whether these should sit within the core.
There was little disagreement though on the crucial importance of security, resilience and cyber security, in particular, in the context of AI and developments in frontier technologies. Respondents emphasised secure, resilient, and adaptable infrastructure, with sufficient flexibility to support future requirements. We envisage a system that will be designed to exacting levels of operational resilience. And the core infrastructure will connect to the Bank’s RTGS service for settlement in central bank money, supporting confidence and financial stability by providing a safe and final means of settlement.
Respondents highlighted common messaging, interfaces and technical standards as important foundations for the new infrastructure. And these, together with ISO20022 messaging, a consistent implementation of standards, and strong governance would be important to support interoperability in its broadest sense.
There were many comments emphasising the importance of a smooth and safe transition to the next generation infrastructure. Planning the transition will be crucial and will need to draw on the input from many players, but it can only be planned once we have a clearer idea of what is being built and hence what is being transitioned to.
The core infrastructure is only part of the ecosystem
The next-generation infrastructure will be a critical layer of the UK retail payments ecosystem. But it is only one layer. It cannot deliver successful payment journeys on its own. Product and scheme arrangements, payment services providers, consumer protection, liability, merchant acceptance, commercial incentives, financial inclusion and access will all need to develop alongside the core. For the core we need to ensure that it can enable what is needed in the product layers that sit above it. And there is also a strong complementary role for the payments industry and financial institutions to leverage the core infrastructure to develop their product offerings to provide open, transparent and accessible payments. This an exciting opportunity to innovate, for all types of customers including the most vulnerable.
The PVDC set out its thinking on this wider picture in its July 2026 update on Roles and Responsibilities in the future Retail Payments Ecosystem Opens in a new window. It is important now that the industry maintains momentum and stays focused, with Pay.UK continuing its vital role as Payment System Operator of the current systems, and the Delivery Company preparing to take forward the Blueprint for the next generation infrastructure.
What happens next
The valuable consultation responses, combined with insightful feedback from wider engagement, provide a strong foundation from which to develop the Blueprint for the next-generation infrastructure. This will set out the high-level design proposals to enable the Delivery Company to take forward the detailed design and delivery of the core.
We are now entering a period of co-creation, bringing together public and private sector expertise. This will enable the golden thread of public policy objectives to run through a design, with industry helping to shape the requirements in a way that will enable them to operate effectively. RPIB, the Design Authority, representatives from the Delivery Company, and industry experts will work together and incorporate feedback from this and our future outreach activities.
The Blueprint will then be handed over to the Delivery Company in Spring 2027, so that they can take forward detailed design, procurement, build and implementation. Ongoing public and private sector engagement will be important in ensuring that the design supports delivery of RPIB’s vision for the new infrastructure and can adapt to the changing technological and demand landscape.
This work does not mean that other innovation should stop and wait. We want it to continue, and we look forward to working with innovators so that it can align with the overall vision.
This is an exciting journey, and we need to keep up momentum. Our destination is a core infrastructure that enables: greater choice, more innovation, and a payments ecosystem that is operationally and financially resilient. The feedback from the consultation has added more detail to our map. And we have a route from high-level design to industry led delivery. I would encourage everyone to move in the same direction together, to point out safe short cuts, and to encourage other passengers to join along the way. The destination is one where we can all thrive.
I would like to thank Katie Britton and Sofia Edrihen Ruiz for helping with the preparation of these remarks.

On 7 November 2025, the PVDC published its strategic outcomes for the future UK retail payments infrastructure, building on the ambitions set out in the government’s National Payments Vision.

Layered models are commonly used to represent complex payment systems and are not specific to this work.

Modular and extensible approach – designing the core infrastructure as a combination of discrete, self-contained components that can be upgraded independently over time, while allowing new functionality and capabilities to be added without requiring fundamental redesign or replacement of the entire core.

Thin core – a core that operates core messaging, clearing, shared services, and settlement coordination services while leaving sufficient room for private sector innovation and competition.

Footnote [4]

Footnote [3]

Heterogeneity in Service Fee Sensitivity: Evidence from ATM Surcharges
Krzysztof Wozniak

Abstract: Service fees continue to proliferate in a wide range of markets, from retail to payments, generating questions about their impact on consumer choice, competition, and fairness. This paper explores how sensitivity to such fees varies across consumers, use cases, and competitive settings, and whether it is affected by consumer learning. I am able to conduct this in-depth empirical analysis thanks to a uniquely detailed, high-frequency panel data set on surcharged ATM cash withdrawals. Results show that average elasticity estimates mask substantial heterogeneity in consumer sensitivity to service fees. I explore ways in which market and behavioral mechanisms can help explain this heterogeneity. Finally, I investigate whether consumers strategically adjust their behavior in response to service fees.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence
articles.text:
Finance and Economics Discussion Series (FEDS)

Twitter

Share

RSS

November 2026

Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence
Nick Carollo, Leland D. Crane, Daniel Garcia Molina, and Joseph Nichols

Abstract: We assess the current evidence on how AI-related investment and the use of AI are affecting the U.S. macroeconomy. Specifically, we document the boom in data center capital investment, the current rate of adoption of AI tools in the economy, the impact of the AI-related investment surge on prices, and discuss whether AI tools have affected the labor market and productivity yet. Driven by current and expected future demand for AI services, investment in data centers, both the physical structures and semiconductor chips and other IT equipment inside the structures, has climbed sharply. AI adoption is growing rapidly both among consumers and firms, though most firms are currently not using AI very intensively or at all. AI model-producing firms have also grown extremely fast, and now account for a noticeable fraction of software industry gross output. Prices have climbed in sectors that provide direct inputs to the data centers, such as memory chips. Effects on the labor market so far appear small and somewhat mixed. Similarly, the effects of AI on aggregate productivity growth also appear to be small so far, and the recent pickup in productivity likely reflects factors that predated the diffusion on generative AI.
Keywords: AI, Artificial Intelligence, Data Centers, Investment, Labor supply and demand, Prices, business fluctuations, and cycles

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesMARKETSGlobal Music Revenues Are Forecast to Rise as Subscriber Growth Beats ExpectationsNov 5, 2026ShareMusic industry forecastThe outlook for recorded musicGrowth markets for streamingOpportunities to grow subscriptionsWhat's boosting live music?How will AI impact music?In Summary Goldman Sachs Research expects global music revenues to grow at an annualized rate of 5.8% to almost $200 billion in 2035 from $112 billion in 2025. Paid subscriptions for music streaming have ample room to grow relative to gaming and on-demand video services. Our analysts see an opportunity for increased conversion from free to paid subscription tiers among older age groups. The market for live music is forecast to grow 6% in 2026 despite economic uncertainty, driven by a strong global arena and stadium business. AI represents an opportunity for the industry as streaming providers and tech companies use the technology to personalize algorithms, curate content, and transform passive listeners into active creators.Global music industry revenues are expected to reach approximately $200 billion annually by 2035 amid an improving outlook for subscription streaming. New subscription models, AI, and direct-to-consumer offerings are creating opportunities for the industry to reach audiences in new ways, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
The music market undershot growth expectations over the last several years. The new forecast represents the first time in three years that Goldman Sachs Research has raised its long-term outlook for the industry, Stephen Laszczyk and Eric Sheridan write in the team’s 2026 edition of the annual “Music in the Air” report. Goldman Sachs Research expects global music revenues to increase at 6.7% year-on-year in 2026 and at a compound rate of 5.8% per year between 2025 and 2035.
“While growth is likely to moderate from the pace observed during the industry's streaming adoption phase, we continue to see a long runway for industry expansion supported by favorable consumer behavior and an increasingly diversified monetization model,” Laszczyk and Sheridan write.
Music streaming subscriptions are growing faster than expected
Paid streaming subscriptions are helping to shore up the outlook for recorded music. After three consecutive downgrades to its forecast for 2030 recorded music revenues, Goldman Sachs Research’s outlook for the segment this year reflects improvements in streaming revenue, physical revenue, and download and other digital revenue.
Subscription streaming revenue is growing faster, mainly because subscriber numbers are increasing more quickly than expected and revenue per user is rising in developed markets. Our analysts are factoring in more consistent price increases from streaming platforms as music labels increasingly incorporate higher royalties into their contracts and streaming platforms introduce new premium service tiers.
At the same time, increasing fan demand for vinyl and CDs is helping lift the outlook for physical music revenues in markets like Japan, South Korea, and the US. “We expect these trends to continue as fans increasingly view physical formats as collectibles rather than as a way to listen, and as artists incorporate physical formats into their album rollouts and tour experiences,” Laszczyk and Sheridan write.
Which markets will drive the growth of music?
Paid subscription streaming revenue beat our analysts’ expectations in 2025, and Goldman Sachs Research expects further growth ahead, driven by emerging markets. Laszczyk and Sheridan forecast the percentage of internet users with paid streaming subscriptions in emerging markets to rise from 10% in 2025 to 15% in 2035, with subscriber numbers boosted by growing populations and increasing internet penetration.
Paid subscriptions in developed markets also have room to grow, according to Laszczyk and Sheridan, who expect the number of paid subscribers in the US, Canada, Europe, and Australasia to rise to 568 million in 2035 from 398 million in 2025.
Only around 53% of Americans subscribed to paid music streaming in 2025, compared with around 60% for gaming and 90% for on-demand video. Goldman Sachs Research expects most developed markets to approach peak penetration for paid music streaming at 60% by 2035.
“Subscribers have been growing at a healthy clip. Going forward, we expect subscribers to grow in the mid-single-digit range over the next 10 years, driven by emerging market penetration and continued growth in developed markets.”Stephen LaszczykGoldman Sachs ResearchOlder age groups and new products could help drive paid music users
Older listeners could be an untapped audience. Data from the UK shows that older listeners are less likely to use paid streaming and less likely to convert from free to paid users.
“We see opportunity for increased conversion from free to paid among older age groups, especially as younger age cohorts who are heavy users of paid streaming services grow older, and as streaming providers adapt their marketing strategies to target older demographics,” Laszczyk and Sheridan write.
Introducing an ad-light tier could also help streaming providers drive subscriber acquisition. Goldman Sachs Research estimates that a small incremental fee of around $1-2 per month for a reduced advertising load could result in subscriber growth. “This follows a similar playbook to what has already been implemented in video streaming,” Laszczyk and Sheridan observe.
If 10% of free streaming users in developed markets shifted to a $1 ad-light tier, global ad-supported revenues would rise by around 8%, Goldman Sachs Research estimates.
Another emerging opportunity in streaming is direct-to-consumer offerings, where artists build a direct relationship with their fans without an intermediary platform controlling access to that audience.
This innovation is still in its early stages, Laszczyk and Sheridan write. But “if this ecosystem continues to develop the way it has been, the direct-to-consumer opportunity could grow from representing tens of millions of dollars of revenue today to hundreds of millions over the next decade.”
Increased touring and new venues are buoying live music
Despite pressure on consumer wallets from tariffs, gasoline prices, and higher interest rates, our analysts expect the market for live music to grow 6% in 2026, driven by a strong global arena and stadium business.
This supports Goldman Sachs Research’s thesis that demand for live events has increased globally since the Covid-19 pandemic, and that the sector is less exposed to economic downturns than other forms of discretionary spending.
Looking ahead, our analysts expect live music to grow at a similar 6% compound rate through 2035, underpinned by an increasing supply of diverse and popular artists touring over the next decade.
Stronger financial incentives to tour and efforts by record labels to promote new talent are set to drive the live music sector, Laszczyk and Sheridan project. And they expect venue capacity to grow, with operators poised to open several dozen new music venues around the world in the next five to seven years.
“Live music is a durable form of spending. If your favorite artist is making their way through town once every so many years, you are likely to prioritize that concert over other forms of discretionary spending.”Stephen LaszczykGoldman Sachs ResearchHow will AI impact the music industry?
AI’s impact on the music industry has been “the biggest debate among music investors over the last year,” Laszczyk and Sheridan say. One concern is that AI-generated music will displace human artists, but Laszczyk and Sheridan believe that fear is overblown for higher-profile artists in the near term. While the team does see some potential for cannibalization by AI over the long term, they expect that it will mostly be limited to lower-value music (including background and study music as well as mid-tier artists).
Only a mid-single-digit percentage of consumers used an AI music generation tool at least monthly as of the fourth quarter of 2025. As of the third quarter of 2025, around 55% of music creators had used an AI tool in the past year, but mostly for production workflow or mastering rather than to generate entirely new songs.
At the same time, AI represents an opportunity for music labels and rights holders: Streaming providers and tech companies can use the technology to personalize recommendations, curate content, and turn passive listeners into active creators.
“We believe that monetization will ultimately make its way back to the rights holders in a way that we think will disproportionately benefit some of these higher-end artists where AI music is likely created off of their image and likeness, their melodies, or their lyrics, given how popular they are,” Laszczyk says.

Modernizing the Payments Operating Model

From fragmented processes to a seamless 24/7 payments system

Isabel Schmidt

calendar_today

25 Sep, 2026

Payments modernization today goes beyond upgrading rails: It’s about redesigning the operating model for a continuous, data-rich – and increasingly intelligent – rail-agnostic payments environment.

As real-time payments, ISO 20022, tokenization, and digital finance arrive in waves at different speeds, the organizations best positioned for what's next will be those that reduce complexity at the core.

This paper traces BNY's journey toward a unified, capability-based platform—and the operating model decisions around data, AI, and resilience that make 24/7 payments possible. Download the full paper to learn more and explore the key questions every payments leader should be asking.

Download the paper

launch

Key Takeaways

Payments modernization should be approached as an enterprise-wide redesign of the operating model, not a rail-by-rail technology upgrade, to build the agility a 24/7 ecosystem demands.A unified orchestration layer with common controls and standardized data across fiat and digital-cash rails resolves fragmentation caused by nearly 100 global real-time payment rails and emerging digital-finance ecosystems.Transaction data and governed agentic AI are core operating capabilities that embed automation directly into workflows and turn payment data into an enterprise asset rather than bolt-on tools.Reliability, resilience and simplification must be embedded as foundational architectural principles, supported by practices like blue-green deployment and consolidated processing, to sustain always-on operations.

Navigating Payment Modernization Challenges

In an interview with Trade Treasury Payments (TTP), BNY’s Isabel Schmidt discusses how banks should handle a growing number of rails and forms of money, and why certainty matters to treasurers as much as speed.

AI is key for 24/7 payments

Agentic AI is emerging as a critical enabler of the 24/7/365 payments operating model. In a recent poll of attendees at the BNY webinar, “Payments Without Pause: The Journey to 24/7/365”:

46%

of respondents said AI and automation will have the biggest impact on treasury operations in the next three years.

44%

said legacy technology was the biggest barrier to 24/7/365 payments

Modernization is about more than speed. It is about building the capacity to adapt: to absorb new rails and digital cash models, manage risk in real time, deploy change safely in a 24/7/365 environment and use data and AI more effectively across operations.

November 2026

Costly Misdemeanours: Labour Market Effects of Low-Level Drink-Driving Violations
Kabir Dasgupta, Marco Francesconi, Jonathan James Linda Kirkpatrick, and Alexander Plum

Abstract: This paper estimates the causal effect of a drink-driving conviction on labour market outcomes. Using linked administrative data and variation in the timing of first convictions in a staggered difference-in-differences design, we compare individuals before and after conviction to those convicted later. We find employment falls by 6–7 percentage points and monthly earnings decline by around 2 percent. The effects are driven primarily by reduced job entry as opposed to job loss. Employment effects are largest in industries where employers are more likely to screen applicants for criminal convictions.
Keywords: Drink-driving convictions, Criminal records and employment, Labour market effects of crime, Administrative data and causal inference

The big question for onshore wind: what to do with ageing turbines?

View Charles Coppins's full profile

Wind and solar are infinite sources of renewable energy. But the equipment that generates power from these resources – the turbines and panels – physically degrades over time and must eventually either be removed or replaced. After a quarter of a century of deployment, renewable project developers are now facing the choice of decommissioning, extending asset life or repowering sites with the latest technology.
What is the scale of decommissioning? Does repowering make economic sense? Who stands to gain most? Soren Lassen and Charles Coppins from our Power and Renewables team explain how the next generation of renewables could deliver more power at lower cost.
How big is the decommissioning challenge?
Large, and growing fast. Of the more than 3.5 TW of wind and solar capacity operational worldwide by the of 2025, Wood Mackenzie forecasts that over 70% will face a decommission, extend or repower decision in the 2040s.
Ageing wind projects are the most pressing. Our latest Horizons report shows that almost 50 GW of wind is now over 20 years old, broadly the design life of these earlier turbines. The number quickly rises to over 230 GW by 2040. And while the rapid deployment of solar PV may have started later, global solar capacity more than 20 years old will overtake wind before 2040.
Does repowering make economic sense?
There’s a compelling case. With capital and operating costs on a par with greenfield projects, the economic advantage of repowering comes mainly from higher output as technology advances. Given the site will always outlast the equipment, repowered projects can also skip grid-connection queues and often clear permitting faster. Location matters. In Germany, for example, decommissioned sites have average wind speeds 4% higher than new greenfield projects, delivering higher capacity factors and a lower levelised cost of energy.
And it isn’t only about economics. Without repowering, growth in global annual wind and solar installations risks stalling. If greenfield renewables additions can’t keep pace as policy support softens, more coal and gas will be required to fill the gap. 
Is technology changing the equation?
Substantially. The average wind turbine rating has increased fourfold over the past two decades and continues to rise. Meanwhile, the efficiency of solar modules has risen by almost 70% over the same period and average solar sites now require around a third less land for the same capacity.
Hardware is also getting more robust. Wind turbine design life has climbed from 20 years to more than 30, while warranties for solar panels have increased by five years as degradation levels continue to improve.
What does this mean for power markets?
Simply decommissioning ageing wind and solar projects does nothing for meeting capacity targets. Take the European Commission's 500 GW wind goal for 2030. Reaching this requires about 37 GW of additions a year through to 2030. If all end-of-design-life projects are decommissioned, around 2 GW more would need to be added annually to achieve published goals.
Repowering can side-step this. Sticking with Germany, we estimate repowering existing projects would raise the country’s onshore wind output by 16% in 2050, which would represent almost a third of the country's current annual wind generation. This matters not only for installation targets but also for consumers as repowered supply could significantly lower power prices.
Who gains most from repowering?
Aside from customers enjoying lower electricity bills, equipment suppliers stand to benefit most. Repowering existing sites means global equipment sales could be more than 60% higher in 2050 than at present even as the pace of annual net additions declines.
The distribution of repowering opportunities is uneven, however. While decommissioning will drive 44% of wind and almost a quarter of solar buildout worldwide in the 2040s, the figures are notably higher in established markets across Europe, Asia and the Americas.
Repowering could usher in an era of renewal and lead to more wind and solar installations than ever before. The impact of this will take years to fully materialise but is already relevant to strategic decision making today. As governments and consumers grapple with volatile fossil fuel prices, planning for future energy renewal opportunities should already be on the agenda.

November 9 – Markets digest the blue wave

Ready to talk?

Markets entered a bout of volatility after the Democratic sweep of Congress in the US midterm elections, and uncertainty about what it means for the AI trade and the buildout of data centres is a part of that, says Christian Nolting, the Private Bank’s Global Chief Investment Officer. “We saw quite a bit of rotation,” Christian says.

Much of the political upheaval has been attributed to voter anger around the cost of living, particularly fuel costs, and Christian says he doesn’t expect those prices to moderate soon. “We do forecast energy prices to stay high for quite some time, but we do not forecast that we go substantially higher again from here.”

US inflation figures are due in the week ahead, as well as third-quarter GDP in the eurozone – but the tremors in markets after the election are likely to remain in the spotlight, Christian says. “The focus at this point in time is the next step for the central banks, and also how is the AI trade doing this week.”

articles.title: The great mid-term rotation
articles.text:
Weekly Market Directions

Inflation

Fixed income

Europe

Commodities

Equity

9 November, 2026

5 minutes

The great mid-term rotation

EDM

Weekly Market DirectionsENFR

The great mid-term rotation

5 minutes

EDM

Weekly Market DirectionsENFR

Summary

The strong rotation fuelled by the US mid-term election results and investor scrutiny of massive corporate capex, is a reminder of the need to diversify outside the AI theme across regions and sectors.

Over the past few weeks, we have seen a rotation away from US tech due to scrutiny of the massive capex and results of the US mid terms.By contrast, global defensive sectors and some regions such as India posted gains.This rotation underscores the importance of a global, diversified approach that avoids concentration in US tech.

The US midterm elections delivered a Democratic sweep of Congress, and markets responded with a dramatic rotation. The shift was swift and decisive: investors moved out of high-growth, technology-heavy businesses into areas of the market that had long been overlooked. The clearest losers were semiconductor and AI-linked stocks, as investors worried about increased regulation in the sector and demanded more clarity on the massive spending plans of large technology companies. The Japanese market, heavily exposed to the global technology supply chain, was also caught in the sell-off. By contrast, European equities held their ground, and the Indian market posted strong gains, reflecting a broader search for alternatives to the US. Defensive global equities — think utilities, healthcare, and consumer staples — quietly outperformed. The message from the markets seems to be that the era of undisputed US technology dominance is being questioned.

This week at a glance

Global equities declined following the US mid-term elections, led by falls in technology stocks. Europe, however, was broadly flat. Bond yields declined across major regions as markets sought safer assets. In commodities, oil prices dropped sharply on expectations of diplomatic progress in the Middle East conflict, while gold rose.

Amundi Investment Institute Macro Focus

AmericasUS Factory Activity Gains MomentumThe Institute for Supply Management's manufacturing index rose to 55.5 in October, above expectations and its second-highest level in over four years. Production reached its best level in several years, a sign of robust industrial momentum. On the labour market front, latest private-sector hiring and weekly jobless claims points to a resilient labour market that supports the broader economic expansion.EuropeBoE Raises Rates as Inflation Outlook WorsensThe Bank of England raised its key interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% on Thursday — its first increase since August 2023. Governor Andrew Bailey signalled that a further increase is more likely than not if energy costs remain elevated, with the Bank now forecasting inflation could reach close to 5% in the second quarter of next year — well above its 2% target. AsiaJapan's Wages Grow at Fastest Pace Since 1997 Nominal wages rose 4.6% year on year in September, the fastest pace in decades. After adjusting for inflation, real wages grew 2.2%, well above economists' expectations. These figures reinforce the view that the wage-growth cycle is becoming more durable, which supports household purchasing power and is a key factor the Bank of Japan monitors when assessing its monetary policy.

Global Markets and EconomyIndustry Perspectives Episode 6GROWTH: Mega Trends - Challenges and OpportunitiesIndustry Perspectives • Podcast • November 12, 2026View TranscriptIn continuing our Industry Perspectives podcast series, we remain focused on the topic of growth. We are joined again by Citi industry experts Rob Rowe and Nathan Sheets in discussing the recent performance of the global economy, looking at the real- world consequences for businesses, nations and individuals.Our latest episode of the Industry Perspectives podcast explores mega trends, comparing emerging and developed market resilience amid geopolitics, AI adoption and rising debt. Also highlighted is the potential for investors, AI's productivity gains and policy priorities—fiscal discipline and innovation—needed to sustain growth.Amanda Hale, Director & Head of Regulatory Services, Global Trustee & Fiduciary, CitiAmanda has over 40 years of experience in the investments industry and has been with Citi since 2008. Prior to joining Citi, Amanda worked in the CIS Policy Team at the Financial Services Authority (FSA), now the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) after having been with HSBC for 26 years in various areas such as Trustee and Depositary Services, Custody, Settlements, Corporate Actions and Income. Amanda currently represents Citi on external industry committees and panel discussions as well as chairing various internal Citi regulatory committees. She demonstrates an excellent understanding of the financial services’ regulatory environment.Andrew Newson, Senior Regulatory Technical Analyst, CitiAndrew has 27 years’ experience working in financial services. Joining Citi in 1999, Andrew worked as a Valuations Officer in the Citibank Private Bank before moving to Switzerland to become a Fund Management Support Manager in Zurich, where he managed a small team. On his return to London, Andrew joined Citibank Global Asset Management as Manager of the Fiduciary department, leading a team conducting post-trade compliance monitoring of private bank portfolios, institutional and sovereign wealth mandates, and Luxembourg Mutual Funds.In 2006, Andrew stepped into the funds business as a Fiduciary Relationship Manager, entrusted with managing key client relationships spanning both UK authorized and unauthorized fund structures. Since 2014, Andrew has been a driving force within Citi's Regulatory Services team, where he plays a pivotal role in preparing and delivering high-impact regulatory updates to clients, translating complex regulatory change into clear, actionable insight. Andrew has also represented Citi as its Technical representative at the UK Depositary Association.Rob Rowe, Interim Head of Research, CitiRob Rowe is the Global Head of Citi Research’s Global Strategy & Macro Group (GSMG) as well as Head of Research for the Americas. GSMG unites all of Citi’s Economists with Fixed Income, FX, Equity and Commodities strategists to create a common team providing research on the world’s major economies and asset classes. Rob has been with Citi for well over 30-years serving in various capacities within markets and research. He originally joined Smith Barney Harris Upham & Company in 1989 working in Investment Banking, Fixed Income sales and Research.
