There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesExchangesPlaying for Scale: The Future of Sports InvestingNov 10, 2026ShareInvestors are finding opportunities in sports as the media rights market surges and team valuations climb, Nicole Pullen Ross, lead of Sports and Entertainment Solutions within Goldman Sachs Private Wealth Management, explains on the Exchanges podcast. Read the related report.
Subscribe: Spotify / Apple Podcasts / YouTube
Download TranscriptKey takeaways:

The value of sports media rights is soaring: The global sports media market grew 41% from 2020 through 2025 and has continued climbing to an expected $67 billion in 2026.

Private equity and institutional investments are accelerating: Surging media rights are the core driver of growth, lifting sports franchise valuations to historic highs.

Infrastructure and real estate are key: Modern venues and surrounding entertainment districts create benefits that go beyond game day and complement technology-driven fan personalization.

Women’s and college sports are attracting investors: Women’s teams that control their own arenas command higher valuations, and new player-pay rules are prompting college athletic departments to weigh new types of financing.

Transcript:
Nicole Pullen Ross: Ultimately, every investor in a sports team is most interested in winning, and so all of the investment that they can make that will help the team become more valuable allows them to invest more in their players and increase their opportunity for winning.
Allison Nathan: A record price for a minority stake in a major basketball franchise. A multi-billion-dollar investment in one of baseball's most iconic organizations. The first billion-dollar franchise in women's professional sports. And a final court approval of a landmark settlement that will allow college athletes to share directly in revenue.
Together, these headlines show how quickly the business of sports is changing. Teams are no longer simply local family-run businesses. They're becoming global investments, attracting large financial firms and driving new opportunities in media, lending, technology, and real estate. I'm Allison Nathan, and this is Goldman Sachs Exchanges.
Today, we're exploring what's driving that change and what it could mean for investors. Joining me is Nicole Pullen Ross, head of Northeast Private Wealth Management and Sports and Entertainment Solutions at Goldman Sachs. Nicole, thanks for joining us.
Nicole Pullen Ross: So happy to be here. Thank you for having me.
Allison Nathan: Nicole, you hosted a whole Goldman Sachs podcast series on investing in sports in late 2024, but at the time, large investment firms were really just beginning to move into the business of sports. So, catch us up. What's happened since then?
Nicole Pullen Ross: It seems like a long time ago, in some ways, and a blink of an eye in others. It's been pretty incredible to see the pace of change over just a couple of years when we last wrote a white paper around investing in sports.
And there are a couple of themes that I would point to that have driven the explosion that we've seen in sports, certainly over the past two years. The first is what's happened around media rights, and the second is the resulting institutional capital, and those two things are very linked.
And I'll start with media rights because that's the core of what's driving revenue growth, given the nature of the media rights contracts that we've seen. And I start with media rights because you think about the value that advertisers find in one of the last places where they can reach their customers, which is around live sports and live events.
And I have to say, being in some of these places where the level of enthusiasm around rooting for the Knicks, for example in the past season or watching your favorite women's soccer team, whatever it might be. The eyeballs are very valuable. And so what that has led to from a media rights perspective is tremendous revenue growth.
And so, the global media rights market has grown 41% since 2020 to about $57.8 billion in 2025 and is expected to reach $67 billion in 2026. So that is the core driver of the growth that we've seen from a valuation perspective. And increasingly streaming has been a meaningful part of that growth. And if you live with someone like I do, my mother-in-law, who is a sports fan but finds it increasingly challenging to find the app that has her favorite game, those streaming services now represent about 20% of that media rights growth. And so, it's pretty significant in terms of how we've seen the space evolve and the players in the space over the past few years.
Allison Nathan: So how has that really changed what teams are worth and how investors are thinking about their future earnings? With exposure to these teams.
Nicole Pullen Ross: Yes. So media rights contracts are shared by the leagues, the teams, and the players, and they have driven the valuations to increase across most major leagues in the ecosystem more broadly.
One of the things that it has done, which is the second point in terms of what's been driving the market, is influence the inflow of institutional capital, and there's been a significant shift there. When you think about the number of private equity transactions that happened in 2025, there were just short of 200.
So 192 private equity transactions in 2025. That compares to just 50 in 2018 when we launched our sports and entertainment business here in wealth management. And so that institutional flow has shown up in a lot of meaningful ways. The NFL, as we all know, in 2024, was the last major league to allow institutional investment, and we've seen that activity continue to grow. And we've seen expansion of valuations to some pretty extraordinary levels since then.
Allison Nathan: And so that's really expanded the ways that teams can actually raise money for investment and growth. If you are the team and you are an investor, an owner, have a stake in the team, and you're making that decision, should we bring in more investors or should we actually borrow money, seeing as there's a lot more capital available, how do you make that decision? What factors are at play?
Nicole Pullen Ross: Interestingly, we included a case study in the white paper that we wrote, called Playing for Scale: The Future of Investing in Sports, from one of our clients who was thinking about this very question, and there are lots of considerations.
One is the stability of the investment that you're looking to make. Another is the return expectation. And if you are investing in an expansion team, a women's expansion team, let's call it that, on one end of the spectrum versus a major league NFL team, which is the most mature, the answer to that question is going to vary.
And we see some clients, we were talking to a client who was focused on a facility for a WNBA team, and the question they were asking themselves is, "Should we take public financing or should we do it ourselves?" And ultimately decided to finance privately because they wanted their local community and the funds there to be put to different use to help the community.
So there are a variety of factors that clients think through in terms of understanding the best return and also how to align that passion that they have around sports and the community impact as well.
Allison Nathan: A lot of this capital flowing into the business of sports is actually flowing into the infrastructure, the stadiums, the restaurants, the shops, all of this development around these core stadiums we've all benefited from that, I think, as sports fans. But construction costs are rising. Interest rates are higher. We'll see if that persists. But how do owners decide whether these projects will pay off?
Obviously, a big investment. And how do they really gain confidence in that decision given the long lead time of construction and so many uncertainties as we go farther out into the future?
Nicole Pullen Ross: Yeah. If you think about the average stadium cost now of $1.7 billion, it's a big decision. And having an appreciation of the complexity of solutions that's available is one of the things that our clients think through.
The other component is making sure that they are building something that has an expanse of life. And so not just the fan experience of today, but how can we make sure that we're using technology and AI and creating a sports ecosystem around the stadium or the arena that all help diversify the revenue streams and help create opportunities for the models to be more attractive in terms of not only looking at game day, but having a facility that can be used year-round and having a community or a smaller city around that stadium or arena are some of the factors that clients consider.
Allison Nathan: Talk to us a little bit more about that technology angle because it is really transforming the experience of fans. What does that look like? Give us some examples of what has evolved.
Nicole Pullen Ross: Yeah. It really ranges. Some of it is athlete immersion, right? And so it's not just about how the athlete performs during the game, but it's all the branding around the athlete. It's the engagement. It's the ability for fans to feel connected in a way that technology allows in a much more impactful way.
It's walking into an arena and the arena recognizing that the restaurant choice that you have takes you through a certain gate and that your order shows up at your seat.
And so that technology and that AI infusion allows for that fan experience to really feel personalized and it allows for the engagement with the athletes to improve as well. Ultimately, every investor in a sports team is most interested in winning, and so all of the investment that they can make that will help the team become more valuable allows them to invest more in their players and increase their opportunity for winning, which was a constant reminder in all the conversations that we had.
Allison Nathan: Nicole, correct me if I'm wrong, but most of our conversation up to now has been about men's sports teams. Women's sports teams are in a very different position, even though they are so much in focus, there's so much buzz about women's teams right now. But most of them still play in rented venues and don't have a permanent home. How important is having that permanent venue to the growth of women's sports?
Nicole Pullen Ross: It's a very big factor and it is also a driver of the valuation growth that we've seen. There's no better example than what is happening in the WNBA right now. The Valkyries are the most highly valued WNBA team at $850 million. And the Atlanta Dream are the least valued team, ranked number 13 at $280 million, I believe is the valuation there.
And one of the factors that contributes to that valuation is the ability to have a permanent facility, and we're seeing this play out real time with the Atlanta Dream and all of the conversations that are happening around where they will be able to play. They now have I think there were 51 games that had a million viewers or more, and so there is an attraction.
Fans want to see and be part of that experience. But the Atlanta Dream plays in a facility that I think holds 3,500 fans. And the expectation, at least what I've read publicly, is that they will hope to play in the main arena, which I think holds 17,000 or so. And so watching that enthusiasm, having surpassed that phase of growth where you kind of need to ramp into a broader stadium, is one of the things that I think will continue to contribute to valuations. And having that permanency is a meaningful factor for sure.
Allison Nathan: What would make achieving that attractive to investors to really draw in the capital?
Nicole Pullen Ross: I think that's a bit of what we're seeing. We did a survey of our family office clients, and one of the top items on their list was investing in sports. And yes, there was the anchor of NFL or men's major leagues, but there was also this broader ecosystem. And so the value of having the real estate investment, the value of investing in the technology, investing in the ability to have exposure to gaming and the betting ecosystem. All of those factors I think are part of the calculation in terms of how you think about not only the permanency of the facility, but also all of the connected business opportunities in the ecosystem.
Allison Nathan: Let's spend a moment on college sports. As I mentioned at the start, there's been a landmark multi-billion-dollar settlement. It's changing how athletes are getting paid. But what does the settlement do? Walk us through it, and what will that really mean for athletes and schools?
Nicole Pullen Ross: Yes, I appreciate the question because it's a topic that we're hearing a lot of interest in. And so as we dig in, we are talking to investors who have spent more time on the college space. And it strikes me, and I didn't realize this several years ago, but college football is the second-largest commercial sport in the US behind football. And so, if you kind of grew up at a southern school or sone of these huge schools, you kind of know that. You've lived that.
Allison Nathan: I believe that. My household Saturdays are very dedicated to college football.
Nicole Pullen Ross: It's extraordinary. It's extraordinary. And so, it's had a tremendous transformative impact on what's happening in the space. And so now that the athletes themselves have the ability to earn an income through name, image, and likeness, the colleges are becoming much more competitive and looking a lot more like a major league team in terms of how they are looking to raise capital to support not only the growth of their current team or to fund their current team, but to fund the growth as well.
And so we're seeing investors think creatively about how they can play a role in that financing process. And so there are examples of private equity firms offering a line of credit for growth for some of those large schools, and a lot of discussion around how there can be a process in place to help fund that growth.
I think it's going to be an interesting few years to see how this all evolves, and there is lots of debate on what the right answer is or isn't, but clear that there will continue to be investment in the space and that the NIL change will have a certainly have a long-term impact.
Allison Nathan: Relatedly, it feels that some of these schools are recognizing that they actually need to have a successful football program or sports program to achieve the rankings and the success they want as a school. It's really a very interesting dynamic. Lastly, let me ask where you see opportunities for investors that are interested in gaining exposure to the business of sports right now.
Nicole Pullen Ross: Clients are answering that question in a variety of ways. They're starting to think about opportunities outside of the US—international expansion.
If you look at any of the major leagues, you're seeing that. You see the NFL playing nine games this season in Europe. You see the NBA looking for opportunities to expand outside of the US as well, and having an increasingly global footprint, both in terms of the teams as well as their media rights strategies.
And so there is this exploration of where you can see more meaningful growth, and that's taking some clients outside of the US, whether it's looking at those major leagues or increasingly trying to figure out ways to have exposure to European football, which continues to be a great opportunity for growth.
And we're seeing this trend that is fueled by things like F1, et cetera, where investors are trying to determine where they can get into a process where there's still meaningful upside potential. And so I think that's taking folks to global opportunities, a lot of interest in women's sports, and then emerging leagues as well, whether it be really creative teams or leagues like what Unrivaled has built, or opportunities around rugby or flag football or whatever the emerging sport might be, where investors are saying, "Okay, I really want growth equity sort of return versus kind of longer term buyout return in the space."
And depending on your view and how you think about risk, longevity, passion, return, et cetera, it takes you to an investment horizon and a scope of investments that is pretty broad with the obviously related amount of risk and return along that line across the spectrum.
Allison Nathan: Let me ask actually a last clarifying question, because when we say client here we're talking about wealthy individuals, we're talking about institutions. Ultimately though, what about regular people who love sports, want to be involved in sports. Are there ways to gain exposure for those clients?
Nicole Pullen Ross: Yes. There are definitely funds that offer broad exposure. There are a few publicly traded teams that you can buy a share in through an exchange, and there's been some activity around some of those names as well. And so I think this broadening of investment reach is not just available to those categories of investors that have traditionally had exposure, but we do see the trend increasing where the access to investments is becoming more broadly available at certainly lower levels than having to write a multi-hundred million or billion dollar check or finance an investment in that way. And so we're certainly seeing much more activity and opportunity broadly speaking.
Allison Nathan: Right. So more opportunity and more access.
Nicole Pullen Ross: More access.
Allison Nathan: Thanks so much for joining
Nicole Pullen Ross: A pleasure. Thank you for having me.
Allison Nathan: This episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges was recorded on Tuesday, October 27th, 2026. If you enjoyed the show, we hope you subscribe on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. And please leave us a rating and a comment. I'm Allison Nathan. Thanks for listening.

This episode was recorded on October 27, 2026.

articles.title: Pakistan's Tariff Regime: Comparative Perspective
articles.text:
Consulting Report

11 Nov 2026

Pakistan’s Tariff Regime: Comparative Perspective

Tariff, para-tariff and implication for export strategy

The National Tariff Policy 2025–30 (NTP) presents Pakistan’s average tariff, including para-tariffs, as higher than those of eight comparator economies: India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Thailand, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Vietnam. This report reassesses the NTP’s international comparisons by examining Pakistan’s customs duties and para-tariffs on a consistent basis alongside those of the nine comparator economies, including Türkiye. The analysis incorporates Pakistan’s recent tariff reforms and available data for the comparator countries.

Pakistan’s average customs duties are in the middle of the study-country range. Its simple-average most-favoured-nation (MFN) tariff is 9.5%, below those of India, Bangladesh and Nepal and equal to Vietnam’s. Its trade-weighted average is 6.7%, also in the middle of the group.

Moving beyond average tariff levels, the analysis of tariff peaks shows that Pakistan’s share of high-duty tariff lines is comparable to the regional level. In 2025, 31.0% of its tariff lines carried duties above 15%, compared with the five-country South Asian average of 30.7%, placing Pakistan fourth among the ten study economies.

Pakistan compares more favourably with its peers when higher thresholds are used to define tariff peaks. A separate sensitivity analysis using common-year 2023 data places Pakistan below the South Asian study-country average at thresholds of 25%, 35% and 50%. This suggests a concentration of moderately high duties rather than an unusually large share of extreme rates compared to regional peers.

Including para-tariffs changes the comparison, but does not make Pakistan uniquely high among the selected economies. Its estimated combined simple average of tariffs and para-tariffs is 17.7%, compared with 28.1% for Bangladesh, 19.3% for Sri Lanka, 17.3% for Türkiye and 16.0% for India. Consistent treatment of these additional charges is therefore essential. Differences in data coverage, reference periods and policy changes mean these estimates remain a best-effort comparison, not a comprehensive measure of all import charges.

Overall, the data do not support the claim that Pakistan has the highest tariff levels among the economies compared. An analysis of simple average tariff rate and export as a share of GDP also show no clear correlation between the two. These findings suggest that Pakistan’s export strategy should rest on how reform would improve export competitiveness rather than on tariff reduction alone. Two broader implications are important going forward. First, tariff reform needs to sit within a broader package that strengthens exporters’ competitiveness, including improvements in energy, logistics, finance and skills. Second, amid rising protectionism, the sequencing of tariff reductions and trade negotiations deserves careful consideration. Preserving scope to offer preferential tariff concessions could help Pakistan negotiate reciprocal access to overseas markets.

articles.title: Global data centre construction to peak in 2030
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

13 Nov 2026

Global data centre construction to peak in 2030

Data centre construction work done in the 25 markets we forecast will grow 45% over the next four years to peak at US$212bn in 2030. Construction activity will then fall 40% through to 2037 but remain more than three times the 2022 level.

What you will learn:

The US remains the largest market for data centre construction activity and will account for over 60% of global spending growth over the next two years. Activity continues to be driven by tech giants (Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Google and OpenAI) building data centres for their own purposes. China is the 2nd largest market.

Australia will be the fastest growing market through to 2028. Ireland will be the 2nd fastest growing market.

New data centre announcements far exceed the capability of the construction industry to deliver the pipeline. Ongoing tightness in many construction labour markets limits the number of projects that can break ground and affects live projects through both input cost escalation (as workers are paid higher wages) and project delays (as work cannot be completed as quickly).

In the US there is a risk that sweeping Democratic victories place greater restrictions on the next wave of data centre projects. We think this risk is more prevalent at the state and local level where governors, utility regulators, and zoning boards set the rates, incentives, permitting and grid access of data centres.

articles.title: The role of refining costs and margins in HICP energy inflation
articles.text: The role of refining costs and margins in HICP energy inflation Prepared by Filippo Durero, Umberto Maglione, Ana-Simona Manu, Aidan Meyler, Mario Porqueddu, Tito Quadri and Ieva RubenePublished as part of the ECB Economic Bulletin, Issue 7/2026.The conflict in the Middle East is continuing to shape energy prices amid significant uncertainty. Brent front-month crude oil prices increased to above USD 110 per barrel at the end of October, close to 60% above pre-conflict levels. As pressures on crude oil prices and their volatility remain elevated, shortages originating from the Middle East, coupled with outages in Russia, have also strained global refinery operations and the supply of refined products, pushing up consumer prices.Global refinery runs have fallen sharply compared with previous years, driven by reduced refinery activity in the Middle East, Russia and Asia (Chart A, panels a and b). Middle Eastern refineries were affected by reduced export capacity on account of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, while Asian refineries reliant on Gulf crude oil have struggled with costly substitutions. China also curbed fuel exports as of March to safeguard domestic fuel supply, with significant cuts continuing until the end of June. However, the restrictions were eased temporarily in July and August. Russian refining capacity has also declined recently following a wave of Ukrainian attacks on energy infrastructure. In response, Russia extended its diesel and petrol export bans until the end of January 2027. For fuel producers, the diesel export ban remained in effect until 31 October 2026, although it was partially eased from 10 October following a supply agreement with the United States. As a result, seaborne diesel imports into the EU were down 56% and petrol imports down 52% at the end of September compared to pre-conflict levels amid limited substitution availability from other countries (Chart A, panel c).Chart ADevelopments in global refinery runs and EU seaborne imports of diesel productsa) Global refinery runs(million barrels per day)b) Total decline in refinery runs since the end of 2025(change between 2025 and May 2026, million barrels per day)c) EU seaborne diesel imports by country of origin(million barrels per day)Sources: Bloomberg, International Energy Agency (IEA), LSEG, ECB and ECB staff calculations. Notes: In panel a), the dashed line represents IEA forecasts; “Range (2015-2025) excluding pandemic” excludes the period from March 2020 to December 2021. In panel b), “APAC” is the Asia-Pacific region excluding China, the Middle East and the EAEU; “EAEU” is the Eurasian Economic Union (Russia and other central Asian countries, according to IEA classifications). In panel c), “ROW” is the rest of the world; “Other Middle East” is the Middle East excluding Saudi Arabia; “Pre-pandemic” refers to the period from 1 January 2018 to 21 February 2020; “Pre-Ukraine war” refers to the period from 21 February 2020 to 24 February 2022; “Pre-Middle East conflict” refers to the period from 5 February 2023 (start of EU embargo) to 28 February 2026; “Middle East conflict” refers to the period since 28 February 2026. The latest observations are for July 2026 (monthly data) for panels a) and b), and 30 September 2026 (daily data) for panel c).The constrained supply of crude oil and refined products has led to a persistent increase in refining margins and costs globally, particularly for diesel (Chart B, panel a). This phenomenon underscores the interconnected nature of liquid fuel markets, where disruptions in one region, such as the Middle East or Russia, have ripple effects across the globe. Elevated diesel refining margins (crack spreads), which surged to around three times pre-Middle East conflict levels in Europe, reflect the tightness of global supply and the inability of regional markets to fully insulate themselves from external shocks (Chart B, panel b).[1] In this box, the terms “refining margins”, “refining costs and margins” and “crack spreads” are used interchangeably. Refining margins are calculated as the difference between the price of the refined product and the price of crude oil. This includes costs which occur in the production of the refined product, such as insurance, transport and labour costs, as well as a mark-up over the cost of production. Petrol refining margins, also increased until September, but weakened sharply in October (Chart B, panel c).Chart BRecent international developments in crude oil and refined product prices and in refining costs and marginsa) Brent crude and refined petrol and diesel prices in Europe(USD per barrel)b) Diesel refining costs and margins (crack spreads)(USD per barrel)c) Petrol refining costs and margins (crack spreads)(USD per barrel)Sources: Bloomberg, LSEG, ECB and ECB staff calculations.Notes: In panel a), all series represent physical/spot prices. Panels b) and c) show diesel and petrol/gasoline refining margins, calculated as product prices minus the regional crude benchmark. All series use the nearest available futures contract. European spreads use ARA ultra-low-sulphur gasoil and Eurobob gasoline against Brent crude. Asian spreads use Singapore 10 ppm gasoil and 92 RON gasoline against Dubai crude. US spreads use New York Harbor ULSD and RBOB gasoline against West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude. The latest observations are for 28 October 2026.In addition to some structural shifts, refining margins in the euro area, measured in real terms, have been elevated and volatile since 2020 (Chart C, panel a). Margins fell in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, rebounded strongly following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, peaked in early 2023, and eased back towards pre-pandemic levels in the second half of 2024. Margins have surged again since the start of the Middle East conflict. This heightened volatility follows a gradual increase in refining margins over the past two decades, driven by structural shifts in the sector.[2] Refining margins have increased in nominal terms over time. After having been very low at around USD 4 per barrel for both petrol and diesel until 2003, margins increased as global refining markets became tighter with the emerging demand from China and averaged around USD 10 per barrel from 2004 to 2021 (with levels typically being slightly higher for diesel than for petrol). Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, margins have averaged around USD 14 per barrel for petrol and USD 28 per barrel for diesel. Historically, margin spikes have been short-lived, as they create incentives to adjust the supply-demand balance as well as the product mix of refineries. The current disruption may be harder and slower to correct.Chart CDevelopments in prices of liquid fuels for transport and heatinga) Components of liquid fuel prices in real terms(2026 euro cent per litre)b) Decomposition of price inflation for liquid fuels(annual percentage changes, percentage point contributions)Sources: Eurostat, LSEG, European Commission (Weekly Oil Bulletin, WOB) and ECB staff calculations.Notes: Liquid fuel prices are calculated as a weighted average of transport (diesel and petrol) and heating oil prices using HICP weights. Panel a): The individual components are shown in 2026 euro cent per litre deflated by HICP inflation. Data for 2026 refer to the year up to 28 October 2026. Panel b): The latest observations are for September 2026.There have also been changes in the dynamics of distribution costs and margins and the tax component of liquid fuel prices since the pandemic and since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Distribution costs and margins rose in 2020 in real terms (perhaps as integrated oil companies sought to offset the decline in sales volumes and refining margins) but have co-moved with refining margins since 2022 and remain at a higher level than before the pandemic. Since 2022, changes in excise duties have partly offset these movements. Having been broadly stable in real terms until 2022, excise duties were reduced in 2022 and 2023. In 2026, the reductions in excise duties, reflecting fiscal measures to curb energy price increases, have been small compared with the rises in crude oil prices and refining and distribution margins.[3] As value added tax (VAT) is levied in percentage terms, the VAT component in euro cent per litre will vary with the sum of the other components (crude oil prices, refining and distribution margins, and excise duties), even if the VAT rate is constant. For consumer prices, changes in refining margins have occasionally been almost as important as developments in crude oil prices, particularly during energy crises (Chart C, panel b). Since the end of February 2026, refining margins have substantially increased, pushing up the rate of inflation for liquid fuels for transport and heating.[4] See Kuik et al. (2026). For a similar decomposition in 2022, see Kuik et al. (2022). Given their importance for HICP inflation, it is useful to capture these dynamics in forecasting models. A real-time forecast evaluation using the ECB’s short-term inflation projection (STIP) energy model suggests that using financial futures to forecast prices for liquid fuels for transport and heating in the euro area results in small improvements, particularly at horizons of 3 to 11 months over the full sample and one month ahead in the pre-pandemic period (until 2019).[5] The STIP energy model used for the evaluation is described in Bańbura et al. (2025). The benefits are less evident during the high-inflation period, when futures prices generally underpredicted subsequent price developments.The STIP energy model shows that refining margins can significantly affect energy inflation. The model was run using two sets of data and assumptions: first using the assumptions for crude oil, gas and refined diesel and petrol based on the cut-off date for the June 2026 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections (21 May); and second using the new data outcomes and the same set of assumptions based on the cut-off date for the September 2026 ECB staff macroeconomic projections (19 August). In both cases, futures for refined product prices from the financial markets were used to inform the outlook. Despite lower oil price assumptions, the September-based forecast yields higher energy inflation, largely because of higher refining costs and margins (Chart D, panels a and b).Chart DPotential role of refining margins in the HICP energy outlooka) Assumptions for the STIP energy model(left-hand scale: euro per litre; right-hand scale: euro per barrel)b) Revision of inflation forecasts from the STIP energy model for liquid fuels for transport and heating: impact of data and changes in assumptions between the June and September 2026 staff projections(percentage points)Sources: Eurostat, LSEG, European Commission (WOB) and ECB staff calculations.Notes: Panel a) compares assumptions based on the cut-off date for the September 2026 projections (19 August, solid lines) and the cut-off date for the June 2026 projections (21 May, dotted lines). Panel b) shows the revision of the forecast annual rate of change between the two cut-off dates. The solid vertical line in the two panels indicates the latest available observation for the September 2026 projections.These findings explain why ECB and Eurosystem staff closely monitor the price trajectories of refined diesel and petrol in their projections. Specifically, financial futures for refined petrol and diesel prices have been used to inform the projections since the start of the conflict in the Middle East to ensure that they are based on all relevant information needed for a proper assessment of the inflation outlook and risks going forward.ReferencesBańbura, M., Bobeica, E., Giammaria, A., Porqueddu, M. and van Spronsen, J. (2025), “A new model to forecast energy inflation in the euro area”, Working Paper Series, No 3062, ECB.European Central Bank (2026a), Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area, June 2026.European Central Bank (2026b), ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area, September 2026.Kuik, F., Adolfsen, J.F., Lis, E.M. and Meyler, A. (2022), “Energy price developments in and out of the COVID-19 pandemic – from commodity prices to consumer prices”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 4, ECB.Kuik, F., Lis, E., Nickel, C. and Porqueddu, M. (2026), “From well to pump: how fuel prices are formed”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 31 July. In this box, the terms “refining margins”, “refining costs and margins” and “crack spreads” are used interchangeably. Refining margins are calculated as the difference between the price of the refined product and the price of crude oil. This includes costs which occur in the production of the refined product, such as insurance, transport and labour costs, as well as a mark-up over the cost of production. Refining margins have increased in nominal terms over time. After having been very low at around USD 4 per barrel for both petrol and diesel until 2003, margins increased as global refining markets became tighter with the emerging demand from China and averaged around USD 10 per barrel from 2004 to 2021 (with levels typically being slightly higher for diesel than for petrol). Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, margins have averaged around USD 14 per barrel for petrol and USD 28 per barrel for diesel. As value added tax (VAT) is levied in percentage terms, the VAT component in euro cent per litre will vary with the sum of the other components (crude oil prices, refining and distribution margins, and excise duties), even if the VAT rate is constant. See Kuik et al. (2026). For a similar decomposition in 2022, see Kuik et al. (2022). The STIP energy model used for the evaluation is described in Bańbura et al. (2025).

articles.text:
Beacon Hospital

Technology and services
Supporting access to advanced healthcare in Ireland

Link copied to clipboard

Macquarie Asset Management is investing in the growth of one of Ireland’s leading private hospitals

Swipe for more

SectorTechnology and servicesSub-sectorHealthcareLocationIreland

Opportunity

Ireland's growing and ageing population is placing greater pressure on healthcare infrastructure and access to timely treatment. This challenge is mirrored across Europe, where longer life expectancy and advances in medical care are also increasing demand for specialist services.1,2
Against this backdrop, investment in modern healthcare facilities, treatment capacity and clinical infrastructure is increasingly important to support patient outcomes and establish long-term resilience across the sector.
Beacon Hospital, located in South Dublin, is one of Ireland's most technologically advanced private hospitals, providing acute care and specialist diagnostic services across a broad range of clinical disciplines to patients from across the country.3
The hospital treats more than 230,000 patients annually and operates 181 inpatient beds, 70 day-case beds, eight operating theatres, three catheterisation laboratories and four endoscopy suites.3 To meet growing demand for its services, investment is needed to expand its capacity and specialist infrastructure.

Approach

In 2024, Macquarie Asset Management (Macquarie) invested in Beacon Hospital through Macquarie-managed funds, supporting the hospital's long-term growth and investment in healthcare infrastructure.4
As part of the acquisition, Macquarie committed additional capital to convert and expand adjacent facilities, supporting plans to increase bed capacity by approximately 30 per cent. The latest phase of this expansion is now underway, with plans to deliver approximately 70 new inpatient beds, a new emergency department, an oncology unit and enhanced staff facilities.5
Further investment has also supported new clinical infrastructure across the existing campus, including a day-case theatre, hybrid operating theatre, Neuro Interventional Radiology laboratory and expanded breast centre.5
Macquarie has also worked with Beacon Hospital to strengthen governance, risk management and sustainability practices – embedding governance standards, introducing a more structured risk management framework and supporting ongoing engagement with clinicians nationwide through programmes such as the hospital’s GP Study Days.5

Outcome

Supported by Macquarie's investment and long-term stewardship, Beacon Hospital is expanding its capacity to meet growing demand for healthcare services and is strengthening its position as a leading provider of specialist care in Ireland.5
The ongoing campus expansion is expected to increase inpatient capacity to more than 250 beds by 2028. Continued investment in facilities, governance and sustainability will help strengthen the hospital's long-term resilience and position it as one of Ireland's most technologically advanced healthcare providers.5
Beacon Hospital has also continued to deliver strong clinical performance, maintaining occupancy of approximately 90 per cent and achieving record outpatient volumes of more than 20,000 visits per month.5
Reflecting its commitment to clinical governance and patient care, the hospital achieved Gold Standard Joint Commission International (JCI) accreditation for the seventh consecutive year in 2025, with a 99 per cent compliance score.6
These outcomes demonstrate how Macquarie's long-term approach can help expand healthcare capacity, strengthen operational resilience and support access to high-quality care.

Demand for high-quality healthcare services continues to grow across Ireland, making investment in healthcare infrastructure increasingly critical. Through our long-term ownership of Beacon Hospital, we are supporting the expansion of clinical facilities, strengthening organisational capabilities and helping create additional capacity that will enable more patients to access specialist care for many years to come.”

articles.title: A case for small-town grit: Sheyenne, North Dakota's quiet comeback | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Podcast
A case for small-town grit: Sheyenne, North Dakota’s quiet comeback

Listen on

Apple Podcasts

Spotify

YouTube

Pod.link

More

Reimagine Rural

Reimagine Rural

HOST:
Anthony F. Pipa

Anthony F. Pipa

Senior Fellow
- Global Economy and Development, Center for Sustainable Development

November 12, 2026

Over the past two decades, the small town of Sheyenne, North Dakota, lost everyday anchors, including its grocery store, restaurant, bank, and school, each closure chipping away at the social fabric of the community.
A local volunteer group, Sheyenne GRIT, has turned a series of community development grants into roughly $800,000 in investments, demonstrating how a modest pool of seed capital can unlock larger opportunities.
Rural revival in Sheyenne has depended less on any single investment than on a steady accumulation of locally driven wins: a new grocery store, rehabilitated houses, a growing annual rodeo, each one signaling that the community is worth betting on.

Aerial view of Sheyenne, North Dakota, from the grain elevator. (Photo by Molly Born)

40 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

I like to get things done, and my parents are like that. My family’s like that. The people of Sheyenne are like that. Like, I’ve also seen many other small towns in North Dakota that are not thriving, and they’re losing resources and losing people. And we’ve been trying to turn the needle in Sheyenne and make sure that doesn’t continue to happen here, that we attract younger families, that we attract workforce, that we have viable housing, that we have essential services.
Joanna Larson, Farmer's Grocery store

In Sheyenne, North Dakota, a shuttered grocery store once signaled decline. Today an honor-system market inside a century-old gas station anchors a broader revival fueled by grassroots grants, rehabbed housing, and a growing roster of community volunteers. This episode of Reimagine Rural explores how a town of roughly 200 people is betting on itself, one investment at a time.
Featuring:

Connie Brown
Gavin Brown
Michelle Gilley
Brent Halseth
Tara Hanson
Megan Langley
Patti Larson
Joanna Larson
Julianna Chenze Millang
Kent Mirey
Sharon Whitmer
