Scenes from Sheyenne, North Dakota

"Welcome to Sheyenne" sign, Sheyenne, North Dakota. (Photo by Molly Born)

Farmer's Grocery along the main road into Sheyenne, North Dakota. (Photo by Molly Born)

Inside Farmer's Grocery in Sheyenne, North Dakota. (Photo by Molly Born)

Suggestion sheet in Farmer's Grocery in Sheyenne, North Dakota. (Photo by Molly Born)

Signs in Farmer's Grocery in Sheyenne, North Dakota. (Photo by Molly Born)

Grain elevator, Sheyenne, North Dakota. (Photo by Molly Born)

Aerial view from atop the grain elevator of Sheyenne, North Dakota. (Photo by Molly Born)

Aerial view of the Larson farm from atop the grain elevator in Sheyenne, North Dakota. (Photo by Molly Born)

At the Youth Garden Club, Sheyenne, North Dakota. (Photo by Molly Born)

01 / 09

"Welcome to Sheyenne" sign, Sheyenne, North Dakota. (Photo by Molly Born)

Transcript

​TONY PIPA: Like many kids in small towns across America, Joanna Larson used to walk to the community grocery store to pick up food for her family.
[music]
A grocery store in a rural area is sacred. If it closes, like it did here in Sheyenne, North Dakota, it can change a place in ways seen and unseen.
[0:20]
Joanna Larson
JOANNA LARSON: And I use a grocery store as just one example, but it’s really other things as well, whether it’s a rural clinic or whether it’s a a gathering space like a senior center, a gas station, or a lunch counter, or a cafe, or a school. Those resources are hard to replace once they’re gone.
TONY PIPA: Joanna Larson is a fourth-generation farmer and rancher from this prairie town of 200 people. That grocery store closure made a lasting impression on her, influencing her educational and work pursuits, and after eight years away, leading her back to her hometown.
JOANNA LARSON: When we lost that, that was something that stands out in my childhood. I think that’s always been in the back of my mind, and has kind of developed my interest in local foods, and a big part of why I I studied agriculture, and wanted to come back to the family farm, and eventually opened a a small store right here on Main Street.
[1:22]
TONY PIPA: That store is an expansion of a roadside stand along a main street in Sheyenne that Joanna ran for two years. She sold her produce and that of other local growers.
JOANNA LARSON: That was pretty successful, I would say. It was not sustainable the amount of time I put in it. But I could see that there was a demand for what we were doing, and I had a vision that potentially if we scaled this to the right size, it could be sustainable.
TONY PIPA: No doubt the demand was there. For years, the nearest grocery store to Sheyenne was 11 miles away. Joanna asked a friend, Gavin Brown, a young contractor from a neighboring town, to help her transform an abandoned gas station along Sheyenne’s main road into her vision. It just opened this past summer. The tape’s a little windy.
[2:11]
GAVIN BROWN SCENE: Well, anyway, thank you all so much for being here. To say I’m shocked with the number of people here on the corner is is an understatement. It’s awesome—
TONY PIPA: — that’s Gavin …
GAVIN BROWN SCENE: —to see you all here. You’ve all mostly been with me through my endeavor of painting and scraping and doing all the fun things. So, I wanna say thank you. There, there is a brick dedicated to this community of Sheyenne, because without this community, I don’t think this would’ve been possible. not only did people give money to support the project, but also a lot of people came to help, to smile, to laugh, to share stories, and that’s what really keeps me motivated. And so, thank you all. I can’t believe I’m getting emotional.
[3:02]
TONY PIPA: Sheyenne is the smallest town I’ve ever visited for the Reimagine Rural podcast, but it’s emblematic of a story happening across rural America. The residents here love their hometown, and they’re willing to get creative and to dedicate their time to gradually bring back essential services that looked like they were gone for good, to create new enterprises that fit with the town’s current incarnation, and to keep it vital and on the map.
[music]
Farmer’s Grocery is eye-catching, one of the very first things you see when you drive into the town. Gavin is 26 now, and he’s been admiring this old gas station for almost half his life.
[3:43]
Gavin Brown
GAVIN BROWN: It was built, I believe, in 1927. It’s of course, you know, your classic American gas station from that era. So, the 1920s, you know, the cars were all narrow, Model A’s. So, there’s an awning off of the front of the building. And and that protrudes out about 12 feet. And then under that awning, of course, would’ve been the old, tall visible gas pumps, you know, you could pull up on either side, and the attendant would come out.
TONY PIPA: One Fourth of July when he was 12 years old, he and his grandmother met the owner.
GAVIN BROWN: You know, he kinda told me what he paid for it. And now, well, at the time it was a dollar, you know. So, even at 12 years old, I was like, “Well, come on now. I got $2.” So, it was always a kind of an attainable dream of mine, even growing up.
So, I’d call him maybe every other year, just to let him know, you know, “Hey, I’m still interested in this building.” And at the time it was used for nothing more than storage. The windows were broken out of it. It was in really miserable shape. But, he always said, “Well, I’ll call you if we decide to sell it.”
[4:56]
TONY PIPA: So, when Joanna expressed interest in expanding the farm stand into a brick-and-mortar space, word got around, as it always does in a small town.
GAVIN BROWN: And I think that might have kinda pushed him to say, “Okay, maybe I will sell this.” But it was just one of those things where it was like, well, I guess now’s the time, so, here I’m gonna go buy a gas station.
And really didn’t have large intentions of doing anything really rapidly with the building. You know? It’s kind of a passion project. So, in the back of my mind I just thought, “Well, at least take the plywood off the windows and put some glass back in and make it look half decent.”
But right away after I visited with the previous owner of the building, Joanna had reached out to me and kinda told me her desires of what she wanted to do with the space or a space. And I I just told her, “Well, I have no problem making that happen.”
[5:56]
TONY PIPA: Joanna and Gavin worked for two and a half years to make Farmer’s Grocery a reality without publicly revealing their plans. Two of those years were construction and renovation.
[6:07]
JOANNA LARSON: We did not tell the community that it was gonna be a store. We kept that a secret because right on Main Street, when you start renovating a building that has been essentially abandoned, busted windows, bad roof, when you start working on something, you get a lot of attention really fast.
So, we didn’t tell anybody what we were doing, just that we were fixing this up And Gavin was working on it whenever he could in his spare time. People were really generous and donated money to him so that he could keep himself fed and and keep working on it.
And that was really inspiring that the community didn’t even care what it was going to be, just that it was going to be fixed up and it wasn’t gonna be an eyesore on Main Street.
We have the historic pumps out front. We have the tin ceiling. We have the old mercantile cases. We have a vintage Coke machine that works and runs. And and when people walk in, it’s like stepping back in time. And as much of an art project as it really became, it’s also incredibly functional and providing a really important need.
[7:19]
TONY PIPA: The business model relies on an honor system. Joanna hired a company specializing in rural grocery store accessibility to help Gavin install remote door access hardware and software so people can access the store 24/7.
[7:34]
JOANNA LARSON: We have the produce still, and we also have a handful of local ranchers bringing animals so that we can butcher and have meat products in the store. And then conventional groceries, all of the essentials, ready-to-eat meals, baking supplies, breakfast items, bread, milk, eggs, cheese, deli meat.
And then a little bit of specialty in some of the clean label foods and foods that might be hard for people to get if they have a allergy or an intolerance. In such a small community, we really need to have a little something for everybody.
[8:12]
TONY PIPA: A sheet of paper on the counter invites residents to share ideas of what they’d like to see on the shelves.
[8:18]
JOANNA LARSON: People are writing their ideas down, and I’ve been taking ideas verbally since we started and trying to source those things. We can’t source everything that people want, unfortunately. Our supply chain is still seriously constrained out here, but we’re doing the best we can and and trying to get what people want.
Like, think about accessing groceries in the middle of a North Dakota blizzard, or being a farmer and working late hours during calving and and not having time to run to town and get milk or get bread. And and so it’s just really essential. And I don’t take food access for granted at all.
[music]
[9:03]
TONY PIPA: I’m Tony Pipa, a senior fellow in the Center for Sustainable Development at the Brookings Institution, and your host for the Reimagine Rural podcast. It’s the podcast where we visit rural places across America experiencing change, and we bring their stories to life while exploring the intersection with policy.
[music]
Sheyenne is in central eastern North Dakota, about two and a half hours northwest of Fargo, but it feels a bit like an old Western town. Here’s Patti Larson, Joanna’s mother, and one of the leaders of Sheyenne’s volunteer community development group.
[9:49]
Patti Larson
PATTI LARSON: I’ve always thought Sheyenne had a a unique brand, that the Main Street sort of has that West, Old West flavor, pioneer spirit. It it was really brought to life in the ‘70s when I was in high school. They kinda redid the storefronts to look like the the Old West.
TONY PIPA: Sheyenne is less than a fourth of a square mile, and driving on the main road, you can pass through it in a matter of seconds.
PATTI LARSON: Our town is so small. There’s 113 houses. We kinda know all of them, and we especially know them all because our church ladies, every year at Christmastime, we go around with cookies.
[10:27]
TONY PIPA: Sheyenne’s vibrant rodeo culture also continues that Western town aesthetic. The July 4th rodeo and the August Sheyenne Stampede events help attract thousands of visitors in the summer months.
[10:43]
SHARON WHITMER: The Rodeo Club was and has been here since 1954.
TONY PIPA: Sharon Whitmer is secretary of the Sheyenne Rodeo Club.
SHARON WHITMER: It’s one of those things that it’s been here, people kind of expect it. It’s like the big highlight of the Fourth of July festivities. People are coming from out of state. And the one lady told me all she did was search for what’s going on on July 4th and found the Sheyenne Rodeo was gonna be happening, and she said that’s what they decided they were gonna come and do.
And when we finally took the big step forward to bring in the Stampede, that has just grown and grown. And every year I’m just amazed. Like, last year we had roughly 2,500 people in attendance, and this year I think they’re looking at probably 3,000 to 3,500.
[11:36]
RODEO SCENE: Go in, get their horses. Come on. Saddle up. Gotta get it branded right on the ribs. Now the run, go.
SHARON WHITMER: You pay it, for a ticket for the whole day, and you get to take in the barrel racing. You get to take in the ranch rodeo. You get to take in all the vendors that are out there, and then you also get a whole night of entertainment. And this year, you know, we’ve got three Nashville recording artists, plus a regional band that, from Minnesota, that’ll open at the beginning and then close with the beer gardens until 2:00 a.m.
TONY PIPA: Wow.
SHARON WHITMER: It actually, you know, I used to say it draws from all the connecting states. And now we’re actually bringing in people from, like, down south and further west and further east. And I think that’s what makes it exciting and so rewarding when you can see that happen.
TONY PIPA: Describe for listeners all the different things that happen. Not everybody’s been to a rodeo that’s gonna be listening to the show.
[12:43]
BRENT HALSETH: So, the barrel race is three barrels set up in a triangle.
[music]
TONY PIPA: That’s Brent Halseth, the rodeo club treasurer.
BRENT HALSETH: And then they run around each barrel in a clover leaf pattern, and obviously the idea is to be as fast as you can. And then in a ranch rodeo, that’s a four-man team, and there’s generally five different events. They range from wild cow milking. It’s catch as catch can, so if you can get on her head and hold her while somebody milks her, have at it.
Range doctoring, you gotta rope the head of a steer and and the heels of a steer, and then fake doctor it. There’s mugging. You gotta rope a steer and then get it tipped over on the ground and tie three legs together. Penning event, you gotta rope a steer, get it into a pen in the middle of the arena. A sled race, which a sled race is kind of, oh boy, pull a sled down with a guy in it, turn around and come back.
So, I come up with the idea, let’s stake a goat at the end. You gotta run down, grab the goat, bring it back to the next guy, hand him the goat, and he’s gotta take it back and put it back on the, the leash. All without letting the goat go and being pulled as fast as you can behind a horse.
TONY PIPA: Here’s Patti Larson again.
[14:13]
PATTI LARSON: Rodeo goes way back. They would just set up a rodeo fence just out in the prairie and work really hard rounding up the cattle, and they built a really nice rodeo arena. The dirt in Sheyenne is sandy, so, it’s just a really nice bed for the horses to run around on.
Rodeo is kind of a, it’s kind of a lifestyle. It’s kind of an attitude. And so, it’s really important to Sheyenne. Although everybody isn’t involved in it, they just like to be part of the watching it happen, and I think it just kind of another tradition that is important to keep people coming back or to be known of, known for.
[14:52]
KENT MIREY: I mean, you get this draw of people into our community. It’s kind of, it’s kinda overwhelming. It kinda almost like it brings tears to your eyes that this can happen in our community.
TONY PIPA: Kent Mirey is a third-generation farmer who’s also in the rodeo club.
KENT MIREY: And it’s getting bigger. I mean, people are starting to call us and ask can we be a sponsor with, of the music. So yeah, it’s pretty cool.
[15:19]
BRENT HALSETH: I I guess to answer your question, how do we handle all these people? We just offer free camping and free parking. We’re, we’re gonna need more volunteers. We’re gonna have to probably start thinking about how are we gonna be able to handle how big this is actually gonna get or how big do we want it to get.
[15:40]
SHARON WHITMER: We are very forward-thinking, and it’s like you’ve got to change, and I’ve said that for a long time, that you’ve gotta be willing to change. You’ve gotta change. If you don’t, you’re gonna sit and be stagnant, and everything’s gonna pretty much just shrivel up and be gone.
TONY PIPA: That ethos is what guides a lot of people in Sheyenne, including Joanna.
[16:09]
JOANNA LARSON: I’m just a go-getter. I like to get things done, and my parents are like that. My family’s like that. The people of Sheyenne are like that. Like, I’ve also seen many other small towns in North Dakota that are not thriving, and they’re losing resources and losing people.
And we’ve been trying to turn the needle in Sheyenne and make sure that doesn’t continue to happen here, that we attract younger families, that we attract workforce, that we have viable housing, that we have essential services.
I know very few people in Sheyenne that are kinda, like, sitting on the sidelines and don’t care what happens to the town. Like, everybody wants Sheyenne to be successful.
[music]
[16:57]
Connie Brown
CONNIE BROWN: I’m Connie Brown. Some people don’t like to say their age, but I’m pretty proud that I’ll be 84 in November, and I’m real proud that I’ve been married 65 years to the same guy.
TONY PIPA: Connie is Gavin Brown’s grandmother, the one he was with when he first noticed the gas station. She’s seen a lot of change over the years. Her sister and brother-in-law, who had moved to Washington State, returned to run the grocery store that closed.
[17:24]
CONNIE BROWN: And another place that was hard for the farmers to lose was our blacksmith shop. I could remember before that closed, thinking, “What would they do without that blacksmith shop to run in and fix up their equipment?” And well, then eventually it did quit, so, they had to start going to New Rockford or buying brand-new stuff. And most of the farmers weren’t… they’d rather fix than buy.
Losing the Tastee-Freez was hard. We we enjoyed that, coming into town on a Sunday night and just everybody would be parked over by the Tastee-Freez. We’d go get our treat, and then we’d all sit around and visit and stuff. I mean, that was, another big social that was cut off.
Back in the days when my husband was farming, one of the biggest things to do was in the morning before they got too much going, they’d go to the elevator and they’d, all the farmers would sit around and talk about the day. A lot of the people end up staying home and losing the friendships and the visiting that they’re, they should be having.
[18:38]
TONY PIPA: In the early 2000s, Sheyenne experienced a series of monumental losses for a small town. In addition to the grocery store closure, the town lost its only fully operating restaurant, the town bank, and the school, all within a matter of years.
CONNIE BROWN: And to see the town lose their school and move to New Rockford, it was a very emotional and hard thing because we lost people, too.
TONY PIPA: Here’s Sharon Whitmer again.
[19:14]
SHARON WHITMER: For me personally, I think it was just, it really created a void. It’s like it was another piece of the community that basically slipped away. And then when you lose your school and all those kids and families, it just was kinda like, okay, now as a community, what do we do? You know? What what can we take hold of and still keep Sheyenne alive and thriving?
[19:42]
Tara Hanson
TARA HANSON: I think it was hard for it to close, but at the same time, I think it was the the community kind of that steppingstone for them to come together and figure out, okay, what are we gonna do with this building because we don’t want it to go to waste. And so, here I am managing a school that is now a lodge.
TONY PIPA: Tara Hanson is a school psychologist who also manages the building, Open Season Lodge & Events Center. Visitors can book an overnight stay in old classrooms or rent out the gym for parties. It’s ideal for groups of hunters and anglers.
TARA HANSON: So, when I walk into each of the rooms that are now, that have beds in them and people come and stay, I call them what they used to be as my school. You know? Like, Oh, here’s the library. Here’s the science room. Here’s the math room. You know, there is that connection. And I think when I tell that story, I think they think it’s even cooler to just kinda stay here because of that background.
[music]
[20:41]
TONY PIPA: Tara is a member of that community development board that includes Sharon Whitmer and Patti Larson.
[20:47]
PATTI LARSON: Sheyenne GRIT, it’s a group of volunteers. We call ourselves GRIT because of the we all agree that we want growth, renewal, imagination, and teamwork. So, when we found out that there was actually some money available that we could spend however we wanted to, it was, like, let’s have a meeting as though we’re gonna win the lottery, and what will we do with it?
[21:11]
TONY PIPA: That money she’s referencing is a project of Strengthen ND, a community development organization based in a small town just six miles south of the Canadian border. Since July 2025, I’ve been co-directing America’s Rural Future, a bipartisan commission co-sponsored by the Brookings Institution and the American Enterprise Institute.
The Commission will recommend improvements to federal rural policy in 2027, sharing what we’ve learned from local rural leaders and residents that we’ve been visiting across the country. And it was during the Commission’s very first public hearing last fall in North Dakota that I met Megan Langley, executive director of Strengthen ND. She spoke passionately about the importance of investing in the leadership of small towns so that local people have the chance to decide for themselves what matters in their community.
[22:07]
MEGAN LANGLEY: We meet people where they are. That means being present in their communities, listening first, and helping them build on what’s already strong.
[22:16]
PATTI LARSON: The the six areas of really concern was housing, and and they included dilapidated houses; businesses and business enhancement; Main Street, because we know it’s our business card for people driving through; events; and then childcare and kid activities. And then we knew that marketing the Sheyenne brand was also a a thing we needed to invest in.
We just got really lucky and wrote up a grant that said we would just try to tackle all these areas. We we formed a board of six women. One one specializes each of the areas, and I was tasked with housing.
[22:57]
TONY PIPA: In 2022, Strengthen ND awarded GRIT a $75,000 Creative Community Solutions Grant. GRIT had been dormant a while, but once it got that investment, Patti and her fellow GRIT members applied for nonprofit status, assembled a six-member board, started holding regular meetings, and began doing some serious grant writing. The other $75,000 came in 2023. They applied again and got another $150,000.
MEGAN LANGLEY: Before that, the community hadn’t received a major state, federal, or philanthropic investment since the 1970s. With that modest…
TONY PIPA: GRIT used the backing from Strengthen ND as a financing tool. Essentially, they put that money in the bank and used it to open up other grant opportunities, $800,000 worth. Since many grants act as reimbursements, applicants have to spend the money upfront. For many small towns, that reality takes them out of the running before they even apply.
[24:03]
PATTI LARSON: If we can always have this little pool of money, that will be our saving grace, because we used to just be able to do fundraisers, but you can’t do enough with $5,000. $5,000 is a great fundraiser for a meal or something, but, you know, for big projects you need upwards of $100,000. Yeah, that’s just a, it’s just a godsend for us.
But also, it brought some agency to our community. Like, Oh, we can do this. And it brought hope for people who had already kinda decided, oh, it’s just, it’s, you know, what can you do? It’s, like, give up.
But now we can do something. It’s important to do stuff. It’s it’s planning for the future. Like, we planted a bunch of trees. We planted, like, 80 trees in the last two years in Sheyenne, and it’s … that alone is hope for the future. You know, someone planted these big shade trees 100 years ago.
[25:02]
TONY PIPA: I heard Patti’s name come up time and again as people described Sheyenne’s growth.
[25:08]
JOANNA LARSON: I’ve just seen her, like, almost have this second act in her life. Like, she’s always been involved in our community my whole life, but after she was done raising us, she just poured all of her energy into, like, every waking hour she’s doing stuff for Sheyenne.
[music]
It’s hard not to be enthusiastic about what she and other people in this community see and hope for and wanna be a part of that.
[25:40]
TONY PIPA: Connie Brown wrote regularly for the Sheyenne Star, a newspaper that GRIT put out for a couple of years. When the support from Strength in ND arrived, she couldn’t help but think of her sister and brother-in-law, the ones who moved back to Sheyenne to run the grocery store, the one that eventually closed.
[26:00]
CONNIE BROWN: At that time, they weren’t talking about grants or anything like that, and I’m so happy they have grants and things now because that may have helped them. It may have been just enough to turn the tide for them.
[26:15]
TONY PIPA: Since housing is a major concern, GRIT used some of that money to clean up dilapidated houses. They were able to purchase and repair a rundown house that had been owned by a retired teacher who left it to her brother in Minnesota after she passed.
[26:31]
PATTI LARSON: It needed a lot of work. He knew about how much Sheyenne meant to her, and he was just so happy to let Sheyenne GRIT take on this as a project.
We purchased the house for $8,000. And it was on a corner lot, but it was totally overgrown with trees, had asbestos tiles in the basement. I did a lot of research. How much is it gonna cost to do this, bring it all up to speed? The garage was almost a tear-down.
But we just started in, and volunteers started showing up, ‘cause, amazingly, people like to paint. People like to do yard work. People just like to do stuff. And then once the trees were cleared, and the scraping of the paint, and started painting it, it’s like, wow, this is really coming to life.
TONY PIPA: They sold the house to a contractor who had a home in California but was in the area doing work in nearby Devils Lake.
PATTI LARSON: So, that was our big first investment. We made, like, twenty-grand, so, wow.
[27:33]
TONY PIPA: The possibility of home ownership was a huge draw for Julianna Chenze Millang, who has lived most of her life in Sheyenne.
[27:41]
JULIANNA CHENZE MILLANG: When it’s so small here, it’s so hard to … [this is a romano] … do anything big-ish. You know? Mm-hmm. We just live in our own little bubble in here in this town.
MOLLY BORN SCENE: Do you like living here?
JULIANNA CHENZE MILLANG: Yeah, I’ve lived here my whole life. It’s cheap to live here. You can actually afford to buy a house here. Well, even driving to New Rockford, 10 miles, the housing price difference is insane, the difference. So, like, it’s so cheap. We just, we’re, we just bought our second house in this town. So, it’s affordable to live here.
MOLLY BORN SCENE: You know, I’m sure it is a great place to raise kids, like…
JULIANNA CHENZE MILLANG: It is, yeah.
MICHELLE GILLEY / GARDEN SCENE: Green, and the yellow ones stay yellow.
JULIANNA CHENZE MILLANG: I mean, do I wish, like, there was more here? Like, maybe a better playground for our kids? Yeah, but they find things to do.
MICHELLE GILLEY / GARDEN SCENE: And butterflies like our… what was down here at the bottom? Butterflies like…
[28:40]
TONY PIPA: One of those things is the Youth Garden Club, run by Michelle Gilley, the county’s extension agent. My producer and I got to tag along one sunny afternoon as Julianna’s nephew and sons identified plants, and then harvested some of the vegetables they’d planted earlier in the summer.
[28:58]
MICHELLE GILLEY / GARDEN SCENE: Monarch butterflies. Yeah. So, this flower is a milkweed. It’s one of the different kinds of milkweed. I think it’s a showy milkweed, not like, so it’s, that’s, we put it in our pollinator garden ‘cause it’s less aggressive than the common milkweed. That is actually kind of a weed in our garden, but we leave it where we can.
So, how is this pollinated? Wind. Wind. Wind. And what kind of flower is this? Uhh … smell it. Dill pickle. Smells like dill. Smells like dill pickles. Yes. So, that’s a different kind of flower, and that shape is an umbel. So, should you take that home and eat it with your cucumbers? Yeah. Yeah. It’s a good idea, but I know you will eat the cucumbers before you get home. True.
What kind of flower is this?
[29:51]
JULIANNA CHENZE MILLANG: Before they started just the kids garden, it was always a massive community garden that I think Patti Jo helped start. And…
TONY PIPA: …that’s Patti Larson, of course …
JULIANNA CHENZE MILLANG: … it was always nice. And then everybody just came up here and helped maintain. And then as the years went by, just slowly grew. And then, like she said, you know, a lot of people were like, Well, we’re just doing our own garden, so the kids can have the entire thing.
TONY PIPA: I gotta say, a garden of this size in a town as small as Sheyenne, pretty impressive.
[30:27]
JULIANNA CHENZE MILLANG: And they’ve learned so much. Like, I mean, it’s not just, like, planting. Right? And then just watching them grow. Like, she teaches them so much about every step, every, like, process. Like, I think, well, I don’t know, I could be wrong, but I swear, I think the kids’ favorite part was putting in the irrigation this year. They had a lot of fun putting that in and learning about it.
[30:52]
MICHELLE GILLEY / GARDEN SCENE: Right now. They’re probably ready right now. When are the onions ready? When they’re popping out. No, not when they’re popping out. When are the onions ready? When they’re falling over. When the stem is bent over and it’s soft when you grab it where it’s bent. Right there. It’s soft. Yes, grab it. These two are ready. This is… Can you pull that onion out and that onion out? Good job. Get the next one too. You wanna dig potatoes next, or… yeah … beans or peas? Potatoes. Okay.
[31:29]
TONY PIPA: During our trip to Sheyenne, we spent a lot of time with Joanna Larson, and we learned so much from her. She and her partner, Ian, who grew up mostly in Texas, but ended up going to high school a couple hours away in Casselton, North Dakota, started their careers in the Seattle area. The work there felt meaningful, and it included dependable salaries and reliable health care.
[31:52]
JOANNA LARSON: Things you don’t have when you farm necessarily. And we started thinking real seriously about making Seattle our home. Frankly, it was felt … unaffordable. We both were making pretty good money. But what was available to us that seemed like a good affordable starter home was, like, you could buy two or three homes in Sheyenne for that amount of money, and it was hard for us to see ourselves there for very long.
So, we decided to go back to school and get more education instead of buying a home, which, many of our peers out in the Seattle area thought we were nuts, and we quit our jobs, and we went to Europe and worked on our master’s degrees.
[32:40]
TONY PIPA: Joanna attended the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences in Uppsala. It’s a place she felt especially connected to. Her great-grandparents were born in Sweden. After a lot of international travel, she and Ian moved to Sheyenne in 2023.
[32:59]
JOANNA LARSON: That all the traveling we did kind of got that out of our system. And I kid you not, we hate leaving Sheyenne. We we don’t even like to drive to neighboring town for appointments. We just, we just want everything here. And maybe part of that is because we got spoiled having all of the amenities and entertainment and everything close when we lived abroad and when we lived out west. So, we think why why can’t we just have everything here in Sheyenne?
[33:34]
TONY PIPA: Joanna knows it’s not entirely realistic to have everything in this small town. But Farmer’s Grocery is one step toward making life better for her neighbors.
[music]
[33:47]
JOANNA LARSON: There is of course a chance that it completely fails and then you have to tell everybody and disappoint everybody that this just didn’t work. But I just think about the people who moved out here, like my my great-grandparents that left Sweden because they were starving and thought that there’s gotta be somewhere better. There’s gotta be somewhere where we can make a life for ourselves.
And they risked everything. They left their communities, they left their families never to return. So, I think when I think about that, it’s like, how can you not try? How can you not kind of put yourself out there? Because if we don’t, I mean, the alternative for a place like Sheyenne is that this experiment fails.
[34:49]
TONY PIPA: At the end of town, a grain elevator stands perched right alongside the main road. The facility caught fire and burned in 2016. At the time, it had been serving 120 farmers in the region. It was rebuilt and opened again in 2017. My producer thought it might be fun to climb to the top and get a bird’s-eye view of the town, and Joanna offered to be her tour guide.
[35:17]
GRAIN ELEVATOR SCENE: Would it be okay if we walk up the stairs? Oh, I don’t care. Go ahead. Okay. Just don’t fly off. Oh, we’re not gonna. If you want me to come back and get you more, just-
These were originally called elevators because the… You saw where the truck could dump the grain in the pit? Yeah. And then these long belts with little buckets on them were the elevators. They elevated the grain all the way to the top.
The whole point of the elevator is that maybe one farmer doesn’t have the best crop that year, and a different farmer has a good crop, and then we can bring it here, and we can blend it off, and then we can make an acceptable product. And that way, we all come together and and are able to market it.
So, I don’t know how high up you wanna go. We, we’re welcome to go to the top, but… yeah, let’s do it. So, this is all your farm?
Yeah. So, this is where I grew up. So, the house, you can’t see it, but it’s just barely behind the trees there.
[36:17]
JOANNA LARSON: We’re ranching. We have about 165 head of cow-calf pairs, and we’re farming conventional crops. So, my folks have corn and soybeans and wheat and alfalfa. And then I myself am growing certified organic vegetables. I’m growing cut flowers that I sell to florists, and also have some of my own cows, and my partner Ian has pigs and ducks.
So, we have a lot of little enterprises going on, and the smaller scale high-value crops like the vegetables and cut flowers are insignificant acreage-wise compared to the other crops my family’s growing, but they’re impactful economically to me.
So, I’m selling most of the produce really locally, and a little bit of farm to school, right down the street in the store, so fresh produce for the community, as well as another rural community up north of here, selling the produce that I raise and some of the beef and pork as well in their store.
[37:28]
GRAIN ELEVATOR SCENE: Yeah, this farm is gorgeous. And you’re in the yellow house right there?
So, that’s where my parents live on. Ian and I live on the other side of town over here in the little, little cottage.
I think you’re probably one of only a handful of people who’ve ever been up here. My dad…
[37:44]
TONY PIPA: Patti Larson and the members of GRIT are thinking about their next project. An especially urgent need now is childcare. After all, to attract and keep a younger generation here, people like her daughter Joanna or Julianna Chenze Millang, it depends on offering the support young families will need.
[38:05]
PATTI LARSON: We have people who would work there. We think we could have up to 15 kids. Yeah. It’s just, like, not easy because you gotta do the building right, and we have to have the person, the manager. We… should we coordinate with a, a childcare that’s already in existence? Or should we start our own, you know?
TONY PIPA: Joanna was more direct in her assessment of how elected officials can help places like Sheyenne.
[38:29]
JOANNA LARSON: I think that the main thing that that our elected officials need to understand is that they’ve gotta be courageous enough to act before it’s too late. I think we saw a little bit of this with the rural grocery crisis, where North Dakota lost a lot of grocery stores in the last decade. And it’s just unfortunate that there wasn’t more done to prevent the loss kinda as it was happening. There was this just attrition going on.
And now they’ve scrambled and provided some limited, much-needed funds, which we’re very fortunate to have received some of those here in Sheyenne. But when you look at all of the stores that applied across the state, and then the small amount that were awarded, it was like putting a Band-Aid on a really bigger problem.
So, that’s that’s the hard part, that sometimes the policy changes move more slowly than the crisis progresses.
[music]
In the next 20 years, I hope Sheyenne is a a great place to raise a family. I mean, I’m, I want, God willing, I want to have kids that grow up here, and I want them to have the same opportunities I had when I grew up here.
[40:12]
PATTI LARSON: Yeah, I would just love to see growth and just happy people living here, taking care of each other like they always have, and just less decay and decline, and more positive things. And there’s definitely, definitely the momentum to do it.
Sheyenne’s not the only little town that’s worth saving. Maddock, Fessenden, you know, quite a few of them just in the, in the 500-mile radius. So, I hope, I hope people realize that when they do policy.
[40:48]
TONY PIPA: Some of those opportunities that Joanna remembered from her childhood, T-ball, a summer theater group, have yet to be realized again. But Patti reminded me about one thing Sheyenne has in spades, people who care about making the place better.
[41:06]
PATTI LARSON: One thing about a small town, civic engagement is just so easy to be a part of. You know, you can be the school board. You can, you can serve on the church board. You can help in any way you can because you’re needed. It’s good to be needed.
[41:26]
TONY PIPA: You know, a rural expert I know often talks about the “STP problem.” The syndrome of having the “same two people” doing everything in town. You would think that that would be even more pronounced in a place as small as Sheyenne. Yet everywhere we turned, it felt like there were lots of people here who were involved in one project or another.
And it was impressive not only to witness this civic energy, but to see the creativity. Joanna, for example, pursuing a business model that would work for the Farmer’s Grocery to serve this place’s needs. Gavin depending upon lots of community support to make the remodel work. GRIT and the rodeo continuing to pump life into new projects.
Will it be enough? The younger generation here is betting that it will be. And that mixture of can-do, collaboration, and commitment certainly seems to give them decent odds of that bet paying off.
Thanks for listening.
[music]

articles.title: U.S. Private Credit Vehicles: Institutional Structure and Aggregate Balance Sheets
articles.text:
FEDS Notes

Twitter

Share

RSS

November 09, 2026
U.S. Private Credit Vehicles: Institutional Structure and Aggregate Balance Sheets
Katie Brinkman, Christine Dobridge, Tim Dore, Simon Glossner, Elizabeth Holmquist, Nam Nguyen, Maria Perozek, and Irina Stefanescu1
1. Introduction

The expansion of private credit has become one of the most significant developments in financial markets over the past decade. Yet, estimates of the size of the market vary considerably, in part because the term private credit is used to describe different instruments, investment strategies, and financial intermediaries. This note provides an overview of the private credit market, describes the principal vehicles through which private credit is financed and held, and uses newly published U.S. Financial Accounts statistics to estimate the size of these vehicles and the composition of their balance sheets.2

U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles held approximately $1.9 trillion in assets at the end of 2025, having grown from roughly $240 billion in 2012.3 Private debt funds (PD funds) represented the largest category, accounting for $940 billion in assets, followed by business development companies (BDCs), interval and tender offer funds, and middle-market collateralized loan obligations (MM CLOs). While these private credit vehicles often invest in similar types of loans, they vary significantly in their asset exposures, funding structures, leverage, and investor bases. For instance, while private credit loans account for almost 80 percent of aggregate BDC assets and all of MM CLO assets, PD funds and interval and tender offer funds tend to be more diversified across asset classes, with private credit loans only accounting for 57 percent and 26 percent of their assets, respectively. BDCs tend to be more highly levered with an average debt-to-equity ratio around 1, compared to ratios of around 0.25 for PD funds and around 0.05 for interval and tender offer funds.

This note is organized as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of private credit market structure and key participants; Section 3 analyzes balance sheets of private credit vehicles, including portfolio composition and debt financing patterns; Section 4 discusses the potential drivers of variation across vehicle types; and Section 5 concludes.

2. Structure of the private credit market

2.1 What is private credit?
In this note, we define private credit loans primarily by the channel through which credit is intermediated.4 Specifically, we use the term to refer to debt instruments extended to borrowers through private negotiation and financed primarily through nonbank investment vehicles, rather than traditional bank balance sheets or securities issued in public debt markets.5 This definition encompasses corporate direct lending, asset-based and specialty finance, real estate debt, infrastructure debt, and other privately negotiated loans. It therefore does not depend on the identity of the borrower, the purpose of the loan, or the assets supporting repayment.6

2.2 How does the private credit market work?
Figure 1 illustrates the private credit ecosystem and the relationships among the principal parties. Investors provide funds to private credit vehicles and in return, they receive claims issued by those vehicles. In turn, private credit vehicles use investor funds to finance loans to nonfinancial businesses and other borrowers, who are then required to repay principal and interest according to the contractual terms of the loans. The following subsections discuss each of these market participants in turn.

Figure 1. Private Credit: From Investors to Borrowers

Accessible version

This framework also defines the perimeter of the market measured in the Financial Accounts and detailed in this note. We focus on private credit loans financed and held through nonbank investment vehicles—namely, PD funds, BDCs, interval and tender offer funds, and MM CLOs. Direct holdings of loans or privately placed debt securities by banks, insurance companies, and other institutional investors are outside the vehicle-based definition of private credit presented here.

2.3 Who are the borrowers and what types of loans do they receive?
Private credit loans finance a broad range of borrowers and economic activities. Nonfinancial corporations—particularly middle-market companies—account for the largest share of private credit debt outstanding, using these loans to finance acquisitions, leveraged buyouts, investment, growth, and refinancing.7 These borrowers are not necessarily excluded from bank or public credit markets but may choose private credit because it can provide speed and certainty of execution, confidentiality, customized financing structures, or the ability to negotiate directly with a relatively small group of lenders. Borrowers may also combine private credit term loans with revolving credit facilities, leveraged loans, and other services supplied by banks.8

The expansion of private credit beyond traditional corporate direct lending has broadened both the borrower and the collateral base. Private credit vehicles also finance real estate, infrastructure, equipment, receivables, inventories, consumer and small-business loans, royalties, and other financial assets or contractual cash flows.

Private credit loans also differ in their seniority and the principal basis on which they are underwritten. They range from first-lien senior secured loans to second-lien and subordinated loans, mezzanine debt and other instruments with debt- and equity-like features. In cash-flow lending, loan size and repayment capacity depend primarily on the borrower's expected operating cash flows, with collateral and enterprise value providing additional lender protection. In asset-based lending, loan size is based primarily on the value of specified assets or contractual cash flows such as receivables, inventory, equipment, real estate, and royalties, which also provide a source of recovery in the event of default. This distinction is not always sharp, as many private credit loans rely both on cash-flow generation and asset values.

2.4 What are the private credit vehicles?
We distinguish private credit loans from the private credit vehicles that finance them and hold them as assets. The principal vehicles considered in this note are PD funds, BDCs, interval and tender offer funds, and MM CLOs.9 These vehicles hold private credit loans, often along with other investments, but differ substantially in their legal structure, investor base, liquidity provisions, use of leverage, and regulatory treatment.

(a) PD Funds
PD funds are privately offered, closed-end investment vehicles that are typically organized as limited partnerships and managed by an affiliated investment adviser.10 They are limited to private offerings to sophisticated investors, including pension funds, insurance companies, endowments, foundations, sovereign wealth funds, family offices, and other institutional or qualified investors. These investors participate as limited partners (LPs), while the sponsor or its affiliate serves as the general partner (GP) and investment manager. Capital is raised through investor commitments and drawn over time through capital calls to fund loan originations and acquisitions. Because investors generally do not have redemption rights before the fund's termination, these funds have a stable capital base and are not subject to redemption-driven liquidity pressures. PD funds span a wide range of private credit strategies with different mandates and risk profiles, including direct lending, mezzanine and junior capital, distressed and special situations, asset-based and specialty finance, private real estate debt, and infrastructure debt.

(b) BDCs
BDCs are specialized investment vehicles created by Congress under the Small Business Investment Incentive Act of 1980 to channel capital to small and mid-sized U.S. businesses. Unlike traditional investment companies that primarily invest in publicly traded securities, BDCs focus on financing privately held and thinly traded companies that typically lack access to public capital markets.11 BDCs are allowed substantially higher leverage than traditional registered investment companies: the statutory baseline allows 1:1 debt-to-equity ratios (or 200 percent asset coverage), and the Small Business Credit Availability Act of 2018 allows a BDC to elect a 2:1 leverage (or 150 percent asset coverage).

There are three different types of BDCs. BDCs can be publicly traded, public and non-traded, or private companies:

BDCs structured as publicly listed companies issue shares that are traded on national securities exchanges. The shares of these BDCs are available to everyone, including retail investors.
Public, non-traded BDCs choose not to list their shares on an exchange and instead offer their securities directly to investors who meet certain suitability standards, typically through broker-dealers or registered investment advisers. Although these BDCs are not traded on an exchange, they typically provide liquidity through periodic redemptions or repurchases of shares.
Private BDCs offer ownership rights to either accredited or qualified investors, such as institutional investors and high-net-worth individuals, depending on their structure. Private BDCs provide liquidity to shareholders only through a liquidity event, such as a liquidation or a merger.

(c) Interval and Tender Offer Funds
Interval funds and tender offer funds are closed-end investment vehicles designed to accommodate illiquid asset classes (e.g., private credit) while providing investors with limited, periodic liquidity through scheduled repurchase mechanisms. The fundamental distinction between the two structures lies in the mandatory versus discretionary nature of their repurchase obligations. Interval funds must conduct periodic repurchase offers at net asset value (NAV) at specified intervals, up to a certain percentage of outstanding shares.12 In contrast, tender offer funds conduct discretionary tender offers and fund managers have flexibility over repurchase timing, frequency, pricing, and offer size.13

(d) MM CLOs
Collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) are financial vehicles that issue securities, in tranches with different risk profiles, backed by pools of loans. MM CLOs are CLOs backed by loans to middle-market companies specifically. The loans underlying CLOs are often originated by direct lenders such as PD funds, BDCs, and asset managers affiliated with life insurers. These lenders, or affiliates of the lenders, then commonly also serve as the CLO managers.

2.5 Who are the investors?
Investors obtain exposure to private credit loans by providing capital to the vehicles that finance and hold them. Depending on the vehicle, investors may acquire partnership interests, shares, or debt and equity securities. The investor base varies substantially across vehicle types. Traditional PD funds raise capital primarily from institutional investors, including pension funds, insurance companies, sovereign wealth funds, endowments, and foundations. BDCs, interval funds, and tender offer funds provide varying degrees of access to individual investors, while MM CLOs are held predominantly by institutional investors. These differences in investor base are closely related to the legal structure, liquidity, and regulatory treatment of each vehicle.

3. Private credit vehicles: Balance sheets

3.1 Size and growth
We use a variety of data sources to construct balance sheet estimates for private credit vehicles and to allocate instruments to holders and borrowers for the aggregates published in the Financial Accounts. See the data appendix for a detailed description of the data and methods underlying the private credit aggregates published in the Financial Accounts, as well as the additional distributional detail provided in this note.

As shown in Figure 2, we estimate that the total assets of U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles reached approximately $1.9 trillion in 2025.14 PD funds are the largest private credit vehicle with $940 billion in assets, followed by BDCs ($570 billion), interval and tender offer funds ($290 billion), and MM CLOs ($50 billion).

Figure 2. Total Financial Assets of U.S.-Domiciled Private Credit Vehicles

Note: Data as of Q4 each year. The key identifies bars in order from top to bottom.

Source: Financial Accounts of the United States.15

Accessible version

This represents substantial growth from 2012, when total assets across these vehicles stood at approximately $240 billion—an eightfold increase over the thirteen-year period. PD funds and BDCs account for most of the growth. PD fund assets have grown by more than $750 billion, from about $175 billion in 2012, while BDCs grew by about $530 billion from a much lower starting level of about $40 billion. Recent growth has been particularly strong, with total assets increasing by 21 percent between 2024 and 2025, driven by the rapid growth of assets held by BDCs (30 percent) and interval and tender offer funds (39 percent).

3.2 Portfolio composition
The composition of assets varies significantly across the different vehicle types. As shown in Figure 3, private credit loans account for only about 57 percent of PD fund assets as of 2025. These funds have significant holdings of corporate equities and debt securities, representing about 18 percent and 13 percent of assets, respectively. Notably, the share of private credit loans has increased over time, with debt securities declining roughly an equal amount, suggesting PD funds are shifting away from secondary market securities toward direct lending relationships.16

Figure 3. Asset Composition of U.S. Private Debt Funds

Note: U.S.-domiciled funds only. Data as of Q4 each year. Excludes dry powder. Missing data on holdings are imputed based on holdings of funds of the same private debt strategy. The key identifies bars in order from top to bottom.

Source: Financial Accounts of the United States.

Accessible version

In contrast, about 80 percent of BDC assets are private credit loans, consistent with their statutory requirements, as shown in Figure 4.

Figure 4. Asset Composition of U.S. BDCs

Note: Data as of Q4 each year. Syndicated loan data available starting 2017. The key identifies bars in order from top to bottom.

Source: Financial Accounts of the United States.

Accessible version

As shown in Figure 5, private credit loans held by interval and tender offer funds account for a significantly smaller share of assets (26 percent), while corporate equities account for 44 percent and debt securities account for almost 14 percent. Finally, MM CLOs invest exclusively in private credit loans.17

Figure 5. Asset Composition of U.S. Interval and Tender Offer Funds

Note: In Panel A, data are quarterly. In Panel B, data are as of Q4 each year. The key identifies bars in order from top to bottom.

Source: Financial Accounts of the United States.

Accessible version

3.3 Debt financing and leverage
As assets have grown, total debt of private credit vehicles has increased significantly since 2012, though leverage ratios have remained relatively stable in recent years. However, leverage varies substantially across vehicle types.

Turning first to PD funds, total debt, defined as loans plus debt securities, grew from about $33 billion in 2012 to $234 billion in 2025 (Figure 6).18 Domestic banks provide almost two-thirds of total debt to PD funds, with other loans and advances accounting for the remainder. Leverage at PD funds, calculated as the ratio of debt-to-equity (or debt-to-NAV), is low on average and relatively stable at around 0.25.19 While average leverage is low, some PD funds have considerably higher leverage. As shown in Panel B of Figure 6, funds at the 90th percentile of the leverage distribution have debt-to-NAV ratios that typically range around 1. Importantly, asset-weighted leverage ratios show similar patterns, indicating that most private credit capital is deployed through funds that have low leverage, while high-leverage outliers tend to be smaller vehicles.20

Figure 6. Debt and Leverage of U.S. Private Debt Funds

Note: NAV is net asset value. Debt is defined as loans plus debt securities. PD funds do not issue debt securities. The difference between total debt and domestic bank loans is other financial business loans and foreign loans.

Source: Financial Accounts of the United States, SEC Form PF.

Accessible version

BDC debt has also grown rapidly since 2012. As shown in Figure 7, BDC debt grew from about $14 billion in 2012 to $260 billion in 2025. Similar to PD funds, banks provide the majority of BDC financing, though corporate bonds are also an important source of funding. BDCs are, on average, more highly levered than PD funds, with average leverage ratios around 1 and 90th percentile leverage around 1.5 in recent years.

Figure 7. Debt and Leverage of U.S. BDCs

Note: NAV is net asset value. Debt is defined as loans plus debt securities.

Source: Financial Accounts of the United States, BDC Collateral.

Accessible version

Like PD funds and BDCs, debt of interval and tender offer funds has increased sharply in recent years. As shown in Figure 8, debt of interval and tender offer funds reached about $21 billion in 2025, with bank loans accounting for about 90 percent of the total. Leverage of interval and tender offer funds is quite low; the average leverage ratio is about 0.05 and the 90th percentile is only about 0.15 during the last few years.

Figure 8. Debt and Leverage of U.S. Interval and Tender Offer Funds

Note: NAV is net asset value. Debt is defined as loans plus debt securities. The difference between total debt and domestic bank loans is federal funds and security repurchase agreements.

Source: Financial Accounts of the United States, SEC Form N-PORT.

Accessible version

4. Interpreting balance sheet differences

The balance sheet differences in portfolio composition, debt financing, and leverage documented above reflect three interconnected factors: regulatory architecture, liquidity obligations, and investor composition.

(1) Regulatory architecture: Different private credit vehicles operate under different regulatory environments, which can constrain and shape the behavior of the funds. For example, BDCs face explicit leverage limits (up to 2:1 debt-to-equity) and asset-composition requirements (70 percent in qualifying assets). Interval and tender offer funds face tighter leverage limits (1:2 debt-to-equity) but fewer asset-composition restrictions, while PD funds have greater flexibility over both leverage and portfolio composition but generally restrict participation to qualified investors. These differences help to explain BDCs' relatively high leverage and concentration in direct middle-market lending relative to interval and tender offer funds, and the greater heterogeneity in leverage across PD funds.

(2) Liquidity obligations: Redemption features vary substantially across private credit vehicles and are related to portfolio liquidity. Private credit vehicles with greater redemption risk are likely to hold a greater share of liquid assets than those that lock up capital for longer periods. PD funds and private BDCs generally provide liquidity only through distributions and liquidation; as a result, they face limited redemption pressures and can maintain greater exposure to illiquid private loans in their portfolios. Perpetual non-traded BDCs typically offer quarterly share repurchases capped at around 5 percent of net asset value, subject to board discretion to limit or suspend repurchases. Recent redemption pressures in these vehicles highlight the liquidity challenges of offering periodic investor withdrawals while holding illiquid private loans. By contrast, interval funds typically offer periodic redemptions of 5 percent of outstanding shares per quarter, requiring greater balance sheet flexibility and more liquid asset holdings.

(3) Investor composition: Investor eligibility requirements help segment private credit across vehicles. PD funds generally restrict participation to investors meeting specified wealth or sophistication criteria, limiting access for retail investors. BDCs and registered interval and tender offer funds can serve a broader investor base, including retail investors. Within these eligibility boundaries, investors' liquidity needs and investment horizons further shape vehicle choice: institutions able to commit capital for longer periods are better positioned to invest in PD funds, while investors seeking greater liquidity may prefer listed BDCs or funds offering periodic repurchases.

Overall, these features help explain the segmentation of private credit across vehicles. Regulatory constraints and investor liquidity needs jointly shape leverage and the capacity to hold illiquid assets, so observed balance sheet differences reflect not only investment strategies but also the institutional structure through which private credit is intermediated.

5. Conclusion

This note provides an overview of the institutional structure of the U.S. private credit market, describing the principal vehicles through which private credit is financed and held, and analyzing the composition of their balance sheets using newly published Financial Accounts data. This analysis complements our previous FEDS Note, “Introducing Private Credit into the Financial Accounts of the United States” (Brinkman et al., 2026).

We document significant differences in asset holdings, leverage, and investor bases across private debt funds, business development companies, interval and tender offer funds, and middle-market CLOs. Understanding this heterogeneity is essential for assessing how regulatory constraints interact with investor preferences to shape private credit vehicles’ balance sheets and investor bases. The data and analysis presented in this note provide a foundation for ongoing monitoring of this evolving market.

Data Appendix

This appendix describes our data sources and methodology.

A.1 Private debt funds
Limited public availability of data on PD fund balance sheets has constrained the ability of policymakers and market participants to assess these funds' asset vulnerabilities and funding resilience. To address this gap, we use confidential fund-level data from SEC Form PF.21 For advisers that meet the reporting requirements, filing is mandatory, meaning that coverage among larger funds is complete, and data on fund assets and liabilities are updated regularly. However, there are two major limitations: (1) Form PF does not explicitly identify PD funds, and (2) detailed balance sheet information is only available for a subset of funds in Form PF data.22

To address the first challenge, we reclassify all Form PF funds into one of nine fund types using signals from fund strategies, fund names, and classifications in other databases.23

Fund Strategy Data: For a substantial share of funds—all funds filing as hedge funds since 2012 and the private equity funds of large private equity fund advisers since 2024—Form PF collects data on each of the fund's investment strategies and the share of the fund's total net asset value devoted to each strategy. We extract signals from these reported strategies when they clearly map to one of our fund types.
Fund Name Data: Fund names also often reveal information about investment strategy. For instance, many funds include phrases such as "Direct Lending" or "Private Equity" in their names. We therefore create a list of keywords and phrases that strongly suggest a particular investment strategy and extract signals from fund names containing those terms.
Classifications in Other Databases: External databases such as Preqin, PitchBook, and Moody's also contain information about fund investment strategies. We match funds in Form PF to these databases using both exact matches on cleaned versions of fund names and fuzzy matches. For each matched fund, we extract a signal from the fund type in the external database, giving higher priority to exact matches than to fuzzy matches in our ultimate classification.

We then use these signals to classify all funds in Form PF with at least one signal into one of the nine fund types.

For PD funds, we refine the classification further to identify the specific private debt strategy of the fund using a similar approach to the one used to classify fund types. We categorize each private debt fund as following one of five strategies: (1) senior direct lending, (2) subordinated direct lending, which includes mezzanine debt funds, distressed debt funds, and similar funds, (3) opportunistic, which includes opportunistic debt funds and special situations funds, (4) asset-based lending funds, which includes real estate debt funds, infrastructure debt funds, and other funds making loans against specific assets, and (5) other debt funds, which includes venture debt funds and other funds that do not belong in the first four categories.

In Figure A1, we present the results of this classification process for U.S.-domiciled funds as of 2025. As discussed above, we estimate that U.S.-domiciled private debt funds held approximately $940 billion in assets as of the end of 2025.24 For comparison, domestic private equity funds are the largest fund category, with almost $5.4 trillion in assets, while hedge funds are the second largest, at about $2.7 trillion in assets. The other remaining funds, which include real estate funds, infrastructure funds, venture capital funds, and liquidity funds, among others, account for about $3.3 trillion in assets.

Figure A1. U.S. Private Fund Assets by Fund Type, 2025

Note: The sample includes only U.S.-domiciled private funds reported on SEC Form PF. All figures exclude dry powder. For funds that report quarterly, we use the last available observation in each calendar year. Panel A shows gross asset value (GAV) by fund type under our new classification: private equity (PE), hedge funds (HF), real estate equity (RE), private debt (PD), and other funds (OTHER). PD includes real estate debt funds and infrastructure debt funds, as well as other private debt funds defined in the text. Real estate equity funds are classified as RE. OTHER includes infrastructure equity funds, venture capital funds, natural resources funds, collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), liquidity funds, and unclassified funds. Panel B breaks down the private debt funds identified in Panel A by strategy: senior direct lending (Sr Direct Lending), subordinated direct lending (Sub Direct Lending), opportunistic investing (Opportunistic), real estate debt funds and other asset-based lending (RE & Other ABL), and all other private debt strategies (Other).

Source: SEC Form PF.

Accessible version

Figure A1 also presents the total assets of domestic PD funds in Form PF for 2025 by debt strategy. Senior direct lending is the largest debt fund strategy, accounting for about $350 billion in assets in 2025. Subordinated direct lending accounted for about $180 billion while opportunistic debt funds controlled approximately $75 billion in assets. Real estate debt funds and other asset-based lending funds, like infrastructure debt funds, held just over $200 billion in assets, with real estate debt funds holding the large majority. Other private debt funds had slightly less than $140 billion in assets.

To address the second data challenge—the fact that detailed balance sheet data are only available for a subset of PD funds—we impute holdings based on funds that do report these data. Importantly, a significant number of PD funds, representing a substantial share of private debt fund assets, report as qualified hedge funds advised by large private fund advisers and are consequently required to report holdings across a wide variety of instruments on a quarterly basis.

Using these funds, we calculate the distribution of assets across different categories (e.g., loans, corporate equities) as a share of total assets for each quarter. We assume that funds with the same private debt strategy (e.g., senior direct lending) that do not report their asset holdings have the same distribution of assets. For these funds, therefore, the imputed asset holdings are calculated as the product of the fund's total assets and the asset ratio for funds with the same private debt strategy in the quarter.

A.2 Business development companies (BDCs)
For BDCs, we use data from BDC Collateral, which parses BDCs' quarterly financial reporting and schedules of investments from their 10-Qs and 10-Ks.

A.3 Interval and tender offer funds
For interval and tender offer funds, we use data from Morningstar and SEC Form N-PORT. Form N-PORT, an SEC filing requirement adopted in 2016 and implemented starting in 2019, requires registered investment companies to report portfolio holdings monthly, with public disclosure occurring quarterly, 60 days after each fiscal quarter-end.

To identify interval and tender offer funds investing in private credit, we begin with Morningstar's list of active and inactive interval and tender offer funds and match it to Form N-PORT filings using CIK and LEI identifiers. Using the detailed holdings data in Form N-PORT, we classify these funds' investments into private credit loans, corporate equity, debt securities, and other instruments.

A.4 Middle-market CLOs
To construct estimates of the outstanding value of private credit loans held by middle-market CLOs, we use data from Moody's Analytics, Inc., Global CLO database, which flags small and middle-market CLOs and includes information on CLO assets, performance of CLO tranches, and attributes of the loans underlying CLOs and the loan obligors.25

References

Avalos, Fernando, Sebastian Doerr, and Gabor Pinter. 2025. "The Global Drivers of Private Credit." BIS Quarterly Review, March 2025, pp. 13–29.

Banegas, Ayelen, Sophia Castelo, Ahmet Degerli, Christine Dobridge, and Will Kennedy. 2026. "Private Credit and Leveraged Loan Markets: Similarities, Differences, and Substitution." FEDS Notes.

Bank for International Settlements (BIS). 2024. "Laying a Robust Macro-Financial Foundation for the Future." BIS Annual Economic Report 2024, Chapter I. Basel: Bank for International Settlements.

Berg, Tobias, and Seung Jung Lee. 2026. "Measuring Counterparty Exposures to Private Credit." OFR Brief No. 26-02. Washington, DC: Office of Financial Research, U.S. Department of the Treasury.

Brinkman, Katie, Christine Dobridge, Tim Dore, Simon Glossner, Elizabeth Holmquist, Nam Nguyen, Maria Perozek, and Irina Stefanescu. 2026. "Introducing Private Credit into the Financial Accounts of the United States." FEDS Notes.

Chernenko, Sergey, Isil Erel, and Robert Prilmeier. 2022. "Why Do Firms Borrow Directly from Nonbanks?" Review of Financial Studies 35(11): 4902–4947.

Erel, Isil, Thomas Flanagan, and Michael S. Weisbach. 2024. "Risk-Adjusting the Returns to Private Debt Funds." Fisher College of Business Working Paper No. 2024-03-006, Charles A. Dice Center Working Paper No. 2024-06.

Haque, Sharjil, Simon Mayer, and Irina Stefanescu. 2026 (forthcoming). "Private Debt versus Bank Debt in Corporate Borrowing." Journal of Financial Economics.

Hinzen, Franz, Giorgio Mondini, Paul Rintamäki, and Sascha Steffen. 2026. "The Cyclicality of Direct Lending." SSRN Working Paper No. 6490423.

International Monetary Fund (IMF). 2024. "The Rise and Risks of Private Credit." Global Financial Stability Report: The Last Mile—Financial Vulnerabilities and Risks, Chapter 2. Washington, DC: International Monetary Fund, April 2024.

Ivashina, Victoria. 2025. "The Role of Private Debt in the Financial Ecosystem." NBER Working Paper No. 34426.

Meisenzahl, Ralf, Jackson Overpeck, and Andy Polacek. 2026. "Life Insurers' Private Credit Investments and Annuity Market Share Capture." Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Working Paper No. 2025-09.

1. We are grateful to Daniel Barth, Mike Batty, Marco Cagetti, Fang Cai, Sophia Castelo, Ahmet Degerli, Giovanni Favara, Matt Hoops, Patrick McCabe, Phillip Monin, Lubomir Petrasek, and Clara Vega for helpful comments and suggestions. We also thank Keely Adjorlolo, Santoro Giuggio, Harrison Karp, and Patrick Schroeder for expertise and assistance with the private credit data. Return to text

2. This note provides complementary details on the integration of the private credit market into the Financial Accounts of the U.S., and it is centered around the private credit vehicles that provide loans to U.S. businesses. For more information, see our previous FEDS Note: "Introducing Private Credit into the Financial Accounts of the United States" (Brinkman et al., 2026). Return to text

3. Foreign-domiciled private credit vehicles that invest in the U.S. held an additional $763 billion in assets. Return to text

4. Our definition builds on the emphasis in recent BIS (2024) and IMF (2024) work on privately negotiated credit intermediated outside traditional banks and public securities markets, while adopting a broader scope with respect to borrower and collateral type. Similarly, Ivashina (2025) states that the appropriate boundary of private credit is determined by how lending is intermediated rather than by the identity of the borrower. Return to text

5. Private credit loans are related to, but distinct from, private placements. Both provide borrowers with financing outside public debt markets and can involve private negotiation and relatively concentrated investor participation. Private placements, however, generally involve the issuance of debt securities, most commonly notes or bonds, directly to a limited group of institutional investors. In the United States, insurance companies are important investors in traditional private placements and commonly hold these securities directly on their balance sheets (Meisenzahl, Overpeck, and Polacek, 2026). The distinction in this note therefore rests on both the form of the instrument and the intermediation structure. Private credit loans are loan instruments financed through nonbank investment vehicles, whereas traditional private placements are debt securities issued by borrowers directly to investors. We exclude privately placed bonds and notes held directly by institutional investors from our estimates of private credit vehicles. Return to text

6. Put differently, private credit encompasses a range of privately negotiated lending activities differentiated by borrower type, collateral, and contractual structure. They are unified by fund-based origination, private negotiation and monitoring, and limited reliance on public capital markets, all of which jointly determine risk, pricing, and control rights (Chernenko, Erel, and Prilmeier, 2022; Avalos, Doerr, and Pinter, 2025). Return to text

7. Middle-market firms are often defined as those with revenues between $10 million and $1 billion (Banegas et al., 2026). Return to text

8. See, for instance, Haque, Mayer, and Stefanescu (2026), Hinzen et al. (2026), and Banegas et al. (2026). Return to text

9. Large alternative-asset managers may operate several of these vehicles through a common origination platform. Loans sourced and underwritten by the same manager can therefore be allocated across affiliated PD funds, BDCs, interval or tender offer funds, and other vehicles, and may subsequently be financed through CLOs. It is therefore useful to distinguish the asset manager or origination platform from the individual legal vehicles through which the loans are financed and held. Return to text

10. Although the funds themselves are exempt from registration as investment companies, their investment advisers are typically registered with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and are subject to applicable reporting, compliance, and fiduciary requirements. Return to text

11. BDCs are closed-end investment companies that elect to be BDCs under Section 2(a)(48) of the Investment Company Act of 1940. A BDC is subject to some but not to all of the limitations and prohibitions of the 1940 Act applicable to typical 1940 Act funds. Several key differences from the 1940 Act funds emerge: a BDC must invest its assets according to specific criteria set out in the 1940 Act that effectively require at least 70 percent of a BDC's total assets to be invested generally in securities acquired from "eligible portfolio companies," defined generally as non-investment companies that are domestic unlisted companies or certain small-cap companies. In addition, BDCs can charge incentive fees based on capital gains and income and must offer managerial assistance to portfolio companies. Return to text

12. When repurchase requests exceed the offered percentage, proration occurs, which can limit investor liquidity. Return to text

13. Both registered interval funds and registered tender offer funds share comprehensive regulatory obligations under the 1940 Act. These include enhanced disclosure through Form N-2 registration statements and Form N-PORT reporting of portfolio holdings, adherence to leverage limitations under Section 18 (generally restricting debt to 33 percent of total assets), and independent board oversight. Return to text

14. Including foreign PD funds and MM CLOs raises the total financial assets to $2.6 trillion. For more details, see our previous FEDS Note: "Introducing Private Credit into the Financial Accounts of the United States" (Brinkman et al., 2026). Return to text

15. Data for interval and tender offer funds begin 2021:Q4. Return to text

16. Consistent with these estimates, using PitchBook data on private debt fund holdings, Erel, Flanagan, and Weisbach (2024) also find that approximately 20 percent of invested capital is held in equity or equity-linked securities. Return to text

17. Prior to launching a CLO, banks commonly provide short-term or "warehouse" financing to CLOs to fund the acquisition of loans. In the Financial Accounts, CLO assets are measured after CLO launch and do not include warehouse loans. Return to text

18. Total debt is a subset of total liabilities, which is calculated as the difference between total assets and equity and includes other unidentified miscellaneous liabilities. Return to text

19. The debt-to-NAV ratios for PD funds, BDCs, and interval and tender offer funds are winsorized at 0.05 and 0.95 levels. Return to text

20. Berg and Lee (2026) also find that leverage is more concentrated in the upper tail, although their study also includes non-U.S.-domiciled PD funds. Their analysis shows that the 95th percentile PD fund has gross-assets-to-net-assets leverage of 3.58 (equivalent to an implied debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 2.58) and that most funds in this highly levered group are relatively small, with just a few exceptions. Return to text

21. Adopted in 2011 as part of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act of 2010, Form PF collects fund-level data from investment advisers registered with the SEC who manage at least $150 million in private fund assets. Smaller advisers do not file Form PF and are not currently included in our estimates. However, we estimate that including private debt funds that file Form ADV but not Form PF does not materially impact our estimates. Return to text

22. The need to reclassify Form PF funds by type is also recognized and discussed in Berg and Lee (2026). Return to text

23. The nine types are: (1) private debt, (2) hedge fund, (3) private equity, (4) venture capital, (5) infrastructure, (6) collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), (7) real estate, (8) liquidity, and (9) natural resources. Note that funds that make equity investments in real estate and infrastructure projects are classified as real estate and infrastructure funds, while funds that invest in loans and other debt investments that finance these projects are classified as private debt funds. Return to text

24. Our measure of assets excludes dry powder, which is capital committed to the fund but not yet drawn down. Dry powder calculated as the difference between gross assets and the value of the fund's assets. In cases where the value of fund assets is not reported, it is estimated as the difference between gross assets and the sum of net assets and total borrowings. Return to text

25. The Moody's Global CLO database is the most comprehensive data source currently available to the Federal Reserve Board for information on middle-market CLOs, however, this dataset may undercount total MM CLO volumes. Return to text

"U.S. Private Credit Vehicles: Institutional Structure and Aggregate Balance Sheets," FEDS Notes. Washington: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, November 09, 2026, https://doi.org/10.17016/2380-7172.4225.
