Pricing behaviour and changing demographics are supporting a boom in the ‘off-peak’ economy…
…which should help the economy run more efficiently…
…though may mean some consumers face more price pressures

Making better use of our scarce resources
The notion of peak and off-peak pricing and availability has been commonplace in many parts of the economy for a long time. But several trends are emerging.
Firstly, pricing behaviour is becoming much more dynamic, with a wider range of services offering pricing to encourage spending into non-peak times.
Secondly, the share of the population able to consume during off-peak times is rising quickly due to a combination of demographic change, more flexible working patterns and a growing share of workers in non-‘nine-to-five’ work. All these trends look set to intensify in the coming years.
What does this mean? Firms clearly want more off-peak custom – it smooths out demand and stops bottlenecks and means that staff are more likely to be fully-employed rather than having down-time. This should mean increases in productivity of assets – a potential efficiency boost to the economy. It should also alleviate bottlenecks in the economy. We wrote back in 2019 that peak-time travel creates unnecessary wastage in the economy, and we’re seeing progress here with travel times becoming more evenly spread outside of peak rush hours since the pandemic. The same is happening with travel, with holidays shifting away from peak summer months.
Spending habits may become harder to track, however, with a greater share of spending volumes enjoyed at lower ‘off-peak’ prices. Whilst there is a gap between peak and off-peak pricing, we may see spending volumes grow, but in a non-inflationary way, if this is simply demand filling the spare capacity in the system.
However, a downside risk is that a positive story for the economy in aggregate could mask growing price pressures for those unable to participate in an off-peak economy, especially as those who work full-time, and in-person.
But, overall, this is a potentially positive step for the global economy. We could remove some bottlenecks and make scarce assets or labour more evenly employed, removing downtime and underuse, with this more optimal use slowly increasing output and lowering prices.

articles.title: Enforcing The Social Safety Net
articles.text:
Enforcing The Social Safety Net

Ernan Cui

Gavekal Dragonomics | 11 Nov 2026

China’s government has long been urged to strengthen its social safety net to alleviate households’ uncertainty about the future, lower their savings rate and thereby unlock stronger consumption. And indeed there has been progress, with the government recently rolling out new social programs, expanding existing ones and promising more funding. The latest Five-Year Plan even enshrines a goal of delivering income growth and a stronger safety net to ensure that “households will have greater financial security, more stable expectations and stronger confidence in consumption.” Today, the various programs that make up China’s social safety net are getting more political attention than in many years.For China’s policymakers, though, the current goal of strengthening the social safety net is mostly about ensuring more of the population is enrolled in official social-insurance programs, rather than increasing benefits or transfers. The heightened focus on coverage has been driven by the spread of informal or “flexible” jobs in which workers rarely pay into the social security system, a trend that raises concerns about both social stability and the financial sustainability of benefits.

articles.title: Energy Turmoil Puts the Gulf of Guinea Back on the Map
articles.text: Source: GettyArticleEnergy Turmoil Puts the Gulf of Guinea Back on the MapTwo decades since Washington elevated West African oil as a strategic priority, the frontier has reemerged as a promising alternative for U.S. energy security.Link CopiedBy Judd Devermont and Gabrielle PosnerPublished on Nov 5, 2026West African energy production is suddenly strategic again. Some two decades ago, U.S. policymakers were inundated with a frenzy of reports, assessments, and testimonials about this region. The National Intelligence Council in 2000 assessed that West Africa would play an increasingly important role in global energy markets, providing 25 percent of North American oil imports by 2015. It spurred the U.S. government to elevate the Gulf of Guinea—defined in its broadest terms as stretching from Mauritania to South Africa—as a strategic energy frontier, driven in part by the need to diversify away from Middle Eastern oil dependence. However, U.S. imports of West African crude and petroleum products reached less than 3 percent in 2015, and the much-touted realignment never came to fruition. Over the intervening years, a combination of record-breaking domestic oil production in the United States and interlocking regulatory and security challenges in West Africa foreclosed this highly touted opportunity.But today’s geopolitical turmoil has reopened it. Between Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022 and the U.S.-Israel war with Iran this year, global energy markets are experiencing continuous shock waves. The International Energy Agency executive director Fatih Birol said that the Middle East conflict constitutes “the greatest threat to global energy security in history”—and that was before the Yemeni Houthis’ latest squeeze of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait left exports even more constrained. These disruptions have supercharged efforts already underway by oil companies to address declining reserves and accelerate exploration after a lull in activities linked to low oil prices in 2015. With energy reserves at their lowest point in four decades and crude prices hovering around $100 per barrel, there is—once again—a U.S. national security imperative to reduce energy market vulnerability to geopolitical conflict. Accordingly, the Economist recently indicated that big oil is “flooding back in” to Africa. This time, though, the Gulf of Guinea’s governments are better equipped to manage persistent challenges and capitalize on renewed interest.The Gulf of Guinea’s AllureThe Gulf of Guinea includes sub-Saharan Africa’s top two hydrocarbon producers, Nigeria and Angola, and a handful of smaller countries that are developing new gas finds or discovering more hydrocarbons near mature fields. A combined 2.7 percent of global gas reserves and 4.5 percent of global oil reserves reside in this region, which also holds significant untapped offshore potential in deepwater blocks. Located on the Atlantic Ocean, Gulf of Guinea producers can supply European and American markets without transiting the chokepoints that a hostile state or nonstate actor can exploit. Importantly, from Washington’s standpoint, no rival holds structural leverage over the region the way that Russia does over Central Asian pipelines or that Iran does over parts of the Middle East. The Gulf of Guinea’s hydrocarbon grade is also attractive to importers. Much of its crude oil is light and sweet, commanding premium prices on global markets and requiring less complex refining than the heavier, sour crudes that dominate much of the Middle East’s export slate.These advantages had set off a new wave of exploration even before the recent disruptions increased the urgency to secure alternative energy sources. Despite inconsistent interest from the United States, there has been massive growth in West Africa’s oil sector. The discovery of Ghana’s Jubilee field marked the first major breakthrough in 2007, followed by large gas discoveries off the coasts of Mauritania and Senegal in the 2010s, major finds off Angola and Côte d’Ivoire, and, farther south along Africa’s Atlantic basin, Namibia’s landmark discoveries in 2022. Now, oil companies are leveraging new technologies, including advanced seismic imaging and improved deepwater drilling, to unlock areas that had yielded little despite decades of seismic surveys and exploration. New licensing rounds are opening acreage in Benin, Cameroon, Gabon, The Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Nigeria, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Sierra Leone.A Landscape of New OpportunitiesMany countries in the region are implementing sweeping, often politically difficult, reforms to make their oil-rich economies more investable. Nigeria and Angola, in particular, have made oil sector reform a centerpiece of their economic development strategies, while newer producers such as Mauritania have sought to build investment regimes more hospitable to international capital. The cumulative regulatory reforms and security investments have contributed to a more welcoming, and potentially more durable, operating environment throughout the Gulf of Guinea. That marks a significant departure from the early 2000s, when the promise of production was limited by a complex regulatory, political, and economic environment. Nigeria has overhauled its oil sector with the passage of the 2021 Petroleum Industry Act (PIA), giving it much-needed regulatory clarity and institutional rigor. The PIA established separate regulatory bodies for upstream and midstream/downstream activities and created the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited to commercialize the state-owned oil company, alongside broader sector-wide reforms. In 2024, a series of presidential directives provided tax incentives and eased operational costs for foreign entrants in deepwater offshore production while also supporting local oil companies onshore. These reforms have complemented significant international interest in deepwater production, most notably Shell’s $5 billion Bonga North deepwater project announced in 2024 and ExxonMobil’s commitment of $1 billion as part of an infill drilling project at the Usan deepwater oil field. Downstream, an indigenous refinery, the Dangote Refinery, is transforming the sector. The 650,000-barrel-per-day (BPD) refinery has made Nigeria a top supplier of jet fuel to Europe.Angola has made similar strides in rejuvenating its oil sector. After years of declining oil production and severe debt challenges afflicting the state-owned oil behemoth Sonangol, the country introduced reforms in 2019. It established the National Agency for Petroleum, Natural Gas and Biofuels to take over regulation of the sector from Sonangol and launched a six-year strategy that established predictable, regular bidding windows for oil block auctions and licensing procedures. Angola has implemented macroeconomic policies to stabilize its economy, including a more flexible and transparent exchange rate regime; introducing a value-added tax; reforming fuel subsidies; trimming the public sector; rationalizing the financial system; and introducing a cash transfer program. To solidify these reforms, the government set an ambitious goal of raising $70 billion in oil sector investments by 2030. In one early success, Chevron announced in August 2026 that it had discovered oil and gas condensate at an ​exploration well and is continuing to explore several Angolan blocks.Mauritania has swiftly established itself as a dependable investment destination. After Kosmos Energy discovered the Greater Tortue Ahmeyim (GTA), a natural gas field on its maritime border with Senegal in 2015, the Mauritanian government subsequently advanced a series of legal and regulatory reforms to improve the investment climate. It also partnered with Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative to establish a data submission portal and “Data Warehouse,” which systematically consolidates all extractive sector data published by private companies and governments. These steps have encouraged more exploration, building on the success of the GTA project. Mauritania recently welcomed Qatar Energy’s exploration and signed a major deal with a Saudi Arabian company to develop, finance, and operate a $700 million power plant.Regionally, some meaningful cooperation has made the Gulf of Guinea’s waters safer for operations. Twenty-five West and Central African states signed the 2013 Yaoundé Code of Conduct to advance a coordinated approach to maritime security through a memorandum of understanding between the relevant subregional bodies and the Gulf of Guinea Commission. The UN Security Council credited the architecture with a measurable decline in piracy incidents since 2021. Most recently, in June 2026, six Gulf of Guinea countries launched the Combined Maritime Task Force to establish a collaborative, rapid response mechanism to deploy the kinetic force needed to effectively combat threats identified under the Yaoundé Architecture.To be sure, the region is not free from insecurity, and policy gains are easily reversible. Each maritime security initiative struggles with persistent underfunding, staffing shortfalls, and unclear divisions of labor among its components. But, together, they comprise an African-led framework that did not exist in the 2000s.A Region Haunted by Old ChallengesDespite this progress, the region faces enduring socioeconomic and policy challenges. Regulatory reform has only made incremental improvements in addressing deep-seated corruption issues. Revenues are frequently siphoned off projects—casting a shadow over exploration opportunities in smaller markets such as Liberia and looming over the more established producers like Nigeria and Angola. Decades of mismanagement of state-owned oil companies have perpetuated Africa’s climate of high-risk investment. Resource nationalism remains a thorny issue to navigate: Last year in Senegal, the former energy minister talked openly about potentially nationalizing the Yakaar-Teranga gas project, operated by Kosmos, a move that would limit private development. The government also has criticized its contract with BP as “unfair.”And security threats linger. Kidnapping for ransom plagues oil-producing regions like the Niger Delta and its offshore waters. Community tensions stem from decades of oil pollution, which has destroyed local fisheries and therefore livelihoods. An already weak pipeline infrastructure is vulnerable to vandalism by militant groups. In Nigeria, especially, these challenges routinely compound to limit crude production. Though 2026 has shown record success in oil production, the country missed its 1.5 million BPD quota (mandated by the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) in all but three months in 2025, accumulating losses worth about $1.31 billion.The global energy transition further complicates the oil sector’s revival in West Africa, requiring new projects to compete amid tightening emissions standards, shifting demand, and growing pressure to decarbonize. Nigeria, alongside its “Decade of Gas” initiative, pledged to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2060 and launched a series of green energy transition initiatives in solar photovoltaic technology and hydropower, among others. At the 2026 Africa Oil Week in Accra, Ghanaian Minister for Energy and Green Transition John Abdulai Jinapor emphasized the need to invest in energy transition technology to secure Africa’s energy supply, though significant deepwater exploration agreements also featured prominently at the conference. Moreover, the energy sector is not immune to geopolitical rivalries. In addition to the Persian Gulf states, China has deepened its commercial involvement in Africa’s energy production. It is especially entrenched in Angola, which has historically signed billions in oil-backed borrowing agreements from China. Nigerian entities are hiring Chinese companies for infrastructure development, equipment, and engineering, including for the Dangote Refinery and the Ogidigben Gas Revolution Industrial Park. Mauritania signed an agreement last year with the Chinese company United Energy Group to produce 1 million tonnes of green ammonia annually. China’s foothold in the energy sector’s infrastructure and financing crowds out U.S. investment and operations. Next StepsNo oil-producing region is risk-free, but the relative reward the Gulf of Guinea offers is meaningful. It is time for U.S. stakeholders to return their focus to the region, especially in the wake of the current global energy crisis. Stakeholders across the U.S. government, private sector, and academia can take several steps to better understand regional dynamics, catalyze investments, and strengthen relations with African counterparts.Refresh perspectives. The Gulf of Guinea’s strategic relevance to U.S. energy security has not been sufficiently studied in decades, downplayed in part due to domestic production and debates regarding climate change and renewables. The net effect has been a decrease in policy engagement and strategic prioritization. Researchers should seek to close these knowledge gaps and challenge assumptions about the region’s current security, governance, and operational dynamics. Congressional delegations and reverse trade delegations can raise awareness and showcase the Gulf of Guinea’s commercial viability, while the private sector can elevate the region through its agenda-setting platforms such as CERAweek, an annual global conference for the energy industry held in Houston, Texas.De-risk investment. The U.S. government should leverage the renewed interest of U.S. energy companies in the Gulf of Guinea to crowd in further investment across the value chain, including infrastructure development, deepwater drilling, and AI-powered prospecting. The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation has been active in deploying its financial and insurance products to secure U.S. energy access in the Indo-Pacific; the institution should leverage its expanded mandate and budget to do the same in Africa.Deploy diplomats. The U.S. government should work more closely with its Gulf of Guinea partners to ensure a greater synergy between government policy reforms and the oil investments they are designed to facilitate. U.S. and African partners are calling for stronger commercial relations, but neither group is investing in the diplomatic capacity required to achieve them. U.S. bilateral engagement with Gulf of Guinea countries and multilateral engagement with regional groupings can help encourage investment in the energy sector, such as through shared protocols and harmonized regulations. In increasingly challenging contexts such as Senegal’s, effective diplomacy can contribute to goodwill toward U.S. companies and help African governments communicate the value of foreign investment in attaining their national development goals.This Time Is DifferentTwo decades ago, Washington’s enthusiasm for the Gulf of Guinea dissipated almost as swiftly as it emerged. An opportunity was lost to increase investments, strengthen partnerships, and diversify access to vital energy sources. Today, the price at the pump evokes renewed urgency to build energy resilience. The Gulf of Guinea provides a viable pathway. The United States should not make the same mistake twice by ignoring this region. It must think creatively and act decisively alongside African partners to realize a shared ambition to increase reliable energy production, strengthen African energy industries, and contribute additional supply to global markets.Get more news and analysis fromCarnegie Africa Program NewsletterThis monthly newsletter is a careful curation of the Carnegie Africa Program’s work and interests. articles.title: Central Bank independence in today’s world - Speech by Andrew Bailey
articles.text:
Central Bank independence in today’s world - Speech by Andrew Bailey

Given at the SIAF Lecture Series, Zurich University

Published on
09 November 2026

In this speech Andrew Bailey argues that today’s shock prone world makes independent and accountable central banks more important than ever, both to control inflation and safeguard financial stability. Andrew is also optimistic about the potential benefits of AI to productivity and sustainable economic growth, but also outlines the financial stability risks posed by AI.

Speech
It is a great pleasure to be here in Zurich.
The main focus this evening is to have a discussion. I am just going to make a few opening comments across the subjects of central bank independence, financial stability and technology – as a prompt to get our discussion going.
We are living through difficult times. Imagine if any of us had been asked ten years ago what were the odds of major military conflicts in Europe and the Middle East at the same time. The economics of these events are supply shocks – which tend to push prices and inflation up and activity down at the same time. Such shocks are challenging for central banks, and particularly when they are large and more frequent. A shock prone world is more difficult.
At the same time, we are seeing growing signs of the beginnings of a positive supply shock coming from AI and the investment required for that. In the UK, economic activity is turning out to be more resilient than we had expected, and some of that is due to AI investment, particularly in the business services sector.
These are challenging times for independent central banks setting monetary policy and for the people we serve. These shocks push inflation away from our targets – our definitions of price stability. Our task is to set interest rates to bring inflation back to target. I do recognise that in Switzerland you have experienced a record of more subdued inflation.
When it comes to the independence of central banks, I would say two things. Yes, these conditions are more challenging. But, it is in the challenging times that we need robust institutions more than ever.
There is though an important further step in this line of argument, which may seem obvious but needs stating. As independent institutions, we are not independent of the people of our countries. We serve them and are accountable to them. This is our public legitimacy. And by this I mean the whole people. I think our independence and legitimacy depends on this – we don’t and shouldn’t select those whom we serve and we are therefore inherently plural in our approach to our societies. This is a critical feature of independence.
Let me turn now to financial stability and central bank independence. Monetary and financial stability are in my view inseparable as the core principles of central banks. They are both equally and firmly anchored around the stability of the value of money. But, notwithstanding this in my experience, the political economy of independence is different. When it comes to monetary policy, while there can be debate around the form and precise structure of the arrangements, the independence of the actual decisions on interest rates is not in doubt. But this does not carry over to financial stability, where the decisions are much more contested. The lobbying moreover is much louder, and the interests much more sharply defined I would argue.
This is illustrated by the current state of affairs. Memories of the financial crisis are receding. But it is contributing to pressure to ease back regulation. I don’t pretend that every one of our rules and regulations in the UK is perfect.
But, I do contend that sustained economic growth depends on financial stability. So, it matters. It also matters that so far we have come through the latest adverse economic shocks with a resilient financial system. That’s not an accident. The post crisis regulatory reforms have made a difference here. And, the final “it matters”, we are seeing the risks shift into new areas of the financial landscape.
Which brings me to my last subject – technology, and particularly AI. I am an optimist on AI, digital technology and most probably robotics too. They have the potential to lift the sustainable growth rates of many economies through raising productivity growth. That is a good thing.
But with that do come risks, the risks of how to come to terms with AI for instance. In our world, Frontier AI has increased the risk from cyber-attacks – something that was already prominent. More broadly, it has led to concerns which may call into question public trust in AI. This is critical. We must act promptly to identify ways to give the public the level of trust they want and deserve. To achieve this, we must be clear what public interest objectives we are pursuing and how we achieve them. A clear case for me is that we need more extensive model testing, pre and post release. This may lead us to conclude that we want more or different points or means of human user intervention in the operation of AI. We also certainly want better incident reporting, monitoring and follow up (to make sure we learn the lessons from them). The key point is that public trust will depend on assured human intervention. AI will succeed as a tool of humans.
Why does this matter for central banks you may well ask? It matters a lot I would argue. Let me briefly set out two reasons for this, which are closely interconnected, and linked to financial stability.
Throughout modern history there has been a close relationship between economic growth, the interest of businesses in fuelling that growth, and the public interest as defined and represented by governments and in some areas of public policy put into effect by institutions such as central banks. You don’t need to take any ideological position to believe in this nexus of connections – you could be Hayek, Keynes, Marx or Schumpeter.
The question we face today is whether AI poses a new and more forceful challenge to the nexus, in the sense that the risk of a loss of public trust requires a careful but determined response to underpin that trust and support the economic growth that we all want to see? My response to this question would be yes it does pose such a challenge. Put simply, if you say “very good things can come from this, but bad things may happen too”, you can’t leave it there. And, it deepens the dependency between commercial success and public policy.
But second, and finally, there is a powerful connection to financial stability here. There is a lot of speculation on the subject of whether there is an asset price bubble in AI, and the financial stability risks that go with that. Bubble spotting is an imprecise science. But, let’s recognise that such a risk exists, which we should do. How might the bubble burst and potentially cause a problem? Four arguments can I think be advanced here.
First, it is the job of financial markets to value uncertain future returns. The returns from AI may be good, but still markets may overvalue them. That’s in the nature of the task of valuing uncertainty.
Second, the returns may be good, and they may match expectations, but they take longer to be realised than predicted. This has been the case historically with big General Purpose Technology innovation – take Edison and electricity for instance. There are good reasons to believe that the world moves faster now, but still the timing may not live up to market expectations.
Third, everyone is priced to be a winner, but history tends to tell us that this is not the case. Remember Netscape.
Fourth, the public trust point – there is a certain fragility created by this nexus. Arguably it is not new. A British Member of Parliament was killed by one of the earliest steam locomotives, people worried about the dangers of electricityfootnote [1]. I would argue that at present the argument seems more powerful with AI – but as I noted earlier, I treat that as a problem to be solved. But, until we have done so it could affect asset valuations.
So, there are clear financial stability risks here, and that’s without talking explicitly about cyber risks.
I said I would use my opening remarks to stir up some questions. Let’s see!
I would like to thank Sarah Breeden, Karen Jude, Clare Lombardelli, Dave Ramsden and James Talbot for their assistance in preparing these remarks.

The originally published speech mistakenly said that a British Prime Minister was killed. We’ve now corrected this.

Footnote [1]
The originally published speech mistakenly said that a British Prime Minister was killed. We’ve now corrected this.

Andrew Bailey
Governor, Bank of England

articles.title: No bank too big to fail, and none too small to resolve − speech by Ruth Smith
articles.text:
No bank too big to fail, and none too small to resolve − speech by Ruth Smith

Given at The Florence School of Banking & Finance Resolution Academy, European University Institute

Published on
23 September 2026

Ruth Smith discusses the Bank’s approach to managing small and medium-sized firm failure within the UK’s resolution framework. She emphasises the evolution of the resolution toolkit to ensure the regime remains robust for small and medium-sized firms, and reflects on the importance of transparency, proportionality and optionality.

Speech
Good evening, everybody. It’s a pleasure to have had the opportunity to listen to many of you over the course of today’s insightful presentations and discussions on banking resolution. Thank you to the European University Institute and Florence School of Banking and Finance for inviting me to speak today.    
Resolution is in many ways a team sport, and events like the Bank Resolution Academy are a real opportunity to learn from one another, understand the parts we each play, and look at what we can learn from a different viewpoint.    
Following on from today’s sessions on resolving medium-sized banks and the tools available to us in a resolution, I hope to provide a UK perspective on how the Bank of England prepares for resolving small to medium-sized firms.    
As you know, in the UK we have resolution regimes for banks and CCPs.  Today I am focusing on banks and will discuss what we mean in the UK when we talk about small to medium-sized firms and our approach to resolution planning for this large and varied group. I will also cover the lessons learned from the resolution of Silicon Valley Bank UK in 2023, and the new mechanisms we have added to our toolkit to improve optionality in a resolution while still seeking to lessen the burden on firms.    
Despite our recent experience of carrying out a resolution, and the improvements we have made as a result of that, there is still plenty of work to do when we consider resolution of smaller firms.   
The UK banking sector   
The UK has a diverse banking system, comprising some of the world’s large globally systemic banks right down to banks who have balance sheets in the tens of millions. This diversity requires flexibility in how our colleagues in the supervisory arm of the Bank of England, the PRA, apply their regulatory focus and equally needs us as the separate but collaborative Bank of England UK Resolution Authority, to tailor our approaches accordingly. Like any successful team, we each have distinct roles, but we are working towards the same objective of a safe and sound financial system.   
The UK remains a competitive and dynamic marketplace with multiple firms engaging in our pre-application process each year via the New Bank Start-up Unit, and the international presence remains strong, with firms of all sizes having UK subsidiaries and branches. Within the sector we see firms successfully entering, embedding their business, adapting to the demands of the marketplace, and in some cases exiting. This breadth of presence requires us, as the UK’s Resolution Authority, to be ready for those firm exits with a flexible and proportionate approach. Perhaps most importantly, we must be aligned to not only our teammates in the PRA, but where those subsidiaries and branches are part of a wider global group, to our resolution colleagues in overseas jurisdictions such as those here today.   
In practice then, what does this diversity of banking sector and tailoring our approach mean for UK resolution planning?     
We think about our banks in three broad groups,footnote [1] the first of which generally comprises our largest banks, where we plan for bail-in.    
We then have what we describe as mid-tier banks, typically with balance sheets in the £25-40 billion range, where firms can be set either a transfer or a bail-in as the preferred resolution strategy. For the firms currently in this range, we generally set a preferred resolution strategy which involves transferring these firms in resolution to a private sector purchaser, or, in the absence of a purchaser, temporarily to a Bank of England owned bridge bank – pending a further sale.    
Following an update to our policy on how much loss absorbing capacity firms must hold, or “MREL policy”, last year,footnote [2] unlike bail-in firms, transfer firms are not required to maintain MREL above minimum capital requirements. However, both bail-in and transfer firms are subject to the Resolvability Assessment Framework, or RAF. The RAF is our framework to assess UK financial firms’ resolvability and depending on the value of deposits held, some of these banks are also required to publicly disclose their own resolution self-assessment.    
In most cases, unless a firm with assets of less than £25 billion were viewed as posing a risk to financial stability, these smaller banks are then assumed to enter liquidation as a means of resolving their business if they are unable to either recover or complete a solvent wind-down. These are the firms we would use the Bank Insolvency Procedure or BIP for and do not hold additional MREL above minimum capital requirements or maintain additional capabilities to prepare for their failure.  BIP involves a rapid pay-out of depositors by the UK deposit guarantee scheme.footnote [3]  
As always there is judgement in setting a preferred resolution strategy, it is not solely based on a firm’s size and as such a transfer strategy can nevertheless be set in circumstances where the Bank assesses that a firm below the £25 billion mark would pose an unacceptable risk if it were to enter modified insolvency.    
Since the 2007-2008 global financial crisis the focus for resolution has rightly been on the largest, most systemic banks, those described as ‘too big to fail’. For these firms, the necessary team may well be large and international, and involve each person playing their role to produce the desired outcome of a smooth resolution.  And, as we look forward at an ever more interconnected system, operationally speaking, for not only our largest firms but smaller banks too, and join this together with our experiences of a small bank failure, we find ourselves working with the same teammates, and asking the same questions about stability and confidence in the wider sector as well as the impact of that failure on the bank’s customers. With this experience still relatively fresh in our minds it is this I want to speak about in depth.   
Our approach to small firms    
For our smallest banks, those typically defined as having less than £25 billion total assets, the plan for the majority of them should they fail is theoretically straightforward. Where a firm experiences severe stress which it is unable to recover from, the simplest solution is a director led solvent wind-down, allowing the firm to exit the market in an orderly manner while remaining a going concern. This enables the firm to stay in control of its own exit, minimising disruption to customers, creditors, and the wider market.    
Not all solvent wind-downs require active involvement from the resolution authority.  The PRA leads the assessment of whether a firm can continue to meet its obligations and execute an orderly exit from the market.  Where there are concerns about the firm’s ability to complete the wind-down solvently, the Bank, as resolution authority, works closely with the PRA to understand what alternative actions may be required, such as a BIP, should the firm’s plans prove no longer credible.    
Across all our work, the close relationship we have with the PRA is one of the most important aspects of our resolution framework. They are a teammate that we cannot be successful without.   
In the situation where a firm enters solvent wind-down, both authorities must be satisfied throughout that the firm’s wind down plan is credible, that it has sufficient resources to meet its obligations to depositors and creditors, and that allowing the firm to continue with their solvent wind-down plan aligns with our respective statutory objectives.  For a smaller firm, where a solvent wind-down ceases to be credible, insolvency may be the only remaining option.    
A BIP is a modified insolvency process. While the BIP shares many of the features of a standard insolvency process, it is specifically modified for deposit takers such as banks and building societies.    
Unlike an ordinary corporate liquidation, a BIP has a key objective of protecting covered depositors, which is done in two possible ways: payout or transfer. A BIP payout involves the insolvency practitioner or bank liquidator winding up the bank, whilst the Financial Services Compensation Scheme, the FSCS, carries out a rapid payout of deposits to the eligible depositors.    
Authorities in the UK have worked to significantly improve the speed and effectiveness of this payout process, learning from our European counterparts, to help ensure that protected depositors can regain access to their funds as quickly as possible. This speed of payout is important in maintaining public confidence in the efficacy of the resolution regime, and in the stability of the wider financial system.   
The second option is a BIP transfer, which involves the transfer by an appointed insolvency practitioner of the firm’s covered deposit book to another firm, with the insolvency practitioner winding up the remainder of the firm. For many of our smaller firms, the BIP provides a credible and proportionate resolution strategy.    
 So far so good and, hopefully, relatively straightforward and with minimal disruption.    
The boundary between BIP and transfer    
However, the small bank sector in the UK is highly diverse, innovative, and faces heavy competition. These characteristics have resulted in many of these smaller firms developing specialised business models which serve key customer groups, sectors, or communities that may not be well served elsewhere in the market or not be able to quickly and easily transfer their banking services to an alternative provider.   
The BIP is ultimately a liquidation procedure, and while it ensures covered depositors benefit from FSCS protection and payout, it is not designed to maintain the continuity of banking services.    
As such, customers of the failed firm may lose access to their existing banking relationships, payments may be disrupted, and those with uncovered deposits may need to wait for distributions through the insolvency procedure. For some smaller firms’ business models this may be acceptable, but for other firms, particularly where customers rely on continued access to banking services to operate on a daily basis, the impact can be significant and potentially outside the risk appetite of the collective authorities.    
This means that the picture in the UK is nuanced, requiring our assessments of whether a BIP would meet our statutory special resolution objectivesfootnote [4] to consider not only the size of a balance sheet, but also the nature of the customers it serves and the services it provides. As the Resolution Authority we need both a clear game plan and the ability to adapt it in real time.    
Lessons learned from SVB UK    
For the Bank, our experience with Silicon Valley Bank UK in March 2023 provides a powerful illustration of why flexibility in resolution planning is so important.    
At the time, SVB UK was a relatively small institution, with a balance sheet of around £12 billion and a preferred resolution strategy of BIP. Following the failure of its US parent and intervention by the FDIC, the Bank announced on Friday 10 March that, in the absence of further information, it intended to place SVB UK into insolvency.    
Based on what was known at that point, insolvency appeared to be the option that best met the public interest and the resolution objectives.   
As the situation developed over the weekend, however, it became clear that many customers relied on SVB UK not just for deposits, but for critical banking and payment services. At the same time, we needed to be cognisant of public confidence in the system against the backdrop of several other small bank failures in the US.   
We therefore kept multiple options open over the weekend, including insolvency. HSBC emerged as the credible bidder able to complete a transaction before markets opened on Monday while ensuring continuity of critical services, and with close liaison with FDIC throughout, and consultation with the PRA, FCA and HM Treasury, we concluded that a private sector transfer would better meet the special resolution objectives than a BIP.   
Unlike a BIP, the transfer provided protection for all depositors, not just those within the covered limits, ensured continuity of banking services, and most importantly protected and enhanced public confidence in the stability of the wider UK financial system in a way that did not incur costs on public funds.     
For me, this evidences that a preferred resolution strategy provides a vital starting point in contingency planning, but authorities need the flexibility, operational readiness and judgement to adapt quickly when executing a resolution as circumstances change in real-time. In the case of SVB UK, that flexibility was critical to achieving a better outcome for customers, for financial stability, and for the public interest.   
With this in mind, I want to speak to three key takeaways from this, our most recent experience of a bank resolution - transparency, optionality and international cooperation.     
Transparency   
First, SVB UK underlined the importance of a transparent resolution regime and communicating clearly and openly with markets, and authorities. The UK’s resolution framework relies not only on the Bank’s powers as resolution authority, but also on firms, investors, and other market participants understanding how these powers are used in practice, so that they can react accordingly.    
During the resolution weekend for SVB UK, both regulatory and finance ministry authorities worked together to consider multiple strategies in parallel. While this demonstrated the flexibility of the UK's framework, it also reinforced the value of ensuring there was common understanding about how different resolution options would be executed in a live event - between authorities, potential buyers, and the firm itself. Success depended on everyone understanding their role and how the wider team would operate under pressure.   
To bolster this shared understanding, in April we published the Bank’s operational guide to transfer resolution. The guide explains how the Bank would use its transfer powers in practice, whether the transfer involves selling the failed firm to a private sector purchaser, or placing it into a temporary bridge bank owned by the Bank of England.    
It aims to provide greater transparency around the key stages of a transfer, including preparatory work for both us and the firm, buyer engagement, transaction execution, and the information needed to support an accelerated sale process.    
By setting out these operational arrangements publicly and in advance of a future stress, the guide explains that transfer is not simply a theoretical power, but a credible and operationally deliverable resolution strategy. It helps firms better understand what may be expected of them, including the importance of maintaining the information and capabilities needed to support a rapid transfer if required.  It provides transparency to all potential stakeholders within a transfer, including prospective buyers, on how the bidding process would run for a transfer, improving the quality of bids, the competitiveness of an auction, and the smoothness of running the process overall.  
We applied the same learnings on transparency and communications to the Bank’s updated operational guide to bail-in resolution.  As firms grow, they face different resolution expectations. The guide provides greater clarity on how the Bank would execute a bail-in, giving firms, investors and other stakeholders a clearer understanding of the practical steps involved. In doing so, it supports preparedness, reduces uncertainty and reinforces the credibility of the UK's resolution framework across the full spectrum of firms.   
Optionality   
Moving on then to consider the optionality that our resolution framework gives us when planning for a firm failure. While the existing regime gave us an effective and flexible set of options that we were able to use to resolve SVB UK smoothly over a weekend, since 2023 we have continued to work very closely with our colleagues in HMT, our finance ministry, to introduce a new choice in our toolkit in the form of the recapitalisation payment mechanism.    
Introduced via the Bank Resolution (Recapitalisation) Act 2025, this tool is intended to cover associated losses or recapitalisation needs in a transfer via a new industry-funded safety net.    
Simply put, assuming the failing firm meets the public interest test, the recapitalisation mechanism allows us to cover certain costs associated with transferring a firm in resolution up front, be that to a private purchaser or a bridge bank, and then recover these from the industry via the financial services compensation scheme levy ex-post. This minimises the risk to public funds while providing options to use stabilisation powers to resolve a smaller firm when in the public interest.  We were fortunate that in the case of SVB UK the write-down of the regulatory capital was sufficient to enable us to transfer the firm to an interested and credible buyer – but this will not always be the case.  
Use of the mechanism may include recapitalisation of a firm during transfer due to a capital shortfall or potentially providing funds to the purchaser upfront and possibly in the form of guarantees to address any material concerns raised during the bidding process.    
For example, we recognise that the circumstances around a failing firm are often uncertain and extremely fast moving, resulting in limited time for due diligence to be conducted by interested buyers and introducing significant barriers which must be navigated to ensure a successful transfer.    
The new mechanism also gives us the space to be more proportionate in terms of what we require from small and medium-sized firms prior to a resolution. As I have noted, transfer firms are no longer required to hold MREL, in part due to the industry-funded safety net that this new mechanism provides.   
This flexibility represents a big step forward in strengthening our resolution toolkit. However, as always, we need to balance the needs of the failing firm with those of the wider financial system – recognising that any funds used to support the transfer are ultimately repaid by the wider industry.    
Importantly, it is not a replacement for BIP – an insolvency procedure is still a viable option for many firms and dependent on the scenario, may still be the right approach to take when considering our resolution objectives. While the use of the recapitalisation payment mechanism will always be situation specific, in all cases, the Bank will seek to use any funds in the most efficient and effective way possible, and the Act will not be used inappropriately to protect creditors from losses.    
This addition to the Bank’s resolution toolkit recognises that the UK runs a non-zero failure regime, and therefore it is important for firms to be allowed to grow but also be allowed to fail and exit the market smoothly – regardless of their size. It places a portion of that accountability back onto industry, not taxpayers, and ensures the Bank as Resolution authority has more options available to it and is ready for multiple failure scenarios without excessive burden on our smaller firms.   
International cooperation and coordination   
Third and finally, SVB UK underlined the importance of close coordination between authorities, particularly where a failing firm forms part of a wider international banking group.    
Effective resolution of cross-border firms requires more than financial resources and legal powers. It also depends on strong cooperation between home and host authorities, shared understanding of the firm's operational dependencies, and a common objective of maintaining critical services for customers. Like any team, it is helpful to train together before a match, and cross-jurisdictional exercises that allow us to practice and understand how we best work together are an important part of preparing for firm failure before the moment of stress arrives.    
While SVB UK involved close coordination between the UK and US authorities, the same principles would apply to firms operating across other jurisdictions.    
As banking groups become international, maintaining these relationships and coordination channels is an essential part of ensuring that resolution strategies remain credible and operationally deliverable.    
Conclusion   
What does the evolution of our framework mean in reality then? For me, it demonstrates that within the UK resolution regime, we have a robust toolkit that gives us confidence in having options to resolve small, medium and large firms.  
But looking ahead, I can still see areas of the banking sector where we could do more, particularly when it comes to small and medium-sized firms, to better prepare ourselves as authorities and prepare firms, in “peacetime”. I have spoken about how flexible options allow us to execute a resolution in more than one way for any given firm, in order to prioritise better outcomes for depositors while still protecting the public purse and wider financial stability.  
We often envisage using these options when presented with new information that challenges our original game plan during a resolution. However, I consider that we can do more to ensure we are always ready, by working with supervisors and firms to use their existing data and regulatory reporting to identify where they may be on the boundary of a BIP or transfer strategy in advance.   
As trailed in our update to the MREL policy last year, we are reviewing the indicative threshold of 40,000 to 80,000 transactional accounts as an intervention point for when a transfer strategy may need to be set for a firm under £25 billion in total assets. In part, this review is taking into account that the recapitalisation payment mechanism gives us more optionality for firms that do not hold MREL, and that consumer banking behaviour has changed since the threshold’s original implementation, making it less in step with the judgements we have to make when setting preferred resolution strategies.   
However, by removing the burden of MREL for such firms, we still need to ensure that we can execute a transfer effectively.  As part of this review, we are working with the PRA to ensure our resolution planning and reporting policies reflect these recent developments. This includes considering the information we require BIP firms to report on regularly. Are we asking the right questions? Is there existing data that firms already have through recovery and solvent exit planning that would better support our shared readiness for resolution planning as a BIP or in preparation for a transfer strategy in the future?  
With a more established resolution regime we must ask ourselves these kinds of questions to ensure we are continually improving and evolving our approach to firm resolution across the sector. I expect that we will publish our updated approach in early 2027 and look forward to hearing industry views in due course.   
A firm’s resolvability journey is never done, and as such our job as resolution authority isn’t either. No single authority can deliver resolution alone; it remains, at its core, a team effort and we will all need to remain live to an evolving sector to ensure our capabilities and policies are in step with the firms we regulate. The world rarely stays still and advances in technology, how firms operate and where the next risk may arise from is a horizon that we must keep at the front of our mind when considering barriers to an orderly resolution. Firms are a part of our team in a resolution, and I hope by continuing to work closely with one another, we can maintain readiness through a proportionate and effective resolution regime.   
I would like to thank Mala Gopalakrishnan, Kat Hind and Amanda Tennant for their help in preparing these remarks. I would also like to thank Geoff Davies, Charlotte Gerken and Dave Ramsden for their helpful comments.    

In general, for the purposes of resolution planning these three groups of firms are categorised as those with total assets of: i) £40 billion or more; ii) between £25 billion and $40 billion; and iii) less than £25 billion.

articles.title: Equities update - Week 45 - November 9th 2026
articles.text: Week 45 saw Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress in the US midterms, ending Republican control from January. The initial relief rally quickly reversed, with the VIX reaching an eight-month high as investors reassessed the pace and cost of the AI buildout. For blockchain equities, the most consequential result may have been in Texas, where governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has called for tighter oversight of data centres. That could slow projects still seeking approvals and make existing power connections more valuable, particularly for miners that already have a customer and can deliver capacity in 2027. Brent’s retreat below USUS$100 and lower Treasury yields offered some relief, although October payrolls rose by 165,000, well above expectations of 70,000, keeping a December Fed hike in play. Corporate progress continued through the sell-off, with Riot securing its US$28bn Corsicana lease, Cipher recognised its first HPC lease revenue at Black Pearl, and IREN’s AI Cloud revenue rose to US$200m from US$71m in the previous quarter. In payments, Samsung Wallet began rolling out USDC with custody support from Coinbase, while Circle agreed to acquire Tazapay to expand its access to local payment networks. Standard Chartered completed live transactions using tokenised deposits for corporate clients in Hong Kong, and Block raised its full-year outlook after reporting 22% gross profit growth. The week brought signed contracts, first revenues and live products across several parts of the Index, even as investors marked down the sector’s growth prospects. Week 45 Key Developments in Blockchain Equities:Index Performance: The Index returned −6.6% over the week, compared with −2.1% for Bitcoin. The US midterm election results drove sharp swings in markets, with the initial relief rally giving way to concerns that greater scrutiny of AI infrastructure could slow development and increase costs. Oil offered some relief, with Brent falling back below US$100 a barrel on hopes of de-escalation in Iran, easing inflation concerns and supporting lower Treasury yields, while gold attracted demand. Friday’s stronger-than-expected employment report added another consideration, October nonfarm payrolls increased by 165,000 against expectations of 70,000, alongside combined upward revisions of 84,000 to the previous two months. Unemployment fell to 4.1% even as participation edged higher, while average hourly earnings rose 0.4% month-on-month, above the 0.3% forecast. The report supports confidence in underlying economic activity, but also gives the Fed greater scope to address persistent inflation, keeping a December rate hike firmly in consideration. Block Index Key Movers: 7-day top performers: Block Inc (+9.2%), Nextera Energy (+7.4%), RIOT Platforms (+7.4%) 7-day worst performers: Cipher Digital (-31.5%), IREN (-31.3%), Hut-8 (-30.8%) US midterms reshape the outlook for blockchain equities, bringing new risks and opportunities – Democrats’ victories in Congress and Gina Hinojosa’s election as Texas governor have brought data-centre approvals and electricity costs into sharper focus. While this creates uncertainty around new developments, the implications for blockchain equities are more balanced than the sector’s sell-off suggests. Slower approvals could make existing power connections and operating sites more valuable, particularly where companies already have customers, established community relationships and a clear route to delivery. For miners that have spent years securing these assets, the political shift could strengthen an advantage that new entrants would find difficult to replicate.Riot stressed that the power interconnections at Rockdale and Corsicana are already fully approved, with both campuses operating for years. Management highlighted these existing connections, substations and community relationships as important advantages in securing its new Corsicana lease. Cipher, speaking before the election, also described exceptionally strong demand for sites available in 2027 and confirmed that Reveille and Ulysses are fully approved for interconnection outside ERCOT’s Batch Zero process. These examples show why the outlook needs to be assessed site by site: restrictions on future development can increase the appeal of capacity that is already further advanced.Hut 8 was similarly constructive, saying it did not expect the election result to change Beacon Point’s outlook and that it expected Texas to remain business-friendly. Management supported the governor-elect’s call for guardrails and argued that responsible development could align with her objectives. Its development opportunities also extend well beyond Texas, with less than 5% of its front-of-meter greenfield pipeline in ERCOT. Beacon Point Phase I still requires completion of the existing audit process, with management expecting final classification in December, but the company’s message was one of continued execution.At IREN, management described customer demand as stronger than ever, pointing to newly signed contracts, expanding customer commitments and one agreement with prepayments covering approximately 90% of the associated GPU investment. It also viewed community expectations that data centres pay their own way as reasonable, highlighting local hiring and closed-loop cooling. Ownership of its land, power and facilities gives IREN flexibility to adjust construction spending as financing conditions change. This matters in the current environment: demand can remain strong while companies take a more selective approach to funding growth.The opportunity increasingly favours operators that can combine established infrastructure with financeable contracts and responsible development. Geographic diversification, including international operations at HIVE and Bitdeer, provides further flexibility. Approvals and construction costs remain important, but greater discipline around new supply could support the economics of well-positioned existing projects.The implications for exchanges, stablecoin providers and tokenisation platforms are different. A Democratic Congress can increase oversight and reshape legislative priorities, while Trump retains executive authority and the presidential veto. The GENIUS Act is already law, and the election does not automatically reverse existing regulatory decisions. Further market-structure legislation will require continued political negotiation, but companies can keep developing services within the frameworks already established.Earnings Recap – Key Holdings:AMD, Block Inc, SBI Holdings, Sony Group, RIOT Platforms, IREN, Core Scientific, Mercari, Circle, Hyperliquid Strategies – PositiveCipher Digital, Hut-8 – MixedMercadoLibre - NegativeOther news - Index constituents:Riot Platforms signed a 15-year powered-land lease covering 910MW of critical IT capacity at Corsicana, representing approximately US$28bn of contracted revenue. Delivery is phased across 2027–28. The structure shifts the modular compute deployment to the tenant, although Riot still estimates approximately US$5.5bn of project capital. Q3 data-centre revenue was US$18.4m, including US$7.7m of base rent. Riot also disclosed approximately US$1.5bn of Bitcoin sales year-to-date, primarily to fund development, illustrating the reallocation of its balance sheet towards AI infrastructure.Circle reported US865m of revenue and reserve income and US$317m of adjusted EBITDA. The results included US182m of ARC token presale revenue, while reserve income declined 8% year-on-year. Circle also agreed to acquire Tazapay, which brings more than US$25bn of annualised payment volume; closing is expected in 2027, subject to approvals. The deal expands local payment connectivity. Separately, Circle said it froze approximately US$1.1bn of USDC associated with the Binance incident in coordination with law enforcement, highlighting the issuer’s role in incident response.Hyperliquid Strategies announced that a subsidiary had applied to become a futures commission merchant, seeking a regulated route to service US clients accessing markets deployed on Hyperliquid. This is an application, with approval and implementation still ahead. The development could extend PURR’s activities beyond its HYPE treasury and staking operations. Quarterly staking revenue and validator commissions were approximately US$12.3m, while US$620.6m of net income primarily reflected unrealised token gains. Holdings reached approximately 38.9m HYPE by 28 October.Bullish named Solana, Aptos and Ethereum as its initial equity-tokenisation network partners, extending its issuer-sponsored approach across multiple chains. Its 3 November announcement also detailed the earlier transfer of 61m reserved Bullish shares, earmarked for the proposed Equiniti acquisition; this was not newly raised capital.SBI Holdings first-half revenue increased 17.2% to ¥1.06trn and attributable profit rose 39.1% to ¥230.6bn, although crypto-asset revenue fell 30.1% and the segment reported a ¥1.6bn pretax loss. Commercial initiatives continued: JPYSC handling balances exceeded ¥30bn, including more than ¥10bn in its lending service, and the tokenised Japanese equity fund JX expanded distribution through Hong Kong’s HashKey Exchange. SBI also announced a US$100m investment in Erebor Bank, which supports blockchain-based settlement and stablecoin deposits and withdrawals, while SBI Securities joined Norinchukin-group partners on a Progmat digital-securities initiative.Standard Chartered launched tokenised deposits for corporate clients in Hong Kong, using its blockchain infrastructure and the HKMA’s Ensemble platform. The release describes live transactions and tokenised money-market-fund settlement, alongside work with Fireblocks and HashKey. The opportunity extends existing treasury and transaction-banking relationships through programmable deposits and around-the-clock transfers across participating banks.Strategy acquired 811 BTC for approximately US$65.5m in the week to 1 November, bringing holdings to 849,327 BTC, and repurchased US$208.2m of STRC preferred shares. Its USD Reserve stood at approximately US$4.79bn, alongside US$132.7m of additional USD cash.Other news – Non - Index constituents:Morgan Stanley said it had tokenised US equities and Treasuries through DTCC’s recently launched service. Its separate plan to support tokenised equities on its own trading platform is now expected in Q1 2027. The development demonstrates use of established post-trade infrastructure, although the bank did not disclose transaction scale.Cross River partnered with Offchain to integrate tokenisation into its lending platform on Arbitrum One, enabling loans to be tokenised at origination. The model connects creation, servicing and distribution of credit assets within the same infrastructure, providing a relevant comparison for Figure’s blockchain-native marketplace.

articles.text:
Investment Insights

2026 Sports Media Update

November 2026

5 minute read

Zachary Baran

SUBSCRIBE TO INSIGHTS

As of May 2026, Arctos is part of KKR Solutions, a new global investing business at KKR spanning investments in premier sports franchises through Arctos Sports and private equity and real assets through Arctos Keystone. Together, these businesses provide bespoke capital solutions, differentiated insights and purpose-built operating capabilities to industry leaders across both markets.
Within Arctos Sports, we focus primarily on investing in professional sports franchises across the four major North American leagues (NFL, NBA, MLB and NHL), supported by deep sector expertise and proprietary research into the factors driving long-term franchise valuations. A key component of our investment thesis is the enduring value of premium live sports media rights, which we believe are becoming increasingly important as streaming reshapes the media landscape and artificial intelligence accelerates content proliferation.
In the analysis below, we examine the evolving sports media rights landscape, the key developments shaping the market in 2026, and why we believe the scarcity and resilience of premium live sports will continue to support long-term growth in franchise valuations.

Sign up to subscribe to the latest insights from KKR

Email Address

Please enter your business email.

Please enter a valid email address.
Please enter a professional email address.

SUBSCRIBE TO INSIGHTS

Key Takeaways
The media rights business is transforming in ways that benefit the Big Four (NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL) and other premium sports leagues.Competition in the video business has changed forever due to streaming, which now represents over 50% of industry economics. Because the industry is so fragmented, retaining must-have content has never been more important.Streaming created an explosion of undifferentiated content, and AI is set to worsen this problem.We believe premium live sports is a safe haven that is both AI-resistant and reliably monetizes audiences at scale – an increasingly scarce asset in the content landscape.

Introduction: The Great Content Glut
Media rights represent an important revenue source for global premium sports leagues, including the “Big Four” in North America (NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL). Media rights deals are typically contracted over multiple years, with annual escalators, and represent a durable driver for franchise valuations. As a firm dedicated to investing in the Big Four and other premium sports, we have spent considerable time and resources on the data and models necessary to understand and forecast media rights values.
We believe three key shifts in the U.S. media marketplace are driving growth in premium sports media rights:
First, the market is digesting the reality of content proliferation, competition and commoditization. Put simply, there is too much video content chasing the same number of eyeballs across the same 24-hour day. Second, a new cohort of streaming-first, diversified tech platforms have emerged as real competitors for sports rights. These businesses are more than just media companies and can amortize rights costs across a broader set of commercial goals. Third, AI is an accelerant: it will make it even easier to create undifferentiated, copiable content at scale, which will worsen the “content glut” and raise the value of anything truly differentiated, authentic and uncopiable.
As a result, traditional media companies face a dilemma. How do media companies protect our subscriber base and advertising business in the face of increasing commoditization and formidable new competitors?
How We Got Here
Media companies, both legacy media companies and Big Tech, generate direct revenues from content via subscriptions and advertising – Subscriber Value (SV) and Advertiser Value (AV). Sports media rights packages represent some amount of future SV and AV that leagues and teams sell to media companies in exchange for fixed, contracted revenue – providing certainty and visibility to franchises in exchange for reliable, often exclusive access to must-have content for networks and streamers. That basic set up is in large part not changing, but the number and kind of partners interested in buying rights packages is.
Just over a decade ago, the media business was highly concentrated and consolidated. There was, in fact, only one television product that most households bought: the cable / linear TV bundle. There were only five, scaled, active bidders on sports rights, and even worse for leagues, losing a rights package was less consequential: no one unsubscribed from the bundle because ESPN/ABC lost NASCAR rights in 2014; they just changed the channel. Margins at media networks were ~40%+ - extremely high by any industry standard.
EXHIBIT 1: Video Landscape In the U.S. Is Highly Fragmented

Estimated Household Penetration by Service Offering (Millions)

Source: SNL Kagan, Company Financials, and Arctos Estimates. As of July 2026.

EXHIBIT 2: Sports Rights Competitors – Then and Now

Source: SNL Kagan, Company Financials, and Arctos Estimates. As of July 2026.

Now, there are at least 11, scaled and capitalized bidders on national and local Big Four sports rights. Most of these players are either streaming-only (Amazon, Netflix, YouTube, Apple) or have both linear and streaming products. Streaming is now >50% of overall industry revenue and ~50% of total media industry EBITDA. The streaming genie is not going back in the bottle: consumer choice is far higher today, and the value proposition is much better. Today, customers can self-curate their own bundle, across many different linear and digital options, and churn at any time. This makes it better than ever to be a media consumer, but harder than ever to be a media company.
As a result, losing must-have sports content today is far more consequential than it was in the bundle world. That would mean risking one of your highest-value subscriber segments to a competitor for as long as the next media deal lasts (often a decade or longer).
Three Updates for 2026
There were several important highlights in 2026 worth addressing.

First, viewership and engagement fundamentals in 2026 are stronger than ever. To unpack this, some context-setting is useful. Over the last 10 years, the media business has “unbundled” – this has meant ever increasing fragmentation and narrowing of audiences. Netflix and YouTube have learned your preferences to such precision that they can use machine learning to curate an engagement-maximizing portfolio of content just for you. There is less “mass media” today – in 1980, 52M homes simultaneously watched the evening news on ABC, CBS, or NBC; today that number is 19M, and falling ~2% per year. Movie theater unit ticket sales are half of what they were in 2002. If the market average ratings point for everything in mass culture is facing this headwind, then (as we like to say) “flat is the new up”. And indeed, viewership has been strong in the Big Four and is growing in part due to new measurement standards. Pro sports is one of the last remaining content niches that durably delivers mass, diversified and heterogeneous audiences at scale.

EXHIBIT 3: Viewership Fundamentals Continue to Deliver for the Big 4
Regular Season Viewership Indexed to 2014

Source: JP Morgan and NBA. As of July 2026. Note: Weighted average of regular season.

Second, some legacy media companies have raised the prospect that they cannot support additional step-ups for must-have sports. Our work suggests that there is more than enough room in aggregate to afford rights just among those incumbents, and that in fact, given the amount of SV and AV that sports rights drive, it could be worse to let must-have rights fall to a competitor than to simply retain them at a step-up. We estimate that legacy media companies spend over $55B on non-sports, non-live content, most of which is less protected from threats like commoditization and competition; they spend $28B on live sports, and only $16B on the Big Four.

EXHIBIT 4: Big Tech Still Has Enormous Dry Powder

Source: SNL Kagan, JP Morgan, Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, and Arctos Estimates. As of July 2026.

Now, this doesn’t mean that leagues and teams will default to the status quo: increasingly, media companies offer different value propositions to leagues in terms of the amount and diversity of audience they can offer. The 11 active media companies that compete for rights are not all created equal, do not all have equal capabilities or have equal balance sheet strength. At the same time, leagues want and need a diverse set of partners. Threading that needle isn’t easy, but it also isn’t new: that is what leagues have done for decades. We think leagues will continue to grow the SV and AV potential of their programming, and over the long-term, the partners with the capabilities to maximize SV and AV will win.
Finally, there’s the topic of “rebundling”. We are seeing signs of rebundling, led by Charter, who has been able to reintegrate the ad-supported streaming platforms of the major network groups (think: Peacock, Paramount+, Disney+, etc.) into their Spectrum basic cable package. However, this is far from a reintroduction of the “one big bundle” market structure that prevailed in pre-internet era. We think this is a rational market evolution that gives these platforms reliable subscriber access for a fair price; but nonetheless, ceding market share to competitors by allowing sports rights to lapse will remain painful, especially if those losses occur to Big Tech, whose platforms live entirely outside of the linear business.
Scarcity Economics
In short, premium sports rights are seeing their already high scarcity value accelerate, driven by persistent market forces that show no signs of letting up. Programming that is evergreen, can retain mass audiences, reliably delivers both SV and AV, and is AI-resistant is in short supply. There are few if any content bets available that can check all four of these boxes – premium sports does.
The specialness of the fan relationship undergirds this – a relationship that takes decades of authentic engagement and powerful memories to build. Authentic fan connection is not something AI can threaten easily. The gap between haves and have-nots is widening in the content world, and premium, global sports is benefiting.
