articles.title: What the Democratic sweep means for markets
articles.text:
Investment Talks

Elections

Geopolitics

Politics

US

Fiscal policy

5 November, 2026

14 minutes

What the Democratic sweep means for markets

EDM

Investment TalksENFR

What the Democratic sweep means for markets

14 minutes

EDM

Investment TalksENFR

Summary

Increased constraints on President Trump, but not a policy reversal: Congress will have greater oversight of foreign policy, funding and appointments, while President Trump retains significant executive authority. This points to more political gridlock, which may constrain policy activism but not fully restore discipline.At the macro level, less fiscal stimulus and greater regulatory scrutiny: increased congressional oversight should limit the scope for further fiscal stimulus. However, this is unlikely to deliver meaningful deficit reduction. Markets would distinguish reduced legislative uncertainty from a genuine improvement in the fiscal trajectory. Greater regulatory scrutiny, particularly of AI and Big Tech, could also slow investment in selected areas, even though more careful consideration of capex and regulatory oversight on AI security may now be welcome.Iran and AI are the two key policy fault lines. Congress may push to reduce funding for the Iran war and challenge tariffs, potentially easing pressure on oil prices and inflation. At the same time, greater scrutiny of AI, Big Tech and data-centre development could weigh on technology investment and valuations.The market reaction points to relief and rotation. The market reaction reflects lower political uncertainty, with bonds benefitting, the dollar weakening and equity leadership broadening beyond US technology. AI, data centres and defence face greater policy risk, but the underlying investment themes remain intact.Investment implications: not a game changer, seek broader diversification in equities. The result is mildly positive for global fixed income, as it could lead to lower inflationary pressure. In US bonds, we continue to favour intermediate maturities. In equities, the election result favours diversification into non-US equities and non-tech sectors.

How is the market reacting to the election result?

The initial market reaction suggests that the blue wave was broader than expected, but not fundamentally surprising. The early sell-off quickly reversed as investors looked beyond the scale of the shift and focused on the removal of a major source of uncertainty. The immediate message is relief – not enthusiasm for the outcome itself.This is not a classic risk-on move. Government bonds are rallying, the dollar is weakening and precious metals are rising. With expectations for the next Fed meeting broadly unchanged, lower yields appear to reflect less risk of an additional fiscal impulse, incremental Treasury supply and term-premium pressure – rather than hopes of easier monetary policy. Gold and silver are benefiting from lower yields and a softer dollar, while retaining value as hedges against future political and institutional confrontation. Acceptance of the result and a less confrontational foreign-policy tone have also reduced immediate tail risks, helping oil retreat.Equity dispersion shows where policy concerns remain. In the US, materials, financials, health care and consumer staples are leading, while technology is participating less fully and energy and industrials are lagging. AI and data-centre names are pricing concerns over tighter permitting constraints, while defence is exposed to greater budget uncertainty. Neither theme is collapsing, however, suggesting that the market is repricing targeted policy rather than a rupture in the earnings regime. The broader rotation is equally revealing. Small caps are outperforming large-cap technology, while European equities and cyclical sectors are benefiting from lower yields and a narrowing US policy premium. This looks like a broadening away from concentrated US growth and pre-election policy winners toward assets benefiting from lower yields, reduced policy exceptionalism and a broader global opportunity set – not a rejection of US risk assets.Options markets went into the vote priced for movement but positioned for relief. Elevated volatility, along with call demand and risk reversals, pointed to a constructive post-election bias. The softer volatility curve and equity rebound suggest uncertainty is clearing to the upside.

Markets price less uncertainty, tighter fiscal constraints, and stronger oversight – not a policy revolution.

The implied message is clear: markets price less uncertainty, tighter fiscal constraints, and stronger oversight – not a policy revolution. Markets today are pricing greater political clarity, but policy risks persist. Reduced legislative optionality does not eliminate execution discretion. The remaining risk is that legislative constraint becomes confrontation through budgets, the debt ceiling, investigations or restrictions on AI investment. For now, clarity and upside optionality are outweighing policy anxiety.

What is the likely election impact on domestic policy?

The Democrats’ message during the election was aimed at Big Tech, AI, and alleged corruption in the administration. Therefore, pushback against the AI data centre buildout should be expected, as well as greater scrutiny of Big Tech. In addition, there are likely to be investigations into President Trump and his administration around his business interests and conflicts of interest; therefore, expect a lot more domestic political noise. Furthermore, as the Senate also confirms Supreme Court justices, Democrats can now block judicial nominations.Importantly, in the Republican and Democratic parties the succession battle now begins. Both parties have big questions to answer over their political positions. The Democrats will see an internal battle playing out between the progressive and more centrist wings, while in the Republican Party MAGA and what it stands for will be questioned.

How do you see foreign policy changing following the election result?

The election results increase pressure on President Trump to de-escalate tensions with Iran, but also the risk of unpredictability.

Since the Democrats won the Senate by a larger margin than expected, they will be able to exercise greater oversight of President Trump’s foreign policy agenda. There will be more scrutiny and therefore more uncertainty. However, a weaker president does not necessarily mean a less assertive foreign policy. President Trump retains executive authority and can still push through his goals on foreign policy and tariffs. Further, since he is now significantly constrained at home, he will likely become more interventionist.In particular, the most immediate impact will likely be on Iran given that the cost of the war for US consumers has been a key issue in this election. While another round of escalation and US/Israeli attacks on Iran are widely expected in the short term, the election results increase the pressure on President Trump to de-escalate over the medium term also because Congress has greater oversight of funding. President Trump’s interests are now also likely to clash with those of Republicans seeking to succeed him. Nevertheless, the election outcome does not change the political realities in the region, and the likelihood of a return to the pre-war status quo remains low. The US has heavily built out its military presence in the Middle East and US and Iranian demands for a compromise remain far apart.Ukraine will likely benefit from more support and pushback against President Trump’s overtures to President Putin, as the Democrats will likely push for increased assistance and better security guarantees. Similarly, for Europe, the election results likely mean more sympathetic voices in Congress and more support for legislation to ensure that US troops remain in Europe. The election result also improves the outlook for US commitment to NATO. The next key piece of legislation to watch is the National Defense Authorization Act, due towards the end of the year, as it outlines US foreign policy priorities and authorises related funding. Nevertheless, there remains fatigue on all sides regarding US involvement in ‘foreign’ conflicts and the desire to reduce defence commitments. Finally, no major change should be expected in US policy towards China, although the results will likely increase support for US allies in South and East Asia.

What are the implications for the US economy?

The Democratic emphasis on redistribution, healthcare support, and benefits for lower-income households could support consumption at the margin.

The Democratic priorities would likely centre on redistribution rather than austerity, with a focus on healthcare. This would include efforts to reinstate the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired at the end of 2025, reverse Medicaid cuts, and expand coverage. The emphasis on redistribution, healthcare support, and benefits for lower-income households could support consumption at the margin, but it would not necessarily materially boost it. The impact on inflation should be limited unless the Democrats secure the reintroduction of Obamacare-related subsidies, which we consider unlikely. As far as investments are concerned, a Democratic sweep should make tighter regulation more likely, probably focusing on areas such as consumer protection, labour impacts, environmental costs, energy consumption, and local permitting. Across the broader economy, given the geopolitical priorities of the current administration, we would expect continued emphasis on innovation, competitiveness, and faster infrastructure buildout in the race for AI dominance.In general, several measures cannot be adopted unilaterally. President Trump has already declared that he will exercise his veto power whenever he deems it necessary, and overriding such a veto would require a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which is clearly out of reach. That said, the new political landscape will create greater checks on presidential power. A Democratic Congress will create more friction for the administration, especially around judicial, regulatory, and Federal Reserve appointments. While the fiscal stance may become more neutral or possibly restrictive next year as stimulus fades, we do not envisage a credible path to a large-scale debt-stabilisation programme. Significant deficits would remain the backdrop, with the Congressional Budget Office baseline pointing to deficits of at least 5.6% of GDP over 2026–36.

What can we expect for markets?

At the margins, the result is mildly positive for global fixed income and mildly negative for AI stocks. Non-tech and international markets may benefit.

Looking ahead there are two major questions that may push markets in opposite directions.Will Congress look to reduce financing for the Iran war and roll back tariffs? If so, this could reduce inflation pressure by pushing oil prices lower and reducing taxes on imported goods. Will Congress want to regulate AI and slow the building of data centres? This could be a direct threat to the revenue growth of tech companies and drive stock prices lower across the sector.On fixed income, the election result is not a game changer, but at the margin can be seen as slightly positive. In the US, we keep a close to neutral stance on duration. We favour intermediate maturities, while we remain more cautious on the long end of the curve, where fiscal credibility and term premium remain key considerations.In equity sectors, AI/Tech names are under scrutiny, but a lot will depend on how much the Democratic Party can change the status quo. More broadly, the AI race is increasingly about execution, not just innovation. Eneregy availablity, infrastructure bottonecks and social accepance – all of which can be shaped by state and federal regulation – may determine the pace and geography of future AI investments. This calls for greater diverisication across the AI value chain, including power infrastructure, grid investment, compute and enabling technologies tied to AI applications. Investors may also seek rotation outside the tech sector and, geographically, beyond the US towards the rest of the world. Some data centre projects may be delayed, but it remains hard to imagine a regime change given the structural investment and the competition with China.With regard to the dollar, looking at past mid-term elections (12 episodes since 1978), the dollar has tended to weaken, with the effect building over the first 6 months, with the weakness looking more persistent in the sweep case and then fading back to flat over a 12-month horizon. Within G10 foreign exchange, the Swiss franc, New Zealand dollar and euro have been the main beneficiaries of dollar weakness at the six-month horizon. Meanwhile, the Japanese yen, Norwegian krone and Swedish krona show little directional bias, and their historical upside in our sample is small.

articles.title: Bank competitiveness and its role for monetary policy
articles.text: Bank competitiveness and its role for monetary policyPrepared by Lorenzo Ferrante, Franziska Maruhn and Carla Valero EscribáPublished as part of the ECB Economic Bulletin, Issue 7/2026.This box provides evidence on bank competitiveness in the euro area and its relationship with monetary policy transmission. Recently, European institutions have been exploring measures to improve bank competitiveness by reducing cross-border fragmentation and simplifying regulation and reporting requirements (European Commission, 2026). The definition of bank competitiveness is not straightforward. Banks are competitive if they generate profits based on a sustainable business model (rather than by exploiting market power) and are adequately capitalised, with affordable access to market-based funding and liquidity, allowing them to maintain lending during episodes of economic or financial disruption and through policy cycles. Bank competitiveness in turn supports the effective transmission of monetary policy.[1] For further discussion on the issues discussed in this box, in particular regarding the definition of competitiveness in the banking sector and the role of capital requirements and fragmentation in the euro area, see, for example, Vujčić (2026), Machado (2026), Elderson (2026) and Buch (2025). Euro area banks are more competitive now than they have been for most of the period since the global financial crisis, as intermediation margins have widened and balance sheets have recovered (Chart A). One way to assess bank competitiveness is through valuation-based measures of their performance. These reflect investors’ perceptions of expected future earnings and therefore provide a market view of expected profitability and performance. The price-to-book ratios of euro area banks have substantially improved in recent years, reflecting stronger balance sheets and higher intermediation margins as net interest earnings have recovered, narrowing the gap to their US peers since 2023, although there are still significant differences across euro area countries (Chart A, panel a). Another way to analyse bank competitiveness is by looking at bank profitability, which has also improved relative to peers outside the euro area (Chart A, panel b). While valuation-based measures focus only on listed institutions and bank profitability is backward looking, a broader metric, based on replicating portfolios, also shows a substantial improvement in recent years (see Altavilla et al., 2024).[2] The measure developed in Altavilla et al. (2024) captures the performance of banks by benchmarking the returns on their balance sheets against the return that a market portfolio with similar maturity and risk characteristics would generate. The “edge” that euro area banks have over the financial markets is now positive, after having been negative for most banks between 2015 and mid-2022. It began to recover during the rapid hiking of interest rates by the European Central Bank (ECB) and eventually returned to positive territory as the yield curve stabilised. Chart APrice-to-book ratio and return on equity for euro area and other banks a) Price-to-book ratio(ratio)b) Return on equity(percentages)Sources: LSEG, ECB (supervisory reporting, consolidated banking data), Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, Moody’s Analytics BankFocus (formerly BvD BankFocus) and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel a): The price-to-book ratio is the ratio of a bank’s share price to its book value per share. Panel b): Return on equity (ROE) is computed on a four-quarter trailing basis. Before 2015, the ROE for the euro area is based on consolidated banking data. The latest observations are for 21 August 2026 for the price-to-book ratio and 2025 for ROE.More competitive banks have demonstrated greater resilience to shocks and transmitted monetary policy more effectively (Chart B). From a monetary policy transmission perspective, bank competitiveness matters, especially if it supports the intermediation capacity of banks over the cycle. During the pandemic shock in 2020 and 2021, more competitive banks were less reliant on lending backed by government guarantees and on the Eurosystem’s targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTROs) and were better able to transmit the monetary policy stimulus (Altavilla et al., 2024). More competitive banks also exhibit a higher pass-through to deposit rates, in particular for household deposits (Chart B, panel a). For corporate deposits the differences are less pronounced, with point estimates differing but confidence bands partially overlapping (Chart B, panel b). It is likely that this reflects the fact that more competitive banks are more able to retain deposits by increasing deposit rates during periods of rising rates and more able to lower rates following monetary policy easing without the risk of losing funding. For lending rates, the pass-through is not dependent on bank competitiveness, indicating that more competitive banks are not achieving a higher remuneration of deposits by extracting higher rents from borrowers.Chart BThe pass-through of monetary policy to deposit rates by bank competitivenessa) Household deposit ratesb) Non-financial corporation deposit rates(x-axis: months; y-axis: percentage points)(x-axis: months; y-axis: percentage points)Sources: ECB (iBSI, iMIR, AnaCredit, SHSG, CSDB, supervisory reporting) and ECB calculations.Notes: Banks are categorised as more competitive or less competitive in each quarter based on the 50th percentile of the “edge” as in Altavilla et al. (2024). Charts show the cumulative change in rates on new business deposits following a 1 percentage point increase in the policy rate. The impacts are estimated using local projection regressions of the change in new business interest rates between t-1 and t+h on the change in the policy rate between t-1 and t (explained by high-frequency monetary policy shocks), where h refers to months. The model includes the lag dependent variable, bank controls and country fixed effects. The latest observations are for March 2026.Gains in cost efficiency are emerging as a driver of recent developments (Chart C). Changes in competitiveness may reflect various drivers. First, the estimated effect of lower capital requirements on competitiveness is not statistically significant, likely reflecting offsetting factors (Chart C, panel a). On the one hand, higher capital requirements may increase transition costs for individual banks with specific vulnerabilities, thereby negatively affecting profitability. On the other hand, these requirements support the resilience of the banking system to adverse shocks and help prevent excessive risk-taking. In addition, in an environment of generally solid bank balance sheets, targeted increases in capital requirements for individual banks can be absorbed and are not a hindrance to the competitiveness of the banking system.[3] See, for example, Behn and Reghezza (2025). Second, a less competitive bank may lose market share against other banks, non-banks or financial assets that offer similar services to customers. Indeed, there is an association between an easing of credit standards originating from perceived increases in competition, as reported in the Bank Lending Survey (BLS), and lower bank competitiveness, even after controlling for observed and unobserved characteristics at bank level and country-specific factors (Chart C, panel b). At the same time, overall competition from non-banks has stabilised in recent years, reflecting specialisation in different customer segments and mutually beneficial interaction between banks and non-banks, for instance via securitisations or mutual exposures. Third, improvements in the cost efficiency of banks have significant and persistent positive effects on bank competitiveness (Chart C, panel c). Thus, it is likely that euro area banks can achieve sustained gains in competitiveness through improved cost efficiency.Chart CImpact of changes in potential determinants on bank competitiveness(x-axis: quarters ahead; y-axis: percentage points)a) Impact of 1 percentage point lower capital requirementsb) Impact of one quarter of BLS-reported competition from non-banksc) Impact of 1 percentage point lower cost-to-income ratioSources: Altavilla et al. (2024), ECB (iBSI, iMIR, AnaCredit, SHSG, CSDB, supervisory reporting, BLS) and ECB calculations.Notes: Results from panel local projection estimations controlling for liquidity, funding composition, and bank and country-time fixed effects. The dependent variable is the difference between the realised return and the replicating portfolio return measured in percentage points. For details, see Altavilla et al. (2024). Panel b) shows the impact of one quarter in which the bank reports an effect from non-bank competition in the BLS. Shaded areas indicate 90% confidence bands. The sample covers the fourth quarter of 2015 to the first quarter of 2026.Investment in digitalisation and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is expected to yield efficiency gains, which can also be achieved by streamlining operations and taking a targeted approach to closing local branches (Chart D). The average size of banking groups in the euro area has steadily increased, while operating expenses (as a share of equity) have generally declined. Banks have reduced their operating expenses by streamlining their group structure, closing a substantial number of local branches and reducing their staff, facilitated by the rise of online banking and digitalisation. Looking ahead, banks are increasingly trying to leverage AI technologies to enhance cost efficiency. Almost half of the references bank executives make to AI adoption specifically focus on potential benefits in terms of cost optimisation in the future (Chart D).Chart DMentions of AI in bank earnings calls by topic(number of mentions per earnings call)Sources: Capital IQ and ECB calculations.Notes: The chart is based on transcripts of 761 earnings calls from 51 euro area banks analysed using a large language model (LLM) and a comprehensive prompt. The LLM identifies mentions of AI and categorises them into five broad themes. Each earnings call can span multiple themes. Data for 2026 refer to earnings calls up to the second quarter of 2026.Euro area banks could become more competitive if progress is made on completing the savings and investments union or through further consolidation (Chart E). Market fragmentation prevents euro area banks from achieving the cost efficiency that would allow them to offer competitive lending terms and conditions to borrowers. More competitive banking groups are typically characterised by greater geographical reach, with benefits in terms of lower cost-to-income ratios (Chart E, panel a). Bank consolidation, including across borders, which has been particularly limited within the euro area, would offer an alternative way to further enhance bank efficiency. Evidence from past mergers demonstrates that such consolidation can enhance the operating efficiency, balance sheet health and sectoral diversification of banks, thereby helping to strengthen their intermediation capacity, while at the same time mechanically increasing their market shares (Chart E, panel b). This, taken by itself, would reduce competition in local banking markets and could weaken monetary policy transmission. However, in the case of cross-border consolidation in a more integrated euro area loan market, larger, more diversified and more competitive banking groups could benefit borrowers by enhancing stability and access to credit through the policy cycle and ensuring that monetary policy impulses reach them.Chart EGeographical reach, consolidation and bank competitivenessa) Relationship between geographical reach and cost efficiencyb) Impact of mergers on bank efficiency and other characteristics(x-axis: geographical reach, kilometres, y-axis: cost-to-income ratio, percentages)(percentages of standard deviation)Sources: ECB (AnaCredit, supervisory reporting), OpenStreetMap and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel a): binned scatter plot based on 1,034 euro area banks. The two grey lines indicate aggregate weighted averages. Geographical reach is measured by the weighted average distance to firms that have borrowed from the bank in the past 12 months (weighted by size of loan). Panel b) shows results from difference-in-difference regressions assessing post-merger changes in banks, including bank and time fixed effects. “Cost-to-income” refers to the cost-to-income ratio, and “NPL ratio” refers to the non-performing loans ratio. Dependent variables are standardised. Effects are cumulated over the years after the merger. Whiskers indicate 95% confidence intervals. The sector concentration of loans is measured by a bank-level Herfindahl-Hirschman index. Panel a) covers the period from the first quarter of 2019 to the second quarter of 2026. Panel b) covers 2011 to 2025.ReferencesAltavilla, C., Begenau, J., Burlon, L. and Maruhn, F. (2024), “Determinants of bank performance: evidence from replicating portfolios”, Working Paper Series, No 2937, ECB, revised January 2025.Behn, M. and Reghezza, A. (2025), “Capital requirements: a pillar or a burden for bank competitiveness?”, Occasional Paper Series, No 376, ECB, October.Buch, C. (2025), “The evidence is in: resilient banks build Europe’s growth on solid ground”, keynote speech at the 2025 European Banking Authority Policy Research Workshop on “Bridging capital and growth – the role of financial structures and intermediaries”, Paris, 19 November.Elderson, F. (2026), “Boosting prosperity through deeper integration”, keynote speech at the conference “Financing Europe: a new era of strategic investment”, Brussels, 12 May.European Commission (2026), “Competitiveness of the Banking Sector and the Single Market in Banking”, Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Central Bank, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions, COM(2026) 615 final, 17 July.Machado, P. (2026), “Competitiveness and simplification – a common agenda for European banks”, speech at the Expansión XVII Financial Forum, Madrid, 28 September.Vujčić, B. (2026), “Resilience, integration and competitiveness: building the future of European banking”, keynote speech at the tenth annual conference of the European Systemic Risk Board, Frankfurt am Main, 2 October. For further discussion on the issues discussed in this box, in particular regarding the definition of competitiveness in the banking sector and the role of capital requirements and fragmentation in the euro area, see, for example, Vujčić (2026), Machado (2026), Elderson (2026) and Buch (2025). The measure developed in Altavilla et al. (2024) captures the performance of banks by benchmarking the returns on their balance sheets against the return that a market portfolio with similar maturity and risk characteristics would generate. The “edge” that euro area banks have over the financial markets is now positive, after having been negative for most banks between 2015 and mid-2022. It began to recover during the rapid hiking of interest rates by the European Central Bank (ECB) and eventually returned to positive territory as the yield curve stabilised. See, for example, Behn and Reghezza (2025).

articles.title: View from the markets: Asia may not follow US rate hikes - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
By Chi Lo, Senior Market Strategist, Asia Pacific, Hong Kong

The forces keeping the US Federal Reserve in monetary tightening mode have not faded. Diesel and petrol prices remain high, artificial intelligence-driven inflation has not eased, and the labour market remains resilient. Housing market weakness and the recent wobble in AI optimism may make the Fed cautious, but core inflation is still skewed to the upside.

Asian central banks have typically followed the Fed’s rate increases. However, it may be different this time unless the Fed’s hikes cause significant exchange rate depreciation in the region.

US inflationary pressures remain

The underlying inflation dynamics in the US have not changed much since the Fed’s rate increase in September. Global energy prices have remained high and tight diesel markets have boosted diesel price inflation (see Exhibit 1). Diesel prices are pivotal to the pass-through to broader inflationary pressures due to the fuel’s widespread use in transport, manufacturing and farming.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh acknowledged recently that tighter financial conditions (due to the rise in bond yields) had helped the Fed to contain inflationary pressures. However, he also stressed that the Fed’s job was to ensure that sector-specific price shocks do not broaden out and that inflation expectations would not be unanchored. So, rising bond yields do not necessarily stand in the way of further rate hikes.

Asia is different

The Fed has already raised rates once in September. October’s stronger-than-expected consumer price index inflation has increased the markets’ conviction of another Fed rate hike in December. Headline inflation came in at 0.4% month-on-month versus the consensus forecast of 0.3% and core CPI was 0.3% versus consensus expectations of 0.2%.

The European Central Bank, the Bank of Japan, the Bank of England and the Bank of Canada have also hiked their rates since September. In Asia (excluding Japan), the picture is more diverse. While a couple of central banks have hiked rates, most have stood pat.

Recent monetary policy cycle experience shows that Asia has not always followed the Fed’s rate moves in lock-step or has followed them with a lag unless the Fed’s hikes triggered sharp exchange rate depreciation. Why is that?

Firstly, Asian central banks have a wider set of policy targets than the Fed. They do not follow the Fed if its moves are inconsistent with their own domestic policy needs. Both market experience and Bank for International Settlements research1 show that Asia’s regional central banks have ‘unwritten targets’ including the exchange rate, economic growth and bond yields.

These factors, in turn, affect domestic inflation. Furthermore, the regional authorities also target headline inflation alongside core inflation. All these are different from the Fed-style dual mandates that put core inflation and maximum employment on an equal footing.

Exchange rate is paramount in Asia

Among these policy targets, the exchange rate is of primary importance for Asian authorities. Fed rate hikes widen the interest-rate differential between Asia and the US and if exchange rates depreciate markedly, this could amplify the inflationary effects on the region’s economies and financial conditions. To contain that potentially greater impact, the regional central banks will follow the Fed or even react more strongly than the Fed’s original move.

However, other than Indonesia and the Philippines, most of Asia’s economies have large current account surpluses (see Exhibit 2) that provide strong support for the region’s exchange rates, thus lessening the pressure to follow the Fed’s rate hikes. The recent downward pressures on Asia’s exchange rates mostly reflect a risk-off sentiment arising from the speed and breadth of the global rates sell-off rather than poor fundamentals and wider interest-rate differentials.

Secondly, despite nine months of high oil prices, core inflation has remained close to, or even lower than, target in most Asian economies, with the notable exceptions of Vietnam and the Philippines (see Exhibit 3). Subsidies have so far helped Asia to contain oil price-induced inflation and the region’s central banks to stay put at low fiscal costs to their treasuries.

However, if the oil shock lasts longer, fiscal pressure will increase and eventually prompt Asian governments to let fuel prices adjust accordingly, unleashing inflationary pressures. This would, in turn, likely prompt regional rate hikes in the wake of those by the Fed.

The bottom lines

The macroeconomic backdrop suggests that Asia is far from being in a broad-based interest-rate hike cycle. Policy rates are currently being driven by the impact of rising oil prices on domestic inflation.

A hawkish Fed may lead to a potential tightening bias in Asia, but it will not likely prompt widespread rate hikes unless interest-rate differentials between Asia and the US result in large and persistent regional exchange-rate depreciation.

Data sources: CEIC, Trading Economics, as of 10 November 2026 (unless otherwise stated). Past performance should not be seen as a guide to future returns.

[1] The Expansionary Lower Bound: Contractionary Monetary Easing and the Trilemma, Bank for International Settlements, 2019.

articles.title: Daily: The risks reshaping global AI investment
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:The AI sell-off and US midterms: Live at the UBS Disruptive Tech Summit (6 mins)
CIO Live Replay: CIO Asia equity strategists on the AI sell-off and opportunities (30 mins)Thought of the dayNVIDIA’s shares fell more than 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday, helping to pull Nasdaq futures around 1% lower and putting pressure on technology-heavy markets in Taiwan and South Korea. The moves followed reports that NVIDIA’s board had met on Wednesday night to discuss whether CEO Jensen Huang should remain in his role, following news that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort and subsequent developments.These headlines come as investors are becoming more selective on the AI trade. Recent technology volatility reflects a shift from rewarding spending commitments toward assessing monetization, balance sheet strength, capacity utilization, and prospective returns. At the same time, underlying demand remains robust: Recent earnings have shown accelerating cloud revenue and expanding orders for computing capacity, and we forecast aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1.0tr in 2026 and USD 1.4tr in 2027.Without taking any views on individual companies, we see several lessons that investors across the technology sector should consider:Key-person risk warrants greater attention. The episode illustrates how leadership and governance can become material investment considerations when a company’s strategy, culture, and market standing are closely associated with an individual. This matters beyond any single company, particularly after several years in which AI-related equity gains have been concentrated in a relatively narrow group of businesses. As investors become more discerning about valuations and returns, governance and clarity around succession planning may play a larger role alongside earnings growth in determining performance.Chip restrictions look unlikely to ease. AI competition between the US and China already operates within tight restrictions on exports of advanced semiconductors. We believe recent developments reduce the likelihood of an easing in current restrictions on advanced AI-chip shipments to China, while scrutiny of where processors are ultimately deployed could increase. Greater restrictions could weigh on sales in certain overseas markets, though they would not necessarily alter underlying AI demand, with compute capacity remaining in short supply.AI is increasingly a geopolitical issue. As advanced computing becomes more strategically important, governments are paying closer attention to where chips are produced, sold, and deployed. This could result in greater tracking requirements, regulatory scrutiny, and friction around global AI supply chains, potentially raising costs and restricting access to some overseas markets. Greater geopolitical competition may also spur investment in alternative supply chains and domestic AI capacity, reinforcing the importance of distinguishing between strong underlying demand and the companies best positioned to capture it.So, while we retain our conviction in the structural AI opportunity, we think these events reinforce the case for greater selectivity and diversification as the tech investment cycle evolves. We continue to favor financially strong hyperscalers; tighter future compute capacity could increase the value of existing infrastructure, while lower future capital spending could support free cash flow. Within AI “picks and shovels” (semiconductors and hardware), we would stay selective and favor quality companies with less margin expansion to unwind, alongside defensive technology exposures such as payment networks and potential beneficiaries of lower memory costs within consumer electronics. For investors whose technology exposure has become overly concentrated, we would consider broadening exposure within technology and diversifying across sectors, asset classes, and geographies.

articles.text:
PORTFOLIO PERSPECTIVES | ARTICLE – 4 min read
The rise of decommissioning bonds in transition finance

By
MALIKA TAKHTAYEVA, ALEXANDER BERNHARDT, JULIEN HALFON 12.11.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article
Decommissioning financing structures and historical precedentsDifferent Decommissioning Financing MechanismsTransition bonds: A new pathway for funding decommissioning: Risks and opportunities through investors’ potential mechanics

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

By Malika Takhtayeva, Alex Bernhardt and Julien Halfon

Decommissioning finance is a specialised subset of transition finance focused on the final stage of an asset’s life cycle, including the physical retirement and dismantling

There has been a shift from traditional balance sheet provisions and general obligation bonds toward ‘labelled’ vehicles which offer investors better visibility, improved risk management, and measurable real-world impact

Modern decommissioning frameworks aim to achieve dual environmental and social outcomes alongside workforce reskilling and community regeneration

Transition finance is any capital that supports high-emitting, carbon-intensive entities or activities to shift toward net-zero alignment.

Unlike ‘green finance’ which primarily funds already low-carbon assets like solar farms, wind power, or electric vehicles, transition finance targets high-carbon or hard-to-abate sectors, such as thermal power generation, steel, cement, mining, oil and gas.

It provides the financial bridge necessary to decarbonise operations, adopt alternative technologies, or systematically wind down carbon-heavy infrastructure.

Transition bonds are therefore a stand-alone bond category distinct from green, social, sustainable (GSS) or sustainability-linked bonds1. The International Capital Market Association’s Climate Transition Bond Guidelines has a non-exhaustive list of eligible project categories. One of these categories is the retirement and decommissioning of high-emission assets, including the permanent early retirement of coal-fired power plants2.

Within the transition finance architecture, decommissioning finance forms a specialised subset, which focuses specifically on the final stage of an asset’s life cycle: the physical retirement, dismantling, safe closure, environmental remediation, and asset / land repurposing of carbon-intensive or environmentally hazardous infrastructure.

While broader transition finance may fund capital expenditure to lower operational carbon intensity (e.g. adding carbon capture to a steel mill), decommissioning finance addresses the capitalrequirements associated with ending high emissions activities entirely while restoring the surrounding ecological and social fabric.

There are various decommissioning financing structures as well as several challenges around labelled decommissioning funding. We outline these below.

Decommissioning financing structures and historical precedents

Historically, bonds dedicated to fund decommissioning obligations were issued as conventional debt, and managed through balance sheet provisions, or kept off balance sheets. Such bonds were rarely (if ever) accompanied by environmental, social or governance commitments / targets or related reporting.

In the case of a general obligation decommissioning bond structure, the debt is traditionally backed by the issuer’s creditworthiness and ongoing commercial revenue streams, rather than revenue generated by the decommissioning process itself.

The bondholders face general corporate credit risk, while the funds are earmarked to offset long-term asset retirement obligations.

The possibility for firms in industries such as fossil fuel exploration and production or power generation to tap sustainable bond markets to finance decommissioning activities is relatively novel. But equally it represents an opportunity for investors to support a low-carbon and just transition – as in our view decommissioning bonds offer:

Better visibility over use of capital: A defined use-of-proceeds framework can allow investors to trace financing to closure, remediation, reserve funding and repurposing rather than to unrestricted corporate expenditure

Potential reduction in long-term issuer risk: Successful prefunding may reduce future liquidity shocks, capital calls and dependence on commodity-cycle cash flows. Markets may reward companies that proactively fund and transparently manage decommissioning, while unfunded companies may face higher risk premia – this is a potential credit benefit, not an automatic result3

Transition and real-world impact: Investors may finance the permanent retirement of high-emitting assets, remediation, methane-risk reduction, biodiversity restoration, recycling, workforce support and site repurposing. These potential positive outcomes need to be connected to investors’ impact objectives

Engagement and stewardship: Investors can differentiate issuers according to funding quality, press for prefunding and insurance, assess decommissioning liabilities as debt-like exposures, and monitor policy and disclosure. A bond framework can create contractual reporting points around which this engagement can be organised

Relative-value opportunities: There is an emerging distinction between well-funded, financially flexible companies and structurally constrained companies. Investors may potentially use funding quality, reserve coverage, transition credibility and liability disclosure as additional dimensions of credit selection

Different Decommissioning Financing Mechanisms

Transition bonds: A new pathway for funding decommissioning:

Emerging frameworks for decommissioning bonds elevate these instruments beyond routine remediation.

Instead of merely paying for toxic cleanup, the use-of-proceeds or target performance metrics are designed to achieve dual environmental and social outcomes with strong governance oversight.

Some of the criteria to be assessed when underwriting a decommissioning bond as a transition finance vehicle follow:

Opportunities for labelled decommissioning bonds should be expected to increase with the potential advent of a Transition fund category in SFDR 2.0 (aka Article 7) and with the ongoing evolution of ICMA and other voluntary transition bond frameworks.

Risks and opportunities through investors’ potential mechanics

Decommissioning finance is shifting from a general balance sheet liability into a strategically structured transition financing opportunity.

With the evolution of transition financing frameworks and SFDR 2.0, issuers may be able to attract specialised capital while mitigating risks and costs associated with long-term asset retirement obligations.

While decommissioning can be financed in many ways, for investors, the potential increase in general obligation funding with use of proceeds tied to decommissioning projects is likely to be of interest.

However, underwriting these issuances will require careful due diligence to ensure that the related decommissioning strategy supports institutions and sectors’ broader transition goals.

Overview

Why invest in this Fund?
The fund seeks to maximize current income exempt from federal income tax to the extent consistent with the preservation of capital. To pursue its goal, the fund normally invests at least 80% of its net assets, plus any borrowings for investment purposes, in municipal bonds that provide income exempt from federal personal income tax. Typically, the fund invests substantially all of its assets in such municipal bonds.The fund invests at least 70% of its net assets in municipal bonds rated, at the time of purchase, investment grade (i.e., Baa/BBB or higher) or the unrated equivalent as determined by Insight North America LLC, the fund's sub-adviser. For additional yield, the fund may invest up to 30% of its net assets in municipal bonds rated, at the time of purchase, below investment grade ("high yield" or "junk" bonds) or the unrated equivalent as determined by the fund's sub-adviser.

Group reorganizations and transformations come in many forms, domestic or cross-border, transaction-driven or strategic. articles.title: Gold Reserve Relocations: Are They Always Bad News for U.S. Dollar Reserves?
articles.text:
FEDS Notes

Twitter

Share

RSS

November 09, 2026
Gold Reserve Relocations: Are They Always Bad News for U.S. Dollar Reserves?
Colin Weiss1
This note reviews several publicized gold reserve relocations by central banks in the Netherlands, France, and Germany since 2013 and any concurrent changes in their U.S. dollar reserve allocations. Generally, the choice of where to custody gold reserves may in part reflect the perceived risk of sanctions or expropriation in the jurisdiction of custody alongside other considerations like the proximity to international gold markets.2 The U.S. dollar share of foreign exchange (FX) reserves may also depend on sanctions risk in addition to other factors like the size and strength of the U.S. economy and the unmatched depth and liquidity of U.S. financial markets. While some countries have accumulated gold reserves stored outside the U.S. as they have reduced the U.S. dollar share of their FX reserves due to sanctions risk, the euro area central banks mentioned above have not followed this pattern. Instead, they continue to hold most of their FX reserves in U.S. dollar assets without substantial declines in the U.S. dollar share following the shift of their gold reserves out of the U.S. For these euro area central banks, the economic benefits of allocating reserves to U.S. dollar assets appear to outweigh any potential costs.

Why custodial location may matter for gold reserves

Before discussing the cases of the euro area central banks that are the focus of this note, I first review why the storage location of a country's gold reserves may have implications for its U.S. dollar reserves. One of gold's potential appeals as a reserve asset is that it can be used to evade financial sanctions and asset seizures imposed by foreign governments, in contrast to foreign currency assets. For these facts to be true, however, the gold cannot be custodied in the country of the sanctioning government.3 In practice, this has meant that central banks concerned about sanctions custody their gold reserves in domestic vaults. Two prominent examples demonstrate this practice.4 First, Russia holds its gold reserves domestically, having stockpiled gold and reduced its dollar holdings during the 2010s amid concerns about U.S. financial sanctions. Second, Turkey repatriated gold held in the U.S. and U.K. in 2018 and also dramatically cut the dollar share of its reserves, actions taken during a period of geopolitical tensions with the U.S. that included President Erdoğan's criticism of the dollar's international role (Arslanalp, Eichengreen, Simpson-Bell, 2025; McDowell, 2023).

Turning to the euro area, Germany, the Netherlands and France, unlike Russia and Turkey, maintained U.S. dollar reserve allocations even after relocating gold reserves out of U.S. 5

2010s relocations: Germany shifted about one-fifth of its U.S.-held gold to domestic vaults between 2013 and 2017. (Bundesbank, 2017). Its dollar share of foreign exchange reserves remained around 90 percent during this period and currently exceeds 80 percent—well above the U.S. dollar's overall share in global FX reserves based on the IMF's COFER data (Figure 1(a)). Similarly, the Netherlands repatriated about two-fifths of its U.S.-custodied gold reserves in 2014 (Carlyle, 2014), with little change to the 83 percent U.S. dollar share of its FX reserves at (Figure (1(b)). While the dollar share did dip to nearly 50 percent in 2018, this large decline proved short-lived.6

Figure 1. U.S. Dollar Share of European FX Reserves

Figure 1a
Note: Shaded region marks years of gold custody transfer.
Sources: Ito and McCauley (2020) and IMF IRFCL.

Figure 1b
Note: Shaded region marks years of gold custody transfer.
Sources: Ito and McCauley (2020) and IMF IRFCL.

Figure 1c
Note: Shaded region marks year of gold custody transfer.
Sources: Ito and McCauley (2020) and DNB Annual Reports.

Figure 1d
Note: Shaded region marks months of gold custody transfer.
Source: IMF IRFCL.

Accessible version

2020s relocations: France repatriated all its U.S.-held gold reserves in 2025 and early 2026 (Banque de France, 2026), yet its U.S. dollar share of FX reserves remained steady at 60 percent (Figure 1(c)), even as the overall U.S. dollar share of global FX reserves in the IMF COFER data declined.7 The Netherlands moved two-fifths of its U.S.-stored gold to London in 2026 (De Nederlansche Bank, 2026). While the U.S. dollar share of its FX reserves did undergo a concurrent 10-percentage-point decline (Figure 1(d)), this share remains above 2018 lows and still dominates Dutch FX reserves.8

In all cases, these central banks continue holding most reserves in U.S. dollar assets, indicating no substantial diversification away from the U.S. dollar.

References

Arslanalp, Serkan, Barry Eichengreen, and Chima Simpson-Bell. (2025). "Our Underappreciated International Reserve System," NBER Working Paper No. 34478.

Banque de France. (2026). "Net profit of EUR 8.1 billion, enabling the clearing of losses carried forward," Press Release (March 25). https://www.banque-france.fr/en/press-release/net-profit-eur-81-billion-enabling-clearing-losses-carried-forward.

Carlyle, Tristan. (2014). "Netherlands Bank Moves 122.5 Tonnes of Gold from New York to Amsterdam," Central Banking (November 21).

De Nederlansche Bank. (2017). 2016 Annual Report. Amsterdam: De Nederlansche Bank, March.

De Nederlansche Bank. (2026). "DNB improves tradability of gold reserves," Press Release (September 2). https://www.dnb.nl/en/general-news/press-release-2026/dnb-improves-tradability-of-gold-reserves.

Deutsch Bundesbank. (2017). "Bundesbank completes gold transfer ahead of schedule," Press Release (August 23). https://www.bundesbank.de/en/tasks/topics/bundesbank-completes-gold-transfer-ahead-of-schedule-646102.

Ito, Hiro and Robert N. McCauley. (2020). "Currency Composition of Foreign Exchange Reserves," Journal of International Money and Finance 102 (102104).

McDowell, Daniel. (2023). Bucking the Buck: U.S. Financial Sanctions and the International Backlash against the Dollar. New York: Oxford University Press.

U.S. Department of the Treasury. (2026). "Treasury Launches Unprecedented Campaign Against Iranian Regime on Economic D-Day," Press Release (August 24). https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0613.

World Gold Council. (2026). "Central Bank Gold Reserves Survey 2026," World Gold Council, June.

1. I thank Shaghil Ahmed and Daniel Beltran for helpful feedback. The views expressed here are solely my own and do not reflect the views of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve or anyone else associated with the Federal Reserve System. Return to text

2. Note that the official statements provided by these euro area central banks about these gold reserve relocations do not suggest concerns about sanctions or expropriation as a key motivation for the shifts. Return to text

3. For example, Venezuela has not been able to access its gold reserves custodied at the Bank of England since 2019 because the British government does not recognize the legitimacy of Nicolás Maduro and his government. Recently, the U.S. Treasury announced sanctions targeting "anyone, regardless of where they are located," operating in the gold sector of Iran's economy (U.S. Treasury, 2026.) Return to text

4. Aside from these examples, recent survey results from the World Gold Council (2026) show a growing number of central banks report a preference for holding their gold reserves in domestic vaults. Return to text

5. Data on currency composition of FX reserves through 2020 are based on Ito and McCauley (2020), who compiled currency shares based on reports from central banks and FX reserve managers. After 2021, I use data from central bank annual reports and the IMF's international reserves foreign currency liquidity (IRFCL) database. Data are as-of year-end except for the 2026 observation for Germany, which is as-of March. Return to text

6. De Nederlansche Bank (DNB) actively manages the currency risk around its foreign currency investments including by hedging currency risk through forward exchange contracts. The U.S. dollar share of its FX reserves reached a local peak in 2015, and the DNB's 2016 annual report notes it reduced its U.S. dollar exposure in that year due to "the high costs of hedging the currency risk" (DNB, 2017). While subsequent annual reports do not explain changes in U.S. dollar exposure, it can plausibly be assumed that some of the movements in the U.S. dollar share of FX reserves reflect changing returns (inclusive of hedging costs) on holding U.S. dollar assets. Return to text

7. The large decline in the U.S. dollar share that occurred in 2023 appears to reflect the sales of U.S. dollar assets by the Banque de France to generate net income at a time when net interest expenses increased rapidly rather than any major preference change around U.S. dollar reserves. Return to text

8. The monthly data in shown in Figure 1(d) come from a different data source than the annual data shown for the Netherlands in Figure 1(b). In principle, these two series should be identical, but, in practice, they are not—especially after 2022. The U.S. dollar share based on the monthly IRFCL data is persistently below that based on the Netherlands' central bank annual report. Return to text

Please cite this note as:
Weiss, Colin (2026). "Gold Reserve Relocations: Are They Always Bad News for U.S. Dollar Reserves?," FEDS Notes. Washington: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, November 09, 2026, https://doi.org/10.17016/2380-7172.4200.

Disclaimer: FEDS Notes are articles in which Board staff offer their own views and present analysis on a range of topics in economics and finance. These articles are shorter and less technically oriented than FEDS Working Papers and IFDP papers.

articles.text:

articles.title: A breakdown of China's government revenue and tax history over nearly 75 years
articles.text:
PIIE CHARTS

A breakdown of China's government revenue and tax history over nearly 75 years

Navneeraj Sharma (Asian Development Bank) and

Arvind Subramanian (PIIE)

November 12, 2026

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Chart Embed

Description
This chart shows China's government revenues from taxes and other sources during 1952–2024.
The overall level of revenues averaged about 30 percent of GDP before China's then-leader Deng Xiaoping's 1978 "Reform and Opening Up" policies. Revenues declined sharply thereafter in the 1980s, increased sharply from the mid-1990s, reaching a peak of about 28.5 percent of GDP in 2015. When adding land sales and retained profits from state-owned enterprises (SOE), revenues peaked at 39 percent in 2018.
The composition of revenues has changed dramatically. In the pre-reform period, a substantial share of overall revenues came as profits of SOEs. Compulsory production quotas at off-market prices, financial repression in favor of SOEs, and strict quotas on consumer goods imports diverting demand to consumer goods produced by SOEs were all implicit ways of extracting revenues, which were reflected in the profits of SOEs.
After the mid-1990s, and consistent with the turn to markets, more modern tax levers have been used, including value-added taxes (VAT), personal and corporate income taxes, and social insurance contributions. Distinctively, revenues from land sales have accounted for a substantial share of revenues since 2003. Throughout its history, therefore, China has generated a substantial share of revenue from sources other than taxes on its people, which is surprising for a communist state.
Regardless of how they are measured, revenues and taxes have been declining for most of the last decade; for example, taxes (excluding social insurance contributions) have collapsed by nearly 5.5 percentage points, from 18.4 percent of GDP in 2012 to 13.0 percent in 2024, and revenues including land sales and retained SOE profits fell 6.5 percentage points, from 39.0 percent of GDP in 2018 to 32.5 percent in 2024. These tax levels are associated with a struggling, lower middle-income country, not an aspiring superpower.
How much of this decline is attributable to growth that is even slower than headline numbers indicate and how much to the tax cuts enacted over the last decade is difficult to say. But it also seems that the government was so reliant on non-tax sources that, once they dried up, it became politically difficult to turn around and impose taxes on the population.
ADDITIONAL NOTES

Subsidies to loss-making SOEs are spending, as in the International Monetary Fund's system of fiscal accounting. China's budget subtracted them from revenue in 1985 to 2006; they are added back here. Before 1985 they were also subtracted, but the amounts were not published, so they cannot be added back; the broadest measure is broken between 1984 and 1985 for this reason, and most of the rise of the bars in 1985 comes from it. Without the add-back, 1985 would be 25.0 percent of GDP, against 25.2 percent in 1984.
Not available, and so left out: subsidies to loss-making SOEs before 1985; social insurance contributions, 1984 to 1988 (they were 0.9 percent of GDP in 1989); the social insurance funds' own income, 1998, 1999 and 2010; government funds inside the budget, 1997 (2.2 percent of GDP in 1998); local state capital budgets, 2007 to 2011 (central government only); and retained SOE profits before 1996.

articles.title: Beyond CCCs, high-yield appears resilient
articles.text:
Economics & markets

Beyond CCCs, high-yield appears resilient

November 10, 2026

Is the high-yield bond market sending a warning? Spreads on CCC-rated bonds have widened by more than 500 basis points from their lowest levels this year, to roughly 1,000 basis points over Treasuries. Meanwhile, spreads on higher-quality BB- and B-rated bonds have remained relatively contained.

Because of their lower credit quality, CCC-rated bonds typically trade at a discount to the rest of high-yield. That discount is now larger than at any point since the COVID-19 market sell-off, raising investor concern about broader credit deterioration. The important question is whether the cracks at the bottom of the high-yield market are a signal for the broader credit market.
A closer look at the Bloomberg U.S. Corporate High Yield Index suggests the picture is more nuanced: stress is concentrated, the market is higher quality than in the past, and attractive income opportunities remain.

The sell-off is sharp, but narrow

Four out of more than 150 CCC-rated issuers make up more than 30% of current CCC-rated bond spreads. Many of the companies most affected are in the telecommunications and media sector, where secular headwinds and company-specific challenges are driving distress.
In other words, this has not been an indiscriminate repricing of credit risk. But that doesn’t mean investors should ignore it. Financial conditions have tightened this year. Interest rates on the broad U.S. bond market have increased by nearly 100 basis points, and this tightening is filtering through to parts of the credit market. Distress often appears first in the lowest-quality companies, which is not uncommon in the later stages of the credit cycle.
Distress in CCCs has been acute, but largely contained, highlighting a sharp divide between the weakest borrowers and the rest of the credit market. In much of the investment-grade and higher-quality high-yield corporate bond universe, fundamentals remain healthy. Corporations have seen record-high earnings. Through November 6, 88% of companies in the Standard & Poor’s 500 Index (S&P 500) had reported third-quarter earnings, with earnings-per-share growth of 29%. Many also have strong and stable balance sheets, conservative management—with low and stable leverage of roughly two times net debt-to-earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, or EBITDA, for S&P 500 companies, the lowest level since 2014—and positive rating trends. Resilient economic growth provides a supportive backdrop.
“In high-yield, you don’t get paid simply for taking more risk,” says Michael Chang, portfolio manager and head of Vanguard’s high-yield corporates team. “You get paid for taking the right risk. In a market where dispersion is increasing, disciplined credit selection becomes increasingly important, both in capturing opportunities and avoiding areas of fundamental weakness.”

High-yield risk has evolved

Today’s high-yield market is markedly different from prior decades. CCCs now make up less than 10% of the market, a more than 50% decrease in their share of the market heading into the Global Financial Crisis.
The improvement in traditional high-yield credit quality reflects a structural shift in credit markets. Over the past decade, a meaningful portion of lower-quality lending has migrated from traditional high-yield into private credit and leveraged loans.
The shift of risk between markets may be masking more volatility to come, particularly in the markets to which CCC-rated risk has moved. Traditional high-yield is often the first market to flash red in its daily trading activity, whereas less liquid markets may take longer to reflect deteriorating conditions. Signs of greater distress are emerging, as seen in rising defaults in private credit and elevated defaults in leveraged loans last year.

Signs of distress emerging in some credit markets

Notes: Data on private credit are annual through 2025 and monthly from January 2026 through September 2026.
Sources: Vanguard calculations based on Bloomberg and Fitch Ratings data as of September 30, 2026.

The opportunity for income

The sell-off in high-yield bonds is idiosyncratic and confined. At the same time, the high-yield bond market offers a higher-quality investment than in the past. The market yielded 8.21% as of November 6, providing a meaningful income cushion even as pockets of distress emerge.
Relative to the complex structures to which investors reached for yield during the low-rate period that preceded 2022, high-yield offers competitive income, transparency, and liquidity.

Navigating the credit cycle

The widening in CCC-rated credit spreads is a reminder that tighter financial conditions are raising the bar for issuers in the weakest corners of the credit market. For now, stress is concentrated, not broad-based. With high-yield credit quality higher today than in past late-cycle periods, and with some credit risk having shifted into leveraged loans and private credit, looking across credit markets and being more discerning will be key to navigating the next stage of the cycle.

articles.title: Settlement reached in Silicon Valley Bank investor class action case | Norges Bank Investment Management
articles.text:
Norges Bank Investment Management and the Swedish pension fund Sjunde AP-fonden (AP7), as Co-Lead Plaintiffs, have reached a settlement in principle of $224.5 million with KPMG LLP, the former external auditor of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB), on behalf of the class of investors in the U.S. securities class action arising from the bank’s collapse in March 2023.
The fund and other SVB investors suffered significant losses on their investments in SVB securities.
“The settlement is an important first step toward recovering investor losses from one of the largest bank failures in U.S. history. It was reached after more than three years of litigation that has helped strengthen legal protections for investors. Investor confidence depends on well-functioning markets and on investors’ ability to enforce their rights”, says Nicolai Tangen, CEO of Norges Bank Investment Management.
The settlement is subject to court approval. The case continues against the other defendants.

articles.title: Annual Outlook 2026 | Economic and Market Outlook
articles.text:
Annual outlook 2026: Investing in tomorrow

In our PERSPECTIVES 2026 publication, we look to the year ahead across our ten key investment themes, identifying opportunities and risks on the horizon.

Get in touch

Click here to activate this content.

Investing in tomorrow – Opportunities and risks

The global economy is in constant flux. Trade flows are shifting, regions are gaining or losing influence, and new technologies are also reshaping the economic map. 2025 has been challenging in some respects, but many local equity indices did deliver very good performance. Given the positive macro environment, we expect 2026 to be another constructive year, albeit with continuing market volatility. Although we anticipate a reduction in some uncertainties, it will definitely not be a time for complacency – especially as global trade relations are far from settled. The continued rise of artificial intelligence (AI) may open up new growth opportunities, which should encourage companies to increase their investment activity, potentially giving fresh impetus to both private and public consumption.

The US administration’s tariffs agenda appears to have now been largely implemented. While the disorientation that followed the declaration of “Liberation Day” in early April still lingers globally and domestically, most US trading partners have managed to significantly reduce initial steep tariff hikes through renegotiation. Overall, markets seem to have priced in the effects of the new environment, with overall tariffs still considerably higher than in January 2025 when the current administration began its tenure.

US growth is likely to be supported by the continuation and introduction of extensive tax relief measures, as well as increased spending on security and defence under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The three interest rate cuts expected from the Federal Reserve by the end of 2026 and planned deregulation in the banking sector should also further improve the investment and consumption environment. What makes these government stimuli remarkable is that they come at a time when the US economy is not in recession but is already growing robustly. The US also appears to be close to full employment. Despite the long-term risks such an environment may pose – including inflationary pressures and rising public debt – we expect fiscal and monetary measures to deliver noticeable economic support in 2026.

We also anticipate that policy will deliver a cyclical impulse in Europe, for example due to Germany’s EUR500bn special fund. Planned investments, particularly in infrastructure and climate neutrality, could trigger a short-term upswing. To achieve sustainably higher growth, however, improving domestic economic flexibility remains crucial to foster entrepreneurial initiatives and create an investment climate that enhances productivity. In my view, urgent action is still needed here.

We maintain a broadly constructive outlook for equity markets in 2026. This will be partly due to strong demand for new AI-based applications, which should continue to drive substantial corporate investment flows. Beneficiaries will not only include US “Big Tech” but also a wide range of sectors – construction (thanks to new data centres), utilities (via higher electricity demand) and industrial and basic materials along the supply chain. Our earnings growth forecasts for companies across all major regions are therefore firmly in double-digit territory.

As outlined in our annual outlook themes, investors should also consider potential risks in equity markets. In the area of highly energy-intensive AI applications, for instance, a global power shortage could dampen investor expectations for progress. Not every stock will be a winner in 2026, and short-term corrections at index level remain possible.

Investors should therefore continue to act with discipline. This means focusing on fundamentals rather than chasing perceived trends, while utilising the broad spectrum of investment opportunities. Diversification remains key. Alongside equities, corporate bonds may be attractive – depending on your risk appetite, both investment-grade and high-yield segments. Gold and some non-traditional investments, such as in private equity or infrastructure, also merit consideration. We explore these in detail in the “Alternative Investments” section of this annual outlook.

Overall, we expect a dynamic year for capital markets in 2026 with numerous compelling opportunities. The central question will be whether constructive forecasts can hold up amid a backdrop of economic and geopolitical challenges. Further disruptions to global trade flows or a renewed escalation of tariff tensions could, for example, temporarily pressure corporate earnings and increase market volatility.

In a complex and uncertain environment, investors would therefore be well advised to actively manage risks. This will enable them to respond to market developments in line with their personal investment strategy. Staying invested with a defined strategic asset allocation will be key, as attempts to perfectly time market entry and exit points can often result in missing the best-performing days and weeks.

I hope you find our annual outlook insightful and full of stimulating ideas for your portfolio. We are always available to review and discuss these ideas and look forward to hearing from you.

Christian Nolting

Global CIO

What the US midterm elections mean for energy
President Trump will retain significant influence over policy. Change will be possible only with bipartisan agreement.

09 November 2026
12 minute read

Email
Share by email
