The language being used to describe the Democratic Party’s successes in the US midterm elections has been dramatic. The results, which will make the Democrats the largest party in both the Senate and the House of Representatives, have been called “an extinction-level event” and “a Chernobyl-level disaster” for the Republicans.
But despite the adrenaline-fuelled commentary, not much will change in US energy policy when the new Congress is seated next year. President Donald Trump has pledged to use his veto power to block legislation he sees as harmful, and the Democrats will not have the two-thirds majorities in the Senate and House needed to override those vetoes. To pass, legislation will need support from Republicans, probably including the president.
Meanwhile, President Trump will retain the ability to implement his agenda through regulations and executive actions. The signature initiatives of his second term, his tariff strategy and the conflict in the Middle East, have been pursued without any formal support from Congress, and he will have broad leeway to take action despite the gains made by Democrats.
The most significant impact on President Trump’s actions is likely to come from increased scrutiny, as a result of Democrats taking control of Congressional committees and setting their own agenda for investigations.
In many areas, the Democrats will not want to force a sharp break with the Trump administration. One of the critical factors behind their election success was American voters’ concern about the cost of living, and the Democrats have pledged to improve the affordability of essentials including energy. They have shown little enthusiasm for taking actions that could restrict oil and gas production and drive up prices.
That said, some aspects of US energy will be affected by the election results, with some impacts growing in significance over time. Wood Mackenzie analysts have been looking at what are likely to be the most material consequences of the elections for US energy.
What could change with a Democratic-controlled Congress
Permitting reform
For the US energy industry, the most important issue in Congress right now is permitting reform: proposed changes in how permits for large infrastructure projects are awarded and reviewed, with the goal of expediting development and controlling costs.
A permitting reform bill with backing from both Republicans and Democrats, the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), was launched last month, and will be voted on in Congress this week.
Wood Mackenzie analysts believe that permitting reform legislation, if passed in a form close to the BAAJA, could make a material difference to development timelines for projects including oil and gas pipelines, power transmission lines and wind farms.
The bill has won bipartisan backing by striking a compromise between the interests of the oil and gas industry and low-carbon energy sectors, with support from groups representing both. But it has also been attacked from both sides, as a “fossil fuel giveaway” and as a way to “re-open the taxpayer and ratepayer spigot to endless and endlessly expensive wind and solar”.
Supporters of the bill have hoped to get it passed this year. But the Democrats’ success in the midterm elections has led some to suggest that they should refuse to support the current proposed legislation, in the hope of securing a better deal when they control Congress next year. Others have argued that the BAAJA, which has support from President Trump, is likely to be the best deal available.
The outlook for the legislation is uncertain, and the energy industry will be closely watching how events in Congress play out over the next few weeks.
Legislation to compel data centre developers to pay for new generation and grid upgrades
Other potentially significant legislation addresses public concerns about data centre development and its impact on electricity costs. The proposed Ratepayer Protection Act was passed with overwhelming support in the House in September, but has not yet come up for a vote in the Senate. If passed, it would require state regulators to consider adopting standards to compel new data centre projects to cover the full costs of the grid and the generation infrastructure needed to support them.
The bill still leaves ultimate decision-making in the hands of the states, and has been criticised for not doing enough to ensure residential customers are protected. Another proposed bill, the GRID (Guarding Ratepayers from Increased Demand-costs) Savings Act, would go further. It would establish a national mandate for data centres and other large loads to cover their associated electricity costs, and direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to establish national rules to enforce that.
Action to protect customers from rising electricity costs has bipartisan support, and will be on the agenda for the next Congress. President Trump launched his own Ratepayer Protection Pledge in March, with backing from the leading tech companies.
However, the president is also a strong supporter of the development of advanced AI capabilities, as both an economic and national security priority for the US. He will be reluctant to impose additional burdens on the industry that could curb its growth. Negotiations over a possible compromise on data centres and electricity bills are likely to take place next year.
State and local restrictions on data centre development
Nearly everywhere they were given the option, voters repudiated data centre development. There were 41 proposals related to data centres on the ballot in 13 states, and on 40 of those a majority of voters backed restrictions on development.
Candidates who spoke out against data centres often did well in state and local races. But opposition to uncontrolled development has been bipartisan, with Republican governors including Ron DeSantis of Florida and Greg Abbott of Texas announcing restrictions.
There has been particular interest in Texas, which has more proposed new data centre capacity than any other state. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who will be the state’s next governor, said that under her leadership “we will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centres until we have those protections”.
She has argued for an extension in the pause in approvals for new data centre projects that was put in place by Governor Abbott. She also wants to ensure that data centres are covering their electricity infrastructure costs. But projects that are already under construction will be allowed to continue, and Governor-elect Hinojosa has said she does not want to stop data centre development altogether.
“We can have economic development and we can have protections for Texans. These things are not mutually exclusive,” she has said.
Wood Mackenzie analysts have modelled a Moderated Demand scenario showing the possible implications for the electricity industry of increased restrictions on data centre development, worsening delays for grid connections and continued equipment shortages. That scenario still envisages significant growth in data centre demand, albeit at a slower pace than in our base case forecast. For a good overview of the outlook for data centre development, listen to Episode 7 of our podcast, The Load Down, from August 2026.
Immigration reform
In an interview over the weekend, President Trump identified immigration law reform as a priority for working with Democrats in Congress. Depending on how the reform is structured, that could help ease the skills shortages that are growing problems for energy and other infrastructure projects.
Ideas for a future Democratic administration
The resounding success for Democrats in the midterms has inevitably raised expectations that they could enjoy further success in the 2028 presidential election. Taking the presidency, and retaining control of Congress, would give the Democrats the ability to reshape the US energy landscape.
Two years is a long time in politics, and any number of events might deliver a different outcome. But that has not stopped speculation about the possible energy policy agenda for a future Democratic president.
One comprehensive set of ideas for the Democrats’ agenda has come from the Thriving Economy Project from the Sustainable Energy & Environment Coalition Institute. The group, working with Democratic House members who are interested in energy and the environment, has produced a “menu of ideas” for the incoming Congress, and the next administration.
Its proposals include tax incentives, regulations and government financing to support the development of low-carbon energy. It addresses issues of environmental protection and emissions reduction to tackle climate change, which were priorities for the Biden administration. But it also has much more of a focus on issues that are of more immediate interest to American voters, including energy prices and the cost of living in general.
Based on that report, and other ideas that have been circulating in Washington, these are some of the possibilities that are being talked about for a future Democratic administration.
An Inflation Reduction Act 2.0
The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, which expanded and extended tax credits for renewable energy, was passed with support only from Democrats, and many of its key provisions were subsequently repealed by the Republicans. Many in the renewables industry want to avoid a repeat of that policy whiplash.
Ray Long, president and chief executive of Acore, the renewable energy industry group, told me on a recent edition of the Energy Gang podcast that the starting principle for any future tax framework should be durability. Banks and investors will have more confidence in the prospects for renewable energy projects if they can expect that taxes and regulations will remain stable through changes of administration and changes of control in Congress. That will mean bipartisan support for any proposed legislation.
Tax incentives that serve bipartisan goals, such as the 45X credits for advanced manufacturing, are most likely to be strengthened.
A windfall tax on oil and gas
The Thriving Economy Project report suggests creating a “strategic energy affordability reserve”, funded by a windfall tax on the profits of the oil and gas industry. If the president declares an energy emergency, funds from the reserve would be released to the states, to help residents with energy bills and transport costs, and to subsidise purchases of energy-efficient appliances.
This proposal is likely to be one of the most controversial for any future administration, if it is taken up in earnest. Disincentivising investment by imposing additional taxes on the oil and gas industry could hit production, working against the goal of bringing fuel costs down.
New controls on energy exports and scrutiny of LNG project approvals
As fuel prices have surged this year, the Trump administration has evaluated possible export controls, but it has not imposed any restrictions. The consensus view in the industry, shared by Wood Mackenzie analysts, is that such controls would have been counter-productive, actually raising costs for American consumers.
However, the Democrats on the Thriving Economy Project have suggested an “energy price safety valve” mechanism that would temporarily constrain exports of LNG, gasoline, diesel and home heating oil.
Their report also says the government could ensure that any new LNG export projects would not raise costs for American consumers before issuing any approvals.
The Biden administration’s review of US LNG exports in 2024 suggested that the industry’s growth would have only a fairly modest impact on the prices paid by American residential customers. Even in the Department of Energy’s low gas supply scenario, projecting growth in LNG exports to meet global demand resulted in modelled residential prices in 2050 rising just 7%. In the middle scenario, modelled prices rise by 4%.
However, those estimates were drawn up before the most recent projections of strong growth in US gas demand for power generation, which could amplify the impact of LNG exports.
A mandate for data centres to use renewables and storage
Although data centre developers can avoid putting additional strain on grid infrastructure by building their own power plants, they can still put upward pressure on gas prices if they are using gas turbines and engines. And if gas prices rise, that will in turn put upward pressure on power prices. To prevent that, the Thriving Economy Project proposes a mandate for all new data centres to use renewables and energy storage for their power supplies.
Power market reform and a review of utility returns
Another focus for the Thriving Economy Project’s is wholesale electricity markets. The report argues that even before the AI boom, there was already a strong case for power market reform to encourage investment in wind, solar, and battery storage. The surge in electricity demand for data centres has made the case for reform urgent, it adds, because better price signals could reduce total system costs.
The report also suggests a review of utility business models to ensure that they prioritise affordability for ratepayers as well as reliability. Regulation could be reformed to strengthen incentives for utilities to bring down costs.

Capital is tilting East: Inside Asia’s AI gold rush
[Music]
Sjoerd Leenart: Welcome to J.P. Morgan's Making Sense channel. I'm Sjoerd Leenart , CEO and head of J.P. Morgan's banking business in Asia Pacific. I look after our strategy and operations across 17 markets in Asia. And today I'm joined by Joyce Chang, chair of global research at J.P. Morgan, to discuss the key takeaways from the investor seminar that we hosted around the IMF World Bank annual meetings, which had returned to Bangkok for the first time in 35 years. Now, Joyce, since the last time you were in Bangkok, the region's GDP has grown nearly ninefold since 1998 to four and a half trillion faster than that of most emerging and developed markets. The 11 countries of Southeast Asia are home to nearly 700 million people and taken together, they would rank as the world's fourth largest economy. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations forms one of the most cohesive and effective associations in the world, next to the European Union. Joyce, it was absolutely great to have you in Bangkok with our clients and J.P. Morgan's senior management team to witness the tremendous growth and opportunities that we see in Asia.
Joyce Chang: Oh, well, Sjoerd, thank you so much. It's just wonderful to be with you. It was my second tour at the IMF World Bank meetings in Bangkok, hosting investor meetings with developed markets and emerging markets policymakers. I was last hosting these meetings in Bangkok in 1991, a year that I was out of graduate school. And during the first decade of my career, I spent a lot of time in the region. And back then, the focus was different. It was on how countries could integrate into a more open global order. Well, today that order is fragmented. Markets are repricing the cost of capital, energy, and access to trade. And the questions have shifted from how to integrate to who pays for security, debt sustainability and resilience. There's just so much to discuss. So Sjoerd, before we get into what we took away from the conference, I really would love to have you talk about your priorities in the ASEAN region and in Asia more broadly.
Sjoerd Leenart: Well, there's a lot of tailwinds that are propelling economies and businesses in Asia. There's what I call the manufacturing renaissance driven by AI data center demand and also the rewiring of global trades and manufacturing capacity. And you see places like Korea, Taiwan, Japan, and to an extent China, they're beneficiaries of that. And then there's certain policy actions that are driving growth. Think of the government stimulus in China, market reforms in Japan and Korea, and then there are places like India or Vietnam or Malaysia, which benefits from a China plus one strategy, but also the growth of domestic demand and the growth of their middle class. So all of that really has led to very divergent, but in totality regional GDP growth of 4.5%. And as you know, that's two, three times what we see in the US and Europe. And on the back of that, you see corporates being active, you see wealth being created, and you see capital markets being both active and very liquid. Now, when we go to a country, we intend to be there forever. So investments, they're going up, they're going down, but they never stop and they're broad based across all these 17 countries. More specifically, we're hiring people to cover the corporate sector, including increasingly mid-cap and innovation economy, private bankers to cover the growing number of wealthy Asian clients. And we're investing in our tech stack in equities, in payments and other products to ensure we are best in class in our delivery.
Joyce Chang: Sjoerd, it's really impressive what I see happening in the ASEAN region. They've really been able to find their place on the value supply chain. So maybe I can just talk a little bit about what we saw and what we heard at the conference on the global macro and the market outlook. What we've seen is that the global economy and markets have been remarkably resilient with AI investment offsetting the energy shocks, also the interest rate shocks that we've seen. But I think one of the concerns is that is this nearing its limits? We've seen some uneven outcomes between AI CapEx beneficiaries and energy shock vulnerabilities. So the IMF still has fairly constructive projections. They are looking at growth at 3.1% this year and actually increasing next year to 3.4%. But we also see a rise in global headline inflation to 4.7% because of higher commodity prices as well. But I think one thing that just struck me was that a lot of the IMF said that resilience is no cause for celebration and bringing very little joy. They're concerned about just the number of shocks the global economy has experienced. And they do point to the flexibility that has come from energy markets, AI related capital spending and fiscal and monetary supports. But they point out that the countries that are benefiting are narrowing, that just 32 countries in the world account for 95% of global growth, down from 54 back in April. But Asia, as you mentioned, Sjoerd, is a bright spot. The regional growth projections continue to be revised up because many countries are benefiting from the ongoing technology boom, notably Korea and several ASEAN economies along with China, India and Japan. But we've also seen some downward revisions in other parts of the globe. In particular, there's a lot of discussion on Europe's need to accelerate reforms to raise productivity and growth since they face aging populations, high energy costs and rising debt burdens in their economies. So we have seen strong performance from Asia, which we both note, but just more challenges in some other parts of the world.
Sjoerd Leenart: Now Joyce, I also wanted to ask you about the strong performance of the equity markets despite all the issues that are going on in the world, rising yields, higher fiscal deficits, heavy issuance across developed markets. What was the investor mood on the market outlook?
Joyce Chang: Well, the investor mood was that two things can be true at the same time, Sjoerd. Overall, even though there was recognition of the higher rates, sentiment was still positive on equities despite the prospect for higher for longer yields. But the prevailing tone compared to earlier this year was selectively risk on. There was more of an emphasis on quality and diversification rather than a universal stance that's tied to the AI CapEx boom. So we think that the AI CapEx plans will continue to drive the market higher over the near term, but there's more concern about the market's capacity to absorb the scale of AI and hyperscaling financing, particularly in the debt markets. And this is in large part because we've seen the surge in sovereign bond yields and developed markets and more competition and higher costs for capital. So compared to some of the conferences that we hosted earlier this year where fear of missing out was really the big driver, this set of meetings surfaced more direct questions about the return on investment and productivity gains. There was also a lot more discussion about second order effects and the growing threat of cybersecurity attacks. And these are greater concerns that we see surfacing across our clients and at J.P. Morgan as well. I do have to say one thing that really stood out to me was that the mood was very constructive on emerging markets. Emerging markets fundamentals are stronger in the cycle. Better external balances, more proactive inflation management, also better fiscal and debt dynamics when you compare it to the developed markets. And we see that policy, when we've met with all of the different central banks and ministries of finance have really anchored basic balances and the strong growth has attracted portfolio flows. We're looking at portfolios coming back to levels that we haven't seen in a number of years. So, Sjoerd I want to ask you, in Asia, we've seen that the AI related companies are half of the regional equity indexes, over 70% of earnings growth. And this is surprise on the upside. We've continued to have to revise these revisions up. How are you looking at the AI financing ecosystem broadly, particularly the build out in debt markets? Because it seems that the AI infrastructure is increasingly capital intensive and debt financed.
Sjoerd Leenart: It's certainly a rapidly emerging theme in Asia. And after the US, we expect actually most data center investments and activity to happen in Asia. There is a big need for computing power here in the region, both from the big Chinese companies, but also from the global hyperscalers who are looking for places where land, electricity, grids are sufficient to support their computing needs in the region. Now, like in the US, we do see some pushback from governments in places like Thailand, Australia, where governments and regulators have put certain projects on pause to assess whether demand for energy does not affect other industries or most importantly, the consumer. How all of it will be financed is, I guess for the market in general, remains a bit of a question mark. And I think here in Asia, we're working hard to find alternative sources of liquidity from private capital to public capital to the debt markets to help finance these projects.
Joyce Chang: Yeah, I really agree with those observations. I mean, from the meetings we have had in Thailand, we continue to see substantial AI CapEx. And most of the hyperscalers investment plans actually seem relatively insensitive to interest rates given some of the strong cash generation and strategic priorities. It's still a hyper growth regime given the earnings visibility. And we actually think that AI CapEx is going to increase to somewhere around one and a half trillion dollars or higher from about 900 billion this year. We see that the demand for computing capacity still exceeds available supply and these infrastructure bottlenecks probably will persist for another two or three years. But the profitability to us that stands out is strongest amongst the North Asian hardware suppliers. This is where we see semiconductor capacity growth that remains well below some of the AI related demand growth. And the leadership is still in place in semiconductors and hardware in Korea and Taiwan, which placed them at the center of the AI investment cycle. Memory chips have also emerged as a really critical component of AI infrastructure with their share of data center spending growing to nearly 50%. So Sjoerd, I want to ask you to talk a little bit more about China. We get a lot of questions about the US-China constructive strategic stability and also about the China 2.0 shock, particularly from our European policy makers. So many have observed that the US China Summit was high on pageantry, but maybe on the outcomes, not so much to talk about with a focus on constructive strategic stability. How have you seen the US-China relationship evolving and how are you looking at the nature of cross-border activity? Are companies more cautious about transactions?
Sjoerd Leenart: Yeah, like global investors, I think we were happy to see these meetings happen. Two have happened. Another two will likely happen this year. And it brings a degree of stability without really a long-term solution. So that's still to be seen. But China is a very big market, 18% of the global GDP. So both corporates and investors need to think how they want to position themselves. And we have to distinguish between those two groups when we think about their China strategy. Corporates, they invest for decades, financial investors, they can obviously move their money around quickly. And I think for the corporate sector, the competitive landscape and the behavior of Chinese consumers has definitely shifted and tariffs are also for them a very significant uncertainty. So, you do see caution and concern, but as I say, it's a big market and companies want to stay invested. So, you see a shift towards more localized operations and also enhancing the product portfolio with more local brands. Now with respect to financial investors, we do see a lot of activity in China. I would say particularly from hedge funds, given the enormous liquidity of the China Hong Kong market and the volatility of those markets. Now not only investors, I would say it's still more cautious as it's unclear whether the consumer, the Chinese consumer and the real estate market have turned a corner. When we look at the behavior of Chinese companies, they continue to go abroad without any pause, more so than ever looking for growth that they can no longer find domestically. And so Southeast Asia, Europe, LATAM, the preferred go-to destinations and the US for obvious reasons seeing less of that Chinese investment. And actually Hong Kong plays a very important role because most Chinese companies would run their regional or global operations through there.
Joyce Chang: No, Sjoerd, I completely agree with those observations. And what I really could see from being in the ASEAN region is that the ASEAN countries are a key beneficiary of regional supply chain reconfigurations in the AI tech cycle. And what we've seen is that China has steadily shifted manufacturing activities to the ASEAN region. Initially, it was to reduce labor costs, but eventually it's been to really adapt to the pivot that we've seen in US trade policy that has favored the ASEAN countries over China in terms of tariff differentials. And so I think that's been an additional tailwind to ASEAN's export performance. But we have seen that it's been a little uneven across the region. There's been a rising tide, which has really helped Vietnam and Thailand as the key recipients of Chinese foreign direct investment. I think that Malaysia and Singapore have also seen their tech exports soar, but Indonesia and the Philippines have lagged a bit due to the smaller manufacturing base. But I agree that we have seen just that a movement of capital and activity towards a variety of markets on China's side. So I want to talk a little bit about the China 2.0 shock because this has been top of mind, particularly as everyone is looking at more turbulence in the bond markets in France and in Europe more broadly. So, we see that China's exports are increasingly absorbing manufacturing output that domestic demand really cannot absorb in China. So a lot of questions have come up about the rebalancing and the consequences of this imbalance, raising concerns that Europe could be the main casualty from the China shock. We are seeing that German has greater direct competitive overlap with China than the US does across autos, manufacturing, machinery, chemicals, and other sectors. And that's made China's export gains more of a problematic for Europe and a larger drag on German's growth. We see that Europe has faced more setbacks here and they're looking at the possibility of adding more sort of trade barriers here, particularly when you look at the auto sector. But I still feel that from the discussions we had, that the recent China and European Union engagement still suggests that there's enough incentives there for both sides to negotiate rather than to enter an uncontrolled trade confirmation. So Sjoerd , I want to just see with you what your thoughts are on any particular opportunities that stand out or that you think will be ones that investors should focus on more in the years ahead or any underestimated risk on your side.
Sjoerd Leenart: Well, as you said, there is a focus on emerging markets and particularly on Asia that we sensed among investors in Bangkok. So I do think a gradual reallocation of money towards that region is happening. But it is, as you alluded to earlier, very uneven. The flows tend to move in and out much more so than what I observe in the US. This year, Korea and Taiwan were obviously darlings in the early parts, but have come off quite significantly. China and Hong Kong reversely have struggled this year after great 2025. And global flows into India have restarted cautiously, I'd say, after we saw 60 billion of outflows over the last two years. And equally in Southeast Asia, you see quite a dispersion between the performance of the markets. So I do feel investors will continue to have to be quite agile in how they reallocate their money between the different Asian markets.
Joyce Chang: Yeah, no, those are great points, Sjoerd . And one thing I just wanted to point out is this was a conference where we had a lot more discussion on cybersecurity risk, that along with global AI systems, they're only as strong as the weakest link and that cyber resilience is really something that will be a greater focus. And many of the discussions I think that stood out were that the number of cyber attacks is growing and that we see that these models can both discover and exploit the vulnerabilities and that what used to be a matter of months has come into hours and soon to minutes as far as the days to exploit these cyber vulnerabilities. So that was also one key takeaway that more focus will be needed on cyber resilience, the crisis preparedness, and also the oversight of critical third party providers here. So Sjoerd, I really want to thank you and the entire Asia Pacific management team for the hospitality. I'm just delighted that you were able to join us today to really bring your on the ground perspectives on what's going on in the Asia region.
Sjoerd Leenart: Well, Joyce, it was an absolute pleasure to have you in Bangkok and it is just unbelievable that you were there as a very young analyst 35 years ago to organize the same conference. It's grown a lot bigger and more important, but it's just wonderful that we had you for all these years with us. So thank you for everything you do for clients and for J.P. Morgan.

Southeast Asia’s economy has grown nearly ninefold since 1998, and the region is now at the center of the global AI investment cycle. In this episode of Making Sense, Sjoerd Leenart, CEO of J.P. Morgan’s banking business in Asia Pacific, sits down with Joyce Chang, chair of Global Research at J.P. Morgan, to unpack key takeaways from the investor seminar hosted around the IMF–World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. They discuss the forces propelling Asia’s growth — from the manufacturing renaissance driven by AI data center demand to divergent policy tailwinds across China, Japan, Korea and ASEAN economies. They also explore the IMF’s latest global outlook, the narrowing base of countries driving world growth and why investor sentiment has shifted from "fear of missing out" to more selective, quality-focused positioning.

articles.title: Macro Signposts | Inflation Is Sticky, But This Isn’t 2022 All Over Again | PIMCO
articles.text:
Tiffany Wilding

11/10/2026

| 6 min read

Share via Email

Share via Linkedin

Share via Twitter

Key takeaways

Inflation was firmer than expected in October, and the pressure was widespread. Higher energy, shipping, and other input costs are reaching consumers. Despite benign wage inflation trends, services categories that are less affected by higher energy prices were also firm.
The Federal Reserve may move to raise rates somewhat more quickly. Fed Governor Waller’s comments Tuesday morning put a 50-basis-point (bp) hike firmly on the table for December. Even if the Fed stops short of 50 bps, speeding up the pace of hikes over the next few meetings seems very likely.
The risk is that inflation remains elevated over the next several months, but we still expect it to ease next year. Shipping disruptions, higher freight costs, and fewer holiday promotions could support prices in the near term. However, falling oil prices, fading supply shocks, and tighter financial conditions, which moderate demand, should also help moderate inflation as we move through next year. This still looks like a rate recalibration, as opposed to a start of a bigger cycle.

October’s U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) data came in hotter than consensus expectations, delivering another disappointing inflation report for a Federal Reserve that has become increasingly vocal about its focus on price stability. Together with Fed Governor Christopher Waller’s comments earlier in the day, the report strengthens the case for another rate hike at the Fed’s December meeting and raises the possibility of a larger 50-basis-point (bp) move.
Our baseline is not yet a 50-bp hike in December. However, we are shifting our forecast to include 25-bp hikes in both December and January, with some risk of another hike in March. If Fed Vice Chair John Williams and Fed Governor Philip Jefferson reinforce Waller’s message in their upcoming comments, that could be enough to shift our December forecast to a 50-bp hike.
Even so, we would characterize the Fed’s current tightening less as the beginning of a new hiking cycle and more as a recalibration of policy aimed at preventing financial conditions from easing in a way that results in a broadening out of inflation from what should have been temporary inflation shocks.

Notable trends in the inflation data

After an uncomfortably firm September reading, inflation was again stronger than the Fed would have liked in October. Core CPI, which excludes the more volatile food and energy categories, rose 0.33% on the month, with firmness relatively broad-based across categories.
Part of that strength continues to reflect higher input costs from energy, chips, tariffs, and shipping being passed through to consumers.
Higher global crude oil prices and stronger refining margins have sharply increased the cost of refined products, including gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel. We estimate that these higher costs are also being passed through indirectly via price increases across retail goods categories and transportation-related services. Altogether, this channel could add roughly 50–60 bps to the year-over-year rate of core inflation this year.
Iran-related shipping disruptions could amplify these pressures. Higher freight and diesel costs, along with shipping delays, have left some retailers with lower-than-normal inventories ahead of the holiday shopping season, according to corporate earnings commentaries.
The good news is that much of this adjustment should already be behind us. Assuming energy prices broadly follow current futures curves, we estimate roughly 70%–80% of the anticipated pass-through has already occurred.
October’s CPI report, however, was not simply an energy story.
Categories that should be less directly affected by these cost pressures, including shelter, recreation, and other non-transportation services, were also firm. These categories tend to be more closely associated with domestic labor market conditions, wages, and underlying inflation, making their strength in October more notable.
So far, labor market fundamentals remain relatively benign. Wage-cost pressures have not reaccelerated in a way that resembles 2021 or 2022. Higher energy, freight, tariff, and chip costs can temporarily raise price levels and year-over-year inflation. The more concerning outcome would be for those first-round price increases to feed into wages, services inflation, inflation expectations, and broader pricing behavior.
We do not yet see convincing evidence that this is happening.

The next few inflation reports could remain uncomfortable

Even as some of the original supply pressures begin to fade, the next several CPI reports could remain firm as past cost increases continue to work through retail prices.
Holiday discounting is one area we are watching closely. Retailers typically discount goods aggressively during the holiday shopping season to drive volumes. This year, however, Iran-related shipping disruptions are raising freight costs, on top of higher diesel prices, while constraining inventories in some categories. Retailers may therefore have less incentive or ability to discount as aggressively as usual.
Because holiday discounting itself is seasonal, smaller-than-usual discounts could mechanically boost seasonally adjusted goods inflation even without another increase in underlying input costs, although the reverse would happen in January and February when lower holiday prices usually revert after the holidays.
This creates the possibility that inflation data remain firm over the next few months even as oil prices and some of the original cost pressures are already reversing.

Implications for Fed policy: watching financial conditions

October’s inflation report strengthens the case for additional Fed tightening, but we still see the current episode as a policy recalibration rather than the start of another prolonged hiking cycle. Based on the CPI data, we estimate core PCE rose roughly 0.36% (month-over-month) in October, lifting the year-over-year rate to around 3.3%. That is uncomfortably high, but still well below the inflation rates reached in 2022.
Policy is also starting from a very different place. The current 3.75%–4.0% fed funds range is roughly 100 bps below our estimated Taylor-rule rate, compared with a gap of around 800 bps in early 2022 (see Figure 1). After several months of firmer inflation, the Fed will likely want to narrow that gap, particularly given the risk of allowing what may be a temporary inflation shock to become more persistent.

Figure 1: The gap between the Fed policy rate and Taylor-rule prescriptions is narrower in 2026 than in 2022

For illustrative purposes only
Source: Federal Reserve Monetary Policy Report (July 2026), Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, and PIMCO calculations as of October 2026, with estimates through December 2027

How much additional tightening is needed will depend on financial conditions. Higher rates across the yield curve, along with more recent weakness in credit and equity markets, are already doing some of the Fed’s work. The San Francisco Fed proxy funds rate (see Figure 1 above), which incorporates broader financial conditions, suggests the effective stance of policy is closer to Taylor-rule prescriptions than the fed funds rate alone would imply.
The Fed therefore needs to maintain restrictive financial conditions, but it does not necessarily need a dramatically higher policy rate to achieve that outcome. If equities rally, credit spreads tighten, and longer-term yields fall while inflation remains firm, the Fed will likely need to hike more. If financial conditions tighten further, markets can do more of the work.
This framework reconciles our expectation for additional hikes with our forecast for substantially lower inflation next year. The Fed can tighten now precisely because it wants to make sure a temporary inflation shock stays temporary.

Demand should moderate as buffers fade

U.S. final domestic demand has remained surprisingly resilient despite this year’s supply shocks. AI-related capital spending has supported investment, although its high import content limits the contribution to U.S. real GDP growth (for details, see the 15 October 2026 Macro Signposts). Consumption has also remained solid, as tax cuts and wealth gains have helped cushion households from higher energy prices and given firms more room to pass higher costs through to consumers.
Those supports should fade. Equity market performance has stalled, the retroactive tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act provided more of a one-time boost, and higher rates and tighter credit conditions should increasingly weigh on activity. In effect, this year’s supply shock hit an economy that had enough demand resilience to absorb it, but that backdrop should become less supportive over the coming quarters.

Bottom line

Our baseline remains that U.S. inflation falls materially in 2027 as the energy shock fades, financial conditions remain restrictive, and demand moderates. The recent decline in oil prices reinforces that view. The Fed’s challenge is to prevent today’s largely supply-driven inflation shock from broadening into wages, services prices, and inflation expectations before those disinflationary forces take hold.
For now, that argues for additional Fed tightening. But we continue to view this as a policy recalibration rather than the beginning of another prolonged hiking cycle. If inflation remains firm while financial conditions ease, the Fed will likely need to do more. If equities and credit weaken further and longer-term borrowing costs remain elevated, markets can do more of the tightening.

articles.title: Trump, Xi, and Putin: What to expect from the APEC summit | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Trump, Xi, and Putin: What to expect from the APEC summit

Jonathan A. Czin,

Jonathan A. Czin

Michael H. Armacost Chair in Foreign Policy Studies,

Fellow
- Foreign Policy, John L. Thornton China Center

Kyle Chan,

Kyle Chan

Fellow
- Foreign Policy, John L. Thornton China Center

Ryan Hass,

Ryan Hass

Director
- John L. Thornton China Center,

Senior Fellow
- Foreign Policy, Center for Asia Policy Studies, John L. Thornton China Center,

Chen-Fu and Cecilia Yen Koo Chair in Taiwan Studies

Scott M. Moore,

Scott M. Moore

Nonresident Senior Fellow
- Foreign Policy, John L. Thornton China Center

Constanze Stelzenmüller, and

Constanze Stelzenmüller

Director
- Center on the United States and Europe,

Senior Fellow
- Foreign Policy, Center on the United States and Europe,

Fritz Stern Chair on Germany and Transatlantic Relations

Yun Sun

Yun Sun

Nonresident Fellow
- Global Economy and Development, Foreign Policy, John L. Thornton China Center, Africa Growth Initiative

November 12, 2026

Russian artist Alexey Sergienko's new pop art painting dubbed "Shenzhen, 26" sits at his gallery in Saint Petersburg on November 12, 2026. (Olga Maltseva/AFP via Getty Images)

21 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Question 1
The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting will take place in Shenzhen, China, on November 18-19, 2026. With another interaction likely between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping on the margins of this summit, what are the major outcomes expected? What will the two leaders seek to accomplish with their third interaction of this calendar year? Can meaningful U.S.-China progress be achieved on artificial intelligence (AI), trade, and other security issues?

Back to top

Kyle Chan

Starting small on AI risks

AI is an increasingly central issue in the U.S.-China relationship. Both countries see AI as a powerful, strategic technology with the potential to reshape geopolitics and the global economy. Both countries also increasingly see AI not just as an opportunity but also as a growing source of risk that needs to be managed. Chinese and American AI models have both been misused to carry out cyberattacks or have acted far beyond the intentions of human users.
On the sidelines of APEC, the United States and China have a chance to begin the long, uncertain road to jointly mitigating these risks. The first step is to establish an incident notification mechanism, which both sides have agreed to in principle. The goal should be to develop not a rigid protocol for comprehensive disclosure but an open communication channel through which each side can share nonsensitive technical information as they feel comfortable. Such information might include which AI models or harnesses were involved, how these tools were misused or misbehaved, and what safeguards or corrective measures proved effective.
In general, expectations for U.S.-China discussions about AI should remain low, and the focus should be on selective communication. Many worry that the United States and China will move too slowly in the face of growing AI risks and rapid improvements in capabilities. But equally worrying is the risk that official U.S.-China AI talks might get derailed at the outset as mounting expectations collide with deep mutual distrust between the two countries. Starting to share limited information at a pace and level that each side feels is appropriate will be a critical early step toward potential future progress on addressing AI risks.

Back to top

Jonathan A. Czin

All thunder, no rain

“All thunder, no rain.” This Chinese aphorism has been an apt description of the last two summits between Trump and Xi—and thus far, it seems likely to apply to this next summit as well. For a long time, in the run-up to such meetings, U.S. diplomats and policymakers would “trade optics for substance”—making concessions to China on protocol in exchange for substantive concessions. Now, both sides appear content to prioritize optics over any substance. The result is pantomime diplomacy.
Theoretically, there is much for the two leaders to discuss—everything from the risks of AI to global hotspots—but it seems more likely than not that these two leaders will miss the moment, again. Instead of engaging constructively, Beijing is capitalizing on its tactical truce with Washington to fortify itself at home and intensify pressure on U.S. allies in the region. Notably, the day after Trump and Xi’s last summit, China’s Southern Theater Command announced a military exercise around Scarborough Shoal—a disputed feature in the South China Sea claimed by both China and the Philippines, a U.S. treaty ally. Tellingly, the move elicited no discernible response from Washington, though the American ambassador to the Philippines did protest.
Xi is likely already looking past Trump and thinking about how the fallout from the U.S. midterm election will affect China policy in the next administration—and whether the United States will revert to a more competitive posture toward China. Xi will host Trump fresh from a major Chinese Communist Party meeting, which fortified Xi’s iron grip on the party and laid the groundwork for his next five-year term, which will begin late next year. Xi’s goal in the meantime remains to do as little as possible to mollify Trump.
The bigger question right now is what will backstop the bilateral relationship in the coming year. The two leaders are supposed to meet one more time in December on the margins of the G20 summit in Doral, Florida, but after that, no meetings are scheduled. And Xi will be increasingly preoccupied with the preparations for next year’s Party Congress as we approach the second half of the year, which will limit his time and bandwidth for another engagement with Trump. In the absence of direct engagement by the top leaders, it remains an open question which force prevails: the inertia of Trump and Xi’s gentleman’s agreement to halt the trade war, or the entropy of the two superpowers’ competitive dynamic.

Back to top

Ryan Hass

Staying the course

Typically, when the leaders of the United States and China meet, it is a major global news event. The planned meeting between Trump and Xi on the margins of APEC may be an exception. The meeting will occur in the aftermath of a resounding reckoning for Trump in the U.S. midterm elections and in the shadow of an expected trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi, and Russian President Vladimir Putin. This will be the third in-person encounter between Trump and Xi of the calendar year. Neither side is preparing ambitious deliverables for this meeting.
Even so, the two leaders will have plenty to discuss. The headline issue will be whether the two leaders agree to extend their trade truce past its current deadline in January. Since Trump and Xi plan to meet again on the margins of the G20 this December in Florida, they may not feel pressure to finalize any trade truce extension at APEC.
The two leaders will be expected to endorse progress on institutionalizing coordination on AI, including through the launch of a bilateral AI dialogue and a bilateral incident reporting channel. Efforts in this space will likely be more focused on agenda-setting and establishing processes and expectations than on any breakthroughs or major deliverables.
Trump and Xi may also use their meeting to announce progress on strengthening military crisis communication, including in the nuclear domain.
The Chinese side likely will use the meeting to amplify the shared definition both leaders have endorsed for the relationship: constructive strategic stability based on fairness, reciprocity, and mutual respect. Beijing values this shared definition as a symbol of both leaders’ investment in preserving bilateral stability and avoiding crises. Although Trump has shown less enthusiasm for the definition, he similarly appears to value keeping the U.S.-China relationship on a relatively stable track for the foreseeable future.
This will be the second consecutive year when Trump will meet Xi on the margins of the APEC economic leaders meeting. Last year, Trump never set foot in the venue where the APEC economic leaders meeting was held. It would not be surprising if Trump skips the summit proceedings this year as well. Trump’s focus will be on meeting other leaders on the summit’s margins, as opposed to the details of the summit meeting itself.

Back to top

Constanze Stelzenmüller

Europe has a stake in the Trump-Xi summit

Not being Pacific Rim nations, the countries of Europe do not have a seat at the table at the APEC meetings. (Despite its Pacific territories of French Polynesia, New Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna, and Clipperton Island, France is not a member.) Yet they will be watching the discussions in Shenzhen with sharp interest. Europe and China’s relationship has undergone drastic change recently, driven not least by Berlin’s volte-face on China trade; the German analyst Thorsten Benner even calls it a second Zeitenwende (historic turn) following the first one on Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Despite Germany’s exploding trade deficit with China and growing concern about China’s aggressive behavior in Europe and its support for Russia against Ukraine, Berlin had long opposed tougher trade measures by the European Union (EU). But in early October, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, together with French President Emmanuel Macron, wrote a strongly worded letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to demand the commission’s decisive action against unfair trade practices, as well as a new EU instrument to counter coercion. It gave the bloc’s trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčović, decisive backing for a trip to Beijing last month. The trade chief managed to avert a full-blown trade war by getting China to agree to restrictions on hybrid car exports.
But as Benner points out, this is only “the beginning of a long, arduous, and risky path to strengthen German and European industry vis-à-vis China.” To work, he argues, it must be flanked by vigorous investment and innovation at home, and a resilient network of partnerships in Asia. Hence, a recent flurry of European leaders traveling to Asia—in the second half of October, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk went to India and Vietnam, while Merz traveled to Singapore, Japan, and South Korea. The larger backdrop for these trips is a massive EU drive for diversification of its Asian partnerships since the Russian invasion—accompanied by a substantive shift from trade, market access, and development to geopolitics, security, and economic resilience. New negotiations were begun with: Singapore (concluded May 2025), Indonesia (concluded September 2025), India (concluded January 2026) and the Philippines (concluded September 2026); negotiations that had been paused for more than a decade were resumed with Thailand (September 2023) and Malaysia (January 2025).
Watching Shenzhen, Europeans will hope for a stabilization of the U.S.-China economic relationship that could benefit them as well. But they also fear a bilateral bargain that redirects Chinese overcapacity to Europe—or one that presumes to set international trade rules for the rest of the world.

Back to top

Yun Sun

The real work happens below the summit

Compared to Trump and Xi’s Beijing summit in May and Washington summit in September, the APEC summit in Shenzhen will be a multilateral occasion. Any potential side meeting between Trump and Xi will be significantly shorter in duration, which means any negotiations over concrete issues will also be limited. Before the Washington summit, it was announced that the two countries’ trade truce would be extended by two months until January 2027. This also alleviates the pressure on the two presidents to deliver major outcomes during their potential bilateral meeting in Shenzhen.
In terms of military security, the two countries have made considerable progress this year. For example, both countries participated in the Indo-Pacific Chiefs of Defense Conference in Canada in late August to early September, where U.S. Pacific Command chief Admiral Samuel Paparo met with the Chinese General Yang Zhibin, the commander of China’s Eastern Theater Command. References to a memorandum of understanding on crisis prevention and communication were also made during the Washington summit. More military-to-military communications could be in the pipeline for 2027. As such, another leadership summit at APEC will be politically significant, and concrete deliverables and meaningful progress on functional issues are more likely to be generated at the working level.

Question 2
There is speculation of a trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin on the margins of the APEC summit. What are the implications of this meeting if it occurs? Will it impact the future trajectory of the Russia-Ukraine war? What message will it send to America’s erstwhile allies and partners?

Back to top

Jonathan A. Czin

A three-way meeting with two winners

It is difficult to envisage a scenario in which a meeting among Trump, Xi, and Putin has a happy outcome for the United States and its interests. The visual from such a meeting alone would be an unsettling imitation of the “Big Three” meeting at Yalta in the midst of World War II. Although this meeting will be more photo op than substance, like the original Yalta, this meeting could pave the way for a carving up of Eastern Europe to accommodate Russian interests. That is a worst-case and perhaps unlikely scenario. But if these three men emerge elated from this meeting, it would likely bode ill for Ukraine—and more importantly, for European security. Last century, an America buffered by two oceans had to learn the hard way that its interests are in fact bound up with the security of Europe and East Asia—yet we seem to periodically need a remedial reeducation in the realities of geopolitics.
Alternatively, if each of these men finds himself frustrated, that is also a potentially dangerous outcome. Acrimony among heads of state is no mere spat—a personal contretemps can have enduring and dangerous consequences, inflaming rather than assuaging the many points of tension and divergence between these leaders.
While Xi and Putin are more likely to humor than to humiliate Trump, even that outcome is a poor one for the United States. It will bait Trump further down his current path of trying to conciliate rather than counter these two strongmen. And, ironically, Trump’s very willingness to participate in such a meeting with so little time to prepare will only make his nominal objective of ending the war in Ukraine even more elusive. Trump has already demonstrated that he has little appetite or wherewithal to avail himself of the leverage he might have over either leader if he were to work in tandem with American allies and partners. And both men know Trump’s time is expiring even more quickly than his leverage—and that he will be irrelevant in a mere 26 months. That is a pittance for two leaders who can measure their tenures in decades, not years. Why would either man make a deal with a leader whose time and leverage are waning? They will only do it if they think they can pilfer more from Trump diplomatically than they will be able to gain from the next American president.

Back to top

Ryan Hass

More downside risk than upside potential for the U.S.

The risk/reward calculation for all three leaders is different.
For Russia, this meeting offers major upside. By sitting down with the leaders of the world’s two most powerful countries in a trilateral format, Putin will be recognized as a major player on the world stage rather than a pariah. He will have achieved his return to the top table in global diplomacy without making any significant concessions on Ukraine or elsewhere.
For China, the meeting will be mixed. On the one hand, Xi will bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter for how China, Russia, and the United States will relate to each other. The meeting will highlight Xi’s statesmanship and China’s centrality in the international system. On the other hand, Beijing will bear the burden of setting an agenda, ensuring a productive exchange, and holding some responsibility for follow-through on any outcomes the meeting generates. Xi typically avoids owning responsibility for high-profile diplomatic events with uncertain outcomes, so this event will stretch the Chinese side’s comfort zone.
For Trump, the meeting will pose greater downside risks than upside potential. Trump will face the risk of being outmaneuvered by more prepared and more cunning leaders. In this triangle, the closest and warmest relationship among the three leaders is between Xi and Putin, who have met over 40 times since 2013 and share a desire to diminish American leadership on the world stage. The meeting’s optics will also send a chill to America’s allies and partners, who will fear Trump is prioritizing his relations with Xi and Putin over their interests and concerns. This chill will be felt most acutely in Ukraine and Taiwan.
Ultimately, symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting. It is unlikely that there will be any breakthroughs on Ukraine or on launching trilateral arms control efforts, Trump’s putative focus for this meeting. Beijing has long been unwilling to enter arms control negotiations until it is closer to reaching parity in nuclear capabilities with the United States and Russia. Beijing is concerned that doing so could lock China into a permanently subordinate position that could expose China to risk. At best, the three leaders could find common principles to endorse, such as maintaining open sea lines of communication, reaffirming that nuclear wars can never be won and should never be fought, and affirming an interest in an end to war in Ukraine, while leaving the terms of such an end ambiguous.

Back to top

Scott M. Moore

A once-unthinkable alignment

Much has been made of Trump’s apparent rapport with the leaders of Russia and China, long regarded as America’s foremost adversaries. But a trilateral summit with Putin and Xi in Shenzhen would go well beyond bonhomie. It would dramatically signal that Washington is prepared to trade the liberal international order it built after 1945 for a concert of authoritarian-nationalist great powers.
The White House has framed the meeting around the legitimate goal of advancing nuclear arms control. But the meeting has broader implications. Holding a three-way meeting with Russia, just as Moscow says it will resume talks with Washington and Kyiv, represents Ukraine’s worst fear: the image of the war being settled among great powers, over Kyiv’s head. Beijing, too, would benefit from being portrayed as a would-be peacemaker, rather than as an enabler for sustaining Russia’s war economy.
The summit may also preview a broader convergence of interests. The Wall Street Journal reports that the Trump administration has encouraged former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán to run for U.N. secretary-general as a joint U.S.-Russia-China candidate. Meanwhile, Beijing reportedly considered a bid to host the 2028 U.N. climate conference, the annual meeting of parties to the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, a treaty from which the United States will formally withdraw in February 2027. Washington is not merely leaving a gap in multilateral leadership. In the Orbán case, it appears to be working with Moscow and Beijing to reshape the multilateral system.
For America’s allies, the message is stark. A trilateral meeting in Shenzhen will reinforce European concerns that their security is negotiable. In Asia, partners such as Japan and Taiwan will wonder whether their own U.S. security commitments are up for negotiation. The result could be that many will hedge, toward Beijing, toward strategic autonomy, or both.
If the summit goes ahead, it will symbolize a once-unthinkable alignment between the United States and the world’s foremost authoritarian powers. It will also speed up the fracturing of Western alliances that Moscow and Beijing have long sought and make it even more difficult to tackle shared challenges and provide global public goods.

Back to top

Constanze Stelzenmüller

No decisions about Europe without Europe

At the time of writing, a Trump-Xi-Putin meeting was still just a Russian proposal, confirmed by the United States but not by China. Even so, it precisely encapsulates what appears to be an emerging political dynamic: Moscow attempting to set a worldwide great-power agenda, Washington appearing to acquiesce, and Beijing hesitating to commit either way. And the mere suggestion of such a “21st-century Yalta”—a tripartite meeting that would presumably decide the future of Ukraine and Europe over the heads of both—has a symbolic impact of its own, even if it never comes to pass.
The timing of this push is significant. Russia, bogged down at Ukraine’s eastern front, is trying to bludgeon Ukrainian resilience with its relentless and indiscriminate bombardments of energy infrastructure and civilian targets, all while losing huge numbers of soldiers. At the same time, it is waging what The Economist calls “a phoney peace … a war of sorts”—increasingly reckless acts of sabotage, assassination attempts, and other dirty tricks—in Europe, in the hopes of undermining its will to defend Ukraine.
The Trump administration, for its part, has just been dealt devastating results in the U.S. midterm elections, with affordability and the unfinished war on Iran topping the list of voter grievances. All the more important, then, to end this other war in Europe, and, based on his recent actions, the president appears to believe that it is best brought to a conclusion by siding with Russia. Trump has praised Russia (“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine”), authorized Russian-origin diesel purchases, waived the Graham Act sanctions, and—according to media reports—is considering relief for a Russian state investment fund which the Biden administration had sanctioned, calling it Putin’s “slush fund.”
But—as Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute, recently pointed out—Europe in 2026 is not the Europe of 1945, when Josef Stalin, Winston Churchill, and Franklin D. Roosevelt met to hash out the shape of the postwar continent. Protests and political differences notwithstanding, today’s Europe has arms, wealth, institutions, allies, and agency. There can be no lasting and legitimate settlement without Ukraine and Europe at the table. To signal otherwise would only cause yet more damage to the transatlantic alliance.

Back to top

Yun Sun

China wants the spotlight, not arms control

Russia has been the primary driver of a potential trilateral summit during APEC, with Moscow circulating the possibility as early as this past summer. The Chinese are not necessarily actively driving such a summit. However, if the United States and Russia clearly call for it, there are few reasons why China would not embrace such an event. In recent weeks, the United States has engaged in active Track 2 diplomacy and dialogue with China and Russia. The Chinese enthusiasm is obvious, despite the struggle over the deliverables and substance of such a summit. Some Chinese officials have suggested that some in China are viewing the trilateral summit as “the most significant meeting in the history of international relations since the end of World War II.” If it happens, China will be presenting itself as the peer of the United States and Russia and playing a pivotal role in U.S.-Russia relations at a historical moment to end the Ukraine war. That is not an opportunity that Beijing would like to miss. In addition, according to Chinese and Russian interlocutors, Russia has made a genuine plea for China to host the trilateral summit. Beijing will have to develop a really strong and convincing argument about why it would refuse to do its Russian partner a solid.
Beijing is likely concerned by Trump’s and Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s references to such a summit containing a trilateral dialogue on arms control and nuclear weapons. China has consistently rejected the concept of U.S.-China-Russia trilateral arms control and nuclear dialogue, citing its significantly smaller nuclear arsenal. The Chinese do not seem to see the Ukraine war as coming to an end so soon. By the time of the APEC summit, the U.S. midterm elections will already be over, and Trump will have lost the motivation to use peace in Ukraine to boost the Republican Party’s popularity. Therefore, a trilateral summit will be unlikely to end the war in Ukraine anyway.

articles.title: Quantitative tightening: the next chapter − speech by Dave Ramsden
articles.text:
Quantitative tightening: the next chapter − speech by Dave Ramsden

Given at the Bank of England, co-hosted by the Money, Macro and Finance Society

Published on
28 September 2026

Dave Ramsden describes the MPC’s September 2026 decision on Quantitative Tightening, alongside the set of announcements by the Bank and HM Treasury which, together, mark the beginning of the next chapter in the approach to unwinding the assets built up through Quantitative Easing.

Speech
Thank you to the Money, Macro and Finance Society (MMF) for co-hosting this event today. It’s a little over three years ago that I delivered my last speech on Quantitative Tightening (QT)footnote [1], where again the MMF kindly co-hosted the event.
In my 2023 speech, I set out what the MPC and Bank had so far learnt after nearly a year of delivering the MPC’s first annual QT decision. After another three years of QT progress and learnings, we are now ready to move to the next chapter.
The MPC’s September decision, alongside the set of announcements from the Bank Executive and HM Treasury (HMT), marked a significant step in the approach to unwinding the assets built up through Quantitative Easing (QE) – a process dubbed QT. Alongside the MPC's decision that it would shift to a multi-year path for QT, the Bank Executive and HMT also released a set of announcements relating to how QT would be implemented in future and the Bank Executive set out its long-term strategy for backing current and future banknote issuance.
I will spend some time today walking through the details of those announcements, both from my perspective as an MPC member, and as the Deputy Governor at the Bank with executive responsibility for the Bank’s balance sheet. I will not focus on the continuing transition to a demand driven, repo led balance sheet though – those aspects of the Bank’s balance sheet have been well explained and detailed by my Bank Executive colleagues in recent speeches and publications.footnote [2]
Much of what I’m covering today is the collective view of the MPC and set out in the September decision minutes, though I will share some personal views too on the monetary policy approach, and highlight when I do. I do also want to note that the MPC considered important institutional questions regarding the potential interaction between monetary and fiscal actions and the independence of MPC decision making over monetary policy, which led to a robust discussion.
As I am marking this as a closing of one chapter of QT, let me also take a step back and provide a longer term, historical perspective. Over my career I’ve been involved, in one way or another, with every QE and QT decision in the UK taken since 2009.
I’ll start with a brief recounting of why we’re undertaking QT, following the rounds of QE that saw a total of £895bn of asset purchases accumulated onto the Bank’s balance sheet. I’ll then look back on the last four years of QT and how the MPC and Bank Executive continued to build on the learnings of the first year of QT that I described in 2023, before then explaining the September announcements, and how QT will operate going forward. I will conclude with some comments on our active monetary policy tool – Bank Rate – and my views on the outlook.
Why is the MPC undertaking QT?
Before getting into the specifics, it’s always helpful to remember why the MPC is undertaking QT in the first place. There are a few good reasons – to create headroom for future QE purchases, and to reduce interest rate risk on the Bank’s balance sheet. But perhaps the most important is that QE was always intended to be a temporary monetary policy stimulus.
Back in 2009 I was Chief Economic Adviser to the Treasury. Amongst other things, that meant I was the HMT representative at MPC meetings and attended the March 2009 meeting when the MPC decided to undertake its first round of QE. The minutesfootnote [3] of that meeting are clear on why the Committee concluded that asset purchases were necessary to meet its 2% inflation target sustainably in the medium term.
There had been several letter exchanges between the Chancellor and the Governor in the early months of 2009, establishing the Asset Purchase Facility (APF) and authorising monetary policy asset purchases through the APF.footnote [4] These lettersfootnote [5] established the framework for QE, including: a clear division of responsibilities between the MPC and HMT; that the Bank would ensure regular reporting of its asset purchase programme to ensure transparency; and that the implementation of the MPC’s decisions on asset purchases would be delegated to the Bank Executive.
A key tenet of QE, communicated consistently through the rounds of QEfootnote [6], is that the MPC would decide on the most appropriate way to unwind its asset purchases. QE is a monetary policy tool to provide temporary stimulus to the economy and deal with specific shocks, to achieve the MPC’s inflation target. It is not intended to be a permanent change to the monetary framework or the Bank’s balance sheet.
By unwinding earlier QE purchases, the MPC reinforces the credibility of QE as a monetary policy tool for the future. As I reiterated recently to the Treasury Committeefootnote [7], QE can support the economy through the most severe stresses, when Bank Rate has reached the lower bound. If the MPC cannot commit to and evidence a credible exit strategy, the viability of the tool in future is put at risk.
In terms of how the MPC has undertaken that unwind, I think it’s helpful to distinguish between the principles that underpin the MPC’s approach to QT, and then the strategy the MPC and the Bank Executive take to execute that unwind. The principles do not change, but the strategy can evolve as the MPC and Bank Executive learn from doing QT over time and respond to market developments.
As a reminder, the MPC’s three key principles for undertaking QT arefootnote [8]:

First, Bank Rate is the MPC’s active policy tool when adjusting the stance of monetary policy.
Second, sales should be conducted so as not to disrupt the functioning of financial markets, and only in appropriate conditions.
Third, to help achieve that, sales should be conducted in a gradual and predictable manner over a period of time.

In terms of the QT strategy, I’d identify three phases, or chapters. Initially a short period from February 2022, where the MPC decided to stop reinvesting maturing gilts and corporate bonds, allowing the stock of assets held in the APF to begin declining naturally. In doing so, the Bank became one of the first major central banks to begin unwinding the extraordinary monetary stimulus put in place following the global financial crisis, the euro area crisis, the Brexit decision, and the pandemic.
By September 2022, the Committee was ready to shift to an annual approach to unwinding asset purchases, through a combination of maturities and sales, supported by the Bank Executive’s work on the operational details of asset sales.footnote [9]
We are now entering a new chapter, the multi-year strategy. We have been working on this for some time and in my view it is a coherent next step. Given my responsibilities at the Bank I’m very focused on the situation in bond markets. But within that context the QT package appears to have been generally well received by markets and market commentators. The different elements seem to have been individually and collectively understood.
Indeed, one of the more common questions I’ve received since the announcement is why didn’t we move to this new approach sooner? In a way, that’s great to hear – clearly the multi-year strategy has been received well. But we shouldn’t forget that the MPC and Bank Executive have learnt a lot over the first few years of QT. And the annual strategy was itself an effective strategy for delivering QT.
To evidence that, and help to answer the question of why we’re moving to the next chapter of QT now, let me provide an overview of the last four years of QT.
Looking back – the annual strategy
Since February 2022, the size of the APF has fallen by over £400bn from a peak of £895bn to around £488bn today, through the MPC’s unwinding of both holdings of gilts and corporate bonds.

Where the Bank’s approach has sometimes been described as different to its peers has been the use of sales to the secondary market, alongside maturities, to deliver the annual reduction in the stock of assets or QT pace. So far, approximately £259 billion of gilts have rolled off through maturities, alongside £129 billion of gilt sales and approximately £20bn of corporate bond sales and maturities. The Riksbank has also used sales to the market in its QT implementation, but other peer central banks, like the Federal Reserve and the ECB, have relied on maturities.
There were good reasons for undertaking sales. It is a prominent feature of UK government debt that the average maturity is much longer than international peers. In implementing QE, the Bank sought to purchase gilts in a way that reflected the structure of the gilt market, consistent with a principle of market neutrality. This meant that QE purchases were conducted across the maturity spectrum of the gilt market, rather than targeting a particular segment of the curve. Given the long maturity profile of UK government debt, this meant that the Bank’s gilt purchases included much longer maturities than many peer central banks.
Relying solely on maturities would have meant the unwind taking over 50 years, as shown in Chart 4. This would have left a significant amount of interest rate risk on the Bank’s balance sheet, limiting the headroom available for future policy interventions and failing in the objective that QE should represent a temporary intervention. Sales to the market have allowed the MPC to reduce the portfolio in a timely manner, retaining future flexibility and credibility of our policy tools.

Monetary policy assessment of QT to date
Starting first with the monetary policy impact of QT, as I set out in my 2023 speech, our strategy for QT has turned off some channels that were important during QE.footnote [10] That should have reduced QT’s potential impact on gilt yields, certainly when compared with the impacts of QE. The main way through which QT does impact financial conditions is through the so-called portfolio rebalancing channel, which can in theory lead to modest increases in gilt yields through term premia.footnote [11]
Term premia can be influenced by a wide range of factors, and isolating the specific effect of QT is not simple, though our estimates suggest the impact of QT has been relatively modest. Other factors influencing term premia over the last four years have been a structural reduction in domestic demand for long-term government debt, global economic policy uncertainty and high issuance of government bonds across countries.
Between the start of QT in February 2022 and late September 2026, 10-year gilt yields rose by around 450 basis points. Term structure model estimates indicate that around 200 basis points of this increase was driven by term premia, with the remaining rise accounted for by higher expected rates, as shown in Chart 5.
