To estimate the specific effect of QT, one approach is to look at movements in term premia in short periods directly around announcementsfootnote [12] of QT policies or around the time of QT auctions; this is the approach taken by Bank staff. This helps to identify the impact of QT because gilt market pricing tends to adjust quickly in response to market news, and the short window helps to limit the influence of other factors on the estimates. But, given that there have been a limited number of QT announcements and auctions and that QT has been operated in a predictable manner, there remains considerable uncertainty around these estimates.
There is also uncertainty around the persistence of QT’s effects on term premia. One drawback of event study estimates of QT (or QE) is that they cannot identify effects that fall outside of the short window used for the estimation. Bank staff’s estimates cumulate effects across QT announcements and auctions going back to 2022 and therefore assume that the effects of QT are highly persistent. While there is, so far, limited evidence on the persistence of QT’s effects, Bank staff analysis of QE has assumed, based on available studies, that impacts may start to fade after one to four years.footnote [13] If the same is true for QT, then these central estimates could overstate its impact on the current level of yields.
In the July Monetary Policy Report, analysis by Bank stafffootnote [14] pointed to an estimated total increase in 10-year gilt yields from cumulative QT to date of 20–30 basis points.footnote [15] Given the overall increase in the term premium for 10-year gilt yields since February 2022, this suggested QT has driven between a tenth and a sixth of that total.
The reaction to the MPC’s September 2026 QT announcement of a multi-year strategy saw yields fall across the curve. The effect was larger at the longer end, for example 30-year gilt yields fell by around 10bps which persisted over subsequent days. The 10-year gilt yields fell by a similar amount with term premia falling around 7 basis points. At the shorter end the effect was smaller and has subsequently reversed. This suggests the market was expecting more QT, either in total or at a higher pace. And some positioning for increases in long-dated yields were subsequently unwound, which may have exacerbated the moves after the announcement. It is also possible that the removal of uncertainty about the path of future QT reduced risk premia.
Other estimates of the impact of QT over the last four years have been published, some of which suggest QT has had a larger impact than the Bank staff’s estimates. But importantly, to the extent any QT impacts – while relatively modest – are coming through, the MPC will have observed the associated effects on asset prices, conditioned its forecasts accordingly and has full flexibility to adjust its active tool – Bank Rate – to the extent that any offsetting action is deemed necessary.
The Bank Executive’s implementation of QT to date
Turning to the implementation of QT, throughout the period from 2022 to 2026, the Bank Executive designed its sales to market approach, such that it delivered the MPC’s QT decision, in line with the MPC’s principles – particularly that sales are conducted so as not to disrupt the functioning of financial markets, and that they should be conducted in a gradual and predictable manner. Subject to that, the Bank Executive should maximise value for money by minimising cost and risk over the lifetime of the APF.
To achieve that, the Bank Executive worked closely with the DMO to design an auction schedule that fitted around gilt issuance and other market events. Auction schedules have been published in advance and sales have been conducted through a consistent auction framework, providing the market a clear view of the QT programme. Together, these features ensured that QT remained predictable, allowing the programme to remain in the background while supporting orderly market functioning.
Gilt sales have been conducted via multi-stock auctions to the secondary market. The auction design itself plays an important role in achieving the value for money objective. By offering multiple bonds in each operation and using a discriminatory price format, the Bank aims to maximise participation and competition, helping deliver value for money across the programme. Offers were ranked and allocated according to the attractiveness of the yield for the Bank.
Over this period, the Bank has sold £129 billion (in purchase proceeds) of the MPC’s APF holdings across 120 auctions, selling gilts across three maturity buckets; short, medium and long.footnote [16] The programme's success can be seen in auction outcomes. We monitor both the level of demand for auctions and the prices achieved relative to prevailing market rates. One measure of demand is the cover ratio – the ratio of offers to accepted bids (Chart 6), while a key pricing metric is the weighted average (WA) spread of accepted prices relative to market mid-yields (Chart 7). To date, QT auctions have received an average cover of 2.3x, meaning there have been 2.3 times more bids than those accepted. And, the average WA spread has been -0.5, meaning that accepted pricing has on average been 0.5bp lower than market mid prices (in favour of the Bank).
These measures suggest that Bank auctions have on the whole consistently attracted strong demand and delivered favourable pricing outcomes. This sentiment is reiterated by market contacts in our MI gathering, who generally describe QT operations as running smoothly and being readily absorbed by the market. These metrics, alongside our market monitoring, indicate that we have achieved our desired aim of reducing the size of the APF in a timely manner while achieving value for money and supporting orderly market functioning.
A key feature of the Bank’s implementation to QT so far has been responsiveness to the needs of the market. Ahead of each annual MPC decision, staff have assessed the capacity of the gilt market to absorb additional supply, and the potential impact to financial markets of different sales paces. That information helps to inform the MPC on potential pace options for subsequent years of QT, in line with the MPC’s principle that sales should be conducted so as to not disrupt the functioning of financial markets. As such, the QT programme has adapted when necessary, including the decision to skew away from longs in September 2025, showing that the Bank is sensitive to changing market conditions.

The next chapter of QT – the MPC’s multi-year strategy
The annual strategy since September 2022 has delivered on the MPC’s principles and provided a solid foundation for the MPC’s decision to shift to a new, multi-year strategy for delivering QT.
There was a lot of information in the set of announcements released just over a week ago and, as I’ve said, these seem to have been well understood and well received. The Governor’s letter to the Chancellorfootnote [17] set out the key elements of the package, taking the current APF stock of £488bn as the baseline, they are:

The MPC’s decision to set a multi-year path for unwind, fully unwinding the stock of gilts held for monetary policy purposes by the end of 2034.
As a result, the Bank would not sell the £222bn of gilts with redemption dates earlier than 2035.
The Bank Executive’s announcement that £120bn of the longest-dated gilts will remain in the APF to back current and future banknote issuance.
The Bank Executive is considering adjusting the way it conducts gilt sales of the remaining £146bn, and intends to implement the MPC’s multi-year plan via sales to the Government rather than to the market.

For me the package was a coherent next step which continue to respect the division of responsibilities between the authorities. Importantly the MPC’s three key principles for delivering QT continue to frame the approach.
The first element of the package is the MPC’s decision to set out a multi-year path for unwinding the APF. Before deciding on the pace of that unwind, there was one critical decision for the MPC to take – the stock of gilts that should be held for monetary policy purposes. This is a key element of the UK’s monetary policy framework, going back to those letters from 2009 that I highlighted.
I have previously set out the case for the MPC to fully unwind its stock of assets built up through QEfootnote [18], but the MPC had yet to take a formal decision on the issue. Consistent with the earlier sets of documentation, the MPC agreed that the stock of assets built up through QE should be fully unwound. Supporting this, the MPC judged that there were no monetary policy reasons to hold a structural gilt portfolio in the APF, particularly given the ongoing and successful transition to a demand-driven, repo led framework for supplying reserves, where money market rates have continued to trade in a narrow spread to Bank Rate.
Having confirmed its desired end point, the MPC discussed the merits of setting out a more forward-looking plan for the remainder of QT. Relative to the annual strategy, shifting to multi-year ensures the pace of QT is as predictable as possible. By removing uncertainty over the pace and end point of QT, the MPC can ensure QT is put even more firmly into the background. As the full intended path for QT can be embedded into financial conditions, this better enables the MPC to take it into account when setting Bank Rate, its primary tool for adjusting the stance of monetary policy.
The MPC’s confirmation that it planned to fully unwind the APF’s holdings of gilts for monetary policy purposes meant the Bank Executive had clarity to confirm the long-term strategy for backing banknotes. The Bank Insights article published alongside the QT announcementfootnote [19] details how banknotes have been indirectly backed by gilts in the APF since 2009. The Bank Executive determined that a portfolio of long-dated gilts would be well suited to backing banknotes as its maturity profile provides a good match for the long-term nature of banknote liability. To ensure notes continued to have appropriate backing, the Bank Executive determined that £120bn of gilts should remain in the APF, no longer held for monetary policy and solely to back notes. Using existing APF gilts to back banknotes avoids the transaction costs associated with purchasing gilts from the market directly onto Issue Department.footnote [20]
That means, of the £488bn of gilts in the APF at the time of the MPC’s September decision, the MPC could determine what the multi-year path should be in the knowledge that £120bn of those gilts would remain in the APF to back notes. In other words, the MPC’s decision on pace would be in relation to the remaining £368bn of gilts.
The MPC discussed the appropriate pace for the multi-year path as part of its September decision. Consistent with previous annual QT decisions, Bank staff assessed the appropriate pace options over the multi-year path, in line with the MPC’s principles that sales should be conducted so as not to disrupt the functioning of financial markets. Given the change in strategy to a multi-year unwind with a fixed pace of sales throughout, the MPC considered the relative benefits of unwinding more quickly or slowly. The MPC recognised the chance that future economic and market shocks could occur over the period of QT unwind and the strategy, including the pace of unwind, has been designed with that context in mind.
After discussion, the MPC unanimously agreed that the remaining £368bn of gilts should be unwound at an annual average pace of £46bn by the end of 2034, through annual sales of £20bn alongside maturing gilts. That means of the £488bn of gilts remaining in the APF, £222bn would be held to maturity (shown by the blue bars in Chart 7), £146bn would be sold (orange bars), and £120bn would remain in the APF to back banknotes (purple bars). The final maturity will be the £28.2bn September 2034 gilt, and the MPC expects that will mark the completion of the QT unwind.

One point of particular discussion amongst MPC members was the extent to which the committee should retain flexibility within that multi-year plan. There’s an obvious trade-off here, the more flexibility the MPC has, the greater its ability to respond to evolving market conditions over time, and potentially increase or decrease its pace of unwind in subsequent years. But on the other hand, a fixed intended pace of unwind would provide more certainty and clarity over the future QT path. On balance, most MPC members felt that the benefits from the predictability of a fixed pace outweighed the loss of flexibility.
The MPC judged that unwinding the APF at a constant and fixed pace would further put QT in the background. Given the variation in the maturity profile in coming years, to make this as simple and transparent as possible, it specified its multi-year strategy as a constant annual sales pace of £20bn each year over the remainder of the path of unwind.
To ensure the MPC’s QT strategy remained consistent with its principles – both that Bank Rate remains the active tool, and that sales do not disrupt the functioning of financial markets – the MPC reiterated that there would only be two specific circumstances where the pace of unwind in the multi-year plan would be reconsidered.footnote [21] These two ‘knockouts’ are designed such that high bars would have to be met in order for them to be triggered, First, if the MPC judged that potential movements in Bank Rate alone were insufficient to meet the inflation target. And second, if markets were judged by the Bank to be very distressed. The Financial Policy Committee would have a role in this second circumstance through its assessment of financial stability.
From my perspective, the obvious example of the first knockout is if repeated shocks mean that Bank Rate is approaching the effective lower bound and there is a risk of running out of headroom to achieve the MPC’s price stability objective. Of course, it would be for the MPC at the time to judge whether the knockout had been triggered, dependent on the circumstances at the time.
The final element of the package set out in the Governor’s letter to the Chancellor is the Bank Executive’s intended approach to implementing the MPC’s multi-year plan. The intended approach – to sell gilts to the Government rather than to the market – has been developed through engagement with HMT and the DMO over the last year, and is subject to final agreement with HMT.
The Bank Executive’s intention to change its approach to gilt sales – subject to HMT agreement – is driven by its responsibility to continue to maximise value for money by minimising cost and risk over the lifetime of the APF, subject to achieving the MPC’s chosen unwind target and in line with the MPC’s key principles. As I’ve described, the Bank Executive’s approach to sales to date has been successful and delivered on its value for money responsibility through careful design of its auctions to market. But given the MPC’s multi-year plan for QT, the Bank Executive is mindful that a portion of the gilts remaining in the APF will likely become less aligned with market demand as unwind continues.
As an alternative, the Bank has engaged with HMT and the DMO to consider a model whereby the MPC’s decision could instead be implemented through APF sales to the Government. At a high level, the model would see HMT instruct the DMO to purchase, over time, the £146bn of 2035-2049 APF gilts that the Bank is selling, which the DMO would on-sell to the National Loans Fund for cancellation and subsequent refinancing, with the DMO better able to align its issuance with market demand. It would also see a return to a single public sector supplier of gilts to the market.
The operational details of this model need to be worked through between the Bank, HMT and DMO. To ensure monetary independence, and to prevent any blurring of fiscal and monetary responsibilities, sales would be set in advance by the Bank Executive and conducted at market prices. This means that sales parameters, including the pace and frequency, would be pre-defined and non-discretionary. The lifetime costs of the APF unwind are neutral whether starting with the longest or shortest maturities. Of course, starting sales from the longest maturity and working backwards reduces interest rate risk on the Bank’s balance sheet the most quickly. Under this sales model, the Bank Executive would therefore expect to sell the £146bn of APF gilts designated for sales to the DMO in reverse order, starting with the longest maturity gilts. The indemnity from HMT to the Bank will remain in place.
The Bank will announce its approach to implementing the MPC’s QT strategy by April 2027. Regardless of the method of sales, the Bank Executive will ensure that the MPC’s agreed sales pace is implemented and full unwind is completed by the end of 2034. The £20bn sales pace refers to the 12-month period following the start of sales; for the avoidance of doubt, if sales were to begin in April 2027, the £20bn of sales would be completed by April 2028. As long as sales begin by end-Q2 2027, the exact start date of the sales programme does not influence the expected end date of the QT unwind, given the MPC expects the final APF gilt held for monetary policy purposes will be the one that matures in September 2034. In the meantime, APF gilt maturities continue, with the next maturity occurring on 22 October 2026.
Once the Bank announces its approach to implementing the MPC’s QT strategy, from my perspective, we will have brought to a close the chapter of QT I first described in 2023. And we will have embarked on the next chapter, which should see the current stock of APF gilts fully unwound for monetary policy purposes over the next eight years.
The MPC’s active monetary policy tool
Before closing, I wanted to share my latest view on the MPC’s active monetary policy tool – Bank Rate. At its September meeting, the MPC voted by a majority of 6-3 to leave Bank Rate unchanged at 3.75%. I voted in the majority, as I have since the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East to hold Bank Rate at 3.75%.
For my part, Bank Rate being the ‘active’ tool doesn’t always mean it has to change. Indeed, a decision to hold can be an active response to the risks to the inflation outlook. In February of this year, prior to the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, I voted in the minority for a cut to Bank Rate to 3.5%. Indeed, with evidence that the disinflation process was on track at the time (and subsequently confirmed from my perspective with the data outturns we have seen this year) I would have expected at least two cuts by now, such that Bank Rate would be at least 0.5% below where it is today, and slightly below the UK OIS curve at the time (shown in Chart 8). Therefore, my holds to Bank Rate since March have effectively delivered a tightening relative to where I thought we might otherwise have been.
I think the tightening we have seen in financial conditions since the outbreak of the conflict, shown by the increase in the OIS curve since February, has helped to limit the potential for some of the direct effects from the energy shock to propagate through to second round effects. But, as I set out in my individual paragraph in the September meeting minutes, I think the risks to the inflation outlook, whether external or domestically generated, have tilted more to the upside. Whilst the policy stance continues to provide restrictiveness, were upside pressures on the inflation outlook to continue to build, there could be a case for increasing Bank Rate.

Looking ahead to upcoming meetings, the inflation pressures I will continue to focus on are external pressures from energy prices, including from crude oil and gas prices as well as those of refined products, but also from extreme weather events and the AI supply chain. Domestically, I will be focused on the outlook for indirect effects, particularly in food prices, and any early signs of second round effects apparent from firms’ responses to the DMP survey and the Bank’s Agents’ intelligence on upcoming wage negotiations, looking ahead to 2027 settlements.
Conclusion
To conclude, based on mine and the market’s current assessment of the economy, I don’t foresee that we will be considering further QE any time soon. However, we have to recognise that the external environment can change very rapidly, as it did with the shocks of the Global Financial Crisis in 2008 and again with the Covid pandemic in 2020.
For today’s purposes let’s assume it doesn’t. In which case, the MPC’s decision at its September 2026 meeting should see the stock of assets held for monetary policy purposes fully unwound by 2034. That will be 25 years after QE was first undertaken. The MPC’s multi-year QT strategy provides a credible and coherent strategy for unwinding QE purchases, which should mean we’ve built a stronger foundation should QE be undertaken again in future.
Back in 2009 I certainly did not envisage that QE would take place in multiple phases over a 12 year period, and would take a similar period to unwind. The last 25 years has raised a lot of questions and points of discussion – in relation to both QE and QT – that need to be worked through. There are further lessons to be drawn from that experience, and more chapters to be written.

For instance, while QE affected gilt rates through a ‘signalling channel’ by changing market expectations for the future path of Bank Rate, the QT strategy is likely to have switched this channel off. During QT, the MPC has used Bank Rate as the active tool of monetary policy, which means that news about QT is not intended to contain any information about the future stance of monetary policy. QE also operated via effects on gilt market liquidity, but as QT sales have been gradual, predictable and only conducted in appropriate market conditions, it has had no marked effect on market liquidity.

This can occur via two main effects. First, increasing the supply of certain bonds can increase the yield on these bonds and on other assets that investors might consider close substitutes (the ‘local supply’ channel). Second, by shifting investors’ portfolios towards longer-dated assets, QT increases the overall amount of duration risk borne by market participants and may therefore increase term premia across the yield curve (the ‘duration channel’).

articles.title: The low-gear labour market − speech by Clare Lombardelli
articles.text:
The low-gear labour market − speech by Clare Lombardelli

Given at the Bank of England Watchers Conference

Published on
10 November 2026

The labour market is cooling mainly through weaker hiring, rather than increased firing. That cyclical slowdown is interacting with a longer-term decline in people’s ability to move into new job opportunities. The result may be greater harm to young people and productivity, without as much easing in wage pressure as the rise in unemployment would normally suggest.

Speech
Introduction
Today I want to talk about an unusual feature of the UK labour market. It is cooling, but mainly through less hiring rather than more firing.
The economy has been more resilient to the recent energy cost shock than expected. Activity has held up better than anticipated, unemployment has risen only gradually, and redundancies remain relatively low. That may sound like good news. In lots of important ways, it is. But a low-hire, low-fire labour market creates its own problems. It protects those already in work while making it much harder for those trying to get in or move on.
This matters because the current slowdown in hiring comes on top of a longer-term decline in mobility within the labour market. People are changing jobs less often. And when they do move, they are less likely to change industry or move into work requiring different skills. The labour market has become less effective at moving people towards new opportunities. The labour market is stuck in low gear.
That has three important consequences.
First, it affects how we interpret the rise in unemployment. If those looking for work are poorly matched to the jobs available, higher unemployment may do less to ease wage pressures than it has in the past.
Second, it can weaken productivity and growth. Moving jobs helps workers find roles where their skills are better used. When that process slows, people miss opportunities to progress and firms find it harder to recruit the staff they need. The costs are falling particularly heavily on young people, for whom the first step into work has become harder.
Third, it can make the economy less able to adapt. That matters as artificial intelligence changes the tasks people perform and the skills employers need. The gains from AI will depend partly on how readily people can move towards the new opportunities it creates.
I will begin with the unusual way in which the labour market is cooling. I will then look at the longer-term decline in job mobility and the particular challenges facing young people. Finally, I will consider what this means for inflation, productivity and the economy’s ability to adapt, before turning to the outlook for monetary policy following last week’s decision.

Cooling through hiring, not firing
The UK economy has, so far, proven to be more resilient to the energy price shock than many expected. We produced our first post-conflict projections just nine weeks after the outbreak. Those were very uncertain times, so we published three scenarios and no central projection.
Chart 1 shows how the economy has evolved in terms of output and unemployment since those projections. Activity has been significantly stronger than the middle scenario from our April report and unemployment has been lower.

Chart 1: Economic activity has been resilient so far (a)

Footnotes

Sources: See our April and November Monetary Policy Reports.
(a) The April scenario contains data up to 2026q1. The November central projection contains data up to 2026q3.

To date, real activity has been unexpectedly robust given the circumstances. That said, the unemployment rate still increased from below 4% in 2022 to peak above 5% late last year. It now stands at 4.7% in the latest data for the three months to August.
This rise in unemployment has been persistent but relatively gradual by historical standards as Chart 2 shows. Unemployment increased for six consecutive quarters from mid-2024 to the end of 2025 but by only around 1 percentage point in total, before falling back in the latest data. Sustained increases of this kind have historically tended to occur around recessions when unemployment typically rose much more sharply following abrupt job losses. Unemployment fell in the most recent data and in our November central projection remains broadly stable in the region of 5%, as shown in Chart 1.

Chart 2: The recent rise in total unemployment has been relatively gradual

Footnotes

Source: ONS.

The headline unemployment rate does not tell us how the labour market is adjusting. To see that, we need to distinguish between people losing existing jobs and people finding it harder to get new ones.
Labour market flows data show that the loosening has not been driven by an abrupt rise in job losses (Chart 3). Redundancies have remained relatively stable. According to the LFSfootnote [1], the redundancy rate is at roughly the same level as it was before the pandemic. This picture is consistent with data on corporate insolvencies, which have been stable or even moderately declining following a slight jump after the pandemic.

Chart 3: There has not been a large rise in redundancies

Footnotes

Sources: HR1 data from Insolvency Service, Management information on Advanced Notification of Redundancy Scheme, LFS redundancy rate from ONS data, Google searches from Google Trends, using keywords "redundancies", "redundancy insurance" and "redundancy calculator".

In contrast, we have seen a larger adjustment in vacancies and other measures of labour demand. Vacancies have fallen and are now well below their pre-pandemic level (Chart 4). The REC measure of labour demand also remains contractionary (below 50), though it has shown signs of improvement. In the recent labour market loosening, firms have so far adjusted much more through reducing demand for new workers than through shedding existing employees.

Chart 4: Demand for new hires has softened

Footnotes

Sources: ONS, KPMG/REC UK Report on Jobs.

Explicitly breaking down the actual rise in unemployment into the separate contributions from hiring and firing shows just how different the recent slowdown has been (Chart 5). Weaker hiring is by far the more significant driver.

Chart 5: Slow hiring has disproportionately driven the recent cycle (a)

Footnotes

Sources: ONS and Bank calculations.
(a) Job finding and separation rates are estimated from changes in the distribution of unemployment by duration rather than directly observed labour market flows. These estimates are used to construct a flows-consistent unemployment rate which may differ from the headline unemployment rate.

The cooling in labour demand has also been uneven across sectors (Chart 6). Vacancy rates are now much more dispersed than before the pandemic. In some industries, including public administration and defence, vacancies remain well above their historical average. In others, notably retail, they have fallen well below it.
This uneven pattern matters because workers do not seamlessly move between industries. When opportunities are contracting in one part of the economy but remain stronger elsewhere, adjustment requires workers to move to areas where staff are more in demand.
Wage growth provides important information on labour market conditions. As Chart 7 shows, pay growth has fallen substantially from its post-pandemic peak. But the latest Bank assessment is that underlying wage growth remains at the upper end of the range consistent with the inflation target, while forward-looking indicators point to continued strength into next year. I will return later to what this combination of weak hiring and continued wage pressure may tell us about the labour market.

Chart 6: Dispersion in labour demand across industries is widening

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

Chart 7: Wage disinflation has slowed

Footnotes

Sources: ONS, DMP Survey, Bank of England Agents and Bank calculations.

Why are firms cutting hiring without making more redundancies?
The labour market is responding to a range of factors. Following the pandemic, it was exceptionally tight, as strong demand ran ahead of the economy’s capacity. More recently, the energy cost shock and heightened uncertainty have affected firms’ decisions.
As the economy reopened from the pandemic, acute labour shortages were widespread. The furlough scheme and wider fiscal and monetary support prevented large-scale unemployment. The rapid expansion in demand then left firms struggling to attract the skills they needed. Bank Agency intelligence and a range of business surveys repeatedly reported acute recruitment difficulties and skills shortages, leading many firms to place a high value on retaining experienced staff (Chart 8 and Chart 4).
Memories of recent labour shortages may have led employers to be more hesitant to make workers redundant, concerned that they will struggle to find the skills they need when activity recovers.

Chart 8: Recruitment difficulties surged after the pandemic

Footnotes

Source: Bank of England Agents.

The conflict in the Middle East has further challenged firms. Disruption to energy supplies has raised oil, gas and other commodity prices, increasing businesses’ costs and squeezing household’s real incomes. Geopolitical uncertainty has also increased, making it harder for firms and households to plan.
Businesses have responded to these pressures in a variety of ways, including absorbing some of the increase in costs in their margins (Chart 9). Profit margins remain compressed as competition and weak demand limit firms’ ability to pass higher costs through to prices. Looking ahead, our Agency network reports that business contacts expect to restore margins through a combination of price increases and further efficiencies such as through procurement and automation.
Part of firms’ adjustment has also been by cost reductions, including hiring restraint, particularly in consumer-facing sectors where intelligence suggests that forward-looking employment intentions remain negative. And while overall employment intentions have recently firmed a little, they remain below normal levels, consistent with continued caution about hiring.
So far, businesses have been able to absorb part of their higher energy costs in their margins. That has probably helped to limit the adjustment in employment, with firms responding through lower hiring, rather than higher redundancies. Heightened uncertainty may be driving the use of margins as a buffer in case the energy cost shock proves only temporary.

Chart 9: Businesses are adjusting in multiple ways

Footnotes

Source: DMP survey.

But that buffer cannot be used indefinitely. The longer energy costs stay high, the greater pressure there will be on businesses to restore margins through other means including higher prices, lower wages or lower employment. A more prolonged shock could therefore force firms to adjust current employment as well as hiring plans.
So the labour market has so far adjusted mainly though weaker hiring rather than higher firing. But this cyclical slowdown has come on top of a longer-term decline in the movement of workers between jobs. I’ll turn to that next.
A less mobile labour market and its effect on young people
We have seen how the current economic cycle has been characterised by unusual stability in the existing workforce. But that cyclical pattern sits alongside a longer-term trend: people are moving less often into, out of, and between jobs.
At any point in time, there is always a substantial amount of movement in the labour market. In 2025, almost 3 million people switched jobs, around one in twelve employed. A further 3.6 million people left employment at some point during the year while about 4.3 million people entered.footnote [2] This underlying amount of change is higher than might be assumed from the stability of aggregate statistics, such as the headline unemployment rate.
People are making fewer job moves
The clearest long-run measure of labour market mobility is the job-to-job switching rate: the share of people moving directly between jobs without a spell of joblessness. It is cyclical, rising in booms and falling in recessions. Chart 10 shows this measure for the last 30 years.

Chart 10: Job-to-job moves are declining (a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations. Data are smoothed using a four-quarter moving average.
(a) The cyclical adjustment (trend) is calculated by estimating the relationship between outturns and the output gap for 1995-2019. Dotted aqua line shows the linear trend of the cyclically-adjusted series.

Despite the volatility, there is a pronounced downward trend. Thirty years ago, more than 3% of employed people changed jobs each quarter. Over the past year, the quarterly rate has been a little above 2%. This is not too far off global financial crisis lows despite much less cyclical weakness.
Mobility is not only about people moving directly between jobs. People also move into and out of employment altogether. Chart 11 combines job-to-job moves with entries to and exits from employment. This more comprehensive measure also shows a long-term slowing.

Chart 11: A broader measure of turnover also shows a slowdown (a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.
(a) The cyclical adjustment is calculated in the same way as the previous chart.

And job moves are becoming narrower
Not only are people moving jobs less often, the moves they make are also becoming narrower (also see Haldane, 2019 Opens in a new window). In the early 2000s, more than half of job switches crossed industry boundaries. That share fell by around ten percentage points during the financial crisis and has not recovered (Chart 12). Moves between broad occupational skill groups have also declined, while moves within the same skill level have become more common (Chart 13).

Chart 12: Fewer workers are moving across industries…

Footnotes

Source: ONS.

Chart 13: …and across skills levels (a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS.
(a) High skill is defined as SOC major groups 1 to 3, medium skill as SOC major groups 4 to 6, and low skill as SOC major groups 7 to 9. Occupational classifications changed in 2021 (for SOC 2020) and in 2011 (for SOC 2010). As such additional care should be taken in interpreting changes around these periods.

Why has job mobility declined?
The decline in labour market mobility reflects a combination of factors.
Structural change across the economy has slowed since its peak in the 1980s Cominetti et al. (2022) Opens in a new window which may have reduced the opportunities for workers to move between jobs and sectors. ONS evidence Opens in a new window finds that job reallocation was lower in 2024 than in 2001 in every industry, showing the trend is broad based rather than concentrated in a few sectors. Research has linked slowing labour market dynamism to a shift towards older, more established businesses (Davis and Haltiwanger, 2014 Opens in a new window).
At the same time, the workforce has aged. This reduces mobility because older workers change jobs, occupations and locations less frequently than younger workers. Rising inactivity associated with ill health also hampers labour market movement. And the move from EU free movement to a migration system more reliant on employer sponsorship and eligible occupations has changed how readily migrant labour can respond to shifts in demand.
These factors may reinforce one another. Fewer fast-growing businesses generate fewer opportunities for people to move into, while a less mobile workforce makes it harder for labour to follow the opportunities that do emerge.
Young people are bearing the greatest cost
The effects of these changes have been highly uneven. Younger workers and new entrants have borne a disproportionate share, even as aggregate employment has remained relatively resilient.
The difficulties facing young people have been well documented. Unemployment among 16 to 24-year-olds has risen much faster than for other age groups (Chart 14). The youth unemployment rate is now more than three times the aggregate rate, its highest relative level since the early 1990s. Despite accounting for only around 12.5% of the labour force, 16 to 24-year-olds account for more than half of the rise in aggregate unemployment since mid-2022 (Chart 15).

Chart 14: Unemployment rates by age

Footnotes

Source: ONS.

The extent of this rise in youth unemployment is similar to that seen in the aftermath of the global financial crisis, even though the wider labour market has deteriorated by far less. Young people now account for around 40% of all unemployment, up sharply since 2021. That is close to the share seen during the aftermath of the 2008 crisis.

Chart 15: Youth unemployment accounts for most of the rise in total

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

The problem goes beyond unemployment (Milburn, 2026 Opens in a new window). Nearly one million 16- to 24-year-olds in the UK are now not in education, employment or training, equivalent to around 13% of that age group. And the problem is entrenched, 45% of people who are NEET at the age of 24 have never worked.
Youth unemployment is not exceptionally high in the UK by international standards. Some other European countries have much higher rates. What stands out more is the gap between young people and the rest of the labour market. Relative to unemployment among prime-age workers, youth unemployment is unusually high in the UK and that gap has widened over time (Chart 16).
So the labour market is behaving very differently for young people than it is for the wider population. Job opportunities for young people have deteriorated by more relative to the national labour market than in other countries. The reasons are complex, but four factors appear particularly important: the low-hire low-fire pattern of adjustment; the concentration of weaker hiring in sectors that employ many young people; the deterioration in young people’s health; and the rising cost and perceived risk of employing inexperienced workers.
By definition, a low-hire, low-fire labour market hurts those entering work for the first time. The composition of labour demand has also moved against some of the routes through which young people traditionally enter employment. This is not simply the unwinding of the exceptional and temporary post-pandemic vacancy boom. Compared with immediately before the pandemic, vacancies are around 14% lower across the economy, but around 19% lower in accommodation and food services and 46% lower in retail. Job opportunities have therefore contracted by more in two sectors that provide important entry routes into work.

Chart 16: The UK has a large youth unemployment gap

Footnotes

Sources: OECD and Bank calculations.

Chart 17 shows the distribution of job seekers and available jobs across industries, splitting job seekers into those who have never worked before and those who have. There is a relative undersupply of jobs in the accommodation, wholesale and retail sectors – the parts of the labour market with the highest concentration of inexperienced job seekers.
Those industries matter because they provide many of the starter jobs through which young people acquire workplace skills and start to build an employment history. Online job posting data shows a similar picture (Indeed, 2026 Opens in a new window). Graduate vacancies are around 7% lower than a year ago and at their lowest level for this time of year since 2020. Summer jobs, another common point of entry into employment, are also at their lowest level in four years.
Young people have experienced a greater deterioration in their health than the wider population, particularly in their mental health. The proportion of adults aged 16-64 meeting the criteria for a common mental disorder increased from 15.5% in 1993 to 22.6% in 2024. Among 16 to 24 year olds that increase was from one in six people to one in four (Fonagy Review, 2026 Opens in a new window). And they face further challenges. This cohort also entered adulthood carrying the effects of the pandemic. Disrupted education reduced learning and work experience, and school absence has remained higher than pre-pandemic levels.

Chart 17: Labour demand and supply mismatch appears worse for starter jobs (a)

Footnotes

Sources: OECD and Bank calculations.
(a) The chart shows the distribution of vacancies and unemployment by previous industry. For people who have never worked, industry is estimated from the sectors that similar first-time job seekers have historically entered over the previous three years.

The relative cost of employing younger workers has also risen because of changes to the National Living Wage. Minimum-wage rates for under-18s and 18 to 20 year-olds have increased faster than the adult rate. In the Bank’s DMP survey 29% of employers affected by the National Living Wage said they would lower overall employment in response.
The drivers of weaker labour market outcomes are difficult to disentangle. The evidence does not allow us to separate precisely effects of weaker demand for young workers from changes in their availability for work.
Through our Agency Network we regularly hear that uncertain demand and higher business costs, particularly energy costs, have depressed overall hiring since the Middle East conflict began. And that higher labour costs are incentivising firms to adopt automation and AI which is further pushing down on labour demand. But for young people in particular, the greater barrier may not be cost alone, but perceived risk. For an employer, taking on a young person involves uncertainty and investment. New entrants need training, supervision and we hear increasingly about work readiness and the need for pastoral support.
Those costs can be worthwhile for firms and transformative for individuals. But when firms face uncertainty, the risk of inaction in terms of pausing hiring new workers is often less than the risk of letting experienced employees go. That asymmetry has contributed to lower hiring of young people.
The human consequences are severe. Work and training provide income, purpose, skills, confidence and social connection. Losing access to them narrows opportunity and damages wellbeing. The effects can persist: unemployment early in working life leaves lasting scars on employment and earnings (Gregg 2001 Opens in a new window; Bell and Blanchflower 2011 Opens in a new window). The size of the affected population means these effects will have a macro impact for the wider economy.
A labour market that is less effective at moving people into work and towards more productive opportunities has implications not only for those directly affected, but also for wage pressure, productivity and the economy’s ability to adapt. I turn to those wider economic consequences next.
Macroeconomic implications
In headline terms, the labour market has proved more resilient than expected, during both the recent energy shock and previous shocks. But resilience in employment does not mean that the labour market is working well for everybody. A labour market can preserve existing jobs while dropping down a gear under the bonnet. Adjustment through weaker hiring rather than higher firing can conceal pressure on young people and new entrants. And it builds on trends of weaker mobility, poorer matching and slower reallocation.
This has three broad macroeconomic consequences.
Higher unemployment may do less to ease wage pressures
First, the interaction between the cyclical and structural stories matters for how we interpret the rise in unemployment.
The cyclical loosening in the labour market has been gradual, occurring mainly through slower hiring rather than abrupt layoffs. But it has happened against the backdrop of a labour market in which people are moving less readily between jobs, industries and skill levels. The combination of those factors presents a risk that jobseekers are not matched quickly enough with the opportunities that are available.
That risk is greater because the slowdown in labour demand has been uneven. Vacancies have fallen much further in some sectors than in others. Adjustment therefore requires more workers to move between industries and occupations at a time when such moves have become less common.
In a more mobile labour market, imbalances between labour demand and supply can be resolved more quickly. Displaced workers find new jobs and compete for available positions. Unemployment then represents a readily available pool of labour, which restrains wage growth.
But if jobseekers are not well matched to the vacancies available, a given rise in unemployment may exert less downward pressure on wages. Unemployment could remain higher for longer without producing the easing in wage pressure that we would ordinarily expect.
That may help explain why wage growth has remained relatively strong even as vacancies and other quantity indicators have weakened. As I showed earlier, pay growth has fallen substantially from its post-pandemic peak. But underlying wage growth remains at the upper end of the range consistent with the inflation target, while forward-looking indicators point to continued strength into next year. That degree of wage pressure sits somewhat uneasily alongside the apparent weakness of the labour market. It reinforces the case for looking closely at whether all the weakness in the quantity indicators reflects a general shortfall in labour demand, or whether some reflects poor matching between jobseekers and the opportunities available.
In the language of our forecast, a persistent reduction in the labour market’s ability to match people with jobs would mean a higher equilibrium unemployment rate (or NAIRU), at least in the short-term. The gap between unemployment and its equilibrium rate would then be smaller than the rise in headline unemployment would suggest.
Given the relatively moderate rise in unemployment so far, I do not think that the equilibrium has changed materially. But these dynamics affect how I interpret the loosening we have seen. If unemployment were to rise further, I will pay close attention to whether that is easing wage pressures or instead revealing the limits of the labour market’s ability to move people quickly into new jobs.
Weaker mobility can reduce productivity and growth
Second, slower labour market reallocation can lower productivity and growth. This has long been recognised in the academic literature. Reallocation enables workers to move to the firms, sectors and occupations where their skills are most highly valued.
Moving up the job ladder is also an important source of earnings growth. Job switchers tend to receive significantly larger pay rises than those who stay with the same employer (Chart 18). The prospect of workers moving can also improve the bargaining power of those who stay, because retaining staff becomes more difficult for employers when alternative opportunities are readily available.

Chart 18: Pay growth of job switchers and stayers

Footnotes

Source: ONS, Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings and Bank calculations.

At the macroeconomic level, job moves can generate productivity gains by producing better matches between workers and employers. Where pay rises reflect those gains, they do not create additional inflationary pressure. Research suggests that moves near the bottom of the job ladder are primarily productivity-enhancing, while moves near the top are more likely to add to wage pressure without generating equivalent productivity gains (Moscarini Opens in a new window & Postel-Vinay, 2023 Opens in a new window).
When reallocation slows, matching deteriorates, human capital accumulates more slowly and productivity suffers. Declining mobility may therefore reflect a labour market that has become less effective at allocating people to the work in which they can be most productive. Allocative efficiency plays an important role in long run productivity growth. Decker et al., (2017) Opens in a new window
Lower turnover is not unambiguously bad. A slower pace of structural change can bring with it fewer involuntary job losses (Cominetti Opens in a new window et al., 2022 Opens in a new window). It is also possible that turnover is lower because better recruitment technology may have reduced the number of very short-lived and unsuccessful employment relationships. Some research has argued that much of the decline in turnover reflects fewer jobs lasting only one or two quarters (Pries and Rogerson, 2022 Opens in a new window).
That may be part of the story, including for the UK. But it sits uncomfortably with wider evidence that matching efficiency has if anything declined over time (Barlevy Opens in a new window et al., 2024 Opens in a new window, or Pizzinelli and Speigner, 2017 for the UK). And with newer evidence suggesting that fewer moves do not simply reflect workers becoming more content to remain where they are. Workers report lower job satisfaction and fewer opportunities for progression (Slaughter, 2026 Opens in a new window). Workers still want better jobs, but a less mobile labour market is providing fewer opportunities to obtain them.
Lower productivity resulting from a less mobile labour market would reduce the economy’s supply capacity over time. That would mean lower growth and, for a given level of demand, greater inflationary pressure. Of course, all else is not equal. How the longer-term effects of lower mobility will sit against the potential productivity gains from the adoption of AI across the economy is uncertain.
The long-term effects on growth are particularly important because they are concentrated among young people. Missing the first steps on the job ladder delays the accumulation of skills and experience. If a large cohort remains detached from work for longer, future labour supply and productivity will be lowerfootnote [3]. A cyclical shortage of entry-level jobs can therefore become a structural loss of productive capacity.
The Government has recognised these challenges and is considering the interaction between young people’s health, skill, work and opportunities. Addressing them would strengthen the economy’s productive capacity and resilience. The forthcoming report from the Alan Milburn’s Young People and Work Review will be an important milestone.
A less mobile labour market is less able to adapt
The third macroeconomic consequence is that lower mobility makes the economy less resilient to shocks and structural change. A fluid labour market absorbs change by moving people from contracting activities towards expanding ones. A rigid one turns change into longer spells of unemployment, lost skills and persistent mismatches.
That matters particularly at a time of rapid technological change. Over time, artificial intelligence is likely to alter the demand for labour across sectors, the tasks people perform and the skills employers need. The eventual adjustment is therefore likely to involve more than simply fewer jobs in certain occupations (Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2019 Opens in a new window; Autor and Thompson, 2025 Opens in a new window).
The contribution of AI related sectors is increasingly visible in UK growth. Bank estimates show that AI-related activity has accounted for around 0.5 percentage points of GVA growth since the beginning of 2026.footnote [4] After allowing for these sectors’ usual contribution, the excess is around 0.3 percentage points – just under one fifth of total GVA growth (Chart 19). Using a more recent historical benchmark gives a similar estimate. This suggests that AI-related activity is becoming increasingly apparent in the UK growth data.

Chart 19: AI-related sectors have boosted growth recently

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

This is consistent with the results in the Bank’s DMP survey. Business leaders are increasing their investment in AI, and expect AI to raise productivity meaningfully over the next few years. They expect this effect to be split broadly equally between increasing output and reducing employment.
Again the effects may fall disproportionately on young people. Some emerging evidence points to weaker hiring of younger workers in occupations most exposed to AI (Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, 2025 Opens in a new window), although other changes, including remote working, may also be contributing (Lambert and Schindler, 2026 Opens in a new window).
Adjustment through fewer vacancies rather than redundancies may be less visible, but it is not necessarily less consequential. If AI takes on tasks traditionally performed by junior staff, it could remove not only an entry-level job but also the opportunity to learn, acquire experience and progress to more skilled and higher-paid work.
On the flip side, there is a more positive possibility. Future cohorts of young people may become more sought after as AI changes the nature of work and demand shifts to AI native employees. But that will depend on the skills they acquire and the opportunities available to put those skills to use.
For the wider economy, the nature and timing of the adjustment matters as much as its eventual scale. If productivity gains come through quickly, they could support growth and real incomes while easing inflationary pressure. But if displacement comes first, while investment, new tasks and retraining take longer, the transition could involve higher unemployment without a corresponding easing in inflation. Who gains matters too. If lower income workers do not benefit, then overall demand may go down. Higher income gainers tend to save more of their income.
Even if new jobs ultimately offset those displaced, they may not emerge at the same time, in the same places, or require the same skills. The labour market’s ability to adapt and move people towards new areas of opportunity will be critical. Greater labour market mobility would reduce the risk that the pace of technological change outruns the capacity of workers and firms to respond.
Monetary Policy
Since I’m speaking at the Bank of England Watchers Conference at a challenging time for inflation, I want to finish by setting out how I am thinking about policy and the outlook following last weeks’ decision.
The framework we are using to think about the impact of the global energy price shock remains the same (Table A). The shock affects inflation through four main channels: direct, indirect, second-round and demand effects. Those channels operate at different speeds and can point to different policy responses. The appropriate stance of monetary policy depends on their balance.
We continue to learn about both the size of the shock and the way it is passing through the economy. Since our assessment in July the energy price shock has proved larger and more persistent. That has increased the direct pressure on inflation, raised the prospect of greater indirect effects as higher costs pass through supply chains, and increased the risk of second round effects through wages, prices and inflation expectations.
At the same time, the offset from weaker demand has so far been smaller than expected. Household spending and business activity have held up better than I anticipated. That resilience is welcome. But it means the shock is producing less disinflationary pressure through the demand channel.
The balance of the four channels has therefore become less favourable for inflation. The inflationary effects of the shock are larger, while its disinflationary effect through weaker demand has been more limited.

Taking these developments together, at our meeting last week, the MPC voted by a majority of 8–1 to increase Bank Rate by 25 basis points to 4%. The scale and duration of the energy shock have generated sufficient inflationary pressure in the pipeline to warrant an increase now. The resilience in activity pushes in the same direction for inflationary risks.
Looking forward, the appropriate path for policy will depend on how the shock continues and how it propagates through the economy. As our scenario analysis illustrates, a variety of alternative paths for the economy are plausible, with different policy implications.
We must be mindful of the uncertainties and risks. The absence of second round effects may be telling us something about the ability of businesses to pass on costs in a weakening economic environment. There is a risk that households and firms exhaust their short-term means of adjusting to cost pressures as the cumulative effects of higher energy costs and tighter financial conditions build. Consumer demand and business activity could then weaken, increasing unemployment and reducing inflationary pressures. The evidence of economic resilience to date sits counter to this, but we cannot dismiss this risk, and it forms the basis of our downside scenario.
My own judgement is that, at present, the balance of risks to inflation remains to the upside. The energy shock has lasted longer and become larger than expected, activity has been more resilient and recent data suggest that underlying disinflation may have stalled. The conditions for persistent inflationary dynamics over the medium-term are crystallising. That warranted an increase in Bank Rate last week. In the absence of evidence of weaker inflation pressures, I continue to think there is likely to be a case for a further increase in rates in the near term.
But that judgement is conditional. This is not just about the conflict and its consequences for energy costs. But also how those feed through to price and wage setting more broadly across the economy. The policy judgement does not depend on a single indicator or variable. It will depend on how the combination of data on pricing, activity and slack come together alongside energy and related prices.
That, together with the considerable uncertainty around the outlook, is a reason to proceed gradually rather than trying to anticipate today the full policy adjustment that will ultimately be needed to return inflation sustainably to target.
Conclusion
Let me conclude.
The UK labour market has been more resilient than expected. Unemployment has risen only gradually and redundancies remain relatively low. But that aggregate resilience conceals a more troubling picture. Firms are hiring less, people are moving between jobs less often and young people are finding it particularly difficult to gain a foothold on the job ladder.
That matters for monetary policy. If those looking for work are poorly matched to the jobs available, higher unemployment may do less to ease wage pressures than it has in the past. It also matters for the economy’s longer-term prospects. A less mobile labour market makes it harder for people to find work in which their skills are best used, weakening productivity and growth.
And it matters for the economy’s ability to adapt. Artificial intelligence could bring substantial gains in productivity and living standards. But realising those gains will require people to move towards new tasks, new skills and new opportunities. If that adjustment is slow, the costs could arrive before the benefits.
The labour market is not standing still. Millions of people still find work and change jobs every year. But it is moving more slowly. Too many people are struggling to get in or move on. The challenge is not simply to keep unemployment low. It is to help the labour market shift up a gear.
In setting monetary policy, I will continue to look beyond the headline numbers: at whether hiring is recovering, whether people can move towards the jobs available, and whether labour market weakness is genuinely easing wage and inflation pressures. That evidence will shape my judgement of how much further monetary policy needs to go to return inflation sustainably to the 2% target.
I would like to thank Maria Balgova, Fabrizio Cadamagnani, Stuart Campbell, Gokce Karasoy Can, Douglas Rendle, Michal Stelmach, Jagdish Tripathy, Hassana Babangida and Brad Speigner for their work in preparing this speech. I am also grateful to Adrian Paul, Chris Young, Harvey Daniell, Ambrogio Cesa-Bianchi, James Bell, Ken Clark, Swati Dhingra, Sarah Breeden, Rohan Churm and Rebecca Maule for helpful comments.

articles.title: Aave’s Proposed V3 Core Cleanup Targets Riskier Collateral
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Aave Moves to Deprecate More Assets as Protocol Cleanup Continues

Written by:

Zack Pokorny
Research Associate

Topics

DeFi

Ethereum

research • November 13, 2026

Aave Moves to Deprecate More Assets as Protocol Cleanup Continues

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.WHAT HAPPENEDThis week LlamaRisk, the primary risk service provider to the Aave DAO, set forth an Aave Request for Comment (ARFC) to begin freezing, migrating, and offboarding a collection of assets from Aave V3 Core, the top DeFi protocol’s most widely used version. The move would be a continuation of a larger campaign by the protocol to tighten its operational risk in the wake of the KelpDAO exploit from April [1][2]. The cleanup effort has also included introducing a framework for assessing protocol risk, deprecating assets with little adoption and implementing updated oracle designs for tail assets on the protocol.Now, LlamaRisk is calling to purge V3 of assets with the following characteristics:Restaking exposure: assets whose backing is delegated to secure other services or networks. rsETH is the main example on the list.Leveraged wrapping strategies: assets where most of the backing is itself a leveraged position in another asset, so the collateral and its underlying move together under stress.Derivatives strategies in the backing: staked or wrapped assets where part of the backing goes into derivatives beyond simple hedging, such as covered-call writing.Custom non-custodial bridge designs: wrapped assets whose backing is held by a purpose-built signer or enclave network rather than an established custodian.Reserves with limited demand: positions too small to justify ongoing maintenance, regardless of asset quality.Issuer risk: issuers with insufficient operational and security resourcing relative to the size of their exposure on Core, as judged by the Aave Risk Framework.The significance of this move rests on the sheer size of the assets recommended to be offboarded. At the time of LlamaRisk’s governance post, it covered $1.33 billion of collateral assets and $1.03 billion of borrowed assets (roughly 8% of outstanding borrows on V3 Core). This potentially poses monumental operational efforts to get the assets migrated and offboarded and could crimp Aave revenue if not migrated effectively. Most of the size comes from assets used in looping strategies (i.e. liquid staking and liquid restaking tokens used to gain leverage to Ethereum’s staking rate). The proposal primarily targets ETH liquid staking/restaking tokens on a USD basis for removal. As demonstrated by Galaxy Research, the strategies in which these asset types are present pose acute risk to Aave in that they carry high amounts of leverage by users borrowing close to their liquidation thresholds. As a result, even small deviations in price as a result of issuer shortcomings can have large implications for Aave.It’s worth noting that Aave is not rejecting these assets outright. The overarching plan is to make V3 Core a place for pooled blue-chip asset lending and borrowing, while V4, which has greater flexibility around risk siloing, can house a fuller spectrum of assets.OUR TAKE Net, this would be a positive step for Aave, and DeFi at large, to take. Aave is now building a more formal view on how assets are constructed and setting risk parameters that align with it, using past failures as a guide. The risk doesn’t fully disappear, however. The attack surface for the assets that remain active will still exist, and attackers will keep finding new angles of exploitation, possibly using AI assistance to break through.This is why collateral listing is a security decision. Lending markets have been a popular route for attackers to turn forged and stolen assets into something they can keep at market value, by converting collateral into liquid assets instantly, at oracle prices, with no real slippage outside of loan-to-value parameters (and the assets they pilfer come at the expense of protocol liquidity providers). In the KelpDAO exploit, attackers minted approximately 116,500 unbacked rsETH tokens and used them as collateral to drain real wrapped ether from Aave’s pools, leaving roughly $200 million in bad debt. In the October Binance exploit, the attackers held USDT that Tether could freeze, so they deposited $60 million of USDT into Aave V3 and borrowed $44.6 million of wrapped ether around 40 minutes before the first freeze. That position stayed overcollateralized, but suppliers’ WETH ended up with the attacker, and recovery now depends on collateral that blacklisting the attacker’s wallet could not automatically retrieve from the pool.From this perspective, the updates being proposed to Aave’s collateral set are about protecting liquidity providers (LPs). For example, on Aave V3 Core every WETH and stablecoin supplier underwrites every listed collateral asset at the same pooled rate, while the extra yield from riskier collateral mostly goes to the borrowers looping it rather than to the suppliers carrying the risk. Narrowing V3 Core to a tighter set of blue-chip collateral would rebalance this trade. LPs would take less tail risk for the same return and attackers would have fewer routes to liquidatingtheir positions into desirable, censorship-resistant assets. What makes this repositioning possible is V4. Before Aave’s latest version launched, its choice was binary: list an asset and have every supplier underwrite it or turn it away and lose the business. V4 removes that tradeoff. Each collateral asset sits in a “spoke” with its own caps, and borrowers pay a premium in proportion to their collateral risk, so suppliers are paid for what they underwrite and exposure to any one asset is bounded and becomes a more explicit choice. That frees V3 Core to concentrate on blue chips while collateral assets the protocol views as riskier can be siloed off and be more compensatory to LPs.The open question around the proposal is migration, and the risk stays in the meantime. A freeze would stop these markets from growing and cut off new collateral as a route for attackers, but it wouldn’t remove the exposure for LPs already on V3 Core. That will only disappear when the borrows backed by these assets are repaid or moved. rsETH has been frozen since April and still backs over $600M of WETH debt, so this process is likely to be slow, and suppliers will carry the legacy risk until it’s done. Notably, LlamaRisk proposed reflecting the Emode configurations of collateral assets being deprecated across those that will remain on the platform (e.g. rsETH’s emode configs will apply to weETH, wstETH, and cbBTC), so borrowers and loopers can swap out their collateral assets to maintain a loan with the same configuration. The plan would work optimally only if V4 absorbs the demand V3 Core is pushing out, or if borrowers swap out deprecated collateral assets for retained ones. If borrowers move to V4 or swap into retained Core collateral, Aave will keep the business and shed the risk. If they leave, Aave will give up revenue to competitors willing to take the risk (a scenario which could also be read as the premium of taking risk being removed from protocol economics). LlamaRisk is betting on the first outcome and moving slowly to get there: positions are frozen rather than forced out, and harsher levers, like higher borrow rates on the leveraged loops that get netted out through incentive programs for users not using collateral on the chopping block, are held back as a last resort. Nonetheless, slowness is a reasonable price given the magnitude of the plan and the possible long-term benefits it should bring to V3 Core and the Aave product consortium generally.

The "Handbook" is a must-have for practitioners, policy makers, academics, and government agencies. It is available as a single volume in print or digital formats, and as chapters for modular use. Additional tools, data and background information are available at worldbank.org/governmentanalytics.

“Governments have long been assessed using aggregate governance indicators, giving us little insight into their diversity and how they can practically be improved. This pioneering handbook shows how microdata can be used to give scholars and practitioners granular and real insights into how states work, and practical guidance on the process of state-building.”
—Francis Fukuyama, Stanford University, author of State-Building: Governance and World Order in the 21st Century

-

"The Government Analytics Handbook is the most comprehensive work on practically building government administration I have ever seen, helping practitioners to change public administration for the better.”
—Francisco Gaetani, Special Secretary for State Transformation, Government of Brazil

—James Robinson, University of Chicago, coauthor of Why Nations FailPublicationData for Better Governance: Building Government Analytics Ecosystems in Latin America and the Caribbean (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2024-11-25) Santini, Juan Francisco; Sacco Capurro, Flavia; Rogger, Daniel; Lundy, Timothy; Kim, Galileu; de León Miranda, Jorge; Cocciolo, Serena; Casanova, ChiaraGovernments in the Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) region face significant developmental and institutional challenges, such as slowing growth, fiscal constraints, and inefficiencies in the public sector. At the same time, governments have invested significantly in government technologies (GovTech), making LAC a global pioneer in management information systems (MISs). This investment creates an opportunity for governments to leverage MIS data to strengthen the functioning of government and achieve development goals—that is, government analytics.

This report provides a conceptual framework to assess and provide guidance on the regional government analytics agenda and how to harvest the benefits of GovTech investments. It examines how government analytics can inform policy making and improve accountability and efficiency, drawing on survey data and successful applications of government analytics. The report also explores the enabling conditions for government analytics—data infrastructure and analytical capabilities—and how to strengthen them. Finally, it provides practical guidance on how to develop a holistic government analytics agenda.

reduce the impact of disasters is based on the task of
improving conditions of use and occupation of territory.PublicationFrom Policy to Practice: Tools for Climate-Responsive Management of Public Procurement and Public Assets in Brazilian States (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2026-03-31) World BankThis report presents a practical, action‑oriented framework to support Brazilian states in translating climate policy commitments into effective implementation through public procurement and public asset management. Developed under the World Bank’s Whole of Economy (WOE) Program, it addresses the persistent gap between policy formulation and operational practice at the subnational level. The guide combines analytical foundations with a comprehensive set of tools designed to integrate climate mitigation, adaptation, and sustainability considerations across the full life cycle of procurement and public assets. It covers institutional assessment, sustainable procurement planning, climate‑responsive asset management, and sustainability reporting, aligned with national legislation and international best practices. By promoting evidence‑based decision‑making and continuous improvement, the report aims to strengthen efficiency, transparency, and climate resilience in state‑level public management.PublicationThe Burden of Road Traffic Injuries in Brazil: Evidence for Policy (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2025-09-08) Lamas, C.B.; Caldeira, G.P.; Obelheiro, M.R.; Bastos, J.T.In 2023, Brazil recorded more than 34,000 fatalities due to road traffic injuries (RTIs). Most of the victims were traveling by motorcycle. This assessment of the burden of RTIs, disabilities, and deaths consists of: (1) a road safety analysis using available official data in Brazil; (2) a computation of globally recognized metrics for assessing the burden of disease, including years of life lost (YLL), years lived with disability (YLD), and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs); (3) a comprehensive cost analysis of traffic crashes in Brazil to estimate expenses related to medical care, hospital stays, production losses, human and administrative costs, property damage, and other traffic-related costs; and (4) the collection and analysis of primary data on RTIs from hospital surveillance and the monitoring of crash victims after hospital discharge—as assessed one and three months after discharge.

Key findings from assessing the burden of RTIs in Brazil using global metrics found that, in 2021–22, RTIs and associated deaths resulted in 1.7 million YLL, 637,000 YLD, and 2.34 million DALYs in Brazil. Males accounted for the majority of the total DALYs at 83.7 percent. Motorcyclists contributed to 55.5 percent of total male DALYs, and 39.0 percent of DALYs among women. An estimate of the total costs of road traffic crashes in Brazil—factoring in medical expenses, hospital care, production losses, human costs, administrative expenses, property damage, and other costs—reveals that the total cost of traffic crashes in Brazil is an estimated US$61.3 billion per year, representing 3.8 percent of GDP. Intangible human costs represent 57 percent of the total cost, while production losses make up 17 percent of the total cost. Based on these and other findings from hospital surveys, the study recommends that Brazilian policymakers: (1) embrace road safety as a high political commitment; (2) shift road design culture and practice; (3) implement evidence-based policy from data-driven analysis; and (4) manage exposure through safer modal split.
