The President of the World Bank Group and Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors submit the Annual Report, together with the accompanying administrative budgets and audited financial statements, to the Board of Governors.PublicationWorld Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2026-08-04) World BankThe World Development Report 2026 assesses what artificial intelligence (AI), as a general-purpose technology, means for 5.6 billion people living in low- and middle-income countries and how it could address development challenges that have resisted solutions for decades. Advancing the AI frontier that relies on semiconductors, data centers, AI-ready training data, and top-level research talent is out of reach for most developing countries in the near term. But adopting AI that is available in the market is not enough because AI’s effectiveness depends on the local context. Adapting AI to solve defined problems in developing countries can do in a decade what might have otherwise taken a century – diagnosing disease, growing small businesses, advising farmers, and delivering public services.

To seize AI’s potential, governments will need to keep strengthening the analog and digital complements that power AI solutions: electricity, internet connectivity, and foundational skills, but also access to compute infrastructure and local language data. Countries will also need to establish frameworks to procure, monitor and evaluate AI applications so that pilots that work well can be deployed on a larger scale. To manage the risks, countries can leverage voluntary standards to facilitate trustworthy AI and turn to existing regulations when markets fail to protect people against the harms of AI. This report urges policy makers in developing countries to be blinded by neither the hype nor the hysteria surrounding AI in the global headlines. It reminds them instead that adopting and adapting AI—with care but without delay—and eventually advancing AI could enable developing countries to solve problems that have resisted solutions for decades.PublicationGlobal Economic Prospects, June 2026 (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2026-06-11) World BankThe global economy is facing a major shock as the Middle East conflict drives sharp energy price increases. Global growth is projected to slow to 2.5 percent in 2026, with emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) facing the weakest per capita income growth since the pandemic. The effects across EMDE regions differ based on direct impact of the conflict, energy exposure, and policy buffers. Risks to the outlook remain skewed to the downside and include escalating hostilities, further commodity market disruptions, and additional geopolitical strains, while broader adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) offers some upside. Policy action is critical: globally to safeguard energy and food security and advance the energy transition, and domestically to control inflation, strengthen fiscal sustainability, and support job creation through investment in physical, human, and digital capital. Compounding pressures from the energy shock, rising debt is driving up sovereign borrowing costs for EMDEs, particularly for those most indebted, underscoring the need for stronger revenue mobilization and improved debt management. Commodity-exporting EMDEs can improve their fiscal resilience by using credible fiscal rules, maintaining well-governed sovereign wealth funds, and diversifying revenue sources to better manage commodity price cycles.PublicationEnABLE Social Inclusion Framework for Results Based Climate Finance Initiatives: Enhancing Access to Benefits while Lowering Emissions (Washington, DC: World Bank, 2025-07-01) World BankThe EnABLE Social Inclusion Framework for Results-Based Climate Finance Initiatives was devised as a key input into the Social Inclusion Strategy and Action Plan of the Enhancing Access to Benefits while Lowering Emissions (EnABLE) trust fund. The framework draws on research undertaken by the scientific community through studies financed by the Forest Carbon Partnership Facility, as well as interviews with practitioners and stakeholders around the world, including civil society organizations (CSOs), representatives of Indigenous Peoples (IPs) and traditional local communities (LCs), and World Bank project teams. The framework is primarily intended to function as a resource for World Bank and other practitioners involved in preparing, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating EnABLE programming, particularly in terms (1) of establishing a common understanding of social inclusion in the context of results-based climate finance (RBCF) and carbon crediting, and (2) developing context-specific operating approaches and strategies. As such, the framework is used by the EnABLE Secretariat and its development partners to identify priority areas and activities for resource allocation and to ascertain whether, to what extent, and how progress toward social inclusion is occurring. The framework can also be applied more generally to carbon crediting initiatives beyond EnABLE and World Bank operations.

articles.title: Principals and Agents – speech by Jonathan Hall
articles.text:
Principals and Agents – speech by Jonathan Hall

Given at CFM-Imperial Workshop on Quantitative Finance (hosted by Deutsche Bank)

Published on
11 November 2026

In his final speech as an external member of the Financial Policy Committee, Jon Hall considers the growing use of AI agents in finance and the potential implications for financial stability. Drawing on principal-agent theory and the Bank of England’s own institutional framework, he discusses how access controls, monitoring and other safeguards could help manage the risks as AI agents become more capable.

Speech
This will be my final speech as a member of the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee (“FPC”). Naturally, that makes me want to reflect on the lessons learned whilst working as a public servant at the Bank. But I also want to look forward and discuss one of the challenges the FPC is likely to face in the years ahead – the growing use of AI agents in finance.
Fortunately, I can do both, as there is a common denominator: the Bank and an AI agent are both delegates in a principal-agent relationship. The Bank of England provides not only proof that delegating authority to powerful agents is not a new issue, but also a framework for how to ensure an “agent” remains transparent, accountable and subject to appropriate constraints.
Of course, AI adoption also brings new challenges, not least the speed and scale at which agents can act and interact. Some guardrails will need to evolve. But by managing risk through both top-down supervision and bottom-up model control, our regulatory framework should be resilient to the adoption of AI technologies.
My remarks will focus mainly on how to mitigate the risks of misalignment between principal and agent as AI becomes more capable. There is, of course, another possible future in which those capabilities fall significantly short of current expectations. That might bring a different set of financial stability risks, particularly given the degree of optimism reflected in market prices. That is a live market issue but not my focus today.

AI risks: a range of possible outcomes

If AI capabilities do continue to improve, then the potential benefits of the technology will be significant. But so will the risks. Whilst investments in monitoring and control won’t be costless, it is only with these investments that individual firms and society realise the upside.
Finally, I should say that this is a follow up to my 2024 speech “Monsters in the Deep?”footnote [1] Since then the use of AI within finance has increased and autonomous trading by AI agents has begun, led by retail investors in non-core markets like crypto and enabled by MCP connections.footnote [2] This remains, however, predominantly a discussion of future risks. The Bank’s recent survey with the FCA found that whilst 80% of respondents use some form of agentic AI only 2% of those agents have broad autonomy.footnote [3] By engaging with the issues now, we can prepare for a potential future world where that latter measure starts to become meaningful.
Delegation and the principal-agent problem
Delegation has many things going for it. It can free up time and resources, making the delegator – the “principal” - more efficient. It can allocate operational elements to specialists, who have the knowledge and experience to execute the task well. And long-term delegation can ensure focus remains on the long-term good, undisturbed by the volatility of short-term incentives and the day-to-day battle for attention. A failure to delegate creates a bottleneck that hinders performance.
But delegation can also be risky. Principals and agents can be misaligned. They can have access to different information sets. Or they can find it impossible to fully specify the problem and its constraints, creating a so-called incomplete contract. The risks can be partially mitigated - through monitoring and control – but this is itself costly in terms of time and resources. So how to proceed?
Fortunately, despite breathless reporting with respect to AI agents, misalignment is not a new problem. In a classic paper, written in 1976, Jensen and Meckling argued that agency costs take three forms: 1) monitoring expenditures by the principal, 2) bonding expenditures by the agent, and 3) the “residual cost” of any divergence between the agent’s actions and those actions that would have maximised the welfare of the principal.footnote [4] Importantly, by spending resources on monitoring and bonding, one can lower both the residual cost and the overall cost.
I will explore the financial stability implications of principal-agent delegation through some case studies. For those wanting to track progress, there will only be three, but the third is the longest!
Case Study I: The Bank of England
One example of a powerful agent with delegated authority is the Bank of England. Here, I will briefly set out the safeguards that Parliament - our principal - has put in place to ensure the Bank always acts in the public interest.
Both theory and the lessons of history tell us that price and financial stability are better safeguarded if they are considered outside the rough and tumble of electoral politics. As Rosa Lastra said, "money should be an element of the constitutional framework of democracy rather than an object of political struggle".footnote [5] But even if you accept this, you may worry that the “unelected bureaucrats” wield too much power. This quick analysis should give you comfort, reducing any perception of a democratic deficit. For those looking for more detail, and a great Christmas present, former Deputy Governor of the Bank Paul Tucker has written an excellent 600page book on this topic.footnote [6]
The Bank of England’s policy committees have what I will call constrained operational independence, where operational independence should be understood as independence with respect to means rather than ends, and the constraint applies to the tools at our disposal. The ends - the narrowly defined mandate and guidance on its interpretation - are subject to clear democratic direction. In the UK this tightly specified goal means that judgement is reserved for execution rather than interpretation.footnote [7] In other jurisdictions the specification is looser. This increases the flexibility of their committees, which may be helpful at times, but also increases the risk of a democratic deficit.
But, in line with Jensen and Mecklings’s analysis and the Nolan principles, Parliament doesn’t rely solely on alignment and tool constraints.footnote [8] They, and the public more generally, also demand that the Bank’s committees conform to high standards of explanatory accountability. This includes transparency in the way decisions are reached - that we make our chain of thought available - and testimony in front of parliamentary committees such as the Treasury Select Committee (“TSC”).
These monitoring requirements are not free for either agent or principal – the production of these documents and the diligent oversight by Parliament require resources of time and effort – but they are necessary to reduce the risk of divergence and to maintain democratic support. As such, they are resources well spent.
In summary, the “independence” of the Bank is constrained by a range of processes and controls, including:

A mandate set out in legislation.
Oversight by Parliament via committees such as the Treasury Select Committee.
Annual guidance from the Chancellor to statutory committees regarding interpretation of the mandate, allowing learning and context-relevant adjustment.
A limited set of tools.
Detailed public reporting to provide transparency with regards views, reasoning and decisions.
A robust process to ensure there are no conflicts (political or financial), including recusals where necessary.
A policy of not commenting on broader issues beyond its remit.

On a personal note, my experience on the FPC is that the alignment is very strong. Although we come from very different backgrounds, and discussions can be robust, everyone fully buys into the mandate and works hard to execute on it faithfully. That’s why I have loved it so much. We also appreciate the importance of transparency and accountability. TSC hearings provide an opportunity for Parliament to question us and challenge our judgements. And events like this one allow us to share our latest thinking and get feedback from experts in the field. The last six years have given me a new-found respect for those that set up the institutional framework.
Case Study II: An AI agent
Although the entities are very different, the same framework applies to any human principal looking to delegate to an AI agent.
In 2024 I discussed model alignment, and I continue to believe that AI agents should be trained to respect the very same rules and regulations as a human employee. Whilst it may be difficult to know the ethical principles with which general models should comply, in finance it is clear. They should comply with the published rules and regulations, and firms should, to the best of their abilities, translate those requirements for the specific technologies and use cases. But this focus on model training is not enough, particularly as it seems that alignment trained through text does not necessarily transfer to agentic behaviour.footnote [9] Therefore, the analysis needs to be augmented in two directions, bringing it in line with principal-agent theory and current AI safety best practice. These are access control and monitoring, which I will discuss in turn.
I think it is fair to say that not all of the safety measures I will outline are being used in production in financial firms today. I would encourage participants to consider what is missing in their controls and to upgrade where necessary as they move to front office and higher stakes deployment. Whilst safety does not come for free, it is in firms’ own interests to reduce their “residual costs”, as they are responsible for the agent’s actions. If the overall costs are too great, then perhaps delegation to an agent is not appropriate.
Access Control:
As everyone here knows, an AI agent is not purely an AI model. It is an AI model wrapped in a harness, and it operates within a series of envelopes and permission structures. If the model is the brain that reasons to decisions, the harness around it supports that reasoning and turns the output into controlled execution. The harness turns an AI model into an AI agent. Amongst other things, the harness specifies the tools available and includes guardrails such as permissions, policies and approvals.
Outside of the harness, at the user-space or operating system level, an AI agent can (and, for high-stakes deployment, should) sit in a sandbox. This further constrains the actions an AI agent can take.

A model becomes an agent when reasoning is connected to tools and execution

Anyone following the Hugging Face incident will know that sandboxes are not fully watertight. They can be undermined if permissioned routes are used in unintended ways or through a “jailbreak”, where an agent locates bugs in the container or operating system and breaks out. But a secure sandbox, configured in line with the Principle of Least Privilege, can a) minimise the possibility that attempted rogue actions will create external harm and b) facilitate monitoring, alerting a manager when prohibited actions are attempted.
Finally, to engage with the external world an AI agent needs to be credentialised. If, for example, it wants to execute a financial transaction on an exchange then it can only do so if it has the appropriate authorisation linked to its unique identity. Fortunately, in financial markets we already have a strong regulatory requirement relating to the identification of algorithms in the UK. This will naturally apply to AI trading agents:
Article 8(3) of UK RTS 22 (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/590)3.
“Where a computer algorithm within the investment firm is responsible for the investment decision in accordance with paragraph 1, the investment firm shall assign a designation for identifying the computer algorithm in a transaction report. That designation shall comply with the following conditions:
(a) it is unique for each set of code or trading strategy that constitutes the algorithm, regardless of the financial instruments or markets that the algorithm applies to;
(b) it is used consistently when referring to the algorithm or version of the algorithm once assigned to it;
(c) it is unique over time.”
This unique identity is a key goal of those in the AI safety community, so it is good to be ahead in this respect. It enables both an audit trail back to the responsible party and a temporary or permanent revocation of access (akin to losing a licence).
As investment firms transition from algos to AI agents, there are two additional factors to consider. First, infrastructure must manage access and tool permissions beyond pure trade execution, ensuring that they are neither overly broad nor overly persistent. And second, permissioning infrastructure must be secure enough to ensure that no rogue agent can steal credentials.
These checks and boundaries, unless compromised, constrain the actions an agent can take, reducing the agency costs borne by the principal.
Monitoring:
If possible, both the internal deliberations and external actions of an agent should be monitored.
Chain of Thought (“CoT”) monitoring has been one of the surprise positives of AI safety so far.footnote [10] For longer chains of reasoning, the model routes intermediate results through a scratchpad, which acts as an externally visible working memory.

Monitoring Chain of Thought

We have been in a bit of a goldilocks zone where, for hard tasks, human understandable CoT increased both performance and safety, but this is somewhat fragile. It could be undermined by training which directly or indirectly reinforces unfaithfulness, or by model improvements.footnote [11] The race is on to make progress on mechanistic interpretability, which monitors and interprets activations and features more directly, before CoT monitoring fails. There seem to have been some interesting developments in this field very recently, but that is beyond the scope of today’s discussion.
The second, and more traditional, form of monitoring is of actions and attempted actions. For this and CoT one of the major issues will be the sheer volume of requests and records. To avoid bottlenecks or alert-management fatigue, firms will need to invest in oversight systems that are scalable and risk based.
Overall, I don’t mean to overstate how easy it is to fully neutralise the risk of a loss of control. This is a difficult problem, and best practice will evolve as capabilities grow. But I also want to push back against any sense of fatalism. The risk and magnitude of harm can be significantly reduced through access restrictions, diligent monitoring and a unique identity.
But even if every firm gets these controls right, does that guarantee a stable financial system? Unfortunately, not.
Case Study III: A swarm of AI agents
That’s all very interesting, you may say, but why is the FPC focused on the riskiness of individual AI agents? Isn’t it supposed to take a more macro view of the financial system as a whole?
Indeed, we are. Specifically, we have the task of identifying, monitoring, and taking action to mitigate systemic risks which increase the likelihood of financial instability.
A stable financial system is one that is able to deliver essential financial services to households and businesses, in bad times as well as good. One service is the provision of liquidity in systemically important markets like government bonds. When multiple financial institutions provide this service in a healthy competitive market, they create a common good, enabling the transfer of financial risk between counterparties and generating valuable financial information on which economic actors can make decisions.
The market is a public good and the service providers are literally the market makers.
This is principal-agent delegation at societal scale. In a market economy, the public, as principal, has delegated the creation of a common good to a swarm of financial market participants. The swarm becomes the agent, and the FPC’s role is to monitor and constrain the swarm, to mitigate risks to that common good.
So, what would cause the loss of this valuable service?
Well, an individual financial institution “fails” to provide the service when it either withdraws from the market or when it shifts to demanding liquidity (for example, rapidly offloading positions into stress). The latter, which is often caused by excess leverage, is more pernicious as it amplifies and transmits shocks.
And a market-wide failure occurs when the (market-share weighted) volume of “failures” exceeds a certain threshold, either because a large individual provider fails to provide the service, or because many smaller providers fail to do so at the same time.
Beyond that threshold there are no longer enough service providers to “make” the market.
The chance of market-wide failure is therefore not only a function of the riskiness of individual institutions but also a function of the concentration and correlation of service providers. The former is easier to get a handle on than the latter. The lesson from the financial crisis is that failures cluster in downturns.footnote [12]
Put simply, there are three dynamics which reduce the health of a financial system, over and above the riskiness of individual institutions:
Dynamic 1: Increased concentration of service providers
Dynamic 2: Increased overall correlation between providers
Dynamic 3: Increased correlation between providers in stress
So, now the financial stability question from an AI perspective becomes clear: How would the delegation of financial service provision to AI agents impact these three dynamics? Would it materially increase concentration or correlation?
I think it is fair to say that at this point we don’t know, but there is a risk that it will. That combination of uncertainty and risk argues for further analysis, both experimental and theoretical, as well as ongoing monitoring of the real world impacts.
Regarding experimentation, the Bank for International Settlements has just launched Project Logos.footnote [13]
The idea is to simulate two broadly matched populations of portfolio managers: one comprising heuristic, rules-based agents with a style that matches the behaviour of a market segment, and the other comprising LLM-based agents prompted to replicate that style. A further population of investor agents will allocate capital. The portfolio manager and investor agents will then make allocation decisions over time in a simulated market.
I will be interested in the answers to a number of questions:

How well can the AI agent match its heuristic pair on day one and how sensitive is it to model type and small differences in prompt?
How much do individual pairs diverge over time?
How correlated are the behaviours of the LLM agents relative to the behaviours of the heuristic agents in good times?
How correlated are the behaviours of the LLM agents relative to the behaviours of the heuristic agents in bad times?

Regarding the theoretical analysis, we can get started right now, and I am interested your opinions.
For dynamic 1 the risk is relatively obvious. Any technology that outperforms in generating returns will, over time, attract more capital and replace historic models. If the benefits of a technology accrue to a small number of providers, then concentration will increase. To some extent this has already happened in many areas such as market making on exchanges, so perhaps the risk that AI adoption makes it even worse is low. Not that that is much of a comfort.
Market concentration is something that we can monitor over time using measures like the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index.

New trading technologies can increase the concentration of liquidity provision footnote [14]

Dynamic 2 is potentially more interesting to discuss, as there are differences in opinion.
One argument against the view that AI adoption will increase correlated behaviour is that sophisticated institutional investors will use AI only for narrow tasks (as illustrated by workflow 1 below) rather than as a generalist (workflow 2), thereby maintaining a healthy separation. This is reinforced by the fact that two further optimisations sit outside the diagram: latency and compute spend.

Correlation: targeted and generalist agents

However, the “bitter lesson” from AI development is that, as compute and data increase, general methods start to outperform human imposed structures.footnote [15] In a horse race, maybe workflow 1 will only outperform for the next couple of model iterations, after which capital allocation will start to flow to workflow 2. This is something we will have to monitor through market intelligence.
Regarding dynamic 3, higher downside tail dependence could be driven by a whole number of factors that become relevant in extreme environments:

General features of foundational models could start to dominate other agent specific factors once the paradigm shifts.
Common failures in models could cause them to all have to reduce the same risk at the same time (as in a flash crash or the bursting of a credit bubble).
Common surprising behaviour in AI agents could cause human managers to shut them down. This raises the question of how the manager will know whether there is a model error or some important, but inscrutable, information in the pattern of prices.

For these risks, aggregate-level tools can reduce instability. Most obvious are circuit breakers, but tools to constrain leverage are also relevant.footnote [16] Over and above these correlated individual “failures”, tail dependence could be driven by emergent multi-agent dynamics. As a general point, the collective behaviour of AI agents is very poorly understood. Their interactions seem to be neither fully rational nor in line with human biases. Research to understand the nuances is ongoing, although each finding risks becoming outdated with the release of a new model.footnote [17]
However, what has become incredibly clear over recent months is that multi-agent dynamics are powerful and capable of causing harm.
For those that haven’t yet read it, I would highly recommend the METR report into the Hugging Face attack.footnote [18] Here I’ll quickly highlight the two features that I found most striking.

Hugging Face: instrumental convergence

Initially, individual agents were working independently on different tasks. But, for whatever reason, around 30% of the tasks were impossible without cheating. The agents' initial goals may have been narrow and idiosyncratic, but when faced with an impossible task they all converged towards the same general goal: to make it look like a problem had been solved even when it was impossible. This is an example of what is called “instrumental convergence”, which was first identified as a risk back in 2008.footnote [19] At this point a weakness in the sandbox became important as it unintentionally allowed communication between the agents.

The development of a hierarchy

The second striking element of the attack was the emergence of a hierarchy within the group of agents, and the significant weight single agents attributed to instructions or information from each other. The failure was, to a large extent, epistemic. The agents converged to a position where they ignored safeguards not because the evidence justified such a position, but because they were biased to conform and respect authority. As can be seen, the first agent was not sufficiently robust to inputs that went against its training.
Could harmful swarm behaviour occur with financial market AI agents? With no constraints, the answer is yes. They could converge over the goal of maximising profit and communicate and collude to achieve that. They could amplify stress through so-called “momentum ignition”, executing trades with the aim of triggering stops from less sophisticated or more constrained (human?) investors.footnote [20] And as discussed back in 2024 and evidenced many times since, agents do engage in collusive behaviour in market pricing experiments.footnote [21]
Many of the mitigants to this are managed at the individual agent level and already covered under regulations. For example, MiFID II currently requires that an algorithm does not contribute to disorderly trading conditions.footnote [22] To ensure AI agents comply with these regulations, managers must tightly control access permissioning, particularly with respect to communication channels.
And importantly, the unique identity requirements will enable an audit trail back to the responsible party and the quarantining of any rogue agent.
There are some forbidden activities, however, that are more difficult to constrain through access permissions. These include tacit collusion, momentum ignition and embedding signals in outputs such as price patterns, volumes or timing.footnote [23] In the short-term the risk will have to be controlled via monitoring, incentivised through the enforcement of current rules on human managers. But in the longer term, as AI capabilities improve, we may well need a more innovative response. footnote [24]
I’ll close my remarks by exploring one such possibility.
Internalising Social Harm
I’ll start with the general idea that public harms are reduced by mechanisms which encourage individual agents to internalise the social costs of their actions - to “internalise the externalities”.
I argued earlier that an efficient market is a common good, because it provides valuable liquidity and price information. Collusive pricing and active shock amplification impose negative externalities by degrading these shared goods.
When an AI agent engages in harmful activity, it does not do so because it is evil, but because of how the principal (who could be) has designed its incentives. The agent’s behaviour is simply the outcome of a system that is becoming better and better at responding to incentives and achieving its goals efficiently. But that does not mean that we should step aside and accept the social costs. Rather it is incumbent upon us to create a better incentive structure such that the function it is minimising includes rather than excludes those external costs.
How could one do that? Well one way, drawing on the broader idea of ‘Guaranteed Safe AI Opens in a new window’, would be to use the incredibly powerful AI models of the future to estimate the ‘market efficiency impact’ of any potential action. footnote [25] I emphasise that this is more of a research project than an endorsed policy proposal. Indeed, it is a research project for those of you in the audience today: if anyone can put flesh on the bones of this idea, you can.
This aim would be narrowly defined: to capture the impact of explicitly prohibited behaviours. For example, it could calculate both the Nash equilibrium price and the price assuming perfect, sustainable competition.footnote [26] Or it could estimate the size of a market move triggered by posting a fake document online or by momentum ignition. The details would need to be worked out but it doesn’t seem too far-fetched. I can imagine doing it myself and I don’t claim to have solved Navier-Stokes!
These calculations could then be used in complementary ways:
Externally, an auditor could use this kind of model to check behaviour. If there was a risk of sanction, perhaps out of a bond held at a trading venue, this would be internalised and improve behaviour.
Internally, a verifier could assure compliance by blocking actions with an estimated market efficiency cost above a certain threshold. As the block vs release boundary could be calculated in advance, this could be integrated into order management infrastructure without delaying execution. This verifier model is perhaps the closest to the original Guaranteed Safe AI proposal.

Internalising social costs: a verifier could block actions whose social costs exceed an agreed threshold

If alignment capabilities improve then a version of this calculation might one day be embedded in training. Free markets champion Milton Friedman once wrote an article called “The social responsibility of business is to increase profits”. But in his closing line he added “… so long as it stays within the rules of the game”. The aim of internalising the calculation would be to align the agent with this nuanced conclusion rather than the sensationalist headline.footnote [27] Of course, it would still have to sit within a framework of monitoring and control, to protect against drift.
I am sure that this sounds overly prescriptive. It does to me too. But perhaps that is because we live in a moral community where there is value in doing the right thing because we choose to, rather than because it is impossible to do otherwise. That’s what makes us moral agents and is why our cars are not restricted to the local speed limit.
But delegating to autonomous AI, whether in financial services or transport, changes that.
I want assurance that my Waymo taxi will comply with the rules of the road. Shouldn’t I also want assurance that my financial agent will comply with rules of the markets?
Conclusion
We may be entering a new age of delegation, but delegation itself is not new.
And neither is the possibility of principal-agent misalignment. That’s why governance, transparency and accountability have always been so important.
Consistent with this, and with recent remarks by Governor Andrew Bailey, I have not been arguing today for new regulations. Rather I have been detailing measures to ensure that the actions of AI agents comply with current regulations.
Whilst investments in monitoring and control won’t be costless, it is only with these investments that individual firms can realise the upside for themselves and for overall growth.
But whatever the future holds, I am confident that the FPC is well positioned to remain an effective agent of Parliament.
Although, I’ll be long gone. Driving off into the sunset in my shiny new autonomous vehicle.
With my seatbelt on.
Thank you for listening and I look forward to your questions.
I would like to thank Harry McHugh for his support drafting this speech. I would also like to thank Andrew Bailey, Sarah Breeden, Carolyn Wilkins, Stephen Blyth, Malek Salisbury-Jones, Amy Lee, Maighread McCloskey, Victoria Monro, Jamie Bell, Michael Salib, Francine Robb, Claire Halsall, Michael Yoganayagam, Henrike Muller, Clare Cowan, Irina Mnohoghitnei, Georgette Graham, and Andy Walters for their comments and assistance.

Asset & Wealth Management

Lazard Asset Management delivers world-class investment solutions and long-term value for our clients.

When clients partner with us, they gain a trusted advocate committed to championing their success and helping them achieve their unique ambitions.As part of Lazard Asset Management, we provide wealth management solutions in the United States through Lazard Wealth and in France through Lazard Frères Gestion.

Lazard Asset Management

At Lazard Asset Management, we have an unwavering focus on delivering differentiated insights and customized solutions for our global client base. Lazard has a distinguished reputation and proven track record for generating alpha, grounded in rigorous investment research and analysis. We focus on high-conviction strategies where differentiated research produces differentiated results.We offer products across a broad spectrum of asset classes, designed for different client types. Our traditional and alternative investment services cover listed equity and fixed income investments in a wide range of global, regional and country specific strategies.

Lazard Wealth

The investment landscape is growing more complex each day, with countless opportunities for you and your family to evaluate.At Lazard Wealth, we help simplify that complexity, working with you to manage, grow and preserve wealth across generations through highly customized investment strategies and tailored advice.Success today requires finding a trusted advisor—someone who can rise above the noise; see the full picture; and provide objective guidance to help you make confident decisions about your future.

Lazard Frères Gestion

Lazard Frères Gestion is the asset management and wealth management company of Lazard Group in France. We serve both institutional and private clients, offering all the flexibility of an entrepreneurial asset management firm, backed by the resources of a large international group.We offer a wide range of investment solutions for our institutional clients and distribution partners: equities, bonds, convertibles, diversified management, and alternative management.Our investment solutions are available through open-ended funds and customized funds, including a range of mutual funds managed by Lazard Asset Management.

Lazard 2030 challenges us to deepen the value we deliver through active management, and that starts with research. Our clients don't just want market exposure — they want conviction, built on a global platform that spans every asset class and every region we operate in.

Chris Hogbin
Chief Executive Officer of Lazard Asset Management

Our Approach

The North American power landscape is evolving
Utilities, hyperscalers, and other offtakers are seeking a broader mix of resources to balance affordability, reliability, and emissions goals – from collocated solar and storage to SMRs and gas. Solar and energy storage are gaining share, bolstered by their cost profile and development timeline. These advantages help meet the surge in demand from data centers and reshored manufacturing. At the same time, geopolitical volatility and supply-chain pressures are reshaping market conditions.
In this environment, utilities, developers, IPPs, and investors need a broad view of the power market to make sound decisions. To reflect this shift, Wood Mackenzie’s longstanding Solar & Energy Storage Summit is expanding to become the North American Power & Renewables Forum.
On the agenda for 2027, we discuss the forces reshaping the power market in North America:
• Can the U.S. achieve energy leadership over the long-term without greater policy consistency?• Tariffs, international conflicts and rising interest rates are adding cost pressures. What level of increase will stifle demand growth?• Has FERC interconnection reform successfully removed blockers to transmission development? Where is further reform needed?• Is USA-made solar and storage cheaper per watt, would it survive without credits, and who absorbs the price difference?• Every major hyperscaler has signed a nuclear PPA; what role will nuclear play in their long-term energy strategy?• To what extent can mature renewable technologies such as wind, solar, and storage contribute to clean firm generation?

Speaking and branding opportunities are now available for 2027

As a commercial partner, your organization will be mixing with the industry decision-makers and influencers who are seeking investment, partnerships, and the latest business enhancing-technologies.

e-STORAGE is the energy storage division of Canadian Solar and a leading energy storage company specializing in the design, manufacturing, and integration of utility-scale energy storage systems. e-STORAGE offers proprietary battery energy storage solutions, comprehensive EPC services, and innovative solutions aimed at improving grid operations. Currently, e-STORAGE operates fully automated, state-of-the-art manufacturing facilities with an annual battery energy storage system capacity of 15 GWh and battery cell capacity of 3 GWh.
https://csestorage.com/

Close

COSSA
COSSA is the leading voice for solar and energy storage in Colorado. As a member-driven nonprofit, COSSA represents a diverse coalition of companies across the clean energy supply chain, from manufacturers and developers to installers, engineers, and advocates. Our mission is to expand solar and storage markets, drive smart energy policy, and generate jobs and prosperity for all Coloradans. Through policy advocacy, regulatory engagement, market development, and member education, COSSA ensures the industry has a seat at the table and a strong future in the state.
https://www.cossa.co/about

Close

Scout Clean Energy
Scout Clean Energy is a leading renewable energy developer-owner-operator headquartered in Boulder, Colorado, responsible for the development of approximately 1,600 MW of operating and under-construction renewable energy assets in the US. Led by renewable energy veterans, Scout is currently developing a pipeline of approximately 21,000 MW of wind, solar and storage projects across 25 states. Scout is a portfolio company managed by Brookfield Asset Management, which acquired Scout in 2022.
https://www.scoutcleanenergy.com/

Close

Let's Share the Sun
Let’s Share the Sun is a non-profit organization dedicated to bringing solar energy to communities in need with little to no access to reliable electricity. Through partnerships, service delegations, and innovative models, we empower individuals and transform lives by providing sustainable energy solutions.

Wood Mackenzie is proud to continue our partnership with Let's Share the Sun to ensure that no victim of domestic violence is left in the dark. Having already equipped four shelters across Puerto Rico with solar PV and energy storage, we are now turning our focus to Casa de Todos. 

Help us bring light and safety to Casa de Todos - Please see further details about the project on the Wood Mackenzie donation page - https://donorbox.org/woodmac-supporting-energy-access-in-pr
https://www.letssharethesun.org/

Close

ES Foundry
Based in South Carolina, ES Foundry is accelerating the U.S. solar industry by onshoring the manufacturing of crystalline solar cells. The company’s state-of-the-art facility in Greenwood produces high-quality solar cells designed to meet the critical needs of U.S. panel manufacturers and address the supply chain demands of developers and EPCs. By offering American-made solar cells, ES Foundry enables customers to unlock an additional 10% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) for domestic content. Backed by a team of seasoned industry veterans, ES Foundry is committed to delivering proven, economical and reliable solar products driving the growth and sustainability of the U.S. clean energy landscape.
https://esfoundrycorp.com/

Close

Thornova Solar
Thornova Solar – US Made. Global Expertise. Reliable Returns.
Founded in 2022, Thornova Solar is a leading FEOC compliant USA-affiliated company with integrated supply chain capabilities, covering the entire production process from silicon wafers and solar cells to modules – based on US-made polysilicon. With our state-of-the-art automated production facilities, Thornova Solar delivers the reliability and performance you expect. We deliver from the US, Kenya or Indonesia – offering the perfect mix and match of DC requirements to achieve the best cost / tax incentive ratio for your projects.
https://www.thornova-solar.com/

Close

Signal Energy
At Signal Energy, we harness creative energy to construct a more resilient future. As a leading and nationally recognized integrated utility-scale energy infrastructure company, we provide full-service EPC (Engineering, Procurement, and Construction) solutions. Signal Energy delivers high-value assets across the power and digital infrastructure sectors, anchored by leading capabilities in solar, battery energy storage (BESS), and high-voltage transmission. Driven by stringent industry standards of safety, quality, and a reputation for on-time delivery, we have successfully built more than 9 GW of generating capacity across 12 states since our founding in 2005. Today, Signal Energy’s workforce of 1,000+ professionals, headquartered in Houston, TX, is committed to de-risking project delivery and ensuring financial outcomes that protect client investments and support the communities we serve.
https://www.signalenergy.com/

Close

Nationwide Transport Services
Nationwide Transport Services is a specialized logistics partner focused on supporting the fast-growing data center and battery energy storage industries. We provide reliable, strategic transportation solutions for critical infrastructure, including oversized equipment, electrical components, backup power systems, and energy storage assets. Our team understands the urgency, precision, and coordination required for high-value, time-sensitive shipments, and we work closely with customers to ensure smooth execution from pickup to delivery. With a strong carrier network, hands-on communication, and a commitment to service, Nationwide Transport Services helps power the projects driving digital infrastructure and energy resilience across the country.
https://ntslogistics.com/

Close

Create Energy
Create is redefining the future of energy with bold, innovative solutions that empower IPPs, developers, EPCs, utilities, communities, and businesses to achieve true energy independence and resiliency. Create develops high performance solar and storage solutions designed to challenge the status quo and drive the next era of the energy sector.
At the center of this approach is OnTrack—a complete, one stop shop solution that enables customers to purchase everything they need directly from Create. By streamlining design, procurement, and installation, OnTrack removes unnecessary complexity and provides a fully integrated path from panel to power. With OnTrack, customers gain simplicity, reliability, and cost savings in a single package—supported by Create’s engineering expertise and long term commitment.

Find out more about OnTrack in the attached PDF.
https://www.create.energy/

Close

Trina Storage
Trina Storage is a global leading battery energy storage system integrator, committed to supporting the energy transition through safe, superior, and cost-effective storage solutions. Based on advanced battery technology, we provide the most reliable energy storage solution – from analyzing the technical challenge, to designing flexible innovations that meet every customer’s unique needs.

With the fast development of energy storage technology and a growing global presence, Trina Storage is well positioned to support the global energy transition. We believe that energy storage is a critical enabler of renewable integration and grid stability. As utilities, developers, and power producers worldwide increasingly adopt energy storage, they face the challenge of identifying partners with proven system integration and large-scale project execution capabilities. Backed by 29 years of global solar experience from Trinasolar, Trina Storage is committed to delivering bankable battery energy storage solutions for utility-scale and hybrid renewable energy projects in the United States and worldwide.
https://www.trinasolar.com/eu/trinastorage/

Close

GridBeyond
GridBeyond is bridging the gap between real-time markets and energy assets, helping businesses thrive in dynamic markets while accelerating the energy transition for a net zero future. Our technology unlocks the latent power within every connected asset - whether its renewables generation, battery storage and industrial load - to ensure each piece can play a vital role in balancing the grid. From advanced demand response to Corporate Power Purchase Agreements and hedging strategies, we unlock new revenue streams and reduce energy costs for industry, while ensuring that green power producers maximise profitability and operational efficiency.

GridBeyond provides a powerful combination of technological excellence, a consultative approach and unrivalled expertise that enables its partners and clients have future-proof access to energy services. Our solutions include Virtual Power Plant (VPP) and Distributed Energy Resource Management Systems (DERMS) to enhance flexibility, resilience, and revenue generation. By connecting Front-of-the-Meter (FTM) assets like renewable energy and battery storage with Behind-the-Meter (BTM) operations, we provide advanced forecasting, control, and energy trading capabilities.
https://gridbeyond.com/

Close

Illumine-i
Illumine International Inc. (Illumine-i) delivers value-engineered solutions to solve critical energy infrastructure challenges, from substation and interconnection design to system optimization and execution support across utility-scale and C&I segments. With hands-on industry experience, we work closely with utilities, developers, EPCs, and IPPs to streamline planning, reduce bottlenecks, and improve project outcomes. In addition to consulting, we offer digital products that enhance design accuracy and accelerate timelines. Our approach focuses on building resilient, high-quality energy assets that improve grid performance, enable faster deployment, and ensure long-term reliability in an increasingly complex energy landscape.
https://www.illuminei.com/

Close

Lens Power & Renewables
Interconnected intelligence across the power value chain.
Assess risk. Make smarter decisions. Strengthen investment strategies.
Our solutions deliver a holistic, 360-degree view of the power value chain, with layers of insight to attract and allocate capital. It's a breadth and depth of information you can't get anywhere else.
https://www.woodmac.com/lens/power-and-renewables/

Close

APA Solar
APA Solar is a leading provider of solar racking and foundation solutions for commercial and utility-scale fixed-tilt and tracker-interface projects. With more than 15 years of advanced engineering experience, APA designs, engineers, and manufactures all products in-house to deliver durable, cost-effective systems optimized for diverse site conditions and rapid installation. As a vertically 
integrated manufacturer, APA continually innovates to reduce hardware and labor costs. Acquired by ARRAY in Q3 2025, APA strengthens ARRAY’s portfolio while maintaining a collaborative, team-first approach with developers, contractors, and EPCs.
https://apasolar.com/

Close

Holland & Hart
At the vanguard of the renewable energy industry for decades, Holland & Hart serves clients in the ever-changing, complex clean energy market.

At Holland & Hart, we are renewable energy industry leaders, serving clients in the complex clean energy market for decades. We help clients capitalize on existing solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, battery, and other renewable energy technologies—as well as innovative new energy opportunities—as part of the global transition to a clean energy economy. We counsel diverse clients—from market newcomers to established companies—on development, construction, procurement, offtake, transactions, and financing. We represent renewable energy buyers negotiating offtake agreements to meet RPS requirements and ESG goals.

Our integrated approach spans tax, environmental permitting, real estate, utility regulation, IP, cybersecurity, and insurance practices. With experience since the industry's inception, we're uniquely positioned to prepare clients for future opportunities in this dynamic market.

Find out more about Holland & Hart’s Renewable Energies Group in the attached PDF.
https://www.hollandhart.com/renewable-energy-and-storage

Close

RavenVolt
RavenVolt, Inc. is a premier nationwide turnkey microgrid EPC firm with a stellar track record across a broad range of energy projects. We have a particular focus on BESS, thermal generator microgrids and custom intelligent switchgear design and manufacture. In the BESS market segment, we cater to both distributed generation and utility projects, serving a broad clientele that includes utilities, IPPs and C&I enterprises. Our project sizes range from 1MW to 100MW and beyond.
https://ravenvolt.com/

Close

Kharon
Kharon helps leading organizations identify a range of sanctions and compliance risks, critical to managing financial crimes, supply chain exposure, export controls, investment risk, and more. Combining cutting-edge technology and data science with industry-leading research, Kharon provides the critical insights required for a comprehensive view of risk and commercial threats.
https://www.kharon.com/

Close

Energy Dome
Energy Dome is a leading provider of innovative capacity solutions for AI infrastructure, powered by its patented CO2 Battery technology. The company’s proprietary system delivers cost-competitive, dispatchable capacity and 24/7 clean power using readily available materials, supporting grid reliability, renewable integration, energy security, and industrial competitiveness. As global electricity demand accelerates, driven by AI workloads, hyperscale computing, and the rapid expansion of data center infrastructure, Energy Dome is advancing the commercial deployment of its technology to deliver reliable, scalable, and lower-emissions power solutions for utilities, energy providers, hyperscalers, and large energy users.
https://energydome.com/

Close

Heliene
Heliene is one of North America's fastest-growing domestic module manufacturers serving the utility-scale, C&I, and residential markets. With an in-house logistics team and remarkably responsive support staff, Heliene delivers competitively priced, high performance solar modules precisely when and where customers need them to accelerate North America's clean energy transition. Founded in 2010, Heliene is recognized as a highly bankable module manufacturer and has production facilities located in Ontario and Minnesota.
https://heliene.com/

Close

Moment Energy
Moment Energy is the world's leading EV battery repurposing company, creating clean, affordable, and reliable battery energy storage systems (BESS) by repurposing retired electric vehicle batteries. Moment Energy works with major automotive companies, including Mercedes-Benz Energy, to support circular economy goals and ensure their batteries are safely used in second-life applications before they are recycled. The team supports utilities, microgrids and commercial customers to improve grid reliability, power EV charging stations and reduce demand charges, all with a sustainable and performant BESS solution made from repurposed EV batteries.
https://www.momentenergy.com/

Close

CALB
CALB is one of the top 5 LFP battery cells and energy storage systems manufacturers. Globally, CALB has already delivered more than 100GWh battery cells for projects located in North America, South America, Middle East and Europe. With strong R&D capabilities and large-scale manufacturing, CALB provides safe, reliable, and high-performance products for utility-scale and commercial applications. With a growing presence in North America, CALB delivers scalable and bankable energy storage solutions, supporting renewable integration and the global energy transition.
https://www.calb-tech.com

Close

Magnum Piering
For over 40 years, Magnum® Piering has been dedicated to designing, engineering, and manufacturing, the most trusted foundation and anchoring products for the Commercial, Electrical Power, Oil & Gas, Renewable Energy and Residential Construction Industries. Magnum® Piering has worked diligently to elevate the standards of the foundation industry with a proven customer support team and through a multi-step quality control system. We are your trusted foundation team.
http://www.magnumpiering.com/

Close

Bachmann Electronic Corp
Bachmann offers a comprehensive range of solutions for wind energy, renewables, energy storage, grid measurement, and control. These solutions include hardware such as controllers, HMIs, software for control and supervision (SCADA) and complete condition monitoring systems (CMS).

Robustness and reliability – Bachmann solutions embody these characteristics, and we therefore perform 100% testing on every single module, including a 48h run-in test. The highly available and durable solutions are designed to withstand the toughest conditions, minimizing both capital and operational expenditure.
https://www.bachmann.info/en

Close

AI Clearing
AI Clearing, headquartered in Austin and founded in 2020, is a global technology leader transforming construction monitoring across renewables, pipelines, and infrastructure. We are the only AI-native solution for solar, wind, transmission lines, pipelines, and civil projects, supporting the full lifecycle from pre-construction through operations. Our platform acts as a single source of truth, integrating drone imagery, CAD/BIM, schedules, and GIS into one environment. Powered by the industry’s largest construction data lake, we deliver automated progress tracking, quality control, and real-time insights in as little as 6 hours—helping teams complete projects 20 days faster, achieve 80% faster inspections, and reduce CAPEX by 4%.
https://www.aiclearing.com/

Close

Hendrix Aerial Cable Systems
Hendrix Aerial Cable Systems, a leader in the electrical utility industry, brings decades of expertise to the renewable energy market. Hendrix spacer cable offers a cost-effective alternative for medium-voltage collector circuits in utility-scale solar and wind applications. By placing multiple circuits on a single pole, you can greatly reduce the right-of-way requirements and eliminate the heat entrapment and de-rating suffered by UG cable. With robust, weather-resistant cables, Hendrix ensures maximum durability and minimal maintenance, making our systems ideal for remote and harsh locations.
https://marmonutility.com/overhead/spacer-cable/

Close

Sieyuan Electric
Sieyuan Electric is a leading power technology company dedicated to "Smarter Power, Better Life." It provides efficient power system solutions across transmission, distribution, energy storage, and digital transformation. With five R&D hubs and over ten manufacturing sites in China, it delivers reliable primary/secondary equipment, power electronics, and EPC services globally.
https://en.sieyuan.com/

articles.title: Lazard’s Levelized Cost of Energy+ (LCOE+)
articles.text:
Lazard’s Levelized Cost of Energy+ (LCOE+)

Lazard's Levelized Cost of Energy+ (LCOE+) analysis was originally developed in 2007 to bring clarity to the evolving cost dynamics of various generation technologies at a time when no industry standard approach existed. It remains a widely cited resource grounded in Lazard's extensive industry expertise and client relationships.

Produced by Lazard’s Power, Energy and Infrastructure advisory group, the LCOE+ gives the sector a common, transparent yardstick for comparing the economics of different power sources. After nearly two decades of annual editions, it offers insight into how technology costs, financing conditions and market pressures shift over time.This 2026 report explores key aspects of energy generation, energy storage and system-level considerations, while reflecting on developments over the past 12 months.

Lazard's 2026 LCOE+ ReportLazard's 2026 LCOE+ report highlights that, despite rising and inflationary cost pressures across all generation technologies, renewables remain the most cost-competitive form of new-build generation on an unsubsidized basis (i.e., without tax subsidies). The report also emphasizes that meeting unprecedented power demand will require both a diverse generation fleet and a thoughtful acceleration of permitting and approval processes. At the same time, rising new-build costs and execution challenges have made replacement capacity more expensive and harder to deliver while load growth drives increased utilization of existing assets, improving their marginal cost relative to new-build LCOEs. Storage costs have also risen this year, reversing recent declines.Read the Report

2026 LCOE+ Report

In today's energy landscape, the relevance of data-driven cost analysis has never been greater. The LCOE+ captures a market defined by unprecedented demand growth, rising costs across every generation technology and an intensifying focus on reliability — making objective, real-world benchmarking more critical than ever for the stakeholders, policymakers and investors shaping the industry's future.

George Bilicic
Managing Director

Dive deeper into lazard's 2026 lcoe+George Bilicic joined the Redefining Energy Podcast to discuss Lazard's 2026 LCOE+ Report and the real cost of power.

Listen Here

We’ve entered a speed-to-power era—demand is outpacing supply, costs are climbing across every technology, and value is shifting to whoever can deliver capacity the fastest, renewables remain the lowest-cost and quickest to deploy resource, but meeting this moment will require a diverse generation fleet.

The income produced by municipal bonds is typically exempt from income taxes at the federal level. Municipal bonds may also be exempt from state and local taxes based on where the investor resides.

In our view, there are many good reasons to invest in the municipal bond market now.
First, muni yields are as high as they've been in 15 years following two years of unprecedented interest rate hikes by the Fed.4
Second, municipal bonds have a long history of low defaults compared to corporate bonds because they fund essential American services.5
Third, the municipal yield curve is steeper than the Treasury yield curve. A steep yield curve means that there is value in duration. Municipal investors who own longer dated munis may be compensated much more than those in longer dated Treasuries.
Fourth, federal, state and in some places local tax rates are high and we don't see them going down. This may provide additional value to the muni tax exemption.

Our high conviction approach to investing aims to deliver a highly competitive yield by exploiting anomalies that exist in the high yield municipal market. The Invesco Municipal Bond team employs a bottom-up, research-oriented approach to generate income-driven total return. Our experienced credit research staff works to uncover value in non-rated bonds, which may offer the potential for higher yield and total return.

We believe in giving investors choices that work for their unique needs. Invesco Rochester High Yield Municipal ETF is an actively managed exchange-traded fund that seeks current income exempt from federal income tax.

We view risk from multiple lenses and manage it using both integrated and independent approaches. First, risk management is embedded within our investment process. Second, multiple governance structures provide independent oversight and monitoring. Third comes senior management and board review.

articles.title: Daily: Rising yields raise the portfolio appeal of bonds and diversified investing
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: The AI sell-off and US midterms: Live at the UBS Disruptive Tech Summit (6 mins)
CIO Live Replay: CIO Asia equity strategists on the AI sell-off and opportunities (30 mins)Thought of the dayHigher global bond yields on recalibrated interest rate expectations and a rebound in appetite for stocks have hurt investors with existing fixed income positions. At the time of writing, the policy-sensitive German 2-year yield stood roughly 17bps higher on the week and was on course for its sharpest weekly rise in two months. And Japanese 10-year yields climbed to their highest levels since 22 October in Asian trading, in tandem with higher US government yields on news that President Trump was not seeking a peace deal with Iran and as investors weighed comments from Federal Reserve President Waller around the possibility of a 50bps rate hike at the Fed's December meeting.But elevated starting yields have restored rather than diminished the appeal of the traditional balanced (60% stock, 40% bond) portfolio. While equities can provide long-term growth, high-quality bonds once again offer meaningful income, potential capital appreciation if growth slows, and a cushion against some equity market declines.Bonds have returned to the core The reset in yields has materially improved the role bonds can play in portfolios. After the global financial crisis, low interest rates left fixed income offering limited income and relatively little protection against an equity market drawdown, while exposing investors to the risk of rising yields. Current higher starting yields matter in several ways. They increase the income available from bonds and provide a greater cushion against negative returns in case rates increase further. They also create scope for capital appreciation if inflation moderates, economic growth weakens, or central banks eventually reduce interest rates. The portfolio role of bonds extends beyond expected returns. High-quality bonds can help preserve capital and may diversify equity exposure when economic growth disappoints. Their senior position in the capital structure also generally makes them less risky than equities issued by the same company.60/40 is stronger, but not invulnerable. The revival of bond yields improves the case for a 60/40 equity-bond portfolio. But it is not guaranteed that bonds will offset every equity decline. The diversification benefit depends partly on why equity markets are falling.High-quality bonds have historically been more effective equity diversifiers during periods of low or stable inflation. If growth weakens and inflation moderates, bond prices may rise as equities come under pressure. If inflation remains elevated and interest rates rise, stocks and bonds can decline together. That distinction is important at present, as investors face several plausible paths for growth, inflation, fiscal policy, energy prices, and geopolitical risk into the year ahead.Completion assets can address different risks. Uncertainty and the need to think in terms of market scenarios makes the case for completion assets stronger. Completion assets can earn their place by doing a specific job that the core may not perform consistently. That might include generating differentiated returns, providing income, reducing sensitivity to equity markets, or helping preserve purchasing power during periods of elevated inflation.Hedge funds may provide alternative sources of return when equities and bonds face pressure at the same time. Real assets can address a different set of risks. Commodities have historically displayed relatively low correlation with traditional asset classes and may benefit when physical supply is constrained or inflation remains elevated. And private infrastructure may offer relatively predictable and potentially inflation-linked income, while providing exposure to long-term investment in electricity networks, data centers, electrification, energy security, and more resilient supply chains.So, the return of meaningful bond yields has made the traditional balanced portfolio relevant again. A diversified mix of equities and high-quality bonds can provide a more credible combination of growth, income, and capital preservation than it could during the low-yield era.We currently rate high grade and investment grade bonds as Attractive. We favor exposure to short- to medium-duration high-quality bonds, while remaining more cautious on longer maturities given fiscal concerns and elevated issuance. We also rate high yield and emerging market bonds as Attractive, supported by elevated yields and, in aggregate, resilient fundamentals.However, 60/40 is a foundation, not a complete answer. We believe investors should also look at commodities, real assets, and select structured strategies as ways to enhance returns, improve portfolio resilience, and best match specific goals with portfolios, subject to careful risk management. Private investments in particular can involve illiquidity, limited disclosure, uncertain cash flows, leverage, capital calls, and blind-pool risk.Finally, portfolio discipline matters as much as portfolio design. A 60/40 US equity-bond portfolio invested in 2020 would have drifted to about 80/20 if left untouched, reflecting the stronger performance of equities. Regular rebalancing helps restore the intended risk profile, reduce unintended concentrations, and prevent recent outperformers from determining the portfolio’s future behavior.

articles.title: Financial resilience in an age of repeated shocks -  speech by Andrew Bailey
articles.text:
Financial resilience in an age of repeated shocks - speech by Andrew Bailey

Given at the Central Bank of Turkey, İstanbul Economic Forum

Published on
08 October 2026

Andrew Bailey says that although the financial system has remained resilient through repeated geopolitical and economic shocks, weaker growth, persistent supply disruptions, rising sovereign debt, leveraged markets and expanding AI-related exposures create risks. Policymakers should therefore pursue sustainable growth, maintain credible monetary and fiscal frameworks, and strengthen core financial markets so they can absorb future shocks without amplifying them.

Speech
The financial system has so far weathered the latest period of uncertainty. But lower growth, repeated supply shocks and changing market structures mean that resilience cannot be taken for granted.
The conflict in the Middle East has created major uncertainty about growth, inflation and interest rates. Existing vulnerabilities in sovereign debt markets, credit markets and asset valuations could crystallise together. The rapid expansion of financing connected with artificial intelligence has created new exposures, while incidents involving frontier AI have underlined the associated operational, cyber and financial risks.
However, an important part of the story so far is economic resilience in the sense that recent supply shocks have hit the world economy at the same time as the potential growth dividends from AI have become clearer.
Moreover, the story of the financial system so far has been one of resilience. Banking systems generally remain well capitalised and we are not seeing funding stress. Despite a succession of economic shocks and heightened volatility, most financial markets have continued to function without a major breakdown in liquidity or trading conditions.
Financial markets have so far withstood significant increases in sovereign bond yields, and most market adjustments have remained orderly. This resilience owes much to the reforms introduced after the global financial crisis. Those reforms are sometimes criticised as burdensome. Today, their value is clear.
But we cannot be relaxed. Experience teaches us that specific problems can emerge even when the wider system appears stable. The lesson of the global financial crisis is that such problems are much easier to manage when the wider system is resilient and the authorities are committed to keeping it that way.
The deeper economic challenge
Behind the immediate risks lie two longer-term developments.
The first is weaker potential growth, driven in many economies by slowing productivity, which determines how rapidly national income and living standards can rise.
The second is the frequency of large negative supply shocks. Covid, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East have each disrupted the supply capacity of economies. Covid was also both a supply and demand shock, with the balance changing over time. But all these episodes were exceptionally large, and they followed one another with unusual speed.
Are repeated shocks the new normal? Central bankers should be wary of becoming political soothsayers. But a more multipolar world, in which economic policy is increasingly an arena for geopolitical competition, may produce more frequent disruptions. We should therefore prepare for a world in which larger shocks are not rare exceptions.
This creates a particular difficulty for monetary policy. A negative supply shock pushes inflation and output in opposite directions, producing weaker output but higher inflation.
The textbook response is to look through a one-off increase in the price level. Interest rates cannot produce more oil or gas, and monetary policy affects the economy with long lags. But looking through a shock is possible only if inflation expectations remain well anchored.
If households and businesses begin to incorporate higher inflation into wage demands and pricing decisions, a temporary shock can become persistent. These second-round effects are slower to emerge. Central banks must make forward-looking judgements and update them as the evidence changes.
The difficulty becomes greater when shocks arrive in quick succession. A recent history of higher inflation can cause people to expect further inflation. The sequencing of Covid and the invasion of Ukraine have made this risk particularly acute.
The interaction with financial stability
Supply shocks can also create tension between monetary and financial stability. Interest rates may need to rise even as economic activity weakens. Debt-servicing costs increase just as household incomes and corporate earnings come under pressure. Asset prices can fall, reducing the value of collateral and restricting the supply of credit.
This is why resilience before a shock is so important. Strong banks and sound household and corporate balance sheets give policymakers room to respond without turning an economic adjustment into a financial crisis.
Fiscal policy faces a related challenge. Lower growth and repeated supply shocks weaken the public finances while increasing pressure on governments to provide support. Higher borrowing costs and weaker growth raise debt-to-GDP ratios. If markets begin to doubt the fiscal trajectory, bond yields can rise further, tightening monetary and financial conditions.
Governments can ordinarily use their balance sheets to cushion a severe downturn and rebuild fiscal space when conditions improve. That is the principle of countercyclical policy. But when shocks become more frequent, underlying growth is weaker, and the succession of shocks leads to a higher level of government debt, this becomes much harder to sustain.
A changing market structure
Global government bond markets have also changed profoundly. They were once dominated by long-term investors, often described as “real money” and “price insensitive”. Today, leveraged investors play a much larger role, while traditional demand for long-duration debt has declined, partly because of changes in pension provision and ageing populations.
This new structure has so far increased the capacity of markets to absorb the additional supply of government debt. But greater absorption has come with greater fragility. Leveraged positions can be unwound rapidly. Losses can trigger margin calls, model-driven repricing and stop-outs, producing further forced selling that can amplify market moves. The buyers are typically more price sensitive.
The same funds may hold large leveraged positions across several countries and asset classes. Deleveraging that begins in one market can therefore spread quickly to others.
The policy response must have several parts.
First, we must pursue sustainable growth. There is no single solution, but major technological advances have historically lifted productivity. Artificial intelligence and robotics can drive scientific discovery, improve efficiency and raise prosperity. Financing that investment is essential. But greater financial exposure to AI also creates risk. If earnings expectations or confidence in the pace of AI adoption were sharply revised, the consequences could spread through equity, credit and sovereign markets. AI safety and financial stability are therefore becoming increasingly connected. Safely deployed, we should see AI as a growth opportunity.
Second, monetary and fiscal frameworks must remain credible. For monetary policy, that means an unwavering commitment to returning inflation to target. I remain sceptical of unconditional promises about future interest rates. The world is too uncertain. But central banks should explain clearly how policy would respond under different economic conditions.
Fiscal policy must likewise be directed towards stability and be seen by markets as credible. Clear frameworks, including fiscal rules, can help contain risk premia when shocks occur.
Third, we must strengthen the resilience of core markets. Greater central clearing, appropriate minimum haircuts and stronger risk management all merit consideration.
There is no quick fix. But the direction is clear: raise sustainable growth, maintain credible policy frameworks, and ensure that financial markets can absorb shocks without amplifying them.
The system has been resilient. Our task is to make sure it remains so.
I would like to thank Nat Benjamin, Sarah Breeden, Karen Jude, Andrea Rosen, Vicky Saporta and James Talbot for their assistance in preparing these remarks.

Andrew Bailey
Governor, Bank of England
