articles.title: Artificial intelligence and European firms: the cost of market-based financing
articles.text: Artificial intelligence and European firms: the cost of market-based financingPrepared by Irene Ferrari, Sofia Gori, Johannes Groß, Fabian Schupp and Sigurd SteffensenPublished as part of the ECB Economic Bulletin, Issue 7/2026.Artificial intelligence (AI) has been the dominant theme in global financial markets since late 2022, with equities in the technology sector outperforming substantially (Chart A). This outperformance has been especially striking in the United States, led by a small group of hyperscalers, and is evident among European firms that occupy upstream positions in the global AI infrastructure buildout. However, AI’s influence on markets extends beyond a narrow set of infrastructure providers and stretches further back in time. Many firms integrate AI into their businesses, either by developing AI-enhanced products or by adopting AI-enabled processes that improve productivity.[1] See, for example, Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020) and Babina et al. (2024). This box therefore introduces a new firm-level measure of AI exposure derived from AI-related discussions in earnings call transcripts. It uses this measure to examine how the AI exposure of European firms is reflected in their equity returns and corporate bond spreads.[2] Earnings calls have previously been used to measure the AI exposure of US firms (see Ca’ Zorzi et al., 2025). Chart APerformance of the STOXX Europe 600 and S&P 500 and their technology subsectors(index: 2 January 2017=100)Sources: LSEG and European Central Bank (ECB) calculations.Notes: The chart shows the levels of European and US benchmark equity indices and their technology subsectors over time. The latest observations are for 15 September 2026.Firms are classified as AI-exposed when their earnings calls link AI to infrastructure provision, product development, or improvements in business processes and productivity.[3] This approach builds on Ferrari et al. (2026). Their prompt allows multi-label classification, anchors AI definitions to the time of each call, and provides a rationale for each flag, aiding interpretability and improving decision quality. Since firms may have an incentive to influence analysts’ perceptions when discussing their AI usage on earnings calls, the model guards against “AI washing” by excluding vague statements that are not explicitly linked to performance. These criteria are applied across STOXX Europe 600 constituents, identifying not only firms that supply AI technology but also firms across all sectors that embed AI in their products and operations. The approach also captures the evolving nature of AI: as the technology matures and diffuses across sectors, firms’ disclosures shift accordingly, allowing a measure grounded in contemporaneous statements to track this evolution. This is valuable given the reliance of analysis on timely identification of AI-related news. Accordingly, AI exposure is measured quarterly from 2017 onwards and treated as time-varying, allowing the analysis to control for firm heterogeneity and sector-specific time variation.[4] The measure correlates strongly with an established sector-level classification provided by Calvino et al. (2024), which combines indicators of AI human capital, AI innovation, barrier-adjusted exposure and AI use. The share of AI-exposed firms has risen markedly since 2022, with AI predominantly mentioned in earnings calls as a source of product innovation and growth (Chart B). 75% of earnings calls mentioning AI refer to product innovation or growth opportunities from an AI-enhanced product offering, while 50% discuss AI-related productivity gains, with some mentioning both. There is clear heterogeneity across sectors and over time: IT firms mentioned AI-related product innovation as far back as 2017, whereas firms in other sectors mainly started to refer to productivity improvements resulting from AI after the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022. This is consistent with the findings of the ECB’s Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises in the euro area in June and December 2025, which show more innovation-oriented cases of AI use in the IT sector and greater emphasis on cost reduction in manufacturing, construction, trade and other services.[5] See Ferrando et al. (2026). Related ECB survey evidence also points to a rapid but uneven diffusion of AI, with around three-quarters of large euro area firms surveyed in 2024 reporting the use of AI in their business operations (Bergeaud et al., 2025). Complementary evidence from the ECB Consumer Expectations Survey shows that the share of workers reporting AI use at work roughly doubled between 2024 and 2026, with substantial heterogeneity across occupations and worker characteristics (Dias da Silva et al., 2026). Chart BShare of AI-exposed STOXX Europe 600 firms and breakdown by AI exposure typea) Overall share(percentages)b) Share by innovation and productivity exposure(percentages)Sources: LSEG and ECB calculations.Notes: The sample includes all STOXX Europe 600 firms and spans from the first quarter of 2017 to the second quarter of 2026. Panel a): quarterly share of earnings calls in which AI is mentioned (left-hand side) and breakdown of earnings calls mentioning AI by exposure type over the sample period (right-hand-side). Panel b): annual share of firms in each Global Industry Classification Standard sector mentioning innovation exposure (left-hand side) and productivity exposure (right-hand side). The 2026 annual share is approximated using the shares for the first and second quarters. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026.Whether AI exposure raises or lowers firms’ financing costs is theoretically ambiguous. AI adoption may boost expected cash flows, lifting equity valuations and reducing perceived credit risk, but only if investors believe that firms are genuinely advancing, and not merely making unsubstantiated claims. On the debt side, AI adoption often requires substantial upfront capital investment concentrated in intangible assets with limited collateral value, potentially raising financing costs. Since these mechanisms operate simultaneously, the analysis examines whether AI exposure is systematically associated with different equity returns and bond financing costs than those faced by firms not exposed to AI.Panel regression evidence points to an equity return premium of around 1.3 percentage points per quarter for AI-exposed firms (Chart C).[6] Since many firms report more than one type of AI exposure, the categories are not mutually exclusive and the analysis therefore focuses on firms’ overall exposure. Quarterly stock returns are regressed on AI exposure flags, controlling for firm-level characteristics, earnings surprises, firm and sector-quarter fixed effects, and sector-specific time trends. This ensures that AI-exposed firms are compared with non-exposed firms in the same sector-quarter, netting out sector-wide movements.[7] Importantly, the premium does not merely reflect the broader tech rally. Excluding the IT sector from the sample leaves the estimated premium similar in magnitude and significance, confirming that the return differential is present across the wider corporate universe. The premium is identified from within-firm variation, comparing the same firm in quarters with and without concrete AI disclosure, net of earnings surprises released at earnings calls and of lagged firm fundamentals and momentum. The regression results align with descriptive patterns in the data: AI-exposed firms recorded higher median annual stock returns than non-exposed firms in most years (Chart C, panel a) and also tended to trade at higher price/earnings ratios (Chart C, panel b). This is consistent with a longer-duration equity profile, whereby much of the value of AI firms is tied to earnings that are expected to accrue far into the future.Chart CStock returns and price/earnings ratios for AI-exposed and non‑AI‑exposed STOXX Europe 600 firmsa) Annual stock market returnsb) Annual price/earnings ratios(percentages)(percentages)Sources: LSEG and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel a): distribution of annual equity returns, weighted by end-of-year market value. Panel b): distribution of annual price/earnings ratios, weighted by end-of-year market value. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026.Non-financial corporate bond markets exhibit a broadly similar pattern to equity markets (Chart D). Panel regressions using quarterly option-adjusted spreads over 2019-26, with bond and issuer-specific controls, show that AI exposure corresponds to spreads that are around 5 basis points tighter – a modest but robust link between AI exposure and a lower market-implied cost of debt.[8] In contrast to the equity findings, none of the three exposure types is individually associated with tighter spreads when entered separately. This suggests that bond markets price overall AI engagement rather than differentiating across specific forms, which is consistent with many firms reporting more than one exposure type. This again aligns with descriptive patterns in the data. AI-exposed issuers consistently exhibit lower spreads than non-exposed issuers, with both the median and interquartile range shifted downward across most years (Chart D, panel a). Exposed firms have also issued a larger share of bonds with maturities exceeding ten years (Chart D, panel b), whereas issuance by non-exposed firms is more concentrated at intermediate maturities. This combination points to more favourable financing conditions, since longer maturities would typically command higher, not lower, spreads.[9] Relatedly, US hyperscalers funding the buildout of AI infrastructure through European corporate debt markets are also found to issue bonds with longer maturities. For these firms, however, AI-related debt issuance is associated with higher, not lower, credit spreads relative to peers, as investors appear to demand a risk premium for the uncertainty surrounding firms’ AI investments. See Duquerroy et al. (2026). Chart DCorporate bond spreads and bond maturity structure for AI-exposed and non‑AI‑exposed STOXX Europe 600 non-financial corporatesa) Option-adjusted spreads(basis points)b) Maturity structure of new bond issuances(left-hand scale: percentages, right-hand scale: percentages per annum)Sources: LSEG, ECB (CSDB, CSEC), ICE, Moody’s Analytics and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel a): annual distribution of option-adjusted spreads over the swap curve. Spreads are winsorised and weighted by the outstanding amount in euro. The sample covers euro-denominated bonds with a residual maturity of between 1 and 30 years, an issued amount above €1 million, and spreads ranging from ‑100 basis points to 3,500 basis points. Panel b): new bond issuance by maturity bucket as a share of the outstanding amount in euro, with the yield to maturity calculated as the average weighted by the outstanding amount in euro. The sample covers euro-denominated bonds with a residual maturity of between 1 and 30 years and an issued amount above €1 million. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026.The findings in this box suggest that AI exposure is positively reflected in equity and corporate bond pricing across the wider economy in Europe. AI’s association with lower market-based financing costs is more widely distributed than the concentrated equity rally in the IT sector suggests. However, this relationship rests on expectations about the technology’s returns. Should those expectations disappoint, valuations and spreads could reprice abruptly and broadly, extending well beyond the firms driving the AI investment cycle. Further analysis is warranted to establish the potential scale of this repricing and its effect on aggregate financing conditions in the euro area.[10] For further information on the valuation risk associated with AI and the potential impact of a correction in US equities on euro area financial conditions, see Andersson et al. (2026). ReferencesAndersson, M., Breckenfelder, J., Corradin, S., Nikolov, K. and Viola, M.A. (2026), “The AI boom: rational enthusiasm or the next dot-com bubble?”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 17 August.Acemoglu, D. and Restrepo, P. (2020), “Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets”, Journal of Political Economy, Vol. 128, No 6, April.Babina, T., Fedyk, A., He, A. and Hodson, J. (2024), “Artificial intelligence, firm growth, and product innovation”, Journal of Financial Economics, Vol. 151, January.Bergeaud, A., González-Torres Fernández, G., Labhard, V. and Sellner, R. (2025), “AI can boost productivity – if firms use it”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 28 March.Calvino, F., Dernis, H., Samek, L. and Ughi, A. (2024), “A sectoral taxonomy of AI intensity”, OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers, No 30, OECD, December.Ca’ Zorzi, M., Lopardo, G. and Manu, A.-S. (2025), “Verba volant, transcripta manent: what corporate earnings calls reveal about the AI stock rally”, Working Paper Series, No 3093, ECB, August.Dias da Silva, A., Lebastard, L. and Sondermann D. (2026), “AI adoption and the productivity promise: what workers report”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 26 August.Duquerroy, A., Furtuna, O., Rahmouni-Rousseau, I. and Vaz Cruz, L. (2026), “Big tech, big debt: when US tech giants tap the euro area bond market”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 31 August.Ferrando, A., Lamboglia, S., Rariga, J. and Schmidt, M. (2026), “Adoption and investment in AI across the euro area: insights from harmonised firm-level data”, Occasional Paper Series, No 395, ECB, July.Ferrari, I., Groß, J., Schupp, F. and Steffensen, S. (2026), “AI Exposure and the Costs of Market-based Financing in Europe: Evidence from Earnings Call Transcripts”, mimeo. See, for example, Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020) and Babina et al. (2024). Earnings calls have previously been used to measure the AI exposure of US firms (see Ca’ Zorzi et al., 2025). This approach builds on Ferrari et al. (2026). Their prompt allows multi-label classification, anchors AI definitions to the time of each call, and provides a rationale for each flag, aiding interpretability and improving decision quality. Since firms may have an incentive to influence analysts’ perceptions when discussing their AI usage on earnings calls, the model guards against “AI washing” by excluding vague statements that are not explicitly linked to performance. The measure correlates strongly with an established sector-level classification provided by Calvino et al. (2024), which combines indicators of AI human capital, AI innovation, barrier-adjusted exposure and AI use. See Ferrando et al. (2026). Related ECB survey evidence also points to a rapid but uneven diffusion of AI, with around three-quarters of large euro area firms surveyed in 2024 reporting the use of AI in their business operations (Bergeaud et al., 2025). Complementary evidence from the ECB Consumer Expectations Survey shows that the share of workers reporting AI use at work roughly doubled between 2024 and 2026, with substantial heterogeneity across occupations and worker characteristics (Dias da Silva et al., 2026). Since many firms report more than one type of AI exposure, the categories are not mutually exclusive and the analysis therefore focuses on firms’ overall exposure. Importantly, the premium does not merely reflect the broader tech rally. Excluding the IT sector from the sample leaves the estimated premium similar in magnitude and significance, confirming that the return differential is present across the wider corporate universe. The premium is identified from within-firm variation, comparing the same firm in quarters with and without concrete AI disclosure, net of earnings surprises released at earnings calls and of lagged firm fundamentals and momentum. In contrast to the equity findings, none of the three exposure types is individually associated with tighter spreads when entered separately. This suggests that bond markets price overall AI engagement rather than differentiating across specific forms, which is consistent with many firms reporting more than one exposure type. Relatedly, US hyperscalers funding the buildout of AI infrastructure through European corporate debt markets are also found to issue bonds with longer maturities. For these firms, however, AI-related debt issuance is associated with higher, not lower, credit spreads relative to peers, as investors appear to demand a risk premium for the uncertainty surrounding firms’ AI investments. See Duquerroy et al. (2026). For further information on the valuation risk associated with AI and the potential impact of a correction in US equities on euro area financial conditions, see Andersson et al. (2026).

articles.title: U.S. Broad Market High Yield
articles.text:
Leveraged Finance

U.S. Broad Market High Yield

Fact Sheet

Table of Contents

Investment Objective
Investment Philosophy
Investment Process
INVESTMENTS
INSIGHTS
ABOUT

Investment Objective
Our U.S. Broad Market High Yield Strategy seeks to maximize excess returns versus the Bloomberg High Yield 1% Issuer Capped Index over the long term.1

Investment Philosophy
In our Broad Market High Yield Strategy, we seek to earn 125 bps of alpha with a tracking error budget of 200 bps versus the Bloomberg Barclays U.S. High-Yield 1% Issuer Capped Index.
We expect tracking error based on historical volatility measured over a long term period to occur from holding position sizes in portfolios that differ from the issuer’s weighting in the benchmark and from holding positions in issuers that are not in the benchmark.
PGIM believes that actively managed high yield bond portfolios, constructed from the bottom up using methodical, research-based subsector and security selection, can lead to consistent outperformance versus the broad high yield index with a high information ratio.
PGIM attempts to achieve this through well-diversified portfolios of performing credits that are carefully researched. Intensive fundamental research is conducted by a large and experienced internal credit research staff to identify strong and improving credits.
The size and experience of the research organization permit us to apply intense focus on individual securities identified from a broad pool of investment opportunities.
Portfolios are then actively managed to capture the best opportunities and minimize credit losses, within an environment of disciplined risk management oversight.
We use a sector based approach, whereby portfolio managers specialize on certain industries (typically 4 to 6 each). As a result of not having to cover the entire universe of industries, our sector PMs can (a) more deeply understand the issuers and trading levels in their sectors to better evaluate relative value and more quickly respond to market opportunities and (b) can have more frequent dialogue with, and as a result get more favorable treatment from, traders at brokers/dealers for secondary trades and also from capital markets/syndicates individuals at underwriters for new issues.
We inherently think long term and are typically patient investors. Also, our institutional client base tends to be more stable (less flows). These two attributes enable us to take advantage of market opportunities because, on a relative basis versus peers, we tend to be liquidity providers as opposed to liquidity takers. In a world of less liquidity, we can take advantage of available market inefficiencies.

Investment Process
1. Senior portfolio manager develops top-down themes by leveraging firm's resources
2. Investment team selects securities and constructs portfolio
Fundamental Value Assessment
Credit analysts evaluate all industries and issuers in the universe. Focus on downside protection:

Asset quality
Capital structure
Covenants

Relative Value Security Selection
Sector portfolio managers and credit analysts evaluate and maximize relative value among approved universe:

Choose credits with strong fundamentals and best relative value

Position Sizing
Sector portfolio managers size positions:

Evaluate industry, issuer and market fundamentals
Achieve top-down beta and curve positioning objectives
Refine position sizes as risk profiles and thresholds change

3. Portfolio managers and risk managers monitor portfolio risk at all levels—interest rate, beta, industry, issuer, and quality

Senior Portfolio Managers

Robert Cignarella, CFA
Head of U.S. High Yield, Co-Head of Global High Yield

Past performance is not a guarantee or a reliable indicator of future results. Your capital is at risk and the value of investments can go down as well as up. Where overseas investments are held the rate of currency may cause the value of investments to fluctuate. Investments in emerging markets are by their nature higher risk and potentially more volatile than those inherent in some established markets. Non-USD securities are converted to USD using a spot rate conversion.

articles.title: Remembering Gary Hufbauer
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

Remembering Gary Hufbauer

Steven R. Weisman (PIIE)

Date
November 10, 2026 1:40 PM

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
You can locate the remarkable professional legacy of Gary Clyde Hufbauer in scores, maybe hundreds, of books, papers, blog postings, and presentations at the Peterson Institute for International Economics for more than 40 years. But his greatest impact here was the friendship, warmth, mentorship, and lessons he imparted to countless colleagues over those decades.
After Gary died this month, at the age of 87, I talked to many colleagues about that professional and personal legacy. Adam Posen, president of PIIE, wrote that Gary was "an extraordinary scholar and person" whose work was a pillar of the Institute's reputation. Gary, he said, embodied "the spirit of the Institute—intellectual engagement, passion to understand and improve the policy world, independence, collegiality, and a deep commitment to bringing economic research to bear on the world's most pressing policy challenges."
Gary was an expert on subsidies, sanctions, trade and tax policy, and much more. He was also the kind of colleague who could persuade you to jump out of an airplane with him. I'll get to that in a minute.
First, I asked Jeff Schott what it was like to work with Gary(link is external) for almost a half century. They started as part of the team at the US Treasury negotiating subsidies agreements for the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) in the 1970s. "I felt like I was always learning from him," Jeff says. "His writing style and analytical style were so clean. He could always get down to the core essence of any issue."
In the early 1980s Gary and Jeff wrote their book Economic Sanctions Reconsidered(link is external), published by PIIE, in which they came up with "nine commandments" on using sanctions, calling for, among other things, working with allies and focusing on limited targets. "We were going to have ten but there was a copyright problem," Jeff said.
Carla Hills got to know Gary when she was US Trade Representative, in the administration of President George H.W. Bush. "Gary was unique," she told me. "He had all the data in his head all the time. He could tell you what the average homeowner will gain or loss of trade off the top of his head."
Outlining the benefits of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) in the 1990s "was a tough position to take," she said. "Labor unions were not in favor, the agriculture community was not in favor. Gary's essays were important in persuading people. But it was never about him. He was the most modest man of extreme brilliance and training. He was never one to say, 'you have to take my view.' He was interested in talking and listening."
I interviewed Gary for a video when he retired in 2018. He recalled that as a student at Harvard, he was influenced by two professors, Gottfried Haberler, a libertarian free-market economist, and Seymour Harris, a Keynesian who had advised President John F. Kennedy. "I got very excited about their work and did my senior thesis on balance-of-payments issues," Gary said. Then he studied at Cambridge University and returned to his beloved southwest at the University of New Mexico as a professor before joining the Treasury Department as a consultant on payment imbalances.
C. Fred Bergsten, a young official running international economics at Treasury in the Jimmy Carter years, invited Gary to become a deputy assistant secretary for trade and investment. Fred founded the Institute for International Economics (now the Peterson Institute) in the early 1980s, recruiting Gary again. "I was just delighted to join him," Gary said.
"Gary was one of the most intellectually curious and creative people I have ever known," Fred told me. "He picked up new topics quickly, with great analysis, but didn't shy from controversy. He was willing to go out on a limb and make estimates and projections even when he knew they weren't going to pass muster for some PhD economists."
The best examples, cited by Fred, were Gary's "big number" of $1 trillion in gains to the US economy from trade expansion, updated to more than $2 trillion in 2017. Also controversial were Hufbauer and Schott's estimates of potential job losses and gains from NAFTA. "The economic purists argued, "How could there be job losses when we're at full employment?" recalled Fred. "But the critics were confusing macro and micro economics. Those estimates by Gary were vitally necessary to inform policy debates."
As a mentor and champion of young people, it would be hard to imagine anyone more inspiring than Gary. "For all Gary's accolades and remarkable and impactful career, what stands out to me was his kindness, humility, and good humor toward his research analysts," says Cathleen Cimino-Isaacs, a former research analyst who now works at the Congressional Research Service. "He never hesitated to elevate and challenge young professionals in a way that made them feel as though they too had meaningful contributions to give."
Daniel Rosen, founder of the Rhodium Group consultancy, told me: "Gary was my professor at Georgetown, and he brought me in as his RA [research assistant]. Gary taught me how to write. He was an absolutely relentless editor and stylist. When I talk about people I've mentored as a professor and at Rhodium, I say Gary Hufbauer was the one who taught me how to do this."
"Over the years, I learned so much from him," writes Anabel González, vice president at the Inter-American Development Bank. "His intellectual depth, extraordinary expertise, pragmatism, creativity, and clarity of thought were truly exceptional."
"Gary Hufbauer was a giant in the trade world and a critical component with Jeff Schott to PIIE's early success," writes Douglas Irwin, the distinguished historian of trade. "I studied the history of US trade policy, but he lived much of it, and he had a great sense for both the economics and politics of trade."
Here are some other recollections I have gathered in recent days. Yuan Liu, a research analyst: "His intellectual depth, extraordinary expertise, pragmatism, creativity, and clarity of thought were truly exceptional. [He was] a wonderful human being and always a pleasure to engage with." Ye Zhang, a former research analyst: "Gary was incredibly generous with his time and extremely patient with his RAs. His feedback on the blog drafts was always full of colorful highlights. I would mark my questions in yellow, and he would patiently answer every single one in green, no matter how trivial."
And these from other PIIE colleagues:
William R. Cline called Gary "a treasured colleague." Monica de Bolle recalls that Gary never failed to jokingly call her Cassandra because of her pessimism about Latin American economies. Ángel Ubide called him "a lovely person and great colleague, always with a smile." Inu Manak said he was "a major source of inspiration for my research on North American integration…. It's hard to imagine the world without him." Joseph Gagnon: "Gary was always a cheerful colleague, even when his economic views were sometimes (not always!) pessimistic." Arvind Subramanian called Gary "an absolute giant." Mary Lovely: "One of the greats." Cecilia Malmstrom: "A legend."
Bob Davis, veteran economics correspondent at the Wall Street Journal: "I considered him…one of the most honest people in Washington—not afraid to make a call and not afraid to admit to a mistake."
But skydiving?
Gary really did love to jump out of planes—with a parachute. Two of his research analysts, Eujin (Jin) Jung and Zhiyao (Lucy) Lu, bravely joined him in 2017 for the drive out to Warrenton, VA, where he waited for the weather to clear while going through his research papers. "That certainly gives you an idea of how dedicated he was to his work," Lucy said. Jin and Lucy did their jumps first with an instructor, followed by Gary in his red jump suit.
Barbara Kotschwar, a 20-something research assistant for Gary in the 1990s, and now director of economic development at the Organization of American States (OAS), says jumping with Gary "was one of the most surreal experiences of my life…. Watching my boss correct a report and then take a swan dive out of an airplane is something I'll never forget."
Interview with Hufbauer from 2018

Data Disclosure

This publication does not include a replication package.

articles.title: Transit-oriented development is good business: How business groups can support their regions by advancing transit-accessible communities | Brookings
articles.text:
Research

Transit-oriented development is good business: How business groups can support their regions by advancing transit-accessible communities

Adie Tomer and

Adie Tomer

Senior Fellow
- Brookings Metro

Ben Swedberg

Ben Swedberg

Research Analyst
- Brookings Metro

November 13, 2026

A Utah Transit Authority (UTA) TRAX light rail train arrives at a station in the Daybreak community of South Jordan, Utah, on April 18, 2024. Photo credit: Jacob Myslinski / Shutterstock

21 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Editor's note:
This report is one component of a three-part series studying the barriers to transit-oriented development (TOD) in U.S. metropolitan areas. It’s accompanied by a statistical survey of over 70,000 roadway corridors owned by state governments and a report on emerging models for state-led TOD governance.

Introduction
Regional business groups are one of the country’s most effective champions for greater public investment in transportation systems. Their diverse membership, topical expertise, and external networks make these civic organizations particularly good at educating lawmakers and the public about the return on investment from new and improved infrastructure.
Their success is particularly clear when it comes to driving investment in mass transit systems. As more metro areas turn to ballot measures to fund significant network expansions and modernization efforts, regional business groups often stump to help earn voter support. And when transit issues are debated in city halls and state legislatures, their leadership is equally adept at working directly with policymakers; for example, the recent instance of fund swapping in Pennsylvania to aid Philadelphia-area transit.
With much of metropolitan America now confronting the interwoven challenges of limited housing supply, rising living costs, and tight public budgets, regions need solutions that can address all three structural challenges at once. Transit-oriented development (TOD) offers one such solution. By building relatively large numbers of housing units in neighborhoods that are pre-developed and transit-served, TOD can bring down housing costs, shorten people’s trips, enhance access to amenities, and save governments money. It’s an ideal issue for business groups to champion.
But delivering TOD at scale will require reforms. Most regions face numerous market and policy barriers to TOD, including complex project financing rules, zoning restrictions, and uncertainty around who pays for necessary infrastructure upgrades. Overcoming such barriers requires the right combination of well-designed policy interventions and consensus-building. Regional business groups are especially well suited to contribute to both civic roles.
Using a mix of desk research and interviews with experts inside and outside business groups, this report builds the case for why regional business groups can help catalyze TOD, and how to bring them into coordinated action at the regional and state level.1 It begins by summarizing TOD-related research, including the established benefits of coalitional advocacy and the limited examination of business groups’ specific roles. The report then turns to how business group leaders should approach building internal support for TOD and what external activities best match business groups’ unique advantages. It concludes with opportunities for other TOD stakeholders to build relationships with business groups and the knock-on impacts for broader network activities.

Transit-oriented development helps cities, businesses, and people thrive
Transit-oriented development is a relatively straightforward real estate concept, although there are specific variations in the definition. At its core, TOD refers to land development around transit lines that is walkable and compact, includes a mix of real estate uses, and offers higher population and job densities than regional averages. Formal definitions often limit TOD’s extent to a quarter- or half-mile surrounding a transit station, but entire neighborhoods could still qualify as TOD across many square miles. Critically, TOD offers residents greater transportation choices to reach destinations, whether by transit, biking, walking, or driving.

Riders wait as an IndyGo Red Line bus arrives at Statehouse station in downtown Indianapolis.
Photo credit: Momoneymoproblemz / Wikimedia Commons

A Rapid Transit vehicle in Charlotte, North Carolina.
Photo credit: Harold Stiver / Shutterstock.com

Capital One Center in Tysons, Virginia, beside the Silver Line’s McLean station.
Photo credit: Duane Lempke / Wikimedia Commons

While exact definitions vary, what’s less variable are the types of benefits TOD can deliver:

TOD can support housing capacity at scale. The blocks surrounding transit stops are ideal for larger, multifamily residential developments. Recent evidence demonstrates numerous metro areas have built many new housing units near rail stations over the last few decades.
TOD promotes a more affordable cost of living. Overall affordability often does not come from reducing housing costs, but more so by enabling households to travel shorter distances and making it easier to own fewer vehicles.
TOD promotes lower costs for local and state governments. Greater density allows more people to use the same number of sidewalks, roadways, water pipes, and parks, effectively lowering service costs per capita.
TOD boosts transit ridership. Putting more households and businesses close to transit increases ridership demand, and those extra riders help cover greater shares of a transit agency’s operating costs.
TOD increases tax returns per developed acre. The more people who live and work in a given acre, the greater the number of tax returns and total revenues generated in that place. This is a well-established benefit of more compact development.
TOD promotes greater accessibility, which itself is an economic accelerant. Concentrating more people and jobs in various nodes—which TOD can do across cities and metro areas—increases job accessibility by transit, biking, walking, and even automobiles. That’s a benefit to businesses of all sizes that need their workers to be able to reliably get to work, and for residents who can access more job opportunities and other amenities. Such accessibility gains are a key feature of agglomeration, or the economic benefits derived from geographic proximity.

Coalitional politics can address barriers to TOD, but the role of regional business groups in supporting TOD is understudied
Even though it promises an impressive set of benefits, actually delivering TOD runs into significant barriers in most metro areas. Local zoning laws can limit development surrounding rail stations and along bus-served corridors, and residents may speak out against changes to those laws. It’s often expensive to upgrade infrastructure such as water and power lines to support larger buildings, and it’s not always clear how much of the investment burden should fall on private developers versus local and state governments. Larger real estate projects often require more complex financing to start with, and public policies—from affordable housing requirements to more typical taxes and fees—can make projects even tougher to pencil out. Even worse: The specific barriers vary from region to region. For one example, see this Urban Institute piece by Yonah Freemark and colleagues summarizing the high land costs, affordable housing requirements, and fee structures in Washington.
Overcoming these kinds of barriers requires deep developmental expertise, strong political communication, and coalitional alignment to persuade policymakers. Fortunately, such dynamics are a rich area of study among researchers. Many studies find that a greater number and variety of stakeholders supporting growth management—or public policies to manage the location and form of physical growth—is associated with the adoption of more reforms in those places. Other studies focus on the ability of developers to effect policy adoption through broader coalitional actions. Some researchers demonstrate the negative effects when external stakeholders don’t align their agendas.
Put simply: While barriers vary across places, coalitions consistently make a positive impact.
While there is a relatively strong record of research into coalitions, there is strikingly little mention of the role of regional business groups. The closest exceptions are mentions of generalized “business interests,” such as in cases from Atlanta and Los Angeles. But even there, the focus is on developers involved directly in TOD, which is different than civic business interests who could mobilize to support it.
That knowledge gap comes at a real expense: limiting the ability of regional business groups to design their engagements based on lessons from their peers, including what kinds of background planning and political engagement tactics work best. Business group executives may wonder how best to invest their operational funds into polling and political communication to reach voters—the literature gives no guidance. The knowledge gap also touches other civic organizations that may want to work with regional business groups. Those stakeholders won’t know whether to engage business groups or, if they do, which activities business groups are best suited to take on. The knowledge gap could especially affect individuals and organizations with a negative perception of business groups.

Regional business groups continue to actively engage in TOD-related activities
Even if there is little published research to date into how regional business groups work within TOD coalitions, several groups around the country have in fact played an active role in supporting TOD in their regions. Their public-facing advocacy tends to split into two common activities.
One is a case-making role. Some regional business groups have published reports and other materials making the case that TOD is beneficial to their region. A common theme is to argue for higher density around transit stations, as evidenced by the San Diego Regional Chamber of Commerce, Austin Chamber in Texas, and the Greater Washington Partnership. Some have done deep dives at specific locations, including reports published with the Urban Land Institute or by business groups representing specific neighborhoods (see this example from Lincoln Square and Ravenswood in Chicago). Some reports are shorter and accessible; some, such as station plans, can be quite detailed.
The other common activity is issuing public statements of support for TOD-related reforms. These are often written endorsements for legislative proposals or related rulemaking, such as those by the Central Maryland Chamber of Commerce, Greater Baltimore Committee, and Austin Chamber. Some efforts involve place-specific reforms, such as those in Charleston, S.C.; Omaha, Neb.; San Diego; and Oakland, Calif. At the state level, California’s CalChamber advocated for statewide upzoning around transit stations, while Chamber of Commerce Hawaii supported a revolving infrastructure fund to support TOD.
The benefits of these activities were reinforced by our conversations with regional business groups. Experts consistently explained that published materials help educate their members and reach other target audiences. Likewise, public statements of support for policy proposals offer elected officials the air cover they may need, or can even sway uncertain ones.
And while correlation isn’t causation, many of these advocacy efforts are associated with tangible policy change. Metro areas such as Austin, Texas; Baltimore; Cincinnati; Salt Lake City; San Diego; and San Francisco have all adopted reforms following outspoken support from a regional business group.
Yet public activities only represent a slice of what regional business groups can do to support TOD. There is still a tremendous amount of internal coordination with members and other outside business interests, private coalition-building with other TOD stakeholders, and networking with policymakers to make all this work more effective. In other words: It’s the private groundwork that makes public impact possible.

How business groups can garner support from their members
While some regional business groups have made major public commitments to support TOD, they are the exception.2 Yet with more metro areas confronting a housing supply crunch, a high cost of living, and tight public budgets, TOD is a natural strategy for business groups to champion.
Making TOD a genuine organizational priority, though, requires thoughtful internal planning. Leaders of regional business groups can’t pursue regional TOD reforms without first gaining the support of their members. TOD and its benefits are intuitive, but many individuals don’t have experience with the topic. This may be particularly true in places where transit systems are nascent, service is relatively limited, there’s been limited recent development of denser neighborhoods, or any combination. As many experts explained, members’ understanding of TOD and transit directly reflects the maturity of the region’s transit system.
If there ever comes a time when a business group’s entire membership will be asked to support regionwide TOD efforts, organizational leaders should expect to have to do some internal educating. Based on expert interviews, we heard the following recommendations for whipping support for TOD among members:

Use accessible topics to educate membership. While business group members tend to have strong business acumen, relatively few specialize in real estate and infrastructure economics. Concepts such as tax revenue generated by developmental acre, real estate development costs, transit agency fiscal affairs, and household travel demand may present a significant learning curve. Additionally, many members don’t operate their businesses or personally reside in TOD-ready locations, which creates an experiential gap.
Business group staff should prioritize more common economic concerns when explaining TOD. Housing scarcity and living expenses are highly resonant and should be priority topics in any internal discussions. Job access for their employees should be well understood among membership and is another area to start. The safety crisis on streets could resonate with some members, especially in health care.
Finally, “NIMBYism” should be addressed thoughtfully. Some members won’t like the idea of converting the neighborhoods where they reside using TOD, but it can be framed differently. One interviewee recommended telling members, “We know you don’t want certain new construction in your neighborhood, so supporting it elsewhere relieves some of that pressure.” Likewise, certain stigmas such as preferring rail-served corridors over bus-served corridors should not be avoided, especially since bus service can anchor TOD. Overall, we consistently heard that members could be persuaded to support TOD based on its merits.

Identify internal champions. Experts told us staff within regional business groups usually rely on a small set of members to externally lead on priority issue areas, and TOD is no exception. Those champions will be among the most knowledgeable actors, making them natural leaders for internal education efforts. Staff should plan their internal activities alongside those members, including which leaders should talk to which members. Multiple experts said that fellow members are the most convincing advocates for reticent members.
Draft compelling, concise materials. Experts frequently noted there is no need to overwhelm members. It likely won’t take considerable time to earn their support, either. Focus on creating polished materials with streamlined messaging and simple facts. One- or two-page fact sheets are ideal and can easily be repurposed for public audiences later.
Don’t just tell—show. Members are likely to gain immense experience from seeing TOD in action. Regional business groups should consider bringing their members to peer markets to see visually impressive TOD projects. These can be coordinated with domestic and international trade missions or during annual fly-in trips to Washington, D.C. Physical, three-dimensional models can have a similar effect, and many developers and governments may be willing to produce such models to demonstrate how station areas and corridors could transform.

How regional business groups can best support TOD coalitions
Once a regional business group’s membership lines up behind TOD, questions about how it can most effectively support overall advocacy naturally emerge. Fortunately, regional business groups offer many strategic advantages for TOD-supportive coalitions. Experts noted multiple areas where business groups can lend their expertise:

Be adaptable to internal and external roles. There’s no question that a business group’s economic knowledge, established networks, and political communication resources can all be useful. But business leaders won’t always be the most known or trusted voice with all constituencies. That includes their potential coalitional partners as well as the lawmakers and public audiences they eventually want to reach. As a first step, business group leadership should feel confident enough to initiate conversations with prospective allies, introduce themselves if necessary, and build a rapport of trust and shared understanding. Once complete, the strength of those coalitional relationships can help business groups decide with whom and when they should be a public communicator (whether as the entire business organization or as members in their individual capacities), versus when to serve as a background orchestrator.
Similarly, business groups’ experience with consensus building is instrumental to design strategies that can win politically. Experts frequently noted that business group members have experience with finding compromise—specifically on how transactional asks can help land bigger, shared prizes. For example, what kinds of infrastructure projects could suburban districts receive so there are more votes to support TOD projects closer to the urban core?

Address economic-oriented knowledge gaps. Any issue-focused political campaign can benefit from highlighting salient economic facts and debunking myths. Business groups have the expertise to answer challenging economic questions, including on how to demonstrate that TOD offers strong return on investment and affordability benefits. These groups also often have funds to help pay for targeted studies.
Short-term job creation should be one argument. Established interests that back highway construction and single-family neighborhood development typically circulate estimates of the number of construction jobs created for every public dollar invested. TOD supporters should have similar figures to make direct comparisons. Specific jobs estimates for unionized workers in the skilled trades are especially valuable.
Accessibility data is a natural area for business groups to lead. Every employer thinks about catchment areas, or how many potential workers or customers can reach their locations within a certain amount of time. Access rates measure that for entire neighborhoods, making them a key data point to show how new TOD could grow the number of people able to reach key destinations, whether it’s a place of work or a place to shop, eat, and meet friends. Business groups could extend the data too, noting that greater multimodal access rates have the potential to attract new talent to specific neighborhoods and the region overall.
Fiscal impacts are well suited for business group involvement too. Policymakers may have limited knowledge about how certain development densities impact tax revenues and future liabilities, which creates an opening for business leaders to educate them. Likewise, demonstrating how TOD can boost transit demand and reduce public subsidies could be especially resonant for lawmakers.

Lead polling of the public and targeted stakeholders. Experts noted that business groups are usually quite experienced with polling. They frequently use different techniques to better understand their target audiences, whether it’s the public or a small set of policymakers. Many business groups will already have connections to regional, statewide, or national pollsters—and if they don’t, their members will. Members are likely to support spending on polling, and the business group could easily pool funds from other coalition members to improve a poll’s design. Once complete, business groups could also socialize the polling results with their peers in other markets.
Multiple experts noted that polling lawmakers about what their districts want most is essential to designing comprehensive investment strategies. For example, a city council member may reveal that their ward only wants new sidewalks and upgraded traffic lights—and that if they receive funds for those purposes, they would be more likely to greenlight funding that could help underwrite TOD or construct new transit lines in other neighborhoods.

Lead study trips. When major public campaigns are starting to approach an inflection point (for example, a referendum vote or major legislative action), business groups are the ideal organization to take elected officials to other markets doing TOD well. Business groups can often cover travel costs, and they have the in-house expertise to design and staff successful study trips. Domestic and international TOD locations are both powerful, though international examples can be more impactful even if significantly more expensive.

Transit advocates, labor groups, and public officials should help to integrate regional business groups into broader coalition activities
Bringing regional business groups into larger coalitions requires more than purposeful action on the part of business leaders. Other coalition members should adjust their own activities to take advantage of the coalition’s new array of topical knowledge, established networks, and public reputations. Examples include:

Transit advocacy organizations. Many metro areas are served by at least one nonprofit organization that does transit advocacy. Policymakers and other stakeholders typically consider these organizations trusted intermediaries to represent the interests of transit riders. Transit advocacy organizations are invariably major supporters of TOD as well.
Even if their core constituencies are different, transit advocacy organizations should form strategic partnerships with regional business groups. The partnerships may already exist in some regions from past ballot referenda or other regionwide transit debates, but if not, they shouldn’t be difficult to start. Experts stressed the need for regular check-in meetings at the executive level. They also noted that coordinating strategic communications should be the top priority, as the two core groups can each reach different audiences.

Seniors and student advocates. Both of these demographic groups can offer powerful engagement around TOD issues. In terms of benefits, each would directly benefit from more infill housing that lowers costs and reduces the need to drive long distances or at all. Each group is also relatively well organized beyond traditional political parties, from local universities for students to a mix of social groups and AARP chapters for seniors. They should each find ways to engage with business groups to help align strategy and find ways to make their voices heard in key debates.
Labor groups. Due to the direct impact on construction jobs, unions representing the skilled trades are already key participants in most regional and state debates regarding infrastructure and real estate policies. Yet labor groups aren’t monolithic; different unions often support different sides of an issue depending on the perceived benefits to their members. Labor politics also vary in every region and state, which makes it impossible to suggest one-size-fits-all solutions.
This is another area where aligning strategic communications with regional business groups is important. Labor groups are also a vital consumer of job-related data. If business groups can confirm which unions will benefit the most from TOD construction, it should be presented to that union’s leadership.

Elected officials. Regional business groups and elected officials already tend to be in close communication. TOD offers a new area where their interests align, yet it’s likely that elected officials who represent TOD-ready districts will benefit most from working closely with their business leadership.
Elected officials have multiple unique tools to help animate business support. Revenue-related instruments such as targeted tax relief and direct investment in new infrastructure will increase the likelihood of business support. As one expert noted, “No business group wants to leave money on the table.” Mayors and governors are especially valuable advocates on the stump; the more they’re willing to argue for TOD-supportive policies—including taking and responding to critiques from TOD opponents—the more business groups will be motivated to wade into debates. Finally, elected officials don’t always need to engage the business community publicly, but they should ensure that they at least maintain back-channel communications, especially if the regional business group could be seen as misaligned with other key constituents.

Turning TOD’s potential into regional action
The case for transit-oriented development is increasingly clear. What’s more difficult is turning that potential into action. Regional business groups can play an important role in a civic-led reform process, but they should not lead every campaign or speak to every audience. Their greatest value will often come from providing economic analysis, convening unlikely partners, testing messages, and giving elected officials the confidence to act.
Business groups’ unique capacities are assets to build around. The next step is for business leaders, transit advocates, labor groups, public officials, and other civic organizations to identify the barriers holding TOD back in their own region, and then build coalitions that maximize the strengths of such diverse membership.

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesMarketsEmerging Market Credit Shows Resilience amid Energy ShockNov 5, 2026Share Weathering recent global shocks with newfound stability, emerging market credit has matured into a resilient and diverse asset class, according to Goldman Sachs Asset Management. As their capital markets and economies have developed over the past decade, emerging market bonds are less constrained by the US dollar. Robust improvements in the quality and depth of financial data are helping drive the growth of emerging market corporate bonds. Investors must be selective in a diversifying market with a rising number of issuers of government and corporate debt.When the Iran war triggered a surge in oil prices this year, many investors may have expected credit markets in the developing world to slide into a selloff.
Instead, emerging market sovereign and corporate bonds weathered the shock with a newfound stability and solid performance for investors.
The development is a key sign that emerging market credit is maturing into a resilient asset class, according to Anupam Damani, co-head and senior portfolio manager of emerging market debt at Goldman Sachs Asset Management. At the same time, investors are rethinking their approach to the market, which has trillions of dollars in outstanding debt.
“Emerging market credit is now unrecognizable, and I mean that in a good way,” Damani says. “These bonds used to come with a crisis label, but this market is no longer monolithic. In my view, it has become a more diverse and resilient asset class, though risks remain.”
To be sure, emerging market bonds run the gamut in terms of risk, and investors must be selective about what they trade in a marketplace with myriad issuers, she adds.
We spoke with Damani about the changing dynamics in the asset class, including the growth of emerging market corporate bonds and a less binding US dollar.
Emerging market credit used to be a byword for volatility. What has changed and what opportunities does the asset class now offer investors?

For a long time, emerging market credit (EM credit) was considered a risk-on or a risk-off trade. Now, there are what we like to call more dispersed opportunity sets, or more names to choose from. We believe this reflects fundamental improvements that may have reduced binary tail risk—the all-or-nothing quality that used to define EM credit. In our view, this has become an asset class where credit selection really matters. The market has matured.
In the sovereign space, for example, you’ll see deep local-currency markets with stronger reserve buffers. This means more liquidity. There are also more credible inflation-policy frameworks and deeper domestic investor bases.
This policy shift seems significant.

It is, and this trend is unfolding across regions, from Asia to Latin America, Eastern Europe, and Africa. I believe these changes have anchored the market very differently than in the past. There used to be only a few countries in the EM sovereign space. Now, there are more than 80 countries offering a far wider range of potential opportunities.
How are investors responding to these changes?

Well, it’s been an evolution. There are countries that are developing strong institutions, and there are always going to be a few countries that are moving backward. This isn’t a linear progression across the asset class. But on an aggregate level, I think there has been a greater focus on fiscal orthodoxy and monetary orthodoxy.
And to see the results, look at how many major emerging markets are running close to their inflation targets, with significant GDP growth, even in the face of the energy supply shock this year. When you look at developed markets, investors are struggling to see the same kind of discipline. Indeed, investors are increasingly demanding a higher risk premium to own some developed market assets.
In my view, what’s interesting is that in emerging markets, there has always been a demand for higher risk premiums because of perceived notions around governance and weakness in policy frameworks. I think this has moved quite a bit.
And corporate bonds? Has that market changed as well?

EM credit used to be largely a sovereign-only market. Today, we have a rapidly evolving market for corporates. And issuers are companies with footprints that extend beyond their borders—they are globally competitive, industry leaders that deal in hard currency. They are supported by local markets, with domestic consumer investor bases that have become larger and deeper in recent years.
In fixed income, we believe emerging market corporates have historically offered attractive Sharpe ratios, or risk-adjusted performance, relative to many other sectors. In our view, this reflects the bonds' strong resilience, credit quality, and lower duration.

Has the role of the US dollar changed in emerging market debt?

Yes. The US dollar constraint is less binding than it used to be in previous cycles. In the 1990s, for instance, issuance was overwhelmingly dollar-driven, so when the dollar appreciated massively, your payment capacity was reduced as the local currency cost of servicing the debt rose. Now that effect is decreasing with the growth of local-currency sovereign debt markets. Emerging market countries are also issuing more debt in euros and renminbi.
Fixed income investors need reliable data to size up credit risk. Are issuers improving the quality of information?

We believe this is an underappreciated development in the EM credit story. There used to be a transparency discount for investors because data on issuers was considered too opaque. If you look at the investable universe in EM corporates today, disclosure looks much closer to what we see in developed markets.
There is standardized reporting of data under International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) or IFRS-aligned frameworks. This improves comparability across regions and sectors, which we didn’t have in the past. Balance sheet transparency is also far stronger.
Issuers have also improved communications with investors—quarterly reporting, presentations, earnings calls, roadshows—just as we see in developed markets. When there are negative developments in a country or broader industry, those communications tend to pick up. You didn’t see this type of healthy dialogue between issuers and investors in the past.
Global markets have recently sustained two shocks: US tariffs and the Middle East energy supply crunch. What is the fallout for emerging market credit?

It’s a pertinent question for the asset class. In our view, what’s important is the convergence around institutional frameworks, orthodox policies on inflation, and stronger international reserve positions. These developments may have increased the ability of emerging markets to better absorb these types of shocks. In this cycle, for example, we have not seen uniform stress across the market but rather a dispersion across credits.
This is an important point. If you look at what’s happening in the Middle East, we have oil prices shooting up. In emerging market credit, we have energy exporters and importers, right? This creates greater differentiation across issuers in the marketplace rather than the broad-based selloffs seen in some prior EM crises.
And it shows that over the years, many developing economies have learned from their mistakes and tried to make changes that make them more resilient. So returns are increasingly driven by fundamentals and valuations, and that is a very different proposition from simply owning what we used to call the EM beta trade.

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesOutlooksThe Global Economy Is Forecast to Grow 2.8% in 2027 as Oil Prices DeclineNov 13, 2026Share Goldman Sachs Research forecasts steady global economic growth in 2027: The US, Japan, and the UK are projected to grow faster than the consensus of economist estimates. Energy prices are expected to flip from an economic headwind to a modest boost next year. AI spending is projected to keep boosting global economic growth in 2027. Our analysts expect nominal global AI investment to rise to $1.8 trillion next year. The risks to Goldman Sachs Research’s forecast “are tilted to the downside”: Tensions in Iran, fiscal deficits, and lower-than-expected AI capex could result in slower global GDP growth.Goldman Sachs Research expects steady global economic growth in 2027, as lower energy prices and still-strong capital expenditures in artificial intelligence (AI) outweigh tighter financial conditions and more neutral fiscal policy.
What is the outlook for global GDP growth in 2027?
Global GDP is predicted to increase 2.8% in 2027, up from 2.7% this year, Jan Hatzius, chief economist and head of Goldman Sachs Research, writes in a report. The economies of the US, Japan, and the UK are among those projected to grow faster than the consensus of economist estimates.
As has been the case for the last several years, our economists are more optimistic than consensus on US economic expansion owing to resilient investment. They are more downbeat on the European growth outlook amid tighter financial conditions and their expectation that higher energy prices will start to bite this winter. Goldman Sachs Research also forecasts continued robust economic expansion in South Korea and Taiwan, reflecting another year of strong AI exports.
While growth is expected to be solid, the risks to Goldman Sachs Research’s forecast for global GDP growth “are tilted to the downside,” Hatzius writes. Renewed escalation in the Iran war could result in another energy price surge. Large fiscal deficits could push up long-term yields more sharply, especially in France. AI capex could be lower than expected because of capacity constraints, regulation, credit market stress, or weaker demand, and Hatzius also sees early signs that AI adoption is weighing on the job market.
“We expect another year of solid but unremarkable GDP growth in 2027, but several of the impulses that shaped global growth in 2026 will look different,” Hatzius writes.
How will oil and energy prices affect GDP growth in 2027?
The headwind from the energy supply shock will likely flip next year as energy prices normalize. The baseline forecast from Goldman Sachs Research’s commodity strategists is that continued Middle East supply adaptation will lower Brent prices to $78 per barrel by the end of 2027, with a similar normalization in global prices for liquefied natural gas.
At the same time, Goldman Sachs Research sees an ongoing drag from energy prices in Europe from delayed energy cost pass-through to consumers.
How financial conditions and the fiscal outlook will affect GDP growth
Lower energy prices should outweigh the effect of tighter financial conditions and a smaller fiscal impulse to GDP expansion in 2027, Hatzius writes. Goldman Sachs Research’s Financial Conditions Index implies a moderate drag on growth over the next few quarters.
While our economists do not “expect meaningful fiscal consolidation” in 2027, the large fiscal expansions of the last few years are fading. The main exception is in Japan, where consumption tax cuts, increased defense spending, and the government’s investment plans are forecast to boost GDP growth by 0.7 percentage point.
“We also expect modestly positive impulses in Germany and the US—where the Democratic victory in November’s US election suggests some of the spending cuts from the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act will be reversed,” Hatzius writes. Our economists project a continued fiscal drag in the UK that leaves the fiscal impulse in developed markets “only slightly positive.”
Will AI boost the global economy in 2027?
Goldman Sachs Research expects AI capex to boost global economic growth again next year. Our analysts forecast that nominal global AI investment will rise to $1.8 trillion in 2027 from $1.1 trillion this year, mostly driven by an increase of over $500 billion in hardware spending in the US. The investment surge is projected to be frontloaded, with the year-over-year change in investment as a share of GDP peaking in the first half of 2027.
“Even with the expected slowdown, the impact on GDP growth will be sizable,” Hatzius writes. Our economists estimate that AI investment will boost GDP growth by 0.4 percentage point globally. In the US, Goldman Sachs Research estimates AI investment will give a 0.6-percentage-point boost to "true" GDP growth after accounting for continued undercounting of semiconductor investment and chip-related intellectual property exports.
The transition to an AI-enabled economy, meanwhile, is occurring in two phases, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The first phase involves an investment boom that raises both corporate profits and global GDP growth but features only limited productivity gains. The second phase involves less hardware investment but more business reorganization, as well as more substantial productivity gains and labor market disruption.
Goldman Sachs Research has argued that AI is likely to displace some jobs and cause a temporary increase in the unemployment rate. Our economists’ baseline expectation is that AI adoption will only have a small effect on the labor market in 2027 and there will be more notable effects in 2028-2029.
What is the outlook for China’s economic growth in 2027?
Goldman Sachs Research forecasts China’s GDP to grow 4.5% in 2027, compared with the consensus estimate of 4.4%. This “reflects very robust expectations for Chinese exports and a further increase in China’s trade surplus,” Hatzius writes.
By contrast, domestic demand growth is predicted to remain weak next year owing to a drag from the property sector and weak underlying consumer spending.
This is expected to result in a modest headwind of 0.1 percentage point to the rest of the world’s GDP growth, with larger drags on growth in manufacturing-heavy economies such as Germany (headwind of 0.3 percentage point) and Central Europe (headwind of 0.2 percentage point).
What is the forecast for inflation in 2027?
Under Goldman Sachs Research’s baseline commodity forecasts for a steady decline in energy prices next year, inflation should slow in 2027, Hatzius writes.
The case for disinflation is particularly strong in the US because the price boosts from tariffs should fully drop out of the year-over-year inflation statistics next spring, he writes. With tariff effects fading and a much smaller inflation boost from the war in Iran, our economists expect core PCE inflation to slow to 2.4% at the end of 2027 from 3.2% at the end of 2026.
“We forecast a steady decline in year-over-year core inflation in the US and a more delayed decline in other major economies once the energy price shock is fully digested,” Hatzius writes.
What is the outlook for the Fed and other central banks in 2027?
Goldman Sachs Research expects “incremental policy tightening” through early 2027 in most major economies, but its economic forecasts support a dovish view on rates next year. Central banks could either deliver gradual normalization cuts later in 2027 as inflation comes down, or they could pivot to cuts sooner if economic growth is slower than projected.
The US Federal Reserve is expected to hike rates in December and March in response to lingering inflation pressures. But our economists say softer inflation data should allow the Fed to cut once in December 2027, followed by three more cuts in 2028 to a terminal rate of 3.25-3.5%.
“Furthermore, we see more dovish rate risks in the US than in most other economies, both because US inflation drivers look more clearly temporary and because the US is most exposed to a downturn in the AI cycle,” Hatzius writes.
Our economists’ views on other major developed markets also skew dovish. The European Central Bank is forecast to deliver its final hike in December, before starting to normalize back toward a 2.25% terminal rate in the fourth quarter of 2027.
Goldman Sachs Research expects a final hike from the Bank of England to 4.25% in February before a hold for the remainder of 2027. Our economists forecast normalization cuts from the BoE to a 3.25% terminal rate, but not until 2028.
“The main outlier to our forecast of only modest further policy tightening is Japan,” Hatzius writes.
Goldman Sachs Research expects the Bank of Japan to hike rates by 25 basis points in December, reflecting recent communication from the central bank highlighting both upside inflation risks and the impact of higher global interest rates on the Japanese yen. With core CPI (excluding fresh food but including energy) likely to rise above 3.5% through next summer, our economists now expect that the BoJ will follow through with additional hikes in March and June for a terminal rate of 2%.

articles.title: Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2026
articles.text: In 2026, 811 million people, 1 in 10, live on less than $3.00 a day, a rate unchanged since 2019. More than half the extreme poor live in nine economies, and by 2030, 87 percent will be in Sub-Saharan Africa, in fragile and conflict-affected situations, or both. Without stronger per capita growth, the number of people in extreme poverty is projected to be higher in 2030 than it is today.Despite the reduction seen in past decades, escaping extreme poverty has not meant reaching security. Nearly half of humanity, 3.7 billion people, still lives on less than $8.30 a day, most of them one shock away from falling back.
