articles.title: Phishing and Fraud Awareness Notice
articles.text:
Phishing and Fraud Awareness Notice

Bridgewater Associates, LP (“Bridgewater”) is a premier asset management firm, focused on delivering unique insight and partnership for the most sophisticated global institutional investors. We have recently become aware of an increase in fraudulent schemes in which unauthorized third parties (often operating through fake websites, social-media profiles, unsolicited e-mail or social media messages, text messages, telephone calls, or other communication platforms) misrepresent themselves as employees, agents, or affiliates of Bridgewater. These bad actors may attempt to obtain confidential personal information, solicit investments (including cryptocurrency investments), offer investment advice, induce the transfer of funds under false pretenses, or may target job seekers purporting to offer jobs at Bridgewater. The fraudulent activity is sophisticated, constantly evolving and frequently mimics the look and feel of genuine Bridgewater communications, and may reference accurate-looking logos, executive names, marketing materials, and the official Bridgewater.com website. We issue this notice to alert current and prospective clients, counterparties, vendors, job applicants, and the general public to these unlawful practices. The actions of these unauthorized persons are in no way associated with Bridgewater.Bridgewater communicates only through official channels, including with its clients, counterparties and job applicants. Bridgewater’s official website is: https://www.bridgewater.com, and our email address ends strictly in “@bwater.com”. No other websites or email domains are authorized by Bridgewater. The only social media accounts authorized by Bridgewater are LinkedIn and Meta (Facebook and Instagram). We only use these authorized social media accounts to issue informational postings. Please be aware that Bridgewater does not conduct business activities, financial transactions, solicit investments or provide investment advice through social-media direct messages, personal e-mail domains, encrypted messaging apps, or public chat platforms, such as Telegram, WeChat, or WhatsApp, or other public platforms. Bridgewater does not hire from social media or conduct interviews via text or messaging services, nor will Bridgewater request any form of payment in connection with the hiring process.Some of the warning signs or red flags that may indicate a scam include: (a) phishing websites that have the look and feel of the official Bridgewater website, (b) variations in email domains that appear to have come from a Bridgewater email address, (c) fraudulent mobile device apps which purport to be an official Bridgewater app, and (d) time bound offers which pressure you to invest immediately.If you have any questions about this notice or the legitimacy of any communication purportedly from Bridgewater, please email our Legal Department at LRG_FraudAwareness@bwater.com. If you believe you may have been the victim of internet crime or fraudulent activity, please report it to law enforcement in your jurisdiction.

articles.title: How Chinese AI Proxy Services Gain Access to U.S. Models
articles.text:
Summary
A shadow market is helping Chinese users sidestep U.S. AI export controls. Proxy services provide access to restricted frontier models, enabling Chinese companies to distill advanced American AI capabilities into their own systems at a fraction of the training cost.
Crypto is helping facilitate the market. Chainalysis research examines the proxy ecosystem’s evolving supply chain and payment infrastructure, finding that 40% of proxy services surveyed accepted cryptocurrency as payment, predominantly stablecoins.
Chinese-linked wallet activity spikes after frontier AI releases. Our research also found that payments from suspected Chinese-linked wallets rise above normal levels in the days following new U.S. model launches, suggesting efforts to quickly access new capabilities, though the data cannot confirm the cause.
Developing frontier AI models is a resource-intensive process with national security implications. For that reason, the U.S. government bars users and companies in China—a key competitor in the global AI arms race—from accessing powerful AI tools like Claude and ChatGPT.Research and analysis from the Chainalysis Global Intelligence Team found that banned suspected Chinese users are accessing models anyway. They are doing it via a shadow economy of export control-sidestepping services that sell access, often at a discount, to the restricted models. Once in, the banned users can cheaply mine the advanced models to improve their own systems for a fraction of the cost.Called “proxy services,” these waystations route queries into AI models while concealing where those requests came from. They take payment in fiat currency, including through China-based payment processors such as WeChat and AliPay. Our survey of 100 proxy services found that 40% also accept crypto as payment, predominately in stablecoins.The above screenshot was taken in August 2026 of one surveyed proxy domain offering crypto payment for users looking to top-up their account balances.Crypto payments are likely part of a deliberate strategy by these proxy services to obfuscate financial infrastructure, bypass state capital controls, and maintain off-grid access for sensitive users.Chinese AI companies use these proxy services to train their own models, undermining U.S. restrictionsBy providing indirect access to advanced American models, proxy services are undermining the national security-focused restrictions that U.S.-based AI labs implement.Through a process known as distillation, Chinese AI laboratories can use the outputs of advanced models to improve their own competing models far more cheaply than they could by training their models from scratch. Anthropic recently accused three China-based AI labs (DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax) of extracting capabilities from Claude using 24,000 fraudulent accounts run through proxy services.And as Anthropic itself outlines, such illicitly distilled models can spread dangerous capabilities as they often lack essential safeguards. Just last month, the National Security Agency warned these models can pose significant risks to critical infrastructure, military, economic, and technology domains.The once informal market facilitating this access has matured into a structured economy, with a segmented supply chain and dedicated financial infrastructure. Providers sell access through credits and account top-ups, creating a commercial ecosystem around unauthorized access to U.S. frontier models.Crypto payments are gaining traction in this commercial ecosystem, offering an alternative for users looking to avoid Chinese digital payment rails.Suspected Chinese wallet activity in the proxy economy spikes after new U.S. model releasesWe analyzed suspected Chinese-linked wallet activity around major U.S. AI model releases. If Chinese developers are using proxy services to extract capabilities from new models—and using crypto to pay for these services—we would expect payments to spike after a release.We found that suspected China-linked wallets do increase their activity in the days following a frontier model release in excess of what we see across all wallets using these services. This pattern is consistent with an effort to gain rapid access to new model capabilities, and may reflect crypto being used as a payment rail to facilitate distillation. The aggregate data cannot, however, confirm what is driving the observed activity.User crypto payments in the ecosystem typically pass through custodial services before reaching proxy providersOur analysis of the wallets paying for AI proxy services found a large concentration of these wallets in China, as well as in Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore, and South Korea, which is consistent with Chinese operators routing through regional proxy corridors to access restricted models.Our research also found that proxy services do not always collect user payments directly. Instead, most use custodial cryptocurrency payment processors. These services can provide a range of benefits, such as adding distance between users and proxy providers, helping bypass state capital controls, and maintaining off-grid access for sensitive users.Given China’s broad restrictions on crypto payment activities, reliance on third-party processors may also appeal to these proxy services as it reduces their exposure to the regulatory and operational risks associated with maintaining their own payment infrastructure.This layered payment structure creates exposure for regulated crypto exchanges and other crypto companies, as funds linked to proxy services can reach regulated platforms with no clear direct ties back to the proxy services.How blockchain intelligence can help crack down on the proxy shadow marketAI proxy services are creating a major enforcement challenge for U.S. efforts to restrict Chinese access to advanced AI. Blocking direct access to frontier models is no longer enough when a mature shadow economy now exists to resell access.The proxy economy’s multi-tier supply chain also makes it particularly difficult to dismantle. Upstream vendors obtain model access through tactics such as account farming and model swapping; proxy services then handle both intermediary and downstream elements, including pooling access, routing queries, and selling subscriptions. When one vendor is disrupted, others can step in.Blockchain intelligence can help investigators trace financial flows across this ecosystem, exposing links between proxy operators, their users, the operational and financial intermediaries that sustain them, and the platforms where funds ultimately land.By mapping these connections, authorities and AI companies can identify critical pressure points, disrupt the infrastructure sustaining these networks, and thereby undermine the shadow market enabling unauthorized access to American AI. FAQWhat are Chinese AI proxy services?Chinese AI proxy services are businesses that resell access to otherwise restricted AI models, such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini, allowing users in China and elsewhere to use systems they may not be able to access directly. Most services offer pay-as-you-go subscriptions, where sign-up is free and then users buy tokens to run queries.Why are AI proxy services a concern for U.S. authorities and AI companies?Beyond individual users accessing AI tools, a key concern is that Chinese AI developers may use proxy services to extract capabilities from U.S. frontier models and train their own systems without incurring the same research and development costs. These efforts circumvent U.S. AI export controls and create security risks if derivative models lack the safeguards of the original systems.How do AI proxy services use cryptocurrency?Cryptocurrency, particularly stablecoins, allows proxy services to accept payments without relying on traditional banking infrastructure. Crypto payments can also reduce payment friction and, depending on the transaction, limit the identity verification required of customers. Chainalysis found that 40% of 100 AI proxy services surveyed offered crypto payments.How do AI proxy services process cryptocurrency payments?Many appear to rely on custodial services and third-party payment processors rather than receiving payments directly from users. These intermediaries help providers create distance between customers and service operators, bypass state capital controls, and maintain off-grid access for sensitive users.How can blockchain intelligence help investigate AI proxy networks?Blockchain intelligence can help investigators and compliance teams trace cryptocurrency flows and map relationships among proxy operators, payment processors, and exchanges. By examining these connections across multiple transactions and services, investigators can identify potential intervention points and better understand the financial infrastructure supporting unauthorized access to advanced AI models. articles.title: How Congress might take back its trade powers and limit Trump's tariffs
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

How Congress might take back its trade powers and limit Trump's tariffs

Inu Manak (PIIE)

Date
November 13, 2026 12:00 PM

Photo Credit: Sipa USA/Michael Brochstein

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
Americans are unhappy with the direction the country is headed and are ready for change. That was the core message from the stunning defeat of the president's party in the midterm elections in November, where the accumulation of unpopular policies—including immigration enforcement, the war in Iran, and tariffs—was thoroughly rebuked. The contribution of those policies to dissatisfaction with the economy is quite clear, and voters expect the incoming Congress to come prepared to tackle them.
Congress may want to start with trade policy. An NBC News exit poll(link is external) from 45 states showed that 66 percent of voters thought President Donald Trump's tariffs had hurt the national economy. With the tariffs' impact being felt by both businesses and consumers, trade policy is an area ripe for reform.
Ending Trump's second-term trade war is also about a lot more than economic costs because the administration has been indiscriminate in targeting allies and adversaries alike. He has focused substantial attention on Canada, which a majority of Americans(link is external) see as misguided. Congress should be equally concerned that Canadians are more likely to view(link is external) the US with suspicion, or as an enemy or potential threat than as a friend.
Reining in the powers that Congress has delegated to the president in the past will not be an easy task politically. Nor will allies suddenly trust the US again even if tariffs are scaled back. Nonetheless, establishing guardrails and repairing alliances are important, and as set out below, there are several ways to do it.
We've Been Here Before
Since Trump's first-term trade war was launched, Congress has debated what kinds of guardrails are necessary to prevent executive abuse of trade authorities. Importantly, while he has used many tools in his battles, some are more harmful than others. Two measures the president uses to avoid accountability are Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, used to impose the "national security" sectoral tariffs, and Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which is propping up baseline tariffs of 10-12 percent on nearly all US imports. While addressing other tariff abuses is important, reducing the economic harm at home and repairing our relationships with allies such as Canada require Congress to close the loopholes in these two statutes.
Since 2018, lawmakers have discussed a range of bills to address different trade statutes and varying concerns with how they are used. Most of those efforts fall within three categories of reforms: limiting executive abuse, improving transparency and procedural concerns, and clarifying the purpose and scope of specific statutes.
The surefire way to prevent executive abuse is to require that Congress vote on any tariffs. This can take two forms. The first is through a joint resolution of disapproval, where both houses of Congress would be able to vote to repeal a president's tariffs. Currently, Section 232 includes a disapproval resolution only for petroleum imports. Senator Rob Portman (R-OH) put forward a bill in 2019 (the Trade Security Act(link is external)) that would expand this to all Section 232 actions. The main problem with disapproval resolutions is that they require Congress to seek repeal of a president's action after it has been taken. Politically, this can be difficult because the president's party may want to avoid openly questioning the president's policy agenda. Some members of Congress may also shy away from voting to repeal actions benefiting some interests in their districts. However, voters' overwhelmingly anti-tariff sentiment could insulate those members from such pressures.
The second, and more robust, option is a joint resolution of approval, which requires Congress to vote on a proposed tariff action before it is taken. This prevents arbitrary imposition of tariffs and ensures that such serious actions are thoughtfully deliberated. A 2019 bill(link is external)—the Bicameral Congressional Trade Authority Act—from Senators Pat Toomey (R-PA) and Mark Warner (D-VA) would have required an approval resolution within 60 days of the president submitting a report to Congress on the proposed action. A 2025 bill(link is external)—the Trade Review Act—by Senators Maria Cantwell (D-WA) and Chuck Grassley (R-IA) would limit new or increased tariffs to 60 days and require a joint resolution of approval to extend them. The bill also would enable Congress to end tariffs at any time through a disapproval resolution. Both approval and disapproval resolutions would be subject to a presidential veto, requiring a two-thirds majority vote of support in both houses to override. The bar would be very high to clear but not impossible.
Another way to limit executive abuse is to narrow the discretion the president has to act. For example, in past Section 232 reform bills, Congress has suggested that the Department of Defense be designated as the appropriate agency to investigate whether a certain product is "being imported into the United States in such quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten to impair national security." Currently, the statute designates the Secretary of Commerce to fulfill that role. Moving this investigative power to the Department of Defense could help ensure that only legitimate national security concerns are being addressed.
Similarly, with Section 301, some have suggested that the investigation conducted by the US Trade Representative (USTR), who is a political appointee reporting directly to the president, be moved to an independent agency(link is external), such as the US International Trade Commission (USITC). This would not only limit the USTR's broad discretion but also ensure that the investigation is data-driven and nonpartisan. A 2023 bill(link is external)—the Global Trade Accountability Act—from Representative Warren Davidson (R-OH) would require the USITC to analyze the impact of some unilateral trade actions on the US economy.
In addition to building backstops to capricious presidential actions, there are other ways Congress could improve transparency in presidential tariff actions and strengthen procedural guardrails. For example, Section 232 could be made subject to judicial review that involves greater scrutiny(link is external) than currently exists, so that court challenges can be seriously considered instead of avoided due to traditional deference to the president on issues relating to national security. The president could also be required to publish or share with Congress the Section 232 reports received from the Secretary of Commerce that are used to make determinations about tariff actions. The first Trump administration's Section 232 investigation on automobiles was released by the Biden administration, for instance. In the second Trump administration, these reports have not been made public, which makes it difficult to assess the rationale behind the actions.
How and why certain products are excluded from tariffs is also a topic Congress may want to address. In 2023, the Government Accountability Office(link is external) critically assessed problems in the Section 232 exclusions process, including the grant of unneeded exclusions. Section 301 does not include a means to grant exclusions, but under the first Trump administration, hundreds of products were exempted from tariffs in an opaque process(link is external). Congress could clarify that exclusions cannot be granted or specify when exclusions would be acceptable (e.g., consumer products, energy, trade agreement partners).
Finally, Congress will need to weigh in on the purpose and scope of these statutes. For example, Congress could define what specific national security threats could warrant tariff actions. For example, the Toomey-Warner bill(link is external) defined national security as "the protection of the United States from foreign aggression; and does not otherwise include the protection of the general welfare of the United States." Congress could also specify where tariffs cannot be applied for national security reasons, such as products where there are no obvious national security applications (e.g., kitchen cabinets and other consumer products, such as groceries(link is external)), towards specific countries that are part of the US defense-industrial base, or security allies.
Such reforms should entail serious reflection about why Congress delegated certain authorities to the president in the first place, and to what end. For example, the primary purpose of Section 301, when it was drafted, was to support the ability of the president to negotiate agreements to reduce foreign trade barriers, rather than to raise US trade barriers. It was, by and large, an investigation-driven enforcement tool to use as leverage in negotiations with a single country(link is external). Today, its application is far removed from that intent. This is one reason why trade experts, including Alan Wolff, the author of the original 301 statute, have been skeptical about the Trump administration's use of Section 301 to impose tariffs allegedly to combat forced labor.
This Time Is Different
The congressional efforts at tariff reform described above suggest that Congress has already put a lot of thought into the persistent problem of executive overreach on trade but has achieved little in terms of concrete outcomes. Political obstacles to action are a main driver of this impasse, but the 2026 midterm election results may have changed past calculations. For one, tariffs are widely unpopular,(link is external) and Democrats spent billions of dollars on TV ads that portrayed tariffs in a negative light. As Democrats take control of both the House and Senate in January, voters are likely expecting the new Congress to deliver on promises to claw back tariffs as one way to lower consumer costs.
Furthermore, Trump's second-term trade war has targeted the whole world, even close US allies such as Canada, and free trade agreement partners such as South Korea. Congress may want to consider Canada-specific legislation, or reforms that prevent the application of tariffs on certain countries entirely. Senator Christopher Coons (D-DE) introduced the Stopping Tariffs on Allies and Bolstering Legislative Exercise of Trade Policy Act(link is external) in 2025, which would limit the president's ability to apply tariffs to members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and major non-NATO allies as well as US free trade agreement partners. However, allies may need more than targeted tariff exemptions to restore trust in the US, when multilateral trade rules and free trade agreements approved by Congress have been violated. Congress may also struggle to build consensus to remove tariffs on all allies, keeping some leverage in place to extract additional concessions.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries—on track to become House Speaker in January—has stated that rolling back Trump's tariffs will be a top priority for Democrats in the next Congress, but he has not specified which tariffs or trade statutes his party will take on. There may be some "low-hanging fruit," such as the authority under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 used by Trump to impose tariffs allegedly to address a US balance of payments problem (tariffs struck down by the US Court of International Trade, although the case is on appeal). Another is the antidiscrimination authority in Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (used against Canada). But tackling these measures will not go far enough in reclaiming trade authorities that Congress has delegated to the president.
Section 338 is also being challenged in court, and Trump's tariffs under that statute could be invalidated. For Canada, those tariffs are also not as economically significant as the Section 232 sectoral tariffs, over which negotiations broke down in August. Therefore, Congress will need to develop a comprehensive reform agenda for the two core statutes that have made the trade wars persist since 2018. Anything less will do little to reduce the uncertainty that has plagued US economic relations since Trump ratcheted up his trade war last year.
Of course, for any legislative action to be successful, a veto-proof majority will be required. That may exist for Canada-specific tariff relief but not for broader efforts. However, Congress may still want to vote on legislation regardless of its probability of passage if only to get members on the record for their views on tariffs. As a matter of internal party politics and positioning for the next election, this may prove useful in identifying those members who are serious about tackling this aspect of affordability from those who are not. The incoming Congress may not be able to achieve comprehensive tariff reform due to internal party pressures and special interest lobbying for continued protectionism. However, the debates that unfold over the next two years can lay important groundwork for the next president and Congress to finally restore checks and balances in trade policy and ensure, as James Madison wrote in Federalist 45, that the powers of the federal government are few and defined.

articles.title: Why AI is sending investors to advisors
articles.text:
Research summary

Why AI is sending investors to advisors

November 09, 2026

Free, general-purpose AI tools offer instant access to financial knowledge. But new Vanguard research reveals AI is delivering something unexpected: a deeper appreciation for humans. Instead of replacing professional guidance, AI is amplifying demand for the expertise of human advisors.

About one-third of Vanguard investors surveyed report turning to AI for financial guidance, for everything from retirement planning to investment decisions. Yet here's the twist: Both advised and self-directed investors say AI has increased, not diminished, the value they place on human advice. In fact, just 2% of advised clients and 3% of self-directed clients say AI has reduced the value of working with a human advisor.
“Investors are defying the popular narrative that AI’s convenience and accessibility are ‘crowding out’ professional guidance,” said Andy Reed, Vanguard head of behavioral economics research. Instead, they’re discovering that exploring financial questions through AI exposes the true complexity of wealth management. This includes the trade-offs between competing goals, the long-term implications of consequential decisions, and the discipline required to sustain a plan through volatile markets. Faced with an abundance of information, many investors are gaining a greater appreciation for financial professionals.

Trust in AI lags far behind use

There’s a clear gap between investors’ use of AI for financial tasks and their trust in its guidance. Among Gen Z, millennial, and Gen X investors, 63% report low or no trust in AI, and only 5%–6% express high trust. Baby boomers and older generations are even more skeptical: 78% report low trust, with just 2% placing high confidence in AI guidance.
The contrast with human advisors is striking. Most investors across all generations maintain high trust in financial professionals, with fewer than 10% expressing low confidence in human guidance. More than 80% of investors say they aren’t comfortable with AI taking action on their behalf—hardly surprising given that just 19% are confident the information they receive from AI is accurate. “Many investors are comfortable taking AI for a test drive, but few are letting it self-drive,” said Reed.

Where advisors maintain the edge

Human advisors retain distinct advantages where judgment matters most. They understand a client's complete financial picture, weigh trade-offs between competing priorities, help navigate decisions with lasting implications, and provide the support and accountability that sustain financial discipline over time. These capabilities—rooted in empathy, experience, and understanding—have proven difficult for AI to replicate.
Interestingly, greater familiarity with AI does strengthen trust. 31% of investors with high AI literacy report having confidence in AI compared with 19% of those less familiar with the technology. This suggests understanding AI plays an important role but doesn’t translate to complete trust. “Investors of all ages tend to agree that high-stakes decisions belong with humans,” said Reed. “There’s an emerging consensus that AI serves best as an exploratory tool rather than a decision-maker.”

What this means going forward

General-purpose AI tools will continue to improve, but closing the trust gap will take time—especially if investor protections aren’t enacted. The technology has proven useful for starting conversations. Human advisors can then provide the judgment, relationships, and holistic guidance needed for consequential decisions. Rather than competing, human advisors and AI may be settling into a complementary dynamic—one that recognizes both the promise of technology and the enduring value of human expertise in navigating financial complexity.

articles.title: The Nvidia Blast Zone
articles.text:
The Nvidia Blast Zone

Laila Khawaja, Arthur Kroeber

Gavekal Research | 12 Nov 2026

The Nvidia scandal now looks certain to topple CEO Jensen Huang, who had affairs with a woman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset, and with one of his subordinates. The questions now are what the longer-term impacts will be both on Nvidia and the US and Chinese AI ecosystems. Understandably, much coverage has focused on the spying and sex angles, but the crucial issues lie elsewhere.The biggest risk to Nvidia is if it or Huang is found to have knowingly colluded in the diversion of export-controlled chips from a Singapore datacenter to unauthorized end-users in China. The biggest risk to China’s AI industry is that the scandal leads to a tightening of US export controls on advanced chips and chip-making equipment, possibly by the end of this year. And while the US AI industry can probably weather the tumult inside Nvidia—especially if the board swiftly ousts Huang and installs credible new leadership—the scandal raises the chance that the incoming Democratic Congress will push for much tougher regulation of the sector.

(Photo by Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)CommentaryEmissaryAfter the Midterm Rout, Can Trump Change Course Without Giving Up Tariffs?Even if the administration maintains its broader trade policy, it should use tariffs more strategically and work with U.S. partners, not against them.Link CopiedBy Barbara WeiselPublished on Nov 6, 2026Among the factors driving the midterm election results, affordability and price increases were often cited as voters’ top issue. The results should motivate the administration of President Donald Trump to adjust its approach to its economic policies, but it may choose to stand firm on trade. Trump proudly embraces the “tariff king” label and views tariffs as an all-purpose tool for securing agreement on trade, investment, and economic security demands.But there are places where the administration can fine-tune its policies without a wholesale shift. Even if it otherwise stays the course, the administration should deploy tariffs more strategically, use them more judiciously in support of a broader U.S. economic agenda, and use carrots—not just sticks—to encourage cooperation from foreign partners. And while it may be tempted to continue to rely on executive action, it should work with the new Congress, which likely will begin to reassert its trade authority and seek more influence in shaping U.S. policy when it takes office in January. More Targeted TariffsOver the past year, the Trump administration has used across-the-board tariffs to pressure U.S. trading partners into bilateral trade agreements. Although tariffs increased government revenues, this blunt instrument also raised business costs and consumer prices, disrupted supply chains, delayed business investment by creating uncertainty, and strained U.S. ties with many partners and allies.In February, the Supreme Court struck down the administration’s broad-based tariffs, ruling that the president does not have the authority to impose tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), the statute on which it relied. Then, the administration launched two investigations under Section 301, which allows the government to investigate and take action against unfair trade practices. The result is expected to produce combined tariffs equal to the invalidated IEEPA rates.The first Section 301 investigation, focused on forced labor, resulted in across-the-board tariffs on sixty economies beginning in July. The administration demanded action on specific labor concerns but offered no clear path to tariff removal even if its demands are met.The second Section 301 investigation covers structural excess manufacturing capacity—for example, a factory with unused capacity that’s kept open by government subsidies—across sixteen economies, including major U.S. trading partners in the Indo-Pacific and Europe, as well as Mexico. The findings, due shortly, will likely include broad-based tariffs but—as with the forced labor investigation—are not expected to outline a path to removing them.Meanwhile, the U.S. government has been negotiating trade agreements with about twenty economies, with commitments that overwhelmingly fall on the partners. Facing U.S. threats of tariffs above IEEPA rates if they fail to agree to U.S. demands, these partners are committing to lowering tariffs on U.S. goods, addressing specific trade barriers, and curbing unfair competition from subsidies or state-owned enterprises, among other requirements.These agreements render the Section 301 tariffs unnecessary. If those tariffs were intended as pressure to get U.S. trading partners to lower their tariffs on U.S. goods and make other changes, they have achieved their goal. U.S. partners will be bound by the obligations in these deals, including those related to excess manufacturing capacity and labor. Additional tariffs merely impose further taxes on U.S. businesses and consumers. They also will not advance the administration’s goal of slashing the U.S. goods trade deficit, which reached a record $135 billion in September—up 2 percent from August and 63 percent year over year.At a minimum, the administration should set out a clear roadmap to phase out all Section 301 tariffs as trading partners address U.S. concerns. The U.S. government should begin by removing tariffs on consumer goods and raw materials or other manufacturing components not already exempted, providing some financial relief to U.S. businesses and consumers in what amounts to a regressive tax on consumers. Speed is essential: The longer the tariffs remain, the harder it will be to give up the revenue and persuade companies to forgo protection they do not need.More Coherent Trade Policy AgendaThe second Trump administration has failed to set clear trade priorities and has pursued policies that lack coherence. Rather than targeting priority countries, Washington imposed sweeping Section 301 tariffs on sixty economies, as though they were all of similar economic significance. It has relied heavily on tariffs as a means to bring manufacturing back to the United States, although they have created business uncertainty and higher production costs. In addition, different government agencies seem to operate in silos. For example, tariffs on steel, aluminum, auto parts, lumber, advanced semiconductors, and other inputs that were imposed under Section 232, which aims to protect national security, have further raised the cost of the domestic industrial production that the Section 301 tariffs were supposed to promote.Trade policy should advance a more holistic approach toward U.S. innovation, competitiveness, resilience, job creation, and growth. Washington should sequence actions to address issues in priority order rather than overload the system and better coordinate both affirmative and defensive actions across agencies. It should use tariffs sparingly and judiciously, employing other tools to achieve its economic goals, protect genuinely strategic sectors, or address specific problems. Going forward, the Trump administration should weigh the downstream effects of tariffs and the costs to consumers more carefully and favor affirmative policies that create new business and market opportunities, rather than reach for tariffs in the first instance.Greater Cooperation with PartnersU.S. trading partners have grown increasingly frustrated with the administration’s unilateral trade actions and have sought to expand their trade with other partners. Over the summer, Trump escalated his trade war with Canada by imposing 50 percent tariffs on a range of Canadian products. The move drew intense opposition on both sides of the border, with many citing the close and longstanding relationship between the neighbors, and it led Canada to intensify its trade diversification efforts. But the United States is deeply integrated in the global economy, which does not operate by zero-sum rules, and its actions will have strategic implications. Moving ahead, the administration should seek to better use its partnerships to advance its economic goals and avoid unnecessarily damaging relations with foreign partners, whose support is essential to addressing international economic challenges and advancing broader U.S. interests. Washington has attacked its partners, often more harshly than its rivals, while demanding their cooperation on multilateral initiatives. Some have participated, but distrust of the United States limits what they can achieve together. Canada would be a good start for this effort. In addition, some countries, such as those in the Indo-Pacific, worry that Washington is missing opportunities to cooperate on shared concerns, including China’s exports of excess industrial capacity and its growing manufacturing trade surplus. They have sought to curb soaring Chinese imports, which have weakened local firms and caused factory closures and job losses, through a variety of measures. But they do not trust that the U.S. government will work with them to manage the issues, despite Washington viewing Beijing as its primary economic, technological, and strategic rival. Instead, these Indo-Pacific countries are attempting to avoid triggering both Chinese retaliation and U.S. accusations that their countries have become bases for China to circumvent U.S. trade restrictions. In other cases, Washington is working with countries that share U.S. concerns about the global impact of China’s industrial overcapacity and recognize the need for collective action. In late September, fourteen G20 trade ministers (including the United States) issued a joint statement on this issue. Without naming countries, the group warned that inaction would cripple industries, cost jobs, and damage economies and agreed to cooperate, initially focusing on autos and electric vehicles, batteries, chemicals, foundational semiconductors, and solar panels. But at the same time, Washington is poised to impose unilateral tariffs on some of these key trading partners.Cooperation on this initiative will already be slow and painstaking, not least in defining excess capacity and agreeing on concrete initiatives to tackle the problem. The Trump administration seemingly believes its unilateral Section 301 tariffs can proceed alongside international coordination efforts, but it minimizes how its action will weaken partners’ commitment to cooperation. It also incorrectly assumes their reliance on the U.S. security umbrella gives them no other choice. Instead of imposing tariffs, the administration should use incentives that reward countries for implementing agreed principles on excess capacity and support them as they take steps to curb China’s massive exports. The ASEAN Summit, which Trump will attend later this month, would be an ideal opportunity to signal a shift in U.S. approach.Congress Should Reassert Its AuthorityCongress has played virtually no role in trade policy during the second Trump administration, but the midterm results may embolden lawmakers. The new Congress may struggle to curb the White House’s use of executive authority, and Trump could veto legislation requiring congressional approval. Still, the scale of the Democratic wave and public anger may prompt the administration to rethink its approach, and it can do so without completely abandoning Trump’s beloved tariffs. Congress may also be able to begin reasserting constitutional authority over trade—a welcome development that will provide healthy checks and balances on the administration’s trade policy.Get more news and analysis fromCarnegie This WeekUnderstand the world with the latest from our scholars around the world.About the AuthorBarbara WeiselNonresident Scholar, Asia ProgramBarbara Weisel is a nonresident scholar in the Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and the former U.S. chief negotiator of the Trans-Pacific Partnership.Recent WorkCommentaryThe Fallout of the U.S.–Canada Trade War Won’t Be Limited to North AmericaBarbara WeiselCommentaryPost U.S.-China Summit: Managed InstabilityBarbara WeiselTradeForeign PolicyEconomyChinaUnited StatesCarnegie does not take institutional positions on public policy issues; the views represented herein are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of Carnegie, its staff, or its trustees.More Work from EmissaryCommentaryEmissaryCentral Asia Wants U.S. Investments.
